units.la: ILLUSTRIS & Magnifice Domine, summa animi subiectione colende. Cum multa aliarelí-gionis Christianæ veritatem contra Atheos, Epicureos & profanos evincant: & nobis omnibusque piis egregiè confirment ac commendent: ab aliarum quoq; gentium & sectarum quarumvis ἐξελοθρη[?]σκείαις placitis, cultibusque commentitiis longissimè secernant, & supra falsarum religionum vanitatem adeò extollant, ut tantùm caput efferat illa, quantum lenta solent inter viburna cupressi: tum illud inprimis irrefragabilem eius autoritatem sancit ac luculentissimè demonstrat, quòd ea sola ab unico & vero Deo, humano generi patefatefacta,[?] Prophetis & Apostolis inspirata, ac de ipsius iussu & voluntate, ad salutem hominum, ac ipsius creatoris cognitionem & gloriam, certus monumentis, quæ Biblia voce recepta dicimus, est perscripta & comprehensa. Nam proculomni dubio, ea demum est vera religio, quæ à Deo Opt. Max. profecta: falsa vero, quæ dæmonum instinctu, vel ab uno quopiam ex-cogitata, vel plurium consensu & ex pacto re-cepta est. Quemadmodum scite scripsit Augu-stinus: Religio vera non à terrena aliqua civitate instituta est, sed cælestem ipsa plane in-stituit civitatem, & eam inspirat ac docet verus Deus, dator vitæ æternæ omnibus suis cul-toribus.
units.tr: Most illustrious and magnificent Lord, to be honoured with the greatest submission of mind. Although many arguments establish the truth of the Christian religion against atheists, Epicureans and profane persons, and commend and strongly confirm it to us and to all the godly, and although they distinguish it sharply from the opinions and fabricated worship of all other nations and sects whatsoever, and so exalt it above the vanity of false religions that it raises its head as much as the cypress does above the pliant viburnum, nevertheless this above all establishes and most clearly demonstrates its irrefutable authority: that it alone, made known to the human race by the one true God, inspired in the prophets and apostles, and written and contained at his command and will, for the salvation of men and for the knowledge and glory of the Creator himself, is set down in those records which we call the Bible by the accepted name. For beyond all doubt, that alone is the true religion which comes from God the best and greatest; but that is false which is devised by demons' prompting or by some single person, or adopted by the agreement and compact of many. As Augustine wrote well: the true religion was not founded by any earthly city, but the heavenly city itself founded it, and the true God, the giver of eternal life to all his worshippers, inspires and teaches it.

units.la: Quod ipsum & gentilium philoso-phorum, legislatorum, & gubernatorum sa-niores agnouisse, vel inde patet, quòd sanctiones suas, θρησκείας[?] & cultus ad eandem origi-nem, numen videlicet (sed suum quisq; ficti-tium seu idolum) retulerunt: uti perhibent historiæ. Minoa Cretensium regem à Ioue, Ly-curgum Laconum νομοθέτῳ[?] à Delphico Apol-line, Numam Pompilium, alterum Romano-rum regem, ab Aegeria nympha, sacra, ritus, leges & instituta divina, se accepisse, & nescio quæ cum illis diis colloquia & congressus iacti-tasse, & ciuibus, rudique popello persuasisse. Falsò id quidem, sed astutè tamen, quòd sub-odoraodorarentur & intelligerent, hominis ratio-nem & conscientiam non nisi hunc pro vero numinis cultu habere, qui ab ipso numine manasset & demonstratus esset.
units.tr: That the wiser of the gentile philosophers, lawgivers and rulers also recognised this is clear from this alone: that they referred their sanctions, religious rites and worship to the same origin, namely a deity (though each his own fictitious deity or idol), as the histories report. They tell that Minos, king of the Cretans, received his sacred rites, laws and divine institutions from Jove; that Lycurgus of the Spartans received them from the Delphic Apollo as lawgiver; that Numa Pompilius, the second king of the Romans, received his sacred rites, ceremonies, laws and institutions from the nymph Egeria, and boasted of I know not what conversations and meetings with those gods, and persuaded the citizens and the rude common people. This was indeed false, but shrewdly done, since they sensed and understood that human reason and conscience hold only that worship of the deity to be true which had flowed from the deity itself and had been shown to be so.

units.la: Verùm enim uerò diuinarum patefactio-num beneficio, non quidem ullo merito nostro, sed mera & singulari Dei φιλανθρωπία, quem, nisi ipso docente, nemo discere potuit, ut Irenæus, imo ipse Filius Dei testatur, nobis benignissimè tributo & communicato, sanè quidem hoc seculo merito gloriari possumus. Habemus enim firmissimum sermonem propheticum: habemus & apostolicum: cui rectè facimus, si attendimus, veluti lucernæ splen-denti in obscuro loco, usq; dum dies illucescat, & lucifer exoriatur in cordibus nostris: ut divinus Petrus monuit 2. Epist.c.1.v.19. Itaq; quotquot hodie Theologi locos communes & materias controuersas methodicè tracta-runt:ferè à sacra Scriptura seu Verbo Dei, quo solo diuinæ istæ patefactiones, eoque vera religio continetur, sunt exorsi, ac de eius authoritate & dignitate sibi primùm agendum & disceptandum existimarunt. Nec immeritò. Est enim sacra Scriptura, proprium principium Theologiæ, ex quo omnes demonstrationes peti & depromi debent: cui si quid consentit, citra tergiuersationem recipiendum: si quid repugnat, sine cunctatione reiiciendum esse, neque vere Christianus ausit inficiari. Rectè igitur hæc tractatio, tanquam fundamentum ceteris controversiis omnibus substernitur, cum absq; ea, quicquid in quæstionem venit, liquidò nequeat definiri. Adigit quoq; ad diligentius huius materiæ examen nostros doctores summa aduersariorum, inprimis eorum qui de societate Iesu se nuncupant, importuni-tas & impudentia: qui si non Pontificis Romani, & unctæ, rasaque cohortis, quam illi Ecclesiæ Catholicæ titulo insigniunt, axioma & auctoritatem supra S. Scripturam extollunt: (quod olim Canonistæ, & alij Paparum adulatores facitarunt: reclamantibus interim eruditis & cordatis viris, qui conscientiam à scientia non divellebant: ut ex Gersonis, Occami, Panormitani, Alphonsi de Castro & aliorum scriptis constat:) saltem Paparum decreta & traditiones sacræ Scripturæ exaquant, & pari fide ac religione tenendas & servandas esse contendunt: imò S. literarum auctoritatem, ab Ecclesia, quam dicunt, id est, suo testimonio suspendunt. Contra quos certè S. scripturæ ὑπεροχὴ αὐτοπιστεύθεν[?] maiestas asserenda est, nisi veritatem prodere velimus. Habet enim, ut Augustinus ait, lib. 12. de Ci-uit. Dei. cap. 9. Scripturæ fides mirabilem auctoritatem toritatem non immerito in orbe terrarum, atque in omnibus gentibus, quas sibi credituras esse, inter cætera quæ dixit, vera divinitate prædixit. Sed cùm de his, aliisq; utilissimis rebus in hoc libro satis copiosè & accuratè disputetur: supervacanea foret oratio prolixior.
units.tr: Yet by the benefit of the divine revelations, not indeed by any merit of ours but by the mere and singular philanthropy of God, whom no one could learn except by his own teaching, as Irenaeus and indeed the Son of God himself testifies, most kindly bestowed and imparted upon us, we can certainly rightly glory in this age. For we have a most firm prophetic word, and we also have the apostolic word, to which we do well to attend, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in our hearts, as the divine Peter warned (2 Pet. 1.19). Therefore, as many as today have methodically treated the common topics and controversial matters of theology have for the most part begun with holy Scripture, or the Word of God, in which alone these divine revelations, and so the true religion, are contained, and they have thought it necessary first to deal with and debate its authority and dignity. Nor without reason. For holy Scripture is the proper principle of theology, from which all demonstrations ought to be sought and drawn; whatever agrees with it must be received without evasion, and whatever conflicts with it must be rejected without hesitation, nor would a true Christian dare to deny this. Rightly, therefore, this treatment is laid down as the foundation for all the other controversies, since without it whatever comes into question cannot be clearly settled. The great importunity and impudence of our adversaries also compels our teachers to examine this matter more diligently, especially of those who call themselves of the Society of Jesus: who, if they do not raise the axiom and authority of the Roman Pontiff and of the anointed and shaven cohort which they label with the title of the Catholic Church above Holy Scripture (which the canonists of old, and other flatterers of the popes, did, while learned and sensible men in the meantime protested, who did not separate conscience from knowledge, as is evident from the writings of Gerson, Ockham, Panormitanus, Alfonso de Castro and others), at least they make the decrees and traditions of the popes equal to Holy Scripture, and contend that they are to be held and observed with equal faith and reverence; indeed they make the authority of the sacred writings depend upon the Church, as they call it, that is, upon its testimony. Against these, certainly, the pre-eminence and self-authenticating majesty of Holy Scripture must be asserted, unless we wish to betray the truth. For, as Augustine says in the twelfth book of The City of God, chapter 9, the faith of Scripture has a wonderful authority, not undeservedly throughout the world and among all the nations; which, among other things, it foretold by true divinity would believe it. But since these and other most useful matters are discussed fully and accurately in this book, a longer discourse would be superfluous.

units.la: Ad T.Cl. Illustris & Generosè Comes, me converto: cui tractatum istum clarissimi & carissimi patris mei, D. Hieronymi Zanchij, quondam in Argentinensi, post Heidelbergensi, tandem Neustadiana Academia professoris solertissi-mi, felicis memoriæ, humiliter offero, dedico, consecro: quem ut T. Cl. serena fronte, vel potius solita benignitate suscipiat, oro. Cui e-nim potius istud opusculum ego meiq; dicari-mus, quàm ei, cuius & summæ sapientiæ, doctrinæ, ac iudicij, de Theologicis inprimis controversiis, exactissimi, & maximè in literatos, adeóque nos ipsos benevolentiæ, plurima extant documenta? cui inter inclytos Germaniæ Comites, ob insignes virtutes, illustri positas loco, & ob Rempubl. præclarè ge-stam, palmam deferunt prudentes: quem denique ob Ecclesiam adiutam, veri-tatem, ve-ritatisque professores defensos, & pios ac exu-les plurimos refocillatos ac sublevatos, certatim orthodoxi laudibus extollunt? Ac sanè quæ T.D. sit in omni literarum genere præstanstantia : quæ cum primis sacrarum rerum cognitio, veræ pietati coniunčta, tum in Deum, tum in patriam nostram, seu Palatinatum, quem vt olim sic etiānum sapientissimis con-siliis pro virili gubernas ; publicè notum est, nec à me prædicari velpotest, vel debet, tanquam impare, & imperito laudum tantarum præconc. Interea tamen iudicium de tractatu isto V.D.defero : quem à Patre meo, ante annos viginti quinq; in Heidelbergensi Academia publicè propositum.plurimi viri doĉti & amici paterni, iampridem efflagitarunt, & in gratiam studiosorum Theologiæ publicari desiderarunt : Quorum voto, quia citius non licuit, iam tandem propinqui & tutores mei satisfaciendum, eumq; leĉtoribus, & Ecclesiis orthodoxis, inprimis cum Pontificiis digla-diantibus, nec inutilem nec iniucundum fore iudicarunt.
units.tr: I now turn to you, most illustrious and noble Count. To you I humbly offer, dedicate and consecrate this treatise of my most famous and dearest father, Lord Hieronymus Zanzius... [see note: name as printed] — namely of Hieronymus Zanchius, of blessed memory, once a most skilful professor at Strasbourg, afterwards at Heidelberg, and finally at the Neustadt Academy; and I pray that your Lordship will receive it with a serene brow, or rather with your customary kindness. For to whom could I and mine more fittingly dedicate this little work than to him, of whose most exact wisdom, learning and judgement, especially in theological controversies, and of whose great goodwill towards men of letters and towards ourselves, very many proofs exist? He whom the wise, among the illustrious Counts of Germany, rank high, placed in an honoured position for his remarkable virtues and for the excellent service he has rendered to the commonwealth; whom, finally, the orthodox eagerly extol with praises for aiding the Church, defending the truth and its professors, and for refreshing and relieving many pious exiles? Indeed, your Lordship's distinction in every branch of learning, especially the knowledge of sacred things joined with true piety, both towards God and towards our fatherland, that is the Palatinate, which you have governed with the wisest counsels, as formerly so still, to the best of your ability, is publicly known, nor can or should it be proclaimed by me, who am unequal to and unskilled in the praise of such great things. Meanwhile, however, I entrust the judgement of this treatise to your Excellency: which many learned men and friends of my father have long demanded to be made public, and have desired it be published for the benefit of students of theology. Since it was not allowed sooner, my kinsmen and guardians, too, have now at last judged that they should satisfy their wish, and that it would be neither useless nor unpleasant to readers and to orthodox Churches, especially to those who wrangle with the Papists.

units.la: De propensione verò G.T.Cl.in D.Zanchÿ familiam, in primis in me, quem è S. Baptismate suscipere dignata est, quia dubitare non licet : equidem obseruantiæ, subiectionis & animi grati testimonium aliquod edendum censui : censuerunt itidem fratres, affines & tutores mei. Cùm verò nil aliud tam præstò sit, nisi chartaceum istud munus : quin & V. Cl. pro heroica sua bonitate nihil aliud à nobis, bis, nisi fortassis ex bibliotheca Opt. patris mei, scripta ad Ecclesiæ vsum accommodata, requirat: in certam spem venio, G.T.D. hanc dedicationem, vt significationem reuerentiæ & studij mei, ceu pro filij T.D. non minus gratam esse habituram, quàm si ab ipso patre meo D.H.Zanchio, p.m. profecta esset: & me in suorum clientum numero habituram, & paterno affectu prosecuturam & complexuram. Quod vt G.V.D. magis magisq; faciat, & me meosq; propinquos, ac Zanchy nomen & scripta sibi commendata habeat, etiam atque etiam oro. Deus Opt. Max. T.Cl. Ecclesiæ suæ, Reip. & nobis omnibus quàm diutissimè conseruet incolumem, saluam & fortunatam, ac de cælis indies copiosissimè toti familiæ vestræ benedicat. Amen. Dab. Neustadij. Eidib. Mart. Anno D.n.I. Christi 1593.
units.tr: As for the favour which your Illustrious Lordship has shown to the family of Zanchius, especially towards me, whom you have deigned to receive from holy baptism, since there is no room for doubt, I have thought some testimony of respect, submission and a grateful mind ought to be given: my brothers, relatives and guardians have likewise thought so. But since nothing else is so readily at hand except this paper gift, and since your Most Illustrious Lordship, in your heroic goodness, asks nothing else from us, except perhaps some writings from my most excellent father's library suited to the use of the Church, I come into a firm hope that your Lordship will take this dedication as a sign of my reverence and zeal, no less welcome than if it had come from my father himself, Lord Hieronymus Zanchius, of blessed memory; and that you will count me among your clients, and will follow and embrace me with fatherly affection. That your Lordship may do this more and more, and may hold the name and writings of Zanchius commended to you, I pray again and again. May God, the best and greatest, preserve your Lordship, your Church, the commonwealth and all of us unharmed, safe and fortunate for as long as possible, and bless your whole household from heaven day by day most abundantly. Amen. Given at Neustadt, on the Ides of March, in the year of our Lord Christ 1593.

units.la: DICTURUS sum, Clarissimi viri, & Ornatissimi auditores, de necessitate, deq; ratione retinendi purumque putum conservandi in Ecclesia verbum Dei: eóque nonnihil de officio Principum in hac re, Ecclesiarum, Pastorum, Doctorum, Studiosorum, deq; Scholarum antiquitate, utilitate & necessitate in regno Christi. Argumentum est, ut videtis, grave, honestum, utile, & vere etiam necessarium in hoc tempore: adde & mea conveniens ac consentaneum conditioni. Cùm enim mihi novo in hac celeberrima Academia Theologo, antequam meum munus obire incipiam, aliqua (ut moris est) habenda esset oratio, qua & Christianam sapientiam, quam Theologiam vocant, lauda-rem, & ad eius studium invenes adhortarer: nul-lum ad rem accommodatius visum est argu-mentum isto, quod tractandum suscepi. Nam & laudes continet verae Theologiae, & satis habet stimulorum ad illius amorem atque studium. Fuerit igitur oratio haec (ut confido) studiosis no-stris neque ingrata, neque inutilis: opto certe, ut sit & gratissima & utilissima. Quare ut me benig-ne & attente audiatis, non tam ego vos rogo, quam ipsius etiam argumenti dignitas & utilitas postulat.
units.tr: I am about to speak, most distinguished sir and most honoured hearers, on the necessity and the manner of keeping the Word of God in the Church and preserving it pure and unmixed; and somewhat also on the duty of princes in this matter, of churches, of pastors, of teachers and of students, and on the antiquity, usefulness and necessity of schools in the kingdom of Christ. The subject, as you see, is weighty, honourable, useful, and truly necessary at this time. Add that it is also fitting and suited to my own condition. For since I am a new theologian in this most celebrated Academy, and before I begin my office some address was to be given (as is customary), in which I would praise Christian wisdom, which they call theology, and exhort the young to its study, I judged no subject more suitable to the matter than the one I have undertaken. For it contains both the praises of true theology and enough spurs to love and study it. This oration will therefore be (I trust) neither unwelcome nor useless to our students; I certainly hope it will be most welcome and most useful. Wherefore, that you hear me kindly and attentively, I ask you less than the very dignity and usefulness of the subject itself requires.

units.la: Ac mihi quidem (ut ad rem ipsam veniam) diu multumq; cogitanti, & in animo volutanti, quidnam illud esset, quod & multis ante seculis, tum Respub. perdidisset, tum Ecclesias evertisset, & nunc etiam (proh dolor) illarum permultis vicunque renovatis atq; instauratis, denuò perniciem facere, & exitium adferre incipiat: illud tandem visum est fuisse & esse in causa, quòd Antichristus, Christi Ecclesias & Scholas blando humanarum doctrinarum veneno inficientibus atq; perdentibus, neque Reges & Principes, qui iuxta vaticinium Isaiae, debuissent esse Ecclesiarum nutritores & protectores, neque etiam reliqui Magistratus, qui patres populorum esse debebant, minimè pro suo officio restiterunt, neque curarunt, ut per veros Episcopos in Ecclesiis, & per sinceros doctores in scholis, verbum Dei, a quo uno tota Ecclesiarum salus dependet, purum sincerumque conservaretur: sed contra potius plerique omnes, feris illis & immanibus bel-luis luis[?] omnia pro libidine vastantibus, non solum conniuerunt, verum etiam, prob Deum atq; hominum fidem opem iam inde ab initio tulerunt, & quotidie etiam ferunt. Qua de re qui dubitet, confido vestrum esse neminem. Nam reapse quam verum hoc sit quod dico, ipsi, sed non sine magno dolore, videmus atque sentimus. Ergo nihil honestius, & Christiano homine ac Principe dignius: nihil ad Respub. & Ecclesiae conseruan-das conducibilius: nihil denique ad salutem cuique comparandam magis necessarium esse potest, quam ut per illos, quorum interest (interest autem omnium pro sua cuiusque rata portione) quam diligentissime curetur, ut reiectis profligatisque in perpetuum omnibus humanis de Religio-ne doctrinis, verbum Dei in Ecclesia, purum putumque conseruetur, & administretur. Hoc est enim fundamentum, in quo salus Ecclesiarum quam maxime nititur. Sic iudico: sic sentio: sic video.
units.tr: For my part, to come to the matter itself: having long and much pondered and turned over in my mind what that thing might be which, both many centuries ago, ruined the commonwealth and overthrew the churches, and now too (alas!), though these have been in many places renewed and restored, begins again to work destruction and bring ruin, I have at last judged that it was and is the cause that Antichrist, infecting and destroying the churches and schools of Christ with the smooth poison of human learning, and neither kings and princes, who according to the prophecy of Isaiah ought to have been the nurses and protectors of the churches, nor the other magistrates, who ought to have been the fathers of the peoples, have resisted as their office required, nor have they taken care that the Word of God, on which the whole safety of the churches depends alone, be kept pure and unmixed through true bishops in the churches and sound teachers in the schools. Rather, almost all of them, while those wild and savage beasts lay everything waste at their pleasure, not only connived but even, by the faith of God and men, have given aid from the very beginning and daily still give it. Concerning this matter, I trust there is none among you who would doubt. For indeed we see and feel, though not without great grief, how true what I say is. Therefore nothing can be more honourable, nothing more worthy of a Christian man and a prince, nothing more conducive to the preservation of the commonwealth and the Church, nothing finally more necessary for obtaining each person's salvation, than that, through those whose concern it is (and it concerns everyone in his own proportion), the greatest diligence be applied so that, all human doctrines of religion having been rejected and utterly overthrown for ever, the Word of God be kept and administered pure and unmixed in the Church. For this is the foundation on which the safety of the churches chiefly rests. So I judge, so I feel, so I see.

units.la: Sic docuit ille omnium excellentissimus & sanctissimus Poeta, qui in primo Psalmo cecinit: Beatum illum fore, qui neglectis omnibus impiorum hominum consiliis, moribus, doctrinis, totum adiicit animum ad unam Domini legem, & in ea dies ac noctes meditatur. Sic Dominus Iesus ipsa aeterna Dei Patris sapientia, confirmauit, cum pro salute nostra, non ad peruestigandas virorum, si Deo placet, sapientissimorum placita, sed ad perscrutandas Scripturas nos ablegauit: Scrutamini (inquiens) scrutamini Scri-pturas. Sic denique (ne singula Scripturarum testimonia[?] proferam) ipse Spiritus S. ubiq; in S. li-teris testificatur, Ecclesiam Dei & colligi & co-agmentari & conseruari verbo Dei. Ergo nihil etiam honestius est, quam ut ipsa Ecclesia, hoc est, nos omni cura & diligentia studeamus ver-bum Dei purum putum apud nos conseruari.
units.tr: So taught that most excellent and most holy Poet, who sang in the first Psalm that he would be blessed who, having disregarded all the counsels, morals and teachings of wicked men, applies his whole mind to the one law of the Lord, and meditates on it day and night. So the Lord Jesus, the eternal wisdom of God the Father himself, confirmed, when he sent us, for our salvation, not to search out the opinions of men, however wise they may be, if it pleases God, but to search the Scriptures: "Search," he says, "search the Scriptures." Finally, so that I do not cite the individual testimonies of Scripture one by one, the Holy Spirit himself bears witness everywhere in the holy letters that the Church of God is gathered, joined together and preserved by the Word of God. Therefore nothing is more honourable than that the Church itself, that is, we, should with all care and diligence strive to have the Word of God kept pure and unmixed among us.

units.la: Ac profecto nihil est, quod magis deceat Ecclesiam, quam ut id apud se purum quam di-ligentissime conseruandum curet, per quod & ipsa fuit mundata ac conseruata, & per quod perpetuò munda scelerisq; pura apud Deum propter Christum asseruatur. Verbo autem mundari nos, mundosq; conseruari, docet luculenter Christus Ioh.17.cum ait, vos mundi estis, per sermo-nem meum.
units.tr: And indeed nothing is more fitting for the Church than to see to it, with the greatest diligence, that the Word, through which it was itself cleansed and preserved, and through which it is kept clean and pure before God for ever for Christ's sake, be kept pure among itself. That we are cleansed by the Word, and that we are kept clean, Christ clearly teaches in John 17, when he says: "You are clean through my word."

units.la: Quid porrò magis honesti & grati hominis postulat officium, quam ut pretiosum thesaurum sibi à suo Principe donatum, ab omni labe purum & vacuum, mundumque custodiat? præsertim, verò si nouerit, hanc etiam sui Principis esse voluntatem. Qui hoc facere negligit: nā dignus ille fuerit, cui tantum thesaurus eripiatur, & alij, qui illum sciat ac velit custodire, donetur. Hoc enim æquitas postulat: hoc docet Natura: sic tradunt sacra litera: sic denique confirmant omnium Gentium & populorum iura atque leges.
units.tr: What more does the duty of an honourable and grateful man require than that he guard, pure and free from every stain and clean, a precious treasure given to him by his prince? Especially if he knows that this is also the will of his prince. He who neglects to do this is worthy to have that treasure taken from him and given to another who knows and wishes to keep it. For equity demands this, nature teaches it, the holy letters so hand it down, and finally the laws and rights of all nations and peoples confirm it.

units.la: Quis autem, per Deum immortalem, pretiosior aut præstabilior thesaurus isto, quo nos Deus O-ptimus Maximus pro sua æterna erga nos bene-uolentia liberaliter donauit, hoc est, Euangelio, inueniri excogitarive potest? Etenim, quantum quaso rei est, Deum rerum omnium conditorem & gubernatorem, è cœlesti throno, nobis homun-cionibus hic humi repentibus, locutum esse? nec locutum tantùm, sed suum etiam cœlestem ser-monem, scriptum nobis reliquisse? Quis non ma-gno sibi ducat honori, si Princeps aliquis, aut Rex, suo se dignetur sermone, & præter hunc suis etiam amicissimis literis? At is, a quo sacrum ha-bemus eloquium, sacramque Scripturam, Deus est, Rex Regum, & Dominus dominantium, qui ius habet in omnium non tantùm facultates & corpora, sed etiam mentes atque animas. Quanti igitur faciendum est ipsius donum? Nos, quos dignatus est hoc honore, Gentiles eramus, nati in peccatis: natura filii irae: alieni diuino à fœ-dere: homines sine Deo: ad quos eloquia hæc Dei non pertinebant : Et tamen hæc à Iudæis ad nos transfulit? Quantum igitur illi debemus: & quanta diligentia sunt nobis hæc custodien-da? Illi, per quos cœlestes hasce diuitias & opes ad nos misit, fuerunt Angeli. Per hos enim suam dedit legem. Fuerunt Prophetæ, afflati Spiritu sancto. Per hos enim vetus Testamen-tum conscriptum est. Fuerunt Apostoli, legati CHRISTI ad omnes Nationes. Per hos enim Novum habemus Testamentum. Fuit denique ipse Filius Dei, idemque Deus IESVS CHRI-STVS. Is enim author totius Scripturæ. Per hosce honoratissimos legatos misit Deus è cœlesti throno in terram hanc, ad nos peccati & Satha-næ vilissima mancipia thesaurum hunc incom-parabilem. Quantam igitur iram Dei, & ruï-nam imminere nobis putamus, si non hunc sum-
units.tr: Who, by the immortal God, could find or devise a treasure more precious or more valuable than that which almighty God, out of his eternal goodwill toward us, has freely given us, that is, the Gospel? For how great a thing is it, I ask you, that God, the creator and governor of all things, should have spoken to us little humans who crawl here on the ground from his heavenly throne? And not only spoken, but also left us his heavenly word in writing? Who would not think it a great honour for himself if some prince or king deigned to address him with his own speech, and besides that with his most friendly letters? Yet he from whom we have the holy oracles and holy Scripture is God, the King of kings and Lord of lords, who has right not only over the goods and bodies of all, but also over their minds and souls. How highly, then, must his gift be valued? We, whom he has deigned to honour in this way, were Gentiles, born in sins, children of wrath by nature, aliens from the covenant of God, men without God, to whom these oracles of God did not pertain. And yet he has brought them to us from the Jews? How much, then, do we owe him, and with how much diligence must we guard these things? The ones through whom he sent these heavenly riches and wealth to us were the angels. For through them he gave his law. There were the prophets, inspired by the Holy Spirit; for through them the Old Testament was written. There were the apostles, ambassadors of Christ to all nations; for through them we have the New Testament. Finally, there was the Son of God himself, who is also God, Jesus Christ, for he is the author of all Scripture. Through these most honourable ambassadors God sent this incomparable treasure from his heavenly throne to this earth, to us, the most worthless slaves of sin and Satan. How great, then, do we think the wrath of God and ruin hanging over us, if we do not with the highest zeal claim this treasure for ourselves as free from every stain?

units.la: mo studio, ab omni labe vacuum nobis asserue-mus?
units.tr: Let us claim it for ourselves, free from every stain, with the highest zeal?

units.la: Verùm, quo etiam modo eum nobis dedit? Primùm oraculis: deinde scripto: confirmatum miraculis: obsignatum sanguine Christi: Spiritu etiam sancto in cordibus nostris inscriptum. Quantum igitur ingrati animi crimen fuerit, si thesaurum hunc tam pretiosum, aut contamine-mus[?] ipsi, aut scientes & prudentes sinamus contaminari? Annon hæc[?] quatuor circumstantiæ, illius, qui dedit: nostrum, quibus dedit: eorum, per quos dedit: & modi, quo dedit: satis luculenter demonstrant, quàm æquum & honestum sit, ut cœlestem hunc thesaurum, diligenter purissimum[?] conservemus: non in cistis, sed in corde, sed in ore, sed in Ecclesiastico ministerio? Has certè circumstantias diligenter examinavit Apostolus, cùm voluit ad obedientiam simul, & reverentiam Evangelij, fideles excitare in Epistola ad Heb.2.dicendo: Propterea, oportet nos diligentius attendere iis, quæ dicta sunt nobis, &c. Legantur reliqua.
units.tr: But in what way has he also given it to us? First by oracles, then in writing, confirmed by miracles, sealed by the blood of Christ, and also written by the Holy Spirit in our hearts. How great, then, would be the crime of an ungrateful mind, if we either ourselves defiled this so precious treasure, or knowingly and prudently allowed it to be defiled? Do not these four circumstances, of him who gave it, of us to whom it was given, of those through whom it was given, and of the manner in which it was given, sufficiently and clearly show how fair and honourable it is that we keep this heavenly treasure carefully and most pure: not in chests, but in the heart, in the mouth, and in the ecclesiastical ministry? The apostle certainly weighed these circumstances carefully when, in the Epistle to the Hebrews 2, he wished to rouse the faithful to obedience and reverence for the Gospel at the same time, saying: "Therefore we ought to give the more earnest heed to the things which were heard by us," etc. Let the rest be read.

units.la: Argumento autem ducto[?] à circumstantia personarum, tum eorum, quibus ablatus est, tum eorum, quibus datus est thesaurus, utitur in Epistola ad Rom.c.11.cùm ait: Dices igitur mihi: Defracti sunt rami, &c.
units.tr: Next, he uses the argument drawn from the circumstances of persons, both of those from whom the treasure was taken and of those to whom it was given, in his Epistle to the Romans, chapter 11, when he says: "You will say then to me: The branches were broken off, etc."

units.la: Sed non minus diligenter dua alia considerandā[?] nobis hic sunt circumstantiæ, quæ ad accuratam huius thesauri custodiam, excitare nos debent: nempe ipsius thesauri qualitas & dignitas: & finis propter quem Ecclesiæ donatus est.
units.tr: But there are two other circumstances that we must consider no less carefully here, which ought to stir us to a careful keeping of this treasure: namely, the quality and worth of the treasure itself, and the purpose for which it was entrusted to the Church.

units.la: Thesaurus ipse pretiosissimus est, coelestis, divinus, quo nihil in mundo praestabilius aut excellentius inveniri: nihil nobis utilius & salutarius donari potuit. Est enim hic ille thesaurus, cuius habendi causa, dividenda sunt omnia, ut Christus docuit: quando in ipso Christo est salus, vita aeterna. Præclara certe & magnifica dona Dei sunt sol, & pluvia, caeteraq; omnia, quae e coelo & terra nobis benigne & liberali manu largitur, ad vitam hanc feliciter transfigendam, necessaria. Præclariora, vires & facultates corporis atq; animi, innumeraq; virtutes, quibus animos mortalium exornat Dominus. Sed quid haec comparata cum verbo Dei aliud sunt, quam plumbum ac ferrum, collatum cum argento atq; auro? Idcirco David, postquam celebrasset coelos & coelorum virtutes, atq; illis dixisset enarrari gloriam Dei: continuò Legem, hoc est, verbum Domini, illis praetulit: atque ab effectis, hanc illis longè praestabiliorem esse demonstravit, dicendo: Lex Domini integra est, convertens animam: testimonium Domini verum, sapientiam suppeditans imperitis. Decreta Domini recta sunt, cor exhilarantia: præceptum Domini repurgatum, illuminans oculos. Legantur reliqua.
units.tr: The treasure itself is most precious, heavenly and divine, and nothing more excellent or outstanding can be found in the world; nothing more useful or salutary could have been given to us. For this is that treasure for whose sake, as Christ taught, all things are to be sold, since salvation and eternal life are in Christ himself. Certainly the sun and rain, and all the other things which God bountifully and generously bestows on us from heaven and earth, necessary for living this life happily, are splendid and magnificent gifts of God. More splendid still are the powers and faculties of body and soul, and the countless virtues with which the Lord adorns the minds of mortals. But what are all these, compared with the Word of God, except lead and iron set beside silver and gold? Therefore David, after praising the heavens and the powers of the heavens, and saying that the glory of God is declared by them, immediately set the Law, that is, the Word of the Lord, above them; and from its effects he showed that this is far more excellent than they, saying: "The law of the Lord is perfect, converting the soul; the testimony of the Lord is sure, making wise the simple. The statutes of the Lord are right, rejoicing the heart; the commandment of the Lord is pure, enlightening the eyes." Let the rest be read.

units.la: Alibi etiam comparat illud auro & argento purgatissimo. Quid vero dicam de Mose? Ostesurus[?] populo, quantum illum Deus praetulisset reliquis Gentibus, hoc unum celebrat: Thesaurum scilicet verbi Dei, id quod postea David in Ps.147. præclare cecinit, cum dixit: Qui annunciat verbum suum Iacobo : iustitias & iudicia sua Israeli. Non fecit taliter omni Nationi:& iudicia sua non manifestauit illis. (Certe reliquis etiam Natio-nibus communia fecerat Deus dona Cœli & Ter-ra: multisq; & praclaris virtutibus illas etiam ordinauerat: atq; ita ornauerat, vt illarum per-multa, ipsis etiam Iudaeis praestantiores fuerint. Qua igitur in re apparebat,populum Dei, Gentibus reliquis omnibus antecellere ? In hac, quod non illis, sed huic tantum suum tradiderat Deus verbum,suaq;patefecerat iudicia. Hoc id ipsum est, quod Apostolus scripsit ad Rom. Quid igitur amplius Iudaeo est ? (in quo scilicet prae-cellat Gentibus) aut quae vtilitas circumcisio-nis ? Multum quidem per omnem modum: atque in primis, quòd concredita sunt illis eloquia Dei. Hoc igitur illud ipsum est, quo nos feliciores & beatiores sumus reliquis populis omnibus, ipsis etiam Iudeis: nempe, quod nobis, & non illis, Euangelium Dei concreditum est. Annon haec luculenta sunt testimonia, testantia & declarantia, quanta sit huiusce thesauri ex-cellentia & dignitas ? Æstiment igitur alij, & magnificiant, quantum velint, diuitias Croesi: triumphos Pompeij:vires Herculis: ingeniū Lu-culli:virtutem Alexandri: doctrinam Aristo-telis aut Platonis:eloquentiam Ciceronis aut De-mosthenis: & si quid aliud in hoc Mundo excel-lens vnquam & admirandum fuit: Nos certè multo pluris faciemus hunc cœlestem thesau-rum: in quo vno salus nostra, vita & felicitas aeterna consistit: vt non sine causa scriptum reliquerit Apostolus, (christum & mortem aboleuisse, & vitam atq; immortalitatem in lucem produxisse per Evangelium : nempe nobis : quòd ea nisi per Evangelium a nobis agnosci percipiue non possit. Quare ab excellentia huiusce thesauri, satis liquido apparet, quanta cura & diligentia custodiendus nobis sit, purumque in Ecclesia conser-vandus.
units.tr: Elsewhere too he compares it to the purest gold and silver. But what shall I say of Moses? Wishing to show the people how much God had preferred them to the other nations, he celebrates this one thing: namely, the treasure of the Word of God. David later sang this splendidly in Psalm 147, when he said: "He declares his word to Jacob, his statutes and judgments to Israel. He has not dealt thus with any nation, and his judgments he has not made known to them." (Certainly God had also given the other nations the common gifts of heaven and earth, and had arranged for them many excellent virtues, adorning them so that many of these were more outstanding even than those of the Jews themselves. In what respect, then, did the people of God appear to excel all the other nations? In this: that God had given his Word and revealed his judgments not to them, but to this people alone. This is the very thing the Apostle wrote in Romans: "What advantage then has the Jew? (in which, namely, he excels the Gentiles) or what is the profit of circumcision? Much in every way; chiefly because the oracles of God were committed to them." Therefore this very thing is what makes us happier and more blessed than all other peoples, even the Jews: namely, that the Gospel of God has been committed to us and not to them. Are these not clear testimonies, witnessing and declaring how great is the excellence and worth of this treasure? Let others, then, esteem and magnify as much as they wish the riches of Croesus, the triumphs of Pompey, the strength of Hercules, the genius of Lucullus, the virtue of Alexander, the learning of Aristotle or Plato, the eloquence of Cicero or Demosthenes, and whatever else in this world has ever been excellent and admirable. We, certainly, will value far more this heavenly treasure, in which alone our salvation, life and eternal happiness consist. The Apostle did not write in vain that Christ has abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the Gospel: namely, for us, because these things cannot be acknowledged or perceived by us except through the Gospel. Therefore from the excellence of this treasure it is clear enough with how much care and diligence it must be guarded by us, and kept pure in the Church.

units.la: Finis porrò præcipuum, propter quem nobis suum verbum Deus & dedit, & reliquit in Ec-clesia, duplex est: gloria ipsius Dei, & salus no-stra. Gloria Dei in hoc cum primis relucet: si is solus agnoscetur, & appareat Ecclesia Doctor, qui è coelo, & non è terra nobis loquatur: & solus etiam a nobis cum summa reuerentia & obedientia audiatur. Nam solus etiam vult audiri: solus vult Ecclesiam suam docere: & hac voce sui verbi, suam declarare præsentiam, qua sua semper adest Ecclesia.
units.tr: Moreover, the chief purpose for which God both gave his Word to us and left it in the Church is twofold: the glory of God himself, and our salvation. The glory of God shines forth chiefly in this: if he alone is acknowledged, and appears as the Teacher of the Church, who speaks to us from heaven and not from earth, and if he alone is heard by us with the greatest reverence and obedience. For he alone wishes to be heard; he alone wishes to teach his Church, and by the voice of his Word to declare his presence, by which his Church is always present with him.

units.la: Finem hunc indicauit sapenumerò Deus in Scripturis per Mosen & Prophetas: quorum testimonia nunc in medium proferre, non est necesse, cùm res sit perspicua. Cùm enim populo mandabat, vt se suumq; Verbum duntaxat audiret: quid aliud hoc præcepto innuebat, nisi idèo se verbum suum, per Prophetas ad illos misisse, vt se loquentem in Prophetis audirent, & præterea neminem? Quid? Annon missum ad nos Filium, diserte hunc solum iubet audiri? Solus igitur vult docere, & audiri in Ecclesia Deus. Quod cùm ita sit, quis non videat, per[?] esse iniquum, vt aliquis alius præter Deum in Ecclesia doceat? aut vt Deus introducatur aliena à sua voluntate, imò & secum pugnantia loqui, idque in medio sua Ecclesia. Atqui id fit, cùm verbum Dei in Ecclesia, humanis corruptum doctrinis proponitur & prædicatur. Ergo, ne tam execra-bile flagitium in Dei maiestatem admittatur: & vt Deus appareat id quod est, verax & constans in suo verbo: & hac ratione sua illi maneat glo-ria, verbum Dei in Ecclesia, ab omni humana vacuum doctrina, purumque putum conseruari & administrari necesse est.
units.tr: God indicated this purpose very often in the Scriptures through Moses and the Prophets, whose testimonies it is now not necessary to bring forward, since the matter is plain. For when he commanded the people that they should hear him and his Word alone, what else did this precept imply, except that he had therefore sent his Word to them through the Prophets, so that they might hear him speaking in the Prophets, and no one besides? What? Does he not, concerning the Son sent to us, expressly command that he alone be heard? Therefore God alone wishes to teach and to be heard in the Church. Since this is so, who does not see that it is wrong for anyone other than God to teach in the Church, or for God to be introduced as speaking things foreign to his own will, and indeed contradictory, and that in the midst of his own Church? Yet this happens when the Word of God in the Church is corrupted by human doctrines and proposed and preached. Therefore, so that such an execrable crime is not committed against the majesty of God, and so that God may appear what he is, true and constant in his Word, and so that his glory remain his in this way, it is necessary that the Word of God in the Church be kept and administered free of all human doctrine, pure and unmixed.

units.la: Salus deinde nostra, in hoc potissimum est po-sita: primum, vt verum Deum agnoscamus, & Mediatorem Iesum Christum. Hæc est (inquit Dominus Iesus Patrem alloquens) vita æterna, vt cognoscant te solum verũ Deum, & quem misisti Iesum Christum. Deinde, vt eum vere colamus cultu: Quicunque invocauerit nomen Domini (inquit Apostolus) salvus erit. Quis autem sine Dei verbo potuisset unquam Deum agnoscere vere, & gratum ei cultum præbere? Ergo, vt Deum, & Christum eiusq; voluntatem & cultum possimus agnoscere, eoq; seruari: suum ad nos misit verbum, vt eo tanquam splendidissimo lumine, quæ alioqui nobis abdita erant, patefie-rent. Proinde Petrus merito scripta Prophetarum, eoq; universam scripturam, comparat lu-cerna lucenti in caliginoso loco, vt eo scilicet Deũ, eiusq; voluntatem & Christum, & quæcunque ad salutem nostram necessaria sunt, perspicue vi-deamus. Quid igitur non solum iniquius, sed etiam nobis detrimentosum esse potest, quam vt, quod nobis facis & luminis ad vitam aeternam praeuntis loco datum est, illud Cimmeriis[?] huma-narum doctrinarum tenebris, vel potius densa & atra ventosaq; caligine, aut nos obscuremus, aut ab aliis obscurari & penitus extingui, prudenter sinamus? Ergo ab ipsa etiam thesauri qualitate, & a duplici fine, propter quem nobis datus est, luce clarius apparet, quanta diligentia & cura debeat a nobis purus in Ecclesia conseruari.
units.tr: Our salvation, moreover, rests chiefly in this: first, that we acknowledge the true God and the Mediator Jesus Christ. "This," says the Lord Jesus, addressing the Father, "is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent." Then, that we truly worship him: "Whoever calls upon the name of the Lord," says the Apostle, "will be saved." But who could ever have truly known God and offered him acceptable worship without the Word of God? Therefore, so that we might be able to know God and Christ and his will and worship, and be kept in them, he sent his Word to us, so that by it, as by a most brilliant light, things which were otherwise hidden from us might be revealed. Accordingly Peter rightly compares the writings of the Prophets, and therefore all Scripture, to a lamp shining in a dark place, so that we may clearly see God and his will and Christ, and whatever is necessary for our salvation. What then can be more unjust, and indeed more harmful to us, than that we, wisely allowing what was given to us in place of a torch and light leading to eternal life, to be darkened by the shadows of human doctrines, or rather by the thick and black and windy mist, either obscure it ourselves or let it be obscured by others and utterly extinguished? Therefore it is clearer than light from the very quality of the treasure and from the twofold purpose for which it has been given to us, with how much diligence and care the pure Word must be preserved by us in the Church.

units.la: Quis vero innumerabiles eximiosq; fructus, quos purum purèq;[?] administratum verbum Dei fidelibus adfert, enumerare, vel explicare queat? Ego certè non possum paucis id clarius & breuius facere, quàm fecerit Apostolus, partim in ea, quam scripsit ad Timotheum posteriore: partim in ea, quae est ad Romanos. In illa ait scripturam sanctam utilem esse πρὸς[?] διδασκαλίαν · πρὸς ἔλεγχον · πρὸς ἐπανόρθωσιν · πρὸς παιδείαν τὴν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ: ut integer sit Dei homo, ad omne bonum opus apparatus: In hac vero ait: Quæcunq; scripta sunt, ea ad nostram doctrinam scripta esse, ut per patientiam & consolationem scripturarum, spem habeamus. His duobus locis, omnes Scriptura utilitates & fructus, vel, ut melius dicam, usus, quam breuissimè simul & dilucidè complexus est Apostolus. Quid enim praeter hac desiderari posset amplius? Nam quaecun-que tradi possunt de religione, & ad salutem nostram pertinentia: illa aut pertinent ad dogmata, aut ad mores, aut ad consolandas afflictorum mentes & conscientias. Si ad dogmata: illa aut sunt vera, aut falsa. Si vera: illa omnia abundè tradit sacra Scriptura: ideo merito ait, illam utilem esse ὠφέλιμον διδασκαλίαν. Si falsa: eadem Scriptura refutari facile possunt. Ideo ait, eam etiam utilem esse ὠφέλιμον ἔλεγχον. Si de moribus agitur: illi aut sunt boni, aut mali. Si mali, eos omnes corrigit Scriptura: idcirco ait, eam utilem esse ὠφέλιμον ἐπανόρθωσιν. Si boni: in illis nos instituit sacra Scriptura, inq; vera iustitia: ita ut quisque ad omne bonum opus apparari, & perfecte instrui per sacram Scripturam possit: ac proinde merito ait, eam utilem esse, ὠφέλιμον διδασκαλίαν τῆς ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ, ἵνα ἄρτιος [?] ἡ ὁ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἄνθρωπος, πρὸς πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθὸν ἐξηρτισμένος. Quid hac Apostolica partitione perfectius? quid absolutius? His vero quatuor, accedit quintus usus: is est consola-tio in adversis, cum patientia seu tolerantia praesentium malorum: & cum spe, certaque expectatione futurorum bonorum coniuncta. Hunc fructum si addas superioribus: nil poteris amplius desiderare. Hanc autem quintam utilitatem, ipsa etiam sacra Scriptura largiter praestat, ut docet Apostolus ad Rom. & nos reapse experi-mur. Nullum est tam grave afflictionum genus, in quo nos positos, non mira afficiat consola-tione S Scriptura. Quamobrem—? Quoniam Deus est, qui ibi loquitur. Deus autem est, qui nos consolatur in omni afflictione[?] nostra. Est enim ipse solus Pater misericordiarum, & Deus omnis consolationis.
units.tr: Who, indeed, could enumerate or explain the countless and outstanding fruits which the Word of God, purely and purely administered, brings to the faithful? I certainly cannot do this more clearly and more briefly than the Apostle did, partly in the passage he wrote to Timothy in the second letter, and partly in the one addressed to the Romans. In the former he says that Holy Scripture is useful "for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness" [πρὸς διδασκαλίαν; πρὸς ἔλεγχον; πρὸς ἐπανόρθωσιν; πρὸς παιδείαν τὴν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ], so that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work. In the latter he says: "Whatever things were written before were written for our learning, that through patience and the comfort of the Scriptures we might have hope." By these two passages the Apostle has embraced, as briefly and clearly as possible, all the uses and fruits of Scripture, or, to speak better, its uses. For what more could be desired beyond these? For whatever can be taught about religion and pertains to our salvation, that either pertains to doctrines, or to morals, or to comforting the minds and consciences of the afflicted. If to doctrines: these are either true or false. If true: Holy Scripture abundantly teaches all of them; therefore he rightly says it is useful for teaching [ὠφέλιμον διδασκαλίαν]. If false: the same Scripture can easily refute them. Therefore he says it is also useful for reproof [ὠφέλιμον ἔλεγχον]. If the matter concerns morals: these are either good or bad. If bad, Scripture corrects them all; therefore he says it is useful for correction [ὠφέλιμον ἐπανόρθωσιν]. If good: Holy Scripture instructs us in them and in true righteousness, so that each person may be equipped for every good work and perfectly trained through Holy Scripture; and therefore he rightly says it is useful for instruction in righteousness [ὠφέλιμον διδασκαλίαν τῆς ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ, ἵνα ἄρτιος ἡ ὁ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἄνθρωπος, πρὸς πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθὸν ἐξηρτισμένος]. What could be more complete or more perfect than this apostolic division? To these four there is added a fifth use: this is consolation in adversity, together with patience or endurance of present evils, and joined with hope and the sure expectation of future good things. If you add this fruit to the previous ones, you can desire nothing more. Holy Scripture itself also supplies this fifth use abundantly, as the Apostle teaches in Romans, and as we ourselves actually experience. There is no kind of affliction so severe that, when we are placed in it, Scripture does not bring a wonderful consolation. Why is this? Because it is God who speaks there. And it is God who comforts us in every affliction of ours, for he himself is the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation.

units.la: Hac omnia bona, larga manu suppeditat Deus divino suo sermone in S Scripturis conten-to: sed eo puro, puréque propositio. Quid igitur utilius, quàm purum Dei verbum in Ecclesia retinere & conseruare ? Certè Ecclesia eatenus seruantur : quatenus retinent purum Dei ver-bum : & eatenus perduntur : quatenus verbum Dei aut prorsus ab illis tollitur : aut humanis do-ctrinis contaminatur atq; corrumpitur : quem-admodum Ecclesia quæ erant in Galatia, & a-lia, tempore etiam Apostolorum : ac deniq; Ro-mana, & quæcunque illam secuti sunt, perspicuè docent. Non est igitur tantum utilis in Ecclesia puritas verbi Dei, sed etiam pernecessaria. Et-enim, quis seruari posset, sine Dei & Christi co-gnitione? Nemo hominum. Quomodo verò Deus & Christus Mediator agnosci verè & salutari-ter a nobis possunt, citra purum ipsius Dei ser-monem? Nullo modo. Non alia profectò ratio-ne Deum agnouerunt & Christum eius veteres Patres, Adamus, Noha, Patriarcha, Moses, Pro-phetæ, Apostoli. Moses quidem summo teneba-tur desiderio videndi Dei faciè ad faciem : & supplex hoc ab illo petiit : sed Deus, hoc, seruo suo alioqui charissimo, aperte denegauit, allata et-iam ratione, cur nollet ei in hac re gratificari : partim quòd fieri nequeat, ut mortalis homo Deum facie ad faciem videat : partim, quòd ei non expediret utile ve esset : propterea, quòd non posset Deum in hac carne facie ad faciem vide-re, quin moriatur : Non videbit (inquit) me homo, & viuet. Patefecit autem se ex sermone ad eum facto, dicens & clamans : Iehoua, Ieho-ua, Deus misericors, beneficus, & quæ sequun-tur Epitheta, quibus se ipse Deus describit, & Mosi cognoscendum præbuit[?]. Ergo ex verbo Dei puro Deus agnoscatur, necesse est. Nam quòd ait Apostolus, invisibilia Dei, per ea, quæ facta sunt, intellecta cognosci: sempiternam quoq; eius virtutem ac divinitatem: cognitio illa imbecilla est, & inefficax, & ea resalutaris esse non potest. Fides enim sine qua servari nemo potest, aut placere Deo, non est ex inspectione rerum creatarum: sed ex auditu (inquit Apostolus:) auditus autem iste, per verbum Christi est. Ad Deum igitur vere & salutariter cognoscendum, eoq; ad salutem consequendam, necessarium est in Ecclesia purum Dei verbum.
units.tr: All these goods God supplies with a generous hand, to those who keep to his divine word in the Holy Scriptures; but to that word in its purity, and purely set forth. What, then, is more useful than to retain and preserve the pure word of God in the Church? Certainly the Churches are preserved so far as they keep the pure word of God, and they are lost so far as the word of God is either entirely taken away from them, or is contaminated and corrupted by human doctrines; as the churches that were in Galatia, and others, even in the time of the Apostles, and finally the Roman church and all those that have followed it, clearly teach. The purity of the word of God in the Church is therefore not only useful but even absolutely necessary. For who could be saved without the knowledge of God and Christ? No one. And how can God and Christ the Mediator be truly and savingly known by us, apart from the pure word of God himself? In no way. Certainly the ancient fathers, Adam, Noah, the patriarchs, Moses, the prophets, and the apostles, did not know God and his Christ by any other method. Moses indeed was held by the greatest desire to see the face of God face to face, and he asked this of him in supplication; but God openly refused this to his servant, otherwise most dear, giving also the reason why he would not grant him this request: partly because it cannot happen that a mortal man should see God face to face, and partly because it was not expedient or useful for him, since he could not see God face to face in this flesh without dying: "No man shall see me and live," he said. But he revealed himself through a word spoken and cried out to him: "Jehovah, Jehovah, a merciful and beneficent God," and the other epithets that follow, by which God describes himself, and he gave himself to Moses to be known. Therefore it is necessary that God be known from the pure word of God. For as to what the Apostle says, that the invisible things of God are known through the things that have been made, namely his eternal power and divinity, that knowledge is weak and ineffective, and it cannot be saving. For faith, without which no one can be saved or please God, does not come from the inspection of created things, but from hearing (says the Apostle); and that hearing is through the word of Christ. Therefore, for the true and saving knowledge of God, and so for the attaining of salvation, the pure word of God in the Church is necessary.

units.la: Deinde etiamsi Deus sese exhiberet visendum universis & singulis hominibus, ita ut eius faciem, sicut faciem hominis intueremur: quem-admodum, cum Christum Apostoli viderunt in gloria sua, in monte sancto, ut loquitur Petrus: tamen nisi eum colamus, ea qua ipse vult cultu ratione: servari nullo modo possumus. Nam illi tantum consortes fiunt salutis, qui Deum in veritate invocant, hoc est, vere colunt. At quisnam divinare possit, quonam Deus delectetur cultu, nisi ipse suo declaret sermone? Nam si nemo novit, quae sunt hominis, nisi (ut loquitur Apostolus) Spiritus, qui in ipso est: quanto minus quae sunt Dei, nisi ipse Deus, & cui ille velit revelare?
units.tr: Furthermore, even if God were to show himself to be seen by all and each of men, so that we looked upon his face as we look upon the face of a man, just as the apostles saw Christ in his glory on the holy mountain, as Peter says, yet unless we worship him in the manner that he himself wills, we can in no way be saved. For only those become partakers of salvation who call upon God in truth, that is, who truly worship him. But who could divine in what manner God delights to be worshipped, unless he himself declared it by his own word? For if no one knows the things of a man except the spirit of man which is in him (as the Apostle says), how much less the things of God, except God himself, and those to whom he wills to reveal them?

units.la: Cùm igitur salutem assequi non possimus, etiamsi eam omni nostra sapientia & viribus prosequamur, nisi Deum recte colamus: & Deus recte coli à nobis non possit, nisi ex puro eius ore nobis innotescat, quànam ratione coli à nobis velit: Quis non videat, quàm omninò necessarium sit, vt purum Dei verbum in Ecclesia habeatur & conseruetur? Dico autem purum verbum, quia purè coli non potest Deus, vbi impurus traditur cultus: Ibi autem impurus est cultus, vbi impura est doctrina. Quod dico, ita perspicuum est, vt probatione nulla opus habeat. Unde enim, quasi vos, impij illi cultus & ἐθελοθρησκείᾳ in Regno Antichristi? nimirum ἐν τῆς ἱεροδιδασκα-λίας ab ea, quam Apostoli putissimam tradiderunt. Ergo si purè velimus Deum coli in Ecclesia: purum etiam Dei verbum in eadem docea-tur necesse est. Hoc est quod Dominus praecipit per Ieremiam 23.cap. dicendo: Propheta, apud quem est somnium, narret somnium: & qui habet verbum meum, loquatur verbum meum verè, hoc est, purè & ex fide. Quid enim paleis cum tritico? hoc est, humanis somniis, cum sermone Dei? Quare sicut eos damnat Dominus, qui sua quidem narrant somnia: sed id faciunt, tanquam sermo esset divinus, & non humana somnia: Ita vult, vt qui verbum Domini adferunt, adferant illud purum putum, nullis humanis contaminatum somniis, tanquam triticum repurgatum, & sine vllis paleis. Quid enim verbo Dei cum nostris somniis? Idem quod luci cum tenebris: veritati cum mendacijs: institutae cum iniquitate: Deo, cum Sathana.
units.tr: Since therefore we cannot attain salvation, even if we pursue it with all our wisdom and strength, unless we worship God rightly; and since God cannot be rightly worshipped by us unless he makes known to us from his pure mouth in what manner he wishes to be worshipped by us: who does not see how absolutely necessary it is that the pure word of God be held and preserved in the Church? I say, however, the pure word, because God cannot be purely worshipped where an impure worship is handed down; and worship is impure where doctrine is impure. What I say is so clear that it needs no proof. For whence, as it were, come those impure worships and will-worship in the kingdom of Antichrist? Assuredly from that holy teaching which the apostles handed down most purely. Therefore, if we wish God to be purely worshipped in the Church, it is necessary that the pure word of God also be taught in it. This is what the Lord commands through Jeremiah in chapter 23, saying: "The prophet who has a dream, let him tell the dream; and he who has my word, let him speak my word truly," that is, purely and in faith. For what has chaff to do with wheat? That is, human dreams with the word of God? Therefore, just as the Lord condemns those who indeed relate their own dreams, but do so as though their words were divine and not human dreams, so he wills that those who bring the word of the Lord should bring it pure and unmixed, free from any human dreams, like wheat cleansed and without any chaff. For what has the word of God to do with our dreams? The same as light with darkness, truth with lies, righteousness with iniquity, God with Satan.

units.la: Nunc satis mihi demonstrasse videor, quod priori loco mihi demonstrandum suscepi: nempe, non solùm honestum, Christianoque homine dignum & vtile esse, sed etiam pernecessarium, vt per eos, quorum interest, curetur, vt reiectis omnibus humanis de religione doctrinis, purissimum putissimum Dei verbum, a quo pura pendet Dei cognitio, purus cultus, pura religio, pura Ecclesia, in Ecclesiastico ministerio retineatur & conseruetur. Sed nondum dixi. Superest enim altera, eaque praecipua & vtilior pars orationis mea, quae est de ratione conseruandi verbum Dei purum in Ecclesia: ideoque de Scholis, explicanda. Verùm quia excludor tempore, differo eam in crastinum diem.
units.tr: Now I think I have sufficiently demonstrated what I undertook to demonstrate in the first place: namely, that it is not only honourable, and worthy and useful for a Christian man, but even absolutely necessary, that by those whose concern it is, care should be taken that, with all human doctrines about religion rejected, the purest and most unadulterated word of God, from which the pure knowledge of God, pure worship, pure religion and pure Church depend, be retained and preserved in the ecclesiastical ministry. But I have not yet said everything. For there remains another part of my discourse, and that the principal and more useful one, which concerns the manner of preserving the word of God pure in the Church, and therefore must be explained with regard to the schools. But since time shuts me out, I defer it until the next day.

units.la: Dixi heri de honesta & vtili necessitate conseruandi in Ecclesia verbum Dei: dicam hodie de vera, qua id possit perfici, ratione.
units.tr: Yesterday I spoke of the honourable and useful necessity of preserving the word of God in the Church; today I shall speak of the true manner by which this can be accomplished.

units.la: Duo sunt hominum genera, per quos Dominus Iesus voluit ordinariè & semper in Ecclesia verbum suum praedicari & explicari: Pastores nimirum, & Doctores: quorum illi ad populum, in Templis: isti verò ad studiosos in Scholis destinati sunt. Ita hinc surgit duplex ratio, qua purum Dei verbum conseruari in Ecclesia possit: quarum prior ad Ecclesiasticos conuentus: altera ad ipsas spectat Scholas. Dicam de utraque, quod sentio, breuiter & liberè: ac spero orationem hanc meam nemini vestrum futuram ingratam. Dicam autem primum de Ecclesiastica: deinde de Scholastica ratione.
units.tr: There are two kinds of men through whom the Lord Jesus has willed that his word be ordinarily and always preached and explained in the Church: namely ministers and teachers; of whom the former are appointed for the people in the churches, and the latter for students in the schools. Thus there arises a twofold method by which the pure word of God can be preserved in the Church: the former concerns the ecclesiastical assemblies, the other the schools themselves. I shall speak briefly and freely about each, as I think, and I hope that this my discourse will be unwelcome to none of you. I shall speak first of the ecclesiastical method, then of the scholastic.

units.la: Quod ad Ecclesiasticam pertinet rationem: illud in primis curandum est, vt ad ministerium verbi non admittantur, nisi homines verè pij, & in S. Literis fideliter explicatis, bene institu-ti, saatq;[?] doctrinæ tenacissimi fortissimiq; defensores, & ad eam aliis tradendam accommodati. Hoc autem est officium Ecclesiarum, Principum, & Magistratus. Hanc admonitionem & observationem tradit Apostolus cum in utraque ad Timotheum, tum in ea quæ est ad Titum: Cum præter alia docet, oportere Episcopum esse διδακτικὸν[?], ὀρθολογοῦντα[?] τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας, ἢ ἀντεχόμενον[?] τῆς καλῆς τῶν διδαχῶν[?] πιστοῦ λόγου[?]. Et id quidem merito. Nam quo pacto ipsi Episcopi poterunt alios fideliter & purè docere: hæreticos confutare: τοὺς ἀντιλέγοντας ἐλέγχειν[?], atq; ita purum retinere Christi in Ecclesia verbum: nisi ipsi prius sanam fuerint puramque edocti doctrinam, & in ea clarè explicanda, & fortiter defendenda exercitati? quæ exercitatio in Scholis inchoari debet. Proinde quam plurimum refert, quibusnam in Scholis edocti & instituti sint illi, qui ad Ministerium Ecclesiasticum promouendi sunt. Etenim qualem quisque didicerit doctrinam, talem & alios doceat ipse, necesse est. Pura igitur doctrina homines, ac sinceris in Scholis educati, eligendi sunt, qui Ecclesiæ purum Dei verbum proponant. Atque, ut ante dixi, hoc est officium Ecclesiarum, Principum, Magistratum.
units.tr: As regards the ecclesiastical method, this above all must be taken care of: that no one be admitted to the ministry of the word unless he is a truly godly man, well instructed in the Holy Scriptures faithfully expounded, a most tenacious and bold defender of doctrine, and suited to pass it on to others. This is the duty of the churches, of princes, and of the magistrate. The Apostle hands down this admonition and observation both in the two letters to Timothy and in the one to Titus; where, among other things, he teaches that a bishop must be "apt to teach, holding fast the word of truth in accordance with sound doctrine" [διδακτικὸν, ὀρθολογοῦντα τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας, ἀντεχόμενον τῆς καλῆς τῶν διδαχῶν πιστοῦ λόγου]; and "to convince those who speak against it" [τοὺς ἀντιλέγοντας ἐλέγχειν]. And rightly so. For how could the bishops themselves teach others faithfully and purely, refute heretics, and thus retain the word of Christ pure in the Church, unless they themselves had first been taught sound and pure doctrine and trained to explain it clearly and defend it boldly? Such training ought to begin in the schools. Therefore it matters very much in which schools those who are to be promoted to the ecclesiastical ministry have been taught and trained. For it is necessary that each one teaches others the kind of doctrine he himself has learned. Therefore men educated in pure doctrine and in sincere schools ought to be chosen to set forth the pure word of God in the Church. And, as I said before, this is the duty of the churches, the princes and the magistrates.

units.la: Deinde ipsis etiam, effectis iam Pastoribus, danda est opera, ut nihil ad populum è suggestis proferant, nisi ipsissimum putissimumq; verbum Dei, idq; tam quod ad doctrinam, quam quod ad illius confirmationem attinet. Nam etiamsi multarum forte scientiarum peritissimi sint, & tamin profanis autoribus, quam in S.do doctoribus[?], tum veteribus, tum recentioribus exercitatissimi, ita ut illorum etiam testimoniis sanam confirmare doctrinam possint: tamen ab huiusce modi hominum tam Christianorum, quam profanorum dictis, quoad eius fieri potest, abstinendum est in suggestis, & nil nisi verbum a Deo prolatum, ad eius Ecclesiam referendum est. Quam ob rem? Primum, quia solus Christus in Ecclesia audiri vult & debet: secundo, quia fit iniuria Scripturae, quasi non sufficiat: tertio, propter utilitatem Ecclesiae, ut illa assuefiat audiendis tantum sermonibus Dei: & hac ratione dum purum Dei verbum residet in animis fidelium, illud vere servetur in Ecclesia. Sic factum fuisse legimus a Mose, & a Prophetis. Etsi enim multa alia praeter verbum Dei, probe tenerent: ad populos tamen in concionibus nil unquam aliud adferebat, nisi quae ex ore Domini accepissent, & ex eius verbo didicissent. Sic Christus, in quo erant omnes thesauri sapientiae ac cognitionis absconditi, egit. Nil enim docebat, nisi quae audivisset a Patre, & in S. literis Prophetarum continerentur. Sic iussi[?] sunt facere Apostoli. Neque enim permisit illis Christus praedicare & docere populos, quaecunque scirent, aut scire possent: sed terminos ac limites praefixit verbi Dei, quos minime fas esset transilire: Praedicate (inquiens) Euangelium: docentes servare, quaecunque praecepi vobis, quasi dicat, nil praeterea. Sic Apostoli obtemperarunt, & sic nobis quoq; faciendum esse docuerunt. Prodeat Petrus: 1. Pet. 4. Si quis loquitur (inquit) quasi sermones Dei: quantò magis igitur, qui Ecclesia Dei conciona-tur? Prodeat & Paulus. Primum præceptum quod tradit Timotheo in priore epistola, cap. 1. de bene regenda & gubernanda Ecclesia, hoc ipsum fuit, quod iam tracto argumentum: nimirum denunciaret illis, qui munus docendi in Ecclesia habebant, μὴ ἑτεροδιδασκαλεῖν: hoc est, neque aliud, neque aliter docerent, quàm ipsi quoque Apostoli docuissent, & adhuc docerent, purum scilicet verbum Dei & purè: μυθολόγους illos appellans, & eorum doctrinam μυθολογίαν, qui- cunq; aliter & aliud docent, quam quod Christus docuit, & docere iussit. Et in altera epistola, cap. 2. iubet Episcopum esse ὀρθοτομοῦντα τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας: non solum iubet, ut nihil aliud secet populo Dei, quam sermonem veritatis: sed etiam iubet, ut illum secet recte, hoc est, prudenter, purè, & secet ad ædificationem.
units.tr: Furthermore, once they have become ministers, care must be taken that from the pulpit they bring forward to the people nothing but the very word of God, purely and wholly, both as regards the doctrine itself and as regards its confirmation. For even if they are most skilled in many sciences, and well practised both in profane authors and in the sacred doctors, both ancient and more recent, so that they could confirm sound doctrine even by their testimonies, nevertheless, so far as it can be done, they must refrain in the pulpit from the sayings of such men, whether Christian or profane, and only the word spoken by God must be brought to his Church. Why so? First, because Christ alone wishes and ought to be heard in the Church; second, because it is an injury to Scripture, as if it were not sufficient; third, for the benefit of the Church, so that it may become accustomed to hearing only the discourses of God; and in this way, while the pure word of God dwells in the minds of the faithful, it is truly preserved in the Church. We read that this was done by Moses and by the Prophets. For although they held well to many other things besides the word of God, nevertheless they never brought to the peoples in their sermons anything other than what they had received from the mouth of the Lord and learned from his word. So Christ acted, in whom were hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge; for he taught nothing except what he had heard from the Father and what was contained in the sacred writings of the Prophets. So the Apostles were commanded to act. For Christ did not permit them to preach and teach the peoples whatever they knew or could know, but he set the limits and boundaries of the word of God, which it would by no means be lawful to overstep: "Preach," he says, "the Gospel; teaching them to observe whatever I have commanded you," as if to say, nothing beyond this. So the Apostles obeyed, and so they taught that we too must act. Let Peter come forward: 1 Pet. 4. "If anyone speaks," he says, "as the oracles of God..."; how much more, then, those who preach in the Church of God? Let Paul also come forward. The first precept which he gives to Timothy in the first epistle, chapter 1, concerning the good ordering and governing of the Church, is that very thing which I am now treating: namely, that he should warn those who had the office of teaching in the Church μὴ ἑτεροδιδασκαλεῖν [not to teach otherwise], that is, that they should teach neither something else nor otherwise than the Apostles themselves had taught and still taught, namely the pure word of God, and purely; calling those who teach otherwise and something other than what Christ taught and commanded to teach "myth-tellers," and their doctrine "myths." And in the second epistle, chapter 2, he bids the bishop be ὀρθοτομοῦντα τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας [rightly dividing the word of truth]: he not only bids him divide to the people of God nothing but the word of truth, but also bids him divide it rightly, that is, wisely, purely, and divide it for edification.

units.la: Docent omnes ij, & alij propè infiniti similes loci, Pastoribus Ecclesiarum in hoc unum omni cura, studio, diligentia esse incumbendum: ut fidelibus in Ecclesia Christi nil nisi purum Dei verbum, idq; purè & fideliter explicatum proponant: quòd hac unica doctrina seruentur Ecclesia. Atque hæc est una vera ratio retinendi in Ecclesia purum Dei verbum, nempe, si Pastores in suo Ministerio se contineant intra limites verbi Dei, non solum quoad ipsam doctrinam, ut scilicet nihil doceant, quod non suppeditet verbum Dei: sed etiam quoad confirmationem doctrinæ, ut scilicet necunde sumant testimonia ad probandum, quàm è fontibus Scriptura-rum: rum: & id quoad eius fieri potest. Hoc addo: quo-niam nonnunquam vsu venit, vt cogantur Pa-stores etiam pro suggestu, praeter testimonia & ra-tiones Scripturarum, vti etiam testimoniis & ra-tionibus hominum tam profanorum, quam et-iam sanctorum, tam ad sua sana dogmata con-firmanda, quàm ad falsa aduersariorum refu-tanda: idque aut propter peruicaciam haeretico-rum, qui dum non acquiescunt Scripturis, aliis rationibus & testimoniis conuincendi sunt: aut propter maleuolorum calumnias, quas aliis, quà Scripturarum testimoniis refellere necesse est: aut denique etiam propter nonnullorum infir-morum fratrum imbecillitatem, qui à veteri su-perstitione non possunt penitus auelli, & in tradi-ta, perque Scripturas confirmata veritate fir-mari: nisi veterum etiam Patrum testimoniis eadem comprobetur. Tunc enim vtile fuerit Ec-clesia, si id fecerit Pastor, modò tamen prudenter & sobriè, praemissa protestatione, se hoc facere co-actum, non egressurum alioqui cancellos sacrâ Scriptura.
units.tr: All these and almost countless other similar passages teach that the one concern, care, study and diligence of the ministers of the Churches must be this: that they set before the faithful in the Church of Christ nothing but the pure word of God, and that explained purely and faithfully; for by this one doctrine the Church is preserved. And this is the one true method of retaining the pure word of God in the Church, namely, if ministers keep themselves in their ministry within the limits of the word of God: not only as regards the doctrine itself, so that they teach nothing which the word of God does not supply, but also as regards the confirmation of the doctrine, so that they take their testimonies for proof from no other sources than the fountains of Scripture, and that as far as can be done. I add this: since it sometimes happens that ministers are compelled even from the pulpit, besides the testimonies and arguments of Scripture, to use also the testimonies and arguments of men, both profane and holy, both to confirm their sound doctrines and to refute the false opinions of adversaries; and this either on account of the obstinacy of heretics, who, since they do not acquiesce in the Scriptures, must be convinced by other arguments and testimonies; or on account of the slanders of ill-wishers, which must be refuted by other means than the testimonies of Scripture; or finally on account of the weakness of some infirm brethren, who cannot be wholly torn away from old superstition and be firmly established in the truth delivered and confirmed by the Scriptures, unless the same is also proved by the testimonies of the ancient Fathers. In such cases it will be useful to the Church if the minister does this, provided, however, that he does it prudently and soberly, having first made a protestation that he is doing this under compulsion, and that he will not otherwise go beyond the bounds of sacred Scripture.

units.la: Caterum extra has tres necessarias causas, quae certè non sape contingunt, non est boni Pastoris & Concionatoris in Ecclesia, extra limites S.Scripturarum, perscripta Poëtarum & Philosophorum, aut etiam Patrum enagari. Hoc enim est contaminare verbum Dei: & Ecclesiam assuefacere dictis hominum magis, quàm S.Scripturarum oraculis audiendis: quod quid aliud est, quàm puritatem verbi Dei paulatim è men-tibus fidelium, eoq; & ex Ecclesia tollere?
units.tr: Apart from these three necessary causes, which indeed do not often occur, it is not the part of a good minister and preacher in the Church, outside the limits of the Holy Scriptures, to bring forth the writings of poets and philosophers, or even of the Fathers. For this is to contaminate the word of God, and to accustom the Church to hear the sayings of men rather than the oracles of the Holy Scriptures; and what else is this than gradually to remove the purity of the word of God from the minds of the faithful and so from the Church?

units.la: Peccant igitur grauissimè contra puritatem verbi Dei illi, qui ostentanda nescio cuius eruditionis gratia, è suggestis varia profanorum, Philosophorum, Poetarum etiam obscoenorum dicta non solum citant, sed etiam integra recitant atq; explicant.
units.tr: They therefore sin most gravely against the purity of the word of God who, for the sake of displaying I know not what erudition, cite from the pulpit not only the various sayings of profane philosophers and poets, even obscene poets, but also recite and explain them at length.

units.la: Non me latet, Apostolum Paulum nonnun-quam in suis sermonibus & Epistolis, profanorum etiam Poetarum dicta, quòd ad rem, quam tractabat, essent accommodata, citasse: ut in Actis illud Arati, τοῦ γὰρ καὶ γένος ἐσμέν [?]: ut in 1. (cor. ιε [?]. illud Menandri, φθείρουσιν ἤθη χρηστὰ ὁμιλίαι κακαί [?]: ut in epist. ad Titum, c. 1. illud Epimenidis, Κρῆτες ἀεὶ ψεῦσται, κακὰ θηρία, γαστέρες ἀργαί.
units.tr: I am not unaware that the Apostle Paul, in his sermons and epistles, sometimes cited sayings of profane poets as well, since they were suited to the matter he was treating: as in Acts the line of Aratus, "For we are also his offspring" [τοῦ γὰρ καὶ γένος ἐσμέν]; as in 1 Cor. 15 the line of Menander, "Evil companionships corrupt good morals" [φθείρουσιν ἤθη χρηστὰ ὁμιλίαι κακαί]; as in the epistle to Titus, chapter 1, the line of Epimenides, "Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, idle bellies" [Κρῆτες ἀεὶ ψεῦσται, κακὰ θηρία, γαστέρες ἀργαί].

units.la: Verum, neq; nominauit Poetas, neq; id fecit frequenter, neq; sine utili causa: sed breuiatantum illorum dicta, raro, sobrie, & quasi obiter, coactus adduxit: ut qui erant ex gentibus, ipsorum quoq; Gentilium dictis, quasi propriis confode-rentur armis. Quid igitur hoc Apostoli exemplum iuuat illos, qui citra ullam necessitatem, aut etiam utilitatem, tantùm ut ostentent nescio quam vanam eruditionem, assuefaciunt mentes fidelium audiendis multorum eruditorum hominum testimoniis? Solus Christus in Ecclesia audiendus est, si volumus puram eius doctrinam in Ecclesia conseruari. Hanc priorem regulam docuit nos Apostolus in altera ad Timoth. epist. cap 2. Quæ audiuisti (inquiens) ex me, inter multos testes: hæc propone fidelibus hominibus, qui erunt ἱκανοὶ, καὶ ἑτέρους διδάξαι [?], nempe eadem, & non alia: quasi dicat, Et ita nostraretineatur doctrina, qua est verbum Dei, in Ecclesia Christi. Atque hæc de officio Pastorum, & depriori conseruandi in Ecclesia verbum Dei, ratione: satis.
