units.tr: But he neither named the poets, nor did so frequently, nor without a useful reason: rather, compelled by necessity, he brought forward only brief sayings of theirs, rarely, soberly, and as it were in passing, so that those who were of the Gentiles might be pierced by their own Gentile sayings as with their own weapons. What then does this example of the Apostle profit those who, without any necessity or even usefulness, merely to display I know not what vain erudition, accustom the minds of the faithful to hear the testimonies of many learned men? Christ alone is to be heard in the Church, if we wish his pure doctrine to be preserved in the Church. The Apostle taught us this first rule in the second epistle to Timothy, chapter 2: "What you have heard from me among many witnesses," he says, "commit to faithful men, who will be ἱκανοὶ [able], and καὶ ἑτέρους διδάξαι [to teach others] also": namely the same things and no others; as if he said, and thus our doctrine, which is the word of God, will be retained in the Church of Christ. And this is enough concerning the duty of ministers and the first method of preserving the word of God in the Church.

units.la: Venio nunc ad alteram: ea est diligens gy-mnasiorum literariorum & scholarum imprimis Theologicarum cura: nimirum, ut qui ad Mini-sterium Ecclesiasticum assumendi sunt, in iis primis Christianæ pieq[?] ad officium illud instituantur. Hæc autem cura partim ad Principes ipsos & Respub. partim ad ipsarum scholarum Doctores: partim denique ad ipsos etiam iuuenes[?] instituendos pertinet.
units.tr: I come now to the second: this is the diligent care of the literary gymnasia and especially of the theological schools: namely, that those who are to be admitted to the ecclesiastical ministry should be instructed, above all, in Christian piety for that office. This care, however, pertains partly to the princes themselves and the commonwealth, partly to the teachers of the schools themselves, and partly finally to the young men themselves who are to be instructed.

units.la: Ac quoad Principes & Respub. pertinet: pri-mum summa diligentia curandum illis est, ut in suis urbibus Scholas habeant, & in iis pios, præstantes, & excellentes viros, qui iuuentutem cum bonas & liberales artes & disciplinas ac linguas tum in primis veram pietatis doctrinam, hoc est, purum Dei verbum doceant: nec non etiam in ipsa pietate, Christianisque & honestis moribus instituant. Deinde, ut hoc commode & felicius fieri possit: debent & Doctores ipsos liberalibus sti-pendiis, & pauperes studiosos honesta aliquara-tione sustentare. Sic Deus docet suo exemplo, cum prospexit Leuitis de urbibus, de decimis, &c. Sic fecit Constantinus Imper. &c. Certè honesta Professorum stipendia, non minus nervi sunt Scholarum, quam pecunia, bellì.
units.tr: As far as the princes and the commonwealth are concerned: first, they must take the greatest diligence to ensure that they have schools in their cities, and in them pious, outstanding and excellent men who teach the youth not only good and liberal arts, disciplines and languages, but above all the true doctrine of piety, that is, the pure word of God; and also instruct them in piety itself and in Christian and honourable morals. Next, so that this may be done conveniently and more successfully, they ought to support the teachers themselves with liberal salaries, and to sustain poor students with some honourable maintenance. Thus God teaches by his own example, when he provided for the Levites with cities, tithes, etc. Thus the Emperor Constantine did, etc. Certainly honourable salaries for professors are no less the sinews of schools than money is of war.

units.la: Postremo debent ipsi pii Principes & Magistratus, Episcopi esse suarum scholarum, hoc est, debent aut per se, si fieri possit, aut saltem per alios subinde visitare Scholas, & inspicere, quantum & quomodo studiosi proficiant, & in literis, & in vera pietatis doctrina: & curare, ut suum quisque faciat officium strenuè & diligenter. Hæc est cura, quam suscipere debent pij Principes & Magistratus, de Scholis aperiendis & bene instituendis ac conseruandis. Sunt enim hæ, si bene sunt constitutæ, non solum utiles Reipub. verum etiam Ecclesiis necessariæ: quando sine ipsis neque Respublica bene habere, neque Ecclesia diu consistere possint. Nam quod attinet ad Respublicas, quantum illa valeant, & quantum sint felices sine viris doctis, & vera sapientia præditis, quorum sapientibus consiliis regantur: satis luculenter docent S. literæ, testantur Philosophi: confirmat experientia. Ecclesiastæ cap.10. Væ tibi ô Terra, cùm Rex tuus puer est. Quid ita? quia puer, imperitus est rerum, indoctus, & insipiens ac stultus. Unde quod Hebraicè est puer נַעַר [?] Germanicè est Narr/stultus. Ideò nomine pueri, quivis imperitus & stultus intelligitur. Quid autem infelicius, quam a stultis & imperitis regi? Hominem imperito nihil vidi iniquius, dicebat ille apud Terentium. Sed tolerabile esset, si Rex puer esset: modò Consiliarij essent probi & sapientes. Sed cum etiam ij sunt insipientes, impij, & improbi: quid illa terra, urbe, & Regno miserius? Ideò bene subdit Salomon, dicendo: Et principes manè commeßantur: hoc est, illi qui deberent vigilantes esse in dandis bonis consiliis, in dicendo iure iis qui petunt, tempus ad hoc destinatum insuinsumunt in epulis, ebrietatibus, voluptatibus. Nam si mane inebrientur, per totum reliquum diem nil boni & recti poterunt praestare. Vae igitur Respub.qua sapientibus & piis viris, quorum consilio regi possint, destituantur. Iesa. 3. ut singulare flagellum, quo nihil detrimentosius regnus accidere possit: minatur Deus se daturum pueros qui regnent, sublatis inde doctis & sapientibus viris. Vidit hoc & Plato sapientissimus proinde scriptum reliquit, Tum demum urbem beatam fore, cum aut Philosophi regnabunt (id est, viri docti & sapientes) aut Reges philosophabuntur, hoc est, operam dabunt studiis bonarum literarum, & verae sapientia. Contra igitur, Tum demum orbis & urbes infelices sunt: cum aut imperiti & stulti regnant aut Reges stultescunt.
units.tr: Finally, pious princes and magistrates ought themselves to be the bishops of their schools; that is, they ought either in person, if that can be managed, or at least through others, to visit the schools from time to time and inspect how far, and in what manner, the students are making progress, both in letters and in the true doctrine of piety, and to see to it that each one performs his duty vigorously and diligently. This is the care that pious princes and magistrates ought to undertake concerning the founding, good organisation and maintenance of schools. For these, if they are well established, are not only useful to the commonwealth but also necessary to the Churches, since without them neither can the commonwealth fare well nor the Church endure for long. As for commonwealths, how much they flourish and how happy they are without learned men endowed with true wisdom, by whose wise counsels they are governed, the Holy Scriptures teach quite plainly, the philosophers bear witness, and experience confirms. Ecclesiastes, chapter 10: "Woe to you, O land, when your king is a child." Why so? Because a child is inexperienced in affairs, untaught, unwise and foolish. Hence the Hebrew word for child, נַעַר [?], in German is Narr, that is, fool. So by the name of child anyone who is inexperienced and foolish is understood. "And what is more unhappy than to be ruled by the foolish and inexperienced?" "I have never seen anything more unjust than a man without experience," says the character in Terence. Yet it would be tolerable if the king were a child, provided that his counsellors were upright and wise. But when they too are unwise, ungodly and wicked, what could be more wretched for that land, city and kingdom? So Solomon rightly adds, saying: "And the princes eat in the morning," that is, those who ought to be watchful in giving good counsel and in pronouncing judgment for those who seek it, spend the time set aside for this on banquets, drunkenness and pleasures. For if they are drunk in the morning, they can perform nothing good or right for the rest of the day. Woe, then, to a commonwealth that is deprived of wise and pious men by whose counsel it might be governed. Isaiah 3. God threatens, as a singular scourge than which nothing more harmful can befall a kingdom, that he will give boys to rule, the learned and wise men having been removed. The most wise Plato also saw this and accordingly left it in writing: that the city would then at last be happy when either philosophers rule (that is, learned and wise men) or kings philosophise, that is, they will devote their efforts to the studies of good letters and true wisdom. On the contrary, then at last the world and cities are unhappy when either the unskilled and foolish rule or kings grow foolish.

units.la: Ac profectò rem ita se habere, & veteres historia tam sacra, quam profana: & nostra haec secula docent. Quando Respub. Israëlis bene habuit? (Cum Reges habuit pios, doctos, inque S. literis exercitatos: ut sub Davide, sub Salomone, sub Iosaphato, Ezechia, Iosia, & aliis similibus. Verissimum igitur est, quod dixi de principio: Res-pub.non posse bene habere, cum destituuntur vi-ris doctis, & vere sapientibus ac piis. At unde ij educuntur? E Scholis. Idcirco etiam Hebræi te-[?]stantur, tum demum Respub. Israëlis felicissime habuisse, cum in Israel frequentes essent Scholae, atq; ut illi loquuntur, cum omnes urbes, oppida, & pagi suas haberent מדרשות ובתי כנסיות [?] בתי hoc est, domos conuentuum, seu synagogas, & domos scrutiniorum, seu studiorum, in quibus S. litera diligenti studio explicarentur. Nam etiam inde boni Reges & Principes, postea quam in S. literis fuissent bene instituti, ad Reipub.gubernacula educebantur. Quantum igitur utilos sint Rebuspub.[?] Schola, satis perspicuum est. Neq; enim nostri instituti est in praesentia, de hac re multa verba facere.
units.tr: And indeed that this is so, both sacred and profane history of old, and these our own times, teach. When has the commonwealth of Israel fared well? When it had kings who were pious, learned and practised in the Holy Scriptures, as under David, under Solomon, under Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah, Josiah and others like them. Therefore what I said at the beginning is most true: a commonwealth cannot fare well when it is deprived of men who are learned, truly wise and pious. But where are such men brought up? In the schools. Hence the Hebrews also testify that the commonwealth of Israel then fared most happily when schools were frequent in Israel, and when, as they put it, all the cities, towns and villages had their own מדרשות ובתי כנסיות [?] בתי, that is, houses of assembly or synagogues, and houses of inquiry or study, in which the Holy Scriptures were explained with diligent application. For from these, too, good kings and princes were afterwards brought up to the helm of the commonwealth, once they had been well instructed in the Holy Scriptures. How useful schools are to a commonwealth is therefore quite clear. For it is not my purpose at present to say much on this matter.

units.la: Caterum, Ecclesiis non solum utiles, sed plane necessariae sunt propter religionem, atque ita necessariae, vt sine iis Scholis, neque doctrina Euangelij pura conseruari, neque ipsa Ecclesia diu possint consistere. Quomodo enim bonam & firmam habere possis Ecclesiam, sine puro Dei verbo? Quomodo autem purum verbum conseruari queat, sine ministerio? Quomodo vero ministerium sine ministris, ad verbum pure administrandum idoneis? At vero quomodo tales habere possumus Pastores sine Scholis? Ergo sine Scholis, e quibus evocari & educi subinde possint viri docti, sapientes & pij, alij ad Resp. alij ad Ecclesias gubernandas, diu conseruari Ecclesia non potest: id quod exemplo non proculpetito[?], confirmari facile potest. Quando enim Ecclesia Romana, ad tantam defecit barbariem doctrina, morum, religionis? Nimirum, postea quam Schola Theologica aut penitus neglecta fuerunt: aut saltem barbaris sophistarum literis corrupta. Sic Julianus ille Apostata, tum maxime nocuit Ecclesiis, cum Scholas bonarum literarum clausit Christianis: putans hac ratione se posse illas funditus tollere. Contra videmus, tum demum in-GermaGermania primùm, deinde in aliis regionibus re-stitutas fuisse Ecclesias, quando cum bonis artibus & disciplinis, studium etiam S literarum restitutum est: & Scholæ verè Theologicæ iterum-beneficio piorum Principum & Rerumpub. apertæ fuerunt. Sunt igitur hæ Scholæ in Repub. Chri-stiana multis nominibus non tantùm vtiles, sed etiam necessariæ, saltem vt in iis, & per has sincera pietatis doctrina retineri possit & conseruari.
units.tr: Furthermore, schools are not only useful but plainly necessary to the Churches on account of religion, and so necessary that without them neither the pure doctrine of the gospel can be preserved, nor the Church itself endure for long. For how could you have a good and firm Church without the pure Word of God? But how can the pure Word be preserved without the ministry? And how can there be a ministry without ministers fit to administer the Word purely? Indeed, how can we have such pastors without schools? Therefore without schools, from which learned, wise and pious men can from time to time be summoned and drawn forth, some to govern the commonwealth and others to govern the Churches, the Church cannot be preserved for long; and this can easily be confirmed by an example not far to seek. For when did the Roman Church fall into such barbarism of doctrine, morals and religion? Surely after the theological schools were either wholly neglected or at least corrupted by the barbarous letters of the sophists. So that apostate Julian did the Churches the greatest harm when he closed the schools of good letters to Christians, thinking that in this way he could utterly destroy them. On the contrary, we see that the Churches were first restored in Germany, and then in other regions, when the study of the Holy Scriptures was restored together with the good arts and disciplines, and truly theological schools were opened again through the good offices of pious princes and commonwealths. These schools, therefore, in the Christian commonwealth are useful in many respects, and indeed necessary, at least so that sound doctrine of piety may be retained and preserved in them and through them.

units.la: Hac de causa videmus non solùm apud populum Dei, verùm etiam apud profanas Gentes, magnam semper adhibitam fuisse curam & diligentiam in hisce Scholis aperiendis, constituen-dis, conseruandis: &, qui in eis docerent, sapien-tibus & doctis viris, vbique locorum perquiren-dis, & amplissimis stipendiis, conducendis: idque vt horum opera cum liberales, artes ac disciplina, tum maximè ipsa religionis doctrina pura con-seruaretur: de quibus Gentium Scholis minimè opus est multa dicere ad vos præsertim viros do-ctos, & antiquarum historiarum peritos. Quis enim nesciat: quanta diligentia Schola curarint, quantaque liberalitate studia & studiosos promouerint Ægyptij, Chaldæi, Babylonij, Persæ, Græci, & Romani? Quis ignoret in quanto pretio apud illos fuerint viri docti, literati, sapientes, atque inprimis doctrina de religione professores & defensores, vt Sacerdotes, Magi, Gymnosophistæ, Philosophi, Pontifices, Augures? Quis com-memoret celeberrima illorum gymnasia, Musæa, Lycæa, Stoas, Tempe, Academias? Sed iis omis-sis, de Scholis populi Dei, tam ante Christum, quam quàm post Christum, nobis dicendum est, ut hic pijprincipes[?], & Christiana Respub. videant, quid circa has Scholas sui sit officij.
units.tr: For this reason we see that not only among the people of God but also among the profane nations great care and diligence have always been applied to founding, establishing and maintaining these schools, and to seeking out learned and wise men wherever they might be found, and engaging them with very generous salaries to teach in them; and this so that through their labour not only the liberal arts and disciplines but above all the pure doctrine of religion might be preserved. There is little need to say much about the schools of the Gentiles, especially to you, learned men, skilled in ancient histories. For who does not know with how much diligence the Egyptians, Chaldeans, Babylonians, Persians, Greeks and Romans maintained their schools, and with how much generosity they advanced studies and students? Who does not know in how high esteem among them were learned, lettered and wise men, and above all the professors and defenders of the doctrine of religion, such as the priests, magi, gymnosophists, philosophers, pontiffs and augurs? Who would recount their most famous gymnasia, Museums, Lyceums, Porticoes, Tempe, Academies? But leaving these aside, we must speak of the schools of the people of God, both before Christ and after Christ, so that these pious princes and the Christian commonwealth may see what their duty is concerning these schools.

units.la: In veteri Testamento videmus passim per to-tum regnum Israëlis fuisse ex iussu Dei institutas & apertas Scholas: in quarum aliis Levitæ, in aliis Prophetæ docebant, Legem Dei explicabant, iuventutem instituebant, & discipulos sibi faciebant, qui postea aut in Templis, aut in Synagogis docerent, & doctrinam Dei ad posteros propagarent.
units.tr: In the Old Testament we see that schools were established and opened by God's command throughout the whole kingdom of Israel: in some of them the Levites, in others the prophets, taught, explained the law of God, instructed the youth, and made disciples for themselves, who afterwards taught in the temples or the synagogues and propagated the doctrine of God to posterity.

units.la: Qui enim erant illi filij Prophetarum, de quibus sæpe fit mentio in libris Regum: nisi studiosi in scholis Prophetarum educati? Atque hoc voluit Amos, cum dixit, Non sum Propheta, nec filius Prophetæ: hoc est, nunquam fui in scholis Prophetarum & literatorum hominum edoctus.
units.tr: For who were those sons of the prophets, so often mentioned in the books of Kings, if not students educated in the schools of the prophets? And this is what Amos meant when he said: "I am not a prophet, nor a son of a prophet": that is, I was never taught in the schools of the prophets and of learned men.

units.la: Qui etiam erant Nazarei: nisi homines ad studia, & ad bonorum morum institutionem segregati, quales olim apud nos Christianos fuerunt sancti Monachi? Hunc iuventutis florem concidisse suo tempore deflet Ieremias, ut verè deflendum est, cum pereunt Scholæ, & cum Scholis iuventus.
units.tr: There were also the Nazarites: were they not men set apart for study and for the training of good morals, like the holy monks who once existed among us Christians? Jeremiah lamented that this flower of youth had perished in his time, as truly it must be lamented when schools perish, and with the schools the youth.

units.la: Quid etiam causa fuit, cur Dominus volue-rit ut 48. urbes cum suburbanis suis darentur Levitis à reliquis tribubus? Hæc præcipua fuit causa, ut passim in toto Regno Israël essent Scholæ & Collegia in quibus Levitæ docerent, & iuvenes in Lege Domini, & bonis moribus instituerent.
units.tr: What was the reason the Lord wanted the 48 cities with their suburbs to be given to the Levites from the other tribes? The chief reason was this: that throughout the whole kingdom of Israel there should be schools and colleges everywhere, in which the Levites would teach and instruct young people in the Law of the Lord and in good morals.

units.la: His autem Scholis & Collegiis moderandis ac regendis præficiebantur semper viri insignes erudieruditione, pietate, prudentia, morum gravitate, tam ex Prophetis, quam ex Leuitis: ut Samuel schola Naiothensi, quae erat in monte sancto[?] in Ramah: ut Helias Gymnasio Hiericontino, & Ramoth Galaad, in cuius locum successit postmodum eius discipulus Helisaeus, atque ita alij aliis. Huc etiam spectat, quòd Dominus voluit, ut Leuitae amplissimos haberent proventus à sin-gulis tribubus, & decimas, & census: hac nimirum de causa, ut ceteris liberati curis, liberius studiis literarum, & Ministerio Ecclesiastico possent vacare. Ac quod Dominus de iis Scholis per Mosen constituerat: illud ipsum pij postmodum Reges seruandum curârunt. Quid? quòd inter ipsas etiam Gentes dispersi Iudaei, suas semper conati sunt retinere Scholas, quas synagogas vocant, in quibus sua calerent studia, & de S. literis inter se dissererent? teste Iacobo in Act.15. Et si collapsa illa fuerunt magna ex parte tempore captiuitatis: certè postliminio reuersi in patriam Principes Iuda, curârunt eas instaurandas, praesertim Hierosolymis, ubi primarium erat Iudaicae Gentis studium, ad quod ex omnibus Regni & Mundi partibus studiosi confluebant, teste Luca in Actis, cap.2.
units.tr: To govern and direct these schools and colleges there were always placed men of distinction, in learning, piety, prudence and gravity of character, drawn both from the prophets and from the Levites: thus Samuel over the school at Naioth, which was on the holy hill at Ramah; Elijah over the gymnasium at Jericho, and Ramoth Gilead, in whose place his disciple Elisha afterwards succeeded; and so on with others. To this also belongs the fact that the Lord willed the Levites to have very ample revenues from each of the tribes, both tithes and dues, for this reason surely: that, freed from other cares, they might devote themselves more freely to the study of letters and to the ecclesiastical ministry. And what the Lord had laid down through Moses concerning those schools, the pious kings afterwards took care to observe. What more? Even among the Gentiles the scattered Jews always strove to keep their own schools, which they call synagogues, in which they pursued their studies and discussed the Holy Scriptures among themselves, as James bears witness in Acts 15. And although those were for the most part fallen during the captivity, the princes of Judah, returning to their homeland by right of return, certainly took care to restore them, especially at Jerusalem, where the chief study of the Jewish nation was, to which students flocked from all parts of the kingdom and the world, as Luke witnesses in Acts, chapter 2.

units.la: De Domino vero Iesu Lucas refert, cùm ingressus fuisset Synagogam, datum ei fuisse librum S Bibliorum, tanquam Doctori, ut aliquid in eo explicaret: ipsum vero fecisse officium. Imò idem Lucas refert, Iesum cum adhuc esset annorum 12. disputasse cum Doctoribus illarum Scholarum, idque cum magna omnium admiratione. Et quidem ipse Dominus Iesus indicauit, se v-trumq; fecisse officium[?], & Ecclesiastici (concionatoris, & scholastici Doctoris, cum dixit, Ego semper docui palàm, & in Templo, & inSyn-agogis. Erant enim illæ Synagogæ, vt ante di-xi, schola & collegia, vbi Lex Domini inter do-ctiores explicabatur, & de Scripturis differeba-tur.
units.tr: Of the Lord Jesus himself Luke relates that when he had entered the synagogue, the book of the Holy Scriptures was given to him, as to a teacher, that he might expound something from it, and that he himself performed the office. Indeed, the same Luke relates that Jesus, while he was still twelve years old, disputed with the teachers of those schools, and this to the great wonder of all. And the Lord Jesus himself indicated that he performed both offices, that of the minister and that of the scholastic teacher, when he said: "I have always taught openly, in the Temple and in the synagogues." For those synagogues, as I said before, were schools and colleges, where the Law of the Lord was expounded among the more learned and the Scriptures were discussed.

units.la: In Actis quoque scriptum reliquit idem Lu-cas, fuisse Hierosolymis habitantes Iudæos, viros religiosos ex omni natione, eorum quæ sub cælo est. Indicat collegia ibi fuisse studiosorum homi-num, qui eò ex omnibus Mundi partibus con-fluerent.
units.tr: In the Acts the same Luke has also left it written that there were dwelling at Jerusalem Jews, religious men from every nation under heaven. He indicates that there were colleges there of studious men, who flocked there from all parts of the world.

units.la: Ibidem cap. 6. mentionem facit collegij Li-bertinorum, Cyrenensium, Alexandrinorum, & Cilicum, & Asianorum, qui disputabant cum Stephano. Contulerant enim eò se omnes isti studiorum gratia.
units.tr: In the same chapter 6 he mentions the college of the Libertines, Cyrenians, Alexandrians, Cilicians and Asians, who disputed with Stephen. For all these had gathered there for the sake of study.

units.la: De Paulo quoque refert idem Lucas, quomo-do è Tarso Ciliciæ, Hierosolymam concesserit, & ibi per Gamalielem in Lege Domini institu-tus fuerit. Quis autem fuit iste Gamaliel? Do-ctor Legis in Academia Hierosolymitana, di-scipulus Simeonis illius, qui Christum in vlnas accepit. Habuit enim illa Schola Hierosolymi-tana multos præclarissimos Doctores, inter quos etiam fuit Hillel, qui anno ante Templi euersia-nem 100 floruit ea in Schola. Certe Paulum post suam conuersionem legimus sæpiùs ingressum fuisse Synagogas Iudæorum, cum illis disputasse, & eiecisse, Iesum esse Christum.
units.tr: Luke also relates of Paul how he came to Jerusalem from Tarsus in Cilicia, and was instructed there in the Law of the Lord under Gamaliel. But who was this Gamaliel? A teacher of the Law in the Academy of Jerusalem, a disciple of that Simeon who received Christ into his arms. For that school at Jerusalem had many most distinguished teachers, among whom was also Hillel, who flourished in that school about 100 years before the overthrow of the Temple. Certainly we read that Paul, after his conversion, very often entered the synagogues of the Jews, disputed with them, and proved that Jesus is the Christ.

units.la: Ex iis & aliis prope infinitis similibus tam Noui, quam Veteris Testamenti locis, facile cuique liquere existimo: primò, fuisse semper ex Dei in-stituto Scholas in populo Dei, usque ad ipsam Hierosolymæ euersionem. Deinde, etiam causam, cur Dominus has instituerit, & tanta diligentia voluerit regi, conseruari, custodiri, grauissimisque & celeberrimis Doctoribus ornari: nempe, vt in eis horum opera, pura doctrina atque religio conseruaretur: quod iis collapsis aut corruptis, non posset diu Ecclesia Dei conseruari. Atq; hæc de Iudaicis Scholis.
units.tr: From these and from almost endless similar passages of both the New and the Old Testament, I think it will be easy for anyone to see: first, that there have always been schools among the people of God by God's appointment, right up to the very overthrow of Jerusalem. Next, also the reason why the Lord instituted them, and willed them to be governed, preserved and guarded with such great diligence, and adorned with most serious and most celebrated teachers: namely, that through their work pure doctrine and religion might be preserved, since, if these had fallen or been corrupted, the Church of God could not long be preserved. And so much for the Jewish schools.

units.la: Venio nunc ad alias, præter Hierosolymita-nam Scholas, quæ post Christum, vbique terrarum, per Apostolos, virosq; Apostolicos instituta fuerunt, vt in eis pura Euangelij doctrina custodiretur, & inde ad posteritatem propagaretur. Habuit enim iam inde ab initio Christiana etiam Ecclesia suas Scholas, in quibus pueri prima religionis elementa discebant: & deinde libros etiam sacros explicari audiebant. Et qui hac docebant, Catechistæ & Doctores vocabantur.
units.tr: I now come to other schools, besides the school at Jerusalem, which after Christ were established everywhere in the world, through the Apostles and apostolic men, so that in them the pure doctrine of the Gospel might be guarded and from there propagated to posterity. For from the beginning the Christian Church too had its schools, in which boys learned the first elements of religion, and then were also made to hear the sacred books expounded. And those who taught these things were called catechists and teachers.

units.la: Ac primùm quidem Antiochia, tempore etiam Apostolorum celebrem fuisse Scholam, & sanctorum doctorumque virorum collegium, docet Lucas in Actis cap.13. In ea, præter alios, Doctor fuit Barnabas, quem postea Spiritus sanctus in-sit[?] inde ad ministerium Apostolatus, Pauli comitem assumi: & Constantini etiam Magni tem-pore illa extabat Schola. Quo etiam ex loco di-scimus, vnde sumendi sint Ministri: nempe ex Scholis, & ex collegiis sanctorum virorum. Ac quoties Apostolus Paulus mentionem facit Catechistarum, & verbi Catechizandi (facit autem sæpe) Scholas indicat Christianas, in quibus innuenes catechizabantur.
units.tr: First, that Antioch, even in the time of the Apostles, was a famous school and a college of holy and learned men, Luke teaches in Acts, chapter 13. In it, among others, Barnabas was a teacher, whom the Holy Spirit afterwards took from there to be a companion of Paul in the apostolic ministry; and that school still stood in the time of Constantine the Great. From this place too we learn where ministers ought to be taken from: namely, from schools and from colleges of holy men. And as often as the Apostle Paul makes mention of catechists and of the word of catechizing (and he often does), he indicates Christian schools, in which young men were catechized.

units.la: In Asia florentissimam instituit Johannes Apostolus Scholam, in ipsa Metropoli, Ephesoè qua multi & magni Episcopi ac Martyres prodierunt, inter quos & Polycarpus fuit, & qui de hac re scribit Polycarpi discipulus Irenæus.
units.tr: The Apostle John established a most flourishing school in Asia, in the metropolis itself, Ephesus, from which many great bishops and martyrs came forth, among whom was Polycarp; and Irenaeus, a disciple of Polycarp, writes about this matter.

units.la: In Palæstina, Cæsareæ fuisse Scholam, docet Gregorius Neocæsariensis, qui ibi operam dedit literis sacris, & inde doctissimus ad Episcopatum assumtus fuit.
units.tr: That there was a school at Caesarea in Palestine, Gregory of Neocaesarea teaches, who there devoted himself to sacred letters, and from there, most learned, was raised to the episcopate.

units.la: De Alexandrina verò omnium in toto orbe celeberrima Schola quid dicam? Scribit Hieronymus, iam inde à temporibus D. Marci, qui Evangelium scripsit, multos & magnos in ea floruisse Doctores: inter hos connumerantur Patanus, Clemens Alexandrinus, Origenes, Hiracles, Dionysius, & alij insignes viri.
units.tr: But what shall I say of the Alexandrian school, the most celebrated of all in the whole world? Jerome writes that from the times of St. Mark, who wrote the Gospel, many great teachers flourished in it: among these are numbered Pantaenus, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Heraclas, Dionysius, and other distinguished men.

units.la: De Schola Bizantina scripsit Gregorius Nazianzenus: & in ea institutum atque eruditum fuisse fratrem suum Basilium narrat.
units.tr: Gregory Nazianzen wrote about the Byzantine school, and he relates that his brother Basil was trained and educated in it.

units.la: Sed quid ego Scholas omnes commemorem? Circumspiciamus & intueamur vetustissima Canonicorum collegia, & Monachorum Monasteria seu Cœnobia: quid de principio hac fuerunt aliud, nisi piorum & studiosorum hominum collegia, & Christiana Academia? Testantur hoc antiquissima, & instructissima, quæ in illis adhuc extant, Bibliothecæ: testantur amplissima facultates, quibus ab Imperatoribus & aliis paten-[?] tibus liberaliter donabantur, pro honesta Doctô-rum[?] & studiosorum sustentatione. Testatur proprie etiam Posidonius in vita Augustini cap 5. [?]& 11. cùm ait, D. Augustinum in Monasterio cum Doctis habitasse, & secundùm Apostolorum regulam vixisse, & è suo collegio, Epi-scopos aliquot, doctissimos viros, Ecclesiis dedisse.
units.tr: But why do I mention all the schools? Let us look around and consider the most ancient colleges of canons and the monasteries or cenobia of monks: what were these at their beginning but colleges of pious and studious men, and Christian academies? The most ancient and most well-equipped libraries, which still survive in them, bear witness to this; the very ample endowments, which were generously given to them by emperors and others, for the honourable support of teachers and students, bear witness. Posidonius too bears witness in the Life of Augustine, chapters 5 and 11, where he says that St. Augustine lived in a monastery with learned men, lived according to the rule of the Apostles, and from his college gave several bishops, very learned men, to the Churches.

units.la: Ex iis autem omnibus, quæ diximus partim de Scholis Christianis & Theologicis, in toto orbe Christiano jam inde ab initio per omnia secula institutis, partim de causis, propter quas tanta diligentia & studio tam a Mose primum & Prophetis, piisque regibus Juda: quam postea ab Apostolis, Christianisque Principibus instituta & conseruata fuerunt: facile quivis videre potest, quam sit necessarium, si velimus & purum Dei verbum, & puras Ecclesias apud nos conseruari, ut cum primis Scholas habeamus optimè constitutas: in quibus tum linguarum cognitio, & liberales artes doceantur, tum maximè puritas Christiana doctrina conseruetur.
units.tr: From all these things which we have said, partly about Christian and theological schools instituted throughout the whole Christian world from the very beginning and through all ages, and partly about the reasons why such great diligence and zeal were devoted to them, first by Moses and the Prophets and the pious kings of Judah, and afterwards instituted and preserved by the Apostles and Christian princes: anyone can easily see how necessary it is, if we wish both the pure Word of God and pure Churches to be preserved among us, to have above all schools that are very well established, in which both the knowledge of languages and the liberal arts are taught, and above all the purity of Christian doctrine is preserved.

units.la: Hanc vero curam cumprimis ad Reges & Principes Christianos pertinere, tum ex iis quæ diximus, tum ex aliis, quæ nisi vitiosam prolixitatem metueremus, dici à nobis, & ex S. literis, historisque Ecclesiasticis demonstrari possent, itidem perspicuum esse potest.
units.tr: That this care especially belongs to Christian kings and princes can also be made plain, both from what we have said and from other things which, were we not to fear a faulty prolixity, could be said by us and demonstrated from Holy Scripture and from ecclesiastical histories.

units.la: Superest igitur, ut de altera Scholarum cura, quæ nimirum ad ipsos attinet Doctores, non nihil breuiter dicamus. De omnibus autem, qui in Scholis profitentur, non est nobis in præsenti sermo: sed de Theologis tantum Doctoribus verba facimus.
units.tr: There remains, then, to say something briefly about the other care of the schools, namely that which concerns the teachers themselves. Concerning all who lecture in the schools, I am not speaking at present; I am speaking only of the teachers of theology.

units.la: Horum in summa, quod ad docendi proprie attinet, duplex est officium. Primum, ut summa Christiana doctrina, ex S. literarum fontibus haustam, methodo συνοπτικὴν[?] collectam, & in certos locos digestam, adolescentioribus breviter & dilucide tradant & explicet, inq; ea quàm diligentissimè illos instituant: quod Graeci κατηχῆν[?] appellarunt. Hoc autem proprie est voce erudire, ἀπὸ τῆς ἠχῆς[?], quod est sonora voce rudimenta religionis tradere: Latini vocant informare. Hoc etiam fuit officium, quod priori loco faciebant Apostoli: cùm variis in locis Ecclesias constituebant. Neque enim mox rudibus populis sacros Prophetarum libros interpretabantur: sed illos primùm catechizabant, hoc est, in praecipuis Christiana doctrina capitibus erudiebant, idq; voce & coram.
units.tr: In sum, as far as teaching proper is concerned, their office is twofold. First, they are to deliver and explain the summary of Christian doctrine, drawn from the fountains of Holy Scripture, gathered by a synoptic method and arranged under fixed heads, briefly and clearly to young people, and to instruct them in it as carefully as possible. The Greeks called this catechizing [κατηχεῖν]. Properly, to catechize [ἀπὸ τῆς ἠχῆς] means to hand on the rudiments of religion by a sounding voice; the Latins call it to instruct. This was also the office which the Apostles performed first, when they established churches in various places. For they did not at once expound the sacred books of the Prophets to rude peoples, but first catechized them, that is, taught them the chief heads of Christian doctrine, and did so by word of mouth and face to face.

units.la: Deinde erectis iam & firmatis Ecclesiis, creatisq; earum Episcopis, curabant, ut sacri etiam libri explicarentur, quorum explicatione fideles in tradita prius doctrina magis ac magis confirmarentur.
units.tr: Then, once the churches were raised up and established, and their bishops appointed, they took care that the sacred books also should be explained, so that the faithful might be more and more confirmed in the doctrine previously delivered by that explanation.

units.la: Possem hoc multis demonstrare, nisi duo sufficerent loci: unus Luc. 1. verf. 4. Alter locus clarior est ad Hebraeos, cap. 6. ubi, quamnam methodum seruârint Apostoli in tradendo Evangelio: & quanam primum ea fundamenta iecerint, antequam ad Propheticorum librorum explicationem veniretur, satis luculenter apparet: cum ait Apostolus: Quapropter omisso, qui in Christo rudes inchoat, sermone, ad per-sectionem feramur, hoc est, ad uberiorem re-rum Christianarum, & S. literarum explica-tionem. Qui vero est, qui in Christo rudes incho-at sermo? Explicat, dicendo: Non rursus fundamenta iacientes poenitentiae ab operibus mortuis, & fidei in Deum, & quae sequuntur. Ibi enim, quae fuerit Catechismi forma, quae-rudes instituebant, perspicue indicatur. Et quidem non dubito, quin omnibus tradiderint, & expli-carint Legem Decalogi: doctrinam de poeniten-tia: Symbolum quod Apostolicum vocatur: & Dominicam precationem, antequam acciperent in manus libros Mosis & Prophetarum enu-cleandos.
units.tr: I could demonstrate this by many examples, but two passages suffice: one is Luke 1, verse 4. The other, clearer passage is in Hebrews, chapter 6, where it sufficiently plainly appears what method the Apostles followed in delivering the Gospel, and how they first laid those foundations before the explanation of the books of the Prophets was undertaken. The Apostle says: "Therefore, leaving the word of the beginning of Christ, let us go on to perfection," that is, to a fuller explanation of Christian matters and of Holy Scripture. "But what is the word of the beginning of Christ?" He explains it by saying: "Not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works, and of faith toward God," and so on. For there it is clearly indicated what the form of the catechism was, by which they instructed the rude. And indeed I do not doubt that they delivered to all and explained the Law of the Decalogue, the doctrine of repentance, the Creed which is called Apostolic, and the Lord's Prayer, before they took up the books of Moses and the Prophets to be unfolded.

units.la: Hanc methodum servavit Dominus, cùm summam suarum Legum, quas postea fusè per Mosen explicavit, duabus tabulis, decemg;[?] pra-ceptis complexus est. Hanc eandem Christus se-cutus est, cùm Legis summam duobus praeceptis, dilectione scilicet Dei & proximi: & summam Euangelij, praedicatione poenitentiae, & remissio-ne peccatorum comprehendit, & docuit. Hanc postea & Patres, tam Graeci, quam Latini, imi-tati sunt: quorum alij certos quosdam locos di-ligenter pertractarunt: alij summam etiam o-mnium locorum communium complexi sunt: ut Theod. ἐπιτομὴ[?] θείων δογμάτων: Augustinus Enchiridio ad Laurentium: Item de fide ad Petrum.
units.tr: The Lord kept this method when he comprehended the sum of his Laws, which he afterwards set out at length through Moses, in two tables and ten precepts. Christ followed the same method when he comprehended and taught the sum of the Law in two precepts, namely the love of God and of neighbour, and the sum of the Gospel in the preaching of repentance and the remission of sins. The Fathers afterwards imitated this, both Greek and Latin: some of them carefully treated certain particular heads, others embraced also the sum of all the commonplaces, as Theodoret in his Epitome of Divine Doctrines, and Augustine in the Enchiridion to Laurentius, and likewise his book On Faith to Peter.

units.la: Ergo de hac docendi methodo dubitandum non est, quin eadem nobis quoque sit imitanda.
units.tr: Therefore there is no room to doubt concerning this method of teaching, that the same method ought to be imitated by us also.

units.la: Cum vero necessaria sit hæc tradendorum ante omnia locorum communium, tanquam primorum principiorum ratio: hinc perspicuum est, quòd id in omnibus tradendis artibus solitum est fieri: siquidem nulla artes, nullaeve disciplinae, recte tradi, utiliterve percipi possunt, nisi prius iaciantur & explicentur fundamenta, quae prima vocantur cuiusque artis principia. Sic Grammaticae praecepta & principia primò docentur pueri, antequam ad Ciceronis aliorumve autorum lectionem admittantur. Sic in Dialecticis: sic Mathematicis: sic denique in Philosophicis & aliis scientiis omnibus fieri consuevit.
units.tr: Since, however, this arrangement of delivering the commonplaces, as the first principles before all else, is necessary, it is plain that this is customary in the teaching of all arts. For no arts or disciplines can be rightly taught or usefully grasped unless first the foundations, which are called the first principles of each art, are laid and explained. Thus boys are first taught the precepts and principles of grammar before they are admitted to reading Cicero or other authors. So it is done in dialectic, so in mathematics, and so, finally, it is customary to do in philosophy and all the other sciences.

units.la: Id certè eò magis in Theologia servandum est, quò perniciosius est in hac errare, quàm in aliis artibus omnibus. Proinde Apostolus Rom. 12. vult, ut qui Scripturas interpretantur, ad analogiam fidei interpretentur. Quanam hæc est? Summa doctrina Christiana ab Apostolis tradita, & ab Ecclesiis omnibus recepta: uti est Symbolum Apostolicum: ut nullam S. Scripturarum interpretationem aut admittamus, aut adferamus, quae cum hac summa doctrina aliquo pugnet modo. Quam regulam si sequerentur illi fratres, qui de Coena nobiscum digladiantur: illam quam urgent verborum Coenae interpretationem, neque ipsi adferrent, neque ab aliis allatam admitterent: cum ex diametro pugnet cum primis fidei nostrae articulis.
units.tr: This must certainly be observed all the more in theology, the more ruinous it is to err in this than in all the other arts. Accordingly the Apostle in Romans 12 wills that those who interpret the Scriptures should interpret them according to the analogy of faith. What is this? It is the sum of Christian doctrine handed down by the Apostles and received by all the churches, such as the Apostles' Creed; so that we should neither admit nor advance any interpretation of Holy Scripture which in any way conflicts with this sum of doctrine. If those brethren who wrangle with us about the Supper followed this rule, they would neither themselves offer, nor admit when offered by others, that interpretation of the words of the Supper which they press, since it directly conflicts with the first articles of our faith.

units.la: Est autem hic notandum, Doctoris qui locos tradit Theologicos, officium esse, non tradere simplicem doctrinam, sed eam etiam firmissimis, quibuscunque potest rationibus & testimoniis confirmare: ac primo loco testimoniis Scripturarum. Quare? Quia non satis est Christiano homini tenere fidem, & principia fidei: sed oportet etiam, ut teneat testimonia Scripturarum, quibus videat fidem suam niti: & ita, cum opus est, sciat fidei sua rationem reddere, sicut 1. Petri, capite 3. iubetur[?] quisque Christianus.
units.tr: It must be noted here that it is the office of the teacher who delivers theological commonplaces not merely to deliver the plain doctrine, but also to confirm it by the firmest reasons and testimonies that he can, and first of all by testimonies of Scripture. Why? Because it is not enough for a Christian to hold the faith and the principles of faith; he must also hold the testimonies of Scripture on which he sees his faith rests, and so, when need arises, he may know how to give an account of his faith, as every Christian is commanded in 1 Peter, chapter 3.

units.la: Ergo Catechistæ seu Doctores, qui in primis fidei capitibus iuuenes instituunt, debent & doctrinam perspicuè tradere, & eam apertis aliquot clarisq; Scriptura testimoniis confirmare, atque hunc in modum pueros instituere. Atque hac de primo Doctorum in Scholis officio, satis.
units.tr: Therefore catechists, or teachers, who instruct young people in the first heads of faith, ought both to deliver the doctrine clearly and to confirm it by some plain and clear testimonies of Scripture, and in this manner to instruct the children. So much on the first office of teachers in the schools.

units.la: Alterum vero est, ut Scripturas methodo ἀναλυτικῇ[?], iuxta analogiam fidei, diligenter & fideliter, pure & sincere, per ipsasmet Scripturas, ad aedificationem, interpretentur. Hoc esse praecipuum illorum officium usque adeo perspicuum est, & è S. literis demonstrari potest, ut in huius probatione immorari, sine iusta reprehensione non possim. Nam quid aliud fuerunt Prophetæ, quam Mosis interpretes? Qua de re loquitur Apostolus, cum ait, Rom. 12. Si quis habet Prophetiam (illam exerceat) iuxta ἀναλογίαν fidei: & cum toties in epist. ad Cor. de Prophetis & prophetandi ratione loquitur: & cum ait 1.Thess.5. Prophetiam nolite spernere: quædere, inquam, loquitur alia, quam de hoc altero, eoque praecipuo Doctorum Ecclesiæ officio, nempe interpretandi Scripturas? An non Christus hoc exercuit, cum venit in Synagogam, & datus ei fuit liber Bibliorum, vt aliquid ibi interpretaretur? An non hoc idem confirmant illi duo discipuli, qui ibant in Emaus, cum post auditum Christum Scripturas explicantem dixerunt: An non cor nostrum erat ardens in via, dum interpretaretur nobis Scripturas? Non est igitur necesse, vt probemus, hoc alterum esse officium Doctorum in Schola, sacros Bibliorum codices interpretari: sed hoc potius observandum est, si velimus purum Dei verbum in Ecclesia conseruari, cumprimis necessarium esse, vt Doctores tum in tradendis locis communibus, purum Dei verbum sequantur: tum in explicandis Scripturis, a puro Dei verbo nunquam deflectant. Quomodo hoc fiet? Si ad Scripturarum interpretationem, non adferant, nisi Scripturas & principia fidei: id quod nihil aliud est, quam, vt loquitur Apostolus, iuxta analogiam fidei Scripturas interpretari. Quomodo enim (vt vnum adferam exemplum) interpretari melius & purius possemus verba Christi de pane, in Coena, quae multi eo rapiunt, vt dicant, ipsum panem vere & proprie esse corpus & carnem Christi, quia sic videntur sonare verba: quam si ad huius loci interpretationem adferamus primum verba eiusdem Christi de Calice, vt ea recitat Lucas & Apostolus, Hic calix, Nouum est Testamentum, &c, & illam Pauli explicationem, Panis, quem frangimus, nonne communio corporis Christi est? Et Petri dictũ Act. 3. cum de Christo, in coelum suo corpore euecto [?] verba faciens, ait: Oportere illum coelo contineri, usq; ad tempus restitutionis omnium: & deinde principia fidei: corpus Christi esse unum, illudq; humanum & finitum: & illud ascendisse in coelos, & iterum venturum esse: & denique locutiones Scripturarum, cum de Sacramentis verba faciunt: ut de Circumcisione, Hoc est foedus meum: de Agno, hic est pascha: de Baptismo, aquam illam, ut vocat Apostolus ad Tit. 3. cap. lauacrum esse regenerationis: cum tantum sit Symbolum interni lauacri Spiritus S. quo regeneramur: & alia similia dicta, Nam haec adferenda sunt ad verborum de Coena interpretationem.
units.tr: The second office is that they interpret the Scriptures diligently and faithfully, purely and sincerely, by the analytic method, according to the analogy of faith, through the Scriptures themselves, for edification. That this is their chief office is so plain, and can be demonstrated from Holy Scripture, that I could not dwell on proving it without just reproach. For what else were the Prophets than interpreters of Moses? The Apostle speaks to this point when he says in Romans 12: "If anyone has prophecy, let him exercise it according to the analogy of faith." And since he so often speaks in the Epistles to the Corinthians about the Prophets and the manner of prophesying, and since he says in 1 Thessalonians 5: "Do not despise prophesying," what, I ask, does he speak of other than this second and especially principal office of the teachers of the Church, namely interpreting the Scriptures? "Did not Christ exercise this when he came into the synagogue, and the book of the Bible was given to him, that he might interpret something there? Do not those two disciples who went to Emmaus confirm the same, when after hearing Christ explaining the Scriptures they said: 'Did not our heart burn within us while he interpreted the Scriptures to us?'" It is not necessary, therefore, that we prove that this second office of teachers in the school is to interpret the sacred codices of the Bible. Rather this should be observed: if we wish the pure Word of God to be preserved in the Church, it is above all necessary that teachers, both in delivering the commonplaces, follow the pure Word of God, and in explaining the Scriptures never turn aside from the pure Word of God. How will this be done? If, for the interpretation of Scripture, they bring forward nothing but Scripture and the principles of faith; which is nothing other than, as the Apostle says, to interpret the Scriptures according to the analogy of faith. For how (to adduce one example) could we interpret the words of Christ about the bread in the Supper better and more purely, when many drag them to this sense, that the bread itself is truly and properly the body and flesh of Christ, because the words seem to sound so? Rather, if we bring forward for the interpretation of this passage first the words of the same Christ about the cup, as Luke and the Apostle recite them, "This cup is the New Testament," etc., and Paul's explanation, "The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?", and the saying of Peter in Acts 3, when speaking of Christ, carried up to heaven in his body, he says that he must be contained in heaven until the time of the restoration of all things; and then the principles of faith: that the body of Christ is one, and that it is human and finite, and that it ascended into heaven and will come again; and finally the forms of speech of Scripture when they treat of the sacraments: as of circumcision, "This is my covenant"; of the lamb, "this is the Passover"; of baptism, that water which the Apostle in Titus 3 calls "the washing of regeneration," since it is only the sign of the inward washing of the Holy Spirit by which we are regenerated; and other similar sayings. For these must be brought forward for the interpretation of the words about the Supper.

units.la: His autem omnibus duo certè ἀποδεικτικῶς e-mincuntur: unum, fieri non posse, & pugnare cum analogia fidei & Scripturis, ut ille panis sit vere & proprie corpus Christi: aut etiam, quod vere & proprie sit in pane, vel coniunctum cum pane. Quare Papalem interpretationem impiam esse, & cum fide Catholica pugnantem. Alterum [?], quod ex illis locis evincitur, est, panem ita esse corpus Christi, sicut circumcisio est foedus Dei: sicut agnus est pascha: sicut aqua est lauacrum regenerationis: nempe sacramentaliter. Possem alia etiam adferre exempla, sed hoc satis est in praesentia. Manifestum igitur est, ad retinendum purum Dei verbum in Schola, non solum locos communes probandos esse testimoniis Scripturarum apertis, sed etiam ipsas Scripturas explicandas & interpretandas esse per Scripturas, & ad fidei analogiam: Nulla autem re magis corrumpi & contaminari puritatem verbi Dei, quam aut dogmata probare, aut Scripturas interpretari, sine verbo Dei, testimoniis tantum & interpretationibus hominum, quicunque illi sint, sive Patres antiqui, sive nostri temporis Doctores, illorumq; autoritate, tanquam sacra anchora niti. Quare debet Doctor in Schola, & dogmata apertis Scripturarum testimoniis, & Scripturas ipsas Scripturis cum analogia fidei interpretari. Hanc Apostolicā interpretandi ratione si omnes sequantur Doctores: fieri certè non poterit, quin purum in Scholis Dei verbum simus semper habituri.
units.tr: Of all these points, two are clearly demonstrated by argument. The first: it cannot be, and it conflicts with the analogy of faith and with Scripture, that this bread is truly and properly the body of Christ, or that what is truly and properly in the bread, or joined with the bread, is so. Hence the Papal interpretation is impious and opposed to the Catholic faith. The second, which is proved from those passages, is that the bread is the body of Christ in the way that circumcision is the covenant of God, that the lamb is the Passover, and that water is the washing of regeneration: namely, sacramentally. I could bring forward other examples too, but this is enough for the present. It is therefore plain that, to keep the pure Word of God in the School, the common places must be proved not only by clear testimonies of Scripture, but also that Scriptures themselves must be explained and interpreted by Scriptures, and in accordance with the analogy of faith. Nothing corrupts and contaminates the purity of the Word of God more than to prove doctrines, or to interpret Scriptures, without the Word of God, relying only on the testimonies and interpretations of men, whoever they may be, whether the ancient Fathers or the teachers of our own time, leaning on their authority as on a sacred anchor. Therefore the teacher in the School ought to interpret doctrines by the clear testimonies of Scripture, and Scriptures themselves by Scriptures, in accordance with the analogy of faith. If all teachers follow this apostolic method of interpreting, it will certainly not be possible that we shall not always have the pure Word of God in the Schools.

units.la: Quod si postmodum libeat Doctori & dogmata iam Scripturis probata, & Scripturas iam Scripturarū interpretationibus explicatas, Patrum etiam & aliorum testimoniis confirmare, praesertim cum venitur ad concertationem cum aduersariis, idq; ut suis ipsorum armis confodi-antur: tantum abest, ut dicamus ei hoc non licere, ut potius si faciat, vehementer laudandum nobis esse videatur. Sic Patres in pugnis & digladiationibus, quas cum Gentibus & Philosophis habebant, soliti sunt dogmata Christiana Scripturis iam probata, Gentilium etiam, Philosophorum Poetarumq; testimoniis, cum poterant, confirmare: ut in eorum libris videre est, praesertim in Iustino Martyre, Clemente Alexandrino, Eusebio Caesariensi, Lactantio, Theodoreto, & Augustino in lib. de civitate[?] Dei, & aliis. Id quod non ita facile est videre in eorum sermonibus seu concionibus, quas ad populum habehabebant fidelem. Est enim longè diuersa ratio Pastorum in Templis, & Doctorum in Scho-lis. Illis negotium est cum fidelibus tantum, vt eos doceant, moneant, corrigant, consolentur: ad quod sufficit verbum Dei: imò alia addere ex profanis, est vt antea ostendi, Ecclesiae detrimen-tosum nisi cogantur, vt ante exposui. At istis negotium est etiam cum haereticis & infidelibus, vt eorum errores refutent: ad quod licet Scripturae sufficiant, tamen utile est, vt aduersarij suis etiam gladiis iugulentur. Ac licet nō semper lectionibus intersint aduersarij, aut nostris nulla cum eis intercedat concertatio: tamen illorum officium postulat, vt armis etiam aduersariorum vtantur propter fideles & Studiosos auditores, qui futuri sunt aut Doctores, aut Pastores, vt ij etiam sciant, quomodo cum aduersariis pugnandum sit: imò in promptu etiam habeant illorum aduersus eos ipsos arma. Haec est causa, cur Patres, non ita in homiliis ad Ecclesiam, quam in disputationibus, pugnis, & libris contra Gentes, Philosophorum & Poëtarum dictis vtantur. Quia eadem res non semper, nec vbique, nec omnibus prodest.
units.tr: But if afterwards a teacher should wish to confirm doctrines already proved from Scripture, and Scriptures already explained by the interpretations of Scripture, also with the testimonies of the Fathers and others, especially when they come to a contest with adversaries, so that they may be pierced with their own weapons, then far from saying that this is not permitted to him, we ought rather to think it greatly to be praised if he does so. Thus the Fathers, in their fights and disputes which they had with the Gentiles and philosophers, were accustomed, when they could, to confirm Christian doctrines already proved from Scripture also with the testimonies of Gentile philosophers, poets and orators, as can be seen in their books, especially in Justin Martyr, Clement of Alexandria, Eusebius of Caesarea, Lactantius, Theodoret, and Augustine in his book on the City of God, and others. This is not so easily seen in their sermons or homilies, which they delivered to the faithful people. For the method of the ministers in the churches is quite different from that of the teachers in the Schools. The ministers have to deal only with the faithful, to teach them, admonish them, correct them, and comfort them; for this the Word of God is sufficient. Indeed, to add things from profane authors, as I showed earlier, would be harmful to the Church unless they were compelled, as I explained before. But the teachers have to deal also with heretics and unbelievers, in order to refute their errors; for this, although the Scriptures suffice, it is nevertheless useful that the adversaries be slain even with their own swords. And although the adversaries are not always present at the lectures, or no contest arises between them and us, nevertheless the duty of the teachers requires that they use also the weapons of the adversaries, for the sake of the faithful and studious hearers, who are to become either teachers or ministers, so that they too may know how one must contend with adversaries, and indeed have ready at hand the adversaries' own weapons against them. This is the reason why the Fathers use the sayings of the Gentiles, philosophers and poets not so much in homilies to the Church as in disputations, combats and books against the Gentiles. For the same thing does not always, nor everywhere, nor for all, do good.

units.la: Proinde non tantum concedi, imò etiam laudari in scholasticis Doctoribus potest, quod in Ecclesiasticis concionatoribus omnino improbandum est. Nunc tenemus, quodnam sit officium Doctorum scholasticorum, & quanam illi vti debeant ratione, si velint puram Christianae doctrinae veritatem in Scholis, ac proinde in ipsis etiam Templis retineri & conseruari.
units.tr: Therefore what may be not only conceded, but even commended, in scholastic teachers, is something that must be wholly condemned in ecclesiastical preachers. Now we have grasped what the duty of scholastic teachers is, and by what method they ought to proceed if they wish the pure truth of Christian doctrine to be kept and preserved in the Schools, and consequently also in the very Churches.

units.la: Reliquum est ad extremū, vt de tertia Scho-larum larum[?] cura, quae ad ipsos Scholares seu studiosos pertinet, disseramus. In hac explicanda, non est opus longa aut accurata oratione, sed uno eoque plano expeditur.
units.tr: It remains at last that we discuss the third care of the Schools, which pertains to the students themselves or the studious. In explaining this, no long or elaborate speech is needed; it can be settled in one plain statement.

units.la: Cum enim inter Doctores & discipulos seu Studiosos mutua sit relatio: explicatis Doctorum officiis, mox & quae sint discipulorum partes facile dignoscitur. Ex iis igitur, quae de duplici Doctorum officio dicta sunt, duplex etiam Studiosorum esse officium, perspicua & plana consecutione colligitur.
units.tr: Since there is a mutual relation between teachers and disciples, or students, once the duties of teachers have been set out, the duties of the disciples are readily recognised at once. Therefore from those things which have been said about the twofold duty of teachers, a twofold duty of students is also gathered by a clear and plain sequence.

units.la: Primum, & cui etiam in primis danda est opera, est, ut attente audiant, diligenter excipiant, & memoriae mandent locorum Theologicorum, quos Communes vocant, doctrinam a piis Doctoribus traditam, & apertis S. literarum testimoniis probatam & confirmatam. Namquā-tum sit, hæc doctrina, hæc methodo tradita, iis qui volunt solidè & purè Scripturas intelligere: paulo ante a nobis ostensum est.
units.tr: The first, and that to which effort must be given above all, is this: that they listen attentively, receive diligently, and commit to memory the doctrine of the theological places, which they call common places, handed down by pious teachers and proved and confirmed by clear testimonies of the Holy Scriptures. How much this doctrine, delivered by this method, helps those who wish to understand the Scriptures solidly and purely, has been shown by us a little earlier.

units.la: Merito autem dixi, hos locos memoriae esse mandandos, quoniam semper debet esse in promptu, tum propter intelligentiam Scripturarum, ad quam sunt ceu [illegible, ~10 letters]: tum propter concertationes cum adversariis doctrinae Christianae, contra quos ii loci sunt ceu quotidia-na arma, quibus nos oportet semper esse munitos.
units.tr: I have rightly said that these places must be committed to memory, since they must always be at hand, both for the understanding of the Scriptures, to which they are as [illegible], and for the contests with adversaries of Christian doctrine, against whom those places are as daily weapons, with which we must always be armed.

units.la: Qua in re peccant permulti Studiosi, qui atten-te quidem hos audiunt, & diligenter exceptos conscribunt: sed postea contenti, se illos habere in cista descriptos, nunquam memoriae mandant. Si similes mihi videntur illis, qui cum nihil tenent Grammatica vel Græca, vel Latina, quæ nihil aliud est, quam loci communes lingua Latina aut Græca, contenti se multos habere Grammaticos in Musæo, accedunt ad lectionem vel Ciceronis, vel Demosthenis. Deinde similes sunt illis militibus, qui freti armis, quæ domi habent, ad bellum accedunt inermes. Ij, si contingat, ut pugnandum sit, coguntur aut succumbere & perire, aut se in fugam vertere: aut hosti dicere: Expecta, dum redeam domum, & sumam gladium, & ita se turpiter dare omnibus ridendos. Neque etiam dissimiles sunt Israelitis, qui minimè curabant, ut legem Domini scriptam haberent in cordibus, propterea quod sibi satis esse viderentur eam habere in tabulis librisq.
units.tr: In this matter many students go wrong: they listen to these attentively, and indeed take them down diligently when received, but afterwards, content that they have them written down in their box, they never commit them to memory. They seem to me like those who, knowing nothing of grammar, whether Greek or Latin, which is nothing other than the common places of the Latin or Greek language, are content that they have many grammarians in their museum, and then come to the reading of either Cicero or Demosthenes. Again, they are like those soldiers who, relying on the arms they have at home, go into battle unarmed. If it happens that they must fight, they are compelled either to give way and perish, or to turn to flight, or to say to the enemy, "Wait until I return home and take up my sword," and so, shamefully surrendering, become a laughing-stock to all. Nor are they unlike the Israelites, who took very little care to have the law of the Lord written in their hearts, because they thought it enough to have it on tablets and in books.

units.la: Debent igitur Studiosi locos communes, etsi non singula verba, quod non probo & est ἀδύνατον[?]: saltem res ipsas & testimonia Scripturarum, quibus confirmati sunt, edificere[?], & in thesaurum perpetuæ memoriæ recondere. Et certè non est perdendus thesaurus memoriæ: perditur autem cùm non exercetur.
units.tr: Students ought therefore to commit to memory the common places, if not every single word (which I do not approve, and is ἀδύνατον [impossible]), then at least the things themselves and the testimonies of Scripture by which they are confirmed, and to store them in the treasury of lasting memory. And certainly the treasury of memory must not be wasted; but it is wasted when it is not exercised.

units.la: Quod ad Scripturarum lectionem & studium attinet: hoc alterum est illorum officium, ut non solùm in Auditorio Doctores suos Scripturarum explicantes attentè audiant, & summam notent: verùm etiam domi illas interpretationes cum doctrina locorum Communium, & cum aliis Scripturis conferant, & an conveniat, necne, videant: imitati hac in re illos Berhoënses, qui (ut Lucas refert Act.17.) cùm audissent Paulum concionantem, & Scripturas Prophetarum de Christo Christo interpretantem : domi consuluerunt Scripturas, an hac ita se haberent, quæ dicebantur a Paulo. Sicut enim publicos scripturarum interpretes audire ipsis ad hoc est vtile, vt habeant studiorum duces, nec fiant αὐτοδίδακτοι[?], quod hominum genus raro Ecclesiæ profuit: ita cum scripturis audita conferre est necesse, ne Pythagoreorum more tantum à suis Magistris pendeant, sed ipsos doctrinæ fontes cognoscant, & dogmatibus Præceptorum suorum fidem habere discant, non quia hominum, quos amant, vel admirantur, sunt placita, sed quia sanctarum scripturarum nituntur auctoritate, & ea vel manifeste ex Dei verbo desumta, vel bona inde consequentia deducta esse intelligunt.
units.tr: As regards the reading and study of the Scriptures, this is their second duty: not only to listen attentively in the lecture-room to their teachers explaining the Scriptures and note the main points, but also at home to compare those interpretations with the doctrine of the common places and with other Scriptures, and to see whether they agree or not. In this they imitate those Bereans who (as Luke relates in Acts 17) when they had heard Paul preaching and interpreting the Scriptures of the Prophets concerning Christ, consulted the Scriptures at home, to see whether those things which Paul said were so. For just as it is useful for students to hear public expositors of the Scriptures, so that they may have guides in their studies and do not become self-taught, a kind of people who have seldom profited the Church, so too it is necessary to compare what has been heard with the Scriptures, lest they depend on their masters only in the manner of the Pythagoreans, but come to know the very sources of doctrine, and learn to put faith in the dogmas of their teachers not because they are the opinions of men whom they love or admire, but because they rest on the authority of the holy Scriptures, and they understand them to be either manifestly taken from the Word of God or rightly deduced from it by good consequence.

units.la: Nec tamen ad familiarem scripturarum cognitionem, quæ in primis in Theologo requiritur, comparandam satis est talis collatio, sed quotidiana insuper atq; attenta lectione priuatim est opus. Consulo igitur, vt nulla dies Theologiæ studiosis abeat, quin & mane aliquam horæ partem priuatæ lectioni, iuxta librorum diuinorum seriem impendant, & vespere diurnarum operarum omnium rationes seuerissimè ipsi à se exigant: cuius diligentiæ incredibile est, quantos breui tempore sint præcepturi fructus.
units.tr: Yet such a comparison is not enough by itself to acquire the familiar knowledge of Scripture that is required above all in a theologian; there is also need of daily and attentive private reading. I advise, therefore, that no day pass for students of theology without their devoting some part of the morning to private reading, following the sequence of the divine books, and that in the evening they demand a strict account from themselves of all the work of the day. It is incredible how much fruit they will soon reap from such diligence.

units.la: Sed nunc finem dicendi faciam, vbi de duobus adhuc studiosos adolescentes monuero.
units.tr: But now I will bring my speech to an end, after I have given two further warnings to the young students.

units.la: Vnum est, ne manibus, quod aiunt, illotis studium hoc, vt diuinissimum, ita maximè arduum attrectent, sed cum reuerentia & necessariis instructis adminiculis ad illud accedant, si modo Laude quid dignum proficere & consequi discedo animum induxerint. Adminicula voco artium dicendi, ac praecipuarum Philosophiae partium, maximè Ethices & Physices cognitionem me-diocrem. Absque his enim non modò plurimas scripturarum sententias non intelligent, sed & multas gravissimas disputationes de Providentia Dei, de Peccato, de Libero arbitrio, de Lege Dei, de virtutibus &c. non assequentur. Sine illis verò, ne quidem, qua[?] assecuti fuerint, commodè tradere aliis poterunt. Et notum est, Apostolum in Theologo requirere facultatem, qua & sermonem rectè secare, atque exhortari auditores per doctrinam sanam, & contradicentes, adversarios redarguere valeat.
units.tr: The first is that they should not take up this study, most divine and at the same time most difficult, with unwashed hands, as they say; rather, they should approach it with reverence and with the necessary aids at hand, if indeed they have resolved to make some progress worthy of praise and to attain it. By aids I mean the arts of speaking and a moderate knowledge of the principal parts of philosophy, above all ethics and physics. Without these they will not only fail to understand very many sentences of Scripture, but they will also not grasp many very weighty disputations concerning the providence of God, sin, free will, the law of God, the virtues, and so on. Without them, moreover, they will not be able to pass on to others, in a suitable manner, even what they have attained. And it is well known that the Apostle requires in a theologian the ability both to handle the word of truth rightly and to exhort hearers through sound doctrine, and to refute opponents who contradict.

units.la: Alterum est, ut in toto studiorum cursu ad rectum scopum oculos perpetuò intentos habeant. Sic enim & currunt alacrius, & currendo propius eum, magno suo & aliorum bono, contingent. Nam & Apostolus eo proposito Timotheum suum ad alacritatem exstimulat praeclarè inquiens: Attende lectioni, exhortationi, doctrinae: Ne negligito donum, quod in te est, quod datum est tibi ad prophetandum cum impositione manuum presbyterij. Haec exercere[?]:in his esto,: ut tuus profectus manifestus sit inter omnes. Attende tibi ipsi & doctrinae: persiste in iis. Id enim si feceris, & te ipsum seruabis, & eos qui te audient. O praeclaros laborum nostrorum fructus, quos certè nec splendida Iurisprudentia, nec sagax Medicina, nec subtilis Philosophia sibi proposites habere, aut praestare potest. Sola Theologia studiostudiosis suis praestat, primùm quidem, vt ipsi-met coelestis sapientia lumine[?] illustrati, veraque pietatis studio quasi innutriti, supra mundum sapiant, & meliores sanctioresq; quotidie evadant, atque ita veram illam εὐδαιμονίαν[?], quam neque Priamica calamitates, neque mors abrumpere possint, apud Deum consequantur.
units.tr: The second is that they should keep their eyes always fixed on the right goal throughout the whole course of their studies. For in this way they will run more eagerly, and by running they will reach that goal more closely, to their great good and the good of others. For the Apostle, with this purpose, spurs on his Timothy to eagerness when he says splendidly: "Attend to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine. Do not neglect the gift that is in you, which was given to you for prophesying with the laying on of the hands of the eldership. Practise these things; be in them, so that your progress may be manifest among all. Attend to yourself and to doctrine; persist in these things. For if you do this, you will save both yourself and those who hear you." O splendid fruits of our labours, which assuredly neither splendid jurisprudence, nor shrewd medicine, nor subtle philosophy can have as their aim or bestow! Theology alone bestows this on its students: first, that, illuminated by the light of heavenly wisdom and as if nourished by a true zeal for piety, they may think above the world and grow daily better and holier, and so attain before God that true happiness which neither the calamities of Priam nor death can break off.

units.la: Deinde verò, vt docendo alios, & viam ad coelestia ex verbo Dei fideliter monstrando, eiusdem illius atque aeterna felicitatis authores plurimi existant, quo labore neq; salutarius quicquam humano generi praestari, neque nobis gloriosius esse ad omnem aeternitatem potest.
units.tr: Then, that by teaching others and faithfully showing the way to heavenly things from the word of God, very many may become the authors of that same eternal happiness; no more salutary work can be done for the human race, and nothing can be more glorious for us throughout all eternity.

units.la: Video quidem fortasse, quid praeterea hîc ex me audire ancant[?] studiosi iuuenes, ânne de nulla vel Patrum, vel Historia Ecclesiastica, vel Commentariorum sacrorum lectione consulam. Sed cogitent, tempus, quo in Academia Doctores praestantes audire conceditur, haud longum da-ri: doctrinam vero longam esse. Illis ergo frugaliter vtantur, dum licet. Catera, quae ad πρᾶξιν[?] Theologiae magis pertinere videntur, minori ia-stura[?], imo maiori suo fructu aggredientur, vbi vivos Magistros amplius audire non dabitur, sed ipsi docendi munus ad iuuentutem vel ad populum sustinebunt. Si qui tamen iudicio sunt cõ-firmatiore, & aliquos etiam ex Antiquitate fru-ctus quasi primitias in Academia decerpere ge-stiunt: me authore illi praecipuos quosdam libellos sibi deligent, quorum lectio tum ad praesentes Controuersias intelligendas aliquid momenti habere, tum animos eorum ad monumenta vetustatis suo tempore auidius euoluenda inflammare possint. Ta-les esse iudico Tertulliani Apologeticum: Cypriani tractatum contra Demetrianum: Ambrosij (alij Prospero tribuunt) libellos de vocatione gentium: Augustini Enchiridion ad Laurentium, libellos de doctrina Christiana: & quaedam posteriora Tomi septimi opuscula: Fulgentij librum primum ad Monimum, : Damasceni libros de Orthodoxa fide: Socratis historiam Ecclesiasti-cam,&c.
units.tr: Perhaps I see what else the young students here want to hear from me: whether I advise them to read nothing of the Fathers, nor church history, nor the sacred commentaries. But let them consider that the time in which it is permitted to hear outstanding teachers in the university is not long, whereas learning is long. Let them therefore use those resources sparingly while it is allowed. The rest, which seem to pertain more to the practice of theology, they will undertake with less loss, indeed with greater profit, when living teachers can no longer be heard at length, but they themselves will undertake the office of teaching among the young and the people. If, however, any who have a more mature judgement and eagerly wish to pluck from the university some first-fruits, as it were, even from antiquity, let them choose for themselves, on my authority, certain outstanding small books, the reading of which may both have some weight for understanding the present controversies and may inflame their minds to unroll the monuments of antiquity more eagerly in their own time. I judge the following to be such: Tertullian's Apologeticum; Cyprian's treatise against Demetrianus; Ambrose's little books on the calling of the Gentiles (others ascribe them to Prosper); Augustine's Enchiridion to Laurentius, his books on Christian doctrine, and some of the later short works in the seventh volume; the first book of Fulgentius to Monimus; the books of Damascene on the orthodox faith; the Ecclesiastical History of Socrates, and so on.

units.la: Sed, quod dixi, finem nunc facio. Oro autem, Deum aeternum Patrem, Domini nostri Iesu Christi toto pectore, ut sanam verbi sui doctrinam, quam in Ecclesiis Palatinatus pro immensa sua bonitate accendit, puram putamque seruare clementer dignetur: benedicat insuper florentis-simae huic Academiae, cuius ciuem me factum esse, merito gaudeo, & nos omnes faciat organa mise-ricordiae salutaria: ad laudem gloriosi nominis sui, & ad aedificationem Ecclesiae suae, per eundem Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, cui honor & gloria in secula.
units.tr: But, as I said, I now make an end. I pray with my whole heart to the eternal Father of our Lord Jesus Christ that he may graciously deign to preserve pure and sound the sound doctrine of his word, which in his immense goodness he has kindled in the churches of the Palatinate; that he may further bless this most flourishing university, of whose citizenship I rightly rejoice to have become a part; and that he may make us all instruments of his mercy, salutary for the praise of his glorious name and for the building up of his Church, through the same Lord our Jesus Christ, to whom be honour and glory for ever.

units.la: DIXI.
units.tr: I HAVE SPOKEN.

units.la: PRÆFATIVNCVLA IN LOCOS COMMUNES: CUR PRIORI LOCO DE sacris Scripturis agendum sit: & qua methodu seruanda.
units.tr: Preliminary remarks on the common places: why the locus on the holy Scriptures must be treated first, and by what method it is to be observed.

units.la: TRACTATVRI sumus, fratres charissimi, locum de Scripturis sanctis. Tractaturo enim locos Theologicos, principiò & ante omnia tractandus est locus de Scripturis sanctis: quòd sine iis tractari explicarive nullus alius possit. Sunt enim Scripturæ sanctæ fundamentum totius Theologiæ, super quod totum corpus Christianæ doctrinæ fundatum & extructum est: imò è Scripturis totum est collectum atque compactum. Quid enim est Theologia, nisi doctrina de Deo, ex verbo Dei desumpta? Merito igitur & nos locum de Scripturis sanctis ante alios omnes tractandum suscepimus. Sunt, & quidem plerique omnes, qui inchoent suos locos, à loco de Deo: quòd cognitio Dei, prima ac præcipua pars sit totius Christianæ sapientiæ, quam Theologiam vocamus: Et sicut ipse est primus ante omnia, sic ante omnia ab eo esse incipiendum. Sed nec Deus ipse, verè & salutariter cognosci à nobis potest fine Scripturis, quæ sunt ipsius sermo, Ioh. 1. Deum nemo vidit vnquam: Filius qui est in sinu Patris, ille nobis enarrauit. Vera igitur docendi Theologiam, communesq; Theologiæ locos tradendi ratio postulat, vt à loco de Scripturis sanctis initium faciamus atq; ducamus.
units.tr: We are about to treat, dearly beloved brothers, the locus on the holy Scriptures. For whoever is about to treat the theological loci, the locus on the holy Scriptures must be treated first and before all others, since no other locus can be treated or explained without them. The holy Scriptures are indeed the foundation of all theology, upon which the whole body of Christian doctrine is founded and built; indeed, the whole of it has been gathered and put together from the Scriptures. For what is theology, except doctrine concerning God, taken from the Word of God? Rightly, therefore, have we also undertaken to treat the locus on the holy Scriptures before all the others.
