There are, and indeed most of them, who begin their loci with the locus on God, because the knowledge of God is the first and chief part of all Christian wisdom, which we call theology; and just as he himself is first before all things, so one must begin with him before all things. But neither can God himself be truly and savingly known by us without the Scriptures, which are his own speech, John 1: "No one has ever seen God; the Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has declared him." The true method of teaching theology and of delivering the common loci of theology therefore requires that we make our beginning and lead off from the locus on the holy Scriptures.

units.la: Methodus verò, quam sequi constituimus, tam in hoc, quàm in aliis colligendis atque tractandis locis, duas habet partes. Prior hæc fuerit.
units.tr: The method, however, which we have resolved to follow, both in this locus and in gathering and treating the others, has two parts. The first shall be this.

units.la: Accipiemus præcipuum aliquem Sacræ Scripturæ contextum, qui copiosiorem illius loci, quem tractandum suscepe rimus, continet doctrinam: illumq; contextum methodo <bl>ἀναλυτικῇ</bl> explicabimus.
units.tr: We shall take some principal context of Holy Scripture which contains a fuller doctrine of that locus which we have undertaken to treat, and we shall explain that context by the analytic method.

units.la: Deinde, quot & quænam quæstiones ad eum locum pertinentes, ex illo contextu colligi possint, indicabimus. Tum demum ad singulas Dialecticè tractandas, accedemus. Quòd si non omnes, quæ ad illum communem locum pertinent quæstiones, in eo Scripturæ continentur contextu: non eas tamen negligemus.
units.tr: Then we shall indicate how many and what questions pertaining to that locus can be gathered from that context. Only then shall we proceed to treat each one dialectically. But if not all the questions that pertain to that common locus are contained in that scriptural context, we shall nonetheless not neglect them.

units.la: Hanc autem priorem methodi partem mihi sequendam delegi, propter maiorem studiosorum vtilitatem.
units.tr: I have chosen to follow this first part of the method for the greater usefulness of students.

units.la: Primùm, Duæ sunt præcipuæ docendi rationes seu methodi: <bl>συνθετικὴ, ἢ ἀναλυτικὴ</bl>[?], hoc est, compositiua, & resolutiua. Compositiua vtimur proprie in locis communibus colligendis & tradendis: Resolutiua in Scri-pturis pturis explicandis. Ergò si primò contextum Scripturæ aliquem explicem, ostenso primum scopo autoris eo in loco: deinde indicatis argumentis, & omnibus quæ ad scopum faciunt: & postea quæstiones seu propositiones, quæ in eo contextu inclusæ habentur, indicem:ac tum demum locum ipsum pertractem: discunt studiosi vtramque simul methodum, tam interpretandi & obseruandi Scripturas, indeque doctrinas colligendi: quàm locos communes tractandi.
units.tr: First, there are two principal ways or methods of teaching: synthetic or analytic, that is, compositive and resolutive. We use the compositive in gathering and delivering common loci; the resolutive in explaining the Scriptures. Therefore, if first I explain some context of Scripture, showing first the author's aim in that place, then indicating the arguments and all that bears on the aim, and afterwards I point out the questions or propositions which are contained in that context, and only then treat the locus itself, students learn both methods together: both of interpreting and observing the Scriptures and gathering doctrines from them, and of treating common loci.

units.la: Deinde facit ad id, vt Theologicæ quæ-stiones explicatæ, memoria facilius retinea-tur. Nam cum ex contextu fuerint erutæ, si contextum habeas ante oculos: mox quæ & quot quæstiones ex singulis dictionibus collectæ fuerint: tibi revocabitur in mentem.
units.tr: Next, this helps the theological questions, once explained, to be retained more easily in memory. For when they have been drawn out of the context, if you keep the context before your eyes, then at once the questions which were gathered from the individual words, and how many, will come back to your mind.

units.la: Habet præterea plus maiestatis & dignitatis, si antequam, quæ tu arte ex verbo Dei congessisti, incipias in medium proferre: aliquid ex simplici Dei verbo prælegatur, super quod tuam omnem extruas orationem: vt semper Christus tam in Schola, quàm in Templo prior loquatur & doceat. Sed cùm ad rem ventum fuerit, quod dico, melius ipsa intelligetis atque sentietis.
units.tr: Moreover, it has more majesty and dignity if, before you begin to bring forward into the open what you have skilfully gathered from the Word of God, something is read aloud first from the simple Word of God, upon which you may build your whole discourse; so that Christ always speaks and teaches first, both in the school and in the temple. But when we come to the matter, you will understand and perceive better what I mean.

units.la: Altera pars methodi, quam in tradendis locis communibus seruaturus sum, hæc est.
units.tr: The second part of the method, which I intend to observe in delivering the common loci, is this.

units.la: Proponam quæstiones singulas seorsim perspicuè atq; distinctè.
units.tr: I shall propose the individual questions separately, clearly and distinctly.

units.la: Deinde, quid de illa sentiant aduersarij, siue Pontificij, siue alij hæretici, siue quocunque appellentur nomine adversarij, bona fide referam: sed eorum rationes ad extremum differam, cùm fuerint refutandæ: idque brevitatis causa, ne eadem cogamur repetere.
units.tr: Then I shall faithfully report what the adversaries think about that question, whether Papists or other heretics, or whatever name the adversaries bear; but I shall defer their arguments to the end, when they are to be refuted, and that for the sake of brevity, lest we be compelled to repeat the same things.

units.la: Tertio loco adferam sententiam Orthodoxam, eamq; certis & brevibus distinctam propositionibus.
units.tr: Third, I shall set forth the Orthodox opinion, and that distinguished into certain and brief propositions.

units.la: Quartò, Propositioni cuique subiiciam eius explicationem, si opus fuerit.
units.tr: Fourth, I shall add to each proposition its explanation, if there is need.

units.la: Deinde, confirmationem è Scripturis: adde etiam, si operæpretium fuerit, Patrum & Conciliorum: imò etiam, si fuerit necesse, Scholasticorum, vbi bene scripserunt. Multa enim scripserunt eorum nonnulli consentanea Scripturis: quæ tamen hodie à Pontificiis impugnantur.
units.tr: Then, confirmation from the Scriptures; add also, if it is worth the effort, that of the Fathers and the Councils; indeed also, if it is necessary, that of the Scholastics, where they have written well. For some of them have written many things agreeing with the Scriptures, which nevertheless are today attacked by the Papists.

units.la: Ad extremum referam adversariorum argumenta præcipua; & ea refutabo, ostensis paralogismis.
units.tr: Finally, I shall set out the chief arguments of the adversaries, and I shall refute them, by exposing their paralogisms.

units.la: Hæc erit nostra methodus, quam spero futuram neque ingratam neque inutilem. Studebo autem, quoad eius fieri poterit, brevitati simul & perspicuitati. Deus nobis suo semper Spiritu adsit, quò possimus omnia ad sui gloriam, & salutem Ecclesiæ, ex puro eius verbo tractare, per Iesum Christum, Dominum nostrum, Amen.
units.tr: This will be our method, which I hope will be neither unwelcome nor useless. I shall strive, so far as it can be done, for brevity and clarity at once. May God always be present with us by his Spirit, so that we may treat all things from his pure Word, to his glory and the salvation of the Church, through Jesus Christ, our Lord. Amen.

units.la: Sed iam tandem aliquando ad rem ipsam veniendum est.
units.tr: But now at last we must come to the matter itself.

units.la: CONtextus Scripturæ sanctæ, quem mihi sumo ἀναλυτικῶς explicandum, vt in-de p oftde postea locum de Scripturis sanctis communem colligam, & tractem: est in altera Pauli Epistola ad Timoth, in cap. 3. ad calcem, qui sic incipit.
units.tr: The context of Holy Scripture which I take up to be explained analytically, so that afterwards I may gather and treat the common locus on the holy Scriptures, is in the second Epistle of Paul to Timothy, at the end of chapter 3, which begins thus.

units.la: Tu autem permane in iis quæ didicisti, & quæ tibi concredita sunt, sciens à quo didiceris: Et quòd à puero sacras literas noueris, quæ te possunt peritum reddere quod ad salutem attinet, per fidem, quæ est in Christo Iesu.
units.tr: "But you continue in the things you have learned and have been entrusted to you, knowing from whom you have learned them; and that from childhood you have known the sacred letters, which are able to make you wise unto salvation, through faith which is in Christ Jesus."

units.la: Tota Scriptura diuinitus (est) inspirata, & vtilis ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad institutionem, quæ (est) in iustitia: Vt perfectus sit homo Dei, ad omne opus bonum perfectè instructus.
units.tr: "All Scripture is divinely inspired and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for instruction, which is in righteousness: that the man of God may be perfect, thoroughly furnished unto every good work."

units.la: Scopus Apostoli in hoc contextu, est vt Timotheum, eoq; omnem pium, confirmet contra omnes Sathanæ & Antichristi tentationes, in retinenda pura doctrina, quam tum è Scripturis sanctis, tum etiam ab ipso Paulo & aliis Apostolis didicerat: utut totus reliquus Mundus perseueret in erroribus, & quotidie proficiat in peius. Hic est scopus.
units.tr: The aim of the Apostle in this context is to strengthen Timothy, and with him every godly person, against all the temptations of Satan and Antichrist, in retaining the pure doctrine which he had learned both from the holy Scriptures and also from Paul himself and the other Apostles, however much the rest of the world persists in errors and daily goes from bad to worse. This is the aim.

units.la: Ideò tota hæc oratio est in genere deliberatiuo: quia vult persuadere Timotheo, vt permaneat in semel recepta & agnita veritate sanctarum Scripturarum: id quod facit aliquot argumentis, quæ mox aperiam & explicabo.
units.tr: Therefore this whole discourse is of the deliberative kind, since it wishes to persuade Timothy to persevere in the truth of the holy Scriptures once received and acknowledged; which it does by several arguments, which I shall soon set forth and explain.

units.la: Occasio, quæ Apostolum mouit ad hanc exhortationem, fuit ei oblata ex iis, quæ pauIô[?] ante dixerat de temporibus periculosis deque variis grauissimisque tentationibus, quæ futuræ erant fidelibus, & præsertim pastoribus, omni ex parte: cùm ab omnibus fere hominibus impiis, quia erunt omnes homines sui amantes: tum inprimis à seducto-ribus, falsisque doctoribus, qui resistent veritati, sicut & Iannes & Iambres restituerunt Mosi: atque ita resistent, vt licet non sint admodum profecturi (nempe apud pios Electos, quia eorum amentia fiet omnibus electis manifesta) tamen quo ad se, & quo ad reliquam hominum multitudinem, quotidiè magis ac magis sint profecturi in peius: errantes ipsi semper, & alios etiam in errorem inducentes. Quid in hoc tempore tantarum tentationum & persecutionum, quas quicunque voluerint piè in Christo viuere, patiantur necesse est: agendum tibi fuerit ô Timothee & cuique pio viro? Fortiter persistendum in semel recepta & cognita veritate Christianæ doctrinæ, & sanctarum Scripturarum. Hæc igitur est adhortatio, quam subdit, dicendo: Tu autem permane in iis quæ didicisti, &c.
units.tr: The occasion which moved the Apostle to this exhortation was offered to him by what he had said a little before about perilous times and about various and most grievous temptations which were to come upon the faithful, and especially upon the ministers, on every side: from almost all impious men, since "all men will be lovers of themselves"; and above all from seducers and false teachers, who will resist the truth, just as Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses; and they will so resist that, although they will not greatly advance (namely among the godly Elect, because their madness will be made manifest to all the elect), yet, as far as they themselves and the rest of the multitude of men are concerned, they will daily advance more and more to the worse, always erring themselves and also leading others into error. What must you do, O Timothy, and every godly man, in this time of such great temptations and persecutions, which all who wish to live godly in Christ must necessarily suffer? One must persist firmly in the truth of Christian doctrine and of the holy Scriptures once received and known. This, therefore, is the exhortation which he adds, saying: "But you continue in the things you have learned, etc."

units.la: Propositio hæc est: Etiamsi futura sint tempora molesta & periculosa, quibus plerique omnes erunt sui amantes, & scelerati homines: & quibus mali homines ac impostores proficient in peius, errantes & inducentes: tamen tu, ô Timothee, non debes iis moueri, ita vt à veritate cognita & recepta vel latum unguem defle-ctas: sed debes in ea fixus & fortis permane-re,& eam aliis prædicare,& ut in ea perseve-rent,adhortari.
units.tr: The proposition is this: Even if the times to come are troublesome and perilous, in which nearly all men will be lovers of themselves and wicked men, and in which evil men and impostors will advance to the worse, erring and leading others astray; nevertheless you, O Timothy, ought not to be moved by them, so as to turn aside from the truth known and received even by a hair's breadth; but you ought to remain fixed and strong in it, and to preach it to others, and to exhort them to persevere in it.

units.la: Quibus autem argumentis vtitur ad per-suadendum[?] Timotheo hanc firmam constantiam in retinenda veritate doctrinæ, quam partim e sacrarum literarum lectione & studio iam inde ab ineunte ætate, partim verò & maxime ex ore Apostolorū didicerat?
units.tr: By what arguments does he persuade Timothy to hold this firm constancy in retaining the truth of the doctrine, which he had learned partly from reading and studying the sacred letters from earliest youth, and partly, and above all, from the mouth of the Apostles?

units.la: Primum,à fide,quæ in depositis seruanda est. Quæ apud nos deponuntur,seu quæ fi-dei nostrę committuntur seruanda:ea etiam bona fide sunt seruanda & custodienda,alio-qui perfidi fuerimus.
units.tr: First, from faith, which must be kept in deposits. Those things that are deposited with us, or that are committed to our faith to be kept, must also be kept and guarded in good faith; otherwise we would be faithless.

units.la: Atqui doctrina veritatis, quam didicisti, tuæ fidei concredita est tanquam pretiosus thesaurus. Tibi igitur ea,bona fide seruanda & custodienda est.Permane igitur in iis quæ didicisti:quia tibi concredita sunt,ut scilicet ea custodias.
units.tr: But the doctrine of truth, which you have learned, has been entrusted to your faith like a precious treasure. Therefore it must be kept and guarded by you in good faith. Persevere, then, in those things you have learned, because they have been entrusted to you, so that you may guard them.

units.la: Atque hinc colligimus, cognitionem ve-ritatis Christianæ seu Euangelij : thesaurum esse pretiosum,apud illos depositum,qui il-lud didicerunt: quem non seruare & custo-dire,maxima sit perfidia & iniquitas.
units.tr: And from this we gather that the knowledge of Christian truth, or of the Gospel, is a precious treasure, deposited with those who have learned it; and not to keep and guard it would be the greatest faithlessness and wickedness.

units.la: Secundum, à perspecta sibi qualitate & autoritate illius, hoc est, Apostoli,à quo hæc didicerat, nempe quòd esset verus Christi Apostolus;quòd haberet Spiritū Dei : quòd nihil doceret,nisi quæ à Christo,& eius Spi-ritu accepisset. Argumentum tale est.
units.tr: Second, from the clearly perceived quality and authority of the one from whom he had learned it, that is, the Apostle: namely, that he was a true Apostle of Christ, that he had the Spirit of God, and that he taught nothing except what he had received from Christ and his Spirit. The argument is this.

units.la: Ab ea doctrina, quam certò scimus nos didicisse ab Apostolis, cùm per Spiritum sanctum locuti sunt, eoque Christi esse doctrinam, nullo modo recedendum est, sed in ea fortiter permanendum. Talis est doctrina, quam didicisti ò Timothee. Tu enim scis, à quo hanc d'diceris[?], nempe non ab impostore, non à Pseudoapostolo, non ab homine mercenario & cauponante verbum Dei: Sed à vero Christi, & fideli Apostolo: qui quot & quanta propter hanc doctrinam passus fit, & adhuc fortiter patiatur, tu ipse nosti. Ergo, &c.
units.tr: One must by no means depart from that doctrine which we know for certain we have learned from the Apostles, when they spoke by the Holy Spirit, and which is therefore the doctrine of Christ, but must remain firmly in it. Such is the doctrine you have learned, O Timothy. For you know from whom you learned it: not from an impostor, not from a false apostle, not from a mercenary man who peddles the Word of God, but from the true Apostle of Christ and faithful one, who suffered, and still bravely suffers, so much and such great things for this doctrine, as you yourself know. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Atque hic habemus quæstionem de autoritate Ecclesiæ, quæ populis omnibus prædicat Euangelium: An ea aliquid valeat: an verò etiam sufficiat ad faciendam fidem, has Scripturas esse verbum Dei, nec ne. Item, An autoritas Scripturarum pendeat ab autoritate Ecclesiæ. Videmus enim hic, quantum valeat, ponderisque habeat certa persuasio & scientia de illorum, qui doctrinam tradunt, autoritate & probitate: ad faciendam fidem, ipsam etiam eorum doctrinam, veram ac diuinam esse: ac proinde in ea esse perseveran-dum. Multum certè valet: sed tamen solanō sufficit. Nam fieri potest, ut etiam Apostolus, vir plenus Spiritu Dei, non semper loquatur ex Spiritu Dei. Exemplum in Petro Antiochiæ, Galat, 2. Idem multò magis sentiendum de Augustino & aliis sanctis Patri-bus. Quare hoc argumentum ab autoritate perpersonæ quæ docet, non vsque adeo firmum est, nisi accedat confirmatio Scripturarum. Ideo firmius subdit argumentum.
units.tr: And here we have the question about the authority of the Church, which preaches the Gospel to all peoples: whether it has any weight, or whether it is also sufficient to make faith that these Scriptures are the Word of God, or not. Likewise, whether the authority of the Scriptures depends on the authority of the Church. For we see here how much weight and importance a certain persuasion and knowledge of the authority and integrity of those who deliver the doctrine has, in making faith that the doctrine itself is true and divine, and therefore that one must persevere in it. It certainly counts for much, but nevertheless it is not sufficient alone. For it can happen that even an Apostle, a man full of the Spirit of God, does not always speak from the Spirit of God. An example is Peter at Antioch, Galatians 2. The same must be thought much more of Augustine and other holy Fathers. Wherefore this argument from the authority of the person who teaches is not so firm, unless the confirmation of the Scriptures is added. Therefore he adds a firmer argument.

units.la: Et quòd ab infantia didiceris S.literas.
units.tr: And that from infancy you have known the sacred letters.

units.la: Tertium argumentum ducitur à certa co-gnitione S.literarum, quæ consentaneæ erant cum doctrina Apostoli. Hoc demum confirmabat Timotheum, Apostoli doctrinam, veram esse, & ea re firmam esse retinendam. Argumentum igitur tale est.
units.tr: The third argument is drawn from the certain knowledge of the sacred letters, which were consonant with the doctrine of the Apostle. This finally confirmed Timothy that the doctrine of the Apostle is true, and that for this reason it must be firmly retained. The argument, therefore, is this.

units.la: In illa doctrina constanter permanendum est, quam agnoscimus certò & ex longo studio conformem esse S.literis. Atqui tu ô Timothee hoc facile nosti. Nam iam indè ab infantia versatus es in S.literis: & eas non tantùm perfunctorie legisti, sed didicisti & optimè nosti, οἶδας[?], Ergo, &c.
units.tr: One must persist constantly in that doctrine which we recognize with certainty, and from long study, to be in agreement with the sacred letters. But you, O Timothy, know this easily. For from infancy you have been versed in the sacred letters, and have not merely read them superficially, but have learned them and know them very well, "you know" [οἶδας]. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Arque hîc videmus, hoc demum verum & firmum esse argumentum, aliquam doctrinam esse veram & Christianam, ideoque in ea esse persistendum: cùm eam agnoscimus consentaneam esse S.literis Propheticis & Apostolicis: Et solam eorum qui do-cent, aut etiam totius Ecclesiæ autoritatem, non ita firmum esse argumentum. Atque ita hîc habemus quæstionem de autoritate Scripturæ: An præcellat autoritati Ecclesiæ, nec ne. Et omninò præcellere, docet Petrus 2.Pet.1. Posteaquam enim ostendisset à sua & aliorum Apostolorum autoritate, certissimum esse Euangelium quod prædicabant de Christo, deque eius gloria & officio, quia scilicet ipsi viderunt gloriam eius, & audiuerunt vocem Patris dicentis: Hic est Filius meus dilectus, &c. dicendo. Non enim indoctas fabulas secuti, notam vobis fecimus, &c. mox confirmat illud argumento certissimo & firmissimo, nempe a Scriptis Prophetarum, dicendo: Et habemus firmiorem Propheticum sermonem, &c. Cur firmiorem vocat Propheticum sermonem? an non quod ipsi Apostoli praedicabant de Christo, firmum certumque erat? Resp. Ita. Sed duabus de causis illud dicit. Primùm, respectu Iudaeorum, quibus erant firmiora Prophetarum scripta, quàm verba Apostolorum. Secundò, quia Apostoli, ut homines, poterant adhuc mutare sententiam, ut Petrus Gal. c. 2. Et de hominibus semper oritur suspicio aliqua: non ita de doctrina iam recepta ab omnibus. Hac de causa laudantur illi Berhoënses, quòd licet scirent, à quo discerent; nempe à Paulo, vero Christi Apostolo: tamen non contenti illa ratione, recurrebant ad firmiorem sermonem Propheticum, confirmatum iam, & de quo dubitare amplius, fas non erat.
units.tr: And here we see that this is the true and firm argument: that some doctrine is true and Christian, and therefore one must persist in it, when we recognize that it agrees with the Prophetic and Apostolic sacred letters; whereas the authority of those who teach, or even of the whole Church, alone is not so firm an argument. And so here we have the question about the authority of Scripture: whether it surpasses the authority of the Church or not. And that it surpasses it altogether, Peter teaches, 2 Peter 1. For after he had shown that the Gospel which he and the other Apostles preached about Christ, and about his glory and office, was most certain, because they themselves saw his glory and heard the voice of the Father saying, "This is my beloved Son, etc.", saying, "For we have not followed cunningly devised fables, we made known to you, etc.", he soon confirms it by a most certain and most firm argument, namely from the writings of the Prophets, saying: "And we have a more sure prophetic word, etc." Why does he call the prophetic word more sure? Was it not that what the Apostles themselves preached about Christ was firm and certain? Answer: Yes. But he says this for two reasons. First, with respect to the Jews, to whom the writings of the Prophets were more certain than the words of the Apostles. Second, because the Apostles, as men, could still change their opinion, as Peter did (Galatians 2); and some suspicion always arises about men, but not so about a doctrine already received by all. For this reason the Bereans are praised, because although they knew from whom they were learning, namely from Paul, the true Apostle of Christ, nevertheless, not content with that ground, they had recourse to the firmer prophetic word, already confirmed, about which it was not lawful to doubt any longer.

units.la: Atque hoc argumentum amplificari potest ab illa parricula[?]: Ab infantia, hunc in modum. Quò quis diutiùs eoque & certiùs nouit sacras literas ac veritatem: eò turpius illi est & perniciosius non in ea constanter perseuerare. Tu Timothee nosti sacras literas eoque veritatem ipsam iam inde ab infanfantia: Quàm turpe igitur & perniciosum tibi fuerit, si non permaneas in iis quæ didi-cisti?
units.tr: And this argument can be amplified from that phrase "from infancy" in the following way. The longer and more certainly someone has known the sacred letters and the truth, the more shameful and harmful it is for him not to persevere constantly in it. You, Timothy, have known the sacred letters, and therefore the truth itself, from infancy. How shameful and harmful, then, would it be for you if you did not persist in those things you have learned?

units.la: Hic etiam duæ sunt quæstiones circa locum de Scripturis: Vna, de lectione Bibliorum: quorum sit ea legere, an tantùm Pastorum & Doctorum, vt Pontificij aiunt: an verò omnium, etiam puerorum. Nam Timotheus iam indè ab infantia legit sacras literas: & hoc in eo laudat Apostolus. Altera: quorum sit docere religionem & S. Biblia: An Pastorum tantùm & Doctorum: an verò etiam omnium patrum & matrum familiàs. Nam mater Lois docuit Timotheum filium.
units.tr: Here there are also two questions concerning the place of the Scriptures. The first concerns the reading of the Bibles: whether it belongs to them to read them only to the ministers and teachers, as the Papists say, or to all, even children. For Timothy has read the sacred letters from infancy, and the Apostle praises him for this. The second: to whom it belongs to teach religion and the holy Bibles: whether only to ministers and teachers, or also to all fathers and mothers of families. For the mother Lois taught her son Timothy.

units.la: Quartum argumentum, à perfectione S. literarum. Sacræ literæ perfectam de æterna salute tradunt doctrinam: ita vt si illis solis adhibeamus fidem, abundè habeamus, quo possimus saluari. Hanc perfectionem ibi habet, cùm ait: Quæ te possunt peritum sen[?] sapien-tem reddere εἰς σωτηρίαν, per fidem quæ est in Christo Iesu. Est autem permanendum in ea doctrina, quæ perfecta est, & salutem adfert æternam. Permane igitur in iis, quæ didicisti è sacris literis.
units.tr: The fourth argument is from the perfection of the sacred letters. The sacred letters deliver a perfect doctrine concerning eternal salvation, so that if we place our faith in them alone, we have enough to be saved. The Apostle states this perfection there, when he says: "which are able to make you wise unto salvation [εἰς σωτηρίαν], through faith which is in Christ Jesus." Now one must persevere in that doctrine which is perfect and brings eternal salvation. Persevere, then, in those things you have learned from the sacred letters.

units.la: Hic etiam duas alias habemus quæstiones circa S. literas. Prima: De perfectione S. literarum: An tradant talem doctrinam, quæ sufficiat ad salutem, nec ne. Paulus aperte affirmat. Secunda: De scopo S. literarum, quis ille sit: Est fides in Christum: per hanc enim seruamur.
units.tr: Here we also have two other questions concerning the sacred letters. The first: concerning the perfection of the sacred letters, whether they deliver such a doctrine as suffices for salvation or not. Paul affirms it plainly. The second: concerning the aim of the sacred letters, what it is: it is faith in Christ, for through this we are saved.

units.la: Quintum argumentum à dignitate & au-toritate sacratum literatum. Perseueran-dum est in doctrina & verbo Dei: quid enim hoc perfectius & dignius? Atqui Scriptura sancta, verbum est Dei. Etsi enim scripta fuit per homines: autor tamen illius est Deus. Fuit enim diuinitus inspirata, nempe illis sanctis hominibus, Mosi, Prophetis, per quos scripta fuit. Est igitur in hac permanendum. Quæ vero ex me clarius didicisti: nosti eadem esse cum iis, quæ tradunt S. literæ. Permane igitur in iis quæ didicisti.
units.tr: The fifth argument is from the dignity and authority of the sacred letters. One must persevere in the doctrine and Word of God: for what is more perfect and worthy than this? But holy Scripture is the Word of God. For although it was written through men, its author is nevertheless God. For it was divinely inspired, namely in those holy men, Moses and the Prophets, through whom it was written. One must therefore persevere in it. And what you have learned more clearly from me, you know to be the same as what the sacred letters deliver. Persevere, then, in those things you have learned.

units.la: His in verbis: Omnis Scriptura diuinitus inspirata est, habemus de sacris literis quæ-stiones sex.
units.tr: With these words, "All Scripture is divinely inspired" (2 Tim. 3.16), we have six questions about the sacred writings.

units.la: Prima: Quænam sint illæ Scripturæ, de quibus Apostolus ait, eas omnes fuisse diuinitus inspiratas. Atque hic habemus quæstionem de libris Canonicis & Apocryphis: seu de partitione Bibliorum in Canonicos & Apocryphos: Et undenam constet, hos esse Canonicos, id est, verbū Dei: alios non item.
units.tr: The first: What are those Scriptures of which the Apostle says that they were all divinely inspired? Here we have the question about the canonical and apocryphal books, or about the division of the Bible into canonical and apocryphal books; and on what basis it is established that these are canonical, that is, the Word of God, and the others are not.

units.la: Secunda: De iis, quibus fuit inspirata, & per quos scripta: quinam illi fuerint.
units.tr: The second: Concerning those to whom it was inspired, and by whom it was written: who they were.

units.la: Tertia: De origine verbi Dei in Ecclesia: An ab iis, per quos fuit scriptum, primam habuerit originem: an vero aliis etiam ante hos, fuerit inspiratum & revelatum: & quomodo seruatum apud illos fuerit sine scripto.
units.tr: The third: Concerning the origin of the Word of God in the Church: whether it had its first origin from those by whom it was written, or whether it was also inspired and revealed to others before these; and how it was preserved among them without writing.

units.la: Quarta: De antiquitate Scripturæ: cuinam primò ita inspirata, vt etiam fuerit ab eo scripta.
units.tr: The fourth: Concerning the antiquity of Scripture: to whom it was first so inspired that it was also written down by him.

units.la: Quinta: De lingua, qua primùm fuit scripta: Deinde, de versione Græca & Latina.
units.tr: The fifth: Concerning the language in which it was first written; then, concerning the Greek and Latin versions.

units.la: Sexta: An liceat, vel vtile sit Scripturam sanctam in linguam cuiusque Gentis popularem còuertere. Nam etiam hæc cõtrouertitur hodie inter multos Pontificios & nos.
units.tr: The sixth: Whether it is lawful, or useful, to translate Holy Scripture into the vernacular of each nation. For this too is today disputed among many Papists and us.

units.la: Sextum argumentum, ab vtilitate maxima S. literarum. Perfistendum est in studio & professione earum literarum, quæ vtilissimæ sunt: & ad omnia, quæ desideramus, vtiliaque nobis sunt, valent.
units.tr: The sixth argument, from the very great usefulness of the Holy Writings. One must persevere in the study and profession of those writings which are most useful, and which avail for everything we desire and that is useful to us.

units.la: Atqui omnis Scriptura, in cuius studio & professione vt perseueres te hortor: vtilis est ad omnia, quæ possis in religione, & ad benè piéque viuendum, desiderare. Nam si cupias scire & docere dogmata fidei: ad ea omnia docenda vtilis est. Est enim vtilis πρὸς διδασκαλίαν, omnium scilicet dogmatum verorum. Si velis refutare falsa: ad id omninò vtilissima est. Est enim vtilis πρὸς ἔλεγχον omnium falsorum dogmatum. Si desideres etiam mores corrigere & tollere, ad hoc vtilis est. Est enim vtilis πρὸς ἐπανόρθωσιν. Si denique animus tibi sit familiam tuam, liberos, Ecclesiam & quosvis instituere in bonis moribus, inque vera iustitia, hoc est, in vera benè piéque viuendi ratione: ad hoc vtilissima est S. scriptura. Vtilis enim est πρὸς παιδείαν τὴν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ.
units.tr: Indeed, all Scripture, in whose study and profession I urge you to persevere, is useful for everything you could desire in religion and for living well and piously. For if you wish to know and teach the doctrines of faith, it is useful for teaching all of them; for it is useful for teaching [πρὸς διδασκαλίαν], that is, of all true doctrines. If you wish to refute falsehoods, it is most useful for this; for it is useful for refutation [πρὸς ἔλεγχον] of all false doctrines. If you also desire to correct and remove morals, it is useful for this; for it is useful for correction [πρὸς ἐπανόρθωσιν]. Finally, if you intend to instruct your household, your children, the Church and whomever in good morals and in true righteousness, that is, in the true way of living well and piously, Holy Scripture is most useful for this; for it is useful for instruction in righteousness [πρὸς παιδείαν τὴν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ].

units.la: Atq; hic habemus multas quæstiones.
units.tr: And here we have many questions.

units.la: Prima: de vtilitate S. Scripturæ: an valeat ad omnia vera dogmata docenda: ac proinde, an vllum dogma fidei, quod non doceat S.Scriptura,fit admittendum in Ecclesia,nec ne. De aliis duabus utilitatibus in sequenti-bus,non est opus vlla quaestione,quia perspi-cuæ sunt.
units.tr: The first: concerning the usefulness of Holy Scripture: whether it avails for teaching all true doctrines; and accordingly, whether any doctrine of faith that Holy Scripture does not teach is to be admitted in the Church or not. Concerning the other two usefulnesses that follow, there is no need for any question, because they are clear.

units.la: Secunda: An tradat omnia, quæ pertinent ad mores, & ad veram pie sanctéque vivendi rationem.
units.tr: The second: whether it hands down everything that pertains to morals and to the true way of living piously and holily.

units.la: Tertia: De intelligentia Scripturarum, & earum perspicuitate. Nam cùm ait, utilis est: subaudiendum, lecta aut audita & intellecta. Nam in cistis sepulta, non prodest: neque etiam lecta & audita: sed non intellecta. Quæstio igitur nascitur: An Scripturæ sint ita perspicuæ, ut possint intelligi necne.
units.tr: The third: concerning the understanding of the Scriptures and their perspicuity. For when it says "it is useful," it must be understood: when read or heard and understood. For buried in chests it does not profit, nor even when read and heard but not understood. The question therefore arises: whether the Scriptures are so clear that they can be understood or not.

units.la: Quarta: De interpretatione & de regulis intelligendi Scripturas.
units.tr: The fourth: concerning interpretation and the rules for understanding the Scriptures.

units.la: Septimum argumentum à fine Scriptu-rarum.In ea doctrina est persistendum, cuius finis est, ut homines sint omnibus numeris perfecti, & ad omne bonorum operum ge-nus perfectè instructi. Est enim hæc doctrina omninò honestissima, sanctissima, &c.
units.tr: The seventh argument, from the end of the Scriptures. One must persevere in that doctrine whose end is that men be perfect in every respect and thoroughly equipped for every kind of good work. For this doctrine is altogether most honourable, most holy, etc.

units.la: Arqui[?] finis huius doctrinæ, quam didici-sti, hic est, ut scilicet perfectus sit homo Dei. Ergo. &c.
units.tr: But the end of this doctrine which you have learned is this: that the man of God may be perfect. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Hic igitur habemus quæstionem de fine Scripturarum. An unus tantùm sit, vel plu-res: & quinam illi.
units.tr: Here, then, we have the question concerning the end of the Scriptures: whether there is only one, or several; and what they are.

units.la: Octauum argumentum, ab altera perse-ctione Scripturarum, quæ est, quòd ea tradit perfectè omnia, quæ ad verè bona opera, ad perfectam bene viuendi rationem pertinent. Argumentum igitur tale est. Non est ab illa recedendum doctrina viro bono, & bonorum operum studioso atque amanti, quæ hominem instruit ad omne bonum & honestum opus. Hoc facit hæc S.Scriptura-rum doctrina. Non enim tantum illius finis est, vt homo sit perfectus, & ad omne bonum opus perfectè instructus: sed etiam hoc præstat, hoc est, hominem perfectè instruit ad omne opus bonum. Ergo, &c.
units.tr: The eighth argument, from the other perfection of the Scriptures, which is that they hand down perfectly everything that pertains to truly good works and to the perfect way of living well. The argument therefore runs thus. A good man, one who is eager and loving of good works, must not depart from that doctrine which instructs a person in every good and honourable work. This is what the doctrine of these Holy Scriptures does. For not only is its end that a man be perfect and thoroughly equipped for every good work, but it also accomplishes this: that is, it perfectly instructs a man in every good work. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Nunc habemus primo analysin huiusce contextus Apostolici, qui est de Scripturis sanctis, deque firma & constanti in doctrina illarum perseuerantia. Deinde videmus, quot quæstiones seu ζητήματα[?] sese hic aperiant, quæ ad locum communem de Scripturis sanctis pertinent. Proinde poteritis iam videre, vel saltem aliquem capere gustu: quam vtilis sit hæc nostra methodus tractandi locos communes: quòd prius eos è Scripturis via Analytica eruimus: deinde via συνθετικῇ[?] tractamus.
units.tr: Now we have first the analysis of this Apostolic context, which concerns the Holy Scriptures and steadfast perseverance in their doctrine. Then we see how many questions, or zētēmata [ζητήματα], present themselves here, which pertain to the common topic concerning the Holy Scriptures. Therefore you can now see, or at least perceive by some taste, how useful this method of ours is in treating common topics: that we first draw them out from the Scriptures by the analytic way, and then treat them by the synthetic [συνθετικῇ] way.

units.la: Sunt autem hæ quæstiones de Scripturis S.ex hoc Apostoli loco collectæ, numero octodecim.
units.tr: Now these questions about the Holy Scriptures, gathered from this passage of the Apostle, are eighteen in number.

units.la: Prima: De custodiendo bona fide thesauro verbi Dei: quia nobis concreditus est. Hanc explicuimus & tractauimus in nostra oratione seu prolegomenis: & qua ratione custodiri possit[?], docuimus.
units.tr: The first: Concerning the keeping of the good deposit of the Word of God, which has been entrusted to us. This we have explained and treated in our oration or prolegomena, and we have taught in what way it can be kept.

units.la: Secunda: De autoritate Ecclesiæ circa S S. quænam illa & quanta sit.
units.tr: The second: Concerning the authority of the Church with respect to the Holy Scriptures: what that authority is and how great it is.

units.la: Tertia: De autoritate S. Scripturæ: quâ illa & quanta sit: & utra maior autoritas, Ecclesia, an Scriptura sancta.
units.tr: The third: Concerning the authority of Holy Scripture: what that authority is and how great it is, and which has greater authority, the Church or Holy Scripture.

units.la: Quarta: De lectione & studio S. scriptura. An omnium sit eam legere, nec ne.
units.tr: The fourth: Concerning the reading and study of Holy Scripture: whether it is for everyone to read it or not.

units.la: Quinta: De officio docendi S. literas: An sit omnium, & quorumnam illud sit.
units.tr: The fifth: Concerning the office of teaching the Holy Writings: whether it belongs to everyone, and to whom in particular it belongs.

units.la: Sexta: De perfectione Scripturarum: An quæcunq; tum ad fidem, tum ad perfectam sanctè viuendi rationem pertinent, abundè tradant: eoq; an sufficiant ad salutem.
units.tr: The sixth: Concerning the perfection of the Scriptures: whether they hand down abundantly everything that pertains both to faith and to the perfect and holy way of living; and whether, for this reason, they suffice for salvation.

units.la: Hinc sequitur septima: An ullum dogma de Religione extra Scripturam sanctam, sit in Ecclesia admittendum, nec ne.
units.tr: From this follows the seventh: whether any doctrine of religion outside Holy Scripture is to be admitted in the Church or not.

units.la: Octava: De partitionibus Bibliorum, quæ apud nos Græcè & Latinè habentur: atq; inprimis: An omnia hæc habenda sint pro Canonicis seu diuinitus inspiratis, ex verbo Dei, necne. Atq; hîc de regulis, unde constet, hos esse verbum Dei, & non alios.
units.tr: The eighth: Concerning the divisions of the Bible that are held among us in Greek and Latin; and above all: whether all of these are to be regarded as canonical, that is, divinely inspired, from the Word of God, or not. And here, concerning the rules by which it is established that these are the Word of God and not others.

units.la: Nona: De iis, quibus Scriptura fuit inspirata, & per quos conscripta, quinam fuerint illi. Atque hanc sequitur
units.tr: The ninth: Concerning those to whom Scripture was inspired, and by whom it was written: who they were. And this is followed by

units.la: Decima: De origine verbi Dei in Ecclesia: An ab iis, per quos fuit scriptum, primam habuerit originem, necne: an verò etiam aliis, ante hos fuerit reuelatum & inspiratum, licet non fuerit scriptum: & quomodo fuerit seruatum.
units.tr: The tenth: Concerning the origin of the Word of God in the Church: whether it had its first origin from those by whom it was written or not; or whether it was also revealed and inspired to others before these, although not written down; and how it was preserved.

units.la: Vndecima: De antiquitate Scripturæ: cui primò ita inspirata fuit, vt etiam ab eo fuerit scripta.
units.tr: The eleventh: Concerning the antiquity of Scripture: to whom it was first so inspired that it was also written down by him.

units.la: Duodecima: De lingua, qua primùm fuit scriscripta Scriptura sacra: Deinde, de versione Græ-ca [?] & Latina.
units.tr: The twelfth: Concerning the language in which Holy Scripture was first written; then, concerning the Greek and Latin versions.

units.la: Decimatertia: An etiam nunc liceat Scripturam sanctam vertere in linguam cuiusque Gentis popularem.
units.tr: The thirteenth: Whether it is now also lawful to translate Holy Scripture into the vernacular of each nation.

units.la: Decimaquarta: De utilitate & usu sanctæ Scripturæ: quotuplex & quinam ille sit. Quanquam hæc explicata fuit magna ex parte in nostra oratione.
units.tr: The fourteenth: Concerning the usefulness and use of Holy Scripture: how many kinds there are and what they are. Although this was explained for the most part in our oration.

units.la: Decimaquinta: De perspicuitate & obscuritate S. Scripturæ.
units.tr: The fifteenth: Concerning the perspicuity and obscurity of Holy Scripture.

units.la: Decimasexta: De officio interpretandi Scripturas in Ecclesia: [?]An sit superuacaneum atque inutile: an vero utile atq; necessarium.
units.tr: The sixteenth: Concerning the office of interpreting the Scriptures in the Church: whether it is superfluous and useless, or rather useful and necessary.

units.la: Decimaseptima: De regulis intelligendi Scripturas.
units.tr: The seventeenth: Concerning the rules for understanding the Scriptures.

units.la: Decima octava: De fine Scripturarum, propter quem data nobis sunt: hoc est, cur voluerit Deus verbum suum manere in Ecclesia scri-ptum.
units.tr: The eighteenth: Concerning the end of the Scriptures, for which they have been given to us; that is, why God willed his Word to remain in the Church in written form.

units.la: Hæ sunt illæ, quas ex hoc Apostoli con-textu colligere potui, quæstiones, ad locum communem de Scripturis sanctis pertinen-tes: in quibus omnia fere, quæ de Scripturis dici possunt, comprehensa sunt. His tamen addi possunt duæ aliæ non parui momenti & utilitatis quæstiones: quarum prima est de summa illius doctrinæ, quam tradit Scriptura sancta, quænam illa sit. Altera sequitur ex hac priore, de discrimine religionis, quæ traditur in S. literis, ab aliis religionibus omnibus.
units.tr: These are the questions which I have been able to gather from this context of the Apostle, pertaining to the common topic concerning the Holy Scriptures, in which almost everything that can be said about the Scriptures is comprehended. To these, however, may be added two other questions of no small importance and usefulness: the first is concerning the sum of the doctrine that Holy Scripture hands down, what it is. The second follows from this former one: concerning the difference of the religion that is taught in the Holy Writings from all other religions.

units.la: Sunt hæ omnes mihi pertractandæ: sed id quàm breuissimè à nobis fiet. Sunt enim permultæ ita perspicuæ, & extra omnem controuersiam, vt non opus habeant multa vel explicatione, vel confirmatione. Quæ-dam etiam sunt à clarissimo pietate & doctrina viro D.D.Vrsino piæ memoriæ, ita explicatæ, vt in illis etiam diu immorari non debeam.
units.tr: All of these I must treat, but I will do so as briefly as I can. Many are so clear and beyond all dispute that they need little explanation or confirmation. Some have also been explained so well by the most distinguished man in piety and learning, D. D. Ursinus of blessed memory, that I need not linger over them.

units.la: Cæterùm, non eo ordine, quo has ex Apo-stoli verbis collegi, à me pertractabuntur hæ quæstiones: sed legitimo ordine: vt hæ priùs pertractentur, quas etiam priùs nosse, necesse est & utile. Age igitur in nomineDomini.
units.tr: However, these questions will not be treated by me in the order in which I have gathered them from the words of the Apostle, but in their proper order, so that those which it is necessary and useful to know first are dealt with first. Come, then, in the name of the Lord.

units.la: QVÆSTIO I. De libris Canonicis & Apocryphis, deq; Bibliorum partitione[?].
units.tr: QUESTION I. On the canonical and apocryphal books, and on the division of the Bible[?].

units.la: VSus in Ecclesia obtinuit, iam inde vsque ab initio, & post hominum memoriam, vt volumen illud totum, quod primùm Græcè, deindè etiam Latinè apud Christianos, pro omnium librorum à condito orbe, sanctissimo & diuinissimo habetur: appelletur Græco nomine, & plurali quidem numero, βιβλία, quod Latinè sonat libros: idque καθ' ἐξοχὴν[?], vt omnes intelligant, non esse hos libros vllius hominis, sed Dei Optimi & Maximi. Et quidem permulti putant, quicunque in hoc volumine continentur libri: eos esse dictatos à Spiritu sancto, eoque verbum Dei esse omnes, & paris authoritatis. Sed qui melioris sunt iudicij, putant ita appella-ri à maiori parte: quòd plerique omnes libri, qui in hoc continentur volumine, sint diui-nitùs inspirati, verbumq; Dei.
units.tr: From the beginning, and within living memory, the custom has prevailed in the Church that the whole volume which the Christians hold, first in Greek and then also in Latin, as the most holy and divine of all books since the creation of the world, is called by a Greek name in the plural, biblia, which in Latin means books; and it is called this kath' exochēn, so that everyone understands that these books belong not to any man but to God, the best and greatest. Indeed, very many think that all the books contained in this volume were dictated by the Holy Spirit, and that therefore all of them are the Word of God and of equal authority. But those of sounder judgment think that it is so called by the greater part, because most of the books contained in this volume are divinely inspired and are the Word of God.

units.la: Prima igitur quæstio hic proponitur de S.Bibliis: an omnes sint Canonici, nec ne Ca-nonici. Pontificij affirmant: & ita ex libris Machabæorum probant orationes pro de-functis, & purgatorium. Nos contrà, alios esse Canonicos, alios Apocryphos.
units.tr: The first question here proposed, then, concerns the Holy Bible: whether all its books are canonical or not. The Papists affirm that they are all canonical, and so from the books of the Maccabees they prove prayers for the dead and purgatory. We, on the contrary, hold that some are canonical and others apocryphal.

units.la: Quadruplex Bibliorum partitio.
units.tr: A fourfold division of the Bible.

units.la: Prima est, in Canonicos & Apocryphos.
units.tr: The first is into canonical and apocryphal.

units.la: Secunda: Canonici secantur in Vetus & Nouum Testamentum.
units.tr: The second: the canonical books are divided into the Old and the New Testament.

units.la: Tertia: Canonici veteris Testamenti in tres classes: primò in תורה legem id est, in libros quinque Mosis: Secundò in נביאים ראשונים ונביאים אחרונים[?] hoc est, in Prophetas priores, & in Prophetas posteriores. Tertiò in scripta כתובים[?] (scilicet sancta) quæ Græci ἁγιόγραφα vocant.
units.tr: The third: the canonical books of the Old Testament fall into three classes: first, the torah, that is, the law, the five books of Moses; second, the nevi'im rishonim and nevi'im acharonim, that is, the former prophets and the latter prophets; third, the ketuvim (that is, the holy writings), which the Greeks call hagiographa.

units.la: Noui Testamenti libri, in tres etiam ordines: Historicos, Epistolas, Apocalypsin.
units.tr: The books of the New Testament likewise fall into three orders: the historical books, the epistles, and the Apocalypse.

units.la: Quarta partitio omnium canonicorum librorum tam Veteris, quàm Noui Testamenti, est à summa totius Scripturæ desumta: ea est in Legem & Euangelium. Dicamus nunc de prima.
units.tr: The fourth division of all the canonical books, both of the Old and the New Testament, is taken from the sum of the whole of Scripture: it is into Law and Gospel. Let us now speak of the first.

units.la: Hæc igitur esto prima partitio Bibliorum, & prima
units.tr: Let this, then, be the first division of the Bible, and the first

units.la: PROPOSITIO I.
units.tr: PROPOSITION I.

units.la: Librorum, qui sunt in volumine tam Latino, quàm Graeco, quod volumen, Biblia appellatur: alij sunt Canonici, alij Apocryphi.
units.tr: Of the books that are in the volume, both Latin and Greek, which volume is called the Bible, some are canonical and others apocryphal.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Canon, Graeca vox κανὼν, est regula seu norma, ad quam aliquid examinatur, sitne purum an adulterinum, rectum, an obliquum, &c. Et Canonicum, quod illi Canoni est omnino ex parte consentaneum.
units.tr: "Canon," from the Greek word κανὼν, is a rule or standard by which something is examined, whether it is pure or adulterated, straight or crooked, and so on. And "canonical" is what is wholly in agreement with that canon.

units.la: Canon primus Scripturarum, ad quem omnia reliqua scripta examinabant Patres in veteri Testamento, an essent Θεόπνευστα, & verbum Dei, nec ne, fuit ipsa Dei תורה per Mosen tradita, partim in externis chartis, partim in cordibus piorum inscripta. Non enim externa illa satis erat: sed opus erat etiam interno Spiritus Canone.
units.tr: The first canon of Scripture, by which the Fathers examined all other writings in the Old Testament, to determine whether they were θεόπνευστα [God-breathed] and the word of God or not, was the very תורה [law] of God delivered through Moses, written partly on outward parchments and partly inscribed in the hearts of the pious. For that outward law was not enough by itself; there was also need of the inward canon of the Spirit.

units.la: Hanc externam תורה acceperunt Israelitae tanquam Dei verbum, sine vllo alio externo Canone, ad quem examinaretur: partim propter autoritatem Mosis, quam ei conciliauerat Deus primùm in Ægypto, deinde in deserto, praesertim in monte Syna. Ipsi enim interfuerunt cùm Moses ascendit in montem, & à Deo Legem accepit: vndè de eius persona, quin amicus esset Deo, non poterant dubitare: ideò nec de Lege, quin à Deo illam accepisset, dubitare volebant: partim etiam acceperant illam Legem pro indubitato Dei verbo, propter autoritatem dignitatem ipsius Legis. Nam viri sancti in-ter eos Spiritu Dei illustrati, agnouerunt scripta Mosis, merum esse Dei verbum, ideoque illud pro tali amplexi sunt.
units.tr: The Israelites received this outward תורה [law] as the word of God, without any other outward canon by which it might be examined. They did so partly on account of the authority of Moses, which God first conferred on him in Egypt and then in the wilderness, especially on Mount Sinai. For they themselves were present when Moses went up the mountain and received the Law from God. Hence they could not doubt his person, that he was a friend of God; and therefore they were not willing to doubt that he had received the Law from God. Partly also they had received that Law as an indubitable word of God, on account of the authority and dignity of the Law itself. For the holy men among them, enlightened by the Spirit of God, recognised that the writings of Moses were purely the word of God, and therefore embraced them as such.

units.la: Adde, quòd eam etiam doctrinam perspexerunt consentaneam esse in substantia, doctrinae quam per successionem à Patriarchis acceperant. His de causis Mosis תורה[?] acceperunt; quia eam agnouerunt pro vero Dei verbo.
units.tr: Add to this that they also perceived that this teaching agreed in substance with the doctrine which they had received by succession from the Patriarchs. For these reasons they received the תורה [law] of Moses, because they recognised it as the true word of God.

units.la: Ad hanc verò, reliqua omnia & dicta & scripta, tanquam ad certum Canonem examinabant: & quæcunque Canoni videbant omni ex parte esse consentanea, tam in doctrina, quàm in cœlesti quadam maiestate sermonis, quæ vndiquaque spirabat diuinam probitatem & sapientiam, ita vt agnoscerent ea esse etiam digna, quæ κανὼν fierent omnis doctrinæ: illa scripta aut verba pro-nunciabant esse verum Dei verbum. Ad hunc enim Canonem iusserat Dominus omnes omnium doctrinas examinari: vt indè agnoscerentur doctrinæ, & Prophetæ ipsi, an essent à Deo, nec ne. Deut.13. Si surrexerit in medio tui Propheta, &c.
units.tr: To this law they examined all the other sayings and writings, as to a fixed canon. And whatever they saw to be wholly in agreement with it, both in doctrine and in a certain heavenly majesty of speech which breathed everywhere the divine goodness and wisdom, so that they recognised these as also worthy to become the canon of all doctrine, they pronounced those writings or words to be the true word of God. For the Lord had commanded that all teachings of everyone be examined by this canon, so that by it doctrines might be recognised, and the prophets themselves, whether they were from God or not. Deut. 13. If there arise in the midst of you a prophet, etc.

units.la: Ad hunc Canonem, omnia Prophetarum scripta examinata: agnita fuerunt esse θεό-πνευστα[?], & digna, quæ vnà cum lege Mosis, essent Canon omnis doctrinæ.
units.tr: By this canon all the writings of the Prophets were examined; they were recognised as θεόπνευστα [God-breathed] and worthy to be, together with the law of Moses, the canon of all doctrine.

units.la: Postmodùm omnia Mosis & Prophetarum scripta & ἀγιόγραφα quæ ab Hebræis recepta sunt; simul fuerunt Canon Scripturarum. rarum,ad quem omnia posteriores Israelitæ, & alij, examinabant aliorum omnium & dicta & scripta. Sic Actor. 17. dicta Pauli ad hunc Canonem examinabant. Sic Christus iubebat suam doctrinam ad hunc Canonem examinari, dicendo Ioh.5[?]. Scrutamini Scriptu-ram, &c. Sic Apostoli sua confirmabant illo Canone veteris Testamenti.
units.tr: Afterwards all the writings of Moses and the Prophets, and the ἀγιόγραφα [holy writings] which were received by the Hebrews, together formed the canon of Scriptures. By this canon the later Israelites, and others, examined all the sayings and writings of all others. Thus in Acts 17 the words of Paul were examined by this canon. Thus Christ ordered his own doctrine to be examined by this canon, saying in John 5: Search the Scriptures, etc. Thus the Apostles confirmed their own teaching by that canon of the Old Testament.

units.la: Nunc vetus Testamentum cum Novo, Canon est Christianis, ad quem omnes doctrinæ examinandæ sunt. De quo Canone 1.Thes.5[?]. Omnia probate, quod bonum est, tenete. Quomodo probabimus? Canone Scri-pturatum[?]. 1.Ioh.4. Nolite omni spiritui credere: sed probate spiritus, utrum ex Deo sint. Quo-modo?ad Canonem S. Scripturæ.
units.tr: Now the Old Testament together with the New is the canon for Christians, by which all doctrines are to be examined. Concerning this canon, 1 Thess. 5: Prove all things; hold fast what is good. How shall we prove them? By the canon of the Scriptures. 1 John 4: Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are from God. How? By the canon of Holy Scripture.

units.la: Canonicos igitur libros vocârunt Patres, omnes eos,quos primùm ad illum Mosis Canonem; deinde ad alterum etiam,Mosis scilicet simul & Prophetarum examinatos: Ecclesia primùm Israëlitica, deinde Ecclesia Christiana, Spiritu sancto edocta: constanter agnouit esse θεόπνευστα[?], & à Spiritu sancto dictatos, perque ipsos Prophetas, Apostolos, atque Euangelistas conscriptos fuisse: eoq; illos purum esse Dei verbum.
units.tr: The Fathers therefore called canonical those books which, having been first examined and approved by that canon of Moses, and then also by the other, namely of Moses and the Prophets together, the Israelite Church first, and then the Christian Church, taught by the Holy Spirit, constantly recognised as θεόπνευστα [God-breathed], dictated by the Holy Spirit, and written through the Prophets, Apostles and Evangelists themselves; and therefore that they are the pure word of God.

units.la: Ac proinde Canonicos vocârunt tum quòd ad Canonem, vt dixi, examinati probati fuerunt: tum quòd ab vniuersa Ecclesia positi sunt in Canone & ipsi eorum librorum, quos Ecclesia agnouit à Spiritu sancto dictatos, & θεόπνευστα[?]: tum denique quòd facti sunt Canon omnis doctrinæ de religione.
units.tr: And accordingly they called them canonical, both because they were examined and approved by the canon, as I have said; and because the whole Church placed them in the canon, and recognised those books as dictated by the Holy Spirit and θεόπνευστα [God-breathed]; and finally because they became the canon of all doctrine concerning religion.

units.la: Nunc tenemus, quos vocent Canonicos: & cur ita vocent.
units.tr: Now we have what they call canonical, and why they so call them.

units.la: Apocryphos appellant eos, qui licet non plane impiam contineant doctrinam: tamen examinati ad Canonem Scripturarum sacrarum non fuerunt agniti ab Ecclesia ita cum Canone omni ex parte conuenire, sicut reliqui, neque illam redolere diuinam maiestatem, sapientiam, veritatem, & coelestem bonitatem ac Spiritum, quem Prophetici & Apostolici: & visi[?] sunt potius Spiritu humano, quàm diuino conscripti.
units.tr: They call apocryphal those which, although they do not contain a plainly impious doctrine, yet, when examined by the canon of the sacred Scriptures, were not recognised by the Church as agreeing with the canon in every respect as the rest do, nor as breathing that divine majesty, wisdom, truth, heavenly goodness and Spirit which the prophetic and apostolic writings breathe; and they seem to have been written by a human spirit rather than a divine one.

units.la: Ideò verò Apocryphi vocati fuerunt (quæ vox Græca significat abscönditum & secretum) partim quia non fuerunt agniti ab Ecclesia pro θεοπνεύστοις[?]: partim quòd nomina autorum, essent abscondita: partim etiam, quòd quædam continerent, quæ Mosi, Prophetis, & Apostolis fuerunt ignota: partim denique quòd propter supra dictas causas, digni non erant, qui legerentur publicè in Ecclesia: Et sic etiam prohibiti fuerunt legi in Ecclesia: vt testatur autor expositionis in Symbolum, apud Cyprianum.
units.tr: They were called apocryphal (a word which in Greek means hidden and secret) partly because they were not recognised by the Church as θεόπνευστα [God-breathed]; partly because the names of their authors were hidden; partly also because they contained some things unknown to Moses, the Prophets and the Apostles; and partly finally because, for the reasons mentioned above, they were not worthy to be read publicly in the Church. And so they were also forbidden to be read in the Church, as the author of the exposition of the Creed in Cyprian bears witness.

units.la: Nunc igitur tenemus explicationem horum nominum, Canonicorum & Apocryphorum: & quid nomine Canonicorum librorum: & quid nomine Apocryphorum intelligendum sit. Non esse autem omnes Canonicos, sed quosdam Apocryphos, paulò pòstdemonstrabimus.
units.tr: We now have, then, the explanation of these names, canonical and apocryphal, and what is to be understood by the name of canonical books and by the name of apocryphal books. That not all books are canonical, but some are apocryphal, we will demonstrate shortly.

units.la: PROPOSITIO II.
units.tr: PROPOSITION II.

units.la: Canonici auctoritatem habent ad constituenda & ad probanda fidei dogmata: Apocryphi vero, etsi utiliter legi possunt: nullam tamen auctoritatem habent vel ad constituenda, vel ad probanda fidei dogmata.
units.tr: The canonical books have authority to establish and to prove the dogmas of faith; the apocryphal books, however, although they may be read with profit, have no authority either to establish or to prove the dogmas of faith.

units.la: Explicatione hic nulla opus est. Quoad 1. probationem attinet, ea est in promptu. Fi-des enim est tantum ex auditu: auditus autem per verbum Dei. Ergo fidei dogmata e solo verbo Dei constitui & probari possunt. Soli autem Canonici, sunt verbum Dei, non autem Apocryphi. Quis igitur non videat, Apocryphos nil valere ad constituenda & probanda dogmata fidei?
units.tr: No explanation is needed here. As for the first proof, it lies ready to hand: faith comes only from hearing, and hearing through the word of God. Therefore the dogmas of faith can be established and proved from the word of God alone. Only the canonical books, however, are the word of God, not the apocryphal ones. Who, then, does not see that the apocryphal books are worth nothing for establishing and proving the dogmas of faith?

units.la: 2. Confirmatur testimoniis Patrum. Hieronymus in praefatione in libros Salomonis aperte testatur. Autor expositionis in Symbolum Apostolicum apud D. Cyprianum, pag. 377. cùm exponit verba: Credo Eccle-siam sanctam, & idem plane scribit. Concilium Laodicenum tempore Damasi Papæ, Canon. 59.
units.tr: Second, it is confirmed by the testimonies of the Fathers. Jerome clearly bears witness in the preface to the books of Solomon. The author of the exposition of the Apostles' Creed, in Cyprian, p. 377, when he expounds the words, "I believe the holy Church," plainly writes the same. The Council of Laodicea, in the time of Pope Damasus, canon 59.

units.la: Hinc apparet, quid de scriptis Patrum sen-tiendum sit, & sententiri ipsi voluerint. Si Apocryphi libri, qui tamen in volumine Bibliorum semper manserunt, propterea quòd valde utilis est illorum lectio: & nulli alij libri, exceptis Canonicis, puriores illis sunt: si inquam libri Apocryphi nullam habent auctoritatem ad constituenda vel probanda fidei dogmata: multò minùs igitur eam habent scripta Patrum, quicunque illi sint. Quod confirmare possem dictis ipsorum Pa-trum: sed hoc alias.
units.tr: From this it is evident what is to be thought of the writings of the Fathers, and what they themselves wished to be thought. If the apocryphal books, which nevertheless have always remained in the volume of the Bible, because the reading of them is very useful, and because no other books, apart from the canonical ones, are purer than they, if I say the apocryphal books have no authority to establish or prove the dogmas of faith, then much less do the writings of the Fathers, whoever they may be, have such authority. This I could confirm by the sayings of the Fathers themselves, but that is for another occasion.

units.la: Nunc venio ad explicationem, quinam Canonici: qui Apocryphi sint.
units.tr: Now I come to the explanation of which books are canonical and which are apocryphal.

units.la: PROPOSITIO III.
units.tr: PROPOSITION III.

units.la: Apocryphi libri sunt: Iudith. Thobias. Esdrae tertius & quartus. Sapientia Salomonis. Sapientia Iesu filij Sirach, qui Ecclesiasti-cus dicitur apud Latinos. Baruch. Epistola Hieremiae. Cap.13.& 14. addita Danieli. Canticum trium puerorum, quod est ad-iectum tertio capiti Danielis. Libri Machabaeorum. Et post 3. versus 10. cap. Esther, reliquum. Reliqui omnes in veteri Testamento Ca-nonici sunt.
units.tr: The apocryphal books are: Judith. Tobit. Esdras the third and fourth. The Wisdom of Solomon. The Wisdom of Jesus the son of Sirach, which among the Latins is called Ecclesiasticus. Baruch. The Epistle of Jeremiah. Chapters 13 and 14 added to Daniel. The Song of the Three Children, which is added to the third chapter of Daniel. The books of the Maccabees. And after verse 3 of chapter 10 of Esther, the remainder. All the rest in the Old Testament are canonical.

units.la: Explicatione nulla hic opus est.
units.tr: No explanation is needed here.

units.la: Unde verò hoc probamus? Ex traditio-ne Ecclesiae, seu ex veteris Ecclesiae consensu & iudicio.
units.tr: How do we prove this, then? From the tradition of the Church, that is, from the consensus and judgement of the ancient Church.

units.la: Hebræi ita senserunt: ideò hos non ha-bent in Canone.
units.tr: The Hebrews likewise thought so, and therefore do not include these in the Canon.

units.la: Iosephus, lib. de antiquitatibus Iudæorum,
units.tr: Josephus, in his book on the antiquities of the Jews,

units.la: contra Appianum Alexandrinum Grammaticum, primò ait Canonicos libros esse xxii. iuxta numerum Hebraicarum literarum: Et hos ait esse: primùm, libros Mosis; quos Hebræi à præcipua parte vocant, תורה [?]: Græci à numero πεντάτευχον [?]: secundò, libros Prophetarum. Tertiò, alios etiam, qui hymnos (vt ipse loquitur) in Deum, ὑμνοῦντες [?] ἐν βίῳ τοῖς ἀνθρώποις πιστεύουσι [?]. Clarius tamen hæc res explicatur apud alios Græcos & Latinos.
units.tr: against Apion the Alexandrian grammarian, first says that the canonical books are twenty-two, according to the number of the Hebrew letters; and he says these are: first, the books of Moses, which the Hebrews call by their principal part, תורה [?]: the Greeks, from the number, Pentateuch [?]; second, the books of the Prophets; third, the others also, which contain hymns (as he himself puts it) to God, and precepts for human life [?]. This matter is explained more clearly, however, by other Greek and Latin writers.

units.la: Hieronymus in prologo in libros Regū, quem prologum vocat Galeatum, & est in Tomo 3. operum Hieronymi: & præponi solet omnibus Bibliis, Confirmat esse tantum 22. libros Canonicos apud Hebræos, sicut etiam 22 literæ: & dum hos numerat, nullam facit mentionem eorum, quos diximus esse Apocryphos: imò nominatim excludit à Canone, librum Sapientiæ Salomonis: Ecclesiasticum: Iuditham: Thobiam: libros Machabæorum.
units.tr: Jerome, in the prologue to the books of Kings, which he calls the Galeatus prologue, and which is in volume 3 of Jerome's works, and is usually placed before all Bibles, confirms that there are only twenty-two canonical books among the Hebrews, just as there are twenty-two letters; and in enumerating these he makes no mention of those we have said are apocryphal. Indeed, he expressly excludes from the Canon the book of the Wisdom of Solomon, Ecclesiasticus, Judith, Tobit, and the books of the Maccabees.

units.la: Autor expositionis in Symbolum Apostolicum super illud, Credo Ecclesiam Sanctam, idem tradit.
units.tr: The author of the exposition of the Apostles' Creed, on the words "I believe the holy Church," teaches the same.

units.la: Eusteb. Cæsariensis Eccles. hist. lib. 3. c. 10. eundem numerum tradit iuxta Iosephum, neq; plures enumerat. Item lib. 4. cap. 26. ex sententia Melitonis Episcopi Sardensis.
units.tr: Eusebius of Caesarea, Ecclesiastical History, book 3, chapter 10, gives the same number, following Josephus, and enumerates no more. Likewise book 4, chapter 26, on the authority of Melito, bishop of Sardis.

units.la: Epiphanius in panario, Tom. 1. libri primi, hæresi 8. quæ fuit Epicureorum, idem habet, nisi quòd cum Ieremia coniungit etjam Epistolam Baruch : & concludit,omnes enumeratos,esse xxii. iuxta numerum Hebraicarum literarum.
units.tr: Epiphanius, in the Panarion, volume 1 of the first book, heresy 8, which was that of the Epicureans, has the same, except that he joins the Epistle of Baruch to Jeremiah; and he concludes that all those enumerated are twenty-two, according to the number of the Hebrew letters.

units.la: Idem Epiphanius lib.de mensuris & pon-deribus, p.604. eundem numerum & ordi-nem librorum Canonicorum tradit,& egre-giè explicat,quomodo, cùm essent numero 27.redacti sint ad 22.nullo tamen excepto.
units.tr: The same Epiphanius, in his book on weights and measures, p. 604, gives the same number and order of the canonical books, and explains admirably how, although they were twenty-seven in number, they were reduced to twenty-two, yet with none omitted.

units.la: Idem super eodem libro de mensuris, p. 14.pulchrè explicat mysterium huius numeri vicenarij cum denario.
units.tr: The same Epiphanius, on the same book of weights and measures, p. 14, neatly explains the mystery of this number twenty combined with ten.

units.la: Hieronymus quoque in prologo Galea-to imitatus Epiphanium, multa de hoc nu-mero xxii.tradit.
units.tr: Jerome also, in the prologue to the Galeatus, imitating Epiphanius, sets out many things about this number twenty-two.

units.la: Hilarius in prologo in Psalmos totidem & eosdem libros enumerat.
units.tr: Hilary, in the prologue to the Psalms, enumerates the same number of books and the same ones.

units.la: Concilium Laodicenum, in Can. 59. eosdem quos & nos antea, enumerat.
units.tr: The Council of Laodicea, in canon 59, enumerates the same books that we have listed above.

units.la: Tomo Concil.1.p.991. in Catalogo Gela-sij excluditur secundus, Machabæorum.
units.tr: In volume 1 of the Councils, p. 991, in the catalogue of Gelasius, the second book of the Maccabees is excluded.

units.la: Augustinus Tom. 7. contra secundam e-pistolam Gaudentij,lib.2.cap.23. Item, Tomo.5.de Ciuit. Dei, lib.18 cap 36 fatetur,li-bros Machabæorum, non esse de Canone Hebræorum, neque paris autoritatis cum Lege & Prophetis: & ideò sobriè esse legen-dos. Atque hæc de libris veteris Testamenti Canonicis.
units.tr: Augustine, volume 7, against the second letter of Gaudentius, book 2, chapter 23. Also, volume 5, On the City of God, book 18, chapter 36, confesses that the books of the Maccabees are not in the Hebrew Canon, nor of equal authority with the Law and the Prophets, and therefore are to be read with sobriety. And so much concerning the canonical books of the Old Testament.

units.la: Ad obiecta Pontificiorum.
units.tr: Against the objections of the Papists.

units.la: At (inquies) Pontificij vrgent alios Patres, qui tam Machabæorum, quàm alios librosàte positos inter Apocrypha, ponunt inter Canonicos: Vt,
units.tr: But (you will say) the Papists press other Fathers, who place among the Canonical books the Maccabees and other books that are set apart among the Apocrypha. For example:

units.la: Augustinus Tom.3. de doctrina Christiana, lib. 2. cap. 8. qui inter Canonicos ponit Thobiam, Iudítham [?], Machabaeos. Vt,
units.tr: Augustine, in the third volume of On Christian Doctrine, book 2, chapter 8, who counts Tobit, Judith [?], and the Maccabees among the Canonical books. For example:

units.la: Patres in Concilio Carthaginensi tertio sub Syricio Papa: receptus fuit inter Canonicos liber Sapientiae: Item, Ecclesiasticus & libri Machabaeorum. Vt,
units.tr: the Fathers at the Third Council of Carthage under Pope Siricius: the book of Wisdom was received among the Canonical books; likewise Ecclesiasticus and the books of the Maccabees. For example:

units.la: Innocentius Papa primus, vt apparet inter eius decreta in Epistola ad Exuperium Tholosanum Episcopum, cap. 7.
units.tr: Pope Innocent I, as appears among his decrees, in the letter to Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse, chapter 7.

units.la: Item Gelasius Papa: nisi quòd Machabaeorum primum tantùm agnoscit pro Canonico: non ita secundum.
units.tr: Likewise Pope Gelasius, except that he acknowledges only the first book of the Maccabees as Canonical, not the second.

units.la: Item in Canonibus, quos vocant Apostolorum, Can. 84. in Tomo Concil. primo, vbi tertium Machabaeorum inter Canonicos ponunt.
units.tr: Likewise in the so-called Canons of the Apostles, canon 84, in the first volume of the Councils, where they list the third book of the Maccabees among the Canonical books.

units.la: Respond. In hac diuersitate iudiciorum tenendae sunt hae regulae.
units.tr: Reply. In this divergence of judgments the following rules are to be held.

units.la: Prima: Libri veteris Testamenti, qui citantur in Nouo à Christo & Apostolis, omnino pro Canonicis habendi sunt.
units.tr: First: The books of the Old Testament which are cited in the New by Christ and the Apostles are to be held wholly as Canonical.

units.la: Secunda: Libri, qui ab omnibus Ecclesiis recepti fuerunt pro Canonicis: ij etiam habendi sunt pro Canonicis citra vllam dubitationem.
units.tr: Second: Those books which were received as Canonical by all the Churches, these too are to be held as Canonical beyond any doubt.

units.la: Tertia: Qui non ab omnibus: sequendum est iudicium Ecclesiarum & Patrum antiquorum, maiorisque auctoritatis, & praeponendum est iudicio posteriorum, & qui mi-noris moris sunt autoritatis ; quales fuerunt illi, quos pro nostra sententia adduximus: Origenes, Epiphanius, Cyprianus, Hilarius, Hie-ronymus, Concilium Laodicenum.
units.tr: Third: Where books were not received by all, the judgment of the Churches and of the ancient Fathers, who had greater authority, is to be followed, and is to be preferred to the judgment of later writers, who have less weight and authority; such as those whom we have cited in support of our opinion: Origen, Epiphanius, Cyprian, Hilary, Jerome, and the Council of Laodicea.

units.la: Primò:illi antiquiores fuerunt illis, quos Pontificij citant: ideò melius iudicium veteris Ecclesiæ & Apostolorum agnoscere potuerunt, quàm posteriores. Et certè regula hæc certissima est: ideò ea etiam utitur Tertullianus, dicendo:Id esse verum, quodcunque prius:id esse adulterinum, quodcunque posterius.
units.tr: First: those were earlier than the writers whom the Papists cite; therefore they were able to recognize the better judgment of the ancient Church and of the Apostles than later writers could. And indeed this rule is most certain; for this reason Tertullian also uses it, saying: whatever is earlier is true, whatever is later is adulterated.

units.la: Secundò:Illi priores Patres pulchrè inter se conueniunt de numero librorum Canonicorum & non Canonicorum: quem consensum non reperies in posterioribus.
units.tr: Second: those earlier Fathers agree admirably among themselves about the number of Canonical and non-Canonical books; a consensus you will not find among the later writers.

units.la: Tertiò: Consentiunt cum Hebræis voluminibus. Certè quos posteriores Patres addunt, nunquam apud Hebræos reperti fuerunt.
units.tr: Third: they agree with the Hebrew writings. Certainly, the books which the later Fathers add were never found among the Hebrews.

units.la: De illis Canonibus,qui dicuntur Apostolorum:liquet, illos non fuisse pro Apostolicis à veteri Ecclesia agnitos:præsertim hunc citatum Canonem de libris Canonicis. Quomodo enim Ecclesia vetus reiecisset utrumque Machabæorum librum, si agnouissent illum Canonem pro Apostolico, qui tres Machabæorum probat?
units.tr: As for those canons which are called the Apostles': it is clear that they were not acknowledged as Apostolic by the ancient Church, especially this cited canon about the Canonical books. For how would the ancient Church have rejected both books of the Maccabees, if they had acknowledged as Apostolic that canon which approves three books of the Maccabees?

units.la: De Augustino: liquidò apparet, vt suprà etiam ostendi ex responsione contra Epistolam Gaudentij secundam: & ex libro de Civitate Dei, illum non agnouisse libros Machabæorum [?] pro Canonicis,ita vt sine dubio admittenda sint omnia, quæ ibi continentur: cùm dicat, eos sobriè esse legendos. Quare, si nos quoque illos nonagnoscamus pro Canonicis:non possumus damnari,quin damnetur Augustinus, & Hieronymus, totaque vetus Ecclesia. Atque hæc de libris veteris Testamenti.
units.tr: As for Augustine: it clearly appears, as I showed above from his reply against the second letter of Gaudentius, and from the book On the City of God, that he did not acknowledge the books of the Maccabees as Canonical, so that everything contained in them must without doubt be admitted; since he says they are to be read soberly. Wherefore, if we too do not acknowledge them as Canonical, we cannot be condemned without condemning Augustine and Jerome, and the whole ancient Church. So much concerning the books of the Old Testament.

units.la: DE LIBRIS NOVI.
units.tr: CONCERNING THE BOOKS OF THE NEW.

units.la: De libris Noui Testamenti citiùs & faci-lius explicatur iudicium. Hæc igitur esto
units.tr: The judgment concerning the books of the New Testament is explained more quickly and easily. Let this therefore be the proposition.

units.la: PROPOSITIO IV.
units.tr: PROPOSITION IV.

units.la: Citra omnem controuersiam Canonici sunt ij libri: Quatuor Euangelistarum libri: Acta Apostolorum:
units.tr: Beyond all controversy, these books are Canonical: the four books of the Evangelists; the Acts of the Apostles;

units.la: Epistolæ Pauli omnes, quæ ipsius habent præfixum nomen: ideò excipitur Epistola ad Hebræos. Epistola Petri prima:& Epistola Iohannis prima.
units.tr: all the Epistles of Paul which bear his name as their heading, excepting therefore the Epistle to the Hebrews; the first Epistle of Peter; and the first Epistle of John.

units.la: PROBATIO.
units.tr: PROOF.

units.la: Eufeb. Cæsar. histor. Ecclesiastica, lib.3 [?] cap. 25. loquens de iis libris: Hæc(inquit) scripta pro indubitatis habentur.
units.tr: Eusebius of Caesarea, Ecclesiastical History, book 3 [?], chapter 25, speaking of these books: These (he says) are held as undoubted writings.

units.la: PROPOSITIO V.
units.tr: PROPOSITION V.

units.la: Reliqui libri, etsi nonnihil de illis dubita-tum tum fuit in veteri Ecclesia à multis: tamen neq; unquam reiecti fuerunt (sicut de Apocry-phu veteris Testamenti dictum est:) neq; et-iam ab omnibus dubitatum de illis fuit. Con-tinent autem doctrinam totam omnino con-sentaneam aliis Propheticis & Apostolicis li-bris. Quare pro ipso Dei verbo agnoscendi & admittendi sunt.
