units.tr: The remaining books, although something was doubted about them by many in the ancient Church, yet they were never rejected (as was said of the Apocrypha of the Old Testament), nor was there doubt about them among all. Moreover they contain a doctrine wholly consistent with the other Prophetic and Apostolic books. Therefore they are to be acknowledged and admitted as the very Word of God.

units.la: TESTIMONIA.
units.tr: TESTIMONIES.

units.la: 1:Tom.Concil.Laodicenum Concilium, omnes quos habemus, pro Canonicis habet, & agnoscit. Fuit autem circa initium Damasi Papae congregatum.
units.tr: 1: The Council of Laodicea, in the first volume of the Councils, holds and acknowledges as Canonical all the books we have. It was assembled about the beginning of the time of Pope Damasus.

units.la: Eufeb. Cæsar. histor. Eccles. lib. 3. cap.25, ostendit de illis dubitatum fuisse, non verum piam sanamq; continerent doctrinam, necne: sed an fuissent scripti ab Apostolis illis, quibus adscribuntur: nunquam autem dicit' fuisse reiectos.
units.tr: Eusebius of Caesarea, Ecclesiastical History, book 3, chapter 25, shows that doubt was raised about them, whether they contained a true, pious and sound doctrine or not; but whether they had been written by the Apostles to whom they are ascribed; yet he never says they were rejected.

units.la: Non secus scribit Hieronymus & alij, quàm dubitatum de illis fuisse, nec dicunt ab omnibus: sed indefinitè.
units.tr: Jerome and others write no differently: that doubt was raised about them, and they do not say by all, but indefinitely.

units.la: Fuisse verò à multis etiam agnitos pro scriptis Apostolorum illorum, quibus inscribuntur: liquet.
units.tr: That they were acknowledged by many also as written by those Apostles to whom they are ascribed, is clear.

units.la: Irenæus Polycarpi discipulus, qui Polycarpus discipulus fuit Iohannis Apostoli, l.3. contra Valentinum, c.18 p.178. verba multa, quæ habentur in Epistola Iohannis secunda ad Electam: omnia attribuit Iohanni Euan-gelistæ geliftæ & Apostolo: & ait, sic eum scripsisse in sua Epistola. Sensit igitur eam fuisse Epistolam Iohannis. Nam ea ipsa verba non habentur in prima Epistola: vt aliquis dicat, inde fuisse accepta.
units.tr: Irenaeus, a disciple of Polycarp, who was a disciple of the Apostle John, in book 3 Against Valentinus, chapter 18, p. 178, attributes to John the Evangelist and Apostle many words which are found in the second Epistle of John to the Elect lady, and says that he wrote thus in his Epistle. He therefore judged it to be an Epistle of John. For those very words are not found in the first Epistle, so that someone might say they were taken from there.

units.la: De Apocalypsi Ioannis, etsi permulti dubitarunt, an esset Iohannis, necne, vt Erasmus in Adventibus recitat: tamen à multis etiam grauissimis Patribus agnitam fuisse pro libro Iohannis, liquet ex iis, quæ in eam Apocalypsin præfatus est doctissimus Bullingerus, & deinde peritissimus Beza: imò ante hos D. Hieronymus in Catalogo scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum: vbi etiam scribit, eam fuisse illustratam Commentariis Iustini & Irenæi, licet non inueniantur iam. Testatur idem & Eusteb. Cæsar. lib.3.cap.25. nem-pe à permultis Patribus fuisse illum librum pro Canonico, & quidem Apostoli Iohannis agnitum.
units.tr: Concerning the Apocalypse of John, although very many doubted whether it was John's or not, as Erasmus recounts in the Adventus, yet that it was acknowledged by many, even very weighty Fathers, as a book of John, is clear from what the most learned Bullinger prefaced to his commentary on that Apocalypse, and then the most skilled Beza; indeed, before these, St. Jerome in his Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers, where he also writes that it was illustrated by commentaries of Justin and Irenaeus, although these are not found now. Eusebius of Caesarea also attests this, book 3, chapter 25: namely, that this book was acknowledged as Canonical by very many Fathers, and indeed as written by the Apostle John.

units.la: Doctrinam verò, quæ in illis continetur, fuisse ab omnibus agnitam pro doctrina Apostolica, itidem liquet: primò, quoniam nemo illam reiecit: secundò, quia qui dubitant an fuerint ab Apostolis scripti, libros eos adscribunt saltem, Apostolorum non discipulis tantùm, sed etiam comitibus. Exempla.
units.tr: But that the doctrine contained in those books was acknowledged by all as Apostolic doctrine, is equally clear: first, because no one rejected it; second, because those who doubt whether they were written by the Apostles at least ascribe those books to the Apostles' companions, not only their disciples. Examples.

units.la: Tertullianus, libro de pudicitia, Epistolam ad Hebræos adscribit Barnabæ, qui comes fuerat Pauli in prædicando Gentibus Euangelio: agnouit igitur esse Apostolicam doctrinam. Hieronymus in catalogo Ecclesiast. scri-ptorum refert de eadem epistola, alios etiam, fuisse, qui autorem illius crediderint fuisse Lucam Euangelistam: alij Clementem, Petri discipulum. Ergo etiam ij agnouerunt, do-ctrinam huius Epistolae totam esse Apostolicam.
units.tr: Tertullian, in his book On Modesty, ascribes the Epistle to the Hebrews to Barnabas, who had been Paul's companion in preaching the Gospel to the Gentiles; he therefore acknowledged it as Apostolic doctrine. Jerome, in his Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers, reports about the same Epistle that others also believed its author to have been Luke the Evangelist, others Clement, the disciple of Peter. Therefore these too acknowledged that the whole doctrine of this Epistle is Apostolic.

units.la: Hieronymus tamen in Epist. ad Galat. i. p. 159. c. Pauli esse Epistolam. Ex iis perspicuum est, nostram quintam propositionem, esse verissimam & certissimam: nempe, etsi de reliquis Noui Testamenti libris, præter illos, quos primo loco recensuimus, dubitatum à nonnullis fuerit, essentne Apostolici, necne: primo tamen non fuisse ab omnibus dubitatum. Secundò, à nemine fuisse unquam reiectos, quemadmodum de Apocryphis veteris Testamenti dictum est. Tertiò, ab omnibus fuisse in illis agnitam Apostolicam doctrinam. Quare nihil esse impedimenti: aut legitimæ causæ, cur non illos possimus & debeamus inter Canonicos connumerare, & pro verbo Dei habere.
units.tr: Jerome, however, in his Epistle to the Galatians, p. 159, [ascribes it to] Paul. From these things it is plain that our fifth proposition is most true and most certain: namely, that although doubt was raised by some about the remaining books of the New Testament, other than those which we listed first, whether they were Apostolic or not, yet first, the doubt was not raised by all. Second, they were never rejected by anyone, as was said of the Apocrypha of the Old Testament. Third, Apostolic doctrine was acknowledged in them by all. Therefore there is no hindrance, nor lawful cause, why we cannot and ought not to number them among the Canonical books and hold them as the Word of God.

units.la: Explicatum iam est id, quod ante omnia erat explicandum: quinam sint Canonici, & qui Apocryphi libri. Nam quæ post hac dicenda sunt, de Canonicis tantùm libris, hoc est, περὶ τῶν πιστευτέων χαρῶν[?], ut loquitur Apostolus, quæ sunt purum Dei verbum, intelligenda erunt: quando quidem suscepi-mus locum tractandum de Scripturis sacris, non de profanis, neque de Apocryphis.
units.tr: What had to be explained before all else has now been explained: which books are Canonical and which are Apocryphal. For what must be said hereafter, concerning Canonical books only, that is, concerning the "faithful" writings [περὶ τῶν πιστευτέων χαρῶν?], as the Apostle puts it, which are the pure Word of God, will be understood in that light, since we have undertaken to treat of the sacred Scriptures, not of profane writings, nor of the Apocrypha.

units.la: Venio igitur ad alias partitiones Bibliorum, quas paucis absoluo.
units.tr: I come therefore to the other divisions of the Bible, which I will dispatch briefly.

units.la: SECVNDA PARTITIO.
units.tr: SECOND DIVISION.

units.la: Propositio VI. Canonici libri secantur in Vetus & Nouum Testamentum.
units.tr: Proposition VI. The canonical books are divided into the Old and New Testament.

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Nomine Testamenti, intelligimus non illud, quod proprie appellatur Testamentum, hoc est, fœdus Dei, quod pepigit cum populo suo, & tandem cõfirmauit per Christum: sed libros omnes, qui ad illud fœdus aliquo modo pertinent. Ideo Vetus, vocamus libros editos ante Christi aduentum: Nouum, libros editos post Christi aduentum.
units.tr: By the name of Testament we understand not that which is properly called the Testament, that is, the covenant of God which he made with his people and at length confirmed through Christ, but all the books which in some way pertain to that covenant. Hence we call the books published before the coming of Christ the Old, and the books published after the coming of Christ the New.

units.la: Probatio.
units.tr: Proof.

units.la: Distinctio seu partitio hæc Apostolica est. 2.Cor.3. In lectione veteris Testamenti manet velamen. Nomine Testamenti apparet intellexisse Apostolum omnes libros Mosaicos & Propheticos. Vetus vero appellauit Testamentum, respectu Noui. Nouum igitur Testamentum iure dicitur liber, continens scripta Apostolorum, post aduentum Christi edita. Nam ideo illos vocauit Vetus Testamentum, vt distingueret à scriptis Apostolorum, quæ sunt post Iohannem. Est igitur certa partitio.
units.tr: This distinction or division is apostolic. 2 Cor. 3: "In the reading of the Old Testament the veil remains." By the name of Testament the Apostle evidently understood all the Mosaic and Prophetic books. He called it the Old Testament with respect to the New. The New Testament is therefore rightly taken to be the book containing the writings of the Apostles, published after the coming of Christ. For he called those the Old Testament in order to distinguish them from the writings of the Apostles, which come after John. The partition is therefore certain.

units.la: TERTIA PARTITIO.
units.tr: THE THIRD DIVISION.

units.la: PROPOSITIO VII.
units.tr: PROPOSITION VII.

units.la: Omnes libri Canonici veteris Testamenti in tres secantur classes ab Hebraeis: Legem: Prophetas: ἁγιόγραφα.
units.tr: All the canonical books of the Old Testament are divided by the Hebrews into three classes: the Law, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa [ἁγιόγραφα].

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Prima est תורה[?], hoc est, lex: in hac sunt quinque libri Mosis, à præcipua parte sic ap-pellati: qui à numero appellantur à Græcis πεντάτευχον[?]: & ab ipsis etiamHebræis חמישה quinque, scilicet libri.
units.tr: The first is Torah [תורה], that is, the Law. It contains the five books of Moses, named after their principal part; the Greeks call them the Pentateuch [πεντάτευχον] from their number. The Hebrews themselves call them Chamishah [חמישה], that is, the five books.

units.la: Secunda classis continet נביאים אחרונים[?] נביאים ראשונים id est, Prophetas priores, & Prophetas posteriores: Nomine autem priorum Prophetarum intelligunt Iosuam: Iudices: Samuelis libros, & Regum. Nomi-ne posteriorum: Iesaiam, Ieremiam, Ezechie-lem, & duodecim Minores.
units.tr: The second class contains the Prophets, Nevi'im [נביאים], namely the former Prophets [נביאים ראשונים] and the latter Prophets [נביאים אחרונים]. By the former Prophets they understand Joshua, Judges, the books of Samuel, and Kings. By the latter: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the twelve Minor Prophets.

units.la: Tertia classis continet כתובים id est, scripta, scilicet sancta, quæ Græci ἁγιόγραφα vocarunt, voce generali, quòd libri sint sancti, & à sanctis scripti, de variis sanctis rebus. Horum nomine intelligunt Iobum: Psal-mos: Proverbia: Ecclesiastem: Canticum Canticorum: Paralipomena: Esdram: Heste-ram: Danielem.
units.tr: The third class contains the Writings, Ketuvim [כתובים], that is, the holy writings, which the Greeks called Hagiographa [ἁγιόγραφα] by a general term, because the books are holy, and were written by holy men, about various sacred matters. Under this name they understand Job, the Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs, Chronicles, Ezra, Esther, and Daniel.

units.la: Hunc ordinem recitat Hieronymus in prologo Galeato. Hoc ordine Dominus Ie-sus complexus est & ipse totum vetus Testa-mentum, cùm dixit Luc. vltimo: O stulti & tardi corde ad credendum iis qua scripta sunt de me, in Lege: (Ecce primam classem: & Prophe-tis (Ecce secundam:) & Psalmis (Ecce tertiam:) in hac enim continentur Psalmi.
units.tr: Jerome recites this order in his Galeatus prologue. In this same order our Lord Jesus also embraced the whole Old Testament himself, when he said in the last chapter of Luke: "O foolish and slow of heart to believe those things which are written of me, in the Law" (behold the first class); "and in the Prophets" (behold the second); "and in the Psalms" (behold the third), for the Psalms are contained in this class.

units.la: Hinc liquet, hunc ordinem librorum ve-teris Testamenti, non esse nouum, sed antiquum, ante Christi aduentum. Hebræi tra-dunt ab Esdra post captiuitatem Babyloni-cam in hunc ordinem fuisse digestos.
units.tr: From this it is clear that this order of the books of the Old Testament is not new but ancient, dating from before the coming of Christ. The Hebrews hand down that they were arranged in this order by Ezra after the Babylonian captivity.

units.la: Libri autem noui Testamenti, in tres clas-ses etiam diuiduntur:
units.tr: The books of the New Testament are also divided into three classes:

units.la: In historias, vt sunt quatuor Euangelista-rum[?], & Actorum Apostolicorum libri:
units.tr: into histories, such as the four Gospels and the book of the Acts of the Apostles;

units.la: Epistolas, vt Pauli & aliorum:
units.tr: into Epistles, those of Paul and of the others;

units.la: Prophetiam, vt est Apocalypsis.
units.tr: into prophecy, such as the Apocalypse.

units.la: QVARTA PARTITIO.
units.tr: FOURTH DIVISION.

units.la: PROPOSITIO VIII.
units.tr: PROPOSITION VIII.

units.la: Omnes libri Canonici tam Veteris, quàm Noui Testamenti, diuiduntur in Legem, & Euangelium.
units.tr: All the canonical books of both the Old and the New Testament are divided into Law and Gospel.

units.la: Hæc partitio à summa doctrinæ sumitur, quæ in S. Bibliis continetur. Tota enim doctrina S. Scripturæ, ad hæc duo capita redigitur, ad Legem, & Euangelium. Nam vbi-que Bibliorum, aut præcepta traduntur de vitandis, & de prosequendis, in quibus duo-bus lex est posita: cum exemplis eorum, qui aut seruarunt Legem, aut transgressi sunt: & cum pœnis contra transgressores: aut doctrina de pœnitentia, & de remissione pec-catocatorum per fidem in Christum: in quibus duabus partibus consistit Euangelium.
units.tr: This division is taken from the sum of the doctrine contained in the holy Bible. For the whole doctrine of Holy Scripture is reduced to these two heads, Law and Gospel. For everywhere in the Bible either precepts are given about what is to be avoided and what is to be pursued, in which two things the Law consists: together with examples of those who either kept the Law or transgressed it, and together with punishments against transgressors; or else there is teaching about repentance and about the forgiveness of sins for those who believe in Christ, and in these two parts the Gospel consists.

units.la: His quatuor partitionibus secanturBiblia 1. In Canonicos & Apocryphos.
units.tr: By these four divisions the Bible is cut up: (1) into Canonical and Apocryphal;

units.la: 2. In Vetus & Nouum Testamentum,
units.tr: (2) into Old and New Testament;

units.la: 3. In Legales, Prophetic os, & ἁγιογράφυς[?].
units.tr: (3) into Legal, Prophetic, and hagiographical [?];

units.la: 4. In Legem, & Euangelium.
units.tr: (4) into Law and Gospel.

units.la: QVÆSTIO II.
units.tr: QUESTION II.

units.la: De mediis, quibus adduci possint homines, ut Canonicos libros vere credant & agnoscant esse θεόπνευστος[?]: & ideo eos, tanquam verum certumq; Dei verbum recipiant & amplectantur.
units.tr: On the means by which men can be brought to truly believe and acknowledge the Canonical books to be divinely inspired [θεόπνευστος?]; and therefore to receive and embrace them as the true and certain Word of God.

units.la: Hactenus, tractata & explicata fuit à no-bis quæstio prima de Scripturis S. ea autem fuit, de Canonicis & Apocryphis libris, deque partitione Bibliorum, quae quadruplex fuit:
units.tr: Thus far the first question concerning the Holy Scriptures has been treated and explained by us; it concerned the Canonical and Apocryphal books and the division of the Bible, which was fourfold:

units.la: Prima fuit huius voluminis, quod & apud Græcos, & apud Latinos pro libro Dei habetur: & Græca voce βίβλια appellatur. Secuimus igitur hoc volumen in Canonicos & Apocryphos libros: ideoq; hæc fuit
units.tr: The first was of this volume, which is held to be the book of God both among the Greeks and among the Latins, and is called by the Greek word βίβλια [books]. We have therefore divided this volume into Canonical and Apocryphal books; and therefore this was

units.la: PROPOSITIO I.
units.tr: PROPOSITION I.

units.la: Librorum qui sunt in volumine tam Græco, quàm Latino, quod Biblia appellatur: alij sunt Canonici, alij Apocryphi.
units.tr: Of the books which are in the volume, both Greek and Latin, which is called the Bible, some are Canonical and some Apocryphal.

units.la: Hic primò explicuimus vocem ἀπόκρυφος[?], vnde Canonici dicti sunt. Secundò, primum κάνονα [?] scriptum, ad quem Patres omnes examinabant doctrinas, fuisse in Ecclesia Israelitica תורת [?] ipsius Mosis: quam Legem Israelitæ acceperant pro certo Dei verbo, permoti primùm autoritate personæ ipsius Mosis, quam autoritatem ei conciliauerat Dominus, tum in Ægypto, tum in deserto, & in monte Syna.Deindè, posteaquam illam, Spiritu sancto illuminati, agnouerunt esse verbum Dei:multò magis amplexi sunt propter autoritatem & dignitatem ipsius Legis. De-nique etiam, quòd nouerunt illam in doctrinæ substantia, consentaneam esse doctrinæ, quam per successionem acceperant à Patribus. Ita hanc Legem sibi constituerunt, sic etiam iubere Domino, pro Canone, ad quem omnes doctrinæ & Prophetæ examinarentur, & ad hunc examinata scripta Propheti-ca, agnita fuisse omni ex parte esse illi con-sentanea, & eodem Spiritu conscripta, quo & Mosaica: proindè hæc, adiuncta Mosaicis scriptis fuisse secundum Canonem Ecclesiæ Israëliticæ, ad quem omnes examinarentur doctrinæ: & ad hunc Canonem voluisse Christum suam examinari doctrinam, cùm subindè ad hunc ad hunc remittebat Iudæos, dicendo: Scrutamini Scripturas, &c, & idem fecisse Apostolos: & Act.17. idem fecisse Ber-rhoënses, cùm ad hunc examinabant doctri-nam Pauli. Et quia scripta etiam omnia Apo-stolica, ad illum Canonem examinata, agni-ta fueta fuerunt, ab eodem dictata fuisse Spiritu, à quo & Mosaica & Prophetica: idcirco hæc illis adiuncta, in Canone ita fuisse posita, vt facta sint nobis tertius & vltimus Canon omnis doctrinæ & omnis religionis, ad quem omnia examinentur, vt Paulus iubet 1. Thes. 5. Omnia probate, quod bonum est, tenete. Ad quid probabimus? Ad Canonem Propheticum & Apostolicum. Sic 1. Ioh. 4. Nolite omni Spiritui credere: sed probate Spiritus, utrum ex Deo sint. Quomodo probamus? Canone hoc S. Scripturarum. Hunc vero postremum esse Canonem, & nullum alium è cœlo exspectandum: liquet Heb. cap. 1 Nouissimè locutus nobis est per Filium, &c.
units.tr: Here we first explained the word ἀπόκρυφος [hidden], whence the books were called Canonical. Second, the first rule [κανών] written, by which all the Fathers tested their doctrines, was in the Israelite Church the Law [תורה] of Moses himself; the Israelites had accepted this Law as the certain Word of God, moved first by the authority of the person of Moses himself, to which authority the Lord had lent weight, both in Egypt and in the desert and on Mount Sinai. Then, after they had been illuminated by the Holy Spirit and had recognised it to be the Word of God, they embraced it much more on account of the authority and dignity of the Law itself. Finally, also because they knew that it was in its substance consonant with the doctrine which they had received by succession from the Fathers. Thus they established this Law for themselves as a rule, and so the Lord also commanded it, as the canon by which all doctrines and prophets were to be examined; and by this canon the prophetic writings, once examined, were recognised to be in every respect consonant with it and written by the same Spirit as the Mosaic writings. Therefore these, added to the Mosaic writings, were in the canon of the Israelite Church according to this rule, by which all doctrines were to be examined; and Christ wished his own doctrine to be examined by this canon, when he repeatedly referred the Jews to it, saying: Search the Scriptures, etc.; and the Apostles did the same; and the Bereans did the same in Acts 17, when they examined the doctrine of Paul by it. And because all the Apostolic writings too, examined by that canon, were recognised to have been dictated by the same Spirit as the Mosaic and Prophetic, therefore these, added to them, were so placed in the canon that they have become for us the third and last canon of all doctrine and all religion, by which all things are to be examined, as Paul commands in 1 Thess. 5: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. By what shall we prove them? By the Prophetic and Apostolic canon. So in 1 John 4: Believe not every spirit, but try the spirits, whether they are of God. How do we try them? By this canon of the Holy Scriptures. That this is the last canon, and that no other is to be expected from heaven, is clear from Heb. 1: God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son, etc.

units.la: Conclusimus, Canonicos in Ecclesia appellari libros, quos Apostolus in epistol. ad Timoth. vocat θεόπνευστος[?]: Apocryphos vero, hoc est, absconditos & ignotos, quos Ecclesia non agnouit consentaneos fuisse Canoni, nec ab eodem Spiritu dictatos, à quo reliqui: sed potiùs humanum quendam spirare Spiritum: ac proindè etiam ab Ecclesia judicatos fuisse indignos, qui in publico cœtu Ecclesiæ palàm legerētur, sed legi tantùm posse priuatim domi. Atque hæc dicta fuere explicandæ primæ propositionis causa.
units.tr: We conclude that those books are called Canonical in the Church which the Apostle in his epistle to Timothy calls θεόπνευστος [divinely inspired]; but Apocryphal, that is, hidden and unknown, are those which the Church has not acknowledged to be consonant with the canon, nor dictated by the same Spirit as the rest, but rather to breathe a certain human spirit; and therefore the Church has also judged them unworthy to be read openly in the public assembly of the Church, but to be read only privately at home. And these things have been said for the sake of explaining the first proposition.

units.la: PROPOSITIO II.
units.tr: PROPOSITION II.

units.la: Canonici habent autoritatem ad constituenda, & ad probanda fidei dogmata: Apocryphi autem nullam. Probavi primò, argumento ducto à fide, quæ est ex solo auditu verbi Dei, Rom. 10[?]. Ad statuenda igitur aut probanda fidei dogmata, solum Dei verbum habere autoritatem: Hoc autem in solis Canonicis continetur.
units.tr: The Canonical books have authority to establish and to prove the dogmas of faith; the Apocryphal books have none. I proved this first, by an argument drawn from faith, which comes from the hearing of the Word of God alone, Rom. 10 [?]. Therefore, to establish or prove the dogmas of faith, only the Word of God has authority; and this is contained only in the Canonical books.

units.la: Secundò, à testimoniis Patrum, Hieronymi in præfatione in lib. Salomonis: Cypriani seu Rufini in Symbolo Apostolorum: Cœcilij Laodiceni, Can. 59 Hinc iotulimus[?], multò minus ergo scripta Patrum hanc habere autoritatem.
units.tr: Second, from the testimonies of the Fathers: Jerome in the preface to the books of Solomon; Cyprian or Rufinus on the Apostles' Creed; Caecilius of Laodicea, Canon 59. Hence [?], much less, therefore, do the writings of the Fathers have this authority.

units.la: PROPOSITIO III.
units.tr: PROPOSITION III.

units.la: Continet qui sint Canonici, qui Apocryphi in veteri Testamento. Apocryphi sunt, Thobias: Iudith: Esdræ tertius & quartus: Sapientia Salomonis: Ecclesiasticus: Ieremiæ Episto-la: Baruch: Canticum trium puerorum, adiectum tertio capiti Danielis: Item 13. & 14. caput Dan. Item libri Machabæorum. Reliqui Canonici.
units.tr: It contains which books are canonical and which are apocryphal in the Old Testament. The apocryphal books are: Tobit; Judith; Esdras the third and fourth; the Wisdom of Solomon; Ecclesiasticus; the Epistle of Jeremiah; Baruch; the Song of the Three Children, added to the third chapter of Daniel; likewise the 13th and 14th chapters of Daniel; and the books of the Maccabees. The rest are canonical.

units.la: Probatio: ex traditione veteris Ecclesiæ, quam primò propter illius autoritatem recipimus: secundò, propter autoritatem ipsorum librorum, in quibus per Spiritum sanctum videmus non hominem, sed Deum loqui. Oues[?] enim voce sui pastoris agnoscunt.
units.tr: Proof: from the tradition of the ancient Church, which we accept first on account of its authority; and second, on account of the authority of the books themselves, in which through the Holy Spirit we see that it is not man but God who speaks. For the sheep recognise the voice of their shepherd.

units.la: In medium igitur adduximus, primum, testimonium totius Ecclesiæ Israëliticæ, quæ nullos unquam alios agnovit pro Canoni-cis, cis, nisi quos habemus in Bibliis Hebraicis, & quos indicauimus.
units.tr: We have therefore brought forward, first, the testimony of the whole Israelite Church, which never recognised as canonical any books other than those we have in the Hebrew Bible, and which we have indicated.

units.la: Deinde ex veteri Ecclesia Christi octo Patres praestantissimos, Hieronymum in prologo Galeato: Cyprianum in Symbolum: Euseb. Caesar. lib. 3. cap. 10. dum recitat sententiam Iosephi: Originem apud Euseb. lib. 6. cap. 25. Melitonem Sardensem Episcopum, apud Euseb. lib. 4. cap. 26. Epiphanium in panario, Tom. primo, libri primi haer. 8. Item lib. de mensuris & ponder. pag. 604. & 614. Hilarium in prologo in Psalm. Concilium Laodicenum, can. 59.
units.tr: Next, from the ancient Church of Christ, eight most outstanding Fathers: Jerome in his Preface to the Galeatus; Cyprian on the Creed; Eusebius of Caesarea, book 3, chapter 10, where he recounts the opinion of Josephus; Origen, in Eusebius, book 6, chapter 25; Melito, bishop of Sardis, in Eusebius, book 4, chapter 26; Epiphanius in the Panarion, vol. 1, book 1, heresy 8; likewise in the book on weights and measures, pp. 604 and 614; Hilary in the preface to the Psalms; the Council of Laodicea, canon 59.

units.la: De libris Machabaeorum, speciatim Ge-lasius excludit a Canone secundum: Augu-stinus utrumque fatetur non esse in Canone Hebraeorum: & sobrie esse legendum, Tom. 7. contra Gaudentij epistolam, lib. 2. cap. 23. Et Tom. 7 [?]. de Ciuitate Dei, lib. 18. cap. 36.
units.tr: Concerning the books of the Maccabees in particular, Gelasius excludes the second from the canon; Augustine acknowledges that neither is in the canon of the Hebrews, and that they are to be read soberly: vol. 7, against the letter of Gaudentius, book 2, chapter 23; and vol. 7 [?], On the City of God, book 18, chapter 36.

units.la: Ad obiecta Pontificiorum, qui alios Patres adducunt,
units.tr: In reply to the objections of the Papists, who bring forward other Fathers,

units.la: Responsum fuit, has tres regulas esse tenendas in hac iudiciorum diuersitate. Primam: Quotquot citantur in Nouo Testamento: eos esse Canonicos. Secundam: Quotquot ab omnibus Ecclesiis & semper: esse eos Canonicos. Tertiam: In aliis, de quibus controuertitur, sequendum esse iudicium vetustioris [?] Ecclesiae, & veteriorum Patrum, maiorisque autoritatis, quia viciniores Apostolis. Item eos, qui melius inter se confentiunt. Tales sunt, quos adduximus pro no-stra sententia.
units.tr: The answer was given that three rules are to be held in this diversity of judgements. The first: whatever books are cited in the New Testament, those are canonical. The second: whatever books have been received by all Churches and always, those are canonical. The third: in other books, about which there is dispute, the judgement of the more ancient Church and of the earlier Fathers, of greater authority because they were nearer the Apostles, must be followed; likewise those which agree better among themselves. Such are the ones we have brought forward in support of our opinion.

units.la: PROPOSITIO IV. De libris Noui Testamenti.
units.tr: PROPOSITION IV. Concerning the books of the New Testament.

units.la: Citra controuersiam Canonici sunt libri Euangelistarum, & Acta, & Epistolæ Pauli cum eius nomine: Epistola Iohannis prima: Petri prima. Euseb. lib. 3. cap. 25.
units.tr: Beyond controversy the canonical books are the books of the Evangelists, and the Acts, and the Epistles of Paul with his name; the first Epistle of John; the first of Peter. Eusebius, book 3, chapter 25.

units.la: PROPOSITIO V. Reliqui, non est ulla legitima causa, cur non debeant inter Canonicos recenseri.
units.tr: PROPOSITION V. As for the rest, there is no lawful reason why they should not be counted among the canonical books.

units.la: Probatio 1. Non fuit ab omnibus de illis dubitatum: imò grauissimi viri eos agnoue-runt, alij alios pro Canonicis. Iren. lib 3. c. 18. Quæ sunt in Epistola ad Electam, adscribit Iohanni Apostolo & Euangelistæ. Clem. Alexandr. Epistolam ad Hebræos Paulo. Iustinus Martyr & Iren. & alij, teste Hieronymo, attribuunt Iohanni Euangelistæ.
units.tr: Proof 1. They were not doubted by all; indeed, very weighty men acknowledged them, some ascribing some of them to others. Irenaeus, book 3, chapter 18, ascribes what is in the Epistle to the Elect to the Apostle and Evangelist John. Clement of Alexandria ascribes the Epistle to the Hebrews to Paul. Justin Martyr, Irenaeus and others, as Jerome testifies, ascribe [the Revelation] to the Evangelist John.

units.la: 2. Nunquam fuerunt ab Ecclesia Catholica reiecti, sicut Apocryphi in veteri Testamento.
units.tr: 2. They were never rejected by the Catholic Church, as the Apocryphal books of the Old Testament were.

units.la: 3. Doctrina approbata omnibus. Tertull. enim lib. de pudicitia dat Epistolam ad Hebræos Barnabæ: alij Lucæ.
units.tr: 3. Doctrine approved by all. For Tertullian, in his book On Modesty, gives the Epistle to the Hebrews to Barnabas; others to Luke.

units.la: SECVNDA PARTITIO.
units.tr: SECOND DIVISION.

units.la: PROPOSITIO VI. Omnes libri Canonici secantur in Vetus & Nouum Testamentum.
units.tr: PROPOSITION VI. All canonical books are divided into the Old and the New Testament.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Nomine veteris Testamenti intelligimus volumen librorum sanctorum ante Chri-stum scriptum,& qui extant.
units.tr: By the name of the Old Testament we understand the collection of the holy books written before Christ, and which are extant.

units.la: Noui,volumen librorum, qui post Christum ab Apostolis conscripti sunt. 2. ad Co-rinth.3.
units.tr: Of the New, the collection of the books which were written by the Apostles after Christ. 2. Corinthians 3.

units.la: TERTIA PARTITIO.
units.tr: THIRD DIVISION.

units.la: PROPOSITIO VII.
units.tr: PROPOSITION VII.

units.la: Omnes Canonici veteris Testamenti in tres classes secantur, Legem: Prophetas: ἁγιο-γραφῆς[?].
units.tr: All the canonical books of the Old Testament are divided into three classes: the Law, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa [ἁγιογραφῆς?].

units.la: In hac propositione explicatum fuit, qui sint in unaquaque classe.
units.tr: In this proposition it was explained which books belong to each class.

units.la: Hanc distinctionem probat Christus Lu-cæ 24.
units.tr: Christ proves this division in Luke 24.

units.la: Noui Testamenti libri etiam in tres clas-ses distinguuntur: in Historias: Epistolas: A-pocalypsin.
units.tr: The books of the New Testament are also distinguished into three classes: the Histories, the Epistles, and the Apocalypse.

units.la: QVARTA PARTITIO.
units.tr: FOURTH PART.

units.la: PROPOSITIO VIII.
units.tr: PROPOSITION VIII.

units.la: Utrumq; Testamentum, in Legem & Evangelium distribuitur.
units.tr: Both Testaments are divided into Law and Gospel.

units.la: Ita conclusum est, quid sibi voluerit Apostolus illa sententia: Omnis Scriptura θεόπνευ-στος (ἐστι:[?]) & quot habeat partes.
units.tr: Thus it has been concluded what the Apostle meant by that saying: All Scripture is divinely inspired [θεόπνευστος (ἐστι:[?])] and how many parts it has.

units.la: Nunc methodus ipsa postulat, ut videa-mus, quænam sint illa media, quibus adduci homines possint, vt hosce libros, quos Canonicos diximus appellari, credant & agnoscant vere esse Θεόπνευστα [?]: ac proinde, vt eos, tanquam certissimum Dei verbum recipiant & amplectantur, & in illorum doctrina permaneant, vt Apostolus hortatur.
units.tr: Now the method itself requires us to see what those means are by which men can be brought to believe and acknowledge that these books, which we have called canonical, are truly divinely inspired [Θεόπνευστα [?]], and therefore to receive and embrace them as the most certain Word of God, and to remain in their teaching, as the Apostle exhorts.

units.la: Etsi enim aliquid ex illis, quæ dicta a nobis sunt, de hac quæstione poterit colligi: tamen vtilitas lectoris postulat, vt seorsum de hac re clarius disseramus.
units.tr: For although some of the things we have said can be gathered from this question, nevertheless the usefulness of the reader requires that we discuss this matter more clearly and separately.

units.la: Ad hunc autem locum tractandum Apostolus nos provocat, imò compellit, cùm Timotheo persuadet, vt permaneat in recepta doctrina, argumento vno ducto ab auctoritate Apostoli, à quo illam didicerat: altero ab authoritate Scripturarum, quas ab infante ætate, per gratiam Spiritus S. noverat: deinde etiam aliis argumentis: quæ explicavimus.
units.tr: Now, the Apostle challenges us to treat this passage, indeed compels us, when he persuades Timothy to remain in the doctrine he had received, using two arguments: one drawn from the authority of the Apostle from whom he had learned it, the other from the authority of the Scriptures, which he had known from infancy through the grace of the Holy Spirit; and then also by other arguments, which we have explained.

units.la: Nunc igitur quæritur, an ad cognoscendum, qui sint libri Canonici, seu quæ sit Scriptura Θεόπνευστος, & quæ non: traditio & auctoritas Ecclesiæ sufficere debeat & possit, necne: & si non sufficit, quænam illa sint media, quibus adduci possint homines, vt hoc vere & certò agnoscant. Quæstio vtilior est quàm forte prima fronte apparet.
units.tr: Now therefore the question is whether tradition and the authority of the Church ought to be sufficient, and are able, to recognise which books are canonical, or which Scripture is divinely inspired and which is not; or not; and if it is not sufficient, what those means are by which men can be brought to recognise this truly and with certainty. This question is more useful than it perhaps appears at first sight.

units.la: Papistæ tantum tribuunt Ecclesiæ, non dicam Catholicæ, quia non possum, sed Romanæ, vt sentiant illius authoritatem vsque adeò magnam esse & efficacem ad fidem faciendam de libris Cano-nicis & non Canonicis, nicis , ut solum eius testimonium sufficere nobis debeat: Imò quicquid iam habet authoritatis sacra Scriptura, propter quam fide digna fit,& pro tali habeatur, totum hoc habere illam ab Ecclesia. Quare authoritatem Ecclesiæ maiorem esse authoritate Scripturarum: atque ita maiorem, ut possit in Scripturis multa dispensare.
units.tr: The Papists attribute so much to the Church, I will not say the Catholic Church, because I cannot, but the Roman Church, that they judge its authority to be so great and so effective in establishing faith concerning canonical and non-canonical books, that its testimony alone ought to be sufficient for us. Indeed, whatever authority holy Scripture now has, by which it is worthy of belief and is held to be such, they say all of this it has from the Church. Therefore the authority of the Church is greater than the authority of the Scriptures, and so much greater that it can dispense many things in the Scriptures.

units.la: Alij, ipsam Scripturam non opus habere alieno testimonio: per se enim ad hoc sufficere, quòd ipsa sese, an sit à Deo, necne inspirata, luculenter patefaciat: sicut Sol suo se lumine, quid sit, declaret: itidem & lucerna accensa: Scripturam autem esse lumen, & lucernam accensam, testimonio Petri & Dauidis. Non igitur opus habere alieno testimonio, quod dicat, hoc est verbum Dei, hoc non est: tantum abest, ut solum testimonium Ecclesiæ sufficere possit.
units.tr: Others say that Scripture itself does not need the testimony of another; for by itself it is sufficient for this, that it plainly reveals itself, whether it is inspired by God or not, just as the sun declares what it is by its own light, and likewise a lamp that is lit; and that Scripture is a light and a lit lamp is shown by the testimony of Peter and David. Therefore it does not need the testimony of another to say, this is the Word of God, this is not; so far is it from being the case that the testimony of the Church alone could be sufficient.

units.la: Nos ad quæstionem his respondemus propositionibus.
units.tr: We answer the question with these propositions.

units.la: PROPOSITIO I.
units.tr: PROPOSITION I.

units.la: Non est cuiuspiam hominis, neque etiam totius Ecclesiæ, sed solius Dei, efficere ut quis certò agnoscat, hanc de qua loquimur Scripturam esse θεόπνευστον[?], alias verò minimè.
units.tr: It is not the task of any man, nor even of the whole Church, but of God alone, to bring it about that someone certainly recognises that the Scripture we are speaking of is divinely inspired [θεόπνευστον[?]], and otherwise not at all.

units.la: A.[?] Perspicua est propositio, ut non opus habeat explicatione: venio igitur ad confirmationem.
units.tr: A.[?] The proposition is clear, so that it needs no explanation; I come therefore to the confirmation.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmation.

units.la: 1 Qui non potest donare Spiritum sanctum & fidem: is certè non potest efficere vt quis agnoscat & discernat verbum Dei, à nō verbo Dei. Ad hoc enim opus est Spiritu sanc□to & lumine fidei: cùm opus sit Spiritus & fidei. 1 Cor.2. Animalis homo non percipit ea, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei,&c. Nos autem Spiritum Dei accepimus: vt sciamus quæ à Deo,&c. Ioh. 6. Apostoli aiunt, Nos credidimus & cognovimus, quòd tu es Christus,&c.
units.tr: 1. He who cannot bestow the Holy Spirit and faith certainly cannot bring it about that someone recognises and distinguishes the Word of God from what is not the Word of God. For this requires the Holy Spirit and the light of faith, since there is need of the Spirit and of faith. 1 Cor. 2: The natural man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God, etc. But we have received the Spirit of God, that we may know the things that are from God, etc. John 6: The apostles say, We have believed and have known that you are the Christ, etc.

units.la: Primò aiunt, Credidimus, deinde cognovimus: vt ostendant, hanc cognitionem rerum diuinarum, opus esse fidei.
units.tr: First they say, We have believed, then we have known, to show that this knowledge of divine things is the work of faith.

units.la: Atqui nemo hominum, nec vniuersa Ecclesia, excepto capite Christo, potest cuiquam largiri Spiritum sanctum & fidem. Est enim donum Dei, Phil.1. Ephes.2. idque tam quoad initium, quàm quoad incrementum, Hebr.12. Huc illud in Actis, 8. Petrus ait Simoni: Pecunia tua tecum sit in perditionem. Existimasti enim donum Dei pecuniis parari posse, hoc est, esse in hominum arbitrio, illum donare cui velint, etiam pro pecuniis, Ergo,&c.
units.tr: But no man, nor the whole Church, except the head, Christ, can bestow the Holy Spirit and faith on anyone. For it is a gift of God, Phil. 1; Eph. 2; and this both as to its beginning and as to its increase, Heb. 12. To this belongs what is said in Acts 8, where Peter says to Simon: Let your money perish with you. For you thought that the gift of God could be obtained with money, that is, that it is in the power of men to bestow it on whom they wish, even for money. Therefore, etc.

units.la: 2. Res spirituales, non possunt nisi lumine supernaturali percipi & vere cognosci: illud autem donare non est, nisi illius, qui est supra naturam, Deus. Non plura addo testimonia & rationes, quia res perspicua est.
units.tr: 2. Spiritual things cannot be perceived and truly known except by supernatural light; but to bestow that light belongs to no one except God, who is above nature. I add no further testimonies and arguments, because the matter is plain.

units.la: PROPOSITIO II.
units.tr: PROPOSITION II.

units.la: Non est etiam Scriptura sancta per sefo-lius hoc efficere: sed opus est Spiritus S. men-tem hominis legentis aut audientis Scriptu-ram, ita illustrante, ut videat, acsentiat, Deum loqui in Scripturis, non hominem.
units.tr: Nor can holy Scripture alone bring this about; but there is need of the Holy Spirit to so illuminate the mind of the man who reads or hears Scripture that he sees and assents that God speaks in the Scriptures, not man.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmatio.

units.la: Si Scriptura S. hoc ex se sola posset prae-stare: omnes qui illam aut audiunt, aut le-gunt, etiam agnoscerent, esse verbum Dei, cum reuera sit verbum Dei. Non omnes au-tem hoc norunt, etsi legunt & audiunt. Hoc liquet exemplis Scripturarum, & quotidia-na experientia. Etsi igitur Scriptura in se lu-men est, lucernaq; accensa, imo Sol splendi-dissimus: tamen, sicut Sol non potest sese caeco homini quis & qualis sit patefacere, nisi caecus aliunde illuminetur: Ita Scriptura non potest sese agnoscendam reipsa praebere cuiquam homini, nisi Sp. S. mens hominis ad videndam Scripturae dignitatem illustretur: & aures ad audiendum Deum in illis loquen-tem, aperiantur. Quare neque Scriptura sua sola dignitate & autoritate quam habet, sine Spiritu sancto sufficit ad hoc, ut quis eam a-gnoscat certum esse Dei verbum.
units.tr: If Holy Scripture could accomplish this by itself, then all who either hear or read it would also recognise that it is the Word of God, since it truly is the Word of God. Yet not all know this, even though they read and hear it. This is clear from the examples in Scripture and from everyday experience. So although Scripture in itself is a light, a lamp kindled, indeed the most brilliant Sun, nevertheless, just as the Sun cannot reveal to a blind man who or what it is unless the blind man is illumined by some other means, so Scripture cannot present itself to anyone as something to be recognised in fact, unless the mind of the man is illumined by the Holy Spirit to see the dignity of Scripture, and the ears are opened to hear God speaking in those writings. Therefore Scripture, by the dignity and authority it has in itself, is not sufficient without the Holy Spirit for anyone to recognise it as the certain Word of God.

units.la: Pelagiani tamen, hoc non admittebant: quia non concedebant, tantam esse naturae nostrae corruptionem, ut mens non possit discernere inter ea quae Dei sunt, & quae nō Dei: inter doctrinam Dei, & doctrinas ho-minum, modò ei offerantur. Ergo uno aut altero testimonio Scripturarum refellantur ipsi,&nostra confirmetur propositio. Actor. prædicante Paulo Philippis ad multas mulieres:omnes quidem audiebant, non de omnibus tamen dicitur, sed de vna tantùm Lydia,Dominum aperuisse illi cor, ut inten-deret iis,quæ dicebantur à Paulo:quantò mi-nùs potuisset intelligere & agnoscere, ea ef-se Dei verba: nisi Dominus ei cor aperuisset Spiritu suo?
units.tr: The Pelagians, however, did not admit this, because they did not grant that our nature's corruption is so great that the mind cannot discern between what belongs to God and what does not, between the doctrine of God and the doctrines of men, when these are offered to it. Let them therefore be refuted by one or another testimony of Scripture, and our proposition be confirmed. In Acts, when Paul preached to many women at Philippi, all indeed were listening, yet it is not said of all, but of Lydia alone, that the Lord opened her heart to attend to the things that were said by Paul. How much less could she have understood and recognised that these were the words of God, unless the Lord had opened her heart by his Spirit?

units.la: Ioannis cap. 8. prædicabat Iudæis multis Christus: alij crediderunt in eum: alij eum habebant pro blasphemo homine : omnes tamen audiebant verbum.
units.tr: In John chapter 8, Christ preached to many Jews. Some believed in him; others held him to be a blasphemer. Yet all heard the word.

units.la: 1.Cor.2 Animalis homo non percipit ea, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei:stultitia enim illi sunt, necpo-test percipere:quia spiritualiter(id est, per Spi-ritum S.)diiudicantur. Quomodo igitur po-test quispiam ex solo auditu Scripturæ, il-lam agnoscere pro Dei verbo,cùm potiùs il-lam iudicet esse stultitiam, stultissimamque doctrinam? Atque hæc satis ad confirmatio-nem secundæ propositionis.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 2: "The natural man does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God; for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot perceive them, because they are spiritually discerned" (that is, by the Holy Spirit). How then can anyone, from the bare hearing of Scripture, recognise it as the Word of God, when he rather judges it to be foolishness, and the most foolish teaching? And these things are enough to confirm the second proposition.

units.la: PROPOSITIO III.
units.tr: PROPOSITIO III.

units.la: Nullis etiam rationibus, siue ab antiqui-tate, siue à consonantia Scripturarum, siue à miraculis, quibus fuit Scriptura S. confirma-ti, siue à complemento vaticiniorum eius, si-ue ab alio quovis loco, deductis, persuaderi [?]illi hominum potest, hos libros esse θεόπνευ-στος, alios nequaquam, sine Spiritu S. intus hoc demonstrante.
units.tr: Nor can it be persuaded to any man, by any arguments whatever, whether drawn from antiquity, from the agreement of the Scriptures, from the miracles by which Holy Scripture was confirmed, from the fulfilment of its prophecies, or from any other source, that these books are θεόπνευστος [God-breathed] and the others are not, without the Holy Spirit demonstrating this inwardly.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmatio.

units.la: Est etiam haec ex testimoniis superius allatis perspicua: praesertim ex illo 1.Corint. 2. Animalis homo non percipit, nec potest percipere. Quem enim intelligit nomine Animalis hominis? hominem, qui rationibus quidem ducatur, sed sine Spiritu Dei. Item ex illo Matt. 11. Abscondisti haec a sapientibus. Item ex illo 1.Cor. 2. Sermo meus & praedicatio mea, non fuit in persuasoriis humanae sapientiae verbis, sed in demonstratione Spiritus & potentiae: ut fides vestra non sit in sapientia hominum, sed in potentia Dei.
units.tr: This is also clear from the testimonies cited above, especially from 1 Cor. 2: "The natural man does not perceive, nor can he perceive." For whom does he understand by the name natural man? A man who is indeed led by reasons, but without the Spirit of God. Likewise from Matt. 11: "You have hidden these things from the wise." Likewise from 1 Cor. 2: "My speech and my preaching was not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that your faith may not rest in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God."

units.la: Ac certè, si illa argumenta hanc haberent vim: citius Philosophi & alij sapientes ad fidem perducerentur, & ad hanc, de qua loquimur, cognitionem verbi Dei, quàm plebei & idiotae: quoniam illi harum [?]sunt rationum capaciores istis. At contrarium affirmat Paulus, 1.Cor. 1. Videte vocationem vestram, quoniam non multi sapientes secundum carnem elegit Deus, sed stulta Mundi elegit Deus. Et ante te ipsum Christus, Matth. 11. Pater gratias ago tibi, quia abscondisti haec a sapientibus.
units.tr: Indeed, if those arguments had this force, philosophers and other wise men would be brought to faith and to this knowledge of the Word of God, of which we speak, more quickly than common people and the unlearned, since they are more capable of these arguments than those. But Paul affirms the contrary, 1 Cor. 1: "Consider your calling, that not many wise according to the flesh were chosen by God, but God chose the foolish things of the world." And Christ himself, before you, Matt. 11: "Father, I give thanks to you, because you have hidden these things from the wise."

units.la: PROPOSITIO IV.
units.tr: PROPOSITIO IV.

units.la: Ergo Spiritus S. qui mentem mentisque oculos aperiat atq; illuminet, non solum necessacessarius est ad hoc, ut quis vere agnoscat Canonicos libros esse θεόπνευστος: sed etiam ad hanc rem ille unus, sine ullo testimonio Ecclesiæ, sineq; ullis rationibus, idoneus est atq; sufficiens doctor.
units.tr: Therefore the Holy Spirit, who opens and illumines the mind and the eyes of the mind, is not only necessary for anyone truly to recognise the canonical books as θεόπνευστος, but also, without any testimony of the Church and without any arguments, he alone is a fit and sufficient teacher for this matter.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmatio.

units.la: 1.Cor.2. Nos autem Spiritum Christi accepimus, ut sciamus, quæ nobis à Deo donata sunt, nempe omnia, inter quæ est etiam verbum. Item, Spiritus autem omnia scrutatur, etiam profunda Dei.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 2: "But we have received the Spirit of Christ, that we may know the things that have been given to us by God," namely all things, among which is also the Word. Likewise: "The Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God."

units.la: Actor.9. Apostolus Paulus certè sine ullo Ecclesiæ testimonio, sineque ullis argumen-tis, solo Spiritu Christi illustratus, agnovit Christum, & quæ Christus prædicaverat, si-bique etiam dixerat, ipsissimum esse Dei verbum. Idem longè ante contigit Mosi & Pro-phetis, cùm afflabantur Spiritu Dei.
units.tr: Acts 9: The Apostle Paul, certainly without any testimony of the Church and without any arguments, illumined by the Spirit of Christ alone, recognised Christ, and that what Christ had preached and had even said to him was the very Word of God. The same happened long before to Moses and the Prophets, when they were inspired by the Spirit of God.

units.la: 1.Ioh.1. Sed vos vnctionem habetis, & nostis omnia. Quæ est ista vnctio? Spiritus S. qui un-git nos in Doctores & Prophetas, ut quæ Dei sunt, probè intelligamus.
units.tr: 1 John 1: "But you have an anointing, and you know all things." What is that anointing? The Holy Spirit, who anoints us as teachers and prophets, so that we rightly understand the things of God.

units.la: 1.Cor.2. Spiritualis homo diiudicat omnia: ipse autem à nemine iudicatur: hoc est, de o-mni doctrina, quæ proponatur, ille qui Spi-ritu Dei præditus est, facilè certum feretiu-dicium, utrum sit θεόπνευστος[?] necne: Ipse au-tem, eiusque doctrina, à nemine, id est, à nul-lo homine, (qui sit sine Spiritu) diiudicatur, discernive potest ab aliis doctrinis: ac proinde necesse est, ut ij homines alieno tan-tum stent iudicio. An non res est perspicua nostro tempore? Cur Papistæ nil urgent, cum nos nostramque damnant doctri[?]nam, nisi Ecclesiæ Romanæ iudicium? Ecclesia (inquiunt) damnat vos vestramque doctrinam ut hæreticam: hoc nobis est satis: volumus disputare: cur, inquam, ita ab aliorum pendent iudicio? quia cum sint sine Spiritu Dei, nullamque teneant Scripturarum cognitionem, non possunt nos diiudicare.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 2: "The spiritual man judges all things, yet he himself is judged by no one." That is, concerning every doctrine that is put forward, one who is endowed with the Spirit of God can easily give a certain judgement whether it is θεόπνευστος or not. But he himself, and his doctrine, is judged by no one, that is, by no man who is without the Spirit, and such a person cannot discern him or distinguish his teaching from other doctrines; and therefore it is necessary that those men should stand solely by another's judgement. Is this not clear in our own time? Why do the Papists press nothing, when they condemn us and our doctrine, except the judgement of the Roman Church? "The Church," they say, "condemns you and your doctrine as heretical: that is enough for us; we want to dispute." Why, I ask, do they depend so much on the judgement of others? Because, since they are without the Spirit of God and hold no knowledge of the Scriptures, they cannot judge us.

units.la: Ex iis omnibus liquido apparet, verissi-mam esse quartam nostram propositionem: Proinde Apostolus merito in contextu, què supra interpretati sumus ad Timoth. non simpliciter ait, Permane in iis, qua audiuisti, sed, qua didicisti, sciens a quo didiceris. Item, de scripturis non dixit simpliciter: Et quod sacras literas legeris: sed, quod sacras literas no-sti. Nam & doctrinam ab Apostolo potuisset audire & S. literas legere, sine hoc speciali S. S. dono: sed illam didicisse, & S. literas nouisse: hoc certè sine Spiritus S. gratia fieri non potuit. Quamobrem non est simplici-ter argumentatus Apostolus ab authoritate sua, & ab authoritate Scripturæ: sed etiam a Spiritu S. qui utramque patefecit Timotheo. Per hunc enim Spiritum, non solum agnoscimus ipsam Scripturam verè esse θεό-πνευστον[?]: sed etiam reipsa sentimus, in hac Scrip-tura certissimam quandam numinis altissi-mi vim vigere, qua sentimus nos suauissimè pertrahi ad hanc Scripturam amandam, amplectendam, & ut pretiosum thesaurum in corde conseruandam: ita ut ab eius studio recedere nequeas neq; dies neq; noctes.
units.tr: From all these things it is plainly apparent that our fourth proposition is most true. Therefore the Apostle, in the context which we have explained above to Timothy, rightly does not simply say, "Continue in the things you have heard," but "in the things you have learned, knowing from whom you have learned." Likewise, concerning the Scriptures he did not simply say, "and that you have read the sacred letters," but "that you have known the sacred letters." For he could have heard the doctrine from the Apostle and read the Holy Letters without this special gift of the Holy Spirit; but to have learned that doctrine and to have known the Holy Letters, this certainly could not happen without the grace of the Holy Spirit. Wherefore the Apostle did not argue simply from his own authority and from the authority of Scripture, but also from the Holy Spirit, who revealed both to Timothy. For through this Spirit we not only recognise that Scripture itself is truly θεόπνευστος [God-breathed], but also actually feel that in this Scripture a most certain power of the Most High God is active, by which we feel ourselves most sweetly drawn to love this Scripture, to embrace it, and to keep it in the heart as a precious treasure, so that you cannot turn away from its study neither by day nor by night.

units.la: Eiusdem etiam vi sentimus nos indies renouari in nouos homines. Nam apertis oculis per Spiritum sanctum videmus Christum in Scripturis: & dum eum ibi contemplamur ceu in speculo: imago Christi, quæ ibi relucet, mentibus nostris imprimitur, ita ut fiamus ei similes in iustitia & sanctitate vitæ 2.Corinth.3. Hoc docuit Apostolus: Ubi Spiritus Domini, ibi libertas. Nos autem omnes retecta facie gloriam Domini in speculo repræsentantes, ad eandem imaginem transformamur à gloria in gloriam, tanquam à Domini Spiritu. Hic igitur Spiritus ille est, qui ita nobis certò & perspicuè ostendit, hanc Scripturam esse certum Dei verbum, ut opus non habeamus vllo Ecclesiæ testimonio, ullisve rationibus. Est enim hæc persuasio cœlestis à Deo.
units.tr: By the same power we feel ourselves renewed daily into new men. For with eyes opened through the Holy Spirit we see Christ in the Scriptures; and while we contemplate him there as in a mirror, the image of Christ shining there is imprinted on our minds, so that we become like him in righteousness and holiness of life. 2 Cor. 3. The Apostle taught this: "Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty. But we all, with unveiled face, reflecting the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord." This Spirit, therefore, is the one who shows us so certainly and plainly that this Scripture is the certain Word of God, that we have no need of any testimony of the Church or of any arguments. For this persuasion is heavenly, from God.

units.la: Cæterùm, ut sciamus, neque testimonium Ecclesiæ, neque auditum verbi esse superuacanea, (sed utilia, & etiam necessaria: ideò illud notandum est, hunc Spiritum non solere à Deo cuipiam communicari (de via ordinaria loquimur)nisi ex auditu verbi. Galat. 3. Ex operibus legis Spiritum accepistis, an ex auditu fidei? Fides certè non datur, nisi ex auditu verbi. Rom. 10. Verbum autem prædicatur ab Ecclesia: quæ publicè testatur, hoc esse verbum Dei: Ecclesiæ autem prædicanti, & hoc esse verbum Dei testificanti, aures minimè præberemus: nisi illius auctoritas atque dignitas, quam illi variis modis conciliauit Deus, nonnihil nos ad eam tanquam fide dignam, audiendam commoueret.
units.tr: Now, so that we understand that neither the testimony of the Church nor the hearing of the word is superfluous, but useful and even necessary, we must note this: God does not usually communicate this Spirit to anyone (we are speaking of the ordinary way) except through the hearing of the word. Gal. 3. Did you receive the Spirit by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith? Faith certainly is not given except through the hearing of the word. Rom. 10. But the word is proclaimed by the Church, which publicly testifies that this is the word of God. Yet we would not pay attention to the Church proclaiming and testifying that this is the word of God, unless its authority and dignity, which God has bestowed on it in various ways, moved us somewhat to listen to it as worthy of trust.

units.la: Quis enim illum audiat, de cuius fide ac probitate dubitet? Hinc consequitur, neque Ecclesiæ testimonium, neque auditum verbi, esse inutilia, sed utilia & necessaria.
units.tr: For who would listen to a man whose faithfulness and integrity he doubts? It follows from this that neither the testimony of the Church nor the hearing of the word is useless, but useful and necessary.

units.la: Quare obseruandum quatuor esse mediorum genera, quibus pedetentim & gradatim efficit in electis Deus, ut Scripturam Canonicam, αὐτόπιστον[?] esse vere & certò agnoscant, inq; ea cognitione indies confirmentur.
units.tr: Therefore we must observe that there are four kinds of means by which God, step by step and gradually, brings it about in the elect that they truly and certainly acknowledge Scripture as canonical and self-authenticating [αὐτόπιστον?], and are daily confirmed in that knowledge.

units.la: 1. Constans & perpetuum Catholicæ Ecclesiæ Testimonium, quod traditionem vocamus.
units.tr: 1. The constant and perpetual testimony of the Catholic Church, which we call tradition.

units.la: 2. Testimonium ipsius Scripturæ, hoc est, Dei, in Scriptura nobis loquentis.
units.tr: 2. The testimony of Scripture itself, that is, of God speaking to us in Scripture.

units.la: 3. Testimonium Spiritus S. intus in corde nobis testificantis & persuadentis, hoc esse verbum Dei; & simul mentem illuminantis, & cœlestem veritatem atque excellentiam verbi ostendentis: atque ita efficientis, ut nos non solùm certò credamus, sed etiam verè agnoscamus, Deum esse eum, qui in Scripturis loquitur.
units.tr: 3. The testimony of the Holy Spirit, testifying and persuading within our hearts that this is the word of God; and at the same time illuminating the mind and showing the heavenly truth and excellence of the word; and so bringing it about that we not only believe with certainty, but also truly acknowledge that it is God who speaks in the Scriptures.

units.la: 4. Multas variasque Scripturæ ipsius demonstrationes, tum ab ipsius in nobis vi & efficacia, tum à multis aliis rebus & esseætis[?] extra nos defumtas[?]: quibus tanquam sigillis veritas in nobis per Spiritum S. obsignatur, & nos in illa magis ac magis quotidie confirmamur, hanc sacram Scripturam verum ac viuum esse sermonem Dei. Dicam breuiter de singulis: idq; eo ordine, quo etiam Deus illis uti solet. Hæc igitur esto in hac quæstione
units.tr: 4. The many and varied demonstrations of Scripture itself, both from its power and efficacy within us, and from many other things outside us: by which the truth is sealed in us through the Holy Spirit, as with seals, and we are more and more confirmed daily in this, that this holy Scripture is the true and living word of God. I shall speak briefly of each of these, in the order in which God is accustomed to use them. This, then, shall be our plan for this question.

units.la: PROPOSITIO V.
units.tr: PROPOSITION V.

units.la: Primum medium, quo Deus uti solet, idq; merito in deducendis nobis ad hanc certam firmamq; sacræ Scripturæ cognitionem: nimirum quòd hæc sit verè θεόπνευστος, ipsiusmque Dei viuentis verbum, est antiquum constansque Catholicæ Ecclesiæ testimonium, quod traditionem Ecclesiasticam vocamus.
units.tr: The first means, which God is accustomed to use, and rightly so, in leading us to this certain and firm knowledge of holy Scripture, namely that it is truly God-breathed [θεόπνευστος] and the word of the living God itself, is the ancient and constant testimony of the Catholic Church, which we call ecclesiastical tradition.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Cùm dico primum, non intelligo præcipuum & efficacius, sed primum ordine. Dixi, Quo solet uti: quia non semper, neq; cum omnibus hoc utitur medio. Certè Moysi & Prophetis, verbum quod proponebat, persuadebat etiam esse certum Dei verbum, sine testimonio Ecclesiæ. Idem de Apostolis, & Paulo cumprimis. Sed ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πλεῖστον[?] hoc utitur medio Deus.
units.tr: When I say "first," I do not mean principal or more effective, but first in order. I said "which God is accustomed to use," because He does not always use this means, nor with everyone. Certainly to Moses and the Prophets, the word they set forth persuaded them that it was the certain word of God, without the testimony of the Church. The same holds for the Apostles, and especially Paul. But God uses this means for the most part [ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πλεῖστον?].

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmation.

units.la: Nunc rem itafe habere, hinc liquidò apparet.
units.tr: That this is so is clear from the following.

units.la: 1. Hæc cognitio, opus est fidei: Ideò Ioh. 6. Apostoli dicunt primùm, (redidimus: Deinde, & cognouimus, quòd tu es Christus Filius Dei viui: Item, quòd habes verba vitæ æternæ. Fides autem ex auditu est, Rom.10. Auditus per verbum Christi, nempe prædicatum: prædicatur autem per Ecclesiam, & non per alios: Hæc enim sola mittitur ad prædicandum, & sola habet verbum. Primum autem quod prædicat Ecclesia: prædicat, hoc esse verbum Dei. Sic Prophetæ primùm dicebant: Factum est verbum Domini ad me. Audite verbum Domini. Ergo primum, quo Deus merito vtitur in ducendis nobis ad hanc Scripturæ cognitionem, quòd fit στόηνδις[?], est Ecclesiæ testimonium.
units.tr: 1. This knowledge is a work of faith. Therefore in John 6 the Apostles say first (we have come to believe) and then (we have come to know) that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God; likewise that you have the words of eternal life. But faith comes by hearing, Rom. 10. Hearing through the word of Christ, namely the word preached. The word is preached by the Church, and not by others, for it alone is sent to preach and alone has the word. The first thing the Church preaches is that this is the word of God. So the Prophets too first said: The word of the Lord came to me. Hear the word of the Lord. Therefore the first means by which God rightly leads us to this knowledge of Scripture, by which it becomes [στόηνδις?], is the testimony of the Church.

units.la: Atque hinc apparet, quàm sit hoc testimonium non solùm non superuacaneum, sed vtile & necessarium. Rom.10. totum quod dixi, tradit Apostolus, cum ait: Quomodo inuocabunt, in quem non crediderunt? Quomodo credent, nisi audiant? Quomodo audient sine prædicante? Quomodo prædicabunt, nisi mittantur? Hæc autem est Ecclesia, quæ milla prædicat. Ergo fides ex auditu.
units.tr: And from this it appears how far this testimony is not only not superfluous, but useful and necessary. Romans 10 sets out the whole of what I have said, when the Apostle says: How shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? How shall they believe, unless they hear? How shall they hear without a preacher? How shall they preach, unless they are sent? But it is the Church that sends preachers. Therefore faith comes by hearing.

units.la: 2. Sic primum, quod mouit Israëlitas, vt crederent, quam Moses adferebat doctrinam, esse Dei: fuit testimonium & autoritas Moysis, qui hoc asseuerabat. Hanc autem ei conciliauerat Deus apud populum, multis magnisq; rationibus.
units.tr: 2. Thus the first thing that moved the Israelites to believe that the doctrine Moses brought was from God was the testimony and authority of Moses, who affirmed it. God had won him this authority among the people by many great reasons.

units.la: Sic quid illud fuit, quod primùm permouit Iudæos, ut audirent Iohannem Baptistam, & illius doctrinam, ut Dei doctrinam acciperent, & deinde etiam ad Chri-stum audiendum accesserint? Illius authori-tas, quòd haberetur pro viro sanctissimo, & in sacris literis docto, & ea re fide dignis-simo.
units.tr: Likewise, what was it that first moved the Jews to listen to John the Baptist, to receive his teaching as the teaching of God, and afterwards to come also to hear Christ? The authority of John, because he was held to be a most holy man, learned in the sacred letters, and for that reason most worthy of trust.

units.la: Sic Pater voluit ipsi Filio suo IesuChristo authoritatem apud Iudæos conciliare, antequam eum mitteret ad prædicandum Euangelium. Quare? ut eo possent facilius permoueri Iudæi ad illum audiendum. Quomodo verò hanc ei conciliauit authoritatem? variis modis, honestate vitæ: experimento & gustu illius sapientiæ, ut quando disputauit cum Doctoribus: testimonio è cœlis, Hic est Filius meus, &c. testimonio Iohannis, Ecce agnus Dei, &c. Quamobrem? Quia noueret Deus Pater, hoc esse primum, quo homines ad aliquem audiendum, & fidem illi præbendam permouentur, nempe authoritatem.
units.tr: So the Father willed to win authority among the Jews for his own Son Jesus Christ before sending him to preach the Gospel. Why? So that the Jews might more easily be moved to hear him. But how did he win him this authority? By various means: by the honesty of his life; by the experience and taste of his wisdom, as when he disputed with the teachers; by the testimony from heaven, This is my beloved Son, etc.; by the testimony of John, Behold the Lamb of God, etc. Why so? Because God the Father knew that this is the first thing by which men are moved to hear someone and to give him faith, namely authority.

units.la: Sic primùm, quo permoti fuerunt Samaritani, ut urbe exirent & Christum audirent, fuit testimonium, & authoritas mulieris illius. Nam apertè dixerunt, se Christo credidisse primùm, propter eius mulieris sermonem, id est, testimonium.
units.tr: Likewise, the first thing by which the Samaritans were moved to leave the city and hear Christ was the testimony and authority of that woman. For they plainly said that they had first believed in Christ because of the woman's word, that is, her testimony.

units.la: Sic Augustinus contra Epistolam Funda-menti scripsit, se fuisse authoritate Ecclesiæ, id est, tot tantorumq; virorum, qui iam inde ab initio eam religionem amplexi fuerunt, dignitate & testimonio permotum, vt Euangelio crederet.
units.tr: Likewise Augustine, in writing against the Letter of Manichaeus (Fundamentum), said that he was moved to believe the Gospel by the authority of the Church, that is, by the dignity and testimony of so many great men who from the beginning had embraced that religion.

units.la: Quid? quòd nemo nostrum est, qui non eodem modo ad Euangelium accesserit? Cur credidimus etiam in Papatu, hoc esse verbum Dei? propter testimonium & authoritatem Ecclesiæ. Quid deinde primùm nos permouit, vt ad Euangelium accesserimus? Authoritas tot tantarumque Ecclesiarum. Ergo quòd agnoscamus nunc verè, hanc Scripturam, verum esse Dei verbum: non parum debemus Ecclesiæ testimonio & traditioni: & huiuscemodi medium, non debemus contemnere aut parui facere, quoniam Deus dignatur hoc vti in deducendis nobis ad veram Scripturæ, quòd verè sit θεόπνευστος[?], cognitionem.
units.tr: What then? Is there not one of us who did not come to the Gospel in the same way? Why did we also believe, even under the Papacy, that this is the word of God? Because of the testimony and authority of the Church. What first moved us afterwards to come to the Gospel? The authority of so many and such great Churches. Therefore, since we now truly acknowledge that this Scripture is the true word of God, we owe no small debt to the testimony and tradition of the Church; and we ought not to despise or make little of this kind of means, since God deigns to use it in leading us to the true knowledge that Scripture is God-breathed [θεόπνευστος].

units.la: Cæterùm, hoc Ecclesiæ testimonium non sufficere ad hanc veram Scripturæ cognitionem, antea demonstratum est. Neque enim hoc solo Ecclesiæ testimonio poterit quispiam adduci, vt verè credat, aut agnoscat hanc Scripturam esse θεόπνευστον[?]: sed ad duo prodest. Primùm ad hoc, vt aures illi præbeamus, & verbum, quod adfert, audiamus: Deinde etiam ad hoc, vt aliquam bonam de hoc verbo concipiamus opinionem, etsi non firmam fidem, quòd sit Dei verbum.
units.tr: Moreover, it was shown earlier that this testimony of the Church is not sufficient for this true knowledge of Scripture. For no one can be brought by this testimony of the Church alone to truly believe or acknowledge that this Scripture is God-breathed [θεόπνευστον]; but it helps in two ways. First, so that we give it our ear and hear the word it brings; then also so that we form some good opinion of this word, even if not firm faith, that it is the word of God.

units.la: PROPOSITIO VI.
units.tr: PROPOSITION VI.

units.la: Alterum medium, est testimonium Scri-
units.tr: The second means is the testimony of Scripture

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Quòd hoc testimonium nobis prosit, & eo ad cognitionem veritatis deducamur, explicandum est: Dum audimus Deum nobis loquentem, si vocis & verbi sono nil aliud accedat, quod mentem nostram percellat: nihil minùs cogitamus, quàm veré Deum esse eum, qui in Scripturis loquitur; imò stultitia videntur ea omnia nobis esse, vt ait 1. Cor.2. Apostolus. Proinde superiùs conclusimus, neq; Scripturam per se, si nil aliud accedat, posse efficere, vt veré agnoscamus, Deum esse, qui in ea nobis loquatur.
units.tr: So that this testimony may help us and lead us to the knowledge of the truth, it must be explained. When we hear God speaking to us, if nothing beyond the sound of the voice and the words reaches our mind to strike it, we think least of all that the one who speaks in the Scriptures is truly God; indeed, all these things seem foolishness to us, as the Apostle says in 1 Cor. 2. Therefore we concluded above that Scripture by itself, if nothing else is added, cannot bring it about that we truly recognise that the one who speaks to us in it is God.

units.la: At est lucerna accensa: est Sol splendidis-simus.
units.tr: But the lamp is lit; the sun is most bright.

units.la: Respon. Quid tum? Sùa se ipse [?]vi & splendore patefacit quid fit, sicuti etiam Sol & lucerna. Verum, sed quibus? Cæcóne? minime. Sed videndi vim & facultatem habenti, & reipsa intuenti. Idem de Scripturis, quæ sunt instar lucernæ lucenti in caliginoso loco, & de nobis, qui nostrapte natura cæci sumus: & nisi per Spiritum S. facultas videndi præbeatur, ea quæ Dei sunt videre ac percipere minimè possumus, dicendum est.
units.tr: Reply. So what? By its own power and brightness it makes clear what it is, just as the sun and a lamp do. But to whom? To the blind? Certainly not. But to one who has the power and ability to see and actually looks. The same must be said of the Scriptures, which are like a lamp shining in a dark place, and of us, who by our very nature are blind: unless the faculty of sight is granted through the Holy Spirit, we can by no means see and perceive the things that belong to God.

units.la: Quare optimè à nobis dictum fuit, hoc et-iam medium per se solum inefficax esse, non in se, sed apud nos, nisi accedat vis Spiritus sancti. Sed bene habet: dum Electi audiunt verbum, adest illis S. S. qui paulatim illos illumiilluminat, fidemque donat, ac persuadet, ut est ad Rom.10. Fides est ex auditu. Item Gal.3. Spiritum accepistis ex auditu fidei. Sed Spiritus ordinarie paulatim progreditur in hac per-suasione.
units.tr: Therefore it was rightly said by us that this means too, by itself alone, is ineffective, not in itself but in us, unless the power of the Holy Spirit is added. But all is well: while the elect hear the Word, the Holy Spirit is present to them, who gradually enlightens them, bestows faith and persuades them, as it is in Rom. 10: Faith comes from hearing. Likewise Gal. 3: You received the Spirit from hearing of faith. But the Spirit ordinarily advances gradually in this persuasion.

units.la: Dum igitur verbum audimus, adest Spiri-tus S. ac dum ille incipit aures mentis aperi-re ad intelligendum: principio videmur nobis audire vocem, aliquid amplius, quàm humanam, resonantem, & cœlestia, non terre-na aut humana loquentem. Sed nondum vere persuasi sumus, Deum illum esse, qui loquitur. Et audimus quidem vocem, quæ multò magis percellit ac permouet mentem, quàm simplex vox & testimonium Ecclesiæ: sed Deum adhuc nō videmus, non agnoscimus. Et licet vi huius vocis magis permoueamur ad credendum, vocem hanc, vocem esse Dei, quàm testimonio Ecclesiæ: nondum tamen sumus vere persuasi. Est enim hoc, initium potius quoddam fidei, ac potius præparatio ad fidem, quàm vera fides.
units.tr: Therefore, while we hear the Word, the Holy Spirit is present, and while he begins to open the ears of the mind to understand, at first we seem to ourselves to hear a voice resounding that is something more than human, speaking heavenly and not earthly or human things. But we are not yet truly persuaded that it is God who speaks. We do indeed hear a voice which strikes and moves the mind far more than a plain voice or the testimony of the Church; but we do not yet see or recognise God. And although by the force of this voice we are moved more to believe that this voice is the voice of God than by the testimony of the Church, nevertheless we are not yet truly persuaded. For this is rather an initial beginning of faith, and a preparation for faith, than true faith.

units.la: Exemplis aliquot è Scripturis desumtis, rem declaro.
units.tr: I will make the matter clear by some examples taken from Scripture.

units.la: Exod.19. Cùm Deus daret Legem per Mo-sen populo: populus audiuit quidem tonitrua & fulgura: sed Deum non videbat. Et quod Moses referebat nomine Dei, audiebat quidem populus: sed in faciem Mosis gloria Dei illustratam, & faciem Dei repræsentantem, non poterat oculos intendere, vt ait Apostolus, propter gloriam vultus eius.
units.tr: Exod. 19. When God gave the Law to the people through Moses, the people indeed heard the thunders and lightnings, but they did not see God. And what Moses reported in the name of God the people heard, but they could not fix their eyes on the face of Moses, illuminated by the glory of God and representing the face of God, as the Apostle says, because of the glory of his countenance.

units.la: Typus illud fuit huius præparationis ad fidem. Cùm audimus in Scripturis ea, quæ ad Legem pertinent, præcepta: comminationes, iudicia in transgressores: videmur quidem audire cœlestia tonitrua, & aliquem quovis homine maiorem ad nos verba facere: sed Deum non videmus, nec possumus eius gloriam in verbo suo alioqui splendentem, præ imbecillitate sensus nostri intueri, hoc est, nondum sumus plenè persuasi, Deũ esse illum, qui in Lege loquitur. Lucæ ulti-mo, duo illi discipuli, qui ibant in Emaunta, dum audirent hominem illum peregrinum (is autem erat Christus) de Christo, deque regno eius loquentem, & Scripturas interpretantem: afficiebantur quidem illorum corda, quia audiebant hominem verba non humana, sed cœlestia proferentem: interim tamen non agnoscebant eum, qui secum loqueretur, esse Christum Filium Dei. Oculi enim eorum tenebantur: ne eum agnoscerent.
units.tr: That was a type of this preparation for faith. When we hear in the Scriptures the precepts that pertain to the Law, the threats and judgments against transgressors, we seem indeed to hear heavenly thunders and one greater than any man speaking to us; but we do not see God, nor, because of the weakness of our sense, can we look upon his glory otherwise shining in his word; that is, we are not yet fully persuaded that it is God who speaks in the Law. In the last chapter of Luke, those two disciples who were going to Emmaus, while they heard that stranger (who was Christ) speaking about Christ and about his kingdom, and interpreting the Scriptures, were indeed moved in their hearts, because they heard a man uttering words not human but heavenly; yet meanwhile they did not recognise him who was speaking with them as Christ the Son of God. For their eyes were held, so that they should not recognise him.

units.la: Idem planè contigit nobis de principio: Cùm audiremus Euangelium: sentiebamus quidem quodam modo corda nostra affici, dum Euangelium audiremus: atque inde ut-cunque agnoscebamus, doctrinam eam non planè esse humanam: sed interim nondum eam veré & plenè agnoscebamus esse ipsum Dei verbum: quia oculi nostri nondum plenè erant aperti, ut possent hoc, & Christum in Euangelio agnoscere.
units.tr: The very same thing happens to us at the beginning: when we first heard the Gospel, we felt in some way our hearts moved while we heard the Gospel; and from this we recognised, in whatever measure, that this teaching was not purely human; but meanwhile we did not yet truly and fully recognise it as the very Word of God, because our eyes were not yet fully open, so that they could recognise this and Christ in the Gospel.

units.la: Est etiam historia apud Marcum, cap.8.de quodam cæco, qui cùm paulatim illumina-retur à Christo, de principio cùm intueretur homines, non eos agnoscebat pro hominibus, sed videbatur sibi arbores sese moventes videre. Quare? quia nondum erat perse-ctè illuminatus. Idem contingit nobis, cùm de principio audimus verbum Dei: Sp.S.in-cipit, quidem aperire oculos, ut videamus, quæ antea minimè poteramus videre: sed nondum plenè sumus persuasi, hoc verbum quod audimus, esse verum certumque Dei verbum.
