En igitur, quale sit hoc alterum de Scripturis testimonium, & quomodo illo utatur Deus, nempe quòd per Spiritum S. mentes nostras paulatim aperiendo, hoc utatur ad trahendum nos ad plenam persuasionem, & cognitionem, hanc Scripturam verè esse θεόπνευστον[?]. Non est quidem per se adhuc satis efficax ad plenam persuasionem: sed tamen efficacius est priore, hoc est, testimonio Ecclesiæ: quia illud testimonium, erat hominum: hoc autem, Dei. Proinde videmus, quantum prosit, & necessarium sit, audire verbum, etiamsi de principio non omnia intelligimus, nec perfectè Deum agno-scimus.
units.tr: There is also the story in Mark, chap. 8, of a certain blind man who, when he was gradually enlightened by Christ, at first when he looked at men did not recognise them as men, but seemed to himself to see trees moving. Why? Because he was not yet perfectly enlightened. The same happens to us when at first we hear the Word of God: the Holy Spirit indeed begins to open our eyes so that we see what before we could by no means see; but we are not yet fully persuaded that the word which we hear is the true and certain Word of God. Behold, then, what kind of second testimony this is concerning the Scriptures, and how God uses it: namely, by gradually opening our minds through the Holy Spirit, he uses it to draw us to full persuasion and knowledge that this Scripture is truly God-breathed. It is indeed not yet sufficiently effective in itself for full persuasion; but nevertheless it is more effective than the former, that is, the testimony of the Church, because that testimony was of men, but this one is of God. Therefore we see how much it helps, and how necessary it is, to hear the Word, even if at first we do not understand everything, nor know God perfectly.

units.la: PROPOSITIO VII.
units.tr: PROPOSITION VII.

units.la: Primo & secundo testimonio accedit ter-tium, illudq; efficacissimum: hoc autem est a-pertum testimonium Spiritus sancti.
units.tr: The first and second testimonies are joined by a third, and this is the most effective of all: this is the manifest testimony of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Hic Spiritus primò plenè persuadet,eum qui nobis in Scriptura loquitur, ipsum esse Deum, cœli & terræ conditorem. Deinde ita plenè illustrat oculos, vt excellentiam di-gnitatemque Scripturæ cœlestem intuea-mur: quo intuitu magis ac magis agnosci-mus,Deum verè huiusce autorem esse, non hominem,aut Angelum. Tunc Solem splen-dentem, & lucernam accensam videmus: tunc verum est,Scripturam sese sua vi prode-re, an sit αὐτόπιστος[?], necne: Tunc cum Sa-maritanis dicimus Ecclesiæ : Iam non credi-mus,propter tuum sermonem: ipsi enim audivi-mus & scimus, quòd hic est verè Servator ille Mundi Christus,
units.tr: Here the Spirit, first of all, fully persuades us that he who speaks to us in Scripture is God himself, the creator of heaven and earth. Then he so fully illuminates our eyes that we behold the heavenly excellence and dignity of Scripture; by this sight we recognise more and more that God, and not man or an angel, is truly its author. Then we see the sun shining and the lamp lit; then it is true that Scripture by its own power makes itself known, and whether it is self-authenticating [αὐτόπιστος]. Then, with the Samaritans, we say to the Church: Now we do not believe because of your words; for we ourselves have heard and know that this is truly the Saviour of the world, Christ.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmation.

units.la: 1.Cor.2. Nos autem Spiritum Domini accepimus,ut sciamus, quæ nobis a Deo donata sunt. Item,Spiritus omnia scrutatur, etiam profunda Dei. Item, Spiritualis homo omnia diiudicat.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 2. But we have received the Spirit of the Lord, that we may know the things that have been freely given us by God. Likewise: The Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God. Likewise: The spiritual man judges all things.

units.la: 2.Cor.3.Nunc autem nos retecta[?] facie, gloriam Domini,ut in speculo intuentes, in eandem imaginem transformamur ex gloria in gloriam,sicut a Domini Spiritu. Ergo quòd agnoscamus, Scripturam esse verbum Dei: hoc cumpri-mis debemus Spiritui sancto qui illud pate-fecit. Nobis verò hoc Spiritu illustratis, & plenè de veritate persuasis, prodest etiam quartum.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 3. But now, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, we are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord. Therefore, that we acknowledge Scripture to be the Word of God, we owe this above all to the Holy Spirit, who has made it manifest. But when we are illuminated by this Spirit and fully persuaded of the truth, the fourth also helps us.

units.la: PROPOSITIO VIII.
units.tr: PROPOSITION VIII.

units.la: Quartum medium, quo vtitur Deus, in confirmandis nobis in perfecta Scriptura cognitione, quòd verè sit θεόπνευστος[?], sunt multa & varia demonstrationes, partim ex iis, quæ Scriptura insunt, partim ex iis, quæ illam consequuntur, deducta.
units.tr: The fourth means, which God uses in confirming us in a complete knowledge of Scripture, namely that it is truly God-breathed [θεόπνευστος], consists of many and various demonstrations, some drawn from those things which lie within Scripture itself, and some from those things which follow upon it.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: Capita locorum tantùm indicabo & ego, quæ forte ab aliis non fuerunt ita obseruata.
units.tr: I too will indicate only the heads of the arguments, which perhaps have not been observed in this way by others.

units.la: 1. Vnum locum constituunt causæ efficientes, hoc est, instrumentales, quibus vsus est Deus in tradenda nobis Scriptura. Ii fuerunt viri sancti, Prophetæ, Moses, Apostoli: Ii testantur, hoc esse verbum Dei. Est autem virorum bonorum admittendum testimonium, Ergo, &c. Sed ego à causa efficiente argumentum compono non contemnendum.
units.tr: 1. One head is constituted by the efficient, that is, the instrumental, causes which God used in delivering Scripture to us. These were holy men: the prophets, Moses, the Apostles. They testify that this is the Word of God. But the testimony of good men must be admitted. Therefore, etc. But I construct an argument from the efficient cause which is not to be despised.

units.la: Si hac Scriptura non est à Deo tanquam à suo autore, necesse est, vt huius autor sit aliqua creatura: non datur medium. Atqui nulla pura creatura potest huius Scripturæ esse autor: id quod mox demonstrabo. Ergo, &c.
units.tr: If this Scripture is not from God as from its author, it is necessary that its author be some creature: there is no other option. But no mere creature can be the author of this Scripture, as I will show presently. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Alia argumenta ducuntur vel ab iis, quæ insunt ipsi Scripturæ: vt à causa materiali, formali, à qualitatibus, ab effectis, proprietatibus: vel ab iis, quæ sunt extra, sed eam consequuntur.
units.tr: Other arguments are drawn either from those things which lie within Scripture itself, such as from the material and formal cause, from its qualities, its effects, its properties; or from those things which lie outside it but follow upon it.

units.la: 1. à materia, id est, à substantia doctrinæ: hæc omnem superat creatum captum.
units.tr: 1. From the matter, that is, from the substance of the doctrine: this surpasses every created capacity.

units.la: 2. à qualitate doctrinæ: nihil vitiosum, carnale, terrenum redolet. Ergo, &c.
units.tr: 2. From the quality of the doctrine: it smells of nothing sinful, carnal or earthly. Therefore, etc.

units.la: 3. à forma dicendi: humilis est, & tamen viuax, trahit omnes in sui admirationem.
units.tr: 3. From the form of speaking: it is humble, and yet lively; it draws all into admiration of itself.

units.la: 1.Cor.2.Non veni in sublimitate sermonis,
units.tr: 1 Cor. 2. I did not come in loftiness of speech,

units.la: 4. à consonantia Scripturarum.
units.tr: 4. From the agreement of the Scriptures.

units.la: à vi regenerandi homines.
units.tr: From the power to regenerate men.

units.la: Extra Scripturam.
units.tr: Outside Scripture.

units.la: ab euentu vaticiniorum; à miraculis. à furore Sathanæ Antichristi cōtra hanc. à conseruatione doctrinæ, contra potentiam Sathanæ. à pœnis, quas persecutores Euangelij dant.
units.tr: From the fulfilment of prophecies; from miracles; from the rage of Satan and of Antichrist against it; from the preservation of the doctrine against the power of Satan; from the punishments which persecutors of the Gospel incur.

units.la: Est Princeps, qui liberos habet in diuersas profectos regiones, idque propter rebellionem contra patrem. Hic senex cùm fit & valetudinarius, antequam grauiori corripiatur morbo, facit & dictat sua lingua Testamentum Notario, qui illud scribit: & quæ habet bona, ea suis legat liberis. Scriptum Testamentum iubet obsignari suis aliquot sigillis. Deinde iubet quibusdam legatis, ut varia huius Testamenti exempla, omnia iisdem sigillis obsignata, ferant ad suos liberos: Testamentum illis legant, & hortentur, domum ut reuertantur ad suos fruendum bonis. Ut verò legati ab ipsis liberis agnoscantur, & ut fides illis habeatur, cuique illorum dat torquem seu cathenam auream ream cum suo insigni appenso.Legati, ut suo pareant Principi, veniunt ad liberos cum Testamento: significant liberis, se legatos esse parentis: se ad illos ferre Testamentum, in quo omnia parentis bona illis legata continentur: rogant, ut se audiant. Illi primùm audiunt, quod de se dicunt Legati, se habere Testamentum patris quod legant: & hoc licet non sint persuasi, tamen aliqua ex parte credunt.Deinde audiunt legi Testamentum: Ac de principio olfaciunt illum esse stylum parentis, sed non sine aliqua adhuc dubitatione. Tertiò, ubi verò totum legi audiuerunt, non semel & iterum, perpensis diligentiùs omnibus quæ lecta sunt: omninò persuadetur, illud verum esse parentis testamentum. Ad extremum inspiciunt etiam sigilla: illis etiam magis ac magis in ea sententia confirmantur, testamentum hoc testamentum esse parentis.
units.tr: There is a Prince who has children who have gone off into various regions, and this on account of rebellion against their father. This old man, being now infirm and sick, before he is seized by a more serious illness, dictates his testament with his own tongue to a notary, who writes it down; and he bequeaths his goods to his children. He orders the written testament to be sealed with several of his seals. Then he orders certain envoys to carry various copies of this testament, all sealed with the same seals, to his children, to read the testament to them and to urge them to return home to enjoy their goods. So that the envoys may be recognised by the children themselves, and so that credit may be given to them, he gives to each of them a golden chain or necklace with his own emblem attached. The envoys, in order to obey their Prince, come to the children with the testament: they tell the children that they are envoys of their father; that they bring him a testament in which all the father's goods are bequeathed to them; and they ask that they be heard. The children first hear what the envoys say about themselves, that they have their father's testament, which they read; and although they are not yet persuaded, they believe it to some extent. Then they hear the testament read; and at the start they perceive that this is the style of their father, but not without some doubt still. Thirdly, when they have heard the whole of it read, not once or twice, and have weighed carefully everything that was read, they are fully persuaded that this is truly their father's testament. Finally they also examine the seals; and they are confirmed more and more in this opinion, that this testament is the testament of their father.

units.la: Hoc simili, puto vobis, quod dixi de quatuor mediis, ita fieri perspicuum, ut nulla opus sit explicatione aut maiore probatione.
units.tr: I think that by this simile what I have said about the four means becomes so clear that no further explanation or greater proof is needed.

units.la: Princeps,est Deus Pater cœlestis: Liberi rebelles, omnes Electi: Testamentum, Scriptura sacra: Bona legata, cœlum, vita æterna: Sigilla, quibus obsignatum est, miracula, vaticiniorum complementa, & alia, unde ducuntur argumenta ad probandum, hanc Scripturam esse verbum Dei: Legati, prophetæ & Apostoli: cathena aurea, qua agnoscuntur, autoritas est, quam illis conciliauit Dominus variis rationibus, quòd veri sint Legati Dei.
units.tr: The Prince is God the heavenly Father; the rebellious children are all the Elect; the testament is holy Scripture; the goods bequeathed are heaven and eternal life; the seals with which it is sealed are the miracles, the fulfilments of prophecies, and the other things from which arguments are drawn to prove that this Scripture is the Word of God; the envoys are the prophets and Apostles; the golden chain by which they are recognised is the authority which the Lord has bestowed upon them by various means, to show that they are true envoys of God.

units.la: Primum igitur, quod filios Dei adducit, ut cogitent credantq; hoc quod adfertur Testamentum, Testamentum esse parentis, est testimonium & auctoritas Legatorum, qui sic assi-mant. Secundum est, testimonium seu verba Testamenti, quae dum audiunt, quo-dam modo agnoscunt verba esse parentis, idque ex spiritu & mente parentis quam tenent. Tertium, plena persuasio, quam post saepius lectum & consideratum Testamentum conceperunt vi Spiritus S. Quartum, inspectio etiam & diligens examinatio sigillorum. Quae haec sunt? Demonstrationes, de quibus dixi, quae ducuntur à materia, forma, &c.
units.tr: First, then, what leads the sons of God to think and believe that what is set before them is the testament of their Father is the testimony and authority of the envoys, who so assert it. Second is the testimony or the words of the testament, which, as they hear them, they in some way recognise to be the words of the Father, and this from the Spirit and mind of the Father which they hold. Third is the full persuasion which they conceived, after the testament had been read and considered more often, by the power of the Holy Spirit. Fourth is the inspection and careful examination of the seals. What are these? They are the demonstrations I spoke of, which are drawn from matter, form, etc.

units.la: Nunc tenemus, quibus rationibus debea-mus nos confirmare in hac sententia, Scripturam hanc ipsissimum esse Dei verbum & θεόπνευστον: eoque in hac constanter perseue-rare, sicut Apostolus hortatus est Timotheum, & nos in ipso.
units.tr: Now we have grasped by what reasons we ought to confirm ourselves in this view, that this very Scripture is the Word of God and God-breathed [θεόπνευστον], and to persevere constantly in this, as the Apostle exhorted Timothy, and us in him.

units.la: Summa: Tria praecipua sunt media, quibus Deus utiturin deducendis nobis ad cognitionem, Scripturam esse θεόπνευστον. Primum, Ecclesiae testimonium externum: secundum, Spiritus S. internum: is ad auditum verbum adest, & persuadet, hoc quod audis, esse Dei verbum: quanquam hoc non omnibus mox, sed gradatim persuadeat: ita ut primo obscurius, deinde clarius hoc faciat, ut supra explicatum est: Tertium [?] est Scripturæ ipsius dignitas & excellentia ac virtus divina, iam perSpiritum sanctum oculis fidelium illuminatis, demonstrata.
units.tr: Summary: There are three chief means by which God uses to lead us to the knowledge that Scripture is God-breathed [θεόπνευστον]. First, the external testimony of the Church; second, the inward testimony of the Holy Spirit, who is present to the hearing of the word and persuades you that what you hear is the Word of God, although he does not persuade everyone at once, but gradually, so that he does this first more obscurely and then more clearly, as was explained above; third, the dignity and excellence and divine power of Scripture itself, now demonstrated to the eyes of the faithful, who have been illuminated by the Holy Spirit.

units.la: QUÆSTIO III. De autoritate Scripturæ & Ecclesiæ: & an Ecclesia ius habeat in Scripturas.
units.tr: QUESTION III. On the authority of Scripture and of the Church: and whether the Church has a right over the Scriptures.

units.la: Nos hic non instituimus sermonem de autoritate Ecclesiæ in universum, sed tantùm & proprie de autoritate Ecclesiæ circa ver-bum Dei.
units.tr: We do not here conduct a discussion on the authority of the Church in general, but only and properly on the authority of the Church with respect to the Word of God.

units.la: De hac igitur quæritur, An autoritas, quam habet Scriptura, habeat ab Ecclesia, necne: ac proinde, an Ecclesiæ autoritas, maior sit autoritate Scripturæ. Sunt duæ quæstiones, sed nos tanquam unam, quæ duabus constet membris, eam tractabimus. Fuit hæc quæstio excitata in Ecclesia, tempore Concilij Constantiensis & Basiliensis, ante annos circiter 161 [?]. Quidam etiam inter Pa-pistas utrumque affirmabant: quidam nega-bant, quemadmodum & nunc non omnes sunt eiusdem sententiæ.
units.tr: The question, then, is this: whether the authority that Scripture has comes from the Church or not; and consequently, whether the authority of the Church is greater than the authority of Scripture. These are two questions, but we will treat them as one, which consists of two parts. This question was raised in the Church at the time of the Councils of Constance and Basel, about 161 years ago. Some even among the Papists affirmed both; some denied them, just as even now not all are of the same opinion.

units.la: Nos utrumque membrum negamus: sed antequam certas afferamus propositiones de hac re, duæ significationes huius vocis Autoritas, explicandæ nobis sunt. Huius enim vocis explicatio, pernecessaria est, tum ad quæstionis intelligentiam, tum ad respon-sionis nostræ explicationem. Age igitur,
units.tr: We deny both parts. But before we set out certain propositions on this matter, we must explain the two meanings of this word Authority. For an explanation of this word is absolutely necessary, both for understanding the question and for explaining our answer. Come, then.

units.la: Prima huius vocis Autoritas, quam Græci ἀξίωσις[?] vocant, significatio, est existimatio, reputatio, seu dignitas, qua quis iudicatur dignus vel fide in verbis; quia agnitus sem-per verax: vel honore, quia agnitus pro vi-ro probo & virtute prædito. Sic Cicero pro Lege Manilia: Et quoniam authoritas multum quoque in bellis administrandis atque imperio militari valet, certe nemini dubium est, quin ea in re idem Imperator (Pompeius) plurimum possit: Sic dicimus aliquem sibi authoritatem comparasse apud homines sua virtute, id est, existimationem, reputationem & dignitatem: verbi gratia. Aliquis semper in verbis suis studuit veritati, ita vt nunquam aliquod in eius verbis inuentum fuerit mendacium aut leuitas: ideo hac virtute sibi hanc apud omnes comparauit authoritatem, vt quo-ties loquitur, fides ei ab omnibus adhibea-tur: & hoc honore & dignitate, dignus iu-dicatur. Hinc fit, vt etiam vulgò, authoritas alicuius accipiatur pro sententia & testimonio alicuius per se fide digno. Vnde dicimus, citare authoritates Patrum, id est, testimonia fide digna. Quare in præsenti quæstione, authoritas proprie significat vim & dignitatem, seu æstimationem, qua fit, vt aliquis per se fit ἀξιόπιστος[?], & pro tali habeatur.
units.tr: The first meaning of this word Authority, which the Greeks call axiōsis [?], is esteem, reputation, or dignity, by which someone is judged worthy of trust in what he says, because he is known always to be truthful; or worthy of honor, because he is known as an upright man endowed with virtue. Thus Cicero, in the speech for the Manilian Law: And since authority also carries great weight in conducting wars and in military command, there is certainly no doubt that the same commander (Pompey) can accomplish very much in this matter. So we say that someone has gained authority among men by his virtue, that is, esteem, reputation and dignity. For example: someone has always strived for truth in his words, so that no falsehood or levity was ever found in what he said; therefore by this virtue he has gained for himself such authority among all that whenever he speaks, he is given belief by everyone, and by this honor and dignity he is judged worthy. Hence it happens that, even in common usage, the authority of someone is taken to mean the opinion and testimony of someone who is trustworthy in himself. Whence we say, to cite the authorities of the Fathers, that is, trustworthy testimonies. Therefore in the present question, authority properly signifies the force and dignity, or esteem, by which someone is in himself trustworthy and is regarded as such.

units.la: Altera significatio nominis Authoritas est potestas, dominium & ius in aliquem, & aliquid agendi: Vt, Magistratus authoritatem habere dicitur in suos ciues, id est, ius & potestatem in illos iubendi, puniendi, &c. Sic etiam Cicero accepit multis in locis. Atque haec est propria significatio Graecae vocis αὐ-θεντίας, qua voce Graeci posteriores significarunt id, quod Latini nomine authoritatis. Nam αὐθέντης [?], idem est quod αὐτεξούσιος [?], dominus, & qui suae est potestatis, iusq; in alios habet, & autor alicuius rei, id est, Dominus primariusq; inventor.
units.tr: The second meaning of the name Authority is power, lordship and right over someone, and the right to act: as when we say that the magistrate has authority over his citizens, that is, the right and power to command them, to punish them, and so on. Cicero also used it in this sense in many places. And this is the proper meaning of the Greek word authentias, by which later Greeks signified what the Latins signify by the name of authority. For authentēs is the same as autexousios, a lord, one who is his own master and has right over others, and the author of something, that is, the chief lord and first discoverer.

units.la: Nunc ad quaestionem iuxta priorem significationem huius nominis intellectam, iis respondeo propositionibus.
units.tr: Now, to the question as understood according to the former meaning of this name, I answer with these propositions.

units.la: PROPOSITIO I.
units.tr: PROPOSITION I.

units.la: Scriptura sacra, quam habet in se authoritatem, hoc est, dignitatem & vim, qua in se ipsa est ἀξιόπιστος [?]: eam non habet ab Ecclesia, sed à Deo.
units.tr: Holy Scripture, which has in itself authority, that is, the dignity and force by which it is in itself trustworthy, does not have this from the Church, but from God.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmation.

units.la: 1. Ab eo suam habet Scriptura authoritatem, à quo etiam, vt ab autore suo, ipsa est. Est autem à Deo, non ab Ecclesia. Ergo, &c. Vt de Sol suam habet lucem? ab eo, à quo etiam esse suum, suamq; substantiam. Sic Scriptura. Ideo enim vera est, eoq; fide digna, quia autorem habet veracem. Idcirco, cum Prophetae inuitabant populos ad audiendum verbum tanquam fide dignum: hanc vnam adferebant causam, Quia Dominus locutus est: Quia Domini est verbum.
units.tr: 1. Scripture has its authority from him from whom it also is, as from its author. But it is from God, not from the Church. Therefore, etc. As the sun has its light from him from whom it also has its being and its substance. So with Scripture: for it is true, and therefore trustworthy, because it has a truthful author. Hence, when the prophets invited the peoples to hear the word as trustworthy, they brought forward this one reason alone: Because the Lord has spoken; Because the word is of the Lord.

units.la: 2. Interrogo Ecclesiam: Antequam ipsa dedisset testimonium Scripturis, & eas declarasset esse θεόπνευστος[?]: vel erant ipsum Dei verbum, vel non erant. Si erant: igitur per se dignae erant fide, nec hanc ab Ecclesia acceperunt autoritatem & dignitatem. Semper enim verbum Domini per se est ἀξιόπιστον. Si non erant: erravit igitur Ecclesia, ne dicam mentita est, dum illos declarauit esse libros θεόπνευστος[?], qui tamen non erant. Non puto, dicturos, Ecclesiam fecisse eos esse verbum Dei, quoniam hoc est nimis blasphemum & ineptum. Quod enim non est verbum Domini: nunquam totius etiam cœli & terræ suffragiis poterit fieri verbum Domini: & perinde esset, ac si diceres: Joannes Baptista testimonium perhibuit de Jesu, quod esset Christus: Ergo fecit illum esse Christum. Effecit quidem suo testimonio, ut agnosceretur pro Christo, sed non effecit, ut esset Christus. Ita Ecclesia suo testimonio effecit, ut Scriptura utcunque agnita fit pro θεοπνευστος[?]: sed non fecit, ut fit verbum Dei. Fuit semper verbum Dei: Ergo fuit semper ex se fide di-gna. Joh 17. Christus ait de suo sermone, antequam esset ab Ecclesia authenticatus, Sermo tuus, ô Pater, veritas est. Ergo verbum Dei, ante Ecclesiæ approbationem, semper ve-rum fuit.
units.tr: 2. I ask the Church: before it had given its testimony to the Scriptures and declared them to be divinely inspired [theopneustos], either they were the very Word of God or they were not. If they were, then they were trustworthy in themselves, and they did not receive this authority and dignity from the Church. For the word of the Lord is always trustworthy in itself. If they were not, then the Church erred, not to say lied, when it declared those books to be divinely inspired, which nevertheless were not. I do not think they will say that the Church made them the Word of God, since this is too blasphemous and absurd. For what is not the Word of the Lord can never become the Word of the Lord by the votes of the whole heaven and earth; and it would be just as if you were to say: John the Baptist bore witness concerning Jesus that he was the Christ; therefore he made him to be the Christ. He did indeed by his testimony bring it about that he was acknowledged as the Christ, but he did not make him to be the Christ. So the Church by its testimony brought it about that Scripture was acknowledged in whatever way as divinely inspired, but it did not make it to be the Word of God. It has always been the Word of God; therefore it has always been trustworthy in itself. In John 17, Christ says of his own word, before it was authenticated by the Church: Thy word, O Father, is truth. Therefore the Word of God, before the approval of the Church, has always been true.

units.la: PROPOSITIO II.
units.tr: PROPOSITION II.

units.la: Sancta Scriptura, quam apud homines[?] nondum Spiritu Dei & vera fide donatos ha-bet bet autoritatem, propter quam incipit admit-ti & audiri tanquam Dei verbum: habet ab Ecclesiæ testimonio & autoritate.
units.tr: Holy Scripture, which among men not yet endowed with the Spirit of God and true faith has authority, on account of which it begins to be admitted and heard as the Word of God, has this from the testimony and authority of the Church.

units.la: Hanc non probamus, quia concedimus Papistis, sed explicamus.
units.tr: We do not approve this because we concede it to the Papists, but we explain it.

units.la: 1. Discrimen est inter habere autoritatem in se, & apud alios. Nouus Rex, ut Dauid, suam habet autoritatem, etiamsi ab aliis non agnoscatur. Homo verax semper est fide di-gnus, etiamsi non habeatur ab improbis pro fide digno:Ita Scriptura etiam non cognita, tamen semper in se suam habet dignitatem, & est fide digna. An non Euangelium etiam apud Turcas est in se fide dignum? Apud alios vero dicitur is obtinere suam dignita-tem, qui iam cognitus est, & pro tali bono viro habetur, qualis est.
units.tr: 1. There is a difference between having authority in oneself and having it among others. A new king, like David, has his authority even if it is not recognized by others. A truthful man is always trustworthy, even if he is not regarded as trustworthy by the wicked. So Scripture, even when unknown, always has its dignity in itself and is trustworthy. Is not the Gospel trustworthy in itself even among the Turks? But among others, that is said to obtain its dignity which is already known and is regarded as such a good man as he is.

units.la: 2. Deinde discrimen est inter veros fide-les, donatosque Spiritu S. & ideo quibus no-ta est dignitas Scripturæ: & inter eos, qui sunt utroq; destituti, & idcirco dignitatem Scripturæ non vident. Apud illos, quicquid habet autoritatis, habet ab Ecclesia, quia cum sint sine Spiritu, & vera fide, nulla alia ratione agnoscunt, Scripturam esse sermo-nem Dei, nisi testimonio Ecclesiæ. Hoc au-tem testimonium solum, non sufficit ad ve-ram cognitionem, ut supra ostensum est. Quare parum etiam apud illos Scriptura ha-bet autoritatis.
units.tr: 2. Next, there is a difference between true believers, endowed with the Holy Spirit, to whom therefore the dignity of Scripture is known, and those who are destitute of both, and so do not see the dignity of Scripture. For those, whatever authority it has, it has from the Church, because since they are without the Spirit and true faith, they recognize Scripture as the word of God in no other way than by the testimony of the Church. But this testimony alone is not sufficient for true knowledge, as has been shown above. Therefore, Scripture has little authority even among them.

units.la: Sancta scriptura, quam apud fideles, & Spiritu Christi donatos, quibus veritas & vis Scripturæ est perspecta, habet authoritatem: non habet tam amplius ab Ecclesia, sed partim a Spiritu S. qui illorum mentes ad dignitatem Scripturæ cognoscendam aperuit: partim a seipsa, quæ ceu lux, fidelium oculos iam apertos sua luce, ita percellit, ut quàm sit ἀξιόπιστος[?], ipsa per se aperte ostendat.
units.tr: Holy Scripture, which has authority among believers and those endowed with the Spirit of Christ, to whom the truth and force of Scripture have been plainly seen, does not have this authority any longer from the Church, but partly from the Holy Spirit, who has opened their minds to recognize the dignity of Scripture, and partly from itself, which, like a light, strikes the eyes of the faithful now opened by its own light, so that it plainly shows in itself how trustworthy it is.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmation.

units.la: Iohan. 4. Iam non credimus propter tuam loquelam, sed quia nos audivimus, & scimus, &c.
units.tr: John 4. Now we no longer believe because of your saying, but because we have heard for ourselves, and know, etc.

units.la: Christus, æstimationem quam de principio habuit apud Samaritanos, ita ut propter illam egressi sint ad illum audiendum ut fide dignum, habuit a mulieris testimonio: sed quam postea habuit iam auditus & cognitus: non certè ab illa, sed à se, suoque sermone habuit. Ita Scriptura, authoritatem, &c. Simile aliud. Venit aliquis vir doctus, sed incognitus plerisque omnibus. Quidam qui eum norant, testantur aliis eum esse virum doctum, & dignum qui audiatur. Ita suo testimonio conciliant ei authoritatem apud alios. Sed postquam auditus & cognitus fuit, authoritatem quam sibi conciliauit, non habet ab illis testibus, sed à se. Hinc etiam liquidò apparet, quid ad alterum quæstionis membrum, An Ecclesiæ autoritas, id est, dignitas, maior sit quàm sanctæ Scripturæ, necne, respondendum sit. Hæc igitur esto
units.tr: Christ received the esteem he had at first among the Samaritans, so that on account of it they went out to hear him as worthy of trust, from the woman's testimony; but the authority he afterwards had once he had been heard and known, he certainly did not have from her, but from himself and his own word. So too Scripture has its authority, etc. Here is another similar case. A learned man comes, but unknown to almost all. Some who knew him testify to others that he is a learned man and worth listening to. In this way by their testimony they win him authority among others. But once he has been heard and known, the authority he has won for himself he does not have from those witnesses, but from himself. From this it is also clear what must be answered to the other part of the question, whether the authority of the Church, that is, its dignity, is greater than that of Holy Scripture or not. Let this then be the proposition.

units.la: Propositio IV.
units.tr: Proposition IV.

units.la: Scriptura sancta longè maioris est in se, & apud omnes esse debet authoritatis, quàm Ecclesiæ: & illius testimonium fide dignius est in se, & apud omnes esse debet, quàm Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: Holy Scripture is by far greater in itself and ought to be of greater authority among all than the Church; and its testimony is more worthy of faith in itself and ought to be among all more worthy of faith than the Church's.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmation.

units.la: 1. Testimonium enim Scripturæ, est ipsius Dei immediate testimonium: Ecclesiæ autem, testimonium est hominum, licet sanctorum. Testimonium autem Dei tanto maius est testimonio omnium hominum, quanto testimonium illius, qui nec falli nec fallere potest, testimonio eorum, qui suapte natura & falli & fallere possunt. Scripturæ igitur testimonium & verbum, semper longè maioris est & esse debet authoritatis, quàm Ecclesiæ: & dicta Scripturarum præferenda omnibus Ecclesiæ decretis.
units.tr: 1. For the testimony of Scripture is the immediate testimony of God himself; but the testimony of the Church is the testimony of men, though holy men. Now the testimony of God is greater than the testimony of all men by as much as the testimony of him who can neither be deceived nor deceive is greater than the testimony of those who by their very nature can both be deceived and deceive. Therefore the testimony and word of Scripture is always by far greater in authority than that of the Church, and the sayings of Scripture are to be preferred to all the decrees of the Church.

units.la: 2. 1.Iohan.5.[?] Si testimonium hominum accipimus, testimonium Dei maius est.
units.tr: 2. 1 John 5. If we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater.

units.la: 3. Act 17. Cur illi recurrunt ad Scripturas? quia sciebant ἀξιοπιστότερα[?] esse S. Biblia, verbis cuiusvis hominis, aut totius Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: 3. Acts 17. Why did they have recourse to the Scriptures? Because they knew that the Holy Bible is more trustworthy than the words of any man or of the whole Church.

units.la: 4. Ipsius dignitas in eo est, quòd est tota θεόπνευστος[?], & nũquam loquitur, nisi ex Deo. At Ecclesia non semper ex Deo loquitur: igi-tur non est tantæ autoritatis.
units.tr: 4. Its dignity lies in this, that it is wholly God-breathed and never speaks except from God. But the Church does not always speak from God; therefore it does not have such great authority.

units.la: Patres omnes tam Græci, quàm Latini, à nostra stant sententia.
units.tr: All the Fathers, both Greek and Latin, stand with our opinion.

units.la: Origenes in Ierem. hom.1. p.645. Necesse est nobis Scripturas sanctas in testimonium vocare. Sensus quippe nostri, & enarrationes, sine his testibus, non habent fidem.
units.tr: Origen, on Jeremiah, homily 1, p. 645. We must necessarily call the holy Scriptures as witnesses. For our senses and expositions, without these witnesses, do not have credibility.

units.la: Cyprianus sermone de lapsis, pagin.228. Hominibus contra Deum credunt, qui contra homines, Deo non credunt.
units.tr: Cyprian, sermon on the lapsed, p. 228. They believe men against God who do not believe God against men.

units.la: Patres iubent omnia sua scripta, & decreta Ecclesiæ, examinari ad Scripturas: igitur sentiebant, has esse maioris dignitatis & autoritatis.
units.tr: The Fathers order that all their writings and the decrees of the Church be examined by the Scriptures; therefore they judged that these have greater dignity and authority.

units.la: Ioh. Gerson, Dicto doctoris autoritate canonica munito, plus quàm declarationi Papæ credendum est.
units.tr: John Gerson: A saying of a teacher fortified with canonical authority is to be believed more than a declaration of the Pope.

units.la: Item, In S. literis erudito, atq; autoritatem Catholicam proferenti, plus est credendum, quàm Generali Concilio.
units.tr: Likewise: One who is learned in the sacred letters and brings forward Catholic authority is to be believed more than a General Council.

units.la: Panormitanus ad Canonem significasti, titulo de Electionibus: Plus credendum est uni prinato fideli, quam toti Concilio aut Papæ, si meliorem habeat autoritatem aut rationem.
units.tr: Panormitanus, on the canon significasti, title on Elections: More credence is to be given to one private faithful person than to the whole Council or the Pope, if he has the better authority or reason.

units.la: Lutherus in libello de Conciliis & Ecclesia.
units.tr: Luther, in his booklet on Councils and the Church.

units.la: Alphonsus de Castro, contra hæres: lib.1. cap.8. ubi præter alia probat, non posse Ecclesiam, nouum fidei articulum condere: posteà etiam sol.18. in hunc scribit modum.
units.tr: Alphonsus de Castro, against the heretics, book 1, chapter 8, where among other things he proves that the Church cannot establish a new article of faith; afterwards also in book 1, chapter 18, he writes in this manner.

units.la: Hoc ex Ecclesia habemus, ut sciamus, quæ sit Scriptura divina. At cum Scripturam esse disinam nobis constiterit, iam ex se ipsa habet, ut ei per omnia credere teneamur: Et hoc adfert simile, admodum accommodatum. Petrus debet Iohanni 100. aureos, & hac de re extat instrumentum (ut vocant) scriptum, & multorum testimonio comprobatum. Si, dum Petrus negat, se Iohanni debere hos 100. aureos, testes illi producantur, & illi testificentur hoc instrumentum verum esse, & legitimum instrumentum, & Petrum verum esse debitorem 100. aureorum Iohanni: nunquid horum testificatio facit, ut instrumentum sit verum, & Petrus verus fiat debitor Iohanni? Minime, Nam etiamsi non fuissent testificati: tamen Petrus debui-set, & instrumentum fuisset verissimum: sed non fuisset agnitum. Ita, etsi Ecclesia testa-ta est, Scripturam hanc esse verum Dei verbum: non tamen effecit, ut sit verbum Dei.
units.tr: We have from the Church that we may know what is divine Scripture. But when it has been established for us that Scripture is divine, it then has from itself that we are bound to believe it in all things. And he brings forward a very apt comparison. Peter owes John 100 gold coins, and about this there exists a written instrument (as they call it), attested by the testimony of many. If, while Peter denies that he owes John these 100 gold coins, witnesses are produced, and they testify that this instrument is true and a legitimate instrument, and that Peter is truly a debtor of 100 gold coins to John: does their testimony make the instrument true, and Peter a true debtor to John? By no means. For even if they had not testified, Peter would still have owed it, and the instrument would have been most true, but it would not have been recognised. So, although the Church has testified that this Scripture is the true word of God, it has not thereby made it to be the word of God.

units.la: Quare posteaquam cognitum est, Scriptu-ram esse verbum Dei: tenemur ei in omnibus parere: etiamsi tota Ecclesia prohiberet: quia parendum est Deo magis, quàm homi-nibus.
units.tr: Therefore, once it has been recognised that Scripture is the word of God, we are bound to obey it in all things, even if the whole Church forbade it, because we must obey God rather than men.

units.la: PROPOSITIO V.
units.tr: PROPOSITION V.

units.la: Sacra Scriptura non solum in se est, & apud omnes esse debet maioris authoritatis, quàm Ecclesia: sed etiam reipsa est apud omnes Spiritu Dei, vera fide, & Scripturarum cognitione praeditos.
units.tr: Holy Scripture is not only in itself, and must be of greater authority for all than the Church, but in fact it is also, for all those endowed with the Spirit of God, true faith, and knowledge of the Scriptures, of greater authority than the Church.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmation.

units.la: 1. Quicunq; non solùm propter testimonii[?] Ecclesiæ credit: verùm etiam per Spiritum sanctum & reipsa nouit, Scripturam sanctam ipsissimum esse Dei verbum, quod nec falli, nec fallere potest, ipsam verò Ecclesiam sua-pte natura & falli & fallere posse: apud ipsum certè maioris est authoritatis sacra Scriptu-ra,quàm Ecclesia. Sciunt enim pluris faciendum esse verbum Dei, quàm omnes homi-nes,&illud maiori[?] dignum fide,quàm omnia hominum dicta. Atqui hoc modo norunt Scripturam esse verbum Dei illi, qui Spiritu sancto,vera fide & Scripturarum cognitione præditi sunt. Ergo apud hos maioris est au-toritatis Scriptura,quàm Ecclesia.
units.tr: 1. Whoever believes not merely on account of the testimony of the Church, but also through the Holy Spirit and in fact knows that Holy Scripture is the very Word of God, which can neither err nor deceive, while the Church itself, by its own nature, can both err and deceive: for him, certainly, Holy Scripture is of greater authority than the Church. For they know that the Word of God is to be valued above all men, and that it is worthy of belief above all the sayings of men. But those who are endowed with the Holy Spirit, true faith and knowledge of the Scriptures know Scripture to be the Word of God in this way. Therefore, for these people, Scripture is of greater authority than the Church.

units.la: 2. Exemplis propositio declaretur & confirmetur.
units.tr: 2. Let the proposition be made clear and confirmed by examples.

units.la: Gal. 1. Si ego aut Angelus de cœlo prædicaue-rit aliud Euangelium, &c. anathema sit. Qua-re hoc ait Apostolus? Quia notat per Spiri-tum sanctum & certissimè norat, hoc Eu-angelium quod prædicauerat, esse ipsissimam Dei verbum, ita ut dubitare de eo nullo am-plius posset modo. Ideò etiamsi tota Ecclesia & omnes Angeli venirent, & aliter docuis-sent, tantum abest, ut voluisset illis maiorem præbere fidem, quàm suo Euangelio, ut po-tius illis dicturus fuisset anathema. Liquet igitur ex hoc loco, authoritatem verbi Dei maiorem apud Apostolum fuisse, quàm totius esset Ecclesiæ, imò & omnium Angelo-rum: rum: & huius rei nullam aliam fuisse ratio-nem, nisi quia per Spiritum S. non autem per hominum testimonium, certus erat de veritate sui Euangelij.
units.tr: Gal. 1. If I, or an angel from heaven, preach to you another gospel, etc., let him be accursed. Why does the Apostle say this? Because he knew, through the Holy Spirit and with the greatest certainty, that the gospel which he had preached was the very Word of God, so that he could no longer doubt it in any way. Therefore, even if the whole Church and all the angels should come and teach otherwise, he would be so far from wishing to give them greater credit than his own gospel, that he would rather pronounce anathema upon them. It is clear therefore from this passage that the authority of the Word of God was greater for the Apostle than that of the whole Church, indeed than that of all the angels; and there was no other reason for this than that he was certain of the truth of his gospel through the Holy Spirit, and not through the testimony of men.

units.la: Sic apud Apostolos omnes, Mariam, Eli-sabetham,&c. maioris erat autoritatis Chri-stus & eius doctrina, quàm tota Ecclesia Hierosolymitana. Quare? quia norant per Spiritum S. hunc esse Filium Dei,& eius do-ctrinam,verum Dei sermonem.
units.tr: So among all the Apostles, Christ and his doctrine were of greater authority than the whole Church of Jerusalem, as were Mary, Elizabeth, etc. Why? Because they knew through the Holy Spirit that this one is the Son of God, and that his doctrine is the true speech of God.

units.la: Sic apud Samaritanos, etsi de principio maior erat authoritas mulieris notæ, quàm Christi,qui erat ignotus: tamen posteaquam per fidem ex auditu verbi eum nouerunt esse Messiam & Filium Dei: longè maioris apud ipsos autoritatis fuit Christus, quàm mulier. Ideò dicebant ei. Jam non credimus propter sermonem tuum, sed quia nos audiuimus, &c. Hinc colligitur necessario.
units.tr: So among the Samaritans, although at first the authority of a woman well known to them was greater than that of Christ, who was unknown, yet after they had come to know through faith, from hearing the word, that he was the Messiah and the Son of God, the authority of Christ among them became far greater than that of the woman. Therefore they said to her: Now we no longer believe because of your saying, but because we have heard, etc. From this a conclusion follows necessarily.

units.la: PROPOSITIO VI.
units.tr: PROPOSITION VI.

units.la: Apud quos Ecclesia maioris est autoritatis, quàm Scriptura: ij nondum per Spiritum S. agnoscunt Scripturam esse verbum Dei, & ideo adhuc nulla vera fide præditi sunt.
units.tr: Among those for whom the Church is of greater authority than Scripture, these people do not yet, through the Holy Spirit, acknowledge Scripture to be the Word of God, and therefore they are not yet endowed with true faith.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmation.

units.la: Liquet ex superiùs dictis per argumentationem à contrario. Si enim præditi essent vera fide & Spiritu Dei, veraque Scripturarum cognitione, vtique maioris apud ipsos esset Scriptura authoritatis, quàm Ecclesia. Hæc patet ex superioribus. Atqui maior apud hos est Ecclesiæ autoritas, quàm Scri-pturæ. Ergò, &c. Cur enim pluris faciunt Ecclesiæ autoritatem quàm Scripturæ? Quia persuasi sunt Ecclesiam constare viris bonis, sanctis, fide dignis, qui non velint fallere, & ita sapientibus, qui non possint falli: de Scripturis autem nondum sunt ita persuasi: es-sent autem persuasi, si haberent Spiritum Dei, veram fidem, & cognitionem Scripturarum. Manifestum igitur est, ideò illos pluris facere testimonium Ecclesiæ, quàm Scripturæ, quia destituti sunt Spiritu Dei. Nam fac, ut per Spiritum sanctum agnoscant Scripturam certissimum esse Dei verbum: tum videbis illos pluris facere Scripturam, quàm Ecclesiam. An non discipuli Iohannis Baptistæ, posteaquam noverunt Christum verum esse Messiam & Filium Dei, illum pluris fecerunt, quàm Iohannem Baptistam & totam Ecclesiam Hierofolymitanam? Omnino. Ergo quod de principio pluris fecerunt Ecclesiam Hierofolymitanam, & secundò Ioannem Baptistam, quàm Christum: argumento fuit, tunc illos nondum per Spiritum sanctum Christum quis esset, agnouisse.
units.tr: It is clear from what has been said above, by argument from the contrary. For if they were endowed with true faith and the Spirit of God, and with true knowledge of the Scriptures, then certainly Scripture would be of greater authority for them than the Church. This is evident from what has gone before. But the authority of the Church is greater than that of Scripture for these people. Therefore, etc. For why do they value the authority of the Church above that of Scripture? Because they are persuaded that the Church consists of good, holy, trustworthy men, who do not wish to deceive, and of wise men, who cannot be deceived; but concerning the Scriptures they are not yet so persuaded. Yet they would be persuaded if they had the Spirit of God, true faith, and knowledge of the Scriptures. It is therefore manifest that they value the testimony of the Church above Scripture because they are destitute of the Spirit of God. For suppose that through the Holy Spirit they acknowledge Scripture to be the most certain Word of God: then you will see them value Scripture above the Church. Did not the disciples of John the Baptist, after they knew Christ to be the true Messiah and Son of God, value him above John the Baptist and the whole Church of Jerusalem? Assuredly. Therefore, that they at first valued the Church of Jerusalem, and secondly John the Baptist, above Christ, was the proof that at that time they had not yet recognised through the Holy Spirit who Christ was.

units.la: Sic apud Augustinum, cùm esset adhuc Manichæus sine Spiritu Dei, & vera cognitione sacræ Scripturæ, maior fuit authoritas Ecclesiæ, id est, tot tantorumque virorum, quos videbat profiteri Christum, quàm Scripturæ & Euangelij. Ideò dixit, Euangelio non credidissem, &c. Sed certè non ita locutus est, posteaquàm Christum nouit & sacras literas. Idem dico de obseruantia Samaritanorum erga mulierem & Christum. Ergo quòd nunc apud Papistas maior sit authoritas Ecclesiæ Romanæ, quàm sacræ Scripturæ: reipsa liquet, illos nondum habere Spiritum Dei, nec veram fidem, nec vllam veram Scripturarum cognitionem, neque agnoscere aut verè credere, Scripturam esse verbum Dei. Nam si hoc agnoscerent, maioris pro-culdubio apud illos esset authoritatis, dignitatis, æstimationis, reuerentiæ, quàm Ecclesia Romana.
units.tr: So with Augustine: while he was still a Manichean, without the Spirit of God and without true knowledge of Holy Scripture, the authority of the Church, that is, of so many and so great men whom he saw professing Christ, was greater than that of Scripture and the Gospel. Therefore he said, I would not have believed the Gospel, etc. But certainly he did not speak thus after he had come to know Christ and the sacred letters. I say the same of the reverence of the Samaritans towards the woman and towards Christ. Therefore, that the authority of the Roman Church is now greater than that of Holy Scripture among the Papists, it is plainly clear in fact that they do not yet have the Spirit of God, nor true faith, nor any true knowledge of the Scriptures, nor do they acknowledge or truly believe that Scripture is the Word of God. For if they acknowledged this, undoubtedly among them the Roman Church would be of greater authority, dignity, esteem and reverence than Scripture.

units.la: Idem contigit nobis, cùm essemus in Papatu, nec dum agnoscueremus Christum & Scripturam, pluris faciebamus Ecclesiam Romanam, quàm sacram Scripturam. At nunc contrà, Dei beneficio. Quare ? quia donati Spiritu Dei melius agnoscimus, quantum discriminis sit inter Scripturam, verbum Dei, & Ecclesiam ipsam cœtum sanctò-rum. Nam agnoscimus quicquid reuerentiæ, fidei & honoris debetur Ecclesiæ, hoc ideò illi deberi, quia retinet verbum Dei, & ex illo loquitur, docet, omnia agit.
units.tr: The same happened to us: when we were in Popery, and did not yet acknowledge Christ and Scripture, we valued the Roman Church above Holy Scripture. But now, by the goodness of God, it is otherwise. Why? Because, endowed with the Spirit of God, we better recognise how great is the difference between Scripture, the Word of God, and the Church itself, the assembly of the saints. For we acknowledge that whatever reverence, faith and honour is owed to the Church, it is owed to it for this reason: that it keeps the Word of God, and speaks, teaches and does everything from that Word.

units.la: PROPOSITIO VII.
units.tr: PROPOSITION VII.

units.la: Quicquid dignitatis habet Ecclesia: habet à sacra Scriptura.
units.tr: Whatever dignity the Church has, it has from Holy Scripture.

units.la: Hac de causa 1. Timoth. c. 3. Columna & firmamentum veritatis appellatur: hac de causa sponsa Christi vocatur, quia sponsi vocem audit & retinet: hac de causa munda & sancta est, quia retinet sermonem Christi, per quem mundata & sanctificata est. Vnde Cæsaris Legatus, qui venit ad Principem nostrum Electorem habet vt audiatur tanquam fide dignus, & ei credatur? habet à literis Cæsaris, quas adfert. Quid dedit autoritatem, & (vt Italicè loquar) credito Ecclesiæ Mofaicæ? Doctrina illa tot miraculis confirmata: quia eam prædicabat & retinebat illa Ecclesia. Sic quid Apostolicæ? Doctrina quam profitebatur tot miraculis confirmata. Ergo doctrina Scripturæ, dat authoritatem Ecclesiæ, non contrà. Est autem certissima illa regula: Propter quod vnum quodque tale est, illud magis tale est. Longè igitur maioris esse autoritatis Scripturam quàm Ecclesiam, Ecclesiam, inquam, veram. Nam falsa & Antichriftiana indigna est, quæ cum sacra Scriptura vllo modo comparetur.
units.tr: For this reason, in 1 Timothy chapter 3, the Church is called the pillar and foundation of the truth. For this reason she is called the bride of Christ, because she hears and holds the voice of the bridegroom. For this reason she is clean and holy, because she holds fast the word of Christ, by which she has been cleansed and sanctified. Hence, why does the envoy of the Emperor, who comes to our Prince Elector, have a right to be heard as trustworthy and to be believed? He has it from the letters of the Emperor which he brings. What gave authority to (to speak in Italian) the credit of the Mosaic Church? That doctrine, confirmed by so many miracles, because that Church preached and held it. Likewise, what gave authority to the Apostolic Church? The doctrine it professed, confirmed by so many miracles. Therefore the doctrine of Scripture gives authority to the Church, not the reverse. Moreover, this rule is most certain: whatever a thing is because of something, that thing is more so. Therefore Scripture is of far greater authority than the Church, I say the true Church. For the false and Antichristian church is unworthy to be compared with holy Scripture in any way.

units.la: Atque hæc fatis de autoritate Ecclesiæ & Scripturæ, quatenus hoc nomen significat æstimationem & dignitatem, qua quis iudicatur fide dignus.
units.tr: And so much for the authority of the Church and of Scripture, insofar as this word signifies the esteem and dignity by which someone is judged worthy of belief.

units.la: RESPONSIONES AD ARGVMENTA.
units.tr: REPLIES TO THE ARGUMENTS.

units.la: Primum ab antiquitate. Autoritas Eccle-sia antiquior est autoritate Scripturæ: fuit enimEcclesia ante Scripturam ullam, ut liquet tam[?] de Ecclesia ante Mosen, quam de Ecclesia Chri-stiana ante scripta Apostolorum. Et Ecclesia suā semper habuit authoritatem & dignitatem, qua digna erat omni fide & reverentia atq; honore.
units.tr: First, from antiquity. The authority of the Church is older than the authority of Scripture: for the Church existed before any Scripture, as is clear both of the Church before Moses and of the Christian Church before the writings of the Apostles. And the Church has always had her own authority and dignity, by which she was worthy of all faith, reverence and honour.

units.la: Ergo suam dignitatem non habet a Scriptura: sed potius contra, ac proinde etiam maior est Ecclesia, quam Scriptura autoritas seu dignitas.
units.tr: Therefore she does not have her dignity from Scripture, but rather the reverse; and accordingly the authority or dignity of the Church is greater than that of Scripture.

units.la: Respond. 1. ad Antecedens. Est falsum, & assumtum etiam falsum: & admittitur fallacia accidentis. Declaro. Scriptura sacra habet suam substantiam & suum accidens. Substantia, est ipsum verbum à Deo revelatum & inspiratum. Ita si definias Scripturam quod ad substantiam attinet, ea nil aliud est, quàm doctrina à Deo sanctis hominibus aut revelata, aut inspirata, ad salutem Electorum. Atque ut breviùs dicam, Scriptura nil est, nisi doctrina θεόπνευστος[?], vt à Paulina locutione non recedam. Accidens verò, est ipsa scriptio, seu exaratio in tabulis & libris. Ita si definias Scripturam à substantia & accidenti simul, sic definienda est. Scriptura est doctrina à Deo sanctis certis hominibus inspirata, & per eosdem, Spiritu sancto di[?]tante conscripta, ad salutem Electorum, & ut illis uti-lis fit ωφέλιμος[?], &c. Ergo si Scripturam spectes quò ad substantiam: illa certè non est posterior Ecclesia, sed contrà. Verbum enim Dei revelatum prius est ipsa Ecclesia, jam à condito orbe: Ecclesia enim col-lecta est verbo, regenerata per verbum: fundata super verbum. Quid autem prius, fundamentum, an domus superstructa? Ergo si substantiam Scripturae spectes, falsum est, Ecclesiam & dignitatem Ecclesiae, priorem esse Scriptura & dignitate Scripturae. Sed si accidens Scripturae: facile damus. Sed tunc nihil concludis: quoniam, etsi ipsa etiam scriptio, suam habeat dignitatem, quatenus & ipsa a Spiritu sancto inspirata, & quodam modo dictata verbotim fuit, ita ut nullum in ea sit iota, quod non sit a Deo inspiratum: unde quod Paulus ait, Scripturam esse θεόπνευστον [?], intelligendum est & quoad substantiam, & quod accidens: etsi, inquam, Scriptura etiam quoad ipsam scriptionem habeat suam dignitatem: tamen dignitas, de qua lo-quimur, praecipue est in ipsa substantia. Hanc autem semper habuit a condito orbe.
units.tr: Reply. 1. To the antecedent: it is false, and the assumption is also false, and the fallacy of accident is admitted. I explain. Holy Scripture has its substance and its accident. The substance is the very word revealed and inspired by God. So if you define Scripture as regards its substance, it is nothing other than doctrine revealed or inspired by God to holy men, for the salvation of the elect. And to say it more briefly, Scripture is nothing but doctrine [theopneustos], not to depart from Paul's expression. The accident, however, is the writing itself, or its inscription on tablets and books. So if you define Scripture by substance and accident together, it must be defined thus: Scripture is doctrine inspired by God to certain holy men, and written down by the same men, moved by the Holy Spirit, for the salvation of the elect and so that it may be useful to them [ōphelimos], etc. Therefore, if you regard Scripture as to its substance, it is certainly not posterior to the Church, but rather the reverse. For the revealed word of God is prior to the Church itself, existing from the foundation of the world: the Church is gathered by the word, regenerated through the word, founded upon the word. Now which is first, the foundation or the house built upon it? Therefore, if you regard the substance of Scripture, it is false that the Church and the dignity of the Church are prior to Scripture and the dignity of Scripture. But if you mean the accident of Scripture, we readily grant it. But then you conclude nothing: since, although the writing itself also has its own dignity, insofar as it too was inspired by the Holy Spirit and in a certain way was dictated word for word, so that there is not a single iota in it that was not inspired by God; hence, what Paul says, that Scripture is [theopneustos], is to be understood both as to substance and as to accident. Yet, I say, although Scripture as to the writing itself also has its dignity, the dignity we are speaking of nonetheless lies chiefly in the substance itself. And this substance it has always had from the foundation of the world.

units.la: 1. Respondeo etiam ad consequentiam: illam non concludere. Oportet enim, ut pendeat ex hac universali: Quicquid est prius, illud est dignius, & gloriosius illo, quod est posterius. Hoc autem videbis non esse in omnibus, & semper verum. Etsi Lex per Mo-sen tradita, prior fuit Evangelio per Chri-stum praedicato & revelato: consequitur igitur Legem Mosis, maioris fuisse dignita-tis & gloriae, quam Evangelium? Apostolus certe 1. Corinth. 3. contrarium demonstrat. Item Iohan. Baptista, prior fuit Christo in carne: Ergo maior Christo? Item, Sacrificia veteris Testamenti pecudum, boum, prio-ra sara sacrificio noui Testamenti, id est, oblatione Christi in cruce: Ergo illa praestantiora isto? Item, Typi & figurae, priores sunt veritate: Ergo etiam pluris faciendae, quàm veritas? Ergo hoc Papistarum argumentum, utraque tibia claudicat, & antecedente & consequentia.
units.tr: 1. I also reply to the consequence: that it does not follow. For it would have to depend on this universal principle: whatever is prior, that is more worthy and more glorious than what is posterior. But you will see that this is not true in all cases, nor always. Although the Law delivered through Moses was prior to the Gospel preached and revealed by Christ, does it follow that the Law of Moses was of greater dignity and glory than the Gospel? The Apostle, at 1 Corinthians 3, certainly shows the contrary. Likewise John the Baptist was prior to Christ in the flesh: therefore is he greater than Christ? Likewise, the sacrifices of the Old Testament, of sheep and oxen, were prior to the sacrifice of the New Testament, that is, the offering of Christ on the cross: therefore are those more excellent than this? Likewise, types and figures are prior to the truth: therefore are they also to be valued more than the truth? Therefore this argument of the Papists limps on both legs, both in its antecedent and in its consequence.

units.la: Secundum argumentum à declaratione & testificatione Ecclesiae.
units.tr: The second argument, from the declaration and testimony of the Church.

units.la: Libri sacri, quòd primò nunc sint authentici dignit q [?] fide: & secundò quòd pro talibus habeantur apud fideles: hanc certè dignitatem habent à sola Ecclesia, quae sua authoritate, hanc illis dedit dignitatem. Nam cùm multi libri in Ecclesia obtruderentur fidelibus, tanquam à Deo inspirati, & eius Spiritu conscripti, Ecclesia agnovit, qui essent verè divini (nempe hos Canonicos) & qui non. Statuit, ut ij ab omnibus haberentur pro Canonicis, & divinis, alij pro Apocryphis. Omnes verò hoc decretum admiserunt propter authoritatem Ecclesiae.
units.tr: Sacred books are authentic and worthy of faith, and, secondly, they are regarded as such among the faithful: this dignity they certainly have from the Church alone, which by its own authority conferred this dignity upon them. For when many books were being thrust upon the faithful as inspired by God and written by his Spirit, the Church recognised which were truly divine (namely these canonical ones) and which were not. It decreed that those were to be held by all as canonical and divine, and the others as apocryphal. And all have admitted this decree on account of the authority of the Church.

units.la: Ergo, quòd Scriptura nunc habeat hanc in Ecclesia apud omnes authoritatem, ut pro verbo Dei agnoscatur & admittatur, habet ab Ecclesiae authoritate.
units.tr: Therefore, that Scripture now has this authority in the Church among all, so that it is acknowledged and admitted as the Word of God, it has from the authority of the Church.

units.la: Respond. ad antecedens .1. Falsum est Scripturam sacram accepisse ab Ecclesia hanc dignitatem, ut sit authentica in se & fide digna. Ecclesia enim nunquam dedit Scripturae hanc dignitatem, ut esset per se ἀξιόπιστος & authentica. Semper enim fuit verbum Dei, & eâ re ἀξιόπιστος: igitur non habet ab Ecclesia: tantum illa testata est & declarauit omnibus, quid & qualis, & cuius esset hæc Scriptura: sed non ei dedit, vt talis esset, hoc est, fide digna. Ioh. Baptista testatus est, & indicauit Iudæis Iesum Christum; sed non fecit vt esset Christus. Aurifaber examinat aurum ad lapidem: deinde vbi agnouit esse bonum aurum, hoc aliis indicat & testatur: Nū igitur dat illi vt sit aurum bonum? Est igitur fallacia figuræ dictionis. Nam aliud est testari aliquid esse tale: aliud facere, vt sit tale.
units.tr: I answer to the antecedent, first: It is false that Holy Scripture received this dignity from the Church, so that it is authentic in itself and worthy of faith. For the Church never gave Scripture this dignity, that it should be trustworthy [ἀξιόπιστος] and authentic of itself. It was always the Word of God, and for that reason trustworthy; therefore it does not have this from the Church. The Church only bore witness and declared to all what and of what kind and whose this Scripture is, but it did not give it that it should be such, that is, worthy of faith. John the Baptist bore witness and pointed out Jesus Christ to the Jews, but he did not make him to be Christ. The goldsmith tests gold on the touchstone; then, when he recognises that it is good gold, he indicates and attests this to others. Does he therefore give it that it be good gold? There is therefore a fallacy of figure of speech. For it is one thing to attest that something is such, and another to make it be such.

units.la: 2. Quòd verò aiunt, Scripturam hanc saltem apud fideles habere abs sola Ecclesia auctoritatem, vt agnoscatur & habeatur pro Canonica & verbo Dei: hoc est falsum. Ab Ecclesia habuit propter illius declarationem & auctoritatem, vt ab hominibus admitteretur pro verbo Dei, & ita audiretur, sed non vt vere crederetur & agnosceretur esse certum Dei verbum: verùm hoc habuit (vt suprà ostensum est) primò à S.S. hoc fidelibus inter audiendū Scripturam persuadente: secundò ab auctoritate & dignitate & excellentia & vi ipsius Scripturæ, iam per Spiritum S. fidelibus patefacta & ostensa. Vnde enim habuit Ecclesia, vt agnouerit, hanc Scripturam esse θεόπνευστον [?] à Spiritu S. sic omnes fatentur. Ab eodem Spiritu etiam singuli veri fideles, eandem accipiunt cognitionem. Est enim eadem ratio singularum partium, quæ & totius. Quare hic etiam est fallacia non causæ vt causæ, Causa enim efficiens, quæ fidelibus verè persuasit & persuadet : item pa-tefecit & patefacit hanc Scripturâ esse ipsum Dei verbum, & Deum in ea loquentem demonstrauit: non fuit Ecclesiæ testimonium & auctoritas: sed Spiritus S. persuadens: & deinde Scripturæ dignitas atque vis, per Spiritum S. fidelium mentibus ostensa: atque ita ostensa, vt eam perspicuè videant & sentiant. Ecclesia autem tantùm hoc effecit suo testimonio & auctoritate, vt homines eam administrarint pro verbo Dei, sed non vt cognouerint, aut etiam persuasi verè de hac re fuerint. Similibus & exemplis declaro hanc ipsorum fallaciam.
units.tr: Second, as to their claim that this Scripture has authority among the faithful, at least, solely from the Church, so that it is acknowledged and held as canonical and the Word of God: this is false. It had from the Church, on account of its declaration and authority, that it be admitted by men as the Word of God and so be heard; but not that it be truly believed and recognised as the certain Word of God. This it has (as has been shown above) first from the Holy Spirit, who persuades the faithful of this while they hear Scripture; secondly, from the authority, dignity, excellence and power of Scripture itself, now disclosed and shown to the faithful through the Holy Spirit. For whence did the Church have, that it recognised that this Scripture is θεόπνευστον [God-breathed] by the Holy Spirit? So all confess. By the same Spirit also individual true believers receive the same knowledge. For the reason for the individual parts is the same as for the whole. Therefore here too there is a fallacy of not-cause as cause. For the efficient cause, which truly persuaded and persuades the faithful, and likewise disclosed and discloses that this Scripture is the very Word of God, and demonstrated God speaking in it, was not the testimony and authority of the Church, but the Holy Spirit persuading; and then the dignity and force of Scripture, shown to the minds of the faithful through the Holy Spirit, and shown in such a way that they clearly see and perceive it. The Church, however, has only brought about this by its testimony and authority, that men have administered it as the Word of God, but not that they have come to know, or even been truly persuaded of, this matter. I explain their fallacy by similar examples.

units.la: Iohan. Baptista testificatur duobus à suis discipulis, inter quos erat Andreas, illum Iesum, quem videbant, esse ipsum Christum Messiam, Filium Dei. Ipsi authoritate Iohan. Baptistæ permoti veniunt ad Iesum, vt videant & audiant. Idem postea Andreas significat Simoni Petro fratri suo: is itidem permotus testimonio & auctoritate Andreæ fratris, venit ad Iesum: & tandem verè credit & agnoscit, illum esse verum Christum & Filium Dei. Dicemusne illos duos discipulos Iohannis, ab ipso Iohanne accepisse, vt crederent in Christum ? Et deinde Petrum hoc accepisse ab Andrea ? Minimè. Nam Matth. 16. Christus ait Simoni: Caro & fan-guis non renelauit[?] tibi, &c. Ergo Christus hanc dignitatem & auctoritatem, vt agnosceretur quis esset, & à multis crederetur in illum, non accepit vel à Iohan. Baptista, vel ab Andrea: sed à Patre, qui suo Spiritu illum patefecit suis electis. Si quis igitur diceret, Andream suo testimonio causam fuisse, vt Petrus crederet in Christum, admitteret paralogismum, qui dicitur, Non causæ vt causæ.
units.tr: John the Baptist bore witness to two of his disciples, among whom was Andrew, that that Jesus whom they saw was the very Christ, the Messiah, the Son of God. They, moved by the authority of John the Baptist, come to Jesus, that they may see and hear. Afterwards Andrew makes this known to Simon Peter his brother; he likewise, moved by the testimony and authority of his brother Andrew, comes to Jesus, and at last truly believes and acknowledges him to be the true Christ and Son of God. Shall we say that those two disciples of John received from John himself that they should believe in Christ? And that Peter received this from Andrew? By no means. For in Matthew 16 Christ says to Simon: "Flesh and blood have not revealed this to you," etc. Therefore Christ did not receive this dignity and authority, that he should be recognised for who he is and be believed in by many, either from John the Baptist or from Andrew, but from the Father, who revealed him to his elect by his Spirit. If anyone therefore said that Andrew was by his testimony the cause that Peter believed in Christ, he would admit the paralogism that is called "not-cause as cause."

units.la: Idem ab exemplo Samaritanorum & mulieris perispicuum fit. Certè mulier non fuit causa, vt crederent illi in Christum, sed tantùm occasio: Itafe [?] habet Ecclesia erga nos, quomodo mulier illa erga Samaritanos, cives suos.
units.tr: The same becomes perfectly clear from the example of the Samaritans and the woman. Certainly the woman was not the cause that they believed in Christ, but only the occasion. The Church stands toward us as that woman stood toward the Samaritans, her fellow citizens.

units.la: Possumus etiam dicere, esse fallaciam à dicto secundùm quid, ad simpliciter. Nam si mulier fuit causa fidei Samaritanis: fuit secundùm quid, non simpliciter.
units.tr: We can also say that this is a fallacy of an argument from what is said in a certain respect to what is said absolutely. For if the woman was the cause of faith for the Samaritans, she was so in a certain respect, not absolutely.

units.la: Tertium. Augustinus Tomo 6. contra epistolam Manichæi, quam vocabant Fundamentum, eo quòd in ea contineretur summa doctrinæ Manichæi, praeter alia habet ibi hæc verba, in cap. 5. [?] Ego verò Euangelio non crederem, nisi Ecclesiæ authoritas me commoueret.
units.tr: Third, Augustine, in volume 6, against the letter of Manichaeus which they called the "Foundation," because the sum of Manichaeus's teaching was contained in it, has, among other things, these words there, in chapter 5: "For my part I would not believe the Gospel, unless the authority of the Church moved me."

units.la: Inde Papistæ inferunt: Ergo fides Augustini in Euangelium, pendebat ab authoritate Ecclesiæ. Ideo enim credidit Euangelio, quia credebat Ecclesiæ, quæ dixit hoc esse Euangelium Christi, verbumque Dei certum.
units.tr: From this the Papists infer: Therefore Augustine's faith in the Gospel depended on the authority of the Church. For he believed the Gospel because he believed the Church, which said that this was the Gospel of Christ and the certain Word of God.

units.la: Ergo authoritas Ecclesiæ, fuit apud Augustinum maior authoritate Euangelij.
units.tr: Therefore the authority of the Church was for Augustine greater than the authority of the Gospel.

units.la: Respond ad antecedens. Sensus Augustini colligendus est ex vera verborum eius intelligentia, & phrasi ac scopo. Illud, Non crederem, nisi me commoueret autoritas Ecclesiae, est pro credidissem & commouisset. Phrasis Augustini.
units.tr: I answer to the antecedent: The sense of Augustine is to be gathered from the true understanding of his words, and from his phrasing and aim. That phrase, "I would not believe, unless the authority of the Church moved me," stands for "I would not have believed and had been moved." This is Augustine's phrasing.

units.la: Nomine Ecclesiae, intelligit totam Ecclesiam Catholicam, quae Euangelium praedicabat & profitebatur. Verbo autem credendi, non intelligit veram & firmam fidem, quantum credebat Euangelio, cum haec scriberet: sed fidem quandam quasi humanam, quam de principio propter Ecclesiae auctoritatem, adhibuit Euangelio. Vera enim non adhibetur propter Ecclesiae authoritatem, sed propter autoritatem Dei loquentis, dignitatem & veritatem Euangelij, quam videmus per Spiritum sanctum illuminati. Sensus igitur est: autoritatem Ecclesiae, sibi multo pluris esse faciendam, quam Manichaei & omnium suorum. Quare?quia illa etiam est, qua primum permotus fuit, ut crederet Euangelio, hoc est, ut illud attente audiret & reuerenter acceperit, & aliqua etiam fide crediderit. Vel etiam si vis eum loqui de vera fide, qua tunc credebat Euangelio, & verbum, Non crederem, retinere in praesenti: perinde fuerit. Erit enim sensus: Ego certe iam non crederem Euangelio, sicut credo: nisi Ecclesia sua authoritate me ad credendum commouisset, & praedicando Euangelium dixisset, Credite Euangelio, quia Domini est Euangelium. Et est sensus, sicut etiam, si Samaritani posteaquam crediderunt in Christum, dixissent: Certe nos non crederemus iam in Christum,nisi autoritas mulieris,quæ nos ad illum videndum & audiendum inui-tauit, commouiflet. O quantum igitur de-bemus huic mulieri. Et sicut fi dixiflent Theflalonicenfes : Nos multum debemus Paulo, & illius authoritatem magnifacere. Quare? quia nisi ille nos sua autoritate com-mouisset, & ad credendum Euangelio exci-taflet sua prædicatione, nos certè iam non crederemus in Christum.
units.tr: By "the Church" he understands the whole Catholic Church, which preached and professed the Gospel. By the word "to believe," however, he does not understand true and firm faith, as far as he believed in the Gospel while writing these things, but a certain faith, as it were human, which at the beginning he gave to the Gospel on account of the authority of the Church. For true faith is not given on account of the authority of the Church, but on account of the authority of God speaking, and the dignity and truth of the Gospel, which we see when illuminated by the Holy Spirit. The sense therefore is: the authority of the Church is to be held of far more account by him than that of the Manichaeans and all their followers. Why? Because it is also that by which he was first moved to believe the Gospel, that is, to hear it attentively and receive it reverently, and to believe it with some faith at least. Or even if you wish him to speak of true faith, by which he then believed the Gospel, and to keep the word "I would not believe" in the present tense, it makes no difference. For the sense will be: "Certainly I would now not believe the Gospel as I believe it, unless the Church had moved me by its authority to believe, and by preaching the Gospel had said, 'Believe the Gospel, because the Gospel is the Lord's.'" And it is the sense as well as if the Samaritans, after they had believed in Christ, had said: "Certainly we would not now believe in Christ, unless the authority of the woman, who invited us to see and hear him, had moved us. O how much then we owe this woman!" And just as if the Thessalonians had said: "We owe much to Paul, and we hold his authority in high esteem. Why? Because unless he had moved us by his authority, and roused us to believe the Gospel by his preaching, we certainly would not now believe in Christ."

units.la: Hunc sensum esse Augustini,liquet,fi quis diligenter illum perpendat locum. Item, ex Commentariis Augustini in illam historiam Samaritanæ Iohan.4. Ait enim, illam fuisse typum Ecclesiæ, quòd sicut illa prædicauit Christum suis ciuibus,sic Ecclesia nobis. Et sicut illi excitati prædicatione mulieris, & eius autoritate, exierunt,audiuerunt Chri-ftum,& in illum crediderunt: sic nos autori-tate & prædicatione Ecclesiæ. Quomodo enim credent, nisi audiant ? Quomodo au-dient fine prædicante ? Sed sicut illi post ve-ram adhibitam fidem Christo & eius Euan-gelio agnouerunt eam sibi datam esse nonà muliere, sed à Spiritu, ex auditu verbi Chri-fti,& proinde dixerunt mulieri , Iam non cre-dimus propter tuum sermonem , sed quia ipsi vi-dimus & audiuimus,&c.Ita nos,&c.
units.tr: This sense of Augustine's is clear enough if one weighs his passage carefully. Likewise, from Augustine's Commentaries on that story of the Samaritan woman in John 4. For he says that she was a type of the Church: just as she preached Christ to her fellow citizens, so the Church does to us. And just as those men, stirred by the woman's preaching and her authority, went out, heard Christ, and believed in him, so we do by the authority and preaching of the Church. For "how shall they believe, unless they hear? And how shall they hear without a preacher?" But afterwards, having adopted the true faith, those men recognised, with respect to Christ and his Gospel, that this faith had been given to them not by the woman but by the Spirit, through hearing the word of Christ; and therefore they said to the woman, Now we believe not because of your saying, but because we ourselves have seen and heard, etc. So with us, etc.

units.la: 2. Ad consequentiam. 1. Illa est contra mentem Augustini ex Augustini verbis col-lecta. 2. Consequentiam hanc,Ergo authori-tas Ecclesiæ maior est autoritate Euangelij colligere ex verbis Augustini, est contra sententiam mentemque Augustini. Hoc liquet ex verbis Augustini in eodem capite. Cùm enim Manichæus appellaret se Apostolum Iesu Christi, & pro tali vellet credi & agnosci, Augustinus ait, se nolle hoc credere, nisi evidentissimè probet: tum quia in Euangelio hoc non legit, illum esse Apostolum Christi: tum quia Catholica Ecclesia hoc prohibeat credi de Manichæo. Hanc autem Ecclesiam tanti se & antea fecisse, & nunc facere, vt nisi fuisset huius authoritate permotus, non vtique crediturus fuisset Euange-lio. Postea subdit: Quòd si forte in Euangelio aliquid apertissimum de Manichaei Apostolo latu innuenire potueris: infirmabis mihi Catholicorum authoritatem, qui iubent, vt tibi non credam. Hactenus Augustinus, Aperte fatetur, authoritatem Ecclesiæ posse infirmari authoritate Euangelij, si quid de Euangelio possit adferri apertum contra Ecclesiæ de Ma-nichæo iudicium. Sic igitur arguo. Si Euangelij authoritas infirmare potest authoritatem Ecclesiæ: vtique illa maior erit ista. Non enim authoritas minor infirmat maiorem, sed maior minorem. Atqui Euangelij authoritas potest infirmare authoritatem Ecclesiæ, de sententia Augustini, vt ibi liquet. Sensit igitur authoritatem Euangelij, maiorem esse authoritate Ecclesiæ. Quare quòd contrarium colligunt Papistæ ex illo Augustini dicto, Non crederem, &c. & produnt suam infci-[?] tiam : & contra sententiam Augustini hoc faciunt.
units.tr: 2. As to the inference. 1. That inference is contrary to Augustine's mind, gathered from Augustine's own words. 2. To draw this conclusion, Therefore the authority of the Church is greater than the authority of the Gospel, from the words of Augustine is contrary to the opinion and mind of Augustine. This is clear from Augustine's words in the same chapter. For when the Manichaean called himself an Apostle of Jesus Christ and wished to be believed and acknowledged as such, Augustine says that he was unwilling to believe this unless he proved it most evidently: partly because he did not read in the Gospel that he was an Apostle of Christ, and partly because the Catholic Church forbids that this be believed of the Manichaean. And he says that he had so greatly esteemed this Church before, and still does, that unless he had been moved by its authority he would certainly not have believed the Gospel.
