Afterwards he adds: But if perhaps you could find something most manifest in the Gospel about the Apostle of Manichaeus, you would weaken for me the authority of the Catholics, who order me not to believe you. Thus far Augustine. He plainly confesses that the authority of the Church can be weakened by the authority of the Gospel, if anything manifest about the Gospel can be brought forward against the Church's judgment concerning the Manichaean. I therefore argue thus. If the authority of the Gospel can weaken the authority of the Church, then certainly the former will be greater than the latter. For a lesser authority does not weaken a greater, but a greater a lesser. But the authority of the Gospel can weaken the authority of the Church, according to Augustine's opinion, as is clear there. Therefore he judged the authority of the Gospel to be greater than the authority of the Church. Wherefore the contrary, which the Papists gather from that saying of Augustine, I would not believe, etc., betrays their own ignorance; and in doing so they act against the opinion of Augustine.

units.la: Si ita sensisset, ut volunt Papistæ: hæc Au-guftini verba essent tanquam plena blasphe-miæ reiicienda. Nam pugnant cum verbo Domini, ut supra à nobis ostensum est, maiorem scilicet esse authoritatem Scripturæ, quàm Ecclesiæ: Contrà vero sentire, est sen-tire, homines esse supra Deum, & maioris authoritatis, quàm Deus sit. Quo quid blasphemius dici potest? Absit autem, ut hoc senserit tantus vir Augustinus. Deinde, falsa etiam ex se est. Vis videre absurditatem huius consequentiæ? Augustinus non credi-disset Euangelio, nisi fuisset Ecclesiæ autho-ritate commotus: Ergo authoritas Ecclesiæ maior fuit & est, autoritate Euangelij. Assume propositionem generalem, quæ silentio præteritur in Enthymematibus, & compone syllogismum: Omne illud, cuius autoritate aliquis commotus, rem aliquam aliam credit, recipit, amplectitur, maioris est authoritatis illa re, quam credit, recipit, amplectitur. Atqui Ecclesia tale quid est cum Euangelio. Nam illius authoritate commotus Augustinus credidit Euangelio, & Euangelium recepit: & idem aliis etiam contigit. Ergo, &c. Quòd falsa sit illa prior propositio, hinc liquet. Liberi, autoritate parentum permoti credunt esse Deum, qui omnia condiderit & regat, & hunc venerantur & invocant. Ergo parentes maioris sunt authoritatis quâ Deus? Iudæi permulti, autoritate Mosis permoti, crediderunt in Christum: unde illud Christi, Si crederetis Mosi, crederetis & mihi: Ergo Mo-ses maioris fuit autoritatis quàm Christus? Sic de Ioan. Baptista: multi huius autoritate permoti, crediderunt in Christum: Ergo ma-ior authoritas Iohannis, quàm Christi? Idem de Samaritanis: Illi permoti autoritate mu-lieris, audierunt & crediderunt in Christum, Ergo, &c. Quis non videat, quàm falsa fit il-la maior propositio? Falsa igitur & conclu-sio. Si sic dicas, Augustinus permotus auto-ritate Ecclesiæ, audiuit crediditque Euange-lio: Ergo tunc autoritas Ecclesiæ maior fuit Augustino, quàm Euangelij: darem. Sed non sequitur: Ergo in se maior est autoritas Ec-clesiæ, autoritate Euangelij. Etiam nunc Pa-pistis permultis maior est autoritas Ecclesiæ Romanæ & Papæ, quàm autoritas Christi & Euangelij. Quis non videat? Cùm illis sit ma-xima religio vel minimum præceptum Papæ violare, mandata autem Christi non curent, & quotidie contemnant. Sed hoc nihil ad quæstionem nostram. Quæstio est de autori-tate Ecclesiæ & Scripturæ in se, utra sit ma-ior: non autem, utra permultis videatur esse maior. Etiam Turcis videtur maior esse au-toritas Mahometis, quàm Christi: igitur est maior? Errant: videtur enim maior, quia cæ-ci sunt. Ita, si Augustino visa fuit ante cogni-tum Euangelium, maior autoritas Ecclesiæ, quàm Euangelij: erravit, quia cæcus erat. Et Papistis videtur maior: Quare?quia cæci.De re igitur disputamus: non de opinionibus hominum.
units.tr: If Augustine had thought as the Papists want, these words of Augustine would have to be rejected as full of blasphemy. For they conflict with the word of the Lord, as we have shown above, namely that the authority of Scripture is greater than that of the Church. To think the opposite is to think that men are above God and of greater authority than God is. What could be said that is more blasphemous? Far be it that so great a man as Augustine thought this. Moreover, the inference is false in itself. Do you want to see the absurdity of this consequence? Augustine would not have believed the Gospel unless he had been moved by the authority of the Church: therefore the authority of the Church was and is greater than the authority of the Gospel. Assume the general premise, which is passed over in silence in enthymemes, and compose the syllogism: Whatever it is by whose authority someone, moved by it, believes, receives or embraces some other thing, is of greater authority than the thing he believes, receives or embraces. But the Church stands in such a relation to the Gospel. For Augustine, moved by its authority, believed the Gospel and received the Gospel, and the same has happened to others also. Therefore, etc. That this first premise is false is clear from this. Children, moved by the authority of their parents, believe that there is a God who created and governs all things, and they venerate and invoke him. Therefore are parents of greater authority than God? Many Jews, moved by the authority of Moses, believed in Christ: whence that saying of Christ, If you believed Moses, you would believe me also. Therefore was Moses of greater authority than Christ? So too with John the Baptist: many, moved by his authority, believed in Christ: therefore is the authority of John greater than the authority of Christ? Likewise with the Samaritans: they, moved by the authority of the woman, heard and believed in Christ. Therefore, etc. Who does not see how false that major premise is? The conclusion is therefore false too. If you say thus: Augustine, moved by the authority of the Church, heard and believed the Gospel; therefore at that time the authority of the Church was greater to Augustine than that of the Gospel: I would grant it. But it does not follow: therefore in itself the authority of the Church is greater than the authority of the Gospel. Even now the authority of the Church of Rome and of the Pope is greater to very many Papists than the authority of Christ and of the Gospel. Who does not see it? For to them the greatest sin is to violate even the smallest precept of the Pope, while they care nothing for the commandments of Christ and despise them every day. But this has nothing to do with our question. The question concerns the authority of the Church and of Scripture in themselves, which is the greater: not which seems greater to very many. The Turks also think the authority of Mahomet greater than that of Christ: is it therefore greater? They are mistaken: it seems greater to them because they are blind. So, if to Augustine, before he knew the Gospel, the authority of the Church seemed greater than that of the Gospel, he was mistaken, because he was blind. And it seems greater to the Papists: why? Because they are blind. We are disputing therefore about the matter itself, not about the opinions of men.

units.la: Denique sentire & dicere, authoritatem Ecclesiæ, maiorem esse authoritate Scripturæ, quæ est verbum Dei: nil aliud est, quàm dicere, homines esse supra Deum. Quanta autem hæc sit blasphemia, quisque cogitet. Declarant hac doctrina Papistæ, se veros esse Antichristos. Antichristi enim proprium est, ut sese efferat supra omne, quod dicitur Deus, ut ait Paulus 2. Thess.2. Et nunc editis etiam carminibus impudenter hoc de Papa prædicant eum esse tanquam Deum, nec Pa-pa damnat. Est enim impressa Romæ imago huius Antichristi, ubi oracula, quæ de Deo, & de Messia Christo sunt apud Prophetas, Papæ attribuuntur: & deinde præter alia sunt ibi hi versus:
units.tr: Finally, to think and to say that the authority of the Church is greater than the authority of Scripture, which is the word of God, is nothing other than to say that men are above God. How great a blasphemy this is, let each one consider. By this doctrine the Papists declare themselves to be true Antichrists. For it is the proper character of Antichrist to exalt himself above everything that is called God, as Paul says, 2 Thess. 2. And now, even in published songs, they shamelessly proclaim this of the Pope, that he is like God, and the Pope does not condemn it. For an image of this Antichrist has been printed at Rome, where the oracles which in the Prophets concern God and the Messiah Christ are ascribed to the Pope; and besides other things there are these verses there:

units.la: Angelicum soluit nomen, pium ipse Michaël: Nam tanquam Deus est, qui ante Mi-chaël erat.
units.tr: The angelic name he has loosed, Michael the pious himself: For he is as God, who was before Michael.

units.la: DE AUTORITATE ECCLESIÆ CIRCA VERBUM DEI quatenus authoritas significat potestatem, dominium & ius in aliquem. QVÆSTIO.
units.tr: On the Authority of the Church with Regard to the Word of God, insofar as authority signifies power, dominion and right over someone. QUESTION.

units.la: Utrum authoritas Scripturæ pendeat ab authoritate Ecclesiæ: ac proinde, An maior sit authoriautoritas Ecclesiæ, autoritate Scripturæ, necne, an potius contrà.
units.tr: Whether the authority of Scripture depends on the authority of the Church; and accordingly, whether the authority of the Church is greater than the authority of Scripture or not, or rather the reverse.

units.la: Ut hæc intelligatur, necesse est ut videa-mus, quænam sit autoritas seu ius Scripturæ in Ecclesiam: & quænam Ecclesiæ circa Scripturam: ac speciatim, An Ecclesia habeat aliquod ius in Scripturam, mutandi aliquid, dispensandi, addendi, minuendi, &c. Nam hoc est præcipuum, quod Papistæ contendunt, & cuius causa tota hæc quæstio de autoritate Scripturæ & Ecclesiæ excitata fuit tempore Concilij Constantiensis & Basiliensis.
units.tr: To understand this, we must see what the authority or right of Scripture over the Church is, and what the Church's right is with respect to Scripture; and in particular, whether the Church has any right over Scripture to change something, to dispense with it, to add to it, to diminish it, and so on. For this is the chief point which the Papists contend, and it is because of this that the whole question about the authority of Scripture and the Church was raised at the time of the Councils of Constance and Basel.

units.la: Autoritas & ius Scripturæ in Ecclesiam, tam multiplex & tam magnum est, ut neque enumerari, neque explicari queat. Ius enim Scripturæ, est ius Dei. Quid autem iuris & potestatis non habet Deus in Ecclesiam, & singulos homines? Dicam tamen quædam, sed breuiter.
units.tr: The authority and right of Scripture over the Church is so manifold and so great that it can be neither enumerated nor explained. For the right of Scripture is the right of God. But what right and power does God not have over the Church and over individual men? Still, I will mention some points, but briefly.

units.la: 1. Scriptura ius habet in Ecclesiam, eam docendi, admonendi, ei consulendi. Idèo dicit 2. Timoth. 3. datam esse θεόπνευστος[?] διδασκαλίαν. Hoc certè non habet Ecclesia in Scripturam. Non est enim Ecclesiæ, corrigere Scripturam, docere, emendare, sed ei subesse, ut discipulum Magistro.
units.tr: 1. Scripture has the right over the Church to teach it, to admonish it, and to counsel it. Hence it is said in 2 Timothy 3 that it was given as "inspired of God, and profitable for teaching" [θεόπνευστος ... διδασκαλίαν]. Certainly the Church has no such right over Scripture. For it is not the Church's place to correct Scripture, to teach it, or to amend it, but to be subject to it, as a disciple to his master.

units.la: 2. Præcipiendi, obligandi conscientias, damnandi, etiam transgressores. Ioh. 12. Sermo meus, quem audivistis, ipse condemnabit vos, &c. In summa, omnia agendi, quæ in Scripturis agit Deus nobiscum. Hoc non habet Ecclesia, neque in Scripturam, neque in ullum homi-nem. Non est enim Ecclesiæ iubere Scriptu-ræ, neque etiam eius præcepta moderari: sed ei parere, & in omnibus obsequentem esse. Unde verò hanc, & omnem aliam habet Scriptura potestatem? ab Ecclesia ne? Mini-mè, sed à Deo, à quo est. 2. Timoth. 3. 2. Pet. 1. Quæ verò & quotuplex est autoritas Ecclesiæ circa Scripturam sanctam? Triplex præcipua.
units.tr: 2. Scripture has the right to command, to bind consciences, to condemn, even transgressors. John 12: "The word that I have spoken shall judge him in the last day." In short, it has the right to do all the things that God does with us in the Scriptures. The Church has no such right, neither over Scripture nor over any man. For it is not the Church's place to command Scripture, nor to regulate its precepts, but to obey it and to be compliant in all things. But whence does Scripture have this power, and every other power? From the Church? By no means, but from God, from whom it comes: 2 Timothy 3; 2 Peter 1. What, then, and how many kinds of authority does the Church have with regard to Holy Scripture? There are three chief kinds.

units.la: Prima facultas est cognoscendi & discer-nendi Scripturam sanctam, à non sancta: Canonicam, à non Canonica. Quomodo? Tum omnes ad Canonem Mosaicum examinan-do: tum etiam Spiritu sancto discernendo & iudicando: atque ita aliis hoc significandi, & ut tales pro Canonicis accipiant, alios reii-ciant, præcipiendi. Ioh. 10. Oues Pastorem se-quuntur, quia nouerunt vocem eius 1. Thess. 5[?]. Omnia probate, quod bonum est, tenete. 1. Iohan. 4. Probate Spiritus, utrum ex Deo sint. 1. Corinth. 11. Inter alia dona concessa Ecclesiæ, est etiam facultas discernendi Spiritus. Dicit enim Apostolus, Alij datur discretio spirituum.
units.tr: The first faculty is that of recognising and distinguishing Holy Scripture from what is not holy, and the canonical from the non-canonical. How? Partly by examining all books by the canon of Moses, and partly by discerning and judging by the Holy Spirit; and thus the Church has the power to signify this to others, and to direct them to accept some books as canonical and to reject others. John 10: "The sheep follow the shepherd, because they know his voice." 1 Thessalonians 5: "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good." 1 John 4: "Try the spirits, whether they are of God." 1 Corinthians 12: Among the other gifts granted to the Church is also the faculty of discerning spirits. For the Apostle says: "To another is given the discerning of spirits."

units.la: Secunda facultas est interpretandi, sed iuxta Scripturas, & ex analogia fidei Rom. 11. Siue Prophetia (quis habeat) iuxta analogiam fidei, (scilicet eam exerceat) 1. Corinth. 12. Inter alia dona Ecclesiæ tradita, est etiam donum interpretandi, quod vocat Prophetare. Alij datur Prophetia, id est, donum interpretandi Scripturas,ait Ambrosius. Ephes.4. Alios dedit Doctores,&c.
units.tr: The second faculty is that of interpreting, but according to the Scriptures and from the analogy of faith: Romans 12: "Whether prophecy (let him have it), let him prophesy according to the proportion of faith" (that is, let him exercise it accordingly). 1 Corinthians 12: Among the other gifts delivered to the Church is also the gift of interpreting, which he calls prophesying. "To another is given prophecy," that is, the gift of interpreting the Scriptures, as Ambrose says. Ephesians 4: "And he gave some teachers," etc.

units.la: Tertia facultas, est facultas & authoritas praedicandi & publicandi Scripturas, & iuxta eas, docendi populos. Matth. 28. Euntes in orbem universum, praedicate Euangelium. Ideo Apostoli praecones appellantur: quia Ecclesiae est praedicare & publicare Euangelium Dei Ephes.cap.4. Alios dedit Pastores.
units.tr: The third faculty is the faculty and authority of preaching and publishing the Scriptures, and of teaching the peoples according to them. Matthew 28: "Go into all the world and preach the Gospel." For this reason the Apostles are called heralds, because it belongs to the Church to preach and publish the Gospel of God. Ephesians 4: "And he gave some pastors."

units.la: Ex iis vero Scripturae locis, quos attulimus de triplici iure Ecclesiae, nempe iudicandi de doctrinis & Scripturis: interpretandi: & praedicandi: hae negatiuae propositiones colligendae & notandae sunt.
units.tr: From those passages of Scripture which we have adduced concerning the threefold right of the Church, namely of judging doctrines and Scriptures, of interpreting, and of preaching, these negative propositions are to be drawn and noted.

units.la: Prima, Circa ius iudicandi de doctrinis: Illud non est restrictum penes Pontif. Romanum, aut advllum[?] aliud hominum genus.
units.tr: First, with regard to the right of judging doctrines: this is not restricted to the Roman Pontiff or to any other class of men.

units.la: Apostolus enim docet, hoc donum distribui fidelibus promiscuè prout visum fuerit Spiritui sancto. Ait enim: Alij datur discretio Spirituum: Et mox: Hac autem omnia operatur unus atq; idem Spiritus, dividens singulis, prout vult.
units.tr: For the Apostle teaches that this gift is distributed promiscuously among the faithful as the Holy Spirit sees fit. For he says: "To another is given the discerning of spirits." And soon after: "But all these things works that one and the same Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will."

units.la: Secunda: Deinde non debet Ecclesia nec potest iudicare de doctrinis, nisi iuxta Canonem scripturarum Propheticarum & Apostolicarum: non iuxta Pontificum, Patrum, & Conciliorum decreta: nisi quatenus confirmata sunt testimoniis Scripturarum. Psalm 118. Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum. 2. Pet.1. Habemus firmum Propheticum sermonem,&c. Idem sentiunt Patres omnes: omnia ad Scripturam examinanda esse: & ita de illis faciendum iudicium, ex Scripturis. Augustinus Tom.7. contra Cresconium. lib.2.cap.31. Nos nullam facimus Cypriano ininriam[?], cum eius quaslibet literas, à Canonica[?] divinarum Scripturarum authoritate distinguimus, Neq; enim sine causa, tam salubri vigilantia constitutus est Canon Ecclesiasticus, ad quem certi Prophetarum & Apostolorum libri pertineant, quas omnino iudicare non audeamus: & secundum quos de caeteris literis vel fidelium, vel infidelium libere iudicemus. Habet igitur Ecclesia ius iudicandi de doctrinis, sed non nisi iuxta Scripturarum sanctarum Canonem.
units.tr: Second: Further, the Church ought not, nor can it, judge doctrines except according to the canon of the prophetic and apostolic Scriptures; not according to the decrees of Pontiffs, Fathers and Councils, except insofar as they are confirmed by the testimonies of Scripture. Psalm 119: "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet." 2 Peter 1: "We have also a more sure word of prophecy," etc. All the Fathers likewise hold that all things are to be examined by Scripture, and that judgment is to be made of them from the Scriptures. Augustine, in the seventh volume, against Cresconius, book 2, chapter 31: "We do no wrong to Cyprian when we distinguish any of his letters from the canonical authority of the divine Scriptures. For the ecclesiastical canon has been established with such salutary vigilance, not without reason, to which belong the certain books of the Prophets and Apostles, which we must by no means dare to judge; and according to which we freely judge the other writings, whether of the faithful or of the unbelievers." Therefore the Church has the right to judge doctrines, but only according to the canon of the Holy Scriptures.

units.la: Tertia: Circa ius interpretandi Scripturas. Ius interpretandi Scripturas: minimè ad solum Pontificem Romanum, & quos ipse ad hoc destinauerit, pertinet: sed ad omnes illos, quibus Deus donum hoc largitus fuerit. Nam Apostolus ait 1. Corinth.12. Alij datur interpretatio sermonum: item, & Alij Prophetia, id est, donum Scripturas interpretandi: Et haec omnia operatur unus atq; idem Spiritus, dividens singulis prout vult,
units.tr: Third: with regard to the right of interpreting the Scriptures. The right of interpreting the Scriptures pertains by no means solely to the Roman Pontiff and to those whom he has appointed for this, but to all those to whom God has granted this gift. For the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 12: "To another is given the interpretation of tongues"; likewise, "To another prophecy," that is, the gift of interpreting the Scriptures. "But all these things works that one and the same Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will."

units.la: Quarta: Ecclesiæ etiam ipsi sanctæ, & quicunq; hoc habent donum aut officium, nequaquam licet Scripturas pro suo capite interpretari: sed omnem Scripturarum interpretationem debet ex ἀναλογίᾳ fidei, & ex ipsis Scripturis colligere. Sic enim ait Ro-man.12. Qui Prophetiam, (hoc est, munus donum interpretandi Scripturas) juxta analogiam fidei, scilicet eam exerceat. Quare si pugnet cum aliis perspicuis Scripturis, aut cum analogia fidei: omnis illa interpretatio reiicienda: ut infinitæ sunt in Papatu, & illa crassa verborum Cœnæ Domini, de carnali præsentia, & de ubiquitate.
units.tr: Fourth: Even the holy Churches themselves, and whoever has this gift or office, may by no means interpret the Scriptures on their own authority; but they ought to derive every interpretation of Scripture from the analogy of faith and from the Scriptures themselves. For thus the Apostle says in Romans 12: "Whoever has prophecy" (that is, the gift or office of interpreting the Scriptures), "let him exercise it according to the analogy of faith." Therefore, if it conflicts with other clear Scriptures or with the analogy of faith, every such interpretation is to be rejected, as are the countless ones in Papacy, and that gross literal reading of the words of the Lord's Supper concerning a carnal presence and concerning ubiquity.

units.la: Quinta: Quod autem attinet ad tertium ius, quod est prædicandi & publicandi hanc Scripturam: primum, hoc ius non restrinxit Dominus ad Papam, ut ille solus possit mittere quos velit: sed toti Ecclesiæ concessum, ut ipsa eligat, quos ad hoc viderit esse idoneos. Act.14.2.Corinth.8. Deinde, ita etiam hoc est concessum ius, ut tamen non liceat quidvis prædicare, sed tantum hanc Scripturam. Matth.28.Gal.1.
units.tr: Fifth: As for the third right, which is that of preaching and publishing this Scripture: first, the Lord did not restrict this right to the Pope, so that he alone could send whom he wishes; but it was granted to the whole Church, so that it may choose those whom it sees to be fit for this. Acts 14; 2 Corinthians 8. Second, this right has been granted in such a way that it is not lawful to preach whatever one likes, but only this Scripture. Matthew 28; Galatians 1.

units.la: Hinc facile liquet, quid ad quæstionem responderi debeat, qua quæritur, An Ecclesia habeat authoritatem aliquid in Scripturis immutandi, addendi, remouendi, dispensandi.
units.tr: From this it is easily clear what ought to be answered to the question which asks whether the Church has authority to change, add to, remove, or dispense with anything in the Scriptures.

units.la: Sunt inter Papistas non pauci, qui afferant: sed adulatores.
units.tr: Among the Papists there are not a few who assert this, but they are flatterers.

units.la: PROPOSITIO.
units.tr: PROPOSITION.

units.la: Ecclesia nullum habet ius in Scripturam addendi, detrahendi, mutandi.
units.tr: The Church has no right to add to, take away from, or change Scripture.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmation.

units.la: 1. Hæc temeritas prohibetur Ecclesiæ, Deut. 4. Non addetis super verbum, quod Ego præcipio praecipio vobis, neq; minuetis ex eo. Idem cap. 5.
units.tr: 1. This presumption is forbidden to the Church by Deut. 4: You shall not add to the word which I command you, nor shall you take away from it. The same in chapter 5:

units.la: Non recedetis ad dextram, neque ad sinistram, id est, nihil mutabis, aut alterabis. Idem 12[?], cap. Galat.1. Si quis praedicauerit aliud Euan-gelium, &c. Gal.3. Hominis testamentum, si fit comprobatum, nemo reiicit, aut addit aliquid, hoc est, non licet addere. Ita lex Mosis, à Deo tradita, non facit irritum nec alterat Testamentum ante à Deo comprobatum erga Christum. Quanto minus igitur potest aut debet Ecclesia abrogare aut alterare sacram Scripturam, vtrumque Testamentum, antea à Deo editum, scriptum & comprobatum, & sanguine Christi confirmatum?
units.tr: You shall not turn aside to the right hand or to the left, that is, you shall change or alter nothing. Also Gal. 1: If anyone preaches to you another gospel, etc. Gal. 3: No one sets aside or adds anything to a man's covenant once it has been ratified, that is, it is not lawful to add. So the law of Moses, given by God, does not annul or alter the covenant previously ratified by God concerning Christ. How much less, then, can or ought the Church to abrogate or alter Sacred Scripture, both Testaments, previously published, written and ratified by God and confirmed by the blood of Christ?

units.la: 2. Iubet etiam Dominus, vt in omnibus rebus dubiis, veritas petatur non ab Ecclesia, sine Scripturis, sed è Scripturis ipsis, Ief. 8. ad Legem & ad testimonium. Deut. 13. iubet, ne audiamus Prophetam quempiam qui aliquid diuer-sum à sacra Scriptura doceat, et-iamsi prædicat verè futura, & edat miracula, imò vt ille lapidibus obruatur. Quare?Qui a execratur Dominus eos, qui in sua Scriptura sancta quippiam mutant. Ideo iubet, dicens: Incedite post Dominum Deum vestrum: Deum timete: illius præcepta custodite: illius vocem audite.
units.tr: 2. The Lord also commands that in all doubtful matters the truth be sought not from the Church apart from the Scriptures, but from the Scriptures themselves: Isa. 8: to the law and to the testimony. Deut. 13 commands that we not listen to any prophet who teaches anything different from holy Scripture, even if he predicts true things and performs miracles; indeed, that he be stoned to death. Why? Because the Lord curses those who change anything in his holy Scripture. Therefore he commands, saying: Walk after the Lord your God, fear God, keep his precepts, and hear his voice.

units.la: Ex iis Scripturarum locis luculenter ap-paret, neque Ecclesiæ, neque vlli hominum licere, quippiam in sacris Literis alterare, mutare, dispensare: sed contrà velle Domi-num, vt omnia ad Scripturas examinentur, tanquam ad lapidem lydium: & quæcunque vel pugnant cum eis, vel diuersa sunt, ea reii-ciantur.
units.tr: From these passages of Scripture it clearly appears that it is lawful neither for the Church nor for any man to alter, change, or dispense anything in the sacred writings; but on the contrary the Lord wills that everything be examined by the Scriptures, as by a touchstone, and whatever is either contrary to them or at variance with them be rejected.

units.la: 3. Sic sentiunt etiam Patres omnes, tam Græci, quàm Latini, vt in ipsorum libris abundè videre est: & Ego alias permultas auctoritates, ex Tertulliano, Irenæo, Cypriano, Origene, Chrysostomo, Basilio, Hieronymo, Augustino, Ambrosio, imò & ex Decretis, distin. 8. & 9. & aliis, cùm agemus de perfectione Scripturarum. In præsentia sufficiat notasse quædam loca. Chrysost. in Matth. expositione secunda, hom. 49. cap. 24. vult Scripturam esse Canonem omnis iudicij de Ecclesia & rebus Ecclesiasticis. August. Tom. 2. Epistol. 166. Idem epist. 3. Item epist. 19. & citatur in decretis, dist. c. Er-gosolis.
units.tr: 3. All the Fathers, Greek as well as Latin, think the same, as may be seen abundantly in their books; and I could cite very many other authorities from Tertullian, Irenaeus, Cyprian, Origen, Chrysostom, Basil, Jerome, Augustine, Ambrose, and even from the Decretals, distinctions 8 and 9, and others, when we treat of the perfection of the Scriptures. For the present it will suffice to note certain passages. Chrysostom, in his second exposition on Matthew, homily 49 on chapter 24, holds that Scripture is the canon of every judgment concerning the Church and ecclesiastical affairs. Augustine, vol. 2, Epistle 166; the same, Epistle 3; likewise Epistle 19, and it is cited in the Decretals, distinction ..., chapter Ergo solis.

units.la: 4. A simili Notarij: Annon Notarij auctoritatem habent scribendi Testamenta, conseruandi, testificandi, publicandi, explicandi: nunquid igitur & alterandi? Et Præco auctoritatem habet edicta Principis publicandi, & de illis testificandi, quòd vera sint Principis edicta: nunquid igitur ius etiam habet in illis quicquam mutandi, addendi, detrahendi? Minimè. Idem dicendum omninò est de auctoritate Ecclesiæ circa Scripturas.
units.tr: 4. By analogy with notaries: do notaries not have the authority to write wills, to preserve, attest, publish and explain them? Do they therefore also have the authority to alter them? Likewise a herald has the authority to publish the edicts of a prince and to attest that the prince's edicts are genuine; does he therefore also have the right to change, add to, or take away anything from them? By no means. The same must altogether be said of the authority of the Church with regard to the Scriptures.

units.la: Ex huius quæstionis explicatione colligitur responsio ad quæstionem, qua speciatim quæritur etiam apud Scholasticos, id est, Sophistas Doctores: An Papa,imò & tota Ecclesia, autoritatem habeat, nouum fidei arti-culum condendi.
units.tr: From the explanation of this question the answer to the question is drawn which is asked specifically also among the Scholastics, that is, the Sophist doctors: whether the Pope, or even the whole Church, has the authority to establish a new article of faith.

units.la: Respondeo his duabus propositionibus.
units.tr: I answer with these two propositions.

units.la: PROPOSITIO I.
units.tr: PROPOSITION I.

units.la: Nemo in Ecclesia, imo neq. tota Ecclesia ius & authoritatem habet, nouum dogma ad fidem pertinens statuendi.
units.tr: No one in the Church, nor even the whole Church, has the right and authority to establish a new dogma pertaining to faith.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmation.

units.la: Liquet hoc ex iis, quae supra à nobis dicta sunt, praesertim ex loco Deuter. Non addas, &c. Sed iis etiam testimoniis & argumentis confirmatur.
units.tr: This is clear from what we have said above, especially from the passage of Deuteronomy, You shall not add, etc. But it is also confirmed by these testimonies and arguments.

units.la: 1. Rom.10. Fides ex auditu: auditus autem per verbum Christi. Hinc colligimus, fidem, sicut ex solo Dei verbo concipitur opera Spiritus S. ita etiam eo solo posse & debere, non autem ulla hominum authoritate niti. Pugnat igitur cum natura fidei, ut ullum fi-dei dogma ab hominibus statuatur, sine ver-bo Dei.
units.tr: 1. Rom. 10: Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ. From this we gather that faith, just as it is conceived from God's word alone by the working of the Holy Spirit, can and ought to rest on that word alone, and not on any human authority. It is therefore contrary to the nature of faith that any article of faith be established by men without the word of God.

units.la: 2. Pugnat etiam cum perfectione Scriptu-rarum. Scriptura tradit omnia, quae ad fidem nostram pertinent, ut alias ostendemus ex hoc Pauli contextu ad Timoth. Ergo nul-lum praeterea fidei dogma tradi ab homini-bus potest.
units.tr: 2. It is also contrary to the perfection of the Scriptures. Scripture delivers all things that pertain to our faith, as we shall show elsewhere from this passage of Paul to Timothy. Therefore no other article of faith can be delivered by men.

units.la: 3. Illud dogma, vel erit cum Scripturis consentaneum, vel dissentaneum. Si consentaneum: non erit igitur ab hominibus, sed ex Dei verbo collectum: quare non erit nouum noűum. Si dissentaneum [?], Scriptura prohibet illud admitti, vt ex Scripturis allatis liquet, Gal. 1. 1. Timoth. 1.
units.tr: 3. That dogma will either agree with the Scriptures or disagree with them. If it agrees, it is not from men but gathered from the word of God, and so it is not new. If it disagrees, the Scripture forbids it to be admitted, as is clear from the Scriptures cited, Gal. 1; 1 Tim. 1.

units.la: 4. 2. Corinth. 1. Non dominamur vestræ fidei: sed adiutores sumus gaudij vestri. Nemini igitur licet dominari alienis conscientiis, nouis fidei dogmatibus.
units.tr: 4. 2 Cor. 1: We are not lords over your faith, but we are workers with you for your joy. No one, therefore, is permitted to lord it over other people's consciences with new articles of faith.

units.la: 5. Patres omnes nobiscum sentiunt: imò & præcipui Scholastici. Thomas 2. secundæ, quæst. 1. articul. 10. Gab. Biel in Magist. sententiarum, lib. 3. distinct. 25. dubio 3. Guil. Ocham, dial. part. 1. lib. 2. cap. 11. Alfonsus de Castro, ibi. c. 8.
units.tr: 5. All the Fathers agree with us, and indeed the principal Scholastics too: Thomas, 2 secundae, question 1, article 10; Gabriel Biel, on the Master of the Sentences, book 3, distinction 25, doubt 3; William of Ockham, Dialogue, part 1, book 2, chapter 11; Alfonso de Castro, ibid., chapter 8.

units.la: PROPOSITIO II.
units.tr: PROPOSITION II.

units.la: Habet verò Ecclesia authoritatem, ita Scripturas per Scripturas, & iuxta analogiam fidei interpretandi, vt si aliquod dogma ibi sit apertum, quod tamen antea non ita fuerit ab omnibus obseruatum: illud possit explicare & definire, & omnibus tanquam veram & certam Dei doctrinam, ad credendum proponere.
units.tr: The Church has authority to interpret the Scriptures through the Scriptures, and in accordance with the analogy of faith, so that if some doctrine is plainly set out in them, which however had not previously been observed by all, it may explain and define that doctrine and propose it to all for belief as the true and certain doctrine of God.

units.la: Explicatio & probatio.
units.tr: Explanation and proof.

units.la: Sic fecit Christus & Apostoli. Doctrinam de iustificatione per solam fidem, quæ omninò aperta erat in libris Mosaicis & Propheticis, sed suo tempore omnibus fere incognita, explicarunt, & in Scripturis contineri neri[?] demonstrârunt: eamque omninò esse recipiendam & credendam, definierunt. Hoc idem hoc tempore factum. Hanc au-toritatem libenter concedimus Ecclesiæ. Cæterùm, hinc colligi non potest, ei licere nouum fidei dogma constituere. Hæc quia perspicua sunt, non opus habent alia con-firmatione.
units.tr: So Christ and the Apostles did. The doctrine of justification by faith alone, which was wholly plain in the books of Moses and the Prophets, but at their time almost unknown to all, they explained, and they demonstrated that it is contained in the Scriptures; and they defined that it is wholly to be received and believed. The same thing has been done in this time. We gladly concede this authority to the Church. However, it cannot be inferred from this that it is lawful for her to establish a new dogma of faith. These points, because they are clear, have no need of further confirmation.

units.la: Liquet igitur ex iis: 1. Quæ & quanta sit autoritas Scripturæ in Ecclesiam: & quæ sit Ecclesiæ, non super, sed circa Scripturam: & quòd hanc ab ipsa etiam habeat Scriptura.
units.tr: It is clear therefore from these things: 1. how great and of what kind is the authority of Scripture over the Church, and that the Church's authority is not over Scripture but concerning it, and that Scripture itself has its authority from the Church.

units.la: 2. Ecclesiam enim nullam habere autoritatem in Scripturam, aliquid in illa mutandi, addendi, detrahendi.
units.tr: 2. For the Church has no authority over Scripture to change, add to, or take away anything from it.

units.la: 3. Ac proinde Scripturæ autoritatem longè maiorem esse autoritate Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: 3. And accordingly the authority of Scripture is far greater than the authority of the Church.

units.la: Sed iam ad quædam Papistarum argumen-ta respondendum est.
units.tr: But now it must be answered to certain arguments of the Papists.

units.la: Primum: Apostoli (inquiunt) multa insti-tuerunt: alia mutârunt, & alterârunt.
units.tr: First: The Apostles (they say) instituted many things, and changed and altered others.

units.la: Exempla.
units.tr: Examples.

units.la: Act.15. decretum faciunt de rebus nouis, & pugnans cum libertate Christiana: illudque Gentibus imponunt tanquam necessarium. Annon abrogata erat Lex? Cur ergo Gentibus mandant, vt abstineant à suffocato & sanguine? Nam de fornicatione & idolothytis nolumus altercari, fatemur ea suis-se à verbo Dei vetita. Sed præceptum de aliis duobus, constat fuisse contra libertatem Christianam, ideóque contra Scripturam: & tamen probatur, quia factum ab Eccle-fia.
units.tr: Acts 15. They make a decree about new matters, one which conflicts with Christian liberty, and they impose it on the Gentiles as necessary. Was the Law not abrogated? Why then do they command the Gentiles to abstain from what is strangled and from blood? For we do not wish to dispute about fornication and food sacrificed to idols; we confess these were forbidden by the Word of God. But the precept about the other two things is plainly contrary to Christian liberty, and therefore contrary to Scripture; and yet it is approved because it was made by the Church.

units.la: Ergo Ecclesia habet autoritatem aliquid etiam contra verbum Dei statuendi, si vide-rit illud expedire.
units.tr: Therefore the Church has authority to establish something even against the Word of God, if it judges that to be expedient.

units.la: Item, Matth. 28[?]. Præceptum habuerunt à Christo, vt Baptizarent in nomine Patris, Filij, & Spiritus sancti: ipsi verò sæpè baptizabant in nomine tantùm Christi, omissa baptizandi forma, quam à Christo acceperant.
units.tr: Likewise, Matt. 28. They had a command from Christ to baptize in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; yet they themselves often baptized only in the name of Christ, leaving out the form of baptism which they had received from Christ.

units.la: Item, Diem Sabbathi, quo iubebantur omnes feriari, & vacare cultui diuino, mu-tarunt ipsi in diem Dominicum: vel, si non ipsi, saltem Ecclesia posterior: id quod ta-men nemo improbat. Licet igitur Ecclesiæ mutare in Scripturis, quod iudicauerit esse mutandum.
units.tr: Likewise, the Sabbath day, on which all were commanded to rest and be free for divine worship, they changed to the Lord's Day; or if not they themselves, at least the later Church; and yet no one disapproves of this. It is lawful therefore for the Church to change in Scripture whatever it judges ought to be changed.

units.la: Respond. Primùm ad Antecedens, negamus tanquam blasphemum totum antecedens: & ratio, cur negemus est: quia Apostoli quicquid egerunt in iis, de quibus postea subduntur testimonia: egerunt ex Spiritu sancto vt ostendemus, & omnes fatentur. Spiritus autem sanctus nihil statuit, quod cum suo pugnet verbo. Non enim sibi ipse est contrarius. Merito igitur negamus Antecedens vt blasphemum in Spiritum san-ctum. Quare loci qui subiiciuntur probatio-nis loco, explicandi sunt iuxta veram intelli-gentiam.
units.tr: Reply. First, to the antecedent: we deny the whole antecedent as blasphemous; and the reason why we deny it is this: whatever the Apostles did in those matters concerning which testimonies are afterwards adduced, they did by the Holy Spirit, as we shall show and as all concede. But the Holy Spirit has decreed nothing that conflicts with his own Word. For he is not contrary to himself. We rightly therefore deny the antecedent as blasphemous against the Holy Spirit. Wherefore the passages that are subjoined in place of proof must be explained according to their true meaning.

units.la: Primus est in Act.15.de mandato, vt abftineant Gentes à suffocato & sanguine.Primò hic est fallacia non causæ, vt causæ. Mandatum enim illud, non fuit proprie factum ab Apostolis, sed à Spiritu sancto. Hic enim illius fuit primarius autor. Liquet ex verbis: Visum est (inquiunt) Spiritui S. & nobis. Primùm, Spiritui S. Ergo ille primarius autor: Deinde & nobis, tanquam instrumentis, quibus hoc inspirauit & reuelauit. Ergo ille autor, non Apostoli. Non secùs hoc fuit, quàm cùm etiam idem Spiritus inspirabat [?] Prophetis, & ipsi loquebantur: Et sic certè videbatur idem Prophetis, quòd antea etiam Spiritui sancto visum fuerat: hoc est, probabant, quòd Spiritus sanctus infpiraffet. Erantne igitur illius doctrinæ ipsi Prophetæ autores? Minimè: sed Deus. Vnde & proprie dicitur verbum Dei. Quòd si aliquando vocantur verba Prophetarum, vt Act. 15. hoc ideò fit, vt significetur, per quos tanquam instrumenta Dei facta sint illa verba. Ita igitur quod dicitur statutum fuisse ab Apostolis: hoc dicitur tanquam de amanuensibus Spiritus sancti, sed Spiritus sanctus author fuit illius decreti.
units.tr: The first is in Acts 15, concerning the command that the Gentiles abstain from what is strangled and from blood. First, here is a fallacy of the non-cause as cause. For that command was not properly made by the Apostles, but by the Holy Spirit. For he was its primary author. This is clear from the words: It seemed good (they say) to the Holy Spirit and to us. First, to the Holy Spirit: therefore he is the primary author. Then, and to us, as instruments by whom he inspired and revealed this. Therefore he is the author, not the Apostles. It was no different from when the same Spirit inspired the Prophets, and they spoke: and in the same way it seemed good to the Prophets what had previously seemed good to the Holy Spirit; that is, they approved that the Holy Spirit had inspired it. Were the Prophets then the authors of that doctrine? By no means; but God. Whence it is properly called the Word of God. But if sometimes the words of the Prophets are called such, as in Acts 15, this is done so that it may be signified through whom those words were made as instruments of God. Thus, therefore, what is said to have been decreed by the Apostles is said as of amanuenses of the Holy Spirit, but the Holy Spirit was the author of that decree.

units.la: Secundò, Quòd verò non puguauerit cum verbo Dei, inde liquet: quia non imponunt hoc præceptum perle necessarium: sed tanquam vtile, tollendi scilicet scandali & offensionis, & contentionis gratia. Nam multi inter Iudæos infirmi nimium offendebantur, quòd viderent, Gentes nihil seruare ex ceremoceremoniis Mosis. Verbum autem Dei tan-tū abest, vt hoc prohibeat, vt potiùs iubeat: nempe, vt si in rebus adiaphoris nos geramus ex præcepto charitatis: ita vt si propter illa-rum vlum frater offenditur, ab illis abstineas. Sic docuerunt Prophetæ: sic Christus: sic postea etiam Apostoli. Ita hoc præceptum charitatis, non est nouum, sed vetus, vt ait Iohannes 1. Iohan. capite 2. Ergo non pugnauit cum verbo Dei, sed fuit consenta-neum.
units.tr: Second, that it did not conflict with the Word of God is clear from this: because they did not impose this precept as absolutely necessary, but as useful, namely for removing scandal and offence, and for the sake of peace. For many of the weak among the Jews were too greatly offended when they saw the Gentiles observing nothing of the ceremonies of Moses. But the Word of God is so far from forbidding this that it rather commands it: namely, that in matters indifferent we conduct ourselves by the precept of charity, so that if a brother is offended by the use of them, you abstain from them. So taught the Prophets; so Christ; so afterwards also the Apostles. Thus this precept of charity is not new but old, as John says in 1 John 2. Therefore it did not conflict with the Word of God, but was consonant with it.

units.la: At illud vocant Apostoli necessarium.
units.tr: But the Apostles call it necessary.

units.la: Respond. Duplex est necessitas, per se, & ex accidenti. Nou [?] primo modo, sed secundo fuit hoc præceptum necessarium, ad tollen-dum scilicet scandalum, id est, propter cha-ritatem.
units.tr: Reply: Necessity is twofold, per se and by accident. It was not necessary in the first way, but in the second way this precept was necessary, namely for removing scandal, that is, on account of charity.

units.la: Tertiò: Neque Christus ita abrogauit le-gem Mosis, vt nullo modo possent amplius seruari illa præcepta, si charitas postularet: sed ita, vt non amplius seruarentur tanquam simpliciter & per se necessaria. Liquet vtrum-que. Apostolus Paulus circumcidit Timo-theum Act.16. quia hoc charitas postulabat. Non fuit igitur sublata lex de Circumcisio-ne, vt nullo modo posset obseruari. Deinde non passus fuit circumcidi Titum, quia vole-bant illū cogere ad circumcisionem tanquā rem necessariam, sine qua non posset seruari.
units.tr: Third: Christ did not so abrogate the law of Moses that those precepts could in no way be observed any longer, if charity required it; but so that they were no longer observed as simply and in themselves necessary. Both are clear. The Apostle Paul circumcised Timothy, Acts 16, because charity required this. The law concerning circumcision was therefore not taken away so that it could in no way be observed. Again, he did not allow Titus to be circumcised, because they wished to compel him to circumcision as a thing necessary, without which he could not be saved.

units.la: Fuit igitur abrogata, vt non amplius esset necessaria, sicut ante, semper, & per se. Quare, si Spiritus sanctus per Apostolos suffit ad tempus, vt gentes abstinerent à sanguine & suffocato, idque nullam aliam ob causam, nisi propter charitatem: nil statuit cōtra Christum, sed cum Christo.
units.tr: It was therefore abrogated so that it was no longer necessary, as before, always, and in itself. Wherefore, if the Holy Spirit through the Apostles sufficed for a time that the Gentiles abstain from blood and from what is strangled, and that for no other cause than charity: he decreed nothing against Christ, but together with Christ.

units.la: Secundus locus est Act. 2. 8. 10. 19. Baptizarunt in nomine Christi, contra mandatum Christi, Matth. 28.
units.tr: The second passage is Acts 2, 8, 10, 19. They baptized in the name of Christ, contrary to the command of Christ, Matt. 28.

units.la: Respondent Primò Patres: etsi baptizarunt in nomine Christi: non sequitur, eos non baptizasse in nomen Patris & Spiritus sancti. Prima ratio: cùm ij tres unum sint: Secunda ratio: Et in nomine Christi, quod significat vnctum, necessariò intelligantur Pater, qui vnxit: Filius, qui vnctus est: & Spiritus sanctus, quo vnctus est. Tertia ratio: Et Christus ait, Qui credit in me, non credit in me (scilicet solum) sed in eum qui misit me. Ergo etiam qui baptizabatur in nomine Christi, non in eum solum, sed etiam in Patrem baptizabatur. Quare quoad substantiam, nihil mutarunt in forma baptismi praescripta à Christo. Et haec responsio Patrum non potest nec debet reiici à Papistis. Sic esset fallacia diuisionis.
units.tr: The Fathers reply first: although they baptized in the name of Christ, it does not follow that they did not baptize in the name of the Father and of the Holy Spirit. First reason: since those three are one. Second reason: and in the name of Christ, which signifies anointed, there must necessarily be understood the Father, who anointed; the Son, who was anointed; and the Holy Spirit, by whom he was anointed. Third reason: and Christ says, He who believes in me, does not believe in me (namely alone) but in him who sent me. Therefore also he who was baptized in the name of Christ was baptized not into him alone, but also into the Father. Wherefore, as to substance, they changed nothing in the form of baptism prescribed by Christ. And this reply of the Fathers cannot and must not be rejected by the Papists. Otherwise it would be a fallacy of division.

units.la: Secundò: Nostri: Ex his locis non potest concludi, Apostolos non vsurpasse formam à Christo praescriptam. Ratio est: quia cùm ita loquitur Lucas, & iussi sunt baptizari in nomine Christi. Item, & baptizati sunt in nomine Christi: non significat, Apostolos iis verbis vsos fuisse: Ego te baptizo in nomine Christi. Sed quid voluit significare? Quidam: voluit luit significare: Eos qui crediderunt in Christum, & nomé dederunt Christo, obsignatos fuisse baptismate Christi, & Christo consecratos, cui etiam dederunt nomen. Hoc enim idem est, atque baptizare in nomen Christi. Quid est enim baptizare aliquem in nomen alicuius? Est illius nomini aliquem obsignare, cui etiam dedit nomen suum. Sic baptizati in nomine Patris, Filij & Spiritus sancti omnes nos dicimur, hoc est, obsignati Patri, Filio, & Spiritui S. in quos etiam credimus: ut sciamus, nos non esse amplius nostros, neque Diaboli, neque Mundi, sed Patris, Filij, & Spiritus sancti: sicut cum merces ab aliquo Mercatore emtæ, obsignatur illius sigillo, cuius factæ sunt, ut agnoscantur non amplius esse illius, à quo emtæ sunt, sed illius, qui emit. Sic quoniam emti sumus sanguine Christi, cum hoc credimus, & nomen damus Christo, professi nos omnino velle esse Christi, & Christo inseruire, quippe qui Christi sumus, & non nostri, neque vllius alius creaturæ: tunc obsignamur Christo, & nomini Christi? Quomodo? intus in animo, sigillo Spiritus sancti: extrà in corpore, sigillo, hoc est, aqua Baptismi. Et quia vtraque obsignatio, Baptismus appellatur, vnus interior, alter exterior: idcirco dicimur baptizari, hoc est obsignari. Cui? Illi, à quo emti, & cuius sumus. Apostolus autem 1. Corinth. 3[?] ait, Nos esse Christi: Ideò non est mirum, si Lucas dicat, omnes eos, qui nomen dederunt Christo, fuisse baptizatos in nomen Christi: quia idem est, quod obsigna-tos fuisse Christo, cuius facti erant, & à quo emti fuerant suo sanguine: sicut ait 1. ad Co-rinth.6. Emti estis pretio magno.
units.tr: Second: our side: from these passages it cannot be concluded that the Apostles did not use the form prescribed by Christ. The reason is this: when Luke says, and they were commanded to be baptized in the name of Christ; likewise, and they were baptized in the name of Christ: this does not mean that the Apostles used those words: I baptize you in the name of Christ. But what did he mean to signify? Some say he meant to signify that those who believed in Christ and gave their name to Christ were sealed with the baptism of Christ and consecrated to Christ, to whom they also gave their name. For this is the same as to baptize into the name of Christ. For what is it to baptize someone into the name of someone? It is to seal someone to the name of him to whom he has also given his own name. So we are all said to be baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, that is, sealed to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, in whom we also believe, so that we may know that we are no longer our own, nor the devil's, nor the world's, but the Father's, the Son's, and the Holy Spirit's; just as when merchandise bought from some merchant is stamped with the seal of him whose it has become, so that it may be recognized that it no longer belongs to him from whom it was bought, but to him who bought it. So, since we were bought with the blood of Christ, when we believe this and give our name to Christ, professing that we wholly wish to be Christ's and to serve Christ, since we are Christ's and not our own, nor of any other creature: then we are sealed to Christ and to the name of Christ. How? Inwardly in the mind, by the seal of the Holy Spirit; outwardly in the body, by the seal, that is, the water of Baptism. And because both sealings are called Baptism, the one inward, the other outward, we are therefore said to be baptized, that is, sealed. To whom? To him by whom we were bought and whose we are. But the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 3 says, We are Christ's. Therefore it is no wonder if Luke says that all those who gave their name to Christ were baptized into the name of Christ: because it is the same as to have been sealed to Christ, whose they had become, and by whom they had been bought with his blood; as he says in 1 Corinthians 6, You were bought with a great price.

units.la: Cæterum hinc non potest colligi, Apostolos hac forma usos fuisse: Ego te baptizo in nomen Christi: non autem illa, in nomine Patris, Filij, & Spiritus sancti. Ego credo Apostolos, uti obsequentissimos discipulos, præceptoris sui formam semper retinuisse. Sed aliud est explicare formam Baptismi, qua usi sunt, quod non facit Lucas: aliud simpliciter narrare ut historicum, quid Apostoli fecerint illis, qui nomen dederant Christo: ait, eos fuisse sigillo etiam Baptismi obsignatos Christo. Quare ex hoc loco colligi non potest, Apostolos mutasse aliquid in Scripturis & præceptis Christi. 3. Alij in nomen Christi, id est, ex mandato & autoritate Christi, Buc. 4. Etiam dici potest, in nomen Christi, hoc est, professi fidem in Christum: sicut etiam 1. Cor. 10. Et in Mosen baptizati sunt, hoc est, professi fidem & fiduciam in Mosen, scilicet in ea, quæ Moses pollicitus fuerat nomine Dei, baptizati sunt, hoc est, in Mare se coniecerunt. Ex harum trium nulla colligi potest, eos usos fuisse hac forma, Ego te baptizo in Christum. Et est fallacia ex i-gnoratione figuræ dictionis.
units.tr: Moreover, one cannot infer from this that the Apostles used this form: "I baptize you in the name of Christ," rather than "in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit." I believe the Apostles, as most obedient disciples, always kept the form of their teacher. But it is one thing to explain the form of baptism they used, which Luke does not do; it is another simply to narrate, as a historian, what the Apostles did for those who had given their names to Christ: he says they were also sealed to Christ by the sign of baptism. Therefore it cannot be inferred from this passage that the Apostles changed anything in the Scriptures and the precepts of Christ. Third, [it is taken as] "in the name of Christ," that is, by the command and authority of Christ, Acts 4. Fourth, it can also be said "in the name of Christ," that is, having professed faith in Christ, just as also 1 Cor. 10: "And they were baptized into Moses," that is, they professed faith and trust in Moses, namely in what Moses had promised in God's name; they were baptized, that is, they threw themselves into the sea. From none of these three can it be inferred that they used this form, "I baptize you into Christ." And this is a fallacy arising from ignorance of the figure of speech.

units.la: Tertius locus est de sabbatho Exod.20.
units.tr: The third place concerns the Sabbath, Exod. 20.

units.la: Respond. Diem sabbathi, in diem Dominicam ab Apostolis per Spiritum sanctum mutatum fuisse, non dubito. Nam huius diei Dominicæ mentio fit in literis Apostolicis. Apoc. I. Ego Johannes fui in spiritu, in Domini-co die. Eodem autem die Dominico, id est, feria prima hebdomadis, solitos fuisse Apo-stolos, & alios Christianos convenire, Coe-nam administrare, collectas facere, & pre-cibus vacare, audireque verbum Dei, quæ antea solita erant fieri die sabbathi: liquet ex iis locis.
units.tr: Reply. I do not doubt that the day of the Sabbath was changed by the Apostles, through the Holy Spirit, to the Lord's Day. For mention of this Lord's Day is made in the apostolic writings: Rev. 1: "I, John, was in the Spirit on the Lord's day." That on this same Lord's Day, that is, the first day of the week, the Apostles and other Christians were accustomed to gather, to administer the Supper, to make collections, to devote themselves to prayers and to hear the word of God, which had formerly been done on the Sabbath day, is clear from those passages.

units.la: Act.20 v.7. Primo autem die hebdomadæ (hic est dies Dominicus) coactis discipulis ad frangendum panem (id est, ad Coenam Domini) Paulus differebat eis, &c. & protendit sermonem usque ad mediam noctem. Græcè est, ἐν τῇ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων[?]: quæ locutio significat primam diem, phrasi Hebraica, sicut etiam Genes. 1. Et factum est mane & vespera, dies unus, id est primus. Sic Matth.28. Cùm ait μιᾶ σαββάτων[?], id est, primo die post Sabbathum: venisse mulieres ad monumentum: id quod expressit Marcus, cap.16. dicendo, Cùm autem surrexisset Iesus πρώτῃ σαββάτου[?], apparuit primum Magdalenæ. Et in quodam veteri Codice additum erat Κυριακὴ[?] Ergo primæ diei nomine Lucas significare voluit, diem quem vocamus Dominicum, quòd eo die Dominus surrexerit. Quare ex hoc loco Actorum colligimus, die Dominica solitos fuisse discipulos Christi convenire, ad audiendum verbum, & Coenam Domini celebrandam: hocest, solitos fuisse vacare cultui diuino, quod præscri-ptum antea erat die sabbathi.
units.tr: Acts 20:7: "On the first day of the week" (this is the Lord's Day), "when the disciples came together to break bread" (that is, to the Lord's Supper), "Paul preached to them, etc., and prolonged his speech until midnight." In Greek it is ἐν τῇ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων [en tē mia tōn sabbatōn], a phrase which in Hebrew idiom signifies the first day, just as also Gen. 1: "And there was evening and morning, one day," that is, the first. So Matt. 28, when it says μιᾷ σαββάτων [mia sabbatōn], that is, on the first day after the Sabbath, the women came to the tomb; which Mark expressed in chapter 16, saying, "But when Jesus had risen πρώτῃ σαββάτου [prōtē sabbatou], he first appeared to Magdalene." And in a certain old codex the word Κυριακὴ [Kyriakē] had been added. Therefore by the name of the first day Luke meant to signify the day which we call the Lord's, because on that day the Lord rose. Hence from this passage of Acts we conclude that the disciples of Christ were accustomed to gather on the Lord's Day, to hear the word and to celebrate the Lord's Supper; that is, they were accustomed to devote themselves to divine worship, which had previously been prescribed for the Sabbath day.

units.la: In priori epist. ad Cor. cap.16. iubet Pau-lus, vt primo die septimanæ collectæ fiant, quas postea ipse erat accepturus pro paupe-ribus,qui erant Hierosolymis.
units.tr: In the first epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 16, Paul orders that on the first day of the week collections be made, which he himself was afterwards to take for the poor who were at Jerusalem.

units.la: Ex iis igitur apparet liquidò, diem hunc, qui dicitur Dominicus, destinatum fuisse ab Apostolis, ad Cœnam Domini celebran-dam, ad audiendum verbum, ad preces,ad collectas,quæ antea solita erant fieri diesab-bathi.
units.tr: From these things, therefore, it clearly appears that this day, which is called the Lord's, was appointed by the Apostles for celebrating the Lord's Supper, for hearing the word, for prayers, and for collections, which had previously been made on the Sabbath day.

units.la: Confirmo testimonio etiam Iustini.
units.tr: I confirm this by the testimony also of Justin.

units.la: Iustinus Martyr in Apolog. secunda ad Antoninum pro Christianis ad calcem, de-scribit, solitos fuisse Christianos die Domi-nico conuenire, audire concionem, sume-re cœnam, & facere collectas pro pauperi-bus, quas collectas Antistes, quem vocat προεστῶτα[?], postea distribuebat viduis, ægro-tis, orphanis, peregrinis. Ex iis liquet Apo-stolos per Spiritum S. vel potiùs Spiritum sanctum per Apostolos, festum solennita-temq; Sabbathi in diem Dominicum trans-tulisse.
units.tr: Justin Martyr, in his Second Apology to Antoninus on behalf of the Christians, near the end, describes that Christians were accustomed to gather on the Lord's Day, to hear a sermon, to partake of the supper, and to make collections for the poor; which collections the president, whom he calls προεστῶτα [proestōta], afterwards distributed to widows, the sick, orphans, and strangers. From these things it is clear that the Apostles, through the Holy Spirit, or rather the Holy Spirit through the Apostles, transferred the festival and solemn observance of the Sabbath to the Lord's Day.

units.la: Cæterùm quæ hinc inferunt Papistæ, sunt ἀσυλλόγιστα.
units.tr: Moreover, the inferences the Papists draw from this are ἀσυλλόγιστα [asyllogista], that is, invalid.

units.la: Primum, Ergo Apostoli aliquid mutarunt in verbo Dei, seu in Scripturis. Quare si hoc licuit Apostolis.2.Ergo licet etiam Ecclesiæ aliquid in Scripturis immutare.
units.tr: First: Therefore the Apostles changed something in the word of God, or in the Scriptures. Wherefore, if this was permitted to the Apostles, then it is also permitted to the Church to change something in the Scriptures.

units.la: Respond. ad primam consequentiam: fallacia est accidentis: Argumentantur enim ab accidenti ad substantiam. Praeceptum enim de sabbatho sanctificando, habet suam substantiam, & suum accidens. Substantia fuit, ut semel in septimana populus universus, a laboribus, negotiis, occupationibus huius saeculi feriaretur, & totus cultui vacaret divino audiendis concionibus, habendis precibus, percipiendis sacramentis, faciendis collectis in usum pauperum. Haec erat ceu substantia praecepti, quod ad externam diei sabbathi sanctificationem attinet. Nam suberat etiam alia substantia, nempe interna quies a peccatis, & spiritualis sanctificatio, de qua ad Hebraeos. Tanquam accidens vero fuit ille certus dies totius septimanae postremus, qui sabbathum dicitur: id quod etiam ex verbis Domini liquet: Sex diebus (inquit) operaberis, & omnia negotia tua conficies: septimo autem die sabbathum Domini est, hoc est, quiescendum est ab operibus & negotiis saeculi, ut totus vaces Domino. Hoc fuit ceu substantia praecepti: & quod ad hanc substantiam attinet, voluit Dominus praeceptum hoc esse perpetuum. Sed quòd talis dies debuerit Iudaeis esse septimus, & ille sanctificandus: ceu accidens fuit: & quod ad hoc attinet, praeceptum illud ceremoniale & politicum fuit: ac proinde usque ad Christum locum habituram: deinde cum reliquis ceremoniis finem acceptuturum[?]. Ergo si ipestemus substantiam præcepti: Apostoli nihil immutarūt. Manet enim adhuc dies unus in septimana, quo feriantur omnes ab operibus & negotiis huius sæculi, & vacatur cultui divino. Sed si spectes accidens: damus, illud esse mutatum. Sed hoc non pugnat cum voluntate Dei in præcepto de sabbatho. Nam quicquid fuit ceremoniale, illud post Christum, liberum mansit Ecclesiæ, idque ex voluntate Dei.
units.tr: Reply to the first consequence: it is a fallacy of accident; for they argue from the accident to the substance. For the precept concerning the sanctification of the Sabbath has its substance and its accident. The substance was that once a week the whole people should rest from labours, business, and the occupations of this world, and should devote themselves entirely to divine worship: hearing sermons, offering prayers, receiving the sacraments, and making collections for the use of the poor. This was, as it were, the substance of the precept, so far as it concerns the external sanctification of the Sabbath day. For there also underlay another substance, namely inward rest from sins and spiritual sanctification, of which the Epistle to the Hebrews speaks. But as an accident was that certain day, the last of the whole week, which is called the Sabbath; this is also clear from the words of the Lord: "Six days you shall labour, and finish all your business; but the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord," that is, one must rest from the works and business of the world, so as to devote oneself wholly to the Lord. This was, as it were, the substance of the precept; and as regards this substance, the Lord willed that the precept should be perpetual. But that such a day should have been the seventh for the Jews, and that this one should be sanctified, was, as it were, an accident; and as regards this, that precept was ceremonial and political, and accordingly would hold its place only until Christ, and then would receive its end together with the other ceremonies. Therefore, if you consider the substance of the precept, the Apostles changed nothing; for one day in the week still remains on which all are freed from the works and business of this world, and devote themselves to divine worship. But if you look at the accident, we grant that this was changed. Yet this does not conflict with the will of God in the precept about the Sabbath. For whatever was ceremonial remained after Christ free for the Church, and this by the will of God.

units.la: Neque vero sine causa, diem sabbathi, quod ad suum attinet accidens, mutarunt in alium diem. Nam utile erat Ecclesiæ, ut hac libertate uterentur Apostoli, quò universis patefieret, Messiam advenisse, eoq; ceremo-niis omnibus finem esse impositum.
units.tr: Nor, indeed, without cause did they change the day of the Sabbath, as far as its accident is concerned, into another day. For it was useful to the Church that the Apostles should use this liberty, so that it might be made plain to all that the Messiah had come and that an end had been put to all the ceremonies.

units.la: Lex enim usque ad Christum: & illa ceremonia usque ad tempus correctionis imposita, Hebr. 9. 10. Hac de causa etiam Paulus Coloss. 2. monet fideles, ut hanc dierum libertatem retineant, nec sinant se in servitutem Mosaicæ legis de sabbathis redigi, cum ait, Nemo vos iudicet in cibo & potu, aut de parte diei festi, aut sabbathorum. Ergo propter hanc libertatem Christianis asserendam, utile fuit mutare sabbathum. Quòd vero non in alium, sed in diem proximè insequentem sabbathum, qui Solis apud Gentes, & fit primus Iudæis, & Dominicus Christianis dicitur, mutarint, duplicem adfert Iustinus in Apologia ad Antoninum, causam: primam, quòd eo die Deus creauit Mundum per verbum suum, per quod verbum postea etiam eundem redemit Mundum. Ergo idem finis manet in obseruatione diei Dominici, qui in sabbathi. Ibi praeter alios fines etiam fuit, vt recordarentur creati Mundi à Deo per verbum, & eorum quae post conditum illum contigerunt, vt quietis Domini,&c. Ita hic, vt scilicet recordemur, Mundum à Deo fuisse conditum, per Verbum, hoc est, Filium suum. Alteram, quòd hoc die Christus resurrexit à mortuis, atq; ita triumphauit de morte, inferno, Sathana: atque ita fides de nostra redemptione per Christum, obseruatione huius diei, in nobis excitetur & refricetur.
units.tr: For the law was until Christ, and that ceremony was imposed until the time of correction, Heb. 9–10. For this reason also Paul, in Col. 2, admonishes the faithful to retain this liberty of days, and not to allow themselves to be brought back into servitude to the Mosaic law concerning Sabbaths, when he says: "Let no one judge you in food or drink, or in respect of a festival day, or of the Sabbaths." Therefore, for the sake of asserting this liberty for Christians, it was useful to change the Sabbath. But that they changed it not to another day, but to the day next following the Sabbath, which among the Gentiles is called the day of the Sun and among the Jews the first, and among Christians the Lord's Day, Justin in his Apology to Antoninus gives a twofold reason: the first, that on that day God created the world through his Word, through which Word afterwards he also redeemed the same world. Therefore the same end remains in the observance of the Lord's Day as in that of the Sabbath. There, besides other ends, there was also this, that they might remember the world created by God through the Word, and the things that happened after that creation, such as the rest of the Lord, etc. So here too, namely that we may remember that the world was created by God through the Word, that is, his Son. The second: that on this day Christ rose from the dead, and thus triumphed over death, hell, and Satan; and thus faith in our redemption through Christ is stirred up and refreshed in us by the observance of this day.

units.la: Ex iis igitur perspicuum est, Apostolos nihil in substantia huius praecepti mutasse: Deinde, quod mutarunt, illud etiam fuisse factum ex voluntate Dei: postremò, ex utilitate Ecclesiae, cuius aedificationi omnes debent seruire ceremoniae.
units.tr: From these things, then, it is clear that the Apostles changed nothing in the substance of this precept; second, that what they did change was also done by the will of God; and finally, that it was done for the benefit of the Church, to whose building all ceremonies ought to serve.

units.la: Ad secundam: Quòd verò sic inferunt, idem licere Ecclesiae.
units.tr: To the second argument: as for the claim that they infer, namely, that the same is permitted to the Church.

units.la: Resp primùm. Cui Ecclesiae? Papisticae? nisi redeat ad obedientiam verbi, vt ei subiecta maneat: nihil habet auctoritatis. Non est enim vera Ecclesia, vt ex Augustino contra Epistolam Paphnutij, cap. 4. colligi poterit, quia discordat à capite Christo. Ecclesia verò nouit, quae sunt à Spiritu sancto tradita & firmata, neminem licere ea violare aut immutare. Deinde, dico licere eo modo, quo & Apostolis licuit: primò, si regantur à Spiritu sancto, ita vt non ipsa Ecclesia, sed Spiritus sanctus autor sit illorum decretorum. Secundò, si nihil immutent, nisi quod verbum Domini doceat esse immutandum: nihil statuant, quod cum verbo Domini pugnet. Sic enim & Apostoli fecerunt. Tertiò, si in rebus adiaphoris, iuxta legem charitatis omnia agant.
units.tr: Answer, first. To which Church? The Papist Church? Unless it returns to obedience to the Word, so as to remain subject to it, it has no authority at all. For it is not the true Church, as can be gathered from Augustine against the Epistle of Paphnutius, chapter 4, because it disagrees with Christ, its head. But the true Church knows that what has been handed down and confirmed by the Holy Spirit may not be violated or changed by anyone. Next, I say that it is permitted in the same way that it was permitted to the Apostles: first, if they are governed by the Holy Spirit, so that it is not the Church itself but the Holy Spirit who is the author of those decrees. Second, if they change nothing except what the Word of the Lord teaches must be changed, and decree nothing that conflicts with the Word of the Lord. For this is how the Apostles acted. Third, if they do everything in matters indifferent according to the law of charity.

units.la: Secundum Argumentum. Ecclesia mutauit, quæ à Spiritu sancto & ab Apostolis fuerunt constituta, vt lex de abstinendo à sanguine & suffocato: Ergo etiam nunc licet.
units.tr: Second argument. The Church has changed what was instituted by the Holy Spirit and by the Apostles, such as the law about abstaining from blood and from what is strangled. Therefore it is permitted now as well.

units.la: Respond. Negatur Antecedens: Nihil enim immutauit, nisi quod Spiritus sanctus voluit cum Apostolis immutari. Nam præceptum illud de abstinendo à sanguine & suffocato, Spiritus sanctus & Apostoli constituerunt, vt ad certum tantùm tempus obseruaretur: deinde non amplius, nempe tantisper dum periculum erat, ne Iudæi exillius transgres-sione offenderentur. Quare non valet consequentia ab isto decreto temporario, ad alia æterna, & quæ Deus vult perpetuò obseruari. Est igitur fallacia ab eo, quod est exacci-denti, ad id quod est per se: & ab eo, quod est simpliciter & semper seruandum, ad id, quod propter aliud, & ad tempus.
units.tr: Answer. The antecedent is denied. For the Church changed nothing except what the Holy Spirit willed to be changed together with the Apostles. For that precept about abstaining from blood and from what is strangled was established by the Holy Spirit and the Apostles to be observed only for a certain time; and then no longer, namely, only for as long as there was danger that the Jews would be offended by its transgression. Therefore the inference from that temporary decree to other eternal decrees, which God wills to be observed forever, does not hold. There is therefore a fallacy in moving from what is accidental to what is per se, and from what is to be kept simply and always to what is to be kept for another reason and for a time.

units.la: QVÆSTIO IV. Deiis, qnibus γραφὴ θεόπνευστος[?] fuit inspirata.
units.tr: QUESTION IV. Of the persons by whom the Scripture was inspired [γραφὴ θεόπνευστος].

units.la: Ex iis, quae de scripturis dixit Apostolus, breuis nempe: πᾶσα γραφὴ θεόπνευστος ἐστι[?], vidimus primum, quaenam sint hae scripturae θεόπνευστοι[?], atque ita egimus de libris Canonicis & Apocryphis. Secundo, quibus mediis agnoscere quis certò possit, quae sint θεόπνευστοι[?], & quae minus: An sufficiat auctoritas & testimonium Ecclesiae, nec ne. Conclusum fuit, in summa opus esse eodem spiritu ad hoc cognoscendum, quo etiam fuerunt inspiratae. Tertiò, cùm haec scriptura sit θεόπνευστος[?], & ideò magnae auctoritatis: & ipsa etiam Ecclesia, quae huic dedit testimonium, non parum sit auctoritatis, propósita fuit quaestio de auctoritate scripturae, & Ecclesiae. Conclusum fuit, quicquid habet Ecclesia dignitatis, aut etiam authoritatis & potestatis, totum hoc illam habere à sacra scriptura, non autem contrà. Longè igitur maiorem esse scripturae auctoritatem, auctoritate Ecclesiae.
units.tr: From what the Apostle said about the Scriptures, namely the brief statement: "All Scripture is inspired by God" [πᾶσα γραφὴ θεόπνευστος ἐστι], we saw first which these inspired Scriptures are, and so we treated the canonical and apocryphal books. Second, by what means one can know with certainty which are inspired and which less so: whether the authority and testimony of the Church suffice for this or not. It was concluded, in sum, that the same Spirit is needed to recognize this, by which they were also inspired. Third, since this Scripture is inspired by God, and therefore of great authority, and since the Church itself, which gave testimony to it, has no small authority, the question was raised about the authority of Scripture and of the Church. It was concluded that whatever dignity, or indeed authority and power, the Church has, it has all of this from holy Scripture, and not the reverse. Therefore the authority of Scripture is far greater than the authority of the Church.

units.la: Nunc igitur methodus docendi postulat, ut videamus, quibusnam fuerit haec scriptura inspirata: Nam si fuit à Deo inspirata: fuit certè aut alicui, aut aliquibus inspirata. Quaestio haec breuis est & facilis, & ferè nihil habet controuersiae. Sic igitur breuiter respondeo iis propositionibus.
units.tr: Now, then, the method of teaching requires that we see to whom this Scripture was inspired. For if it was inspired by God, it was certainly inspired to someone or to some people. This question is brief and easy, and has almost no controversy in it. So I answer briefly with these propositions.

units.la: PROPOSITIO I.
units.tr: PROPOSITION I.

units.la: Scriptura, quod ad summam substantiam attinet: non primùm Mosi, sed longè ante Mosen, iam indè ab initio orbis conditi, Ad primùm, & deinde aliis multis Patribus, inspi-rata & revelata fuit.
units.tr: Scripture, as far as its main substance is concerned: was inspired and revealed not first to Moses, but long before Moses, from the beginning of the created world, first to Adam, and then to many other Fathers.

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Cùm dico, multis, eos intelligo, quibus apparuit Dominus: ut Nohæ, ut Abrahæ, ut Isaaco & Iacobo: inspirata & revelata fuit.
units.tr: When I say "many," I mean those to whom the Lord appeared: such as Noah, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; it was inspired and revealed to them.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmation.

units.la: Nam Ecclesia iam inde ab initio Mundi habuit semper penes se Verbum Dei (sine quo Ecclesia esse non potest) idq; partim in-spiratum à Deo & revelatum: partim per Pa-trum traditionem, ad Mosen usque conti-nuatum & conservatum in Ecclesia, verùm ἄγραφον[?]. Illud autem verbum ἄγραφον idem fuit in substantia, cum ea salutis doctrina, quam nunc habemus in sacris Literis: id quod nemo inficiatur. Scriptura igitur sacra, quod ad suam attinet substantiam, hoc est, qua-tenus doctrina est cœlestis & divina, non fuit primùm inspirata & revelata Moysi: sed jam inde à condito orbe, aliis Patribus.
units.tr: For the Church from the beginning of the world always had with it the Word of God (without which the Church cannot exist), and this was partly inspired and revealed by God, and partly continued and preserved in the Church from the Fathers' tradition down to Moses, but unwritten [ἄγραφον]. That unwritten word was the same in substance as the doctrine of salvation which we now have in the sacred Letters, which no one denies. Therefore holy Scripture, as far as its substance is concerned, that is, insofar as it is heavenly and divine doctrine, was not first inspired and revealed to Moses, but from the creation of the world, to other Fathers.

units.la: PROPOSITIO II.
units.tr: PROPOSITION II.

units.la: Scriptura verò sacra, non solùm quatenus doctrina est cœlestis, sed etiam quatenus est Scriptura: inspirata fuit primùm Moysi: deinde aliis Prophetis: postremò Apostolis.
units.tr: But holy Scripture, not only insofar as it is heavenly doctrine, but also insofar as it is written Scripture: was first inspired to Moses, then to other Prophets, and finally to the Apostles.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmation.

units.la: Primus enim, qui cœlestem doctrinam literis commiserit & scripserit, fuit Moses. Nam quòd quidam scribunt de libro Enochi: illud nihil habet firmitudinis. Etenim, etiamsi libentissimè concedam, Epistolam Iudæ, epistolam esse [illegible, ~10 letters]: tamen indè colligi nequit, ab Enocho quippiam fuisse conscriptum, & posteritati relictum. Non enim fit ibi mentio libri aut scripti cuius-piam: sed tantùm habet hæc verba Iudæ: προεφήτευσε[?] δὲ καὶ τούτοις ἕβδομος ἀπὸ Ἀδὰμ Ἐνὼχ λέγων, &c. Annon potuit hæc prophetasse sine scripto?
units.tr: Moses was the first who committed the heavenly doctrine to letters and wrote it down. For as to what some write about the book of Enoch, that has no firmness. For even if I most willingly grant that the Epistle of Jude is an epistle [illegible, ~10 letters]; yet it cannot be concluded from it that anything was written by Enoch and left to posterity. For no mention is made there of any book or writing, but only Jude has these words: "Enoch also, the seventh from Adam, prophesied, saying, etc." [Jude 14]. Could he not have prophesied this without writing?

units.la: At propria verba recitat Enochi: unde hæc potuit habere, nisi ex libro Enochi?
units.tr: But Enoch's own words are recited: from where could Jude have had them, unless from the book of Enoch?

units.la: Respond. Non hoc consequitur. Nam potuit illud habere ex traditione: ita ut illud Enochi dictum fuerit in omnium ore. Aut forte, quod per traditionem in Ecclesia multos duraverat annos & sæcula, illud ab aliquo deinde alio fuit in chartas relatum. Ex hoc igitur loco Iudæ nil certi potest concludi de libro Enochi. Quare stat sententia, Mosi primùm ita fuisse scripturam, id est, doctrinam Dei inspiratam; ut ipse prior eam quoque scri-ptis commendarit. Confirmatur hæc sen-tentia, primùm testimonio Christi. Nam cùm citat scripturas, primum semper locum dat Mosi: Et quidem Lucæ 24. cùm de indu-stria, & ex professo vellet scripturis omni-bus probare, oportuisse Christum pati, & ita intrare in gloriam suam. Incipit à Mose, deinde à Prophetis: & ita interpretabatur illis (inquit Lucas) in omnibus scripturis, qua de ipso erant.
units.tr: Answer: this does not follow. For he could have had it from tradition, so that the saying of Enoch was in everyone's mouth. Or perhaps, since it had lasted by tradition in the Church for many years and ages, it was afterwards put into writing by some other person. Therefore nothing certain can be concluded from this passage of Jude about the book of Enoch.
