Wherefore the opinion stands that Scripture was first written thus by Moses, that is, the doctrine of God inspired, so that he himself first also committed it to writing. This opinion is confirmed, first, by the testimony of Christ. For when he cites the Scriptures, he always gives the first place to Moses. And indeed Luke 24, when he wished deliberately and expressly to prove from all the Scriptures that "Christ ought to suffer, and so enter into his glory. He began from Moses, then from the Prophets, and so he interpreted to them" (says Luke) "in all the Scriptures, the things which were concerning him."

units.la: Certè si quid etiam ante Mosen fuisset de se scriptum:non illud omisset.
units.tr: Certainly, if anything had been written about himself even before Moses, he would not have omitted it.

units.la: Secundò, testimonio Hebrœorum omnium, qui nullum antiquiorem Mosè scriptorem agnoscunt.
units.tr: Second, by the testimony of all the Hebrews, who acknowledge no writer older than Moses.

units.la: Tertiò, testimonio omnium Patrum. Singulorum testimonia non recito, quia res foret nimis prolixa, deinde inutilis: sed legatur Iustinus Martyr ἐν τῷ λόγῳ παραινετικῷ[?] πρὸς Ἕλληνας, pag.14. Ibi ex ipsis etiam profanis scriptoribus demonstrat, Mosen fuisse omnium scriptorum, tam Philosophorum, quàm Poe-tarum, & legislatorum, antiquissimum. Imò etiam evidentissimè ostendit, quicquid boni de Deo, rebusque diuinis scriptum reliquerunt Orpheus, Homerus, Solon, Pythagoras, Plato', & alij Græci: totum illud eos sumsisse ex libris Mosis: præsertim postea quam in Græcam linguam versi fuerunt. Eadem post Iustinum scripta reliquit Eusebius Cæsariensis in Libro excellentissimo, cui titulum fecit προπαρασκευὴ εὐαγγελικὴ[?], lib.10. cap.2. & 3. Item Tertullianus in Apologetico, cap.19. Ergo citrà omnem controversiam Moses non solùm primus fuit, cui Deus suam doctrinam ita inspiravit, ut eam etiam dictante Spiritu sancto conscripserit: verùm etiam omnium aliorum, inter Græcos scriptorum, antiquissimus. Quare sacra scriptu-ra omnium est librorum antiquissima. Catalogus autem scriptorum huiusce γεα-[?] φῆς Ἱστνύσυ[?], & qua quisq; lingua scripserit: hic est.
units.tr: Third, by the testimony of all the Fathers. I do not recite the testimonies of each one, because the matter would be too lengthy and then useless; but let Justin Martyr be read, in his hortatory discourse to the Greeks, p. 14. There he demonstrates, even from the profane writers themselves, that Moses was the oldest of all writers, both philosophers and poets and lawgivers. Indeed he shows most evidently that whatever good they left written about God and divine things, Orpheus, Homer, Solon, Pythagoras, Plato, and the other Greeks, they took all of that from the books of Moses, especially after these were translated into the Greek language. The same things, after Justin, Eusebius of Caesarea left written in his most excellent book, which he entitled the Preparation for the Gospel, book 10, chapters 2 and 3. Likewise Tertullian in the Apologeticus, chapter 19. Therefore, beyond all controversy, Moses was not only the first to whom God inspired his doctrine in such a way that he also wrote it down under the dictation of the Holy Spirit, but also the most ancient of all other writers among the Greeks. Wherefore Holy Scripture is the most ancient of all books. The catalogue of writers of this kind, and in what language each one wrote, is this:

units.la: Primus, Moses[?] scripsit libros quinque: quos etiam πεντάτευχοι[?] Græci vocârunt, à numero. Scripsit autem Hebraica lingua, & quidem cùm esset in deserto dux populi. Excipiuntur postremi versus in fine Deuteronomij: vbi de morte Moses sermo est. Nam hos non potuit scribere Moses, sed Iosua scripsisse creditur.
units.tr: First, Moses wrote five books, which the Greeks also called the Pentateuch, from the number. He wrote them in the Hebrew language, and indeed while he was leader of the people in the desert. The last verses at the end of Deuteronomy are excepted, where the account is of Moses' death. For Moses could not have written these; Joshua is believed to have written them.

units.la: Secundus, Iobus Idumæus, scripsit librum, cui suum præfixit nomen. Scripsit autem partim Hebraicè, partim Arabicè, partim Syriacè, vt Hieronymus testatur in Iobum. Quanquam non desunt inter Hebræos, qui velint, huius etiam libri autorem & scriptorem fuisse Mosen.
units.tr: Second, Job the Idumaean wrote a book, to which he prefixed his own name. He wrote partly in Hebrew, partly in Arabic, partly in Syriac, as Jerome testifies on Job. Although among the Hebrews there are not lacking those who would have Moses also to be the author and writer of this book.

units.la: Tertium, Eleazarus, Aaronis filius, & perpetuus comes Iosuæ, creditur fuisse scriptor libri Iosuæ. Quanquam plerique omnes velint, Iosuam ipsum eum librum scripsisse, sicut & Moses suos.
units.tr: Third, Eleazar, son of Aaron and the constant companion of Joshua, is believed to have been the writer of the book of Joshua. Although nearly all want Joshua himself to have written that book, just as Moses wrote his own.

units.la: Quartus, Samuel Propheta, & Rector populi, scripsit primo librum, qui Iudicum dicitur: (vt tradunt Hebræi) lingua Hebraica. Sunt tamen qui velint, Iudices ipsos, suasque temporis res gestas conscripsisse: à Samuele verò, omnia illa Iudicum monumenta, in vnum tandem volumen fuisse redacta. Secundo, scripsit librum Ruth, de omnium Hebræorum sententia. Tertiò, scripsit librum primum, qui Samuelis inscribitur apud Hebraeos, & primus Regum dicitur Latinis, vsque ad 25. caput, vbi ipsius mors describitur. Reliqua capita, & totus secundus liber, creditur à Dauide Rege fuisse conscriptus.
units.tr: Fourth, Samuel the prophet and ruler of the people first wrote the book which is called Judges, (as the Hebrews relate) in the Hebrew language. There are, however, some who would have the judges themselves to have written their own deeds of their time, and that afterwards by Samuel all those monuments of the Judges were finally brought together into one volume. Second, he wrote the book of Ruth, according to the opinion of all the Hebrews. Third, he wrote the first book, which among the Hebrews is entitled Samuel, and is called the first of Kings by the Latins, down to chapter 25, where his own death is described. The remaining chapters, and the whole second book, are believed to have been written by King David.

units.la: Quintus, Reliqui duo libri, qui Melachim seu Regum appellantur, partim à Dauide, partim à Salomone, partim ab aliis Prophetis, qui illis vixerunt temporibus, creduntur fuisse scripti:ita ut quisque illorum, res suo tempore gestas monumentis mandarit, à Spiritu sancto afflati.
units.tr: Fifth, the remaining two books, which are called Melachim or Kings, are believed to have been written partly by David, partly by Solomon, partly by other prophets who lived in those times; so that each of them, inspired by the Holy Spirit, committed to monuments the deeds performed in his own time.

units.la: Dauid suos scripsit Psalmos, Hebraicè, quos Hebraei vocant Tehilim. Qui ipsius non sunt: ab aliis quorum inscripta sunt nomina, Spiritu itidem Dei afflatus compositi & conscripti fuerunt: sed postea ab Eldra omnes in vnum volumen redacti sunt.
units.tr: David wrote his Psalms in Hebrew, which the Hebrews call Tehillim. Those which are not his own were composed and written down, likewise inspired by God's Spirit, by others whose names are inscribed on them; but afterwards all of them were brought together into one volume by Ezra.

units.la: Sextus, Salomon, Dauidis filius, scripsit Proverbia Mischli: Ecclesiastem, quem vocant Cohelet, & Schir Haschirim, id est, Canticum Canticorum.
units.tr: Sixth, Solomon, son of David, wrote the Proverbs (Mishlei), Ecclesiastes, which they call Qoheleth, and Shir ha-Shirim, that is, the Song of Songs.

units.la: Septimus, Esdras sacerdos, scripsit primum & secundum: quorum primus Esdrae: alter Nehemiae dicitur, quòd gesta Nehemiae cum primis contineat. Scripsisse etiâ creditur (quanquam nil certi) duos libros, qui ab Hebraeis vocantur Dibre Hajomim, hoc est, verba dierum, id est, Diaria: & à Graecis παραλειπομένων, hoc est, derelictorum: quòd ea complectuntur, quae in libris Regum derelicta sunt. Ideo in Hebraicis Bibliis collocantur post duos libros Esdrae, quòd credantur ab ipso fuisse conscripti, vel saltem in ordinem redacti.
units.tr: Seventh, Ezra the priest wrote the first and second books; of which the first is called Ezra's, the other Nehemiah's, because it contains chiefly the deeds of Nehemiah. It is also believed (though nothing certain) that he wrote two books, which by the Hebrews are called Dibre Hayyamim, that is, the words of days, that is, Diaries; and by the Greeks paraleipomenōn, that is, of things left out, because they comprehend what was left out in the books of Kings. Therefore in the Hebrew Bibles they are placed after the two books of Ezra, because they are believed to have been written by him, or at least put into order.

units.la: Osanus[?] Mardochaeus Iudæus, vir nobilis, & generosus, scripsit librum, qui dicitur Hester. Sic Kimchi, & alij.
units.tr: Mordecai the Jew, a man noble and generous, wrote the book which is called Esther. So Kimchi and others.

units.la: Iesaias, Ieremias, Ezechiel, Daniel, Duodecim minores Prophetæ, suam quisq; scripsit Prophetiam. Summam enim suarum concionum notabant: deinde à piis Regibus curatum, vt in certa redigerentur volumina. Sic etiam scribit Iustinus Martyr, in altera pro Christianis apologia ad Antoninum Imperatorem, p.146. v.13. [illegible, ~60 letters]
units.tr: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, the twelve minor Prophets each wrote his own prophecy. For they noted down the sum of their sermons; then, by pious kings, care was taken that they should be brought into fixed volumes. So also Justin Martyr writes, in the second apology for the Christians to the Emperor Antoninus, p. 146, v. 13. [illegible, ~60 letters]

units.la: Hi igitur sunt, quibus hæc veteris Testamenti scriptura θεόπνευστος fuit inspirata. Et de iis ait Petrus 2.Pet.1. Spiritu sancto inspirati locuti sunt ij Dei homines.
units.tr: These, therefore, are the ones to whom this Scripture of the Old Testament was inspired, θεόπνευστος [theopneustos]. And of them Peter says, 2 Pet. 1: "Holy men of God spoke, moved by the Holy Spirit."

units.la: Quæstio: At fuerunt ne plures iis, quibus Deus inspirauerit scripturam θεόπνευστον[?]? Et pluresne iis quos habemus sacri libri?
units.tr: Question: Were there more than those to whom God inspired Scripture, θεόπνευστον [theopneuston]? And are there more than those whose sacred books we have?

units.la: Respond. Fuerunt alij & libri θεόπνευστοι, & viri, quibus inspirata fuit scriptura θεόπνευστος, de quibus certissima habemus in scripturis testimonia: sed perierunt, præsertim in templi incendio, & vrbis destructione, cùm populus fuit abductus in Babylonem; Qui autem desiderantur, sunt ij:
units.tr: Answer: There were also other books θεόπνευστοι [theopneustoi] and men to whom Scripture was inspired, θεόπνευστος [theopneustos], about whom we have most certain testimonies in the Scriptures; but they have perished, especially in the burning of the temple and the destruction of the city, when the people were led away into Babylon. Those which are missed are these:

units.la: 1. Liber bellorum Domini, de quo Num.21. fit mentio.
units.tr: 1. The Book of the Wars of the Lord, of which mention is made in Num. 21.

units.la: 2. Liber iustorum, de quo Iosue, cap.10.
units.tr: 2. The Book of the Upright, of which in Joshua, chap. 10.

units.la: 3. Liber Nathani, Prophetae &
units.tr: 3. The Book of Nathan the Prophet, and

units.la: 4. Liber Gad Prophetae, de quibus. 1. Pa-ral.29.
units.tr: 4. The Book of Gad the Prophet, of which 1 Chron. 29.

units.la: 5. Sermones Ahiae Silonitae Prophetae: &
units.tr: 5. The Sermons of Ahijah the Shilonite, the Prophet; and

units.la: 6. Visiones Addo videntis, id est, Prophetae, quarum mentio fit 2. Paral.9.
units.tr: 6. The Visions of Iddo the seer, that is, the Prophet, of which mention is made in 2 Chron. 9.

units.la: 7. Proverbia multa, & Carmina, a Salomone edita & scripta, quæ non extant, & de quibus mentio fit, in Reg.3[?].cap.4.
units.tr: 7. Many proverbs and songs, put forth and written by Solomon, which do not survive, and of which mention is made in 1 Kings 4.

units.la: 8. Liber Salomonis, de omnibus arboribus, hoc est, de natura arborum & stirpium.
units.tr: 8. The book of Solomon on all trees, that is, on the nature of trees and plants.

units.la: 9. Eiusdem liber de quadrupedibus ani-mantibus.
units.tr: 9. The same book on four-footed animals.

units.la: 10. Eiusdem de volucribus.
units.tr: 10. The same on birds.

units.la: 11. Eiusdem de serpentibus.
units.tr: 11. The same on serpents.

units.la: 12. Eiusdem de piscibus: De quibus omnibus Salomonis libris in 3. Reg.cap.4.
units.tr: 12. The same on fishes. Of all these books of Solomon, see 1 Kings 4.

units.la: Item ex Patribus hi etiam colliguntur deesse.
units.tr: Likewise, the Fathers also gather that the following books are missing:

units.la: 1. Liber descriptionum Ieremiae 2. Ma-chab.2.
units.tr: 1. The Book of the Descriptions of Jeremiah; 2. Maccabees 2.

units.la: 2. Commentarij Nehemiae.
units.tr: 2. The Commentaries of Nehemiah.

units.la: 3. Hymni Dauidis super duo millia. Atha-nasius in synopsi scripturarum.
units.tr: 3. The Hymns of David, two thousand in number. Athanasius, in his synopsis of the Scriptures.

units.la: 4. Ezechielis liber unus: Iosephus, ut refert Athanasius in synopsi. Duos enim scri-psit.
units.tr: 4. One book of Ezekiel; Josephus, as Athanasius reports in the synopsis. For he wrote two.

units.la: §.[?] Liber historiarum, ab Esaia scriptus: Beda, T.4. in Esdram,lib.2.cap.9.
units.tr: §.[?] The Book of Histories, written by Isaiah: Bede, vol. 4 on Ezra, book 2, chapter 9.

units.la: Cæterùm,etsi ij libri ἀπόκρυφοι[?] desideren-tur: tamen nihil decedit de doctrina ad salu-tem nostram necessaria. Nam diuina proui-dentia tantum seruatum est librorum,quan-tum satis erat ad cognoscendum Deum, e-jus voluntatem, Christum, eoque viam sa-lutis.
units.tr: Moreover, although those books [ἀπόκρυφοι[?]] are wanting, nothing is taken away from the doctrine necessary for our salvation. For by divine providence there has been preserved of the books just so much as was sufficient for knowing God, his will, Christ, and thereby the way of salvation.

units.la: Atque hæc de illis, quibus scriptura vete-ris Testamenti, de qua proprie loquitur Apostolus 2. Tim.3.satis.
units.tr: And so much concerning those books of the Old Testament, of which the Apostle speaks properly in 2 Tim. 3.

units.la: Cæterum de iis, quibus scriptura Noui Testamenti inspirata: & à quibus in literas redacta fuit, facilior & certior est responsio.
units.tr: As for those books of the New Testament, by whom they were inspired and by whom they were committed to writing, the answer is easier and more certain.

units.la: Extra controuersiam est, Euangelistas omnes sua scripsisse Euangelia, idque affla-tos Spiritu sancto. De actis Lucas ipse te-statur.
units.tr: It is beyond controversy that all the Evangelists wrote their own Gospels, and that they did so inspired by the Holy Spirit. Luke himself bears witness concerning the Acts.

units.la: De Epistolis etiam Paulo ascriptis, nemo dubitat, quin à Paulo fuerint conscriptæ: si unam excipias ad Hebraeos. Sed nihil etiam est firmæ rationis, firmive testimonij, cur non sentiendum sit, fuisse & hanc à Paulo exaratam: cùm & Clemens Alexandrinus, & alij nonnulli antiqui Patres affirment.
units.tr: Concerning the Epistles also ascribed to Paul, no one doubts that they were written by Paul, with the exception of the one to the Hebrews. Yet there is no firm reason or firm testimony why we should not hold that this one too was written by Paul, since both Clement of Alexandria and several other ancient Fathers affirm it.

units.la: De Epistolis Canonicis antea à nobis di-ctum fuit, quid sentiam: itidem de Apocaly-psi. Ego non dubito,omnes hosce libros ab illis fuisse scriptos, quibus etiam ascribun-tur, & quidem omnes Græca lingua. Nam quòd de Euangelio Matthaei & de Epistola ad Hebræos nonnulli scribunt, Hebraica lingua fuisse scriptos: Ego neminem lego, qui scribat, se hos duos libros, aut saltem alterutrum vidisse Hebraicè scriptos: tantùm omnes referuntaliorum sententias, & dicta: ut quòd Euseb. Cæsar. libr. 5. cap. 10. de Euangelio Matth. scribit: ex aliorum sententia & rumore scribit. Idem dico de iis, quæ scribit Hieronymus. Ita de Irenæo lib.3. cap.1. Affirmat Matthæum Hebraicè scripsisse: sed non ait, se vidisse. Neq; etiam ullam video rationem, quæ concludat. Quòd enim scribunt quidam, Ideo Hebraicè fuisse utrumque scriptum: quia ad Hebræos scribebatur: nihil est. Nam eadem ratione dicendum fuerit, etiam Epistolam Petri fuisse Hebraicis literis scriptam: quia scripta fuit ad Iudæos, qui erant in dispersione Ponti, & Galatiæ, & Cappadociæ. Imò contrà retorqueo: Quia Apostoli omnes mandatum habebant à Christo, ut Gentibus omnibus prædicarent Euangelii, & per totum orbem propagarent: verisimilius est, omnes ea lingua suos conscripsisse libros, quæ toti orbi notior esset. Hæc autem tunc temporis fuit Græca. Nihil igitur peccauerimus, si credamus, omnes libros Noui Testamenti Græca lingua fuisse conscriptos.
units.tr: Concerning the Catholic Epistles, I have already said what I think; likewise concerning the Apocalypse. I do not doubt that all these books were written by those to whom they are also ascribed, and indeed that all were written in the Greek language. For as to what some write, that the Gospel of Matthew and the Epistle to the Hebrews were written in the Hebrew language, I read of no one who writes that he had seen these two books, or at least one of them, written in Hebrew; they all merely report the opinions and sayings of others, as when Eusebius of Caesarea, book 5, chapter 10, writes concerning the Gospel of Matthew that he writes on the opinion and rumour of others. I say the same of what Jerome writes. Thus Irenaeus, book 3, chapter 1, affirms that Matthew wrote in Hebrew, but does not say that he himself had seen it. Nor do I see any reasoning that proves it. For the argument of some, that both were therefore written in Hebrew because they were written to the Hebrews, is nothing. For by the same reasoning it would have to be said that the Epistle of Peter was also written in Hebrew letters, because it was written to the Jews who were scattered through Pontus, Galatia and Cappadocia. Indeed I turn the argument back the other way: since all the Apostles had a command from Christ to preach the Gospel to all the Gentiles and to spread it through the whole world, it is more likely that they all wrote their books in that language which was best known to the whole world. This at that time was Greek. We shall therefore not err if we believe that all the books of the New Testament were written in the Greek language.

units.la: Nunc igitur tenemus etiam de quarta quæstione, qui nam illi fuerint, quibus Deus ita hanc scripturam inspirauit, ut eam etiam scripserint. Hinc colligimus, præter hos, alium admittendum esse neminem, qui dicat, suam doctrinam sibi esse inspiratam à Deo. Nam si fuerit huic θεόπνευστος γραφὴ consentanea: non fuerit ei nuper revelata, sed è scripturis desumta: si dissentanea: non à Deo, sed à Diabolo sit revelata, necesse est.
units.tr: Now then we hold also concerning the fourth question, who those were to whom God so inspired this Scripture that they also wrote it down. From this we gather that, beyond these, no one else is to be admitted who says that his doctrine has been inspired in him by God. For if it agrees with this θεόπνευστος γραφή, it was not newly revealed to him but was drawn from the Scriptures; if it disagrees, it is necessarily revealed not by God but by the Devil.

units.la: QVÆSTIO V. De origine & progressu Verbi Dei in Ecclesia.
units.tr: QUESTION V. Concerning the origin and progress of the Word of God in the Church.

units.la: Hinc vero perspicuum fit, quid ad quintam quæstionem, quæ est de origine, & pro-gressu Verbi Dei in Ecclesia, respondendum sit.
units.tr: From this it becomes clear what must be answered to the fifth question, which concerns the origin and progress of the Word of God in the Church.

units.la: PROPOSITIO.
units.tr: PROPOSITION.

units.la: Hoc verbum ex Dei ore, tanquam ex fonte effluxit[?], perque mentes, & ora, & manus horum sanctorum virorum, tanquam per Canales, opera Spiritus sancti ad nos usque derivatum est, & ad posteros in finem usque Mundi derivabitur: Deo scripturas in Ec-clesia conservante: & Ministerium Verbi custodiente.
units.tr: This Word has flowed out from the mouth of God, as from a fountain, and through the minds, mouths and hands of these holy men, as through channels, by the work of the Holy Spirit, has been carried down to us, and will be carried down to posterity until the end of the world, God preserving the Scriptures in the Church and the Ministry of the Word keeping them.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmation.

units.la: Hoc ita perspicuum est, ut probatione nō opus habeat. Est enim scriptura θεόπνευστος: Ergo primum à Dei ore & Spiritu est. Deinde per homines sanctos, quibus fuit inspirata, ad nos transmissa. Hæc duo consequantur. Est necesse ex hac dictione θεόπνευστος. Accedat&illud 2.Pet.1. Prophetia propria in-terpretatione non fit: sed Spiritu sancto inspirati, locuti sunt sancti Dei homines. Item Hebr.1.
units.tr: This is so evident that it needs no proof. Scripture is θεόπνευστος: therefore it is first from the mouth and Spirit of God. Then it has been transmitted to us through the holy men to whom it was inspired. These two things follow necessarily from this word θεόπνευστος. Add that passage of 2 Pet. 1: "No prophecy is made by private interpretation, but holy men of God spoke, being moved by the Holy Spirit." Likewise Heb. 1:

units.la: Multifariam multisque modis olim Deus lo-cutus est, novissime autem in Filio, &c.
units.tr: "God, who at various times and in various ways spoke of old, has at the last spoken to us in his Son," etc.

units.la: Duraturum verò in Ecclesia, in finem usque seculi: inde liquet, Matth.28. Ecce ego vobiscum sum, usq; in consummationem seculi. 1. Pet.1. Verbum autem Domini manet in aeternum. 1. Corinth.11. Mortem Domini annunciabitis, donec veniat. Ergo usque ad Domini reditum, Ministerium & verbi, & sacramentorum in Ecclesia continuabitur.
units.tr: That it will endure in the Church until the end of the age is clear from Matt. 28: "Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the world." 1 Pet. 1: "But the word of the Lord endures forever." 1 Cor. 11: "You proclaim the Lord's death until he comes." Therefore, until the Lord's return, the ministry both of the Word and of the sacraments will continue in the Church.

units.la: 2. Thes.2. De Antichristo ait, illum à Domino paulatim interfectum iri spiritu oris sui, donec per illustrem aduentum Christi tandem penitus aboleatur. In finem igitur usque Mundi, verbum in Ecclesia servabitur. Est igitur hæc origo, & progressus verbi Dei in Ecclesia diligenter observandus: quia multum facit ad fidem nostram fulciendam.
units.tr: In 2 Thess. 2 he says of Antichrist that he will be gradually slain by the Lord with the breath of his mouth, until at the glorious coming of Christ he is at last utterly abolished. Therefore the Word will be preserved in the Church until the end of the world. This origin and progress of the Word of God in the Church is therefore to be carefully observed, because it contributes greatly to strengthening our faith.

units.la: Duo sunt modi, quibus Deus verbum suum ad nos misit iam inde ab initio Mundi, & conservauit & conservat in Ecclesia, usq; ad finem seculi: Viva vox: & scriptio. Uterque autem per Spiritum sanctum efficax est in electis atq; fidelibus.
units.tr: There are two modes by which God has sent his Word to us from the beginning of the world, and has preserved and preserves it in the Church until the end of the age: the living voice and writing. Both are made effective through the Holy Spirit in the elect and faithful.

units.la: Ac primùm quidem à condito orbe usq; ad Mosen, nulla usus est scriptione in chartis, sed tantùm voce & scriptione in cordibus, idq; per annos circiter bis mille, & quadringentos, 2400 Per illud enim tempus, sine ullo scripto Deus modò per Filium λό-γον sub specie humanæ formæ Patribus apparentem, locutus est: modò per Spiritus sancti afflatum, intus tantùm in animo loquentis: modò per Angelos è cœlo demissos: modò per ministerium ipsorum etiam hominum. Totum hoc quod dico, etiam vel mediocriter versatis in sacris Literis, perspicuum est.
units.tr: And first, indeed, from the creation of the world until Moses, he used no writing on paper, but only voice and writing in hearts; and this for about two thousand four hundred years. For during that time, without any written record, God spoke, now through the Son, the Word, appearing to the Fathers under the form of a human shape; now through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, inwardly only in the mind of the one speaking; now through angels sent down from heaven; now through the ministry of men themselves. All that I am saying is evident even to those moderately versed in the Holy Scriptures.

units.la: Filium Dei subinde Patribus in spectro humanæ formæ apparuisse, & familiariter cum illis locutum fuisse: docent scripturæ, & Patres confirmant. Quis enim fuit ille, per quem formatus fuit Adamus: deinde admonitus, ne ederet de pomis illius arboris: & post peccatum fuit obiurgatus, promissione etiam de salute per futurum semen sublevatus? Quis, inquam, ille fuit? Ille λόγος, per quem facta sunt omnia (inquit Iohannes) & sine quo factum est nihil, quod factum est. Iohan. 1. Omnia per ipsum facta sunt: Ergo etiam Adamus huius manibus formatus, & huius ore edoctus, admonitus, reprehensus, confortatus. Idem est, qui apparuit Nohæ, Abrahæ, à duobus Angelis comitatus, qui luctatus est cum Iacobo. Idcirco appellatur Malcach, id est, Angelus, nempe Patris: quia à Patre mittebatur, & per illum loquebatur.
units.tr: That the Son of God from time to time appeared to the Fathers in the appearance of a human form and spoke with them familiarly, the Scriptures teach and the Fathers confirm. For who was he through whom Adam was formed, then warned not to eat of the fruit of that tree, and after the sin was rebuked, and raised up even with the promise of salvation through the future seed? Who, I say, was he? He is the Word "through whom all things were made" (says John), "and without whom nothing was made that was made." John 1: "All things were made through him." Therefore Adam too, formed by his hands, and instructed, admonished, rebuked and strengthened by his mouth. He is the same who appeared to Noah and Abraham, accompanied by two angels, and who wrestled with Jacob. For this reason he is called Malcach, that is, Angel, namely of the Father, because he was sent by the Father and spoke through him.

units.la: Huc facit, quod Hof. 12. legimus de hoc Angelo, qui luctatus est cum Iacobo. Quem enim primò vocavit Hosea v. 4. Malcach id est, ἄγγελον[?] Angelum: postea vocat v.s. Iehouam[?] Deum Zebaoth.
units.tr: To this purpose is what we read in Hos. 12 about this Angel who wrestled with Jacob. For Hosea at verse 4 first calls him Malcach, that is, ἄγγελον[?] Angel; afterwards, at verse 5, he calls him Jehovah, God of Hosts.

units.la: Et Patres, praesertim Tertullianus & Irenaeus scribunt, Patrem nunquam solitum fuisse cuipiam apparere in aliquo spectro: sed tantum Filium. Ideo vocant Patrem in-visibilem, Filium visibilem: non quidem quod ad essentiam divinitatis attinet. Est enim Filius tam ἀόρατος[?] (ut loquitur Apostolus) quàm Pater: sed ideo visibilem, quòd in spectris ipse apparebat, non Pater. Et addit Irenaeus: hoc optimè convenisse Filio: quia voluit praeludio quodam ostendere, quid postea reipsa esset facturus: nempe sumturus humanam carnem, non amplius speciem humanae carnis, sed veram humanam carnem, idque ὑποστατικῶς.
units.tr: And the Fathers, especially Tertullian and Irenaeus, write that the Father never used to appear to anyone in any form, but only the Son. Therefore they call the Father invisible and the Son visible: not indeed as regards the essence of the Godhead. For the Son is as invisible (as the Apostle puts it) as the Father; but he is called visible because it was he himself, not the Father, who appeared in forms. And Irenaeus adds that this agreed very well with the Son, because he wished by a kind of prelude to show what he was afterwards actually going to do: namely, to take on human flesh, no longer the appearance of human flesh but true human flesh, and that hypostatically.

units.la: Proverb. 8. locus est insignis de hac re. Ibi sapientia Patris, quae est filius Dei, loquitur, & ait primùm se fuisse cum Patre, antequam quicquam conditum esset:2.se cum Patre omnia composuisse & creasse: 3. se fuisse & esse omni tempore cum Patre coram eo ludentem, & deliciis fruentem. 4. Se etiam in orbe terrarum ludere, & delicias sibi esse cum filiis hominum. Λόγῳ[?] igitur & Sapientia Patris, ille est, qui forma humani corporis sumta, ludebat cum Patribus, & hoc erat illi in deliciis, versari scilicet cum hominibus.
units.tr: Proverbs 8 is a notable passage on this matter. There Wisdom, which is the Father's Son, the Word of God, speaks and says: first, that she was with the Father before anything was created; second, that she arranged and created all things together with the Father; third, that she was and is with the Father at all times, playing before him and delighting in him; fourth, that she also plays in the world and her delight is with the sons of men. Therefore it is the Word and Wisdom of the Father who, having taken on the form of a human body, played with the Fathers, and this was his delight, namely to dwell with men.

units.la: Obiect. At Heb.1.dicitur: Olim locutus est in Prophetis, nunc in Filio. Resp. Intelligit de externo omnibus visibili, & ordinario in Ecclesia[?] ministerio. Quare dubium non est, quin Filius Dei fuerit ille primus, per quem Pater Verbum suum attulit Mundo.
units.tr: Objection. But Hebrews 1 says: God, who at various times and in various ways spoke in the prophets, has in these last days spoken to us by a Son. Answer: it refers to the external and ordinary ministry in the Church, which was visible to all. Hence there is no doubt that the Son of God was that first one through whom the Father brought his Word to the world.

units.la: De illius spiritu, quod scilicet per illius etiam afflatum intus in animis loqueretur sanctis Patriarchis & Prophetis: liquet ex 2.[?] Pet.1.Spiritu sancto inspirati, locuti sunt Dei homines. Ergo etiam Patriarchae, & alij sancti viri.
units.tr: That he also spoke within the souls of the holy Patriarchs and Prophets through his inward breathing, namely by his inspiration, is clear from 2 Peter 1: Men spoke from God, moved by the Holy Spirit. Therefore the Patriarchs too, and the other holy men.

units.la: Locutum vero etiam esse per Angelos: historia itidem Geneseos & Exodi, docet abundè. Nam per Angelos saepe locutus est cum Abrahamo, & Lotho, & Iacobo. Gal.3. ait, per Angelos datam fuisse legem.
units.tr: That God also spoke through angels, the histories of Genesis and Exodus likewise teach abundantly. For he often spoke through angels with Abraham, Lot and Jacob. Galatians 3 says that the law was given through angels.

units.la: Per ipsum etiam ministerium hominum verbum suum praedicasse, propagasse, conseruasse in Ecclesia: luce clarius est. Nam in hunc etiam finem primis illis Patribus loquebatur ipse per Filium, per Spiritum S. per Angelos: ut ipsi postea idem verbum aliis annunciarent, & ad posteros propagarent.
units.tr: That he also preached, propagated and preserved his Word in the Church through the ministry of men is clearer than light. For to this end also he spoke to those first Fathers himself, through the Son, through the Holy Spirit and through angels, so that they in turn might announce the same Word to others and pass it on to posterity.

units.la: Accipe testimonium unum. Gen.19. Non ce-
units.tr: Take one testimony. Genesis 18: Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?

units.la: labo Abrahamum quaecunq; facturus sum. Qua-re? Cum (inquit) Abrahamum futurum sit in gentem magnam: Hoc quoque, scio, quod manda-turus sit filiis suis, & domui suae post se, ut custo-diant viam meam. En cur revelabat verbum Patribus: nempe ut ipsi illud idem traderent filiis suis & posteritati: atque ita successione quadam seruaretur in Ecclesia.
units.tr: Why? Because, he says, Abraham is going to become a great nation: I know that he will also command his sons and his household after him to keep my way. See why he revealed the Word to the Fathers: namely, that they might hand the same down to their sons and posterity, and so it might be preserved in the Church by a kind of succession.

units.la: Haec est illa traditio Patrum, per quam fi-ne scripto verbum Dei conseruatum est in Ecclesia, usq; ad Mosen. Adamus igitur fuit primus inter homines praeco Dei, & praedicator verbi. Deinde Seth, eius filius, & sic deinceps, ne singulos commemorem vsque ad diluuium. A diluuio, Mundo jam nouo, & quasi altero, Noha cum liberis, maximè cum Sem, unde sancti propagati sunt, verbum Dei in Ecclesia praedicârunt & conseruarunt, semper viua voce, sine scriptis, ad Mosen usque.
units.tr: This is that tradition of the Fathers, by which the Word of God was preserved in the Church without writing, up to Moses. Adam, therefore, was the first among men as herald of God and preacher of the Word. Then Seth, his son, and so on in turn, not to mention each one, down to the flood. From the flood, with the world now new and as it were a second one, Noah with his children, above all Shem, from whom the saints were propagated, preached and preserved the Word of God in the Church, always by living voice, without writings, up to Moses.

units.la: Nunc tenemus originem & progressum verbi, usque ad Mosen: & quem modum seruarit Deus in hoc verbo propagando, per il-lud tempus annorum scilicet 2400.
units.tr: Now we have the origin and progress of the Word up to Moses, and the manner God observed in propagating this Word during that period of about 2400 years.

units.la: Nunc de secundo modo, quo scilicet per scripturam, verbum suum in Ecclesia propa-gauit & conseruauit, in hoc usque tempus, & conseruaturus est in finem usque Mundi, dicendum est.
units.tr: Now we must speak of the second manner, namely how through Scripture he has propagated and preserved his Word in the Church up to this time, and will preserve it to the end of the world.

units.la: Primus, cuius opera usus est Deus in ver-bo suo literis committendo: fuit Moses, quemadmodum ante demonstrauimus. Huic principio magnam conciliauit apud omnes tam Ægyptios quàm Israelitas auctoritatem, tum in Ægypto, editis per eum permultis & obstupescendis miraculis: tum in deserto frequentissimis cum illo habitis familiaribus colloquiis, & aliis rationibus multis.
units.tr: The first whom God used to entrust his Word to letters was Moses, as we showed before. To this beginning he won great authority among all, both Egyptians and Israelites: in Egypt, through the very many and astonishing miracles he performed; and in the desert, through the most frequent familiar conversations he held with him, and through many other means.

units.la: In quem verò finem tantam ei conciliauit auctoritatem Deus? Ut plus fidei à populo præberetur [?] scriptis, quæ Moses, nomine Dei, erat illis traditurus: atque ita cognoscerent omnes,omnes, hanc Mosis scripturam, esse ipsissimum Dei verbum. Conciliauit igitur Moysi Deus tantam autoritatem, non tam propter Mosen, quàm propter populi autoritatem, & salutem. Hunc finem diserte Dominus aperit Mosi, dicendo; Exod. 19. Ecce ego veniam ad te, in densa nube, vt audiat me populus tecum loquentem: & credat tibi in perpetuum.
units.tr: But to what end did God grant him such great authority? That more faith might be given by the people to the writings which Moses was to hand down in God's name; and thus all might know that this Scripture of Moses is the very Word of God. God therefore conferred such authority on Moses not so much on account of Moses as on account of the authority and salvation of the people. The Lord clearly reveals this purpose to Moses, saying: Exodus 19: Behold, I will come to you in a thick cloud, so that the people may hear me speaking with you, and may believe you forever.

units.la: Conciliata Mosi autoritate, & ostenso fine Deus suo exemplo indicat ei, quid sibi faciundum sit. Legem enim, hoc, est, summam doctrinae coelestis, quam antea solitus erat tantùm voce Patribus tradere, & quam etiam prius Mosi ore ad os (vt more scripturae loquar) hoc est, coram explicuerat, scribit ei in duabus tabulis: hoc exemplo significans, se velle, vt haec doctrina in literas & libros posthac referatur.
units.tr: Once Moses' authority was established and the purpose shown, God by his own example indicates to him what must be done. For the law, that is, the sum of heavenly doctrine, which he had previously been accustomed to hand down to the Fathers only by voice, and which he had earlier explained to him mouth to mouth (to speak in the manner of Scripture), that is, face to face, he writes for him on two tablets; by this example signifying that he wishes this doctrine to be henceforth recorded in letters and books.

units.la: Mosesitaq; agnita Dei voluntate, totam coelestem doctrinam, quam partim à Patribus per traditionem accepérat: partim à Spiritu sancto per afflatum internum didicerat: & simul quaecunque sibi, & populo, toto vitae suae tempore, per annos 120. con-tigerant, in literas redegit, & populo exhibuit.
units.tr: Moses, therefore, having recognised the will of God, reduced to writing the whole heavenly doctrine, which he had partly received from the Fathers by tradition and partly learned from the Holy Spirit through inward inspiration; and at the same time everything that had befallen him and the people during his whole life, over 120 years, and he presented it to the people.

units.la: Populus vniuersus accipit scripturam Mosis tanquam ipsum Dei verbum: ac certè consensus iste totius illius populi & Ecclesiae, magno fuit & esse debet argumento, scrip-ta Mosis, verum esse Dei verbum. Nam quòd Dathan, Core, & Abiron contradixe-rint: illud non solùm non infirmat autorita-tem doctrinæ Mosis, sed magis confirmat. Deus enim illos ita seueriter puniuit, vt hac ratione aperte declarárit, Mosen sibi fuisse amicissimum: & quæ ille tradidisset, ea esse à Deo, ipsaque Dei eloquia.
units.tr: The whole people received the writing of Moses as the very Word of God; and certainly that consent of the whole people and Church was, and ought to be, a great argument that the writings of Moses are the true Word of God. For that Dathan, Korah and Abiram contradicted him: this not only does not weaken the authority of Moses' doctrine, but rather confirms it. For God punished them so severely that by this means he openly declared that Moses was most dear to him, and that what he had handed down was from God and was the very oracles of God.

units.la: DE PROPHETIS.
units.tr: ON THE PROPHETS.

units.la: Postmodum excitauit varios Prophetas, atque his primùm, sicut & Mosi, autoritatem conciliauit variis rationibus. Deinde, per ora horum hominum verbum prædicauit: & ad extremum etiam, per horum manus con-scripsit. Et hunc tenorem continuauit per annos circiter 1200. vsque ad Malachiam: post quem nullus vsque ad Iohannem Baptistam & Christum fuit in Ecclesia, Prophe-ta: neque etiam vsq; ad Apostolos, vllus Ecclesiasticus scriptor, cuius opera vsus fit Deus in suo verbo literis committendo. Nam Machabæorum scriptura non est ἀπόκρυφ[?]ος, vt antea ostendimus.
units.tr: Afterwards he raised up various prophets, and to these first, just as to Moses, he gave authority by various means. Then, through the mouths of these men he proclaimed the word, and finally, through their hands he also committed it to writing. He continued this course for about 1200 years, down to Malachi. After him, until John the Baptist and Christ, there was no prophet in the Church, nor, until the Apostles, any ecclesiastical writer whose work God used in committing his word to letters. For the writings of the Maccabees are not apocryphal, as we showed earlier.

units.la: Cæterum, hoc notandum est, Doctrinam Dei per Moysen traditam, Gentibus etiam communicatam fuisse: non tantùm voce, vt Ionas Nineuitis: sed etiam scriptis: idque tum tempore Prophetarum, tum etiam postea. Primùm Assyrijs illis, qui abductis decem tribubus, habitabant in Samaria, & aliis vrbibus Regni Israël[?]: curauit Deus per Regem Assyriorum, vt lex Moysis traderetur & explicaretur, indeque discerent colere verum Israelitarum DEVM. 4.Reg.17.
units.tr: Moreover, it should be noted that the doctrine of God delivered through Moses was also communicated to the Gentiles, not only by voice, as Jonah to the Ninevites, but also in writing; and this happened both in the time of the prophets and also afterwards. First, God arranged, through the king of the Assyrians, that the law of Moses should be delivered and explained to those Assyrians who, after the ten tribes were carried off, lived in Samaria and the other cities of the kingdom of Israel, so that they might learn to worship the true God of Israel. 4 Kings 17.

units.la: Secundò, Ante ipsum Ptolemæum Philadelphum, Regem Ægypti, imò & ante Alexandrum magnum (teste Aristobulo in lib. quem ad Regem Ptolemæum conscripsit) libri Moysis translati fuerunt in linguam Græcam quanquam malè: ut etiam inde Græci, quænam esset Dei voluntas, quæve doctrina salutis, discerent. Scribuntur hæc ab Eufeb. Cæsar, de præparatione Euangelica, lib.13.cap.7.
units.tr: Second, before Ptolemy Philadelphus, king of Egypt, and even before Alexander the Great (on the testimony of Aristobulus, in the book he wrote to King Ptolemy), the books of Moses were translated into the Greek language, though badly, so that the Greeks too might learn from them what the will of God was and what the doctrine of salvation was. These things are written by Eusebius of Caesarea, in the Preparation for the Gospel, book 13, chapter 7.

units.la: Tertiò, Admonitione verò Demetrij Pha-leraei, Regis Ægypti Bibliothecarij, & iussu atq; sumtibus regis Ægypti, cui Ptolemæus Philadelphus nomen fuit, per septuaginta duos doctissimos Hebræos, ex singulis tri-bubus sex, translata fuerunt scripta Moysis (De iis certum est.) Quidam volunt etiam scripta Prophetarum, & ἁγιόγραφα.
units.tr: Third, at the suggestion of Demetrius of Phalerum, librarian of the king of Egypt, and by the command and at the expense of the king of Egypt, whose name was Ptolemy Philadelphus, the writings of Moses were translated by seventy-two very learned Hebrews, six from each tribe. This is certain. Some hold that the writings of the prophets and the Hagiographa were translated too.

units.la: De hac 72. seniorum Iudæorum historia & versione, extant testimonia apud omnes scriptores. Indicabo præcipuos.
units.tr: Testimonies to this history of the seventy-two elders of the Jews and their version are extant among all the writers. I will name the chief ones.

units.la: Iosephus de Antiquitatibus lib.12.cap.2.
units.tr: Josephus, Antiquities, book 12, chapter 2.

units.la: Aristæus qui à Ptolemæo ad summum Pontificem Iudæorum, pro hac re missus fuerat legatus, librum scripsit, qui etiamnum extat. In eo totam historiam diligenter explicat.
units.tr: Aristeas, who was sent as envoy by Ptolemy to the high priest of the Jews for this matter, wrote a book which still survives. In it he explains the whole history carefully.

units.la: Tertullian. in Apologetico, pag.845.c.19.
units.tr: Tertullian, in the Apologeticus, p. 845, c. 19.

units.la: Iustinus Martyr, in exhortatione ad Gent.
units.tr: Justin Martyr, in the Exhortation to the Greeks.

units.la: Irenæus contra Valentinum, lib.3.cap.24. Epiphanius libr. de mensuris & ponderi-bus,pag.606.
units.tr: Irenaeus, against Valentinus, book 3, chapter 24. Epiphanius, book on weights and measures, p. 606.

units.la: Athanasius[?] in Synopsi.
units.tr: Athanasius, in the Synopsis.

units.la: Euseb.Cæsar.histor.Ecclesiast.lib.7[?].cap 8.
units.tr: Eusebius of Caesarea, Ecclesiastical History, book 7, chapter 8.

units.la: Item, de præparatione Euangelica, lib.8. cap.1.
units.tr: Likewise, in the Preparation for the Gospel, book 8, chapter 1.

units.la: Augusti. T.5. de Ciuitate Dei,lib.18. cap. 42.43.
units.tr: Augustine, vol. 5, On the City of God, book 18, chapters 42, 43.

units.la: Item, T.3. de doctrina Christiana, lib.2[?]. cap.15.
units.tr: Likewise, vol. 3, On Christian Doctrine, book 2, chapter 15.

units.la: Hi patres perspicuè describunt hanc hi-storiam de septuaginta duobus interpreti-bus:& quanti sit faciendâ illa versio, docent. Ego, quæ de hac historia controuertantur inter Hieronymum & Augustinum,& alios, in præsentia non disputo,neq; quid sentiam, dico ; quia hoc non est præsentis instituti. Hæc tantùm retuli,ut ostendam, quomodo Deus sua prouidentia, suum in Mundo con-tinuarit ad nos usq; verbum.
units.tr: These Fathers describe this history of the seventy-two interpreters clearly, and teach how great a value that version has. As for what is disputed about this history between Jerome and Augustine and others, I do not discuss it at present, nor do I say what I think, because that is not the purpose of the present undertaking. I have only related these things to show how God, by his providence, has preserved his word in the world and carried it down to us.

units.la: Quàm autem fuerit non solùm utilissimâ, sed etiam necessaria Ecclesiæ hæc 70. inter-pretum conuersio, inde satis liquet: quòd Apostoli hac semper usi sunt, cùm Gentibus prædicarunt. Fuit igitur propter Gentes ne-cessaria. Atque hæc 70. Interpretum versio facta fuit anno ante Christi aduentum, cir-citer 272.
units.tr: How useful, indeed how necessary, this conversion of the seventy interpreters was for the Church, is clear enough from this: the Apostles always used it when they preached to the Gentiles. It was therefore necessary for the sake of the Gentiles. And this version of the seventy interpreters was made about 272 years before the coming of Christ.

units.la: Post Prophetarum omnium & mortem & silentium, & post sparsam aliquam ex parte inter Gentes S. Bibliorum doctrinam, pe-70. Interpretum versionem : continuatum quidem fuit verbum Dei in populo Iudaico, per Pontifices, in Ministerio publico: sed non sine corruptelis, successu temporis: ita vt in aduentu Christi magna ex parte corrupta esset doctrina, non in Bibliis, sed in publico Ministerio. Et credo, hanc doctrinae corruptelam coepisse in Israële, postquam autore Iasone, Pontifice Maximo, Ethnicae literae coeperunt publicè doceri Hierosolymis, anno ante Christum, circiter 174. Vide 2. Mach. 4.
units.tr: After the death and silence of all the prophets, and after the doctrine of the Holy Scriptures had been partly scattered among the Gentiles, and after the version of the seventy interpreters, the word of God did indeed continue among the Jewish people through the priests in public ministry; but, as time went on, not without corruptions, so that at the coming of Christ the doctrine was for the most part corrupted, not in the Bible but in the public ministry. And I believe this corruption of doctrine began in Israel after, under the high priest Jason, Greek learning began to be taught publicly at Jerusalem, about 174 years before Christ. See 2 Maccabees 4.

units.la: Verùm quod ad scripta attinet, nihil novi fuit post Malachiam scriptum, quod verè possit dici ἀντιλεγόμενον[?]. De scriptis enim Machabeorum antea dictum est.
units.tr: Yet as far as writings are concerned, nothing new was written after Malachi that could truly be called disputed. For the writings of the Maccabees were discussed earlier.

units.la: Scripserunt etiam Hebraei suas Δευτερώσεις[?], de quibus saepe apud Hieronymum & Eusebium: hoc est, secundas iteratasque legis explicationes, idque etiam Graecè: & eas exteris quoq; hominibus communicabant: sed Δευτερώσεως[?] scriptura non fuit. Fuerunt autem hae Δευτερώσεις, nihil aliud, quàm dictorum Mosis & Prophetarum, non satis suo iudicio explicatorum, dilucidior interpretatio, & quasi totius legis compendium atque expositio.
units.tr: The Hebrews also wrote their Deuterôseis, of which Jerome and Eusebius often speak; that is, second and repeated explanations of the law, and this also in Greek; and they shared these with outsiders too. But the Deuterôseis were not Scripture. They were nothing other than a clearer interpretation of the sayings of Moses and the prophets, which had not been explained sufficiently by their own judgment, and a kind of summary and exposition of the whole law.

units.la: Primus, qui hoc opus aggressus est, fuit Iesus, filius Syrach, cuius librum habemus, qui Ecclesiasticus Latinis dicitur. Inter hos fuit etiam Ionathan Chaldaeus.Hic, vt etiam Chal- daei legere possent Biblia, imitatus exemplum 70. Interpretum, conuertit Biblia, ex Hebraica, in Chaldaicam linguam, anno ante natum Christum, circiter 40.
units.tr: The first who undertook this work was Jesus, son of Sirach, whose book we have, which is called Ecclesiasticus in Latin. Among these was also Jonathan the Chaldee. He, so that the Chaldeans too might be able to read the Bible, imitating the example of the seventy interpreters, translated the Bible from Hebrew into the Chaldee language, about 40 years before the birth of Christ.

units.la: Circa hoc idem tempus, Simeon Hilleles, doctor in schola Hierosolymitana, ille qui (vt scribitur) Christū excepit in vlnas, egregia quædam scripsit. Post hunc, ipse etiam Gamaliel, Simeonis fi non filius, saltem discipulus (vocatur enim BenSimeon) legis explanationes edidit, ad cuius etiam pedes institutus fuit Apostolus Paulus.
units.tr: About the same time, Simeon Hillel, a teacher in the school at Jerusalem, he who (as it is written) took Christ into his arms, wrote certain excellent things. After him, Gamaliel himself, if not the son of Simeon, at least his disciple (for he is called Ben-Simeon), published explanations of the law, at whose feet the Apostle Paul was also instructed.

units.la: Omnes hos commentarios, & S. Bibliorum, legisq; Domini explicationes, Hebraei Graeca voce, appellarunt [illegible, ~9 letters]. Cæterum nihil horum scriptorum agnitum fuit aut receptum ab Ecclesia pro θεοπνεύστῳ[?].
units.tr: All these commentaries, both on the Holy Scriptures and on the explanations of the Lord's law, the Hebrews called by a Greek word [illegible, ~9 letters]. Yet none of these writers was acknowledged or received by the Church as divinely inspired.

units.la: Tandem igitur venit Iohannes Baptista: mox Christus: horum neuter quippiam scripsit: sed Euangelium utrque voce tantum prædicauit. Ac proprie Ioannes quidem Baptista Christum venisse, præsentem esse, non tam verbis, quam digito etiam demonstrauit. Christus vero Euangelium ita prædicauit, vt etiam quæ fuerant à Prophetis de se prædicta, reipsa compleuerit: atque ita adimpleuerit, vt nihil reliquerit vel dicendum, vel adimplendum. Huc illud Ioan.15[?]. Omnia quæcunque audiui à Patre, nota fecI vobis. Item illud, Matth.5[?]. Iota vnum, aut vnus apex non præteribit a lege, donec omnia fiant.
units.tr: At last, therefore, came John the Baptist; soon after, Christ. Neither of them wrote anything, but each proclaimed the Gospel by voice only. John the Baptist in particular showed that Christ had come and was present, not so much by words as even by pointing with his finger. Christ, however, proclaimed the Gospel in such a way that he also fulfilled in fact what had been foretold of himself by the prophets, and so fulfilled it that he left nothing either to be said or to be fulfilled. To this belongs that saying, John 15. All things whatsoever I have heard from the Father, I have made known to you. Likewise that, Matthew 5. One jot or one tittle shall not pass from the law until all things are fulfilled.

units.la: Euangelij vero doctrinam à se prædicatam, miraculis permultis & manifestis confirmauit. Cur autem Christus nil sua manu scripserit: non est curiose investigandum. Illud tantum dicam, quod etiam de corpore Mosis ab omnibus piis viris scribitur: ideo noluisse Deum, ut ubinam sepultum esset, rescire tur, ne illo Israelitæ ad idola-triam abuterentur. Si etiam Christus quippiam scripsisset: quata idololatria erga ipsius scripturam admissa fuisset? Nam si cauda et-iam asini cuiusdam, quia creditur fuisse illius, quem equitauit Christus, cum venit Hierosolymam: adoratur à Mundo: quanto magis fuisset adorata scriptura ipsius manuscripta? Deinde, voluit hunc honorem deferre suis discipulis. Satis etiam fuit discipulis dictasse Magistrum, quæ vellet ab ipsis postea scribi.
units.tr: The doctrine of the Gospel which he preached he confirmed by very many manifest miracles. Why Christ wrote nothing with his own hand is not something to be investigated with curiosity. I will say only this, which is also written by all pious men about the body of Moses: that God did not want it to be known where he was buried, lest the Israelites should abuse it for idolatry. If Christ too had written something, how great an idolatry would have been committed toward his own writing? For if even the tail of a certain donkey, because it is believed to have belonged to the one on whom Christ rode when he came to Jerusalem, is worshipped by the world, how much more would his own handwritten writing have been adored? Then, he wished to confer this honor upon his disciples. It was enough for the disciples that the Master dictated to them what he wished to be written afterwards by them.

units.la: Quomodo igitur Christus Jesus Euange-lium ipse prædicauerit, idque in Judæa tantum, habemus.
units.tr: Thus we have how Christ Jesus himself preached the Gospel, and that only in Judea.

units.la: Jam vero, ut doctrina hæc cœlestis toti orbi innotesceret: discipulos sibi collegit, quos etiam testes suæ doctrinæ apud omnes mortales esse voluit: atq; hos idcirco appel-lauit Apostolos, quia per totum terrarum orbem erat illos ablegaturus. Actor. 1. Vos eritis mihi testes in omni Judæa & Samaria, & usq; ad ultimum terræ. Homines fuerunt simplices, candidi, sine dolo, iusti, veraces, probi, per omnia veri, eoque fide digni. Hos per triennium habuit testes suæ doctrinæ, suæ vitæ, suorum divinorum operum. Post suam à mortuis resurrectionem, iniunxit illis, ut irent per universum orbem, & Euangelium omni creaturæ prædicarent, & sibi testes essent vsque ad vltimum terræ,
units.tr: Now, so that this heavenly doctrine might become known to the whole world, he gathered disciples to himself, whom he also wished to be witnesses of his doctrine before all mortals; and he therefore called them Apostles, because he was going to send them away through the whole circuit of the earth. Acts 1. You shall be my witnesses in all Judea and Samaria, and even to the uttermost part of the earth. They were men simple, sincere, without guile, just, truthful, upright, in every way true, and therefore worthy of trust. For three years he had them as witnesses of his doctrine, of his life, and of his divine works. After his resurrection from the dead, he charged them to go through the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature, and to be his witnesses even to the uttermost part of the earth.

units.la: Post ascensionem vero, misit super eos Spiritum sanctum iuxta suam promissionem, ut omnes intelligerent, è coelo hos confirmari legatos Christi. Ac per hunc spiritum, eos omni linguarum genere, omnique virtute ad illud officium feliciter perficiendum instruxit. Ita instructi, ab Hierosolymis tandem exeunt, & per vniuersum orbem, Euangelium prædicant: Deo illud signis & miraculis confirmante, ut est apud Marcum, vltimo, & ad Hebr.2. Posteaquam autem aliquot annos voce tantum prædicassent verbum Dei: illud etiam tandem in literas, propter posteros retulerunt, inspirati semper à Spiritu sancto. Post Apostolos nil scriptum, quod ἀποτύπωτον[?] vocari possit. Sunt hæc omnia ita perspicua nobis Christianis, ut nulla egeant probatione. Fuit tamen verbum hoc Dei, prædicatione etiam post Apostolos in Ecclesia conseruatum, & adhuc seruatur. Etsi enim per multa secula, propter somnolentiam Episcoporum, loco verbi Dei, multæ ἑτεροδιδασκαλίαι obtrusæ & intrusæ fuerunt in Ecclesias Christi: tamen ad extremum, Dei misericordia factum est, ut multi afflati spiritu Dei, & donati vera scripturarum intelligentia, luce huius sacræ scripturæ, multos & maximos dispulerint ex Ecclesia errores, & falsos cultus: & purum Dei verbum in Ecclesia restituerint.
units.tr: After the ascension, he sent the Holy Spirit upon them according to his promise, so that everyone would understand that these legates of Christ were confirmed from heaven. And through this Spirit he equipped them with every kind of tongue and every power to carry out that office successfully. Thus equipped, they at last went out from Jerusalem and preached the Gospel throughout the whole world, God confirming it with signs and miracles, as is found in Mark at the end, and in Heb. 2. After they had preached the word of God by voice alone for some years, they also at last committed it to writing for the sake of posterity, always inspired by the Holy Spirit. After the Apostles nothing was written that could be called [apotypoton?]. All these things are so clear to us Christians that they need no proof. Yet this word of God was preserved in the Church after the Apostles also by preaching, and it is still preserved. For although over many centuries, because of the drowsiness of the bishops, many [heterodidaskaliai] were thrust and forced into the churches of Christ in place of the word of God, nevertheless in the end, by the mercy of God, it came about that many men, inspired by the Spirit of God and endowed with a true understanding of the Scriptures, by the light of this holy Scripture drove out many and great errors and false worship from the Church, and restored the pure word of God in the Church.

units.la: Nunc tenemus, quam originem habuerit, & quem progressum fecerit ad nos usq; verbum Dei.
units.tr: We now hold what origin the word of God had, and what progress it has made down to us.

units.la: QUÆSTIO VI.
units.tr: QUESTION VI.

units.la: De causis, cur primum voce tantum: deinde etiam scripto, verbum suum Deus voluerit in Ecclesia propagari, & conseruari.
units.tr: Concerning the causes why God willed his word to be propagated and preserved in the Church first by voice alone, and then also in writing.

units.la: Nunc breuiter dicendum est, primùm quam ob causam Deus voluerit tam longo tempore, nempe à condito orbe usque ad Moisen, Ecclesiam esse sine verbo Dei scripto, & voce tantum illud propagari & conseruari. Deinde cur illud, tam legem quàm Euangelium, tandem in literas atque chartas referri: & hac ratione ad nos usque, imò etiam in finem usque seculi, in Ecclesia custodiri & asseruari[?] constituerit.
units.tr: Now we must briefly say, first, for what reason God willed that the Church should be without the written word of God for so long a time, namely from the creation of the world until Moses, and that it should be propagated and preserved by voice alone. Then, why he determined that this word, both the law and the Gospel, should at last be committed to letters and pages, and in this way be preserved and secured in the Church down to us, and indeed even to the end of the age.

units.la: Quod ad primum attinet, hac una respon-deo[?] propositione.
units.tr: As regards the first, I answer with this one proposition.

units.la: Quod Deus voluerit de principio, Ecclesiam esse sine verbo scripto: id propter bonum & utilitatem Ecclesiæ voluit.
units.tr: That God willed, from the beginning, that the Church should be without the written word: he willed this for the good and advantage of the Church.

units.la: Explicatio & Confirmatio.
units.tr: Explanation and Confirmation.

units.la: Primùm, Ecclesiæ illi, quæ fuit sine scri-ptura, utilius fuit & melius ea secum ratione fuisse actum: nempe frequenti apparitione Filii Dei, non raris Dei per Angelos collo-
units.tr: First, it was more useful and better for that Church, which was without Scripture, that it was dealt with in this way: by the frequent appearance of the Son of God, the not infrequent conversations of God through angels,

units.la: I. Ecclesiæ illi, quæ fuit sine scriptura. [?] quiis,&Spiritus fanéti afflatibus;quàm fi fo-lum Dei verbum, in literas relatum accepif-set. Annon utilius atque melius & gratius est, Deum præsentem & coràm loquentem audire, quàm eius tantùm literas legere? Quis non malit amicum coràm audire,quàm eius legere literas? Idcirco Apostolus comparans hanc Dei cognitionem, quam hic habemus ex solo verbo, cum illa, qua dona-bimur ex ipsius conspectu, illam vocat ex parte,hoc est,imperfectam,& in Ænigmate, hoc est,obscuram. Hanc verò alteram, perfectam,& à facie ad faciem.Ita certè Patribus longè melius fuit& gratius frui illis frequentibus Filij Dei visionibus, colloquiis, spiritusq; sanéti afflatibus,& audiro verbo:quàm si illis priuati, solum habuissent scriptū ver-bum. Idem de Apostolis dico: longè certè gratius fuit & iucundius esse cum Christo,& eius frui præsentia atque sermonibus, fine ipsius scriptura: quàm si illius præsentia de-stituti, eius habuissent scripturam aliquam. Quid est enim melius,esse testem oculatum, an tantùm auritum?
units.tr: I. For that Church which was without Scripture, [?] and the inspirations of the Holy Spirit, than if it had received only the word of God, recorded in letters. Is it not more useful, better and more pleasing to hear God present and speaking face to face than merely to read his letters? Who would not rather hear a friend in person than read his letters? Therefore the Apostle, comparing this knowledge of God which we have from the word alone with that which we shall be given from his sight, calls the former partial, that is, imperfect, and in a riddle, that is, obscure. But the other he calls perfect, and face to face. So certainly it was far better and more pleasing for the Fathers to enjoy those frequent visions, conversations and inspirations of the Spirit of the Son of God, and to hear the voice, than if, deprived of these, they had had only the written word. I say the same of the Apostles: certainly it was far more pleasing and delightful to be with Christ and to enjoy his presence and discourses, without his writing, than if, bereft of his presence, they had had some writing of his. For what is better: to be an eyewitness, or only an earwitness?

units.la: Quæstio:Sed quid de illis piis,quibus non folebat apparere Filius Dei, neq; etiam Angeli? ut ante Mosen?
units.tr: Question: But what of those pious people, to whom the Son of God did not customarily appear, nor even the angels? As before Moses?

units.la: Resp. Etiam illi sciebant, Deum & Angelos apparere & loqui cum suis Maioribus è populo suo: propterea quòd & hoc refere-batur ad se, à suis Maioribus dicentibus, Vi-di Dominum: Dominus locutus est ad me, & huiusce rei multa videbant& certissima signa, nempe miracula : idcirco etiam magna & certissima fide verbum ab illis excipiebant. Hoc autem fuit illis utilius, quàm si solum in scripto habuissent verbum. Ergo ea ratio, quātum[?] urebatur Deus, sine scripto in revelando suo verbo, cessit illis Patribus in maiorem utilitatem, quàm si tantum scriptum habuissent verbum.
units.tr: Answer: They too knew that God and the angels appeared and spoke with their forefathers from among their people, because this too was reported to them by their forefathers saying, I have seen the Lord: the Lord has spoken to me, and they saw many very certain signs of this, namely miracles; therefore they also received the word from them with great and most certain faith. Moreover this was more useful to them than if they had had the word only in writing. Therefore that method, by which God used, without writing, in revealing his word, turned out to the Fathers for greater advantage than if they had had the word only in writing.

units.la: Idem dico de illis,qui non viderunt Christum, sed Apostolos duntaxat praedicantes audierunt sine scripto Euangelio. Apostoli enim testabantur illis, se cum Christo fuisse, & post resurrectionem cum illo manducas-se, & caetera. Et quae docebant, se suis oculis vidisse, suis auribus audivisse, suis manibus contrectasse: ideoque esse certissima. Deinde suum hoc testimonium miraculis confirmabant: hinc fiebat, ut auditores, operâ Spiritus sancti, certissima fide verbum Apostolorum amplecterentur, non ut verbum hominum, sed ut verbum Dei. Hoc igitur fuit utilius, quàm si non audivissent Apostolos, & scriptum tantum habuissent Euangelium. Ecquis nostrum est, qui non maluisset ipsos audire Apostolos, sine ipsorum scriptis, quàm nunc tantum illorum videre scripta? Fuit igitur illa ratio propagandi Euangelij sine scripto, Ecclesiae illi primitiuae, utilissima & iucundissima.
units.tr: I say the same of those who did not see Christ, but heard the Apostles alone preaching, without the written Gospel. For the Apostles testified to them that they had been with Christ, and had eaten with him after the resurrection, and so on. And what they taught, they said they had seen with their own eyes, heard with their own ears, handled with their own hands, and therefore that it was most certain. Then they confirmed this their testimony by miracles; hence it came about that the hearers, by the work of the Holy Spirit, embraced the word of the Apostles with the most certain faith, not as the word of men, but as the word of God. This therefore was more useful than if they had not heard the Apostles and had had only the written Gospel. Which of us would not have preferred to hear the Apostles themselves, without their writings, rather than now to see only their writings? That method of propagating the Gospel without writing was therefore most useful and most pleasing to the early Church.

units.la: Secundo : Ecclesiae etiam insequenti, quae scripturas erat acceptura, profuit utilis, quidem vtilior, quàm si illi priores, imme-diatè scriptum accepissent verbum, sine illis diuinis apparitionibus, collocutionibus, afflatibus. Illa enim prior ratio propagandi verbi ἀγράφῳ[?], sed coniuncta cum illis frequentibus apparitionibus, colloquiis & afflatibus diuinis: & maiorem fidem conciliauit futurae scripturae, quàm haec per se sola habuisset. Liquet hoc ex verbis Domini ad Mosen Exod. 19. Nunc veniam ad te in caligine nubis, vt audiat me populus loquentem ad te, & credat tibi in perpetuum. En causam, cur Dominus voluerit prius sine scripto loqui cum Mose, & Mosen cum populo, quàm legem simplici scripto obsignatam, populo exhibere: vt scilicet plus autoritatis & fidei hac ratione conciliaretur & Moysi & eius scriptis. De hac re etiam posteri gloriabantur, cùm dicebant, Iohan. 9. Scimus, quia Mosi locutus est Deus, quasi dicerent, ideo certissima est Mosis doctrina. Hac eadem ratione vsus est & Apostolus, vt fidem faceret sibi, & suo Euangelio, cùm dixit. 1. Corinth. 9. Annon & ego Dominum Iesum vidi? Item, cùm Gal. 1. ait, suum Apostolatum & Euangelium se accepisse non ab hominibus, neq; per homines, sed a Iesu Christo. Totum igitur illud tempus, quod scripturam praecessit, fuit posteris ceu quaedam μεταγραφικὴ[?], ad scripturam maiori cum reuerentia, certioriq; fide excipiendam, audiendam legendam. Et fuit scripturae ipsi ceu quoddam praeiactum diuinae cognitiohis fundamentum,cui postmodum ipsa infe-quens inniteretur. Oportuit enim, ut Deus prius declararet suis illis apparitionibus, & familiaribus colloquiis, se curā habere humani generis, se nos amare, se velle, nos ad cognitionem veritatis fuæq; voluntatis venire, quàm suam scripto tradere legem: quia illud faciebat ad nostram utilitatem. Quare utilissimum fuit Ecclesiæ,& præcedenti Mo-sen, & subsequenti, ut Deus in propagando suo verbo usus sit prius illà prima ratione, per vocem & traditionem, quàm ista posteriori, per scripturam. Atque idem plane dico de Ecclesia Apostolica.
units.tr: Second: It was also useful to the following Church, which was to receive the Scriptures, indeed more useful than if those earlier people had immediately received the written word without those divine appearances, conversations and inspirations. For that earlier method of propagating the word unwritten, but joined with those frequent divine appearances, conversations and inspirations, both won greater faith for the future Scripture than this would have had by itself alone. This is clear from the words of the Lord to Moses, Exod. 19. Now I will come to you in the darkness of a cloud, so that the people may hear me speaking to you, and may believe you forever. Here is the reason why the Lord willed first to speak without writing with Moses, and Moses with the people, before presenting the law sealed in plain writing to the people: namely so that by this method more authority and faith might be won both for Moses and for his writings. Later generations also boasted of this matter when they said, John 9. We know that God has spoken to Moses, as if to say: therefore the teaching of Moses is most certain. The Apostle used this same method, so that he might win faith for himself and for his Gospel, when he said, 1 Cor. 9. Have I not also seen the Lord Jesus? Likewise when he says in Gal. 1 that he received his apostleship and Gospel not from men, nor through men, but from Jesus Christ. The whole time, therefore, which preceded Scripture was for posterity like a certain transcription, to receive, hear and read the Scripture with greater reverence and more certain faith. And it was, as it were, a certain foundation of divine knowledge laid before the Scripture itself, on which the following Scripture would afterwards rest. For it was fitting that God should first declare, by those appearances and familiar conversations, that he takes care of the human race, that he loves us, and that he wishes us to come to the knowledge of the truth and of his will, rather than to deliver his law to us in writing, because that served our advantage. Wherefore it was most useful for the Church, both before Moses and after him, that God in propagating his word used the first method, by voice and tradition, before the later method, by Scripture. And I say exactly the same of the Apostolic Church.

units.la: Voluit enim Christus suos Apostolos ce-lebres, venerandos, suspiciendos, & maxima autoritate insignes reddere, idque variis donis, certitudine eorum quæ erant scripturæ publica & visibili super ipsos in vrbe celeberrima Hierusalem, Spiritus sancti missione: constanti per ipsos in toto terrarum orbe Euangelij prædicatione: cognitione linguarum: videndi miracula, omnemque genus morbos solo verbo curandi, quin &mortuos ad vitam revocandi: plusquam heroica in omnibus aduersis animi fortitudine atque constantia: voluit, inquam, Deus his rationibus celebres suos reddere Apostolos, ante-quam suum Euangelium per ipsorum manus, in literas referret. Quam ob causam? Propter maiorem Ecclesiæ etiam insequentis vtilitatem, hoc est, ut porrò plus fidei scriptis præberetur Apostolicis, propter confir-mata iam tot signis atq; miraculis, tum ipso-rum Apostolorum autoritatem, tum doctri-næ ab ipsis prædicatæ primùm, deinde etiam in literas redactæ, veritatem: atq; ita & Ele-ctorum salus magis ac magis promoueretur: &reprobo rum infidelitas inexcusabilis red-deretur, & autoritas ipsius scripturæ Apo-ftolicæ, confirmaretur:& ex consequenti, fa-luti posterorum, qui non Apostolos ipsos prædicantes audituri, sed ipsorum scripta tantùm lecturi erant, consuleretur.
units.tr: For Christ willed to make his Apostles famous, venerable, worthy of respect, and distinguished by the greatest authority, and to do so by various gifts: by the sending of the Holy Spirit, which made certain for them the public and visible sign of their office in the most famous city of Jerusalem; by the constant preaching of the Gospel through them throughout the whole world; by the knowledge of languages; by the power to see miracles and to heal every kind of disease by the word alone, and even to raise the dead to life; and by a courage and steadfastness in all adversity more than heroic. God willed, I say, to make his Apostles famous by these means before he committed his Gospel to writing through their hands. Why so? For the greater usefulness of the Church that was to follow, that is, so that more faith might be given to the Apostolic writings, since both the authority of the Apostles themselves and the truth of the doctrine they first preached, and afterwards committed to writing, had already been confirmed by so many signs and miracles; and so that the salvation of the elect might be promoted more and more, the unbelief of the reprobate might be made inexcusable, the authority of the Apostolic Scripture itself might be confirmed, and, as a consequence, the salvation of posterity might be provided for, since those who were not going to hear the Apostles preaching in person, but were only going to read their writings, would be helped.

units.la: Quod verò ad fecundum attinet huiusce quæstionis membrum: hac etiam vnica re-spondemus propositione.
units.tr: As for the second part of this question, we answer it also with this single proposition.

units.la: PROPOSITIO II.
units.tr: PROPOSITION II.

units.la: Quòd Deus, tam ante Christum per Mo-sen & Prophetas, quàm post Christum per Apostolos, non contentus viva voce, scripto etiam voluerit verbum suum in Ecclesia pro-moueri & custodiri: hoc fecit propter utilita-tem & salutem Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: That God, both before Christ through Moses and the Prophets, and after Christ through the Apostles, not content with the living voice, also willed to have his word propagated and preserved in the Church in writing: he did this for the usefulness and salvation of the Church.

units.la: Explicatio & Confirmatio.
units.tr: Explanation and Confirmation.

units.la: Hæc Ecclesiæ vtilitas, quam ex verbo Dei scripto consecuta est, & consequitur: ex non scripto autem non ita fuisset adepta, qua-druplex est.
units.tr: This usefulness of the Church, which it has obtained and still obtains from the written Word of God, and which it would not have obtained in the same way from the unwritten word, is fourfold.

units.la: Prima fuit & est: quòd iam habet certissi-mum canonem, ad quem omnes de religio-ne doctrinæ, & libri examinari possunt, & ita legitimi à nothis, & diuini ab humanis, facile discerni. Estne haec parua & contemnenda vtilitas? Sic ad legem Mosis iam scriptam & certam, miraculisque Dei confirmatam, tanquam ad lapidem lydium examinarunt priores Israelitae, omnia Prophetarum dicta & scripta. Sic posteriores, ad Mosaica & Prophetica examinarunt omnes aliorum doctrinas & libros: & quænam sincerae ac diuinae, quae minus, certissimè agnouerunt. Sic Christus suam ad hunc canonem examinatam, demonstrauit Iudaeis, esse vere caelestem ac diuinam doctrinam. Sic Apostolus gloriatur, se doctrinam de iustificatione tradere, quae testimonio legis & Prophetarum sit comprobata. Quare? quia ad scripta Mosis & Prophetarum examinata, deprehensa fuit, esse illis consentanea: Sic Berhoënses Act.17. doctrinam Pauli ad hunc scriptum Canonem, tanquam ad Heraclium lapidem probarunt: inde facti certi de veritate doctrinae Apostolicae, eam amplexi, & salui facti sunt. Itane utilitas haec parui est facienda? Qui potuissent tam facile & cito discernere doctrinam Spiritus sancti ab humana, nisi hunc scripti verbi canonem habuissent? Quid de nobis dicam? Quiunquam potuissemus in tantis Papatus tenebris, in tanta doctrinarum varietate, quænam vera esset, quæve falsa, diiudicare, nisi hanc habuissemus integram puramque scripturam, certum doctrinarum omnium indicem? Habent autem hunc Canonem nonem omnes per totum terrarum orbem diffusæ Ecclesiæ. Hinc fit, ut inter omnes, qui hunc sequuntur Canonem, certa fit consensio in doctrina salutis: atque hæc est communio sanctorum. Quanta hæc est utilitas? Ergo, ut omnes omnium temporum Ecclesiæ, certiores fieri possent, an sanam de Deo rebusq; diuinis sequerentur doctrinam verumque Dei cultum, hæc ne: voluit Deus, ut sua voluntas, totaque cœlestis de religione doctrina, in libros referretur: & ij libri in omnem æternitatem seruarentur. Huc spectat illud, 1. Iohan. 4. Probate spiritus, utrum ex Deo sint, Ad quod examen? scripturarum.
units.tr: The first was and is this: that it now has a most certain canon, by which all teachings and books concerning religion can be examined, and so the legitimate may easily be distinguished from the spurious, and the divine from the human. Is this a small and contemptible usefulness? Thus the earlier Israelites, using the law of Moses, already written, certain, and confirmed by the miracles of God, as a touchstone, examined all the sayings and writings of the Prophets. Likewise the later ones examined by the Mosaic and Prophetic writings the teachings and books of others, and knew most certainly which were sincere and divine and which less so. Thus Christ, demonstrating to the Jews that his doctrine, examined by this canon, was truly heavenly and divine. Thus the Apostle boasts that he teaches the doctrine of justification, which is confirmed by the testimony of the Law and the Prophets. Why? Because, when examined by the writings of Moses and the Prophets, it was found to agree with them. Thus the Bereans (Acts 17) tested the doctrine of Paul by this written canon, as by the Heraclean stone; having thus become certain of the truth of the Apostolic doctrine, they embraced it and were saved. Should this usefulness be counted as small? How could they have so easily and quickly distinguished the doctrine of the Holy Spirit from the human, had they not possessed this canon of the written Word? What shall I say of ourselves? Could we, in such darkness of the Papacy, in such variety of doctrines, have judged which was true and which false, unless we had this whole and pure Scripture, a certain index of all doctrines? All the Church spread throughout the whole world now has this canon. Hence it comes about that among all who follow this canon there is a certain agreement in the doctrine of salvation: and this is the communion of the saints. How great is this usefulness? Therefore, so that all the Churches of all times might be more certain whether they followed sound doctrine concerning God and divine things and the true worship of God, God willed that his will and the whole heavenly doctrine of religion be set down in books, and that those books be preserved for all eternity. To this refers the text of 1 John 4: Test the spirits, whether they are of God. By what test? By the Scriptures.

units.la: Atque hæc est causa, cur Papa & Anabaptistæ nollent hanc extare scripturam: vel saltem nollent à quopiam legi. Quid ita? Ne suæ impostura possint ad hanc coticulam examinati & agnosci: Similes illis, qui falsas & adulterinas circumferunt monetas: ij nolent ullum extare βάσανον [?] seu indicem, ad quem probentur. Utilitas igitur hæc prima, maxima est.
units.tr: And this is the reason why the Pope and the Anabaptists would not want this Scripture to exist, or at least would not want it to be read by anyone. Why so? So that their deceptions may not be examined and recognised by this touchstone.
