By this particle, therefore, I show that nothing can be delivered concerning religion which is not contained in the Scriptures; and consequently that it is not lawful for anyone to establish in the Church either articles of faith or precepts binding the conscience concerning the sacrament and other actions. Now let us come to the confirmation.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmation.

units.la: Huc pertinent, quæcunque supra attuli- mus è Scripturis, vt ostenderemus, Scriptu- ram ideò inspiratam, & per sanctos homines in libros relatam, vt nos nihil lateret eorum, quæ ad salutem pertinent, & vt ellet nobis instrumentum ad salutem æternam. Hinc enim sic argumentari licet.
units.tr: To this belongs everything I have already cited from the Scriptures, to show that Scripture was therefore inspired and committed to books by holy men, so that nothing of what pertains to salvation would be hidden from us, and so that it would be for us an instrument to eternal salvation. For from this we may argue thus.

units.la: Scriptura in hunc finem tradita est, vt nihil nos lateret eorum, quæ ad veram pietatem pertinent, & ad vitam æternam consequendam necessaria sunt: atq; ita nobis esset instrumentum ad salutem æternam.Hocan-tè demonstratum est. Ergo Scriptura sancta continet omnia, quæ ad salutem necessaria sunt, idque perspicue: alioqui latérent nos, si non etiam perspicuè essent tradita. Nunc specialia afferam argumenta & testimonia.
units.tr: Scripture has been handed down for this end: that nothing of what pertains to true piety and is necessary for attaining eternal life would be hidden from us, and that it would thus be for us an instrument to eternal salvation. This has been demonstrated above. Therefore Holy Scripture contains everything that is necessary for salvation, and it does so plainly; otherwise these things would be hidden from us, if they were not also handed down plainly. Now I shall bring forward special arguments and testimonies.

units.la: Doctrina illa de religione, deque æterna salute,cui nihil Deus vultaddi,aut etiam diminui, perfecta sit necesse est: ac proinde contineat omnia, quæ ad salutem necessaria sunt, oportet. Quis hanc propositionem queat inficiari:Est enim deducta[?] à definitione perfecti. Illud est perfectum in suo genere, cui nihil in eo genere aut addi, aut diminui potest. Accommoda hanc definitionem perfecti ad quascunque velis res: & videbis eam esse certissimam atque verissimam. Sic perfectum Scriptura vocat Deum: quia nihil illi addi vel essentiæ, vel virtutis, vel potentiæ potest.Sic perfectum dicimus hominem, quâ homo:cui nihil deest vel in anima,vel in corpore:&cui etiam nihil potest adimi,quin mox desinat esse perfectus.Propositio igitur certissima est: Illam de religione deque salute æterna doctrinam,cui nihil addi, nihilve diminui potest,esse perfectam,eoque continere omnia,quæ ad salutem necessaria sunt, idq; perspicuè. Atqui talis est doctrina Scripturæ sacræ,&ipsa Scriptura, vt mox ostendam. Ergo,&c.
units.tr: That doctrine of religion and of eternal salvation, to which God wishes nothing to be added or even diminished, must necessarily be perfect; and therefore it must contain everything that is necessary for salvation. Who could deny this proposition? For it is derived from the definition of the perfect. That is perfect in its kind to which nothing in that kind can be added or taken away. Apply this definition of the perfect to whatever things you like, and you will see that it is most certain and most true. Thus Scripture calls God perfect, because nothing can be added to Him in essence, virtue, or power. Thus we call a human being perfect, insofar as he is a human, to whom nothing is lacking either in soul or in body, and from whom nothing can even be taken away without at once ceasing to be perfect. The proposition is therefore most certain: that doctrine of religion and of eternal salvation, to which nothing can be added nor anything diminished, is perfect, and therefore contains everything that is necessary for salvation, and does so plainly. But such is the doctrine of Holy Scripture, and Scripture itself, as I shall show presently. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Esse verò Scripturam talem,cui nihil addi aut diminui possit ac debeat, liquet ex iis lo-cis. Deut.4.f.12. Non addetis ad verbum,quod vobis loquor,nec auferetis ex eo. Ac ne Papista aliquis excipiat, & dicat, Neque nos sentimus addendum esse illis, quæ ad internam eoque ad spiritualem pietatem & Dei cul-tum attinent: sed tantùm de externis ceremoniis est controuersia. Obsecro,considerate mihi, de quibusnam rebus loquatur Dominus in eo cap. Deuter. 4. De quibusnam? De ceremoniis,sacrisque ritibus,& de iudicialibus legibus. Sic enim ait Hebraicè: Et nunc Israel audi. Hachukim, & hamifch-jatim,id est,statuta & iudicia. Vox illa,Hachu-kim, proprie significat ceremonias,ritus,cultus. Voluit igitur docere Dominus,non solùm præceptis moralibus, & de interno cultu: sed neque præceptis de ceremoniis & ritibus quippiam esse addendum, aut imminuendum.
units.tr: That Scripture is such that nothing can or ought to be added to it or taken from it is clear from these places: Deut. 4.12: "You shall not add to the word which I speak to you, nor take away from it." And lest some Papist should except and say, "Neither do we think that anything is to be added to those things which pertain to inward, and therefore spiritual, piety and the worship of God, but the controversy concerns only external ceremonies": I beg you to consider with me what things the Lord is speaking of in that chapter of Deuteronomy 4. Of what things? Of ceremonies, sacred rites, and judicial laws. For thus He says in Hebrew: "And now, Israel, hear: the hachukim and the hamishpatim," that is, "statutes and judgments." The word hachukim properly signifies ceremonies, rites, and forms of worship. The Lord therefore intended to teach not only with respect to the moral precepts and inward worship, but also that nothing is to be added to or diminished from the precepts concerning ceremonies and rites.

units.la: Quod si dicas, Cur igitur Christus immutauit,cum instituit Baptismum? Responsio facilis est: voluit idem Dominus, vt tunc ceremoniae illae mutarentur, & aliae succederent, quia vsq; ad tempus correctionis erant impositae, Heb.9. Quòd si excipias: igitur illud praeceptum nihil ad nos pertinet. Respon.Imò:id quod liquet, si finem praecepti spectes. Quis finis? Vtiis[?] & quidem solis, quae Deus praecepit, simpliciter obediremus, nihil addendo, nihil imminuendo. Ergo cùm idem Deus per Filium praecepta etiam tradiderit de ceremoniis Noui Testamenti, & velit vt eis simpliciter obedias, manet vis praecepti illius: Nihil addas, nihil imminuas.
units.tr: But if you say: why then did Christ change them when He instituted Baptism? The answer is easy: the same Lord willed that those ceremonies should then be changed and others should succeed them, because they had been imposed only until the time of correction (Heb. 9). But if you except: then that precept does not pertain to us. The answer: On the contrary; this is clear if you look to the purpose of the precept. What is the purpose? That we should simply obey the things which God has commanded, adding nothing and diminishing nothing. Therefore, since the same God, through the Son, has also handed down precepts concerning the ceremonies of the New Testament, and wills that you obey them simply, the force of that precept remains: "Add nothing, diminish nothing."

units.la: Deinde Christus quoq; idem aperte mandat Matth.28. Baptizate eos in nomine Patris, Filij, & Spiritus sancti, docentes seruare quaecunque praecepi vobis. Quid hoc est, nisi ne addatis, neimminuatis? Item, quid illud est, quod ait Apostolus 1.Cor.11. Ego accepi a Domino, quod & tradidi vobis? nisi mihi, neq; cuiquam hominum licet de Coena aliter docere, quâ acceperimus à Domino? hoc est, non licet neque addere, neq; imminuere. Quid etiam illud est, quod ait 1.Tim.1. Praecipe & denuncia μὴ ἑτεροδιδασκαλεῖν[?], nisi non licet neq; addere, neq; imminuere? Quid etiam illud est, quòd Tertullianus lib. de praescriptionibus, pag.109 discernit Christianos ab Haereticis, quòd haeretici adulterent scripturas additione, detractione, transmutatione: Christiani vero nequaquam? Vis igitur illius praecepti in Deut. de non addendo vel minuendo aliquid in præceptis Dei, etiam de ceremoniis & ritibus sacris, manet perpetuò, & ad nos pertinet.
units.tr: Moreover, Christ Himself openly commands the same thing in Matthew 28: "Baptize them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you." What is this, if not: do not add, and do not diminish? Likewise, what is that which the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 11: "I received of the Lord that which also I delivered to you"? Is it not that it is not lawful for me, or for anyone, to teach about the Supper otherwise than as we have received from the Lord? That is, it is lawful neither to add nor to diminish. What also is that which he says in 1 Timothy 1: "Charge and declare that they teach no other doctrine" [μὴ ἑτεροδιδασκαλεῖν]? Is it not that it is not lawful either to add or to diminish? What also is that which Tertullian, in his book On Prescription, page 109, distinguishes Christians from heretics by: that heretics corrupt the Scriptures by addition, subtraction, and alteration, but Christians by no means do so? The force, therefore, of that precept in Deuteronomy, not to add or diminish anything in the precepts of God, including those concerning ceremonies and sacred rites, remains perpetually and pertains to us.

units.la: Idem præceptum repetitur à Salomone Prouer.30. Omnis sermo Dei purgatus est, scutum est his, qui eo nituntur : Ne addas sermonibus eius, ne te redarguat, & mendax inveniaris. Hic per Salomonem Spiritus sanctus præceptum illud ad totam Dei doctrinam extendit, nihil esse addendum doctrinæ & sermoni diuino: & rationem addit, quia scilicet purgatus est. Cùm igitur etiā doctrina Christi, sermo sit Dei, & is purgatissimus: consequitur necessariò, nihil ei esse addendum; proinde ita esse perfectum, ut omnia ad veram pietatem spectantia contineat. Addit Salomon, sermonem Domini esse scutum iis, qui eo nituntur. Valet igitur contra omnes hostes, Sathanam, Mundum, peccatum. Sic Eph.6 scutum fidei, quia scilicet nitimur verbo Dei. Stat igitur argumentum à nobis allatum, deductum à definitione perfecti, perfectæq; doctrinæ.
units.tr: The same precept is repeated by Solomon in Proverbs 30: "Every word of God is pure; He is a shield to those who trust in Him. Do not add to His words, lest He reprove you and you be found a liar." Here through Solomon the Holy Spirit extends that precept to the whole doctrine of God, that nothing is to be added to the divine doctrine and word, and He adds the reason, namely, because it is "pure." Since therefore the doctrine of Christ also is the word of God, and that most pure, it follows necessarily that nothing is to be added to it; and so it is perfect, so that it contains everything that pertains to true piety. Solomon adds that the word of the Lord is a shield to those who trust in it. It therefore avails against all enemies: Satan, the world, and sin. So in Ephesians 6, "the shield of faith," because, of course, we lean upon the word of God. The argument brought forward by us therefore stands, derived from the definition of the perfect and of perfect doctrine.

units.la: Sequitur argumentum ab effectis perfectæ doctrinæ.
units.tr: There follows an argument from the effects of perfect doctrine.

units.la: 3. Perfectissima est illa doctrina, quæ sa-pientem facit ad salutem & vitam æternam consequendam: quæ hominem ad opus bonum perfectè instruit: per quā regeneratur in Filium Dei: per quam liberatur à seruitute peccati & Sathanæ: quæ denique hominem saluat,& beatum efficit,& vnit Deo & Chri-sto. Hæc enim sunt illa effecta,quæ quæruntur,& quæ expectantur à doctrina de religio-ne:ita vt hæc effecta consecuti, nihil præterea desideremus,aut opus habeamus. Atqui talis est doctrina S.Scripturæ.
units.tr: 3. That doctrine is most perfect which makes a person wise unto salvation and the attaining of eternal life; which fully equips a person for every good work; through which he is regenerated into a son of God; through which he is freed from the bondage of sin and of Satan; which, in short, saves a person, makes him blessed, and unites him to God and to Christ. For these are the effects which are sought and expected from the doctrine of religion, so that, having obtained these effects, we desire nothing further and have no need of anything else. But such is the doctrine of Holy Scripture.

units.la: 1. Quòd faciat sapientem ad salutem & vitam æternam,liquet: 2,Tim 3. Et quòd S.li-teras nosti,quæ te possunt sapientem efficere ad sa-lutem.
units.tr: 1. That it makes a person wise unto salvation and eternal life is clear from 2 Timothy 3: "And that from a child you have known the holy letters, which are able to make you wise unto salvation."

units.la: 2. Quòd instruat ad omne opus bonum: liquet ex eodem loco: Omnis Scriptura diuinitus inspirata,&c. vt perfectus sit homo Dei, ad omne opus bonum perfectè instructus.
units.tr: 2. That it instructs unto every good work is clear from the same passage: "All Scripture is divinely inspired, etc., that the man of God may be perfect, thoroughly furnished unto every good work."

units.la: 3. Quòd per eum regeneremur liquet ex 1.Petr.1. Renati non ex semine mortali, sed ex immortali, per sermonem Dei viui, & manentis in æternum.
units.tr: 3. That through it we are regenerated is clear from 1 Peter 1: "Born again not of corruptible seed but of incorruptible, through the word of the living God, which abides forever."

units.la: 4. Quòd liberet à seruitute peccati. Iohan.8. Si manseritis in sermone meo, veritas liberabit vos.
units.tr: 4. That it frees from the bondage of sin: John 8: "If you abide in my word, the truth will make you free."

units.la: 5. Quòd saluet [?], liquet Rom.1. Euangelium Dei virtus est in salutem omni credenti, nempe huic Euangelio.
units.tr: 5. That it saves is clear from Romans 1: "The gospel of God is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes," namely, this gospel.

units.la: 6. Quòd beatum efficiat, liquet Psalm.1. Beatus qui in Lege Domini meditatur die ac nocte.
units.tr: 6. That it makes blessed is clear from Psalm 1: "Blessed is the man who meditates in the law of the Lord day and night."

units.la: 7. Quòd vniat nos cum Apostolis,& cum Patre ac Filio eius, liquet 1.Ioh.1. Hoc scribimus vobis, vt & vos communionem habeatis nobiscum: & communio nostra sit cum Patre, & cum Filio eius Iesu Christo.
units.tr: 7. That it unites us with the Apostles, and with the Father and His Son, is clear from 1 John 1: "These things we write to you, that you also may have fellowship with us; and our fellowship is with the Father, and with His Son Jesus Christ."

units.la: 4. A causa efficiente simul & finali. Deus hanc scripturam Patribus inspirauit, Moysi, Prophetis, Apostolis, & per eos in libros retulit ac scripsit, idque propter salutem nostram, hoc est, Electorum omnium, Rom.4. & 15. 2.Tim.3. 1.Tim.4. Et ut utilis esset ὡς διδασκαλίαν [?] omnis scilicet pietatis: ὡς ἐλεγχον, omnis scilicet erroris: ὡς ἐπανόρθωσιν, hoc est, ad correctionem omnis scilicet malae vitae & malorum morum: ὡς παιδείαν in omni iustitia: & in summa, ut homo esset perfectus & integer, ut nihil in eo deesset, nihilve esset luxatum: sed integra nova creatura. Ergo hanc scripturam dedit ita perfectam, ut nihil in ea possit desiderari, quod ad salutem & aeternam vitam pertineat: alioquin accusaretur Deus aut insciitiae, quod nesciuerit perfectam dare: aut invidiae, quod noluerit dare perfectam: aut impotentiae, quod non potuerit perfectam dare & relinquere: quae omnia blasphemia sunt in Dei sapientiam, bonitatem, omnipotentiam.
units.tr: 4. From the efficient and at the same time the final cause. God inspired this Scripture in the Patriarchs, Moses, the Prophets, and the Apostles, and through them committed it to books and wrote it, and that for our salvation, that is, of all the elect (Rom. 4 and 15; 2 Tim. 3; 1 Tim. 4). And that it might be useful: for teaching, that is, of all piety; for refutation, that is, of all error; for correction, that is, for the amendment of all bad life and evil morals; for instruction in all righteousness; and, in sum, "that the man might be perfect and complete, so that nothing in him would be lacking, nor anything in him be out of joint, but he would be a whole new creature." Therefore God gave this Scripture so perfect that nothing can be desired in it which pertains to salvation and eternal life; otherwise God would be accused either of ignorance, that He did not know how to give a perfect one; or of envy, that He did not will to give a perfect one; or of impotence, that He could not give and leave a perfect one. All of which are blasphemies against the wisdom, goodness, and omnipotence of God.

units.la: 5. A causis instrumentalibus, seu ab officio Apostolorum, qui fuerunt amanuenses Christi & Spiritus sancti.
units.tr: 5. On the instrumental causes, or the office of the Apostles, who were the amanuenses of Christ and of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Christus omnem docuit doctrinam, quae ad salutem nostram pertinebat. Iohan.15. Omnia quaecunque audivi a Patre meo, nota feci vobis. Apostolis praecepit, ut eandem salutis doctrinam, reliquis omnibus praedicarent & notam facerent in finem vsque Mundi, ut & illi participes fierent salutis, Matth.28. Praedicate Euangelium, docentes seruare omnia quæ mandaui vobis. Præceptum hoc est, de officio Apostolorum in patefaciendo Euangelio omnibus Gentibus, vsque in finem seculi. Nam hoc declarat promissio, Ecce ego vobis-cum sum vsq; ad consummationem seculi. Vobiscum (inquit) scilicet Apostolis. Vbi?In vestro Ministerio. Quovsque?vsque ad con-summationem seculi. Officium igitur illorum fuit, prædicare vsque ad consumma-tionem seculi. Atqui hoc non potuerunt viua voce, quia moriendum erat. Ergo horum officium fuit, scriptis committere totam Euangelij summam, & eam per scripta omnibus in finem vsque Mundi prædicare. Atqui Apostoli fuerunt obsequentes Christi, & amarunt omnes electos, etiam nos: & percupidi fuerunt nostræ salutis: sciuerunt etiam & potuerunt totam salutis doctrinam literis committere, & ad nos transmittere. Ergo dubitari non potest fine iniuria Apostolorum, quin totam salutis doctrinam literis commiserint, & ad nos transmiserint.
units.tr: Christ taught the whole doctrine that pertained to our salvation. John 15: All things that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you. He commanded the Apostles to preach and make known the same doctrine of salvation to all others until the end of the world, so that they too might become partakers of salvation. Matt. 28: Preach the gospel, teaching them to observe all things that I have commanded you. This command concerns the office of the Apostles in making the Gospel known to all nations until the end of the age. For this is declared by the promise, Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the world. "With you," he says, that is, with the Apostles. Where? In your ministry. How long? Until the end of the world. Their office, therefore, was to preach until the end of the world. But they could not do this by the living voice, because they were to die. Therefore their office was to commit the whole sum of the Gospel to writing, and to preach it by writing to all until the end of the world. Now the Apostles were obedient to Christ, and loved all the elect, including us, and they were most eager for our salvation. They also knew and were able to commit the whole doctrine of salvation to letters and to transmit it to us. Therefore, without doing injustice to the Apostles, it cannot be doubted that they committed the whole doctrine of salvation to writing and transmitted it to us.

units.la: Confirmatur hoc argumentum ab Apo-stolis, amanuensibus Christi & Spiritus san-cti eorumque officio, argumento ducente ad absurda.
units.tr: This argument is confirmed from the Apostles, the amanuenses of Christ and of the Holy Spirit, and from their office, by an argument leading to absurdities.

units.la: Si Apostoli non omnia nobis scripta reliquerunt, quæ ad salutem necessaria sunt: consequitur primùm, illos aut nesciuisse, aut noluisse, aut oblitos fuisse, aut non potuisse hoc efficere. Sunt autem hæc omnia absurdissiabsurdissima & blasphema in ipsum etiam Spiritum sanctum. Nam Spiritus S. in ipsis erat, loquebatur, scribebat, charitate implebat & sapientia. Sciuerunt igitur, quia pleni sapientia: voluerunt, quia pleni in charitate erga posteros omnes: Non sunt obliti, quia Spiritus S. non obliuiscitur eorum, quæ ad salutem nostram necessaria sunt: potuerunt, quia Spiritus sanctus vires suppeditabat. Ergo quemadmodum scripserunt ea quæ habemus: si quæ etiam præter hæc fuissent necessaria, vtique etiam scribere non neglexissent.
units.tr: If the Apostles did not leave us in writing everything that is necessary for salvation, it follows, first, that they either did not know it, or were unwilling, or forgot, or were unable to accomplish this. But all these things are most absurd and blasphemous even against the Holy Spirit himself. For the Holy Spirit was in them, speaking, writing, filling them with love and wisdom. They knew, therefore, because they were full of wisdom; they were willing, because they were full of love toward all posterity; they did not forget, because the Holy Spirit does not forget those things that are necessary for our salvation; they were able, because the Holy Spirit supplied them with strength. Therefore, just as they wrote those things that we have, so, if anything beyond these had been necessary, they would certainly not have neglected to write it as well.

units.la: Secundò, sequeretur, Iohannem mentitum, qui dixit Iohan. 20. Hæc autem scripta sunt, ut credatis, quòd Iesus est Christus, & ut credentes haberetis vitam æternam. Quibus verbis testatur, se nihil omisisse eorum, quæ ad salutem necessaria erant.
units.tr: Secondly, it would follow that John lied, who said in John 20: But these things are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, and that believing you may have eternal life. By these words he testifies that he omitted nothing of those things that were necessary for salvation.

units.la: 3. Consequeretur, Paulum insulsè & imprudenter se gessisse in suis scriptionibus. Nam in suis Epistolis, quas multas scripsit, de multis, etiam minimis rebus, ut de modo prophetandi, de velandis capitibus mulierum, de collectis, quo die sint faciendæ, & aliis infinitis id genus. Si igitur qui de iis rebus tam diligenter scripsit, aliquid eorum, quæ ad salutem sunt necessaria, omisisset: quanta fuisset Apostoli imprudentia, infulsi-tas, oscitantia? Sed illos summam doctrinæ ad salutem necessariæ scriptis complexos fuisse liquet. Luc. 1. in præfatione. I. Cor. 15. Notum vobis facio Euangelium, quod euangeli-zaui vobis, quod & accepistis, in quo & statis, per quod etiam seruamini, &c.
units.tr: 3. It would follow that Paul acted foolishly and imprudently in his writings. For in his Epistles, which he wrote in great number, he wrote about many things, even very small matters, such as the manner of prophesying, the veiling of women's heads, the collections, on what day they are to be made, and countless others of that kind. If, therefore, he who wrote so carefully about those things had omitted anything necessary for salvation, how great would have been the Apostle's imprudence, foolishness, and carelessness? But it is clear that they comprised the sum of doctrine necessary for salvation in writing. Luke 1, in the preface. 1 Cor. 15: I make known to you the gospel that I preached to you, which you also received, in which you also stand, by which also you are saved, etc.

units.la: LOCI ALIQUOT E SCRIPTURIS, quibus idem confirmatur: debere scilicet nos esse contentos scripturis: & extra has nihil de religione admittere.
units.tr: SOME PASSAGES FROM THE SCRIPTURES, by which the same is confirmed: namely, that we ought to be content with the Scriptures, and to admit nothing concerning religion outside them.

units.la: Deut.28. Dominus postquam suam explicasset legem, adiecit promissiones non tam de rebus temporalibus, quàm de coelestibus, sub illis tanquam sub typis conclusas. Et Apostolus Galat.3. summam repetit, dicendo: Qui fecerit hac homo, viuet in illis. Sic Ezech.20. Dedi eis statuta mea, & iudicia mea indicaui eis, in quibus homo, si ea fecerit, viuet. Mortem verò non minatur, nisi verbi sui transgressoribus.
units.tr: Deut. 28. After the Lord had explained his law, he added promises not so much concerning temporal things as concerning heavenly ones, enclosed under those things as under types. And the Apostle in Gal. 3 repeats the sum, saying: He who does these things shall live in them. Likewise Ezek. 20: I gave them my statutes, and I showed them my judgments, in which a man, if he does them, shall live. He threatens death only to the transgressors of his word.

units.la: Matth.19. Si vis ad vitam ingredi, serua mandata.
units.tr: Matt. 19: If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments.

units.la: Marc.16. Qui crediderit (Euangelio) saluus erit. Ergo non sunt necessaria, quae praeter scripturam obtruduntur.
units.tr: Mark 16: He who believes (the Gospel) will be saved. Therefore those things that are thrust upon us besides Scripture are not necessary.

units.la: Ierem.19. Iudæi permulti exemplo Abrahæ, qui filium voluit immolare, commori, filios suos immolabant & comburebant igne, proculdubio hac mente, ut Deo gratifica-rentur, quasi hoc ei placerer. Sed arguit ipse hoc factum, & minatur exitium, & praeter alia ait: Ego hac non praecepi, non sum locutus, nec ascenderunt in cor meum. Docet hic locus, non esse etiam omnia scripturarum exem[?]plaimitanda: sed tantùm legem & verbum Dei, & eorum exempla, quatenus sunt con-sentanea legi Dei, omnibus traditæ.
units.tr: Jer. 19. Many Jews, following the example of Abraham, who wished to sacrifice his son, sacrificed and burned their sons with fire, undoubtedly with the intention of pleasing God, as if this were pleasing to him. But he himself condemns this deed, and threatens destruction, and among other things says: I did not command this, I did not speak it, nor did it come into my heart. This passage teaches that not all the examples in the Scriptures are to be imitated, but only the law and the word of God, and their examples, insofar as they agree with the law of God, are given to all.

units.la: Luc.16. Habent Mosen & Prophetas: quasi dicat, Isti sufficiunt ad cognoscendum, quæ ad salutem necessaria sunt.
units.tr: Luke 16: They have Moses and the Prophets: as if he were saying, these are sufficient for knowing those things that are necessary for salvation.

units.la: 1. Cor.1. Apostolus propter Euangelium, quod Corinthiis prædicauerat, dicit, eos re-pletos esse omni cognitione (quæ scilicet ad sa-lutem necessaria est) adeò ut nulla alia reve-latio aut doctrina exspectanda illis sit, nisi revelatio Domini Iesu Christi, cùm scilicet apparebit in fine Mundi. Sic enim ait: Gra-tias ago Deo, quod ditati estis in omnibus in ipso (Christo) in omni sermone, & omni cognitione, adeò ut non destituamini ullo dono, exspectantes revelationem Domini nostri Iesu Christi. Ergo præter doctrinam Apostolicam, & Euangelium Christi, nil est admittendum, sed illa doctrina contenti, exspectare debemus Christi adventum.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 1. The Apostle, on account of the Gospel that he had preached to the Corinthians, says that they were filled with all knowledge (which, of course, is necessary for salvation), so that no other revelation or doctrine is to be expected by them, except the revelation of the Lord Jesus Christ, namely when he will appear at the end of the world. For he says: I give thanks to God that you have been enriched in everything in him (Christ), in all speech and all knowledge, so that you lack no gift, awaiting the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, besides Apostolic doctrine and the Gospel of Christ, nothing is to be admitted; but content with that doctrine, we ought to await the coming of Christ.

units.la: 2. Iohan.1. Qui permanet in doctrina Chri-sti, hic habet Patrem & Filium. Ergo doctrina Christi sufficit ad salutem. At quæ est doctrina Christi? Illa quæ fuit tradita ab initio per Apostolos ante mortem ipsius Iohannis. Sic enim ait 1. Iohan. 2. Vos quod audiuistis ab initio, in vobis permaneat. Si in vobis per-manserit quod audiuistis ab initio: & vos in Patre ac Filio manebitis. Quod supra dixit, Qui permanet in doctrina Christi: hic habet Patrem & Filium: Hic ait, Si permanserit quod audiuistis ab initio: vos in Patre & Filio manebitis.Doctrina igitur CHRISTI est, quae ab initio tradita fuit. Quaecunque ergo postea inuenta, ad doctrinam CHRISTI non pertinent. In illa autem qui permanet: habet Filium & Patrem. Ergo doctrina de principio ab Apostolis tradita, sufficit ad salutem,
units.tr: 2 John 1: Whoever abides in the doctrine of Christ has the Father and the Son. Therefore the doctrine of Christ is sufficient for salvation. But what is the doctrine of Christ? That which was delivered from the beginning through the Apostles, before the death of John himself. For he says in 1 John 2: What you heard from the beginning, let it abide in you. If what you heard from the beginning abides in you, you also will abide in the Father and the Son. What he said above, Whoever abides in the doctrine of Christ has the Father and the Son, he says here, If what you heard from the beginning abides, you will abide in the Father and the Son. The doctrine of Christ, therefore, is that which was delivered from the beginning. Whatever was discovered afterwards, therefore, does not pertain to the doctrine of Christ. Whoever abides in that has the Son and the Father. Therefore the doctrine delivered by the Apostles from the beginning is sufficient for salvation.

units.la: Quem(Christum )nos praedicamus,admonentes omnem hominem, & docentes omne hominem in omni sapientia, vt statuamus omne hominem perfectum in Christo Iesu. Ergo sola Apostolica doctrina continet omnem sapientiam: & valet ad reddendum hominem perfectum in Christo.
units.tr: Whom (Christ) we preach, admonishing every man and teaching every man in all wisdom, that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus. Therefore the Apostolic doctrine alone contains all wisdom, and is effective in making a man perfect in Christ.

units.la: Ibidem: Et vos,qui quondam eratis alienati & hostes,mente operibus malis intenta, reconciliauit in corpore illo carnis suae,&c.si quidem permanetis in fide fundati & firmi, nec dimouemini à spe Euangelij, quod audiuistis. Hinc peti-tur Propositio: Si quis in ea fide,quam Apo-stoli praedicarunt,permanet,nec dimouetur à spe illius Euangelij, quod praedicatum fuit ab Apostolis, & auditum tunc temporis in vniuerso mundo: is certè particeps est beneficij Christi,id est, reconciliationis cum Patre, & est in conspectu Dei sanctus, irreprehensibilis. Haec est Apostoli. Atqui doctrina,quae nunc traditur in Papatu,de Missa, de inuocatione mortuorum, &c. non fuit tunc praedicata ab Apostolis, nec in vniuerso Mundo tradita. Ergo,&c. Satis confirmatam esse doctrinam nostram testimoniis Scripturae iudico. Nunc igitur progrediar ad testimonia Patrum.
units.tr: In the same place: And you, who once were alienated and enemies in mind, engaged in evil works, he has reconciled in the body of his flesh, etc., if indeed you continue in the faith grounded and steadfast, and are not moved away from the hope of the Gospel that you heard. From this the proposition is drawn: If anyone continues in that faith which the Apostles preached, and is not moved from the hope of that Gospel which was preached by the Apostles and heard at that time throughout the whole world, he is certainly a partaker of the benefit of Christ, that is, of reconciliation with the Father, and is holy and blameless in the sight of God. This is the Apostle's teaching. But the doctrine that is now taught in the Papacy, concerning the Mass, the invocation of the dead, etc., was not preached at that time by the Apostles, nor delivered throughout the whole world. Therefore, etc. I judge that our doctrine has been sufficiently confirmed by the testimonies of Scripture. Now therefore I shall proceed to the testimonies of the Fathers.

units.la: Irenæus lib.3. cap.1. Non enim per alios dispositionem salutis nostræ cognoscimus, quàm per testimonios, per quos Euangelium peruenit ad nos, quod quidem tunc praeconiauerunt, post vero per Dei voluntatem in Scripturis nobis tradiderunt, fundamentum & columnam fidei nostræ futurum Scriptura. Nec enim fas est dicere, quoniam ante praedicauerunt, quam perfectam haberent agnitionem, sicut quidam audent dicere, gloriantes emendatores se esse Apostolorum. Tria hic docet: 1. Apostolos omnia ad salutem pertinentia nouisse. 2. eadem nobis voce primùm communicata esse. 3. quæ antea praeconiauerunt, eadem scripta nobis reliquisse.
units.tr: Irenaeus, book 3, chapter 1: "For we do not come to know the plan of our salvation through anyone else than those through whom the Gospel has come down to us. They first proclaimed it, and afterwards, by God's will, handed it down to us in the Scriptures, to be the foundation and pillar of our faith. For it is not right to say that they preached before they had perfect knowledge, as some dare to say, boasting that they are correctors of the Apostles." Here he teaches three things: 1. that the Apostles knew everything pertaining to salvation; 2. that the same things were first communicated to us by the living voice; 3. that what they had earlier preached, they afterwards left to us in writing.

units.la: Idem lib.2. cap.46. Cum vniuersa Scriptura & Prophetica & Euangelica in aperto & sine ambiguitate, & similiter ab omnibus audiri possint, &c. Quia de cogitatione eorum, qui contraria opinantur de Patre, nihil aperte nec ipsa dictione, nec sine controuersia in nulla omnino dictum sit Scriptura, & ipsi testantur dicentes, in abscondito hac eadem saluatorem docuisse non omnes, sed aliquos discipulorum, qui possunt capere, &c.
units.tr: The same, book 2, chapter 46: "Since the whole of Scripture, both prophetic and evangelical, can be heard openly and without ambiguity, and alike by all, etc. For Scripture has nowhere said anything openly, either in its wording or without controversy, about the thought of those who hold contrary opinions concerning the Father; and they themselves testify, saying that the Saviour taught these same things in secret, not to all, but to some of the disciples who are able to grasp them, etc."

units.la: Et cap.47. Credere debemus Deo, rectissimè scientes, quia Scripturae quidem perfectae sunt, quippe a Verbo Dei & Spiritu eius dictae: nos autem secundum quod minores sumus, & nouissimi a Verbo Dei & Spiritu eius, secundum hoc & scientia mysteriorum eius indigemus.
units.tr: And chapter 47: "We ought to believe God, knowing most rightly that the Scriptures are indeed perfect, since they were spoken by the Word of God and his Spirit; but we, insofar as we are lesser and the last, are by the Word of God and his Spirit, and in accordance with this, we need the knowledge of his mysteries."

units.la: Id.lib.s. Oportet confugere ad Ecclesiam, & eius sinu educari, & Dominicis scripturis enu-triri. Plantatus est Ecclesia paradisus in hoc mundo. De omni ligno paradisi escas manduca-bis, inquit spiritus Dei, hoc est, de omni Scriptura Dominica manducate.
units.tr: The same, book 5: "It is necessary to take refuge in the Church, to be brought up in her bosom, and to be nourished by the Lord's Scriptures. The Church is a paradise planted in this world. 'Of every tree of the paradise you shall eat food,' says the Spirit of God; that is, you shall eat of every Scripture of the Lord."

units.la: Tertullianus de præscript. hæret. cùm alia multa, tum hæc scribit: Nobis verò nihil ex nostro arbitrio indulgere licet, sed nec eligere, quod aliquis de arbitrio suo induxerit. Apostolos Domini habemus autores, qui nec ipsi quicquam ex suo arbitrio, quod inducerent, elegerunt, sed acceptam à Christo disciplinam fideliter nationibus assignauerunt. Itaq; etiamsi Angelus è cœlis aliter euangelizaret, anathema diceretur à nobis. Idem paulò pòst: omnia Domini dicta omnibus posita esse. Id.lib.cont.Hermog. Adoro Scripturæ plenitudinem, quæ mihi factorem manifestat & facta. In Euangelio verò amplum & ministrum atq; arbitrum rectoris inuenio sermonem. An autem de aliqua subiacente materia facta sint omnia, nusquam adhuc legi. Scriptum esse doceat Hermogenis officina, aut timeat va illud, adiicientibus aut detrahentibus destinatum. Idem de resurrect.carnis. Hæreticos vocat Lu-cifugas scripturarum, & ait, aufer hæreticis, quæ cum Ethnicis sapiunt: vt de solis scripturis quæstiones suas sistant, & stare non possunt. Idem ad-uersus hæret. nobis curiositate non opus est post Christū Iesum, nec inquisitione post Euangelium, &c. Idem de carne Christi ait: nihil recipiendū esse, quod non habeat testimonium scripturæ.
units.tr: Tertullian, in the Prescription against Heretics, writes, among many other things, these: "For us it is not permitted to indulge anything at our own pleasure, nor even to choose what someone has introduced of his own will. We have the Apostles of the Lord as authors, who themselves chose nothing of their own will to introduce, but faithfully handed on to the nations the teaching received from Christ. Therefore, even if an angel from heaven should preach otherwise, let him be anathema to us." Shortly afterwards he says: "All the sayings of the Lord have been set before all." In his book against Hermogenes: "I adore the fullness of Scripture, which reveals to me both the Maker and the things made. But in the Gospel I find a full and ministering word and the arbiter of the Master. Yet I have never read anywhere whether all things were made out of some pre-existing matter. Let the workshop of Hermogenes teach that it is written; or let him fear that woe which is destined for those who add or take away." In his book on the resurrection of the flesh he calls heretics "fleers from the Scriptures," and says: "Take away from heretics whatever savours of the Gentiles, so that they may rest their questions on the Scriptures alone, and they cannot stand." In his book against heretics: "We have no need of curiosity after Christ Jesus, nor of inquiry after the Gospel, etc." Concerning the flesh of Christ he says that nothing is to be accepted which does not have the testimony of Scripture.

units.la: Iustinus Martyr confugiebat ad scripturas, vt in omnibus tutus effet. In Triphone. Item in expos. Symboli, pag. 195. in rebus religionis non esse agendum auctoritate humana.
units.tr: Justin Martyr took refuge in the Scriptures, so as to be safe in all things. In Dialogue with Trypho. Likewise in his exposition of the Creed, p. 195: in matters of religion, one must not act on human authority.

units.la: Cyprian. lib.1. epist.8. sacrilegum esse quicquid excogitatum ab hominibus. Idem ad Pop. semper recurrendum esse ad scripturas. Idem epist 63. ad Caecil. Christum solum esse audiendum, & nullum praeterea, &c. Imprimis epist. 74. Unde est ista traditio? vtrumne de dominica & Euangelica auctoritate descendens, an de Apostolorum mandatis atq; Epistolis veniens? Ea enim facienda esse, quae scripta sunt, Deus testatur, & proponit, ad Iesum Naue dicens: non recedet liber legis huius ex ore tuo, &c. vt observes facere omnia, quae scripta sunt in eo. Item Dominus Apostolos suos mittens, mandat baptizari Gentes & doceri, vt observent omnia, quaecunque ille praecepit. Tum subiungit: si ergo aut in Euangelio praecipitur, aut in Apostolorum Epistolis aut Actibus continetur, vt a quacunq; haeresi venientes non baptizentur, sed tantum manus illis imponatur in poenitentiam, observetur divina haec & sancta traditio.
units.tr: Cyprian, book 1, letter 8: "It is sacrilege whatever has been devised by men." The same, to the people: "one must always have recourse to the Scriptures." The same, letter 63, to Caecilius: that Christ alone is to be heard, and no one besides him, etc. Especially letter 74: "Whence is this tradition? Does it descend from the authority of the Lord and the Gospel, or does it come from the commands and letters of the Apostles? For God testifies and sets forth that those things are to be done which are written, saying to Joshua: 'The book of this law shall not depart from your mouth,' etc., that you may observe to do all things which are written in it. Likewise the Lord, sending his Apostles, commands that the nations be baptized and taught to observe all things whatsoever he commanded." Then he adds: "If therefore it is either prescribed in the Gospel, or contained in the Epistles or Acts of the Apostles, that those coming from any heresy are not to be baptized, but only hands are to be laid upon them for repentance, let this divine and holy tradition be observed."

units.la: Origenes tom.1. Hom.1. in Ierem. Necesse est nobis, scripturas sanctas in Testimonium vocare. Sensus quippe nostri & enarrationes sine iis testibus non habent fidem. Et hoc quod dictum est, In ore duorum vel trium testium stabit omne verbum, magis convenit ad interpretantis probationem, quam ad quorumcunq; hominum numerum, vt firmem verbum intelleEius mei[?], accipiens duos testes, de nouo & vetere Testamento, accipiens tres testes, de Euangelio, de Propheta, de Apostolo. Sic enim stabit omne verbum. Item in Leuit. Homil. ς[?].
units.tr: Origen, vol. 1, homily 1 on Jeremiah: "It is necessary for us to call the holy Scriptures as witnesses. For our own senses and explanations have no credit without those witnesses. And what is said, 'In the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word stand,' applies more to the proof of the interpreter than to any number of men; so that I may confirm the word of my understanding, taking two witnesses, from the Old and New Testament, taking three witnesses, from the Gospel, from the Prophet, from the Apostle. For thus shall every word stand." Likewise in Leviticus, homily [?].

units.la: Idem Tom. II, in Matth. hom. 25[?]. Debemus ad testimonium omnium verborum, quae proferimus in doctrina, proferre sensum scripturae quasi confirmantem, quem exponimus, sensum, &c. Vide locum prolixum satis & luculentum.
units.tr: The same, vol. 2, on Matthew, homily 25[?]: "For the testimony of all the words which we set forth in teaching, we ought to set forth the sense of Scripture as, so to speak, confirming the sense which we expound, etc." See the passage, which is quite long and lucid.

units.la: Idem ad Rom. c. 3[?]. Paulus Doctoribus Ecclesiae exemplum praebet, ut quae loquuntur ad populum, non propriis praesumta sententiis, sed divinis munita testimoniis proferant. Item paulò post: Si ipse tantum ac talis Apostolus authoritatem dictorum suorum sufficere posse non credit, nisi doceat in Lege & Prophetis scripta esse, quae dicit: quanto magis nos minimi hoc observare debemus, ut non nostras, cum docemus, sed S. Spiritus sententias proferamus.
units.tr: The same, on Romans, chapter 3[?]: "Paul offers an example to the teachers of the Church, that what they say to the people they should set forth not as presumptions of their own opinions, but fortified by divine testimonies." Likewise shortly afterwards: "If so great and such an Apostle does not believe that his own statements can suffice for authority, unless he shows that they are written in the Law and the Prophets, which he asserts, how much more ought we, the very least, to observe this, that when we teach we set forth not our own opinions but those of the Holy Spirit."

units.la: Idem in c.16.ad Rom.l.10. Vide quàm proximi periculis fiant hi, qui exerceri in diuinis literis negligunt, ex quibus SOLIS huiusmodi examinationis agnoscenda discretio est.
units.tr: The same, on Romans chapter 16, on Romans 10: "See how close to dangers those are who neglect to be exercised in the divine writings, from which ALONE the discernment of such an examination is to be recognised."

units.la: Idem homil. 3. & 10. in Genesin docet.
units.tr: The same teaches in homilies 3 and 10 on Genesis.

units.la: BASILIVS in Moralib. Reg 80. Si omne, quod ex fide non est, peccatum est: fides autem ex auditu, auditus autem per Verbum Dei: sine dubio cum quicquid extra diuinam Scripturam sit, ex fide non sit, id peccatum est.
units.tr: Basil, in the Moralia, rule 80: "If everything which is not of faith is sin, and faith is by hearing, and hearing by the Word of God, then without doubt, since whatever is outside the divine Scripture is not of faith, that is sin."

units.la: Id in Moralib. Reg.26[?] Quicquid vel dicimus vel facimus,id testimonio divinarum lite-rarum confirmari debet.
units.tr: The same, in the Moralia, rule 26[?]: "Whatever we either say or do ought to be confirmed by the testimony of the divine letters."

units.la: Id.Confess.[?] de vera ac pia fide, pag. 47. Manifestissimum infidelitatis argumentum, signumque superbiæ certissimum, si quis eorum, quæ scripta sunt, aliquid velit reiicere, aut eorū quæ non scripta sunt, introducere, cùm Dominus noster dicat: Oves mea vocem meam audiunt, alienam autem non sequuntur. Item. Apostolus ab hominibus sumto exemplo, Galat.3. vehementissimè interdicit, ne quid eorum, quæ in Divinis literis habentur, deleatur, aut, quod absit, addatur.
units.tr: The same, in the Confession [?] on the true and pious faith, p. 47: "It is a most manifest proof of unbelief, and a most certain sign of pride, if anyone wishes to reject any part of those things which are written, or to introduce any of those things which are not written, since our Lord says: 'My sheep hear my voice, but they do not follow another's.' Likewise the Apostle, taking the example from men, in Galatians 3, most vehemently forbids that anything of those things which are contained in the divine letters be deleted, or, which God forbid, be added."

units.la: Idem in Epist. 80. ad Eustathium : Non putamus æquum, esse vt quæ apud ipsos obtinuit loquendi consuetudo, pro lege ac canone habeatur recta doctrina. Si enim ad probandam doctrinam rectam valet consuetudo, licet & nobis omnino hac in re illos imitari. Stemus itaq; arbitratu inspirata à Deo Scriptura, & apud quos inveniuntur dogmata divinis oraculis consona, illis omnino veritatis adiudicetur sententia.
units.tr: The same, in Letter 80 to Eustathius: "We do not think it fair that the manner of speaking which has prevailed among them should be held as a law and rule of sound doctrine. For if custom is valid for proving sound doctrine, we too may by all means imitate them in this matter. Let us therefore stand by the Scripture inspired by God, and wherever doctrines are found consonant with the divine oracles, let the judgment of truth be wholly adjudged to them."

units.la: Id.in quæst.comp.q.1.pag.560. Eorum quæ apud nos in usu sunt, tam verborum quam rerum, alia distincte tradita sunt in scripturis, alia praetermissa. Scripta nullo modo omittenda sunt: de iis autem, quæ praetermissa sunt, regulam habemus à Paulo traditam: Omnia mihi licent, sed non omnia expediunt.
units.tr: The same, in Quaestiones compendiosae, q. 1, p. 560: "Of those things which are in use among us, both of words and of things, some are distinctly handed down in the Scriptures, others are passed over. What is written must in no way be omitted; but concerning those things which are passed over, we have a rule handed down by Paul: 'All things are lawful for me, but not all things are expedient.'"

units.la: ATHANASIUS libr. cont. idola : Sufficiunt sancta & divinitus inspirata Scriptura ad OMNEM veritatis instructionem seu indi[?]ationem. Nota istud Omnem:idq; sic extat in veterib. exempl. tùm Basileens. tùm Lugdunens. ne quis Iesuita calumnietur, à nobis id assutum esse.
units.tr: Athanasius, in the book against idols: "The holy and divinely inspired Scriptures suffice for the ENTIRE instruction or indication of truth. Note this word 'entire'; and so it stands in the old copies, both Basel and Lyon, lest any Jesuit calumniate us, as if we had added it."

units.la: Idem in Synopsi, Scripturam esse ancoram-& sustentaculum fidei nostræ.
units.tr: Likewise in the Synopsis: Scripture is the anchor and support of our faith.

units.la: CHRYSOSTOMUS Tom.2. in Matth. Homil.1. Scripturis opus esse, quia multi do-ctrinam corrumpant. Homil.49. Qui sunt in-Christianitate, conferant se ad Scripturas, quia nulla alia probatio poterit esse vera Christiani-tatis,quam Scriptura divina.
units.tr: CHRYSOSTOM, vol. 2, On Matthew, Homily 1: There is need of the Scriptures, because many corrupt doctrine. Homily 49: Those who are in Christianity should betake themselves to the Scriptures, because no other proof of true Christianity can exist than divine Scripture.

units.la: Ibidem. Quum videritis abominationem-desolationis, idest, hæresin impiam, fugite ad montes, &c. Montes sunt scripturæ Apostolorum & Prophetarum, de quibus dictum est: Illuminas tu mirabiliter à montibus æternis: & de Ecclesia dicit: Fundamenta eius in montibus san-ctis. Vide & cap.7.in Matth. Homil.20. &c.15[?] Hom.52.
units.tr: Ibid.: "When you see the abomination of desolation", that is, impious heresy, "flee to the mountains", etc. The mountains are the Scriptures of the Apostles and Prophets, of which it is said: "You wonderfully give light from the everlasting mountains." And of the Church he says: "Its foundations are on the holy mountains." See also chapter 7 on Matthew, Homily 20, etc., 15[?] Homily 52.

units.la: Idem Hom.13.in Genef. Scriptura non fi-nit auditorem errare,&c. Sed quia pleriq; non ut commodi quippiam ex S. literis aucupentur, sed voluptatis gratia aures accommodant his, qui talia tractant, & propterea non eos, qui magus pro-sunt, sed qui magis oblectant, ut audire possint, querunt: oro, ut omnibus illis praeclusis auribus, ad amussim Canonem S.Scriptura sequamur.
units.tr: The same, Homily 13 on Genesis: "Scripture does not allow the hearer to err", etc. But since most people do not seek to gather any profit from the Holy Letters, but lend their ears for pleasure to those who handle such things, and therefore seek not those who benefit them most but those who delight them most, so that they may be heard: I beg that, with all those ears shut, we follow the canon of Holy Scripture exactly.

units.la: Idem Tomo 4. in 2. ad Thessal.[?] c 2. Hom. 3. & 10. ait Omnia in Scripturis esse manifesta, quæ sunt necessaria.
units.tr: The same, vol. 4, on 2 Thessalonians, chapter 2, Homilies 3 and 10, says: "All things that are necessary are manifest in the Scriptures."

units.la: Idem in homil. Psal. 95. Non oportet quicquam dicere sine testibus, solaque animi cogitatione. Nam si quid dicitur absque Scriptura, auditorum cogitatio claudicat, nunc annuens, nunc haesitans, & interdum sermonem ut frivolum aversans, interdum ut probabilem recipiens. Verum ubi è Scriptura divina vocis prodiit testimonium, & loquentis sermonem, & audientis animum confirmat.
units.tr: The same, in Homily on Psalm 95: "One must not say anything without witnesses, relying on the thought of the mind alone. For if anything is said apart from Scripture, the thought of the hearers limps, now assenting, now hesitating, and sometimes rejecting the discourse as frivolous, sometimes accepting it as probable. But when the testimony of the divine Scripture has come forth from the voice, it confirms both the speaker's discourse and the hearer's mind."

units.la: Idem Hom.13. in 2.Ep. ad Corinth. Quo-modo non absurdum est, propter pecunias aliis non credere, sed ipsas numerare & supputare, pro rebus autem amplioribus aliorum sententiam sequi simpliciter, praesertim cum habeamus omnium exactissimam trutinam, & gnomonem, ac regulam, divinarum, inquam, legum assertionem. Ideo obsecro omnes vos, ut relinquatis, quidnam huic vel illi videatur, deque his a Scripturis haec omnia inquirite.
units.tr: The same, Homily 13 on 2 Corinthians: "How is it not absurd, on account of money, to not trust others but to count and reckon the money themselves, yet in matters of greater weight to simply follow the opinion of others, especially since we have the most exact balance, and gnomon and rule, namely the assertion of the divine laws? Therefore I beg all of you that you leave aside what seems so to this or that person, and seek out all these things from the Scriptures."

units.la: Id.Hom.58. in principium c.10. Ioan Me-ritò ostium Scripturas appellat, quoniam nos ad Deum ducunt, & eius nobis cognitionem aperiunt: ipsa ones [?] faciunt, ipsa custodiunt, neq; lupos irrumpere permittunt. Tanquam enim ostium firmissimum haereticos arcent, & in tuto constituunt, neq; nos, modo velimus, aberrare sinent. Et, Quisacra non utitur Scriptura, sed ascendit aliunde, id est, non concessa via, fur est.
units.tr: The same, Homily 58 on the beginning of John chapter 10: "He rightly calls the Scriptures a door, since they lead us to God and open to us the knowledge of him. They themselves make us sheep, they themselves keep us, and do not allow wolves to break in. For as a most firm door they keep heretics away and set us in safety, nor will they allow us to wander, if we are willing." And: "He who does not use Scripture as the sacred way, but climbs up some other way, that is, not by the permitted way, is a thief."

units.la: Id Hom. 9. Ep. ad Colos. Nolo expectare alium magistrum. Habes verbum Dei. Nemo te potest sit docere. Hac omnium malorum causa est, quod Scriptura ignoratur.
units.tr: The same, Homily 9 on the Epistle to the Colossians: "I do not wish to await another teacher. You have the Word of God. No one can teach you. This is the cause of all evils, that Scripture is ignored."

units.la: Idem in 2. Timoth.hom.9. Si quid vel discere vel ignorare opus sit[?], in Scripturis disca-mus.
units.tr: The same, on 2 Timothy, Homily 9: "If there is anything that we need to learn or to be ignorant of, let us learn it from the Scriptures."

units.la: Id.de oran.Spir. Si quis eorum, qui dicun-tur habere Spiritum sanctum, dicat aliquid ex seipso & non ex Euangelio, ne credite. Manes dicit quod Sol & Luna opifices sunt. Ubi legisti hoc? Ex quo non legit hac scripta, sed a seipso loquitur, manifestum est, quod non habet Spiritum sanctum.
units.tr: The same, On the Holy Spirit: "If anyone among those who are said to have the Holy Spirit says something from himself and not from the Gospel, do not believe him. Manes says that the Sun and Moon are craftsmen. Where did you read this? Since he does not read these writings but speaks from himself, it is plain that he does not have the Holy Spirit."

units.la: Idem Tom. 4. in epist. ad Tit. Hom.1. Omnia Euangelium continet, & praesentia & futura, honorem, pietatem, fidem, simul omnia praedicationis verbo conclusit. Sicut enim praeco praesentibus omnibus in theatro praedicat, ita & nos publice praedicamus, ea ratione, ut nihil addamus, sed ea tantum, quae audivimus, praedicamus.
units.tr: The same, vol. 4, on the Epistle to Titus, Homily 1: "The Gospel contains all things, both present and future, honour, piety, faith; it has embraced all things together in the word of preaching. For just as a herald, with all present in the theatre, proclaims, so also we publicly preach, with this principle, that we add nothing, but proclaim only those things which we have heard."

units.la: Vide & Tom. 3. Serm. de libello repudij. col.961.
units.tr: See also vol. 3, Sermon on the bill of divorce, col. 961.

units.la: Hieronymus pro nobis facit, ut videre est ex plurimis locis: ut Ep. ad Paulinum, quae praefigitur Bibliis. Tom. 2. contra Helui-gium, pag. 13. Tom. 8. in Psal 98. & in Psal 86. in Comment. in Haggaeum, cap. 1. pag. 229. 230 Tom. 9. in Matth. cap. 13. & 23. Quod de Scripturis auctoritatem non habet, eadem facilitate contemnitur, qua probatur Tom. 9. in Ep. ad Tit. c. 1. Sine auctoritate Scripturarum garrulitas non habet fidem.
units.tr: Jerome supports us, as can be seen from very many places: as in the Letter to Paulinus, which is prefixed to the Bibles; vol. 2, against Helvidius, p. 13; vol. 8, on Psalm 98 and on Psalm 86; in the Commentary on Haggai, chapter 1, pp. 229, 230; vol. 9, on Matthew, chapters 13 and 23: "What has no authority from the Scriptures is rejected with the same ease with which it is asserted." Vol. 9, on the Epistle to Titus, chapter 1: "Without the authority of the Scriptures, idle talk has no credibility."

units.la: Ambrosius Tom. 1. de virgin. libr. 3. cap. 114. Ostendit non esse Christiani, cum non habet testimonium Scripturae, in Religione aliquid asserere.
units.tr: Ambrose, vol. 1, On Virgins, book 3, chapter 114: he shows that it is not the mark of a Christian to assert anything in religion when he has no testimony of Scripture.

units.la: Idem in comment.in 16 cap.Lucæ.
units.tr: The same, in the commentary on chapter 16 of Luke.

units.la: In lib.1.ad Gratianum de fide,cap.4.
units.tr: In book 1, to Gratian, On Faith, chapter 4.

units.la: In Com.in 1.Cor.4.Tom.4.
units.tr: In the commentary on 1 Corinthians 4, vol. 4.

units.la: Augustin.lib.2.de doctr.Christ.cap 9. In iis, quæ aperte in Scriptura posita sunt, inveniuntur illa omnia, quæ continent fidem, mores que viuendi, spem scilicet atque caritatem. Id. Tomo 6 contra Prif.& Orig. ad Orof.cap.8. Item contra Faustum Manich. libr.10 cap.5. Tom.7. de nat. & grat, cap.61. Item contra Maxim.Arian. libr.3. cap. 14. Nec ego Niceenum, nec tu debes Ariminense, tanquam præiudicaturus proferre concilium: nec ego huius auctoritate, nec tu illius detineris. Scripturarum auctoritatibus, res cum re, causa cum causa, ratio cum ratione concertet.
units.tr: Augustine, book 2, On Christian Doctrine, chapter 9: "In those things which are set out plainly in Scripture, all those things are found which contain faith and the rules of living, namely hope and love." The same, vol. 6, against Priscillian and Origen, to Orosius, chapter 8; likewise against Faustus the Manichaean, book 10, chapter 5; vol. 7, On Nature and Grace, chapter 61; likewise against Maximinus the Arian, book 3, chapter 14: "Neither I nor you ought to bring forward the Council of Nicaea, as if to settle the matter, nor am I bound by its authority, nor are you bound by that of Rimini. Let the matter contend with the matter, the cause with the cause, and reason with reason, by the authorities of the Scriptures."

units.la: Idem Tom 2.Epist.42.ad Madaur. Ep.157. ad Optat. Tom.7. de vnitate Eccl. cap.3. De pecc.merit.libr. 2, cap, 36. de Baptismo contra Donatist.lib.2.cap.6. {e}Afferamus diuinam stateram de Scripturis sanctis, & in illis quid sit grauius appendamus.
units.tr: The same, vol. 2, Letter 42 to Madaurus; Letter 157 to Optatus; vol. 7, On the Unity of the Church, chapter 3; On Sins and Merits, book 2, chapter 36; On Baptism against the Donatists, book 2, chapter 6: "Let us bring forward the divine balance of the Holy Scriptures, and in them let us weigh what is heavier."

units.la: Id. contra Crescon. Gramm. lib.2. cap.32. Canon Ecclesiasticus constitutus est, ad quem Prophetarum & Apostolorum libri pertinent, secundum quos de cæteris literis vel fidelium vel infidelium iudicemus.
units.tr: The same, Against Cresconius the Grammarian, book 2, chapter 32: "The ecclesiastical canon has been established, to which belong the books of the Prophets and Apostles, according to which we judge the other writings, whether of the faithful or of the unfaithful."

units.la: Vide & ep.48. & in Tom.2.
units.tr: See also Letter 48 and vol. 2.

units.la: Et Tom.9.in c.10 Ioh.Tractat.49.
units.tr: And vol. 9, on John chapter 10, Tractate 49.

units.la: Similes loci plures apud hunc Patrem oc-currunt.
units.tr: Several similar passages occur in this Father.

units.la: Leo primus Epist.ad Fabian.idem docet. Poterant ex aliis quoque Patribus plura testimonia allegari: Sed nunc methodus postulat, vt respondeamus ad argumenta con-tratria Papistarum.
units.tr: Leo the First, in his Letter to Fabian, teaches the same. Many more testimonies could be alleged from the other Fathers too, but now the method requires that we answer the contrary arguments of the Papists.

units.la: ARGUMENTA CONTRA perfectionem scripturarum: quod Christus non omnia docuerit, quae ad salutem necessaria sunt: Et si docuit, non omnia tamen ab Apostolis sunt scripta, sed multa per traditionem relicta in Ecclesia.
units.tr: ARGUMENTS AGAINST the perfection of Scripture: that Christ did not teach everything that is necessary for salvation; and even if he did, not everything was written down by the Apostles, but much was handed down through tradition in the Church.

units.la: Sunt autem tres classes argumentorum, quae Papistae contra hanc doctrinam adferunt. 1. Quaedam sumuntur ex quibusdam scripturarum dictis, sed perperam intellectis quibus videtur cocludi, non omnia esse scripta, quae ad salutem necessaria sunt, sed multa fuisse tantum per traditionem relicta in Ecclesia. 2. Quaedam sumuntur ex quibusdam dogmatibus & institutis, quae ab universis Ecclesiis pro piis & veris admittuntur. Contendunt autem haec non habere aperta testimonia in scripturis. Esse igitur aliqua ad fidem ideoq; ad salutem necessaria, quae non sint in scripturis. 3. Quaedam deniq; sumuntur ex Patribus, qui multa videntur statuere, in Ecclesia esse observatu necessaria, quae tamen in scripturis non habeant certum testimonium.
units.tr: There are three classes of arguments that the Papists bring against this doctrine. (1) Some are drawn from certain sayings of Scripture, but misunderstood, from which they seem to conclude that not everything necessary for salvation has been written, but that much was left only through tradition in the Church. (2) Some are drawn from certain doctrines and institutions which are admitted by all Churches as pious and true, but they contend that these have no clear testimony in Scripture. There are therefore some things necessary for faith, and hence for salvation, that are not in Scripture. (3) Finally, some are drawn from the Fathers, who seem to lay down that many things are to be observed as necessary in the Church, which nevertheless have no certain testimony in Scripture.

units.la: Ad argumenta prima classis.
units.tr: To the arguments of the first class.

units.la: Iohan.16. Adhuc multa habeo, quae vobis dicam,&c. Inferunt hinc: 1. Ergo Christus non omnia docuit ad salutem necessaria, 2. Sed post Euangelium multa reliquit magisterio & revelationibus Spiritus sancti docenda partim per Apostolos, partim per Apostolorum successores & Ecclesiam usque in finem Mundi. 3. Non possunt autem illa multa alia esse quàm ea, quæ hactenus Ecclesia definiuit & definit. 4.Credendum igitur est, quæ præter Euangelium in Ecclesia à Patribus in Conciliis præsertim, quæ Ecclesiam totam repræsentant, constituta sunt, ea omnia esse à Spiritu sancto.
units.tr: John 16: "I still have many things to say to you," etc. From this they infer: (1) Therefore Christ did not teach everything necessary for salvation. (2) But after the Gospel he left many things to be taught by the teaching and revelations of the Holy Spirit, partly through the Apostles, partly through the successors of the Apostles and the Church until the end of the world. (3) Now those many things cannot be other than those which the Church has hitherto defined and still defines. (4) It must therefore be believed that whatever has been established in the Church, beyond the Gospel, by the Fathers, especially in Councils which represent the whole Church, all of these are from the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Resp. Antequam respondeam, notandum hoc argumentum non esse nouum, & à Papistis inuentum. Antiquum est, & à veteribus hæreticis, tempore Irenæi & Tertulliani excogitatum. Sic Manichæus dicebat, se esse hunc Spiritum promissum, qui deberet nouam adferre veritatem. Vide Augustin, contra epistolam Fundamenti. Nam ut suas hæreses obtrudere possent Ecclesiis, abutebantur hoc loco Christi ad ostendendum, 1. Non omnia nouisse Apostolos. 2. eoque non omnia ad salutem necessaria docuisse. Et quidem colorem adhibebant ad hoc facilimè persuadendum. Dicebant enim hoc decere ut defendant. Cedere enim in Ecclesiæ dedecus, & contra Ecclesiæ esse dignitatem, dicere omnia tradita fuisse ab Apostolis, quasi non reseruata essent alia etiam. Legatur Tertull. de præscript. hæret. pag. 103. Et Irenæus lib.3.cap.1. Ex iis enim quæ ij Patres tres ibi scribunt, colliguntur ea, quæ dixi. Quare videmus Papistas veteres hæreses revocasse in Ecclesiam. Nunc ad responsionem.
units.tr: Reply. Before I answer, it should be noted that this argument is not new, nor was it invented by the Papists. It is ancient, and was devised by the old heretics at the time of Irenaeus and Tertullian. Thus Manichaeus said that he was this promised Spirit, who was to bring a new truth. See Augustine, against the letter of Fundamentus. For in order to force their heresies upon the Churches, they abused this passage of Christ to show (1) that the Apostles did not know everything, and (2) therefore had not taught everything necessary for salvation. And indeed they used a pretext to persuade people of this very easily. For they said it was fitting to defend it thus: it would be a disgrace to the Church, and contrary to the Church's dignity, to say that everything had been handed down by the Apostles, as if some things had not also been reserved. Let Tertullian, On the Prescription of Heretics, p. 103, be read, and Irenaeus, book 3, chapter 1. For from what those Fathers write there, the points I have mentioned are gathered. Hence we see that the Papists have revived the old heresies in the Church. Now to the reply.

units.la: Resp. 1. in genere: deinde ad præcipuos paralogismos. In hoc loco est paralogismus, quem vocant figuræ dictionis, hoc est, ex ignorantia veræ διανοίας huius loci Christi. Hæc enim Christi verba ita interpretantur, quasi dicat, se nondum illos docuisse omnia quæ ad salutem faciunt: sed hoc officium te reseruare Spiritui sancto, qui posteá doceat, quæ supersunt docenda, ad salutem ipsorum necessaria. Sed hallucinantur. Christus enim non hic loquitur de rebus ad salutem consequendam cognitu necessariis, hæc antea reuelarat, vt ait Iohan.16[?]. Quæcunque audiui à Patre, nota feci vobis sed hic loquitur Christus de iis, quæ ad propriam Apostolorum consolationem pertinebant. Fuerant enim magna affecti tristitia ex eo, quòd Dominus dixerat de suo discessu ex hoc mundo, hoc est, de sua morte: quasi verò destituti præsentia Christi corporali, destituendi etiam essent omni ope, omnique magistro & consolatore, & soli in Mundo hoc imbecilli & ceu pupilli relinquendi. Sed Christus ostendit, tantum abesse, vt propter suum discessum debeant tristitia affici, vt potius lætandum sit. Quare? Proterea, quòd hoc futurum illis sit vtilissimum: contrà detrimentosum, si non discedat ex hoc Mundo. Ideo praeposuit propositionem hanc, Expedit vobis, vt ego vadam. Quomodo? Explicat & probat, dicendo: Nisi (inquit) ego abiero: paracletus non veniet ad vos: quasi dicat: hoc autem esset vobis detrimento-sum. Si autem abiero, mittam eum ad vos: quasi dicat, hoc autem erit vobis vtilissimum. Sequitur: Ergo expedit vobis, vt ego vadam: quasi dicat, Si expedit, habetis igitur cur læ-temini, non cur tristemini. At quomodo erit nobis vtile, si mittas hunc spiritum paracle-tum? Resp. Probat ab effectis Spiritus S. in ipsis Apostolis. Nam cùm venerit (inquit) ille arguet (scilicet per vos) Mundum de peccato, &c. hoc est, ille non erit vobiscum, vt ego hac præsentia corporali extra vos, sed habitabit in vobis, in vestris animis, eos replens sapientia, fortitudine, vi dicendi, convincendi Mundum vniuersum, non Iudæos tantum, sed etiam Gentes, etiam sapientissimos, & fortissimos ac sanctissimos quosque. Quibus de rebus? De peccato, quòd scilicet omnes, qui non credunt in me, adhuc sint in peccato. De iustitia, quòd scilicet iustitia vera coram Deo, non sit posita in operibus, quæ ab hominibus præstari possint, sed in mea obedientia, morte, resurrectione, ascensione in cœlum, & perpetua pro credentibus in me, apud Patrem intercessione. Et hoc est, Quia vado, &c. Quare per me solum homines iustificari. De iudicio, quòd scilicet princeps huius Mundi mundi iam condemnatus sit, & ex consequenti omnes qui sunt de hoc Mundo, cum illo damnandi: ac proinde contrà, qui non sunt de hoc Mundo, sed in me credunt, futuros beatos mecum apud Patrem, ad quem vado. Hæc est autem summa doctrinæ Euangelij. Sensus est: Spiritus iste efficax erit in vestra prædicatione, quia convincet, ἐλέγχει[?]: Ergo expedit, ut vadam. Proinde hæc debent vos consolari, quæ scilicet Spiritus sanctus per vos effecturus est.
units.tr: Reply: first in general, then against the principal paralogisms. In this passage there is a paralogism which they call a fallacy of expression (figura dictionis), that is, arising from ignorance of the true meaning (diánoia) of this saying of Christ. For they interpret these words of Christ as if he said that he had not yet taught them all that pertains to salvation, but that this task was reserved for the Holy Spirit, who would afterwards teach what remained to be taught, necessary for their salvation. But they are mistaken. For Christ does not here speak of things necessary to be known for obtaining salvation; these he had already revealed, as John 16 says: "All that I heard from the Father I have made known to you." Rather, Christ here speaks of those things which pertained to the Apostles' own consolation. For they had been greatly affected with sorrow because the Lord had spoken of his departure from this world, that is, of his death; as if, being deprived of the bodily presence of Christ, they were also to be deprived of all help, of every teacher and comforter, and left alone in this world, weak and as orphans. But Christ shows that so far is it from being the case that they ought to be saddened by his departure, that they ought rather to rejoice. Why? Because this would be most useful to them; on the contrary, it would be harmful if he did not depart from this world. Therefore he put forward this proposition: "It is expedient for you that I go away." How so? He explains and proves it, saying: "Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come to you," as if to say: that would be harmful to you. "But if I go away, I will send him to you," as if to say: this will be most useful to you. It follows: "Therefore it is expedient for you that I go," as if to say: if it is expedient, you have therefore reason to rejoice, not reason to grieve. But how will it be useful to us, if you send this Paraclete Spirit? Answer: he proves it from the effects of the Holy Spirit in the Apostles themselves. For "when he comes," he says, "he will convict" (namely, through you) "the world of sin," etc. That is, he will not be with you as I am, by bodily presence outside you, but he will dwell in you, in your souls, filling them with wisdom, strength, and power of speech, to convict the whole world, not only the Jews but also the Gentiles, even the wisest, strongest and holiest of all. Concerning what things? "Of sin," namely that all who do not believe in me are still in sin. "Of righteousness," namely that true righteousness before God is not placed in works which men can perform, but in my obedience, death, resurrection, ascension into heaven, and perpetual intercession before the Father for those who believe in me. And this is what "because I go, etc." means: that men are justified through me alone. "Of judgment," namely that the prince of this world has already been condemned, and consequently all who are of this world are to be condemned with him; and accordingly, on the contrary, those who are not of this world but believe in me will be blessed with me before the Father, to whom I go. This, however, is the sum of the doctrine of the Gospel. The sense is: this effective Spirit will be at work in your preaching, because he will convict (elégchei). Therefore it is expedient that I go. Accordingly, these things ought to comfort you, namely what the Holy Spirit is going to accomplish through you.

units.la: Postea subdit, Multa alia habeo, quæ vo-bis dicam, &c. Quæ sunt ista alia? Augustinus ait, non posse sciri, cùm Dominus non explicuerit. Verum: sed si Dominus ea saltem per transennam indicet, si non proprie & in specie, saltem in genere? Primùm, ex contextu, hoc est, tam ex scopo huius sermonis, & ex præcedentibus, quàm ex subsequentibus apparet, Christum hic loqui tum de donis Spiritus sancti, quæ effusurus erat in Apostolos, tum de iis, quæ per Apostolos iam suis donis instructos, erat facturus Spiritus sanctus ad glorificandum Christum. Supra ait, Expedit ut vadam: probat, quia Spiritus sanctus descendet super vos, & tunc ille per vos arguet.
units.tr: Afterwards he adds: "I have many other things to say to you, etc." What are these other things? Augustine says they cannot be known, since the Lord did not explain them. True; but if the Lord indicated them at least obliquely, if not properly and specifically, at least in general? First, from the context, that is, both from the aim of this discourse and from what precedes and what follows, it appears that Christ here speaks both of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which he was about to pour out upon the Apostles, and of those things which the Holy Spirit was going to accomplish through the Apostles, already equipped with his gifts, for glorifying Christ. Above he says, "It is expedient that I go"; he proves it, because the Holy Spirit will descend upon you, and then he will convict through you.

units.la: Post hæc verba, Multa habeo,&c. continuat sermonem Dominus de eodem Spiritu, deque iis, quæ in Apostolis, perque Apostolos operaturus erat, dicendo: Is deducet vos in omnem veritatem. Item, Quæ ventura sunt,revelabit vobis. Item, Ipse glorificabit me. Quæ omnia spectant ad scopum, & ad illam propositionem, Expedit vobis, ut ego vadam. Ergo etiam hæc multa, de quibus dicit, Multa habeo, quæ vobis dicam, eodem spectant, & de iisdem Spiritus sancti donis & effectis, hoc est, quæ per Apostolos erat effecturus, intelligenda sunt.
units.tr: After these words, "I have many things," the Lord continues his discourse about the same Spirit, and about those things which he was going to work in the Apostles and through the Apostles, saying: "He will guide you into all truth." Likewise, "He will declare to you the things that are to come." Likewise, "He will glorify me." All these things look to the aim and to that proposition, "It is expedient for you that I go." Therefore these many things also, of which he says, "I have many things to say to you," look to the same thing, and must be understood of the same gifts and effects of the Holy Spirit, that is, of those which he was going to effect through the Apostles.

units.la: Deinde ex iis, quæ postea per Apostolos Spiritus sanctus effecit in mundo, admiranda atque obstupescenda, & quæ nunquam putarent se præstituros Apostoli, neque unquam sibi potuissent persuadere: intelligimus, quæ sint illa multa, de quibus dicit Chri-stus, &Adhuc multa habeo, &c. Quid egit Spiritus sanctus in Apostolis, & quid per Apostolos? Apostolos ipsos admirandis & multis donis instruxit: cognitione Scripturarum, & vera Oraculorum Propheticorum intelligentia, cognitione & usu omnium linguarum, ut edendi stupenda miracula, virtute & efficacitate in sermonibus, tanta animi altitudine & fortitudine, & in dicendo παῤῥησίᾳ, ut nihil metuerint propter Christum: de quibus donis partim in Actis, partim in Epistolis Apostolicis, 1. Corinth. 12. ipsi nunquam sperarent, se tot tantisque donis instructum iri. Deinde per hos ita instructos, convertit Mundum, omnesque Gentes brevi tempore ad Christum: demolitus est (ut loquitur Paulus 2. Corinth. 10.) omnem altitudinem, omnes munitiones, omnia consilia Mundi, & adegit rebelles ad obediendum Christo: effecit, ut Reges colla subdiderint Christo: evertit i-dola, & regnum ac fidem Christianam stabi-livit. Quanta hæc sunt? Hæc certè nunquam Apostoli potuissent non solum sibi persuadere & credere, sed ne cogitare quidem: præ-fertim[?] quod Conversio Gentium ad Christum, & propagatio gratiæ ad Gentes erat illis incredibilis. Sed posteaquam per Spiritum sanctum viderunt rem ipsam: tunc agnoverunt, &c. Huc spectat illud Ephes.3. Huius rei gratia,&c.vsq; ad versum 7.
units.tr: Next, from those things which the Holy Spirit afterwards effected in the world through the Apostles, which are wonderful and astonishing, and which the Apostles themselves would never have thought they would accomplish, nor could ever have persuaded themselves of: we understand what those many things are of which Christ says, "I still have many things to say, etc." What did the Holy Spirit do in the Apostles, and what did He do through the Apostles? He equipped the Apostles themselves with admirable and many gifts: knowledge of the Scriptures, and a true understanding of the prophetic oracles; knowledge and use of all languages; the power to work astonishing miracles; virtue and efficacy in their speeches; such loftiness and strength of spirit, and boldness [parrhesia, παῤῥησία] in speaking, that they feared nothing for Christ. Of these gifts, some are described in the Acts, and some in the Apostolic Epistles (1 Cor. 12), which they themselves would never have hoped they would be furnished with, so many and so great. Then, through these so equipped, He turned the world and all nations to Christ in a short time; He tore down (as Paul says, 2 Cor. 10) every height, every fortress, every counsel of the world, and brought rebels to obey Christ; He caused kings to submit their necks to Christ; He overthrew idols, and established the kingdom and the Christian faith. How great are these things! Certainly the Apostles could never have persuaded themselves of these things, nor believed them, nor even thought of them, especially since the conversion of the Gentiles to Christ and the spread of grace to the Gentiles was incredible to them. But after they saw the thing itself through the Holy Spirit, then they recognised it, etc. To this refers that passage of Ephesians 3, For this cause, etc., down to verse 7.

units.la: Hæc sunt illa multa, quæ tunc Christus tacuit, quia Apostoli non potuissent tunc hæc intelligere: sed promisit se effecturum, ut tandem in veritatem harum rerum, per Spiritum sanctum adducerentur. Proinde voluit concludere, Expedire ipsis, ut iret ad Patrem, & ita tristitiam illis levare, & contra consolari.
units.tr: These are those many things which Christ then kept silent about, because the Apostles could not then understand them; but He promised that He would bring it about that they would at last be led into the truth of these things, through the Holy Spirit. Accordingly, He wished to conclude that it was expedient for them that He go to the Father, and so lighten their sadness and, on the contrary, console them.

units.la: Nunc quàm omnia verba huc congruant, videamus. Multa habeo,&c. quæ scilicet ad vestram consolationem pertinent. De qua re multa? De hoc Spiritu, quæ vobis donaturus est, & quæ per vos effecturus. Sed vos non potestis portare modo: hoc est, sed vos hæc nunquam potestis vobis persuadere & credere, imò nec intelligere, vsque adeò multa & magna sunt.
