(Cum autem venerit Spiritus ille,&c. hoc est, Etsi verò in præsentia non potestis illa intelligere: tamen per Spiritum sanctum in vobis fient, & tunc vos harum rerum veritatem & complementum videbi-tis : Spiritus ille sanctus deducet vos in omnem veritatem: Quam omnem veritatem? In ve-ritatem horum omnium, quæ nunc taceo, sed eventura sunt: deducet in veritatem, spectandam, oculis inspiciendam: quasi di-cat, deducet ille vos in rem præsentem, & ef-ficiet, ut quæ iam ego taceo, propter vestram imbecillitatem, & quæ nunc vos non potē-stis mente capere, tunc oculis ipsis cernatis, & quasi manu palpetis. Sensus est, Spiritus sanctus omnino re ipsa præstabit, quæ ego tacitus promitto.
units.tr: Now let us see how all these words agree with this. "I have many things, etc.," which of course pertain to your consolation. About what thing are there many? About this Spirit, whom He will give you and whom He will bring about through you. But "you cannot bear them now": that is, you can never persuade yourselves of these things and believe them, nor indeed understand them, so great and so many are they. ("But when that Spirit comes, etc." that is, although indeed you cannot understand those things at present, nevertheless they will be made in you through the Holy Spirit, and then you will see the truth and fulfilment of these things.) "That Spirit of truth will lead you into all truth": what all truth? Into the truth of all these things which I now keep silent about, but which are about to happen: he will lead you into the truth, to be looked at and inspected with the eyes; as if He were to say, that Spirit will lead you into the present reality, and will bring it about that what I now withhold because of your weakness, and what you cannot now grasp in your mind, you will then see with your very eyes and, as it were, touch with your hand. The sense is: the Holy Spirit will certainly accomplish in very deed what I promise in silence.

units.la: Confirmat hoc à fide Legati, hoc est, Spi-ritus sancti, quem missurus erat Christus tanquam legatum suum, & executorem suorum consiliorum & promissorum. Ideo ait, Non enim ille loquetur à semetipso, &c. Facit Spiritum sanctum suum legatum, & suum executorem, sicut & ipse fuerat Legatus Patris, & executor mandatorum eius. Sicut autem probauerat, se fidum fuisse legatum Patris, ex eo, quòd nihil loquebatur ex se, aut aliquid agebat ex se, sed tantùm loquebatur quæ audiuerat à Patre: unde dicebat, Ameipso non loquor: Ita hic ostendit, hac eadem locutione, Spiritum sanctum futurum suum fidum Legatum & executorem. Ille enim legatus dicitur fidelis, qui nihil loquitur ex se, nihilque agit, nisi quatenus habet in mandatis. Hoc igitur significat, cùm ait: Non enim loquetur à semetipso: sed quæcun-
units.tr: He confirms this from the faithfulness of the envoy, that is, of the Holy Spirit, whom Christ was about to send as His envoy and executor of His counsels and promises. Therefore He says, "For he will not speak of himself, etc." He makes the Holy Spirit His envoy and His executor, just as He Himself had been the envoy of the Father and the executor of His commands. Now, just as He had proved that He had been a faithful envoy of the Father, from the fact that He spoke nothing of Himself, nor did anything of Himself, but only spoke what He had heard from the Father, whence He said, "I do not speak of myself": so here He shows, by this same manner of speaking, that the Holy Spirit will be His faithful envoy and executor. For that envoy is called faithful who speaks nothing of himself and does nothing except insofar as he has it in his commission. This therefore is what He means when He says: "For he will not speak of himself: but whatever he hears,"

units.la: cum leg. ‚ und Lesarten (none printed; omitted) que audiet, scilicet ex me, loquetur per vos, & faciet. Ideo etiam infra ait, De meo accipiet. Sensus est; Dubium non est, quin Spiritus sanctus facturus sit in vobis, & per vos illa multa & admiranda, quæ decreui per vos fieri: sed taceo propter vestram imbecillitatem: atque ita fitis per eum tanquam in rem præsentem deducendi ad perspiciendam veritatem horum omnium. Quare dubium non est? Quia fidus erit meus legatus & executor. Et quæ ventura sunt, revelabit vobis. Quidam sic: Quæ ventura sunt vobis viventibus, de conversione scilicet Gentium: illa vobis nunciabit, id est, patefaciet. Quomodo? Reipsa præstando, & executioni mandando. Et sic Ephes. 3. Nunc autem revelatum est sanctis Apostolis[?] eius & Prophetis per Spiritum. Sed potest etiam referri ad futura post eorum mortem: quasi dicat: Non solum per vos viventes efficiet, quæ taceo mirabilia, sed etiam quæ futura sint post vos mortuos, propter doctrinam, quam prædicabitis, vobis indicabit. Prædicit igitur, eos donatum iri dono Prophetiæ, id est, prævidendi quæ futura in Ecclesia fuerint. Videmus hoc imple-tum. Apostoli prædixerunt de venturis in Ecclesiam lupis, Antichristis: sed tamen etiam prævuiderunt, quomodo Christus semper esset triumphaturus. Qualis illa Prophetia de Antichristo tam perspicua, tam clara, quæ est 2. Thess. 2. Qualis illa Apocalypsis? An non hæc etiam magna Spiritus dona? Concludit: Ipse me glorificabit, scilicet, per vos, quasi dicat: Summa haec est, quod Spiritus per vos glorificabit me. Quomodo? Propagando regnum meum, complendo oracula Prophetarum. Haec certe glorificatio non consequeretur, si ego non abirem, & mitterem hunc Spiritum. Ergo expedit, ut vadam.
units.tr: (leg. ‚ und Lesarten; none printed, omitted) "that he will hear," namely from me, "he will speak through you, and will do." Therefore He also says below, "He will receive of mine." The sense is: there is no doubt that the Holy Spirit will bring about in you, and through you, those many and wonderful things which I have decided are to be done through you; but I keep silent because of your weakness; and thus, through Him, you will be led, as into a present reality, to behold the truth of all these things. Why is there no doubt? Because he will be my faithful envoy and executor. "And he will show you the things that are to come." Some interpret thus: the things that are to come while you are living, namely the conversion of the Gentiles, these he will announce to you, that is, make known. How? By actually accomplishing them and carrying them into effect. And so Ephesians 3: "Now it has been revealed to the holy apostles of his and prophets by the Spirit." But it can also be referred to things future after their death: as if He were to say: not only will he bring about through you while you are living the wonderful things I am keeping silent about, but he will also show you, on account of the teaching which you will preach, what will be in the future after you are dead. He foretells, therefore, that they would be granted the gift of prophecy, that is, of foreseeing what things would be in the future in the Church. We see this fulfilled. The Apostles foretold of the wolves and Antichrists who were to come into the Church; yet they also foresaw how Christ would always be about to triumph. What of that prophecy about Antichrist, so plain and so clear, which is 2 Thessalonians 2? What of the Apocalypse? Are not these also great gifts of the Spirit? He concludes: "He will glorify me," namely through you, as if to say: the sum of it is that the Spirit will glorify me through you. How? By propagating my kingdom, by fulfilling the oracles of the prophets. Certainly this glorification would not follow if I did not go away and send this Spirit. Therefore it is expedient that I go.

units.la: Sed esto: loquatur de doctrina, deque rebus, quas ante non audierint: Non sequitur tamen prima illatio, Ergo non omnia ne-cessaria ad salutem audiuerunt à Christo A-postoli. Nam primò fieri potuit, ut essent a-lia, quae non ad summam doctrinae de salute pertinerent: ut quod Spiritus sanctus esset illos afflaturus spiritu Prophetico, ut futura praeuiderent, sicut videmus, multa praedixis-se Apostolos per Spiritum S. ut 2. Thessal. 2. de Antichristo: 1. Tim. 4. Spiritus autem manifestè dicit, quod in nouissimis diebus desciscent quidam à fide spiritibus seductoribus attendentes ac doctrinis daemoniorum, &c. Quare ἀσυλλό-γιστῳ[?] est illa ratio.
units.tr: But grant it: let him speak of the teaching and of things which they had not heard before. Yet the first inference does not follow, "Therefore the Apostles did not hear from Christ all things necessary to salvation." For first it could be that there were other things which did not pertain to the sum of the doctrine of salvation: such as that the Holy Spirit would breathe upon them with the prophetic Spirit, so that they might foresee future things, as we see the Apostles to have foretold many things through the Holy Spirit, as in 2 Thessalonians 2 concerning Antichrist; 1 Timothy 4: "Now the Spirit clearly says that in the latter days some will fall away from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits and doctrines of demons," etc. Wherefore that reasoning is a non sequitur.

units.la: 2. Etiamsi loquebatur de doctrina salu-tis: non tamen sequitur, nouam hanc tradi-turum fuisse Spiritum sanctum, & non fuisse traditam prius à Christo. Nam sic possunt verba exponi: Deducet vos in omnem veritatem, non inauditam & nouam, sed in vete-rem, & à me auditam: verùm alio modo, quà ego, deducet in veritatem, hoc est, si excide-rint, in memoriam reuocabit: si non fuerint bene intellecta, efficiet, ut melius intelliga-tis. Et hanc interpretationem docet Christus, cum ait de spiritu suo, Ioh.14. Ille vos docebit omnia (id est, melius persuadebit) & suggeret vobis omnia, quæcunque dixi vobis. Quare fallacia est accidentis. Non enim loquitur de nova doctrina, sed de novo docendi modo. Et quid est inferre, Ergo Christus non omnia docuit Apostolos, nisi dicere, Christus mentitus est, cum dixit Ioh.15 [?]. Omnia quæcunque audivi a Patre, nota feci vobis?
units.tr: 2. Even if he was speaking of the doctrine of salvation, it does not follow that the Holy Spirit would hand down a new doctrine, and that it had not been handed down before by Christ. For the words can be explained thus: "He will lead you into all truth," not unheard of and new, but into the old truth, which was heard from me; but in another way than I did: he will lead into the truth, that is, if things have slipped out of mind, he will recall them to memory; if they have not been well understood, he will bring it about that you understand them better. And Christ teaches this interpretation when He speaks of His Spirit, John 14: "He will teach you all things (that is, will persuade you better) and will bring to your remembrance all things whatsoever I have said to you." Wherefore the inference is a fallacy of accident. For he does not speak of a new doctrine, but of a new manner of teaching. And what is it to infer, "Therefore Christ did not teach the Apostles all things," except to say, "Christ lied, when He said, John 15: 'All things whatsoever I have heard from the Father I have made known to you'?"

units.la: 3. Esto etiam, ut Christus, cum hæc diceret, nondum omnia revelarit Apostolis: sequitur ne, Ergo nunquam revelavit ipse? Imo contra promittit hic Christus, se alia illis dicturum. Est enim aperta promissio, Multa habeo quæ dicam, Non nunc, sed aliàs. Ergo tandem dixit. Stat enim promissio. At quando postea dixit? Resp. Post resurrectionem. An non post resurrectionem multa eis dixit, quæ antea non dixerat? Lege Evangelistas, Matth. 28. & Marc. 16. Ite in universum Mundum, prædicate Evangelium omni creaturæ. Ecce ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus usque ad consummationem seculi. At non de se, sed de spiritu loquitur sancto? Resp. Quasi vero non idem sit, qui in Apostolis loquebatur Christus, qui & spiritus Christi.
units.tr: 3. Granted that Christ, when he said these things, had not yet revealed everything to the Apostles: does it follow, then, that he never revealed it himself? On the contrary, Christ here promises that he will tell them other things. For the promise is plain: I have many things to say, not now, but at another time. So he did tell them at last, for the promise stands. But when did he tell them afterwards? Answer: after the resurrection. Did he not, after the resurrection, tell them many things that he had not told them before? Read the Evangelists, Matth. 28. and Mark 16.: Go into all the world, preach the Gospel to every creature. Behold, I am with you always, even unto the end of the world. But he does not speak of himself, you say, but of the Holy Spirit? Answer: as if it were not the same Christ who spoke in the Apostles, the Christ who is also the Spirit of Christ.

units.la: Ad secundam illationem. Esto, multa reli-querit docenda spiritui.
units.tr: To the second inference. Granted, he left many things for the Spirit to teach.

units.la: 1. Non sequitur, hæc fuisse ex eorum nu-mero, mero, quæ sunt necessaria ad salutem. Stat enim sententia Christi de iis vera. Iohan. 15. Quacunque audiui a Patre, notafeci vobis. Sed quæ illa multa? Illa, quæ ad formam Eccle-siæ pertinent, vt multa apud Apostolum 1. Cor.11.14[?] Item de rebus futuris.
units.tr: 1. It does not follow that these were among those things which are necessary to salvation. For Christ's saying stands true about them: John 15. All things that I have heard of my Father I have made known to you. But what are those many things? Those which pertain to the form of the Church, as many things in the Apostle, 1 Cor. 11.14[?]. Likewise things concerning the future.

units.la: 2. Sed sunt o de illis, quæ ad salutem ne-cessaria sunt: Ergo hinc sequitur Apostolos omnia tandem cognouisse per Spiritũ Christi. Si enim hoc promitrit Christus:vtiq; impleuit promissum. Promisit autem dicendo, Deducet vos in omnem veritatem. Quis igitur audeat dicere, Apostolos non agnouisse o-mnem veritatem? Et sic Tertull. exponit & argumentatur in libr. de præscriptionibus, pag.103. & Irenæus lib.3.cap.1. idem concludit Est hæc antiqua hæresis Valentini & aliorum hæreticorum, Apostolos nõ omnia ne-cessaria ad salutem nouisse. At dem (ait quis) omnia nouisse, non tamen omnia docue-runt, sed partem.
units.tr: 2. But some of those things are necessary to salvation. Therefore it follows from this that the Apostles at last came to know all things through the Spirit of Christ. For if Christ promised this, he certainly fulfilled the promise. He promised, however, when he said, He will lead you into all truth. Who, then, would dare to say that the Apostles did not know all truth? Tertullian also expounds and argues thus in the book On Prescription, p. 103, and Irenaeus, book 3, chapter 1, draws the same conclusion. This is the ancient heresy of Valentinus and other heretics, that the Apostles did not know all things necessary to salvation. But grant (someone says) that they knew all things, yet they did not teach them all, but only a part.

units.la: Respon. Hoc etiam impium est sentire. Nam si non docuerunt, aut non docuerunt de industria, quia noluerunt. At hoc fuisset crimen invidiæ, & contra charitatem, & contra officium suum: aut ex obliuione, & hoc est contra Spiritum S. qui in illis habitabat, quasi oblitus sit cum illis nostræ salutis. Sunt hæc absurda. Ergo falsum, quod ais, partem. Ideo Tertullianus & Irenæus con-tra contendunt, Apostolos omnia docuisse, quæ ad salutem erant necessaria. At do, docuisse, nempe ore: sed non scri-pserunt omnia.
units.tr: Answer: this too is impious to think. For if they did not teach them, either they did not teach them on purpose, because they were unwilling; but that would have been a crime of envy, and against charity, and against their office; or else it was through forgetfulness, and that is against the Holy Spirit, who dwelt in them, as if he had forgotten our salvation along with them. These are absurd. Therefore what you say, a part, is false. This is why Tertullian and Irenaeus contend against it, that the Apostles taught all things that were necessary to salvation. But grant that they taught them, namely by word of mouth, but did not write everything down.

units.la: Resp. Si hoc non fecerunt, aut de industria omiserunt, aut ex obliuione, aut exim-potentia. Omnia absurda: cùm Spiritus suppeditârit charitatem, memoriam salutis nostræ, & vires. 2. Sequeretur, Paulum valdè imprudentem fuisse, qui scripsit multa de rebus, non ita necessariis, si neglexisset necessarias. Sic Iren.lib.3. cap.1.
units.tr: Answer: if they did not do this, then either they deliberately omitted it, or through forgetfulness, or through inability. All absurd, since the Spirit supplied them with charity, memory of our salvation, and strength. 2. It would follow that Paul was very imprudent, who wrote many things about matters not so necessary, if he had neglected necessary ones. So Irenaeus, book 3, chapter 1.

units.la: Ita illatio tertia corruit. Si enim illi omnes necessaria scripserunt. Non igitur per Ecclesiam Spiritus sanctus subindè noua docet. Est contra Apostolum Hebr.1. Nouissimè (id est, non amplius posthac noua locuturus) locutus est in Filio, Et contra Patres Tertull. & Irenæum.
units.tr: So the third inference collapses. For if they all wrote down what was necessary, then the Holy Spirit does not teach new things from time to time through the Church. This is against the Apostle, Heb. 1.: In these last days (that is, not going to speak new things any more after this) he has spoken to us by the Son; and against the Fathers, Tertullian and Irenaeus.

units.la: Illatio quarta, Credendum est, quæ præter Euangelium à Patribus in Conciliis præsertim, quæ Ecclesiam totam repræsentant, constituta sunt, ea omnia esse à Spiritu sancto.
units.tr: Fourth inference: One must believe that whatever has been established by the Fathers, especially in Councils, which represent the whole Church, apart from the Gospel, all of it is from the Holy Spirit.

units.la: At 1. non possunt tradere sine verbo Christi, Rom.10. Unde igitur probas per Scripturas, quæ tradidit Ecclesia sine Scripturis, ea esse à Spiritu sancto? 2. Quomodo possunt esse à Spiritu sancto, quæ pugnāt cum Scripturis? Vt Canon Constantinop.de non dando calice. Ita in fumum dissipatur Scriptura.
units.tr: But first, they cannot hand down anything without the word of Christ, Rom. 10. Whence, then, do you prove by Scripture that what the Church handed down without Scripture is from the Holy Spirit? Second, how can those things be from the Holy Spirit which fight against the Scriptures? Such as the canon of Constantinople about not giving the cup. Thus Scripture is dissipated into smoke.

units.la: Et cùm ais, Hæc esse illa omnia: Respon.1. Augustinus in hunc locum. Ecquis ille, qui audet dicere, quæ sint illa, cùm Christus noluerit explicare. 2. Hæc quæ ais esse illa multa, non possunt esse. Nam de illis dixit Christus, quòd non possint portare illa Apostoli. Ista autem non sunt ita difficilia intellectu, quin possint ferri. Ergo, &c. Quid ergo Spiritus sanctus sibi reseruauit? vt doceret vngere, & baptizare campanas, & similes nugas?
units.tr: And when you say, these are those all things: Answer: first, Augustine on this passage. Who is he who dares to say what those things are, since Christ was unwilling to explain them? Second, these things which you say are those many things cannot be them. For Christ said of those things that the Apostles could not bear them. But these are not so difficult to understand that they could not be borne. Therefore, etc. What, then, did the Holy Spirit reserve for himself? To teach anointing, and baptizing bells, and similar trifles?

units.la: Secundus locus, Ioh.21. ad calcem, Multa alia sunt, quæ fecit Iesus, quæ si scribantur sigilla-tim, ne mundum quidem ipsum opinor capturum eos, qui scriberentur, libros.
units.tr: The second passage, John 21, at the end: There are also many other things which Jesus did, which, if they were written every one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written.

units.la: Resp. Sed idem docet tot scripsisse, quot ad salutem nostram sufficiunt cap. 20. ad finem, dicendo: Hæc autem scripta sunt, ut credatis, quòd Iesus est Christus ille Filius Dei, & ut credentes vitam habeatis per nomen eius. Per-secta igitur doctrina, quia per illam fide ac-ceptam, possumus consequi vitam æternam. Sic Cyrill. in Iohan. lib.12. cap.68. Ita Augustinus in hunc locum. Ideo notandum, non dicere Euangelistam, Multa alia docuit Christus, quasi hæc, quam tradit ex ore Christi do-ctrina, sit imperfecta: sed ait de miraculis & Actis. Deinde etiamsi diceret, Multa alia do-cuit: non possent tamen intelligi multa, id est, diuersa: quia hæc, quæ habemus, non suf-ficerent ad salutem. Sufficiunt autem teste hic eodem Iohanne. Ergo, &c. Est igitur sal-lacia accidentis: quia ab eo, quod est aliud numero, argumetaris ad id, quod est aliud in substantia: vel ὁμωνυμίας, At excipies. Si non alia, id est, diuersa ab iis, quæ habemus, egit aut docuit: & tamen multa alia egit & docuit, eaque non sunt ne-cessaria ad salutem, quia omnia necessaria habemus in iis quæ extant scripturis: sequitur multa egisse Christum superflua.
units.tr: Answer: but the same passage shows that he wrote as many as suffice for our salvation, at the end of chapter 20, saying: But these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life through his name. Therefore the doctrine is complete, because by faith received through it we can attain eternal life. So Cyril, on John, book 12, chapter 68. So Augustine on this passage. Therefore it should be noted that the Evangelist does not say, Christ taught many other things, as if the doctrine he hands down from the mouth of Christ were imperfect; but he speaks of miracles and deeds. Moreover, even if he said, Christ taught many other things, nevertheless the many could not be understood as different, that is, diverse things, because what we have would not be enough for salvation. Yet by John's own testimony here, they are enough. Therefore, etc. This is therefore a fallacy of accident, because you argue from what is other in number to what is other in substance; or it is an equivocation. But you will object: if he did not do or teach other things, that is, things different from those we have, and yet he did and taught many other things, and these are not necessary to salvation, because we have all necessary things in those which are extant in the Scriptures, it follows that Christ did many superfluous things.

units.la: Respon. Est paralogismus non causæ vt causæ.Non est enim hæc causa,cur alia mul-ta gesserit & docuerit, vt scilicet doceret diuersa: sed fuit, vt eandem doctrinam variis docendi modis exponeret, & variis mira-culis confirmaret. Non sequitur igitur fuisse superuacanea, cùm suum habuerint finem.
units.tr: Answer: this is a paralogism of non-cause as cause. For this is not the reason why he did and taught many other things, namely in order to teach different things; but it was so that he might set forth the same doctrine in various ways of teaching, and confirm it by various miracles. It does not follow, therefore, that they were superfluous, since they had their own end.

units.la: Simile. Apostolus etiam ad Romanos: variis & multis argumentis docet, hominem iustificari sola fide. Ergone superuacanea sunt omnia argumenta præter unum præcipuum ? Chrysostomi testimonio confirmatur Interpretatio Actor.1. Scripsi de omni-bus quæ cœpit Iesus & facere & docere: Non dixit omnia, sed de omnibus, scilicet ad salutem necessariis.
units.tr: Parallel. The Apostle also, to the Romans, by various and many arguments teaches that man is justified by faith alone. Are then all the arguments superfluous except the one chief one? The interpretation of Acts 1. is confirmed by the testimony of Chrysostom: I wrote of all the things that Jesus began both to do and to teach. He did not say all things, but of all things, namely those necessary to salvation.

units.la: 3. Act.1. post resurrectionem, per dies 4o. fuit Christus cum discipulis, & loquens de Regno Dei: & tamen admodum pauca describit Lucas & Euangelistæ. Non ergo o-mnia scripta.
units.tr: 3. Acts 1. After the resurrection, for forty days, Christ was with the disciples, speaking of the kingdom of God; and yet Luke and the Evangelists describe very few things. Therefore not everything was written down.

units.la: Respo. Locutus est de regno Dei, sed non diuersa in substantia ab illis, quæ ante etiam mortem docuerat. Neque tamen sequitur, Ergo superuacanea: quia valebant ad con-firmandos Apostolos in iam ante audita recepta doctrina Euangelij. Et ita Cypr. exponit tract. 40. qui est de idolorum vanitate, ad calcem. Aut enim, apparuisse per 40. dies, ut denuo ad praecepta vitalia instrui possent, &c.
units.tr: Answer: he spoke of the kingdom of God, but not things different in substance from those which he had taught even before his death. Nor does it follow, therefore, that they were superfluous; for they were of value for confirming the Apostles in the doctrine of the Gospel already heard and received. And so Cyprian expounds it in tract 40, which is on the vanity of idols, at the end: for either he appeared for forty days so that they might again be instructed in the vital precepts, etc.

units.la: 4. Actor. 20. Apostolis ait, Christum solitum fuisse dicere, Beatius esse dare, quam accipere. Nullus tamen Euangelista retulit hoc. Ergo non omnia scripta.
units.tr: 4. Acts 20. He says to the Apostles that Christ was accustomed to say, It is more blessed to give than to receive. Yet no Evangelist reported this. Therefore not everything was written.

units.la: Respon. Quid ineptius hoc argumento? 1. Si non scriptum ab Euangelistis, scriptum est ab Apostolo Paulo. 2. Etsi hoc dictum non fuisset in literas relatum, non propterea tamen doctrina salutis esset manca.
units.tr: Answer: what could be more absurd than this argument? First, if it was not written by the Evangelists, it was written by the Apostle Paul. Second, even if this saying had not been recorded in writing, the doctrine of salvation would nevertheless not be deficient.

units.la: 5. Act. 15. Visum est Spiritui S. & nobis, ut abstineatis a sanguine, suffocato, idolothytis, & fornicatione, &c. Quaedam igitur didicerunt a Spiritu sancto, & non a Christo.
units.tr: 5. Acts 15. "It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us that you abstain from blood, from what is strangled, from idolothytes, and from fornication, etc." Some things, therefore, they learned from the Holy Spirit, and not from Christ.

units.la: Resp. 1. Nihil novi fuit hic constitutum, quod summatim in lege antea non fuisset traditum. De idolothytis & fornicatione liquet: de aliis duobus suffocato & sanguine, liquet hinc, quia nihil prohibent, nisi ne dent scandalum infirmis fratribus ex Iudaismo, sua libertate. Non esse autem in rebus adiaphoris scandalo offendendum fratrem, antea docuerat Prophetae & in primis Christus. Matth. 18. Va[?] qui scandalizaverit unum ex iis pusillis,
units.tr: Answer. 1. Nothing new was laid down here that had not already been handed down in summary form in the law. The point about idolothytes and fornication is clear; the other two, what is strangled and blood, are also clear from this, since they forbid nothing except that they should not give offence to weak brethren from Judaism by their liberty. That a brother is not to be offended by scandal in matters indifferent, the prophets and above all Christ had taught beforehand. Matt. 18. "Woe to him who shall offend one of these little ones."

units.la: 2. Quod vero dicunt, Visum est Spiritui S. non autem Christo: hoc ideo faciunt, ut ostendant Spiritum sanctum idem sibi di-ctitasse, &itasse[?], quod antea etiam Christus docue-rat de non praebendo scandalo fratribus in-firmis: & ita confirmare, quod Christus de Spiritu dixerat, Non loquetur a semetipso: De meo enim accipiet, & annunciabit vobis. Proin-de non sequitur, illos aliquid noui tum didi-cisse: imo hoc nil fuit, quam declaratio eius, quod dixerat Christus, Ioh. 14. Suggeret vobis omnia, quacunq; dixi vobis.
units.tr: 2. As for their saying, "It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit," and not to Christ, they do this so as to show that the Holy Spirit dictated to them the same thing that Christ had already taught earlier about not giving offence to weak brethren; and thus to confirm what Christ had said of the Spirit, "He shall not speak of himself; for he shall receive of mine, and shall declare it to you." Therefore it does not follow that they learned anything new at that time. Indeed, this was nothing but a declaration of what Christ had said, John 14. "He shall bring to your remembrance all things whatsoever I have said to you."

units.la: 6. 1.Cor.7. Multa tradit Apostolus, & insti-tuit in Ecclesiis, quae tamen non accepit a Christo. Ergo non omnia Christus docuit necessaria ad salutem Ecclesiarum. Illud li-quet 1.Cor.7. Iubet fidelem retinere infidelem-coniugem, si velit manere: sin minus, sinat abire: & postea ait, se hac docere, non Dominum praecipere. Ita cap.14. multa alia.
units.tr: 6. 1 Cor. 7. "The Apostle hands down many things, and instituted in the churches, which nevertheless he did not receive from Christ." Therefore Christ did not teach everything necessary for the salvation of the churches. That is clear from 1 Cor. 7: "He commands the believing husband not to put away the unbelieving wife, if she is willing to remain; but if not, let her depart," and afterwards he says that he teaches this, "not the Lord commanding." So also in chapter 14, many other things.

units.la: Resp. Negatur antecedens, Apostolum scilicet non accepisse a Christo, quae docuit: Aperte enim ait, εAn experimentum quaeritis eius, qui in me loquitur, Christi? Item 14.de illis praeceptis a se traditis in Ecclesia, aperte ait esse Domini mandata, dicendo: Si quis sit inter vos Propheta, aut spiritualis, agnoscat quae scribo, Domini esse mandata.
units.tr: Answer. The antecedent is denied, namely that the Apostle did not receive from Christ what he taught. For he plainly says, "Do you seek a proof of him who speaks in me, Christ?" Likewise, in chapter 14, concerning those precepts he had laid down in the Church, he plainly says they are the commandments of the Lord, saying: "If anyone among you is a prophet, or spiritual, let him acknowledge that the things I write are the commandments of the Lord."

units.la: εAt 1.Corinth.7. ait, Non Dominus, sed ego.
units.tr: "But in 1 Corinthians 7 he says, Not the Lord, but I."

units.la: Resp. Discrimen facit Apostolus inter praecepta Christi: quaedam sunt, quae ex ipsius ore expressa, tradita sunt Apostolis omnibus, ut illud de non dimittenda uxore, eiusdem scilicet religionis, nisi propter adulterium: alia sunt non ex ore immediate Christi expressa, sed ex eius generali doctrina de charitate per Spiritum sanctum, quo duce scripturas interpretabantur Apostoli, collecta: ut illud 1. Corinth. 7. Ideo ait, Puto autem, quod & ego Spiritum Dei habeam. Pulcre enim illud congruit cum charitate. Idem dico de aliis praeceptis. 1 Corinth. 11. & 14. Est igitur fallacia ὁμωνυμίας [?]: quia praeceptum Christi accipitur bifariam, ut declaratum est. Papistae autem uno semper modo accipiunt.
units.tr: Answer. The Apostle makes a distinction between the precepts of Christ. Some are those that were expressed from his own mouth and delivered to all the apostles, such as that about not dismissing a wife of the same religion, except on account of adultery. Others are not expressed directly from the mouth of Christ, but gathered from his general teaching about love, through the Holy Spirit, under whose guidance the apostles interpreted the Scriptures; such as that in 1 Corinthians 7: "So I say, but I think that I also have the Spirit of God." For this fits beautifully with love. I say the same of the other precepts, 1 Corinthians 11 and 14. There is therefore an equivocation of terms, since the precept of Christ is taken in two ways, as has been explained. The Papists, however, always take it in one way only.

units.la: 7. 1. Thessal. 4. Nostis quae praecepta (παραγ-γελίας, hoc est, accepta mandata) dederimus vobis per Dominum Iesum: Et tamen haec non sunt scripta: nec etiam exponit, quae fuerint. Ergo multa mandata Christi in Ecclesia, relicta per Apostolos sine scripto.
units.tr: 7. 1 Thess. 4. "You know what precepts (παραγγελίας, that is, received commandments) we gave you through the Lord Jesus." And yet these were not written down, nor does he explain what they were. Therefore many commandments of Christ were left in the Church by the apostles without writing.

units.la: Respon. 1. Damus hic loqui Apostolum de praeceptis seu mandatis, quae per manus accipiuntur & traduntur. Qui enim mandat, dicitur διαγγέλλειν [?], hoc est, per alium significare: Qui vero denunciat, quasi per manus acceptum, παραγγέλλειν [?], hoc est, per alium significare: ac proinde loqui Apostolum hic de iis, quae acceperat à Christo, voce, non scripto: sicut & 1. Corinth. 11. de Coena ait, Ego accepi à Domino, quod & tradidi.
units.tr: Answer. 1. We grant that the Apostle here speaks of precepts or commandments that are received and handed on by hand. For one who commands is said to "announce" (διαγγέλλειν), that is, to signify through another; but one who charges, as something received by hand, "delivers a charge" (παραγγέλλειν), that is, to signify through another. And accordingly the Apostle here speaks of those things which he had received from Christ by word of mouth, not in writing; just as in 1 Corinthians 11 he says of the Supper, "I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you."

units.la: Sed 2. quod postea aiunt, non esse scripta, nec exprimi, quaenam haec fuerint, negamus. Nam mox Apostolus, quaenam fuerint haec mandata Domini, declarat, dicendo: Enimvero haec est voluntas Dei (nempe) sanctificatio vestra, ut scilicet abstineatis à fornicatione:& quæ sequuntur vsq; ad ea verba: Pro-inde, qui hac reiicit, non reiicit hominem, sed Deum. Sunt igitur scripta hæc mandata Do-mini. Quare pudeat Papistas hæc scribere impudentissima mendacia.
units.tr: But secondly, as to what they say afterwards, that these were not written down and it is not expressed what they were, we deny it. For immediately the Apostle declares what these commandments of the Lord were, saying: "For this is the will of God, namely your sanctification, that you abstain from fornication," and what follows, down to these words: "Therefore, he who rejects these things does not reject man, but God." These commandments of the Lord are therefore written. Wherefore let the Papists be ashamed to write such most shameless lies.

units.la: 8. 1. Cor.II. Cùm docuisset, velandas esse mulieres, cùm in Ecclesia orant, aut Prophetant: postea subdit, Si quis videtur contentiosus esse, nos talem consuetudinem non habemus, neque Ecclesia Dei. Ecce vrget eos (inquiunt) vt curent mulieres velandas, & obediant sine contentione, in re non magni momenti, & vrget hoc, consuetudine sola Ecclesiæ, sine vllo scripto. Ergo parendum Ecclesiæ in rebus etiam leuibus, sine contentione, tantùm propter consuetudinem.
units.tr: 8. 1 Cor. 11. When he had taught that women must be veiled when they pray or prophesy in the Church, he afterwards adds: "If anyone seems to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor does the Church of God." Behold, they urge (they say) that women be veiled and obey without contention in a matter of no great moment, and they urge this on the sole basis of the custom of the Church, without any writing. Therefore one must obey the Church even in light matters, without contention, merely on account of custom.

units.la: Respon. 1. ad Antecedens: scio multos sic interpretari, vt illa verba, Nos non habemus talem consuetudinem, referantur ad mulieres velandas: quasi dicat: Quòd si quis renuat velare mulieres, & velit esse sine velo: agat vt velit. Quod nos attinet Hebræos, & Ecclesias Dei, non habemus talem consuetudinem, scilicet permittendi, vt mulieres sint detecto capite. Sed tamen mihi magis placet, vt referantur hæc verba, ad contentio-sum esse, vt fit sensus: Quòd si quis in hac re indifferenti, nolit acquiescere nostræ sententiæ, sed contendere: nos certè nolumus contendere. Non enim habemus talem consuetudinem, contendendi scilicet, neque etiam Ecclesiæ Christi. Et ita est. Verus Christianus fugit contentiones inanes & φι-λονεικίας[?].
units.tr: Answer. 1. As to the antecedent: I know that many interpret the words, "We have no such custom," as referring to the veiling of women, as if he said: If anyone refuses to veil women and wishes to be without a veil, let him act as he wishes. As for us, the Hebrews and the churches of God, we have no such custom, namely of permitting women to be with uncovered heads. But I prefer that these words be referred to "contentious," so that the sense is: If anyone in this indifferent matter is unwilling to acquiesce in our opinion, but contends, we certainly are unwilling to contend. For we have no such custom, namely of contending, nor does the Church of Christ. And so it is. The true Christian flees empty contentions and strifes.

units.la: 2. Ad illationem. Neque nos negamus, Ecclesiæ consuetudines esse seruandas etiam in leuibus rebus & adiaphoris: idq; propter pacem & charitatem, modo illæ res non pugnent cum verbo Dei: deinde maneant adiaphorç[?], hoc est non iniungantur tanquam necessariæ ad salutem; & sub pœna (vt vocant Papistæ) peccati mortalis, & vacuæ sint ab omni superstitione. Sed quid hoc ad rem, de qua disputatur? & ad consuetudines, quæ sunt in Ecclesia Romana, aut pugnantes cum verbo Dei, aut coniunctas cum superstitione, & cum laqueis conscientiæ? Deinde loquimur de iis, quæ ad salutem sunt necessaria, non de rebus adiaphoris. Quare locus hic nihil facit ad rem.
units.tr: 2. As to the inference: we also do not deny that the customs of the Church are to be observed even in light matters and things indifferent, and that for the sake of peace and charity, provided those things do not conflict with the word of God; and further that they remain indifferent, that is, are not imposed as necessary to salvation, and under penalty (as the Papists call it) of mortal sin, and are free from all superstition. But what does this have to do with the matter under dispute? And with the customs that exist in the Roman Church, which either conflict with the word of God or are joined with superstition and with snares of conscience? Moreover, we are speaking of those things which are necessary to salvation, not of things indifferent. Wherefore this passage has nothing to do with the question.

units.la: 9. 1Corinth.ii, Cùm explicasset de Cœ-na quæ erant essentialia, postea dixit, Cætera, cum venero disponam. Hic (inquiunt) Apostolus promittit, se viva voce & coram dispositurum, quæ pertinebant ad modum communionis, & celebrandi Cœnam: & alia ad statum Ecclesiæ pertinentia. Non est autem dubitandum quin præstiterit promissa. Multa igitur sunt, quæ pertinent ad bonum & salutem Ecclesiæ, quæ non scripta.
units.tr: 9. 1 Cor. 11. When he had explained the essential things about the Supper, he afterwards said: "The rest I will set in order when I come." Here (they say) the Apostle promises that he will set in order, by word of mouth and in person, the things that pertained to the manner of communion and of celebrating the Supper, and other things pertaining to the state of the Church. Yet there is no doubt that he performed what he promised. Therefore there are many things which pertain to the good and salvation of the Church that were not written.

units.la: Resp. ad Antecedens. 1. Illud verbum Dis-ponam, quod Græcè est διαλέξομαι[?], non semper significat, noua ponere statura: sed significat etiam, ea in ordinem redigere, quæ antea fuerant confusa.Et sic accepit hoc verbum Apostolus 1.Corinth.7. Cum dixit, Et sic omnibus Ecclesiis διατάγμαι[?], ordino, constituo, nempe ut quisque in sua se vocatione contineat, nec ordines politicos confundat: seruus maneat seruus: circumcisus ne adducat praeputium. Quare ex hoc loco 1.ad Corinth.11. nil potest concludi de nouis ordinationibus à Paulo institutis in Ecclesia Corinthiaca,circa Coenam Domini,aut aliis. Nam fieri potest, vt verba fecerit de multis grauibus rebus, quae in ea Ecclesia fuerint confusae & disturbatae, & pollicitus sit, se cum venerit,curaturum, vt omnia ad pristinum bonum statum restituantur. Quale erat, quòd inter se essent diuisi.
units.tr: Answer to the antecedent. 1. That word "I will set in order" (Greek διαλέξομαι, or rather διατάξομαι), does not always signify to lay down new ordinances, but also signifies to bring into order things that had previously been confused. And the Apostle takes the word in this way in 1 Corinthians 7, when he said: "And so I ordain (διατάσσομαι) in all the churches," that is, he lays down that each person should remain in his own calling, and not confuse the civil orders: a slave should remain a slave; the circumcised should not seek to remove the foreskin. Therefore from this passage in 1 Corinthians 11 nothing can be concluded about new ordinances instituted by Paul in the Corinthian Church concerning the Lord's Supper or other matters. For it may be that he spoke of many weighty matters that had become confused and disturbed in that church, and promised that when he came he would take care that all things be restored to their former good state. Such as the fact that they were divided among themselves.

units.la: 2. Quod aiunt illum disposuisse, quomodo Missa esset celebranda, & communio sumenda: quis ferat has ineptias?
units.tr: 2. As for their claim that he laid down how the Mass should be celebrated and how communion should be taken: who could put up with these silly inventions?

units.la: Ad illationem: Concedimus, multa fuisse instituta ab Apostolis in Ecclesiis, quae non sint scripta: sed negamus fuisse talia, quae ad salutem essent necessaria.
units.tr: To the inference: We grant that many things were instituted by the Apostles in the churches which are not written down; but we deny that there were any such things as were necessary to salvation.

units.la: 10. 2. Timoth 2. Tu ergo Fili, confortare in gratia, quae est per Christum Iesum: & quae audisti a me inter multos testes: haec committe fidelibus hominibus, qui erunt idonei ad alios quoque docendos. Hic Apostolus (inquiunt) loquitur de doctrina salutis. Dicit se eam tradidisse Timotheo non per scripta, sed coram inter multos testes: & tamen hanc non explicat. Ergo in Ecclesia relicta est doctrina ad salutem neccessaria, quæ tamen scripta non est.
units.tr: 10. 2 Timothy 2. Therefore, my son, be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus; and the things you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit these to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also. Here the Apostle (they say) speaks of the doctrine of salvation. He says he delivered it to Timothy not in writings but in the presence of many witnesses; and yet he does not explain it. Therefore a doctrine necessary to salvation has been left in the Church, which nevertheless is not written down.

units.la: Resp. ad Antecedens: quòd aiunt hanc doctrinam ab Apostolo non fuisse explicatam in libris, cùm hoc probauerint, manum dabimus. Quomodo tantus Apostolus tam diligenter de multis rebus adiaphoris scripsit, vt liquet in epistola ad Corinth. & ad Timoth. & postea neglexit eam doctrinam literis committere quæ necessaria erat ad salutem? Quare quod inferunt: Ergo aliqua doctrina ad salutem necessaria, in Ecclesia relicta est sine scripto: totum hoc ἀσυλλόγιστον[?] est.
units.tr: Reply to the antecedent: that they say this doctrine was not explained by the Apostle in the books, we will concede, since they have proved it. How could so great an Apostle have written so carefully about many matters of indifference, as is clear in the epistles to the Corinthians and to Timothy, and afterwards have neglected to commit to writing that doctrine which was necessary to salvation? Therefore what they infer, "Therefore some doctrine necessary to salvation has been left in the Church unwritten," is entirely ἀσυλλόγιστον[?], that is, without valid reasoning.

units.la: II. Johan. Canonica. Plura habeo quæ scribam, sed nolui per calamum & atramentum: spero enim me venturum ad vos, & ore ad os loquiturum. Ergo multa docuit coràm, quæ scripta non sunt.
units.tr: II. John, Canonical Epistle. I have many things to write to you, but I did not wish to do so with pen and ink; for I hope to come to you and speak face to face. Therefore he taught many things orally which are not written down.

units.la: Resp. 1. Non dicit, docere & tradere doctrinam salutis, sed locuturum se ore ad os. Erant igitur secretiora quædam ad illos pertinentia tantùm, quæ nolebat literis committere. Quare nihil concludunt de doctrina salutis. 2. Esto: de doctrina salutis loquatur: non sequitur tamen illatio, illam igitur non esse comprehensam in suis epistolis.
units.tr: Reply: 1. He does not say that he teaches and hands down the doctrine of salvation, but that he will speak face to face. There were therefore certain more secret matters pertaining only to them, which he did not wish to commit to writing. Hence they conclude nothing about the doctrine of salvation. 2. Granted that he speaks of the doctrine of salvation: the inference does not follow, that it was therefore not contained in his epistles.

units.la: 12. Ioh.14.&16. Item Actor.1. Promittitur Ecclesiæ S.S. vt illi semper assistat, & deducat in omnem veritatem. Atqui hoc esset superuacaneum, si omnia essent scripta. Ergo, &c.
units.tr: 12. John 14 and 16. Likewise Acts 1. It is promised to the Church of the Holy Spirit that he will always be present with her and lead her into all truth. But this would be superfluous if everything had been written. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Resp. Negatur Minor, & est fallacia non causæ. Causa enim, cur Spiritus S. datus sit Ecclesiæ, & singulis fidelibus, non est, vt nouam subinde doceat doctrinam, sed alia sunt causae multae, ut regatur in suis actionibus, ut defendantur a Sarhana : Item ut eam in recepta doctrina conferuet, & in fide. Quare nil concludit.
units.tr: Reply: The minor premise is denied, and it is a fallacy of non-cause. For the cause why the Holy Spirit was given to the Church and to individual believers is not so that he may from time to time teach a new doctrine, but there are many other causes: that she may be governed in her actions, that she may be defended against the Sarhana; likewise that she may preserve that doctrine which has been received, and the faith. Therefore it concludes nothing.

units.la: 13. ✱Act.10.11. Apostoli etiam post acce-ptum Spiritum S.ignorabant, An ad gratiam Euangelij admittendi essent Gentiles: Ergo non omnia didicerunt à Christo: nec statim à Spiritu sancto : sed longo post tempore, cùm placuit Deo. Quare idem fit in Ecclesia, ut successiuè multa reuelentur.
units.tr: 13. Acts 10 and 11. The Apostles, even after receiving the Holy Spirit, did not know whether Gentiles were to be admitted to the grace of the Gospel. Therefore they did not learn everything from Christ, nor immediately from the Holy Spirit, but after a long time, when it pleased God. Hence the same thing happens in the Church, that many things are revealed successively.

units.la: Resp. ad Antecedens. 1. Falsum assumunt: imò Christus praedixerat saepe, ut Matth.11. Multi venient ab Oriente. Item Matth.28. & Marc.16. Praedicate Euangelium omni creatu-ra. Item, Docete omnes Gentes. Sed quòd etiam post resurrectionem dubitarint, idcirco factum est, quia videbatur absurdum & inauditum, quòd Gentes deberent esse participes gratiae. 2. Non erat haec res ex illorum genere, quae necessaria cognitu sunt ad salutem: Nos autem de iis disputamus. Nihil igitur concluditur.
units.tr: Reply to the antecedent. 1. They assume what is false: indeed Christ had often foretold it, as in Matthew 8: Many shall come from the east. Likewise Matthew 28 and Mark 16: Preach the gospel to every creature. Likewise, Teach all nations. But that they doubted even after the resurrection happened for this reason, because it seemed absurd and unheard of that the Gentiles should be partakers of grace. 2. This matter was not of the kind which is necessary to know for salvation; but it is about these things that we are disputing. Nothing therefore follows.

units.la: 14. ✱Ad extremum vrgent nomen Traditionis ex Epistolis Pauli, ut 1. Corinth.11. Laudo vos, quod omnia mea memoria tenetis & sicut tradidi vobis, traditiones tenetis παραδόσεις κα-τηχήσεις[?]. Ibi tamen non exprimuntur. 2. Thess. 2. Itaque state fratres & tenete traditiones, quas didicistis, sive per sermonem, sive per Epistolam nostram. Traditiones autem sunt doctrinæ, & ordinationes atque institutiones non scriptæ, sed per manum traditæ, & ob hanc causam vocantur traditiones. Ergo Apo-li multa reliquerunt in Ecclesia non scripta: tam de doctrina salutis, quàm de ordinationibus Ecclesiasticis. Quare non omnia ad salutem necessaria, sunt in literis S. com-prehensa.
units.tr: 14. Finally, they press the name of Tradition from the Epistles of Paul, as in 1 Corinthians 11: I praise you, that you remember all my teachings and hold to the traditions, as I delivered them to you, παραδόσεις κα-τηχήσεις[?]. There, however, these things are not stated. 2 Thessalonians 2: So then, brethren, stand firm and hold to the traditions which you were taught, whether by word or by our epistle. Now traditions are doctrines, and ordinances and institutions not written down but handed down by hand, and for this reason they are called traditions. Therefore the Apostles left many things unwritten in the Church: as much of the doctrine of salvation as of ecclesiastical ordinances. Hence not everything necessary to salvation is comprehended in the Holy Scriptures.

units.la: Resp. ad Maiorem: Damus multas παραδό-σεις ab Apostolis in Ecclesiis [?]raditas [?] & reliquas.
units.tr: Reply to the major premise: We grant that there were many παραδόσεις handed down by the Apostles in the churches [?] and the rest.

units.la: Ad Minorem: Non uno modo tantùm accipitur nomen Traditio. Ideò hìc est ὁμω-νυμία.
units.tr: To the minor premise: The name Tradition is not taken in only one way. Therefore here there is ὁμωνυμία, that is, equivocation.

units.la: 1. Aliquando accipitur pro doctrina, quo vis modo primitus tradita, sive viva tantùm voce, sive per scripturam. Sic Act. 6. Lex scri-pta Mosis, vocatur Traditio: Homo iste (de Stephano loquitur) non cessat loqui verba adversus locum sanctum, & legem. Audivimus enim eum dicentem, quòd Iesus Nazarenus destruet locum istum, & mutabit τὰ ἔθη, ἃ παρέδωκεν ἡμῖν Moses. 2. Thess. 2. Tenete traditiones, quas didicistis sive per sermonem, sive per Epistolam nostram. Ergo si quid etiam doceat per solam epistolam, illud vocat Traditionem.
units.tr: 1. It is sometimes taken for doctrine, in whatever way it was first delivered, whether by living voice alone or in writing. Thus in Acts 6 the written Law of Moses is called Tradition: "This man (he is speaking of Stephen) does not cease to speak words against this holy place and the law. For we have heard him say that Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and change the customs τὰ ἔθη, ἃ παρέδωκεν ἡμῖν Moses, which Moses delivered to us." 2 Thessalonians 2: "Hold the traditions which you were taught, whether by word or by our epistle." Therefore, if he teaches anything through the epistle alone, he calls that Tradition.

units.la: 2. Accipitur pro doctrina, primùm quidem viva voce, sine scripto tradita, sed postea in literas etiam relata. Sic 1. Cor. 11. Doctrinam de Cœna, quam tradiderat primùm voce, & postea etiam scripto, vocat nomine Traditionis, dicendo: Ego enim accepi à Domino,quod & tradidi vobis. Sic 1.Thess. 4. Rogamus & obsecramus in Domino Iesu vt quem-admodum accepistis a nobis, quomodo oportet vos ambulare, & placere Deo, sic etiam ambulet is, vt abundetis magis. Scitis enim,quas παραγ-γελίας dederim vobis: & mox partem eorum, quæ tradiderat voce, etiam scripto repetit.
units.tr: 2. It is taken for doctrine which was first delivered by living voice, without writing, but afterwards was also related in writing. Thus in 1 Corinthians 11 he calls the doctrine about the Supper, which he had first delivered by voice and afterwards also in writing, by the name of Tradition, saying: For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you. So in 1 Thessalonians 4: We ask and beseech you in the Lord Jesus, that as you received from us how you ought to walk and to please God, so you would walk, that you may abound more and more. For you know what commands I gave you παραγγελίας; and soon after he repeats in writing part of what he had delivered by voice.

units.la: 2.Thess 1.[?] Tenete traditiones quas didicistis, siue per sermonem (primum) siue (postea) per Epistolam nostram. Hoc modo tota doctrina Euangelij in sacris literis comprehensa, appellari potest Traditio: quia scilicet primum fuit viua voce tradita, Deinde in libros relata. Sic Cyprianus totam Christi doctrinam, quæ in sacris Literis continetur, vocat sæpe Dominicam Traditionem.
units.tr: 2 Thessalonians 1 [?]: Hold the traditions which you were taught, whether by word (first) or (afterwards) by our epistle. In this way the whole doctrine of the Gospel comprehended in the sacred writings can be called Tradition, because it was first delivered by living voice, and then carried into books. So Cyprian often calls the whole doctrine of Christ, which is contained in the sacred Scriptures, the Lord's Tradition.

units.la: 3. Accipitur pro doctrina & institutione Patribus voce tantum tradita, & perpetua successione, quasi per manus ad posteros, sine vllo scripto deriuata: id quod multi Patres Græci vocant verbum ἄγραφον. Talis fuit doctrina ante Moisen, Patribus tradita, & ad Mosen vsque sine vllo scripto, continuata. Ergo etiamsi in Epistolis Apostolicis, sæpe mentio fiat παραδόσεων, & παραγγελιῶν: tamen non inde sequitur, Apostolos multas traditiones instituisse in Ecclesia, quæ non sint in sacris Literis contentæ. Nam semper dicam, quæ primum voce tradiderunt, eorum deinde summam scriptis cōplexi sunt, vt liquet de Cœna 1.Cor.11. Item 2.Thess.4. De præceptis honestæ vitæ. Item de Ecclesiasticis[?] ordinibus, de quibus 1. Corinth. ii. 14. Deinde, etiamsi dem, aliqua fuisse ab Apostolis instituta, quæ scripta non reliquerint: tamen semper dicam, & sic etiam contendo, nil ab illis fuisse institutum, quod non habuerit fundamentum in verbo Dei, hoc est, in literis Propheticis, & in doctrina Christi, ab Euangelistis etiam postmodum comprehensa libris. Præterea dicam, illa quæ scripta non tel[?] quærunt, non fuisse ad salutem necessaria. Quare hoc etiam argumentum nihil concludit contra nostram thesin, Omnia ad salutem necessaria, in sacris Literis perspicuè continneri.
units.tr: 3. It is taken for doctrine and institution delivered by the Fathers by voice alone, and derived by perpetual succession, as it were by hand to posterity, without any writing: which many of the Greek Fathers call the unwritten word, ἄγραφον. Such was the doctrine before Moses, handed down to the Fathers and continued without any writing until Moses. Therefore, even if in the Apostolic epistles mention is often made of παραδόσεις and παραγγελίαι, it does not follow from this that the Apostles instituted many traditions in the Church which are not contained in the sacred writings. For I will always say that what they first delivered by voice, they afterwards embraced in writings in summary, as is clear about the Supper in 1 Corinthians 11; likewise 2 Thessalonians 4 about precepts of honest living; likewise about ecclesiastical orders, concerning which 1 Corinthians 14. Then, even if I grant that some things were instituted by the Apostles which they left unwritten, I will still always say, and also contend, that nothing was instituted by them which did not have its foundation in the Word of God, that is, in the prophetic writings and in the doctrine of Christ, afterwards also comprehended in the books of the Evangelists. Moreover I will say that those things which are not sought in writing were not necessary to salvation. Therefore this argument also concludes nothing against our thesis, that all things necessary to salvation are clearly contained in the sacred writings.

units.la: Ad argumenta secunda Classis,
units.tr: To the second class of arguments

units.la: 1. Ad salutem necessarium est, credere & scire, hoc quod habemus in libris, quos vocant Canonicos, esse verbum Dei: Et de hoc nulla est controuersia. Atqui hoc non tradit scriptura. Neque enim illa explicat, qui sint Canonici, qui minùs: sed ex sola habetur traditione. Ergo aliqua sunt necessaria ad salutem, quæ non continentur in sacris Literis, sed tantùm habentur ex traditione Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: 1. It is necessary for salvation to believe and know that what we have in the books which they call Canonical is the Word of God; and about this there is no controversy. But Scripture does not teach this. For it does not explain which books are canonical and which are less so; this is known from tradition alone. Therefore some things are necessary for salvation which are not contained in the Holy Scriptures, but are had only from the tradition of the Church.

units.la: Resp. Negatur Minor, nempe quòd scriptura non tradat, se esse verbum Dei: & quòd sola Ecclesiæ traditione hoc agnoscatur. Antea a nobis in quæstione secunda de scripturis declaratum est, quibus modis agnoscere certò possimus, hanc scripturam esse verbum Dei: & in summa demonstratum, Ecclesiæ traditionem, ad hanc rem multū prodesse, sed non sufficere: quòd opus fit Spiritu sancto oculos ad cognoscendam aperiente & persuadente: hoc autem habito, mox scripturam sese patefacere, cuius fit verbum. Nam etiam non alia ratione illi primi Patres hoc agnouerunt, nisi partim traditione, partim autem & maximè Spiritu sancto scripturæ ipsius dignitatem, veritatem, & cœlestem maiestatem demonstrante. Est igitur fallacia non causæ vt causæ. Non enim sola Ecclesiæ traditio hoc præstat: sed etiam, idque in primis, scripturæ ipsius dignitas, per Spiritum sanctum nobis patefacta. Alioqui si valeret argumentum: hoc etiam valeret: Ecclesia est illa, quæ primùm prædicat verbum, & hanc doctrinam, Christum esse Filium Dei, verumque Deum. Ergo quòd Christus sit verus Deus, non habemus nisi ab Ecclesia per traditionem, & non è scripturis. Est autem hoc impium. Ergo, &c.
units.tr: Reply. I deny the minor premise, namely that Scripture does not teach that it is the Word of God, and that this is recognised by the tradition of the Church alone. Earlier, in our second question concerning the Scriptures, we explained by what means we can know with certainty that this Scripture is the Word of God, and we showed in summary that the tradition of the Church helps greatly in this matter, but is not sufficient; for the Holy Spirit is needed to open and persuade the eyes to recognise it. Once this is granted, Scripture itself straightway makes manifest whose word it is. For the first Fathers also recognised this in no other way than partly by tradition, but chiefly by the Holy Spirit, who demonstrated the dignity, truth and heavenly majesty of Scripture itself. It is therefore a fallacy of not the cause as the cause. For the tradition of the Church is not alone in accomplishing this; the dignity of Scripture itself, revealed to us through the Holy Spirit, does so too, and chiefly so. Otherwise, if the argument held, this would hold as well: the Church is that which first preaches the Word, and this doctrine, that Christ is the Son of God and true God. Therefore we have the fact that Christ is true God only from the Church through tradition, and not from the Scriptures. But this is impious. Therefore, and so on.

units.la: Scio non deesse, & ex Patribus & è nostris, qui scribant, hoc nos habere ex sola Ecclesiæ traditione: sed intelligunt quoad initia huius cognitionis primumque testimonium: non autem quoad veram certamque cognitionem. Illud certum & firmum semper manet Rom. 10. Fides ex auditu: auditus per verbum Christi. Non potest igitur verè credi hoc esse verbum Dei, nisi ex auditu[?] huius verbi, opera Spiritus S. illuminantis & docentis.
units.tr: I know that there are not lacking, both among the Fathers and among our own writers, those who write that we have this from the tradition of the Church alone; but they mean this with respect to the beginnings of this knowledge and the first testimony, not with respect to the true and certain knowledge. That remains always certain and firm: Romans 10, "Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ." Therefore it cannot truly be believed that this is the Word of God unless from the hearing of this Word, by the work of the Holy Spirit illuminating and teaching.

units.la: 2. Articulum de Trinitate est necessarium ad salutem, de omnium consensu:& tamen hoc non habemus è scripturis, sed ex traditione sola Ecclesia.
units.tr: 2. The article concerning the Trinity is necessary for salvation, by the agreement of all; and yet we do not have this from the Scriptures, but from the tradition of the Church alone.

units.la: Resp. Alterum huius propositionis membrum salsissimum est, & impiissimè scriptum. Ergo fides nostra in primo articulo religionis nostrae pendet non è scripturis, sed à sola Ecclesiae traditione? Contrarium docent scripturae ipsae tam in veteri, quàm Novo Testamento, vt aliàs ostendam: Duo loci satis sunto[?] in praesentia. Iohan. 16. Cùm venerit Paracletus, quem ego mittam à Patre, spiritus veritatis, ille vos deducet in omnem veritatem. Ille accipiet de meo. Hic habes Patrem, à quo Christus erat Spiritum S. missurus. Habes Filium, qui mittit: Spiritum sanctum missum: etsi tamen unum tantum Deum, ubiq; docet scriptura.
units.tr: Reply. The second part of this proposition is most insipid and written most impiously. Therefore is our faith in the first article of our religion dependent not on the Scriptures but on the tradition of the Church alone? The Scriptures themselves, both in the Old and in the New Testament, teach the contrary, as I shall show elsewhere. Two passages are enough for the present. John 16: "When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send from the Father, the Spirit of truth, he will lead you into all truth. He will take from what is mine." Here you have the Father, from whom Christ was to send the Holy Spirit. You have the Son, who sends; the Holy Spirit is sent. And yet Scripture everywhere teaches only one God.

units.la: 1.Ioan.5. Tres sunt qui testimonium dant in coelo, &c.
units.tr: 1 John 5: "There are three who bear witness in heaven, etc."

units.la: Tertullianus contrà sentit, quàm Papistæ, lib. contra Praxeam, scripturas omnes praedicare Trinitatem, & unum Deum.
units.tr: Tertullian thinks otherwise than the Papists, in his book against Praxeas, that all the Scriptures proclaim the Trinity and one God.

units.la: 3. Christum esse coaequalem & consubstan-tialem ὁμοούσιον Patri, credimus omnes, & necessa-rium est articulum in Ecclesia. Nec tamen è scripturis habetur, sed ex traditione. Ergo, &c.
units.tr: 3. We all believe that Christ is co-equal and consubstantial with the Father, homoousios, and it is necessary for the Church to hold this article. Yet it is not had from the Scriptures, but from tradition. Therefore, and so on.

units.la: Resp. Falsum assumtum. Zach.13. Excitare ogladie[?] in Pastorem meum, & in virumsocium, parem, coaequalem mihi. Est autem de Christo intelligendum, quia Christus de se hoc citat testimonium. Iohan.10. Ego & Pater unum sumus. Iohan.5. Æqualem se faciens Deo. Item, Ego in Patre, Pater in me. Iohan.10. Facis te Deum, cum sis homo.
units.tr: Reply. The assumption is false. Zechariah 13: "Awake, O sword, against my shepherd, and against the man who is my fellow, equal to me." This must be understood of Christ, because Christ cites this testimony about himself. John 10: "I and the Father are one." John 5: "making himself equal to God." Likewise, "I am in the Father, and the Father in me." John 10: "You make yourself God, though you are a man."

units.la: Deinde, quomodo igitur Patres refutarunt Arium, si scripturis non potuit convinci? Quomodo verum illud, scripturam valere ad ἔλεγχον? Augustinus contra Maximin. demonstrat id ex sacra scriptura.
units.tr: Then, how did the Fathers refute Arius, if he could not be convicted from the Scriptures? How is that true which says that Scripture is sufficient for refutation? Augustine, against Maximinus, demonstrates this from Holy Scripture.

units.la: 4. Duas esse naturas in Christo, humanam & divinam, articulus est ad salutem cognitu necessarius. At non est in Scripturis.
units.tr: 4. That Christ has two natures, human and divine, is an article necessary to know for salvation. But it is not in the Scriptures.

units.la: Resp. Falsissimum hoc est. Iohan.10. Potestatem habeo ponendi Animam, & potestatem habeo iterum sumendi eam. Ergo Deus & homo. 2. Corinth.13. Mortuus ex infirmitate, vivit ex virtute Dei. 1 Petr.3. Mortificatus quidem carne, vivificatus autem spiritu, &c.
units.tr: Reply. This is most false. John 10: "I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again." Therefore God and man. 2 Corinthians 13: "He was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God." 1 Peter 3: "put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the spirit, etc."

units.la: 5. De duabus in Christo voluntatibus nihil esse expressum in Scripturis.
units.tr: 5. Nothing is expressed in the Scriptures about two wills in Christ.

units.la: Resp. Imo 1. sunt in Christo duæ naturæ distinctæ, humana & divina: Ergo duæ voluntates. Utraque enim suam habet voluntatem. 2. Patres damnarunt Monotheletas in Concilio Constantinopolitano 6 ex scripturis, Ergo &c. 3. Luc.22. Pater, transfer at calixi-fte: veruntamen non mea, sed tua voluntas fiat.
units.tr: Reply. Indeed: 1. there are in Christ two distinct natures, human and divine; therefore two wills, for each nature has its own will. 2. The Fathers condemned the Monothelites at the Sixth Council of Constantinople from the Scriptures; therefore, and so on. 3. Luke 22: "Father, if you are willing, take this cup from me; nevertheless, not my will, but yours be done."

units.la: 6. De anima & mente Christi nihil esse in sacra Scriptura. Resp. Nego. Matth. 26. Tristis est anima mea usque ad mortem. Heb.2. Per omnia fratribus similis factus, excepto peccato. Luc.2. Iesus profecit sapientia. Ergo habebat mentem, ubi sapientia.
units.tr: 6. Nothing about the soul and mind of Christ is in Holy Scripture. Reply. I deny it. Matthew 26: "My soul is sorrowful even unto death." Hebrews 2: "made like his brothers in every respect, except sin." Luke 2: "Jesus increased in wisdom." Therefore he had a mind, in which there was wisdom.

units.la: 7. Spiritus sanctus procedit à Patre & Filio: ut omnes concedunt: non tamen est hoc in Scripturis. Ergo,&c.
units.tr: 7. The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, as all concede; yet this is not in the Scriptures. Therefore, and so on.

units.la: Resp. August. contra Maxim. Arriminens. Episcopum, lib. 13. c.14. & deinceps contrarium probat e scripturis. Ioh.15. Ego mittam, eum à Patre, &c.
units.tr: Reply. Augustine, against Maximinus, the Arian bishop, book 13, chapter 14, and onward, proves the contrary from the Scriptures. John 15: "I will send him from the Father, etc."

units.la: 8. De virginitate Maria etiam post partum: & tamen unde e scripturis probari po-test?
units.tr: 8. The virginity of Mary, even after the birth, is also held; and yet from what Scripture can it be proved?

units.la: Resp. Epiphanius contra Antidico Ma-rianitas, lib. 3. Tom. 2, conatur e scripturis probare. Idem alij. Sed ego dicam, hoc ideo nos credere, quia pium est sic sentire de virgine Maria, cùm nullum habeamus certum in contrariam partem testimonium, & multis aliis de causis. Cæterum, nego talem esse articulum fidei, ut qui hoc non credat, idcir-co pro hæretico haberi debeat, aut obiturus ille sit mortem æternam.
units.tr: Reply. Epiphanius, against Antidicomarianites, book 3, vol. 2, attempts to prove it from the Scriptures, and others likewise. But I say that we believe this because it is pious to think thus of the Virgin Mary, since we have no certain testimony to the contrary, and for many other reasons. Moreover, I deny that it is such an article of faith that whoever does not believe it should therefore be held a heretic, or that he will undergo eternal death.

units.la: 9. Symbolum Apostolicum quàm necessa-rium sit, ut firma fide credamus & confitea-mur, nemo est qui nesciat. Non est tamen in scripturis.
units.tr: 9. How necessary it is that we believe and confess the Apostles' Creed with firm faith, no one is ignorant. Yet it is not in the Scriptures.

units.la: Resp. Etsi non ibi sit hæc forma & ordo verborum: est tamen tota doctrinæ substan-tia. Fallacia igitur Accidentis.
units.tr: Reply. Even if this form and order of words is not there, the whole substance of the doctrine is there. This is therefore a fallacy of the accident.

units.la: 10. Baptizandos etiam esse paruulos, non habemus (inquiunt) expressum in sacris Literis: & tamen damus omnes, esse baptizan-dos.
units.tr: 10. They say that we do not have it expressed in the Holy Scriptures that infants are also to be baptised; and yet we all grant that they are to be baptised.

units.la: Resp. Etsi non extet præceptum Christi verbis expressum hac de re: ex ipsis tamen scripturis, vti ex doctrina de fœdere, & de filiis fidelium perspicuè & necessariò colli-gitur, vt suprà à nobis ostensum fuit. Iubet enim Christus obsignari sibi, quicunque in suum fœdus recipiuntur, Matth. 28. Atqui filij fidelium in fœdus sunt recepti, 1.Cor.7. Item Marc.10. Horum enim est regnum cœlo-rum.
units.tr: Reply. Even if no precept of Christ expressed in words exists on this matter, it is nevertheless clearly and necessarily gathered from the Scriptures themselves, as from the doctrine of the covenant and of the children of believers, as was shown above by us. For Christ commands that whoever are received into his covenant be sealed to him, Matthew 28. But the children of believers have been received into the covenant, 1 Corinthians 7. Likewise Mark 10: "For of such is the kingdom of heaven."

units.la: 11. Ad Cœnam admittendas esse mulieres, non est expressum in sacris Literis. Chri-stus enim Cœnam egit tantùm cum discipulis.
units.tr: 11. Women are not to be admitted to the Lord's Supper; it is not expressed in the Holy Scriptures. For Christ celebrated the Supper only with the disciples.

units.la: Resp. Etsi in illa Cœna non legantur vllæ interfuisse mulieres: non tamen inde sequitur, ex Christi igitur doctrina non haberi, mulieres ad Cœnam esse admittendas. Apostolus enim apertè ait, quod tradidit Corinthiis, se à Domino accepisse, 1. Corinth. 11. Atque is docuit, etiam mulieres debere ede-re de pane Domini. Probet autem seipsum homo. Homo autem significat tam fœminam, quàm masculum. Item sacramentum Paschæ tam à mulieribus quàm à viris edebatur: Ergo & Christi Cœna, quæ in eius locum successit. Item tam mulieres debent edere de carne Christi spiritualiter, quàm viri, Ioh.6. Nisi manducaueritis carnem meam, & biberitis sanguinem meum, non habebitis vitam in vobis. Ergo etiam de sacramento carnis.
units.tr: Reply. Even if no women are read of as present at that Supper, it does not follow from this that it is not had from the doctrine of Christ that women are to be admitted to the Supper. For the Apostle plainly says that what he delivered to the Corinthians he had received from the Lord, 1 Corinthians 11. And he taught that women too ought to eat of the bread of the Lord: "But let a man examine himself." Now "man" signifies a woman as much as a man. Likewise the sacrament of the Passover was eaten by women as much as by men; therefore also the Supper of Christ, which succeeded in its place. Likewise women ought to eat of the flesh of Christ spiritually, just as men do, John 6: "Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you have no life in you." Therefore also of the sacrament of the flesh.

units.la: 12. Descensus Christi ad inferos non est expressus in sacris Literis: & tamen confitemur omnes in symbolo.
units.tr: 12. The descent of Christ into hell is not expressed in the sacred Scriptures; and yet we all confess it in the creed.

units.la: Resp. Etsi nonnullis videtur haec particula longè post prima illa concilia, vt Nicaenum, &c. adiecta fuisse: neque enim huius fit mentio in symbolis veterum Conciliorum: tamen collectam hanc esse è scripturis, liquet. Non loquor iam de intelligentia horum verborum, sed de verbis ipsis. In Psalmo 16. qui de Christo est, teste Petro Actor. 2. & Paulo, Actor.13. Christus sic alloquitur Patrem: Non derelinques animam meam in-inferno.
units.tr: Answer: Although it seems to some that this clause was added long after those first councils, such as Nicaea, etc., for no mention of it is made in the creeds of the early councils, it is nevertheless clear that it has been gathered from the Scriptures. I am not speaking now of the meaning of these words, but of the words themselves. In Psalm 16, which is about Christ, as Peter witnesses in Acts 2 and Paul in Acts 13, Christ addresses the Father thus: Thou wilt not leave my soul in hell.

units.la: 13. Quòd Maria sit & debeat vocari Mater Dei.
units.tr: 13. That Mary is and ought to be called the Mother of God.

units.la: Resp. Imò hoc definitum secundùm scripturas à Patribus in Conciliis, vt Chalcedonensi, &c. Item Luc.1. Elisabeth ait: Et unde hoc mihi, vt veniat Mater Domini mei ad me? Quem vocat Dominum? Deum. Idem igitur sunt mater Domini, & mater Dei. Item Luc.1. Quod nascitur ex te sanctum, vocabitur filius Dei. Si quod natum est ex Maria, filius Dei est & Deus: quis non videat, eam matrem esse & appellari debere Dei, propter hypostaticam unionem duarum naturarum, & communicationem idiomatum.
units.tr: Answer: Indeed, this has been defined according to the Scriptures by the Fathers in councils, such as Chalcedon, etc. Likewise, in Luke 1, Elisabeth says: And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me? Whom does she call Lord? God. The mother of the Lord and the mother of God are therefore the same. Likewise, in Luke 1: That which is born of you shall be called holy, the Son of God. If what was born of Mary is the Son of God and God, who does not see that she is, and ought to be called, the mother of God, on account of the hypostatic union of the two natures and the communication of properties?

units.la: 14. Quòd beatorum Animæ statim à corpore exutæ, clara visione, diuinitatem videant, &c. Resp. Imò habetur cùm aliis in locis, tum 2. Corinth. 5. Ibi enim ponit apertè duplicem fidelium statum: vnum in hoc corpore, alterum extra corpus. Et dum fumus in corpore, ait nos peregrinos esse à Domino. Cùm soluti fumus à corpore, ait nos peregrinari à corpore, & præsentes adesse apud Dominum. Ergo Animæ fidelium solutæ à corporibus, migrant ad Dominum, & ante illum stant, eumque vident.
units.tr: 14. That the souls of the blessed, immediately stripped of the body, see the divinity with a clear vision, etc. Answer: Indeed, this is found both in other places and in 2 Corinthians 5. For there he plainly sets out a twofold state of believers: one in this body, the other outside the body. And while we are in the body, he says we are pilgrims away from the Lord. When we are loosed from the body, he says we are away from the body, and present with the Lord. Therefore the souls of believers, loosed from their bodies, migrate to the Lord, stand before him, and see him.

units.la: 15. De sanctificatione Diei Dominicæ; non habemus in scripturis: & tamen nemo est, qui non hunc sanctificet diem.
units.tr: 15. We do not have in the Scriptures the sanctification of the Lord's Day; and yet there is no one who does not sanctify this day.

units.la: Resp. Imò è scripturis colligimus, Apoc.1. Actor.20. 1.Corinth.16. Quæ enim solebant fieri die sabbathi, Apostoli transtulerunt in diem Dominicam, vt ibi liquet: neque hoc ex se, sed iuxta voluntatem Dei, qui volebat, vt etiam dies sabbathi, quatenus ceremonialis erat, corrigeretur: quando omnia ceremonialia vsq; ad tempus correctionis fuerunt imposita, Heb 9.
units.tr: Answer: Indeed, we gather it from the Scriptures: Revelation 1, Acts 20, 1 Corinthians 16. For the Apostles transferred to the Lord's Day what used to be done on the Sabbath, as is clear there; and this was not done on their own initiative, but according to the will of God, who willed that even the Sabbath day, insofar as it was ceremonial, should be corrected, since all ceremonial things were imposed until the time of correction, Hebrews 9.

units.la: Argumenta tertia Classis, sumpta ex Patribus,
units.tr: The third class of arguments, taken from the Fathers

units.la: PATRES antiquissimi, qui aut Apostolorum discipuli fuerunt, aut saltem non ita multò post Apostolorum tempora vixerunt, testantur, multa fuisse per Apostolos in Ecclesia constituta ad pietatem pertinentia, idque ore tantùm, de quibus nullum Apostolicum extat scriptum: & harum traditionum multas commemorant Patres: dicuntque his non minùs fidei esse adhibendum, quàm scriptis: & ad has provocant, cùm disputant cum hæreticis. Est igitur falsum quod dicitis, (aiunt Pontificij) omnia ad salutem necessaria & ad pietatem pertinentia, contineri in scripturis. Illud verò Assumtum conantur probare testimoniis Patrum in medium allatis, & primò:
units.tr: The most ancient Fathers, who were either disciples of the Apostles or lived not very long after the times of the Apostles, testify that many things pertaining to piety were established in the Church by the Apostles, and that these were by word of mouth only, of which no Apostolic writing exists; and the Fathers mention many of these traditions, and say that they are to be received with no less faith than the writings; and they appeal to these when they dispute with heretics. It is therefore false, say the Papists, what you assert, that all things necessary for salvation and pertaining to piety are contained in the Scriptures. They try to prove this assumption by testimonies of the Fathers brought forward, and first:

units.la: Irenæus lib.3. cap.1.2.3. 4. duo in summa docet esse, quibus Christiana religio nititur: primum quidem scripturam sanctam: deinde traditionem Apostolicam: & ad hæc duo provocant veri Christiani. Contrà verò Hæretici aut scripturas negant, si non in totum, saltem ex parte: aut traditionem: aut utrumque. Proinde cùm negantur scripturæ, aut reiiciuntur, quasi non sint perfectæ, docet confugiendum esse ad Ecclesias Apostolicas, & in primis ad Romanam, ubi retinentur puræ traditiones Apostolicæ. Hæc est summa doctrinæ Irenæi de iis traditionibus. Scribebat autem adversus Valentinum & eius discipulos, qui non agnoscebant unum tantùm Deum conditorem Cœli, prædicatum à Prophetis.
units.tr: Irenaeus, book 3, chapters 1, 2, 3, 4, teaches in summary that there are two things on which the Christian religion rests: first, the holy Scripture, and then the Apostolic tradition; and true Christians appeal to these two. On the contrary, heretics either deny the Scriptures, if not entirely, at least in part, or deny the tradition, or both. Therefore, when the Scriptures are denied or rejected, as if they were not complete, he teaches that we must flee to the Apostolic Churches, and especially to the Roman, where the pure Apostolic traditions are kept. This is the sum of Irenaeus' teaching about those traditions.
