Only those churches could give certain testimony on these matters, because, having been founded and taught by the Apostles not so very long before, and having kept in all doctrine, not so much in writing as also by word of mouth, the doctrine and the understanding of Scripture which they received from the Apostles by living voice, they still retain it to this day. The Fathers proved this because, from the time those churches were planted and taught by the Apostles, they had never varied in doctrine; their testimony therefore ought to be admitted as most certain and most true. But if anyone should reject even this, and despise the authority of the churches, they said that they could no longer dispute with such men. Did they not then rightly appeal to the churches, and to such churches? Did they not then rightly say that there was no longer any need to dispute with these heretics on the Scriptures alone?

units.la: Atque ita apparet Quartum, Cur scilicet illi Patres remiserint ad Ecclesias illas pro intelligentia scripturarum, & pro veritate: quia scilicet apud illas manebat veritas, & vera scripturarum intelligentia, sicut fuerat ibi relicta ab Apostolis. Hanc causam aperte affert Tertullianus, cum dicit: Ubi enim apparverit esse veritatem disciplina & fidei Christiana: illic erit & veritas scripturarum, & expositionum, & omnium traditionum Christianarum.[?]
units.tr: And so it appears, fourth, why those Fathers referred to those churches for the understanding of Scripture and for the truth: because, namely, the truth remained with them, and the true understanding of Scripture, just as it had been left there by the Apostles. Tertullian plainly states this cause when he says: For where the truth of the Christian discipline and faith has been shown to be, there will also be the truth of the Scriptures, and of the interpretations, and of all the Christian traditions.

units.la: Sed quid haec Patrum dicta iuvant Papi-stas contra nos? Agant Papistae nobiscum sicut illi Patres agebant cum illis Haereticis: probent sua per scripturas apertas: probent per receptam apud omnes traditionem sym-bolum scilicet Apostolicum, imo & per alias traditiones, hoc est, symbola, veterum Ecclesiarum: adferant illum scripturarum sen-sum, qui non pugnet cum scripturis & symbolis: tum demum, si non acquieverimus, provocent ad Ecclesias omnes, quae ab Apo-stolis plantatae & edoctae, eandem semper re-tinuerint, & adhuc retineant doctrinam, quam ab Apostolis acceperunt. Provocent etiam ad Ecclesiam Romanam, sed probent sicut Patres faciebant, in hac Ecclesia nullam factam esse mutationem in doctrina & cultu diuino, ab eo tempore, quo fuit ab Apostolis instituta, & tum demum, si non acquieuerimus, clament, nobiscum non esse amplius disputandum. Videmus itaq; quomodo intelligendum sit illud quintum dictum, hoc est, verba Irenæi & Tertulliani, quæ supra recitauimus: & quam merito illud dixerint & scripserint aduersus tales hæreticos, qui neque scripturas, quæ contra se fecerunt, neq; verum & simplicem sensum aliarum[?], neq; receptam ab omnibus traditionem, hoc est, doctrinam symboli, neq; deniq; omnium Ecclesiarum, quæ nunquam ab eo tempore, quo fuerunt ab Apostolis doctæ & institutæ, ab illorum doctrina recesserunt, testimonium admittebant. Ac proinde apparet, hæc Pa-trum dicta, nihil aduersus nos facere, qui & scripturas omnes Canonicas, & simplicem illarum sensum, & communem symboli traditionem amplectimur: & si etiam adferant testimonia Ecclesiarum verè Apostolicarum, quas constet nihil unquam variasse in doctrina, libentissimè amplexuri illa fumus.
units.tr: But what do these sayings of the Fathers help the Papists against us? Let the Papists deal with us as those Fathers dealt with those heretics: let them prove their positions from plain Scriptures; let them prove them by the creed, the Apostles' Creed, which is received by all, and even by other traditions, that is, the creeds of the ancient churches; let them bring forward that sense of the Scriptures which does not conflict with the Scriptures and the creeds. Then at last, if we do not agree, let them appeal to all the churches which were planted and taught by the Apostles, and have always kept, and still keep, the doctrine which they received from the Apostles. Let them also appeal to the Roman Church, but let them prove, as the Fathers did, that in this Church no change has been made in doctrine or in divine worship since the time it was founded by the Apostles; and then at last, if we do not agree, let them cry out that there is no longer any need to dispute with us. We see, therefore, how that fifth saying, that is, the words of Irenaeus and Tertullian which we quoted above, is to be understood, and how rightly they spoke and wrote it against such heretics, who admitted neither the Scriptures, which were against them, nor the true and simple sense of the other passages, nor the tradition received by all, that is, the doctrine of the creed, nor finally the testimony of all the churches, which, from the time they were taught and founded by the Apostles, never departed from their teaching. And so it appears that these sayings of the Fathers do nothing against us, who embrace all the canonical Scriptures, their plain sense, and the common tradition of the creed; and if they bring forward the testimonies of churches truly Apostolic, which it is established never varied in doctrine, we will most willingly embrace them too.

units.la: Summa hæc est: Quia apud illas Ecclesias manebat veritas doctrinæ Apostolicæ, & manebat integer scripturarum sensus, quem Apostoli apud illas reliquerant: id quod con-stabat, quia nunquam facta fuerat ulla do-ctrinæ mutatio apud illas: ideo Patres me-ritô ritò illarum autoritatem magnificabant, & præscribebant hæreticis: Et si hanc reiicerent, cum illis disputandum esse negabant: idque tum demum hoc dicebant, cum sua probarent scripturis, & communi receptá-que traditione: hæretici verò neq; illas, ne-que hanc admittere voluissent.
units.tr: The sum of this is: because the truth of Apostolic doctrine remained with those churches, and the whole sense of Scripture which the Apostles had left with them remained; which was evident, because no change of doctrine had ever been made among them: therefore the Fathers rightly magnified their authority and set it against the heretics; and if the heretics rejected it, they said that there was no need to dispute with them. And they said this only when they had proved their own positions from the Scriptures and the common and received tradition; but the heretics would admit neither the one nor the other.

units.la: Cæterùm, Patres nunquam fidem Apostolicam vllis alligarunt locis aut personis. Inde illud Tertull. de præscript. hæret. pag. 96. Non esse veritatem ex personis, sed personas ex veritate indicandas. Item pag. 109. Unde autem extranei & inimici Apostolis Haeretici, nisi ex diuersitate doctrinae, quam vnusquisque de suo arbitrio aduersus Apostolos aut protulit, aut recepit? Volebant autem omnia probari per scripturas, id quod liquet. Sed scripturarum sensum in præcipuis capitibus religionis, volebant sumi ex symbolo, & ab illis Ecclesiis, apud quos constabat manere veritatem fidei Christianæ, non autem ab illis, apud quas non maneret hæc veritas. Ideo ait pag. 109. Illic igitur & scripturarum & expositionum adulteratio deputanda est, vbi diuersitas inuenitur doctrinae, diuersitas scilicet doctrinae, ab ea, quam tradiderunt Apostoli.
units.tr: Moreover, the Fathers never bound the Apostolic faith to any places or persons. Hence that saying of Tertullian in De praescriptione haereticorum, p. 96: Truth is not to be judged by persons, but persons by the truth. Likewise p. 109: For whence came the heretics, strangers and enemies of the Apostles, except from the diversity of doctrine which each one, at his own pleasure, either set forth or received against the Apostles? They wished, however, that everything be proved by the Scriptures, as is clear. But they wanted the sense of Scripture in the chief heads of religion to be taken from the creed, and from those churches where the truth of the Christian faith was known to remain, and not from those where this truth did not remain. Therefore he says on p. 109: There, then, both the corruption of the Scriptures and of their interpretations is to be reckoned, where a diversity of doctrine is found, namely a diversity of doctrine from that which the Apostles handed down.

units.la: QUÆSTIO IX. De legendis cuiq; hominis scripturis.
units.tr: QUESTION IX. On the reading of Scripture by each person.

units.la: Post quæstionem de utilitate & perfectio-ne scripturarum, sequitur ordine legitimo quæstio de legendis & audiendis scripturis. Nam cùm Apostolus ait 2. Timoth. 3. Omnis scriptura divinitùs inspirata, utilis est ad doctrinam, &c. Item, quòd potest sapientem facere ad salutem: videndum est, quosnam possint sapientes facere, & quibus utilis sit ad doctrinam. Non certè illis, qui hanc scripturam in libris tantùm & cistis, & Musæis tenent, sed nunquam legunt, nunquam audiunt: verùm illis, qui eam legunt, audiunt, intelligunt, fide recipiunt. Ideo subiecit Apostolus, dicendo: Quæ te possunt facere sapientem per fidem, quæ est in Christo Iesu. Item Rom. 1. Euangelium est potentia Dei in salutem omni credenti. Fides autem est ex auditu. Rom.10.
units.tr: After the question concerning the usefulness and perfection of the Scriptures, there follows in proper order the question concerning the reading and hearing of the Scriptures. For when the Apostle says, 2 Timothy 3, "All Scripture is divinely inspired and profitable for teaching, etc.," and likewise that it "can make the wise man wise unto salvation," we must consider who may be made wise by it, and to whom it is profitable for teaching. Certainly not to those who keep this Scripture only in books, chests and bookcases, but never read it and never hear it; rather to those who read it, hear it, understand it, and receive it in faith. Therefore the Apostle added, saying: "which are able to make you wise through faith which is in Christ Jesus." Likewise Romans 1: "The gospel is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes." And Romans 10: "Faith comes from hearing."

units.la: Quæstio igitur hæc proponitur: An officium sit cuiusq; Christiani, imò cuiusvis hominis, operam dare sacris Literis, non solùm audiendis, cùm explicantur in Templo & in schola, sed etiam domi legendis & scrutandis, nec ne.
units.tr: The question, then, is put forward: Whether it is the duty of every Christian, indeed of every person whatever, to devote himself to the holy Literature, not only to hearing it when it is expounded in the temple and in the school, but also to reading and searching it at home, or not.

units.la: Papistæ permulti, præsertim hoc tempore, negant permittendum esse cuique legere scripturas, vt mulieribus, Laicis, indoctis, pueris, militibus, plebeis: Hoc esse officium Ecclesiasticorum & Theologorum, doctorumq; virorum. Quas adferant rationes, ad extremum breviter recitabo & refutabo. Sententiam nostram continet hæc
units.tr: Very many Papists, especially in this age, deny that it should be permitted to everyone to read the Scriptures, such as women, laymen, the unlearned, children, soldiers and common people; they say this is the duty of ecclesiastics and theologians and learned men. I shall briefly recite and refute the reasons they advance, at the end. Our opinion is contained in this thesis.

units.la: THESIS.
units.tr: THESIS.

units.la: Cuiusq; Christiani officium est operam da-re sacris Bibliis, non solùm audiendis cùm explicantur aut in templo, aut in schola, sed etiam domi legendis & scrutandis.
units.tr: It is the duty of every Christian to devote himself to the holy Bibles, not only to hearing them when they are expounded either in the temple or in the school, but also to reading and searching them at home.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmation.

units.la: 1. Præceptum Dei est, ad singulos homines pertinens, ut se & Christum nobis loquentem audiamus, nempe quoties ille ad nos verba facit, & nos illum audire possumus. Testimonia Prophetæ subinde inculcant, Audite verbum Domini. De Christo Paterait Matth.17 Ipsum audite. Atqui loquitur nobis non solum è suggesto & è Cathedra per Doctores & Pastores, sed etiam in sacris Literis. Ibi enim docet, præcipit, promittit, minatur. Ergo cuiusque Christiani est, cùm vacat, Christum in scripturis loquentem audire: id quod fit legendo.
units.tr: 1. It is a command of God, pertaining to each individual person, that we hear both himself and Christ speaking to us; namely, as often as he addresses us and we are able to hear him. The testimonies of the Prophets repeatedly urge, "Hear the word of the Lord." Concerning Christ the Father said in Matthew 17: "Hear him." But he speaks to us not only from the pulpit and from the chair through the teachers and ministers, but also in the holy Scriptures. For there he teaches, commands, promises and threatens. Therefore it is the duty of every Christian, when he has leisure, to hear Christ speaking in the Scriptures; which is done by reading.

units.la: 2. Christi præceptum est ad singulos spectans, Iohan. 5. Scrutamini scripturas. Solebant igitur omnes Iudæi libros sacros legere.
units.tr: 2. The command of Christ pertains to each individual, John 5: "Search the Scriptures." All the Jews therefore were accustomed to read the sacred books.

units.la: 3. Col.3. Toti Ecclesiæ & singulis fidelibus, qui Colossis erant, mandat Apostolus, ut in ipsis etiam ædibus priuatis, sermo Christi, hoc est, doctrina Euangelij & sacrarum literarum, inhabitet affluenter, docentes se mutuo & admonentes sui quemq; officij, nempè è scripturis. Sermo (inquit) Christi, ἐνοικείτω ἐν ὑμῖν πλουσίως ἐν πάσῃ σοφίᾳ· διδάσκοντες καὶ νουθετοῦντες[?] ἑαυτούς. Vbi illud verbum ἐνοικεῖν diligenter considerandum est. Significat enim dome-sticam inhabitationem.
units.tr: 3. Colossians 3. The Apostle commands the whole Church and the individual faithful who were at Colossae that the word of Christ, that is, the doctrine of the gospel and of the holy Literature, should dwell richly in their very private houses, "teaching and admonishing one another, each of his duty"; namely from the Scriptures. "The word of Christ" (he says) "let it dwell in you richly in all wisdom: teaching and admonishing [?] yourselves" [ἐνοικείτω ἐν ὑμῖν πλουσίως ἐν πάσῃ σοφίᾳ· διδάσκοντες καὶ νουθετοῦντες ἑαυτούς]. Where the word ἐνοικεῖν must be carefully considered. For it signifies a domestic indwelling.

units.la: 4. Quisque tenetur non solùm cùm opus est, suam profiteri fidem: sed etiam cur sic credat, sperét & viuat, rationem reddere, 1.Pet.3. Parati sitis reddere rationem (ἕτοιμοι[?] δὲ ἀπο-λογίαν) omni poscenti, de ea quæ in vobis est spe. At quomodo hoc fecerit Christianus, nisi sese exerceat in sacris Literis? Neque enim aliunde ratio petenda est fidei & spei nostræ, nisi è scripturis, quibus vnis nititur. Meritò autem hoc exigit Apostolus à singulis Christianis: quoniam turpissimum est, Christianum eum appellari debere, qui nesciat è scripturis rationem adferre eorum quæ profitetur & agit: quando idem turpe est in omni alia professione tam disciplinarum quàm artium: nempe, vt aliquis profiteatur se esse Philosophum aut Medicum, qui nesciat rationem adferre eius quam profitetur artem. Profectò huiusmodi homines apud nos exsibilantur & ridentur: quanto turpius id fuerit Christiano?
units.tr: 4. Each person is bound not only, when need arises, to profess his faith, but also to give an account of why he so believes, hopes and lives: 1 Peter 3, "Be ready to give an account" (ἕτοιμοι δὲ ἀπολογίαν) "to everyone who asks you about the hope that is in you." But how could a Christian do this unless he exercises himself in the holy Literature? For the reason of our faith and hope is not to be sought anywhere else than in the Scriptures, on which alone it rests. The Apostle rightly requires this of each Christian, since it is most shameful that someone should be called a Christian who does not know how to give an account from the Scriptures of the things he professes and does; just as it is equally shameful in every other profession, of the sciences as of the arts: for example, that someone should profess himself a philosopher or a physician who does not know how to give an account of the art he professes. Such men are certainly hissed and laughed at among us; how much more shameful would this be for a Christian?

units.la: §. Deuter. 6. toti populo suo sic mandat Dominus: Erunt verba ista (legis) quæ ego præcipio tibi hodiè, super cor tuum, recense-bisq; ea filiis tuis, & loqueris de iis cùm sedes in domo tua, & cùm ambulas per viam: cùm vadis dormitum, & cùm iterum surgis: ligabis denique in signum super manum tuam, eruntq; monitoria inter oculos tuos. Scribes enim supra postes domus tuæ, & in portis tuis. Eadem repetit Deut.11. Hinc perspicuum fit, voluisse Deum, vt in singulis ædibus haberetur lex Domini eaque scripta, non certè ut ibi otiosa lateret, sed ut à cunctis legeretur, audiretur, atq; ita cœlestis doctrina per omnes ætates, perpetuaque successione incorrupta seruaretur & propagaretur. Et quidem Iudæi præceptum illud obseruarunt & adhuc obseruant. Nulla est enim domus apud Iudæos, in qua libri sacri non habeantur, & statis temporibus universa familia audiente, non legantur. Quin etiam pueri à teneris annis, Bibliis legendis assuefiunt: mulieres etiam incumbunt sacrarum Literarum lectioni & studio. 2. Timoth.1.[?] Annon igitur interest & Christianorum id ipsum facere? Nam præceptum illud Dei de scripturis domi legendis, non ad solos pertinet Iudæos, sed etiam ad Christianos, & quidem in primis ad Christianos, quippe qui verus nunc sunt populus Dei: Et præceptum illud, non iudiciale neque ceremoniale est, sed morale ad primam pertinens tabulam: ut nemo rergiuersari possit, causans illud es-se cum reliquis ceremonialibus & iudicialibus per Christum abrogatum. Imò Christus, cùm dixit, scrutamini scripturas, & cùm arguit Pharisæos, quòd non legerent scripturas, illud proprie omninò confirmauit: & univer-se quicquid in veteri Testamento reperitur, ad fidem in Dominum, ad charitatem in pro-ximum, & ad vitam sanctè traducendam per-tinens: totum illud à Christo confirmatum esse, perspicuum est.
units.tr: §. Deuteronomy 6. The Lord thus commands his whole people: "These words (of the law) which I command you today shall be upon your heart, and you shall recount them to your sons, and you shall speak of them when you sit in your house and when you walk by the way, when you lie down and when you rise again; you shall bind them finally as a sign upon your hand, and they shall be reminders between your eyes. For you shall write them upon the posts of your house and upon your gates." The same is repeated in Deuteronomy 11. From this it is clear that God wished the law of the Lord to be kept in each household and written there, not indeed that it should lie idle there, but that it should be read and heard by all, and so the heavenly doctrine be preserved and propagated uncorrupted through all ages by continual succession. And indeed the Jews have observed that precept and still observe it. For there is no house among the Jews in which the holy books are not kept, and at fixed times, with the whole family listening, they are read. Moreover, children from their tender years are accustomed to reading the Bibles; women too apply themselves to the reading and study of the holy Literature. 2 Timothy 1. Does it not then concern Christians to do the same? For that command of God concerning reading the Scriptures at home pertains not only to the Jews but also to Christians, and indeed chiefly to Christians, who are now the true people of God. And that precept is not judicial nor ceremonial, but moral, belonging to the first table; so that no one can shuffle off, pleading that it was abrogated by Christ together with the other ceremonial and judicial laws. Indeed, Christ, when he said "search the Scriptures," and when he rebuked the Pharisees because they did not read the Scriptures, plainly confirmed that very thing; and it is clear that generally whatever is found in the Old Testament pertaining to faith in the Lord, to love of neighbour, and to living holily, all of that has been confirmed by Christ.

units.la: 6. 2. Petr. 1. Ad universos scribens Chri-stianos stianos, & non tantum ad sacerdotes ait. Habemus firmum Propheticum sermonem, cui dum attenditis velut lucernæ splendenti in obscuro loco, benè facitis, donec dies illucescat, & lucifer oriatur in cordibus vestris. Docet iis verbis, non solum tunc temporis Christianos omnes solitos fuisse scripturas Prophetarum diligenter legere: sed etiam, quicunque hoc idem faciunt, illos recte facere: Male igitur, qui hoc facere negligunt.
units.tr: 6. 2 Peter 1. Writing to all Christians, and not only to the priests, he says: "We have the firm prophetic word, to which you do well to attend as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star arises in your hearts." By these words he teaches not only that at that time all Christians were accustomed to read the writings of the Prophets diligently, but also that all who do the same now do rightly; so those who neglect to do this do wrongly.

units.la: 7. Prou. 2. Deus per Salomonem unum-quemque hortatur, ut penes se reponat verba & præcepta sua, & aures sapientiæ accommodet. Legantur & quæ de eadem re initio cap. 4. scribit: Vbi & præceptum ad singulos pertinens de studio legis Domini, & magnifica promissio, illos attingens, qui huic studio incumbunt. Quid igitur garriunt impij, le-ctionem scripturarum non ad omnes per-tinere?
units.tr: 7. Proverbs 2. Through Solomon God exhorts each one "to store up his words and commands within himself and to incline his ears to wisdom." Let also what he writes at the beginning of chapter 4 be read on the same matter: there is both a command pertaining to each individual concerning the study of the Lord's law, and a magnificent promise reaching those who devote themselves to this study. Why then do the wicked prattle that reading the Scriptures does not pertain to all?

units.la: 8. Quid verò minetur Dominus iis, qui negligunt legem suam audire, sed eam reii-ciunt, legatur Ierem. cap. 9. An non etiam reii-ciunt, qui nolunt scripturas legere cùm possint?
units.tr: 8. What the Lord threatens against those who neglect to hear his law but reject it, let them read Jeremiah chapter 9. Do not those also reject it who are unwilling to read the Scriptures when they are able to?

units.la: 9. Actor.17. De Beroënsibus, qui erant Thessalonicæ, viris nobilibus traditur, cùm audiuissent Apostolum, eos quotidie scrutatos fuisse scripturas, ut viderent, an ita se res haberet in scripturis, sicut audiuerunt ab Apostolo prædicari. Quid hoc exemplum docet, nisi tempore Apostolorum pios quoque solitos fuisse sacras Literas quàm diligentissimè etiam domi legere & perscrutari? ac proinde idem nobis esse faciendum, si vere inter pios connumerari, & de religione nostra certiores fieri velimus? Quo etiam ex loco colligere promptum est, nihil Christianis hominibus de religione admittendum esse, nisi quod deprehenderint consentaneum esse cum sacris Literis.
units.tr: 9. Acts 17. Concerning the Bereans, who were in Thessalonica, it is recorded of these noble men that when they heard the Apostle, "they searched the Scriptures daily, to see whether those things were so as they had heard preached by the Apostle." What does this example teach, except that in the time of the Apostles even the pious were accustomed to read and examine the holy Literature most diligently, even at home? And therefore that we too ought to do the same, if we wish to be counted among the pious and to be more certain about our religion? From this passage too it is easily gathered that nothing should be admitted by Christians concerning religion except what they have found to agree with the holy Literature.

units.la: 1. Corinth. 14. Ostendit Apostolus hanc fuisse consuetudinem in Ecclesia Christi receptam, vt fideles simul conuenirent omnes & de doctrinis, quæ piæ, quæ minus, diiudicarent. Quoties conuenitis, vnusquisque vestrum canticum habet, doctrinam habet, &c. Item (alteri[?] diiudicent.. At quomodo hanc diiudicationem facere illi rectè potuissent, qui in sacris Literis non fuissent exercitati? Quomodo verò in iis exercitari, nisi etiam domi in illis legendis & meditandis sese occupassent? Quandoquidem igitur singulorum est Christianorum facere iudicium de doctrinis, singulorum etiam est sacras Literas legere & perscrutari.
units.tr: 1 Corinthians 14. The Apostle shows that this custom was received in the Church of Christ: that the faithful should all come together and judge which doctrines were godly and which less so. "Whenever you come together, each one of you has a psalm, has a teaching, etc." Likewise: "let the others judge..." But how could those who had not been practised in the Holy Scriptures judge this rightly? And how could they be practised in them unless they also occupied themselves with reading and meditating on them at home? Since, therefore, it is the duty of each individual Christian to judge doctrines, it is also the duty of each individual to read and search the Holy Scriptures.

units.la: 1. Cor. 14. Dum etiam ibidem præcipit, vt mulieres, si quid volunt discere, maritos domi interrogent: an non satis inuenit, debere singulos viros ita esse in S. Literis exercitatos, vt possint mulieribus suis in omnibus, quæ de pietate interrogant, abundè è scripturis satisfacere? At quomodo hoc fieri, nisi quotidie aliquid legam in scripturis, & illud diligenter examinem?
units.tr: 1 Corinthians 14. Where he also instructs there that "if women want to learn anything, let them ask their husbands at home": does he not clearly show that each man ought to be so practised in the Holy Scriptures that he can fully satisfy his wife, out of the Scriptures, in everything she asks about piety? But how can this be done unless I read something in the Scriptures every day and examine it diligently?

units.la: 12. 1. Timoth. 3. Persiste in iis, qua didicisti, & qua tibi concredita sunt, sciens a quo didice-ris, & quod a puero sacras Literas noveris. Et quinam Timotheum adhuc puerum sacras Literas docuerunt, nisi mater Eunice, & avia Lois? Non enim didicit a Patre, qui Gentilis erat & infidelis. De matris autem & aviae pietate ac fide testatur 2. Timoth. 1. Docet etiam hic locus, receptum fuisse apud Christianos, & vere pios homines, ut parentes, etiam ipsae matres, liberos suos, domi sanctas docerent literas.
units.tr: 12. 1 Timothy 3. "Continue in those things which you have learned and which have been entrusted to you, knowing from whom you learned them, and that from childhood you have known the Holy Scriptures." And who taught the boy Timothy the Holy Scriptures, if not his mother Eunice and his grandmother Lois? For he did not learn from his father, who was a Gentile and an unbeliever. Concerning the piety and faith of his mother and grandmother, 2 Timothy 1 bears witness. This passage also teaches that it was received among Christians, and among truly godly people, that parents, and even the mothers themselves, should teach the holy letters to their children at home.

units.la: 13. Actor. 8. Eunuchus Candaces Æthiopum Reginæ præfectus, homo Gentilis, cum peregrinaretur, & curru veheretur, non iacuit ibi otiosus, sed legebat Iesaiam Prophetam. An non igitur domi verisimilius est, aliquam sibi partem temporis solitum fuisse deligere, qua aliquid in scripturis legeret? Quàm autem Deo probata fuerit hæc Eunuchi Gentilis diligentia & assiduitas in sacris scripturis legendis, perspicuum facit id quod sequitur in historia. Misit enim ad eum Dominus Philippum, qui loca Iesaiæ quæ legebat, sed non intelligebat, explicaret, in pietate Christiana institueret, & tandem baptizaret. Quidni igitur dicamus Deo probari eorum Christianorum quicunque sint, studium, qui etiamsi non omnia intelligant, scripturis tamen legendis non defatigantur? Quid ni dicamus, Deum illis missurum, qui explicent, si non alios, saltem Spiritum sanctum?
units.tr: 13. Acts 8. The eunuch, the officer of Candace, Queen of the Ethiopians, a Gentile, when he was travelling and being carried in his chariot, did not lie there idle, but was reading the prophet Isaiah. Is it not then more probable that at home he was accustomed to set aside some portion of his time in which he might read something in the Scriptures? How acceptable this diligence and constancy of the Gentile eunuch in reading the Holy Scriptures was to God, the sequel of the story makes plain. For the Lord sent Philip to him, who explained the passages of Isaiah that he was reading but did not understand, instructed him in Christian piety, and at last baptised him. Why then should we not say that the zeal of whatever Christians, who, even if they do not understand everything, nevertheless do not tire of reading the Scriptures, is approved by God? Why should we not say that God will send to them someone to explain, if not others, at least the Holy Spirit?

units.la: 14. Ephef.6. Patres nolite ad iracundiam provocare liberos vestros, sed instruite illos in timore Domini, &c. Quomodo verò hoc fecerint Patres, sine lectione scripturarum?
units.tr: 14. Ephesians 6. "Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the fear of the Lord, etc." But how would the Fathers have done this without reading the Scriptures?

units.la: 15. Ad Romanos, & alibi salutat priuatas familias, & eas vocat Ecclesias. Quamobrem ita vocat? Quia in ædibus priuatim precabantur, quæ etiam in Ecclesia publicè. Preces enim fiebant simul à tota familia, & scripturæ legebantur & explicabantur.
units.tr: 15. In the letter to the Romans, and elsewhere, he greets private households and calls them churches. Why does he call them so? Because they prayed privately in their houses, which they also did publicly in the Church. For prayers were made together by the whole household, and the Scriptures were read and explained.

units.la: 16. 1.Thess.5.[?] Ad vniuersos singulosque fideles scribens, ait: Adhortemini vos mutuo, & edificetis singuli singulos. Volebat igitur Apostolus, vt singuli essent sibi mutuò doctores & pastores. Quomodo autem hoc potuis-sent præstare officium, sine assidua scriptu-rarum lectione & cognitione.
units.tr: 16. 1 Thessalonians 5. Writing to all the faithful and to each one, he says: "Exhort one another, and let each of you edify the other." The Apostle therefore wished each one to be a teacher and minister to one another. But how could they have performed this office without constant reading and knowledge of the Scriptures?

units.la: 17. 1. Timoth. 2. Deus vult omnes homines saluos fieri, & ad cognitionem veritatis venire. Ergo cuiusque hominis est, dare operam legendis S. Bibliis, vt per hæc ad cognitionem veritatis perueniant.
units.tr: 17. 1 Timothy 2. "God wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth." Therefore it is the duty of every person to take pains over reading the Holy Bible, so that through these they may come to the knowledge of the truth.

units.la: 2.Timoth.2. Quæ audiuisti à me inter multos testes, hæc propone fidelibus hominibus, qui eruntidonei ad alios quoq; docendos. Vult igitur Apostolus, non solùm sacerdotes, sed etiam Laicos ita proficere in scripturis, vt etiam aliosipsi possint docere.
units.tr: 2 Timothy 2. "What you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit to faithful men, who will be fit to teach others also." The Apostle therefore wills that not only priests but also laymen should advance in the Scriptures so far that they can also teach others.

units.la: Atque vt speciatim ad multos Laicorum hominum gradus descendam, Deut.17. Præcipit Regibus, vt legem Domini penes se scriptam habeant, & in eo libro, cunctis diebus vitæ suæ legant. Legantur & hæc loca, 1.Sam.8.12. 1. Reg.5.8.10 2. Reg.22. 2. Paral.1.9. Prouerb. 20.21.25.49.31. Ecclef.10. Psal.20.101. Ier.22. Iosu.1. Ne recedat volumen legis huius de manu tua.
units.tr: And, to come down specifically to the many ranks of lay men, Deuteronomy 17 commands kings to keep the law of the Lord written beside them, and to read in that book all the days of their life. Let these passages also be read: 1 Samuel 8:12; 1 Kings 5:8, 10; 2 Kings 22; 2 Chronicles 1:9; Proverbs 20, 21, 25, 49, 31; Ecclesiastes 10; Psalms 20, 101; Jeremiah 22; Joshua 1: "Let not this book of the law depart out of your hand."

units.la: Quod quisque teneatur, si vacet, sacras Scripturas legere, testimonia ex Patribus.
units.tr: That each person is bound, if he has leisure, to read the Holy Scriptures: testimonies from the Fathers.

units.la: Hieronymus Tom. 9. ad Paulam & Eustochium in proœmio Enarrationis Epistolæ Pauli ad Ephes. pag. 202. & rationem ducit ab officio hominis, qui & ratione præditus est, & loqui potest. Locus incipit: Cùm enim à cæteris animantibus, &c. Tomo 6. in initio: Qui nescit scripturas, nescit Dei veritatem, eiusque sapientiam.
units.tr: Jerome, vol. 9, in the preface to his commentary on the letter of Paul to the Ephesians, to Paula and Eustochium, p. 202, and he draws the argument from the duty of man, who is endowed with reason and can speak. The passage begins: "For since from the other animals, etc." In vol. 6, at the beginning: "He who does not know the Scriptures does not know the truth of God and his wisdom."

units.la: Idem in proœmio in primum librum Commentariorum in Iosuam, Ignoratio (inquit) scripturarum, ignoratio Christi est.
units.tr: The same, in the preface to the first book of his commentaries on Joshua: "Ignorance of the Scriptures," he says, "is ignorance of Christ."

units.la: Epistola ad Paulinum cum primis legatur, quæ præfigitur Bibliis, & est de lectione sacrorum Bibliorum.
units.tr: The letter to Paulinus should be read first of all, which is prefixed to the Bibles and is concerned with the reading of the holy Bibles.

units.la: Idem Tom. 1. pag. 66. ad Demetriadem epistola de virginitate seruanda. Hortatur cumprimis, vt animum suum amore sacræ lectionis occupet: & inter alia sic etiam ait: Ama scripturas sanctas, & amabit te sapientia: dilige eam, & seruabit te: honora illam, & amplexabitur te.
units.tr: The same, vol. 1, p. 66, in the letter to Demetrias on keeping virginity. He urges above all that she occupy her mind with love of holy reading; and among other things he also says: "Love the holy Scriptures, and wisdom will love you; esteem her, and she will keep you; honour her, and she will embrace you."

units.la: Epistola ad Saluinam, quæ est pag. 73. de viduitate seruanda, ad idem studium illam hortatur: Semper (inquit) in manibus tuis sit divina lectio. pag.76.
units.tr: In the letter to Salvina, which is on p. 73, on keeping widowhood, he urges her to the same zeal: "Let the divine reading always be in your hands," he says. p. 76.

units.la: Idem in epistola ad Furiam viduam, quæ est pag.79. facit officium. Ad multas autem scripsit fœminas: & nonnullis aliquot dedicauit libros. Omnia hæc argumento sunt, Hieronymum voluisse, vt omnes, etiam fœminæ in legendis sacris literis occuparentur.
units.tr: The same, in the letter to Furia the widow, which is on p. 79, performs the same office. He wrote to many women, and dedicated several books to some of them. All these things are evidence that Jerome wished all people, even women, to be occupied in reading the holy letters.

units.la: Notandum vero, quod est in fine Com-mentariorum in Nahum: Futurum ait, vt sub Christi aduentum ad exercendum iudicium, populus vndique ad discendas sacras literas confluat. Annon nunc id est tempus?
units.tr: It must be noted also what is at the end of his commentary on Nahum: he says that it will come to pass that, before the coming of Christ to execute judgment, people from every side will flock together to learn the holy letters. Is not now that time?

units.la: Chrysost. Tom. 1. in Genesin homil. 35. quæ sic incipit, Ingens bonum est diuinarum scripturarum peritia, scribit idque in initio homiliæ: fieri non posse, vt is qui diuinis scripturis magno studio feruentique desiderio vacat, semper negligatur: quoniam licet desit nobis hominis magisterium: ipse Dominus tamen supernè corda nostra intrans, illustrat mentem, rationi iubar suum infundit, detegit occulta, doctórque fit eorum quæ ignoramus: tantùm nos quæ adsunt, adferre velimus. Ne vocetis (inquit) Magistrum super terram.
units.tr: Chrysostom, vol. 1, on Genesis, homily 35, which begins thus, "Great is the good of skill in the divine Scriptures," he writes this at the beginning of the homily: "It cannot be that he who is devoted with great zeal and fervent desire to the divine Scriptures is ever neglected; for although the teaching of a man is lacking to us, the Lord himself, entering our hearts from above, illumines the mind, pours his light into reason, uncovers hidden things, and becomes the teacher of what we do not know, provided only that we wish to bring what is at hand." "Call no one," he says, "Teacher upon the earth."

units.la: Frequentissimè Patres suos populos ad legendas etiam domi scripturas hortabantur.
units.tr: The Fathers very frequently exhorted their peoples to read the Scriptures, even at home.

units.la: Origenes Tom.1. in Exod.hom.12. Totum populum ad hoc studium hortatur.
units.tr: Origen, vol. 1, on Exodus, homily 12: he exhorts the whole people to this zeal.

units.la: Idem Tom.1.in Leuit.hom.9.p.169.suadet populo, vt non solùm det operam audire in Ecclesia verbum Dei, sed etiam in ipsorum aedibus exerceri & meditari in lege Domini die noctuq;: quòd ibi etiam sit Christus,& vbiq; adsit quaerentibus se.
units.tr: The same, vol. 1, on Leviticus, homily 9, p. 169, urges the people not only to take pains to hear the word of God in the Church, but also to be exercised and to meditate in the law of the Lord day and night in their own houses, because Christ is there too, and is present everywhere to those who seek him.

units.la: In Iosuam,hom.20.pag.364.multis demonstrat, & Deo & Angelis probari,nobis verò vtile esse, si legamus scripturas, etiamsi non plane intelligamus. Quo pacto fuerit ipse à parente domi exercitatus in sacris literis, Eufeb.Ecclesiast.hist.lib 6.cap.20.
units.tr: In Joshua, homily 20, p. 364, he shows at length that it is acceptable both to God and to the Angels, and useful to us, if we read the Scriptures even when we do not fully understand them. In what way he himself was exercised at home in the holy letters by his father, see Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 6, chapter 20.

units.la: Chrysostomus verò quàm frequens & feruens fuerit in excitandis cuiusque ordinis hominibus ad lectionem sacrarum scripturarum, libri ipsius & praesertim homiliae testificantur.Legatur in Epist.ad Colos. cap.3, hom.9.in ea verba, Sermo Christi inhabitet in vobis opulenter. Compellat Patresfamilias,& iubet,vt sibi emant Biblia,& in illis domi legant & meditentur, quòd nemo possit melius illos docere,quàm illa. Et praeterea alia haec etiam habet verba: Hoc (inquit) demum malorum omnium causa est, quòd scripturae ignorantur, Col.1291.C.
units.tr: How frequent and fervent Chrysostom was in stirring up people of every rank to the reading of the Holy Scriptures, his books and especially his homilies bear witness. See on the Epistle to the Colossians, chapter 3, homily 9, on the words "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly." He addresses the heads of households, and bids them buy the Bibles for themselves and read and meditate on them at home, because no one can teach them better than those. And besides he has these other words also: "This," he says, "is at last the cause of all evils, that the Scriptures are ignored." Col. 1291.C.

units.la: Idem in Genesin homil.21.col.155. hortatur vniuersum populum ad studium sacrae Scripturae.
units.tr: The same author, in Genesis, homily 21, col. 155, urges the whole people to the study of Holy Scripture.

units.la: Idem hom.29. In Scripturis enim inueniri pharmaca ad omnem spiritualem morbum. Idem Tom.3.in Ioann.c.8.homil.52.Vult libros sacros domi ab omnibus volui: & licet simus duri: tamen continuando lectionem scripturae, aliquam aslequemur[?] utilitatem. Simile: Qui assidet unguentariae tabernae, etiam inuitus accipiet odorem.
units.tr: The same, homily 29: For in the Scriptures are found remedies for every spiritual disease. The same, Tom. 3, on John, ch. 8, homily 52, wishes the sacred books to be had at home by everyone, and says: even if we are dull, yet by continuing in the reading of Scripture we shall gain some benefit. Similarly: he who sits beside a perfume shop will receive the scent even against his will.

units.la: Augustinus Tom.2.Epistola 3 ad Volusianum, scribit, scripturas legendas esse non tantum doctis, sed etiam indoctis, adeoque omnis generis hominibus. Deum enim in illis loqui ad cor indoctorum atque doctorum. Scripsit & hic Pater multas epistolas ad varias matronas, & viduas & puellas: Ad Paulinam, Probam, Efdiciam, Iulianam, Fabiolam, Feliciam, Florentinam puellam, Italicam, Maximam. Et inter eius sermones etiam unus est, qui inscribitur de studio sapientiae & meditationis legis Dei.
units.tr: Augustine, Tom. 2, Epistle 3, to Volusianus, writes that the Scriptures are to be read not only by the learned but also by the unlearned, and indeed by men of every kind; for God speaks in them to the heart of the unlearned as well as of the learned. This Father also wrote many letters to various matrons, widows and girls: to Paulina, Proba, Eudoxia, Juliana, Fabiola, Felicitas, Florentina the girl, Italica, Maxima. And among his sermons there is one entitled On the Study of Wisdom and the Meditation on the Law of God.

units.la: Id. August. Tomo 10. de verbis Domini, serm.45. in initio: Praeceptum illud Christi, Scrutamini Scripturas, non ad Iudaeos tantum, sed ad singulos Christianos pertinere contendit.
units.tr: The same Augustine, Tom. 10, On the Words of the Lord, sermon 45, at the beginning, contends that the precept of Christ, Search the Scriptures, pertains not only to the Jews but to each individual Christian.

units.la: Ambrosius Tom.3.pag.321. legatur sermone 35. de ieiunio Domini ad finem, adhortatio, ut omnes accipiant panem scripturarum, & in illis exerceantur. Item Tom.4. in Psal.118. sermone 21. qui est pag.581. Omnes fideles hortatur ad scripturarum lectionem. Idem de offic.lib.1[?] c.22. Sit igitur sermo huiusmodi de scripturis maxime. Leo I. ep.22. ad clerum & populum Con-stantinopolit. idem tradit.
units.tr: Ambrose, Tom. 3, p. 321: read sermon 35, On the Lord's Fasting, toward the end, where he exhorts that all should receive the bread of the Scriptures and be exercised in them. Likewise Tom. 4, on Psalm 118, sermon 21, which is at p. 581, exhorts all the faithful to the reading of Scripture. The same, On Duties, book 1, ch. 22: let such discourse be, above all, about the Scriptures. Leo I, Epistle 22, to the clergy and people of Constantinople, delivers the same.

units.la: Quid haec demonstrant, nisi tunc etiam Laicos ita dedisse operam sacris Literis, ut possent cum Philosophis disputare, & eos convincere?
units.tr: What do these things show, except that the laity too in those times devoted themselves to the sacred letters so that they could dispute with the philosophers and refute them?

units.la: Scripturas cuiq; legendas esse, ra-tiones aliquot.
units.tr: That the Scriptures are to be read by each person: several reasons.

units.la: Scripturam sacram voluit populo He-braeo, Hebraica lingua, & quidem omnibus notissima tradi. Obsecro in quem finem, nisi ut ab omnibus legeretur & intelligeretur? 1. Corinth. 14. Hanc caulam docet Apostolus, cùm etiam iubet in Ecclesia vti lingua omnibus nota. Quamobrem? vt ab omnibus intelligatur, & ne alter alteri fiat barbarus. Multò minùs voluit Deus nobiscum ita loqui, vt non posset à nobis intelligi.
units.tr: God willed that the sacred Scripture be delivered to the Hebrew people in the Hebrew language, and indeed in a language most familiar to all. For what purpose, I beg you, except that it should be read and understood by all? The Apostle teaches this reason in 1 Corinthians 14, when he also orders that a language known to all be used in the Church. Why? So that it may be understood by all, and lest one become a barbarian to another. Much less did God wish to speak with us in such a way that it could not be understood by us.

units.la: Eadem de causa, cùm voluit suam legem non amplius inter Iudaeos contineri, sed ad omnes etiam Gentes propagari, immisit in mentem Ptolemaeo Philadel. Regi Aegypti, vt eam curaret per 72. Doctores Hebræos linguæ etiam Græcæ peritissimos, eo quo narrat Aristæas modo, in Græcam linguam conuerti, quò posset ab omnibus etiam Gen-tibus legi & intelligi. Erat enim tum temporis Græca lingua omnibus fere populis ac Gentibus nota in Asia, Africa, Europa. Cùm verò hæc fere in Africa atque Europa cum suo imperio interiisset, & Latina jam longiùs[?] latiusq; cœpisset propagari: voluit hanc sacram Scripturam latinam quoque fieri. Quam ob rem? Profecto, vt ab omnibus pos-set legi, percipi, memoriæ mandari. Denique voluit, vt omnes nationes, Germani, Itali, Galli, Hispani, Dalmatæ, Angli, Poloni, in sua quiq; lingua, eam haberent.
units.tr: For the same reason, when he willed that his law should no longer be confined among the Jews but spread also to all the Gentiles, he put it into the mind of Ptolemy Philadelphus, king of Egypt, to take care that it be turned into the Greek language by seventy-two Hebrew teachers, very skilled also in Greek, in the manner Aristeas relates, so that it could be read and understood by all the Gentiles as well. For at that time the Greek language was known to almost all peoples and nations in Asia, Africa and Europe. But when this language had nearly perished in Africa and Europe along with its empire, and Latin had begun to spread further and wider, he willed that this sacred Scripture be made Latin too. Why? Surely so that it could be read, grasped and committed to memory by all. Finally, he willed that all nations, Germans, Italians, French, Spaniards, Dalmatians, English, Poles, have it in their own tongue.

units.la: 2. Quì etiam fit, vt in sermonibus Patrum, etiamsi inculcentur scripturæ, autores tamen librorum, & capita non ita, vt nunc, citen-tur? Inde, quia populi ita erant exercitati in sacris Bibliis, vt sententia aliqua audita, mox intelligerent, cuius esset, & è quoto capite sumta fuisset. Hoc verò arguit, illos domi etiam vacasse sacrarum literarum lectioni.
units.tr: 2. It is also the case that in the sermons of the Fathers, even when Scripture is pressed upon the people, the authors of the books and the chapters are not cited as they are now? The reason is that the people were so practised in the sacred Bibles that, on hearing some sentence, they at once understood whose it was and from which chapter it had been taken. This indeed shows that they also devoted themselves at home to the reading of the sacred letters.

units.la: 3. Scriptura sacra, thesaurus est pretiosissi-mus vniuersis ac singulis hominibus à Deo donatus, vt fruantur & inde ditescant, vt et-iam Apostolus loquitur 1. Cor. ii. An non i-gitur magna tyrannis prohibere homines à fruitione sui thesauri?
units.tr: 3. Sacred Scripture is a most precious treasure given by God to all and each of mankind, so that they may enjoy it and be enriched by it, as the Apostle also says in 1 Corinthians 2. Is it not, then, a great tyranny to prohibit men from enjoying their own treasure?

units.la: 4. Permittuntur omnes Gentes legere scripturas, & prohibentur Christiani?
units.tr: 4. Are all nations permitted to read the Scriptures, and Christians forbidden?

units.la: 5. Pepigit Deus fœdus suum non cum sa-cerdotibus tantùm & Monachis, sed cum omnibus, etiam plebeis, etiam mulieribus, et-iam paruulis: Cur igitur non liceat vnicuique pactiones fœderis legere, vt sciat quid Deus illis promittat, quid vicissim ab illis sti-puletur?
units.tr: 5. God made his covenant not only with priests and monks, but with all, including common people and women and even little children. Why, then, should it not be permitted to each person to read the terms of the covenant, so that he may know what God promises him and what in turn he requires from him?

units.la: 6. Vita nostra perpetua est militia super terram, Iob. 7. Scriptura autem sacra, nostra sunt arma contra hos hostes, Ephes. 6. Cur non igitur tam vulgus & idiotæ his armis induantur, ut queant pugnare? Quomodo hoc? Legendo, studendo Bibliis. An non plusquam hostile est exarmare, quos oportet perpetuo esse armatos?
units.tr: 6. Our life is a continual warfare upon the earth, Job 7. Now the sacred Scripture is our weapons against these enemies, Ephesians 6. Why, then, should not the common people and the unlearned be armed with these weapons, so that they can fight? How so? By reading and studying the Bible. Is it not more than hostile to disarm those who ought to be always armed?

units.la: Responsiones ad exceptiones.
units.tr: Responses to objections.

units.la: 1. Omnes, qui scripturas lectitant, fiunt hæretici, Vide Tertull. de præscript. Hæret. pag.IIo[?].
units.tr: 1. All who read the Scriptures become heretics. See Tertullian, On the Prescription of Heretics, p. 2[?].

units.la: Resp. O maledicam vocem Quid] hoc aliud est, quàm dicere, quod Deus dedit pro medicamento animorum, illud esse venenum? & eo accersi morbum, quod aduersus morbum datum est? Contrarium traditur Iohan. 6[?]. 2. Timoth. 3. Scriptura valet πρὸς[?] ἔλεγχον, ad omnes scilicet hæreticos conuin-cendos. Contrarium tradit Psalm. 1. Beatus vir, &c. Contrarium etiam docuerunt Patres: Chrysost. in primis, homil. 3. de Lazaro: vbi dicit, ignorationem Scripturæ esse cau-sam hæreseos. Et alij Patres, Cum hæretici maximè Ecclesiam perturbarent, Ariani, Manichæi, Valentiniani, Marcionitæ, Sa-belliani, plurimique defecerent ad Gentili-tatem, tum maximè omnibus suadebat, ut vacarent scripturarum lectioni. Imò, si veli-mus hæresibus resistere, opus est scriptura-rum lectione. Nam sic ait Apostolus, πρὸς[?] ἔλεγχον. Audi & Chrysost. in Matth. 24. cap. expositione 2. homil. 49. Vide Cyprianum pag.177. Imò hæc est causa hæresum,ignora-tio & negleƈtio scripturarum: Chryf. de La-zaro,hom.ȷ.teste, vt diximus.
units.tr: Reply: Oh, what a cursed saying! Is this anything other than saying that what God gave as a medicine for souls is poison, and that the disease is brought on by the very thing given against disease? The opposite is taught in John 6[?]. In 2 Timothy 3 Scripture is profitable for refutation [πρὸς ἔλεγχον], that is, for convicting all heretics. The opposite is taught in Psalm 1: "Blessed is the man," etc. The Fathers also taught the opposite. Chrysostom above all, in homily 3 on Lazarus, where he says that ignorance of Scripture is the cause of heresy. And other Fathers: when heretics were especially disturbing the Church, the Arians, Manichaeans, Valentinians, Marcionites, Sabellians, and when very many were defecting to paganism, then above all they urged everyone to devote themselves to reading the Scriptures. Indeed, if we wish to resist heresies, there is need of the reading of the Scriptures. For the Apostle says so, [πρὸς ἔλεγχον]. Hear also Chrysostom on Matthew 24, exposition 2, homily 49. See Cyprian, p. 177. Indeed, this is the cause of heresies: ignorance and neglect of the Scriptures, as Chrysostom says in his homily on Lazarus, 1, as we have said.

units.la: Sed quinam sunt, qui hæc scribunt & dicunt?Papistæ. Quid istis est hæresis? Doctri-na, quæ cum ipsorum de iustificatione, de fide, de sacramentis pugnet. Verum igitur dicunt.Nam doctrina quam tradunt S. Lite-ræ,pugnat cum ipsorum.
units.tr: But who are those who write and say these things? The Papists. What is heresy to them? Doctrine that conflicts with their own teaching on justification, on faith, on the sacraments. So they speak truly in this sense: for the doctrine that the Holy Scriptures teach conflicts with theirs.

units.la: Quòd fi tamen aliqui iis abutantur ad hæ-reses:hoc ex accidenti, id est, ipsorum vitio, non scripturarum fit. Sic de Epistolis Pauli scribit Petrus. Qui (inquit) praui homines, deprauant ad suam perditionem.. Quot etiam sunt,qui vino ad suum interitum abutuntur? 1. Cor. 1. Paulus prædicat Christum, sua certè natura sapientiam & virtutem : interim non omnibus erat virtus & sapientia, sed aliis stultitia,aliis scandalum. Item Apostoli erant sua doctrina aliis odor mortis. Quibus? iis qui pereunt.
units.tr: But if some nevertheless abuse them for heresies, this happens by accident, that is, through their own fault, not through the fault of the Scriptures. So Peter writes concerning the Epistles of Paul: "Which (he says) the unlearned and unstable wrest, as they do also the other Scriptures, unto their own destruction." How many also abuse wine to their own ruin? In 1 Corinthians 1, Paul preaches Christ, who is certainly by his nature wisdom and power; yet not to all was he power and wisdom, but to some foolishness, to others a stumbling block. Likewise the Apostles, by their teaching, were to some the savour of death. To whom? To those who perish.

units.la: Contra hanc diabolicam vocem,oppono Christum Ioh. 8. Qui ex Deo est, verba Dei audit,propterea vos non auditis,quia ex Deo non estis. Hos autem paulò ante dixit, esse ex Pa-treDiabolo natos.Sic igitur sentiamus iuxta hanc Christi infallibilem regulam: Qui de-lectantur verbo Dei audiendo legendo, meditando, & ad idem alios hortantur: hos dare testimonium,se esse ex Deo. Contrà,Qui non delectantur, & alios etiam ab eius le-ctione dehortatur, hos verè ex Diabolo esse.
units.tr: Against this diabolical saying I set Christ in John 8: "He that is of God hears God's words; therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God." He had said a little earlier that these men were born of their father the Devil. So let us therefore think, according to this infallible rule of Christ: those who delight in hearing, reading, and meditating on the Word of God, and urge others to the same, give evidence that they are of God. On the contrary, those who take no delight in it, and even dissuade others from reading it, are truly of the Devil.

units.la: Exceptio II[?].
units.tr: Objection II[?].

units.la: 2. Scriptura nihil[?] aliud est, quàm materiali-tis & rixarum. In Colloquio VVormatiensi, Anno 57[?].
units.tr: 2. Scripture is nothing other than a source of strife and quarrels. At the Colloquy of Worms, in the year 57[?].

units.la: Resp. Diabolica blasphemia est: imò est norma & causa pacis & componendarum rixarum.
units.tr: Reply: It is a diabolical blasphemy; rather, it is the rule and cause of peace and of settling quarrels.

units.la: Exceptio III.
units.tr: Objection III.

units.la: 3. Scripturam nemo per se potest intelligere.
units.tr: 3. No one can understand Scripture by himself.

units.la: Resp. Quasi verò Spiritus sanctus non adsit invocantibus se? Quasi etiam non possit quisque interrogare doctiorem se. Vide Hie-ronymum in fine Nahum.
units.tr: Reply: As if the Holy Spirit were not present to those who call upon him! As if each person could not also ask someone more learned than himself. See Jerome at the end of Nahum.

units.la: Esse hoc officium maximè Doctorum & Pastorum.
units.tr: That this duty belongs chiefly to teachers and ministers.

units.la: Etsi verò omnium Christianorum est stu-dere sacris literis: præcipuum tamen hoc est officium Doctorum & Pastorum Ecclesiæ, & eorum qui se ad huiusce modi ministerium Ecclesiasticum præparant: idque pro-pterea, quòd aliorum præceptores, ductores & doctores constituti sunt. Quis autem du-bitat, debere doctorem discipulis esse do-ctiorem? & ductores exercitus, peritiores rei militaris, quàm reliqui milites? Sed audia-mus scripturas.
units.tr: Although it is the duty of all Christians to study the sacred letters, this is nevertheless the particular duty of the teachers and ministers of the Church, and of those who prepare themselves for this kind of ecclesiastical ministry; and this is so because they have been appointed as the instructors, guides and teachers of others. Who, however, doubts that a teacher ought to be more learned than his pupils, and that the leaders of an army should be more skilled in military affairs than the rest of the soldiers? But let us hear the Scriptures.

units.la: Leuit. 10. præcipit Deus Leuitis, ut legem atque statuta à se tradita populum fideliter doceant. Malach. 2. Labia sacerdotis custo-dient. dient scientiam, & legem requirent ex ore eius. Hos. 4. Quia repulisti scientiam, repellam & ego te, ne sacerdotio fungaris mihi. Matth. 5. Vos estis lux Mundi & sal terrae. 1. Timoth. 3. Oportet Episcopum esse διδακτικὸν [?]. 2. Timoth. 1. & 2. ut sciat ὀρθολογεῖν [?]. Tit. 1. Oportet esse tenacem eius qui secundum doctrinam est sermonis: potens et-iam sit exhortari per doctrinam sanam, & τῶν ἀντιλεγόντων ἐλέγχειν [?]. Ier. 23. Ministros Ecclesiarum, qui ignorantes verbum Dei populo obtrudunt sua somnia, vocat onera, quae proiici a facie Domini oporteat. Ezech. 22. 24. Tales vult Dominus Templi ministros eligi, qui inter caetera docere etiam possint populum, quid inter sanctum & profanum interfit. Qui id non possunt, eos excludit, & perpetua vult notari ignominia. Quid haec docent, nisi Pastores ita debere esse exercitatos prae caeteris in sacris Literis, ut populum possint docere: Et si id nequeant, officio & loco submovendos esse?
units.tr: In Leviticus 10 God commands the Levites to teach the people faithfully the law and the statutes given by him. Malachi 2: "The lips of the priest shall keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law at his mouth." Hosea 4: "Because you have rejected knowledge, I also will reject you, that you shall not serve as priest to me." Matthew 5: "You are the light of the world and the salt of the earth." 1 Timothy 3: "A bishop must be apt to teach" [διδακτικόν]. 2 Timothy 1 and 2: that he may know how to handle the word rightly [ὀρθοτομεῖν]. Titus 1: "He must hold fast the faithful word as he has been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convict the gainsayers" [τῶν ἀντιλεγόντων ἐλέγχειν]. Jeremiah 23: he calls the ministers of the Churches who, ignorant of the word of God, foist their own dreams upon the people, burdens which must be cast from the face of the Lord. Ezekiel 22 and 24: the Lord wills that such ministers of the Temple be chosen, who among other things can also teach the people what difference there is between the holy and the profane. Those who cannot do so he excludes, and wills that they be marked with perpetual disgrace. What do these passages teach, except that ministers ought to be so trained above others in the sacred Letters that they can teach the people; and that if they cannot, they should be removed from their office and place?

units.la: Extant etiam hac de re Canones antiqui, & Patrum sententiae.
units.tr: There also exist ancient canons on this matter, and the opinions of the Fathers.

units.la: Distinct. 36. 37. 38. Decretalibus de Ele-ctione: de aetate & qualitate ordinandorum. Episcopus Catinensis per Honor. 3. propter ignorationem scripturarum depositus est ab officio, Decretal. Can. Quamvis multos. Et id merito, Ecclesiasticum enim ministerium situm non est in frigidis ceremoniis & cantionibus, sed cum primis in diligenti scripturarum explicatione. Quomodo autem officium hoc præstare possunt scripturarum ignari? Quomodo falsa euertere dogmata? Quomodo vitia prudenter reprehendere? Quomodo afflictos consolari? Hæc enim omnia è scripturis petenda sunt.
units.tr: Distinction 36, 37, 38; in the Decretals, On Election; on the age and qualifications of those to be ordained. The Bishop of Catania, through Honorius III, was deposed from his office on account of ignorance of the Scriptures; Decretal, canon "Quamvis multos." And rightly so: for the ecclesiastical ministry does not consist in cold ceremonies and chants, but above all in the diligent explanation of the Scriptures. How, however, can those ignorant of the Scriptures perform this office? How can they overthrow false dogmas? How prudently reprove vices? How console the afflicted? For all these things must be sought from the Scriptures.

units.la: Fatemur igitur libenter, Ministrorum Ec-clesiæ, & eorum qui ad Ministerium Eccle-siasticum sunt promouendi, cum primis esse officium, ita sacris Literis operam dare, ut in illis sint omnium exercitatissimi: Et hac de causa Apostolum hic Timotheum speciatim monere, ut attendat sacris Literis: sed hinc non consequitur, Ergo horum tantùm esse studere Bibliis, à Laicis autem idem officium minimè requiri. Nam etiam 1. Tim. 3. requi-rit ab Episcopo, ut sit irreprehensibilis, unius uxoris maritus, sobrius, pudicus, non vinolentus: Consequiturne, Ergo hæc ab aliis non Epi-scopis minimè requiri? Nequaquam. Sed be-ne sequitur, Ergo etsi hæc ab omnibus fide-libus exiguntur: cum primis tamen ab Episcopis, quos oportet esse virtutum omnium exemplaria in Ecclesia. Idem de lectione stu-dioque scripturarum dicendum est. Et res confirmatur exemplo in veteri Testamento. Leuitis cum primis mandabatur, ut verbum Domini populo explicarent: interim non excludebantur alij, qui non erant è tribu Le-ui, ut multi Prophetæ, ab eodem officio, & Christus, qui erat ex tribu Iuda, id fecit officij.
units.tr: We therefore willingly grant that it is the chief duty of the ministers of the Church, and of those who are to be promoted to the ecclesiastical ministry, to devote themselves to the sacred Letters in such a way that they become the most practised in them all. And for this reason the Apostle here specifically admonishes Timothy "to attend to the sacred Letters." But it does not follow from this: therefore only these men ought to study the Bible, and the same duty is in no way required of the laity. For 1 Timothy 3 also requires of the bishop that he be blameless, the husband of one wife, sober, chaste, not given to wine. Does it follow: therefore these things are in no way required of others who are not bishops? By no means. But it rightly follows: therefore, although these things are required of all the faithful, nevertheless especially of bishops, who ought to be examples of all virtues in the Church. The same must be said about reading and devotion to the Scriptures. And the matter is confirmed by the example in the Old Testament. The Levites in particular were commanded to explain the Word of the Lord to the people; yet others who were not of the tribe of Levi were not excluded from this office, as many prophets were, and Christ, who was of the tribe of Judah, performed this office.

units.la: QVÆSTIO X. De versionibus Bibliorum.
units.tr: QUESTION X. On the translations of the Bible.

units.la: Quæstionem nonam sequitur decima, quæ de Bibliorum est versionibus. Nam si Biblia cuique Christiano legenda sunt, legi autem non possunt, nisi in eam vertantur linguam, quam quisque intelligat, neque omnes unam & eandem percipiunt linguam: ex una igitur lingua in aliam convertantur necesse est. Quare merito agendum nunc est de variis Bibliorum versionibus.
units.tr: The ninth question is followed by the tenth, which concerns translations of the Bible. For if the Bible is to be read by every Christian, and it cannot be read unless it is turned into the language that each person understands, and not all understand one and the same language, then it is necessary that it be translated from one language into another. Therefore it is rightly our business now to deal with the various translations of the Bible.

units.la: Duo autem nobis agenda sunt: primum de versionibus Græcis & Latinis, de quibus apud veteres autores al quid memoriæ prolditum est. Deinde quæstio explicanda, An præter illas, utile etiam sit, & an forte etiam necessarium, in linguam cuiusq; Gentis propriam Biblia convertere, nec ne. Nam non desunt, qui etiam hoc inficientur: imò qui etiam dicant non licere.
units.tr: We have two things to deal with. First, the Greek and Latin translations, of which some memory has been handed down by the ancient authors. Second, the question to be explained: whether, besides those, it is useful, and perhaps even necessary, to translate the Bible into the proper language of each nation, or not. For there are not lacking those who deny even this, indeed who say that it is not lawful.

units.la: Quod ad primum igitur attinet: prima & principalis, maximæq; omnium autoritatis versio, versio fuit ex Hebræa lingua in Græ-cam per 72. Interpretes, Hebræos quidem homines genere ac gente, sed lingua non tam Hebraica, quàm etiam Græca insignes excellentissimosq; viros, & omnium qui tum temporis essent inter Hebræos, sanctissimos simul & doctissimos Legis Doctores.
units.tr: As to the first point, then: the first and principal translation, and the greatest in authority of all, was the translation from the Hebrew language into Greek by the Seventy-two Interpreters, men Hebrew indeed by birth and nation, but outstanding and most excellent men in the Greek language as well as the Hebrew, and at once the most holy and most learned teachers of the Law among all the Hebrews of that time.

units.la: Quo tempore, & quo autore ij Hebræi Biblia fecerint ex Hebræis Græca, satis inter omnes constat, nempe nō ita multò post mortem Alexandri Magni, autore Ptolemęo Philadelpho Ægyptiorum rege, posteaquam regnasset annos 17. à quo anno vsque ad Augustum Regem Romanorum intercesserunt anni 249. Anno autem Augusti 42. nascitur Christus.
units.tr: When and at whose instigation those Hebrews made the Greek Bible from the Hebrew is fairly well agreed by all: namely, not long after the death of Alexander the Great, under Ptolemy Philadelphus, king of the Egyptians, after he had reigned seventeen years. From that year until Augustus, king of the Romans, there intervened 249 years. In the forty-second year of Augustus, Christ was born.

units.la: Cæterùm, quænam conuerterint, & quomodo conuerterint, & qua fide conuerterint, non eadem prorsus est omnium scriptorum de hisce tribus capitibus sententia.
units.tr: Moreover, what they translated, and how they translated it, and with what fidelity they translated it, is not at all the same opinion of all writers on these three heads.

units.la: Nam quod ad libros conuersos attinet, sunt qui velint, legem duntaxat, hoc est, quinque libros Mosis, fuisse per hosce 72. viros, sic iubente Philadelpho, in Græcam linguam conuersos, idque intra spacium 72. dierum: reliquos verò libros ab aliis postmodum factos fuisse Græcos. In hac sententia esse videtur Aristæus, qui hanc historiam Græcè scriptam nobis reliquit, & qui scribit, se vnum ex illis fuisse, qui à Rege Hierosolymam ad Eleazarum sacerdotem pro iis interpretibus missi fuerunt. Is enim mentionem tantùm facit legis. Huius sententiæ videtur esse &c &c Iosephus Flauius, grauissimus autor, lib. de antiquit. Iud. 12.[?] cap. 2. Nam mentionem tan-tùm facit legis.
units.tr: For as to the books translated, there are some who wish that only the Law, that is, the five books of Moses, was translated into the Greek language by these seventy-two men, as Philadelphus commanded, and that within the space of seventy-two days; and that the remaining books were afterwards made Greek by others. Aristeas seems to be of this opinion, who left us this history written in Greek, and who writes that he himself was one of those who were sent by the King to Eleazar the priest for those interpreters. For he makes mention only of the Law. Flavius Josephus, a most weighty author, in book 12 of the Antiquities of the Jews, chapter 2, seems to be of this opinion, etc. For he makes mention only of the Law.

units.la: 2. Sunt verò multò plures, & grauissimi scriptores, qui scribant, non solùm legem, sed omnia sacra Biblia fuisse per hos 72. Interpretes conuersa. Inter hos est Iosephus Hebr.filius Gorionis, lib. 3. cap. 2. Irenæus, lib.3.cap.25.Iustinus Martyr in exhortatione ad Gentes pag.17.
units.tr: 2. But there are far more, and most weighty, writers who write that not only the Law but all the holy Bible was translated by these seventy-two interpreters. Among these is Josephus the Hebrew, son of Gorion, book 3, chapter 2; Irenaeus, book 3, chapter 25; Justin Martyr in his Exhortation to the Gentiles, page 17.

units.la: Epiphanius libr. de mensuris & ponderi-bus, pag. 606. Euseb. Cæsar. histor. Eccle-siast.lib.5. cap.8. Athanas. in synopsi scriptu-rarum, Theodoretus Cyr.Episcopus: Augu-stinus de doctrina Christiana, libr.2. cap 15. Item de ciuitate Dei, lib.18. cap.42.43. Et idem liquet ex desiderio Ptolemæi, quod fuit, ut omnibus bonis libris instrueretur e-ius Bibliotheca.
units.tr: Epiphanius, in his book On Weights and Measures, page 606; Eusebius of Caesarea, Ecclesiastical History, book 5, chapter 8; Athanasius in the Synopsis of the Scriptures; Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus; Augustine, On Christian Doctrine, book 2, chapter 15; also On the City of God, book 18, chapters 42 and 43. And the same is clear from the desire of Ptolemy, which was that his library be furnished with all good books.

units.la: Ad id verò, quod obiicitur ex Aristea & Iosepho, mentionem tantùm fieri legis, re-sponsio facilis est: nomen legis sæpe accipi pro tota sacra scriptura veteris Testamenti. Exempla, Psal 1. Ioh.15. Ut impleretur sermo, qui in lege eorum scriptus est, Oderunt me im-merito. Matth.5. Iota unum,aut unus apex ne-quaquam præterierit ex lege, usque dum omnia facta fuerint.
units.tr: To what is objected from Aristeas and Josephus, that only the Law is mentioned, the answer is easy: the name "Law" is often taken for the whole of the holy Scripture of the Old Testament. Examples: Psalm 1; John 15, "That the word might be fulfilled that is written in their law: They hated me without a cause." Matthew 5, "One jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled."

units.la: Quod ad secundum: sunt qui velint hos 72. seniores, simul eodem in loco congre-gatos, simul etiam conferendo, Biblia ver-tisse. Ita scribit Aristæas, quem habemus Græcè. Eadem scribit Iosephus Flauius, lo-co supra citato. Idem sentit Hieronymus. Contrà tamen sentiunt alij & grauissimi qui-dem illi atque antiquissimi scriptores, quo-rum etiam libros & capita, in quibus hac de re scribunt, supra citauimus: Iosephus He-bræus Ben Gorionis ex Hebræo per Mun-sterum verso. Iustinus Martyr in exhortatione ad Gentes. Irenæus. Hi apertissimè scribunt, Ptolemæum curasse, ut diversæ sic-rent cellulæ, idque ad Pharum insulam, in quibus singuli illi interpretes Biblia con-verterunt: idque ut melius appareret eorum fides & diligentia in vertendis Bibliis, neque ex communi consilio aliquid vel omittere, vel mutare ob aliquam invidiam possent. Et quidem Iustinus ait, se vestigia illarum cellularum vidisse, & illorum locorum indigenas hoc tanquam per manus à Patribus acceptum, sibi narrasse. Illi certè duo, Iustinus & Irenæus, antiquissimi sunt scriptores, quibus consentit Tertullianus in Apologet. cap.191.[?]
units.tr: As to the second point: there are some who wish that these seventy elders, gathered together in one and the same place, also translated the Bible by comparing together at the same time. Aristeas, whom we have in Greek, writes thus. Flavius Josephus writes the same, in the place cited above. Jerome holds the same view. On the other hand, however, other and indeed most weighty and most ancient writers, whose books and chapters, in which they write on this matter, we have cited above, hold a contrary view: Josephus the Hebrew, son of Gorion, translated from the Hebrew by Münster; Justin Martyr in his Exhortation to the Gentiles; Irenaeus. These write most plainly that Ptolemy arranged for separate cells to be set up, and that at Pharos island, in which each of those interpreters translated the Bible, so that their faith and diligence in translating the Bible might better appear, and so that they could not omit or change anything by common counsel for fear of any ill will. And indeed Justin says that he himself saw the traces of those cells, and that the natives of those places told him this, as handed down to them by the Fathers. Those two, Justin and Irenaeus, are most ancient writers, with whom Tertullian agrees in his Apology, chapter 19 [?].

units.la: Hos postea secuti sunt Epiphanius, quan-quam hic aliquid diversum scribit, binos scilicet, & binos fuisse distributos illos 72. interpretes, ita ut in 36. domunculis omnes essent à se invicem divisi & separati. Certè non omnes simul inter se contulisse uno & eodem consensu scribunt isti Patres. Quibus subscribunt alii quàm plurimi, Theodo-retus Cyrens[?] Episcopus: Eusceb. Cæsariensis. Augustinus.
units.tr: After these followed Epiphanius, although he writes something different here: namely that the seventy interpreters were divided into pairs, and two by two, in thirty-six little houses, so that all were separated and divided from one another. Certainly these Fathers write that they did not all compare with one another in one and the same agreement. To them subscribe very many others: Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus; Eusebius of Caesarea; Augustine.

units.la: Verum est ab Hieronymo has cellulas derideri passim in suis libris, præsertim in A-pologia adversus Rufinum pag. 224[?]. Tom 2. Sed nihil certi adfert in contrarium ex antiquis monumentis. Interim verò magna est Iustini cum primis & Irenæi & Tertul-liani autoritas, ut de posterioribus Patribus taceam. Hinc factum est, vt maxima semper in autoritate fuerit hæc 72. Interpretum versio, vt etiam Hieronymus cogatur 70. Inter- preres[?] laudare.
units.tr: It is true that Jerome everywhere mocks these cells in his books, especially in his Apology against Rufinus, page 224 [?], Tom. 2. But he brings nothing certain to the contrary from the ancient records. Meanwhile the authority of Justin above all, and of Irenaeus and Tertullian, is great, not to mention the later Fathers. Hence it has come about that this version of the Seventy-two Interpreters has always been of the greatest authority, so that even Jerome is compelled to praise the Seventy Interpreters.

units.la: Quod ad tertium attinet: neque Hieronymus ipse dubitat de fide & diligentia 70. Interpretum: ac proinde quòd multa ab Hebræis voluminibus diuersa in hac quam nos habemus versione Græca reperiantur: hoc aut 70. interpretum inscitiæ, aut aliorum malitiæ, qui versionem 70. corruperint, attribuendum esse, sicut de Aquila scribit Epiphanius.
units.tr: As to the third point: Jerome himself does not doubt the faith and diligence of the Seventy Interpreters; and therefore, that many things found in this Greek version which we have differ from the Hebrew volumes, this must be attributed either to the ignorance of the Seventy Interpreters or to the malice of others who corrupted the version of the Seventy, as Epiphanius writes concerning Aquila.

units.la: Diuersissimam esse versionem Græcam ab Hebraica veritate, nemo est quin videre possit, si cum illa hanc conferat. Vbi autem huius diuersitatis culpa hæreat, an in 70. ipsis, an vero in aliis, an partim in ipsis, partim in aliis, operæ pretium fuerit inuestigare & intelligere. Non totam residere in 70. liquidò apparet non tam testimonio Hieronymi & aliorum, sed etiam ex collatione eorum Bibliorum Græcorum, quæ impressa circumferuntur, cum codicibus antiquis. Ego certè olim vidi Romæ apud Basilium Zanchium propinquum meum, permulta in ipsius Bibliis Græcis ad exemplum codicis vetustissimi manu scripti, quod est in Vaticano, emendata. Multa igitur aliunde errata irrepserunt in Biblia 70. Interpretum. Non totam etiam huius diuersitatis causam ita hærere in aliis, vt nihil residear 70. Interpretibus, inde colligere possumus, quòd ab Euangelistis & Apostolis multa ex veteri Testamento citantur, quæ cum Hebraica veritate non vsquequaq; congruunt, sed tantùm cum 70. Non est autem vllo modo concedendum, Apostolos citaffe ex Bibliis Græcis dicta, quæ aliter fe haberent, quàm in ipsis Bibliis, quæ tunc in manu omnium versabantur, continerentur & legerentur. Et tamen hæc dicta aliter fe habent in Bibliis Hebraicis, & consentiunt cum Græcis. Ergo horum saltem locorum ab Apostolis citatorum diuersitas, ab ipsis 70. fit interpretibus, necesse est. Quòd fi quis excipiat, hanc lectionis diuersitatem non esse abs 70. interpretibus, quasi aut nescierint aut noluerint fideliter vertere ex Hebraica veritate, sed adscribendam esse Rabinis, qui post 70. secuti sunt, ab ipsis nimirum Hebraica Biblia fuisse corrupta, idque adductis odio Christianorum, ne veritatem haberent Hebraicorum librorum: hic facilè reiicietur & refelletur. Nam fi Hebraica Biblia corrupta fuerunt ab Hebræis, hoc factum est aut ante Christi aduentum, aut post. Si ante: Christus certè reprehendisset Pharifæos & ipsorum Patres de corruptis Bibliis, sicut & de reliquis minoribus peccatis arguebat. Non hoc fecit, imò semper hortatus est ad horum Bibliorum lectionem. Ergo, &c. Si post: vel hoc contigit tempore Apostolorum, vel post illud tempus. Si tempore Apostolorum : Apostoli certe hoc a-nimaduertissent, & tum Hebros reprehen-dissent, tum Gentes & reliquos de hac read-monuissent , tum etiam corrigenda Biblia curassent. Atqui nihil horum est ab Apostolis factum. Si post tempus Apostolorum : aliqui etiam ex illis Apostolicis Patribus hoc observassent, & aliquam huius rei in suis scriptis mentionem fecissent, & Biblia suæ pristinę[?] veritati restituenda curassent: Ac præter alios Hieronymus in Hebraicis L. versatissimus, & diligentissimus He-braicorum Bibliorum indagator & observator, hoc observasset, notasset, corrigi curasset: præsertim quia non deerant Hebraica Ex-emplaria, quæ iam inde ab Apostolis in Ec-clesiis & scholis à se institutis, relicta fue-rant. Atqui nihil horum legimus fuisse ob-servatum aut factum ab Hieronymo vel aliis Patribus. Imò contrà Hieronymus præter alios, ad Hebraica semper exemplaria pro-vocat, & ea in linguam convertit Latinam. Non est igitur verisimile, nec probabile, He-braica Biblia aut ante Christum, aut tempore Apostolorum aut etiam post obitum Apostolorum fuisse ab Hebræis corrupta. Nam quibus volebant corrumpere ? Sibi? Hoc est stultum cogitare. Nobis Christianis? At iam veritas Christiana erat confirmata. Item multa erant apud Christianos vera & pura Bibliorum etiam Hebraicorum exem-plaria, ad quæ illa sexaminata[?], mox & facilè potuisset cognosci, an essent corrupta, nec ne corrupta: atqj ita apud Imperatores Christianos Hebraei illi accusari & convinci, falsi & sacrilegij.
units.tr: That the Greek version is very different from the Hebrew truth, no one can fail to see if he compares the one with the other. But where the fault of this difference lies, whether in the Seventy themselves, or in others, or partly in the Seventy and partly in others, it will be worth the effort to investigate and understand. That the fault does not rest wholly in the Seventy is clear not only from the testimony of Jerome and others, but also from the collation of those Greek Bibles which circulate in print with ancient manuscripts. I myself once saw at Rome, at the house of my kinsman Basilius Zanchius, very many passages in his Greek Bibles corrected according to the example of a most ancient manuscript codex, which is in the Vatican. Many errors therefore crept into the Bible of the Seventy from elsewhere. That the cause of this difference does not lie wholly in others, so that nothing remains to be attributed to the Seventy Interpreters, we can gather from this: that many passages of the Old Testament are cited by the Evangelists and Apostles which do not at all agree with the Hebrew truth, but only with the Seventy.
