Yet it must in no way be conceded that the Apostles cited from the Greek Bibles sayings which stood otherwise than they are contained in the Bibles themselves, which were then in the hands of all and were read. And yet these sayings stand otherwise in the Hebrew Bibles, and agree with the Greek. Therefore, at least for these passages cited by the Apostles, the difference must necessarily come from the Seventy Interpreters themselves. But if anyone should except that this variety of reading is not from the Seventy Interpreters, as though they had either not known or not wished to translate faithfully from the Hebrew truth, but that it is to be ascribed to the rabbis who followed after the Seventy, and that the Hebrew Bibles were corrupted by them, moved of course by hatred of the Christians, so that they would not have the truth of the Hebrew books: this will easily be rejected and refuted. For if the Hebrew Bibles were corrupted by the Hebrews, this happened either before the coming of Christ or after. If before: Christ certainly would have rebuked the Pharisees and their fathers for the corrupted Bibles, just as he also reproved them for the other lesser sins. He did not do this; rather he always urged them to read these Bibles. Therefore, etc. If after: either this happened in the time of the Apostles, or after that time. If in the time of the Apostles: the Apostles certainly would have noticed this, and then would have rebuked the Hebrews, and would have admonished the Gentiles and the rest about this matter, and would also have taken care that the Bibles be corrected. But nothing of this was done by the Apostles. If after the time of the Apostles: some of those Apostolic Fathers would also have observed this, and would have made some mention of it in their writings, and would have taken care that the Bibles be restored to their former truth. And besides others, Jerome, most versed in Hebrew and most diligent investigator and observer of the Hebrew Bibles, would have observed it, noted it, and taken care to correct it; especially since there were no lack of Hebrew copies, which had been left from the time of the Apostles in the churches and schools which they had founded. But we read that nothing of this was observed or done by Jerome or the other Fathers. On the contrary, Jerome, besides others, always appeals to the Hebrew copies and translates them into Latin. It is therefore neither likely nor probable that the Hebrew Bibles were corrupted by the Hebrews, either before Christ, or in the time of the Apostles, or even after the death of the Apostles. For whom did they wish to corrupt them? Themselves? That is foolish to think. Us Christians? But the Christian truth was already confirmed. Likewise there were among the Christians many true and pure copies even of the Hebrew Bibles, by which those [copies] might have been examined, and it could soon and easily have been recognised whether they were corrupted or not; and thus those Hebrews would have been accused and convicted before the Christian Emperors of falsehood and sacrilege.

units.la: Deinde, si Hebraei corrupissent Christianorum causa: oportuisset illos ea sic corrupta exhibere Christianis. At Christiani non accepissent: tum quòd non opus habuissent, tum quòd non si Iudæis fuissent. Non est igitur vllo modo probabile, Hebraica Biblia fuisse à quopiam depravata. Quare cum diuersa sint à versione septuaginta Interpretum, & huius diuersitatis causa non sit in Hebraica, in Græca sit necesse est: quòd scilicet aut non vsque adeò fuerit omni ex parte fideliter translata à 70. Interpretibus, aut ab aliis fuerit corrupta.
units.tr: Next, if the Hebrews had corrupted the text for the sake of the Christians, they would have had to present those corrupted copies to the Christians. But the Christians would not have accepted them: partly because they had no need of them, and partly because they would not have been Jews if they had. It is therefore in no way probable that the Hebrew Bibles were corrupted by anyone. Since, then, the Septuagint differs from them, and the cause of this difference is not in the Hebrew, it must be in the Greek: either the Seventy translators did not translate faithfully in every respect, or the text was corrupted by others.

units.la: Corruptas sententias non citassent Apostoli: Ergo saltem quantum ad hæc dicta quæ citantur ab Apostolis attinet, necesse est dicamus, ita fuisse à septuaginta translata ex Hebræo, sicut ab Apostolis citantur. Sunt autem diuersa ab Hebraica veritate: diuersè igitur sunt Biblia, aliquibus saltem in locis, ab Hebraica veritate interpretati. Quod cum ita sit: magnus & difficilis hic oritur scrupus, qui multum mihi quoque alias fecit negotij. Quisnam ille est? Dicam. Apostoli ad comprobandam Euangelij veritatem, vsi sunt sæpissimè versione septuaginta Interpretum, diuersa à veritate Hebraica: Quod autem est diuersum à veritate, illud falsum sit, necesse est. Falso igitur vsi sunt ad veritatem confirmandam?
units.tr: The Apostles would not have cited corrupt sentences. So at least as far as those passages that the Apostles cite are concerned, we must say that the Seventy translated them from the Hebrew just as the Apostles cite them. But they differ from the Hebrew truth; so the Bibles were translated differently from the Hebrew truth, at least in some places. Since this is so, a great and difficult scruple arises here, which has also caused me much trouble at other times. What is it? I will say. The Apostles, to confirm the truth of the Gospel, very often used the version of the Seventy translators, which differs from the Hebrew truth. But what differs from the truth must be false. Did they therefore use something false to confirm the truth?

units.la: Resp. Negatur Minor. Non enim omne diuersum à vero, proprie falsum est: sed illud tantum, quod ita est diuersum, vt pugnet cum vero. Exemplum: vt, Christus est Deus, Christus non est Deus: & in aliis propositionibus, quæ sibi opponuntur vel contrariè, vel negatiuè, vel contradictoriè. Sed in nomine ὁμωνύμῳ, etsi multa habeat significata diuersa, non tamen contraria. Ideo etiamsi tu vnam, & ego aliam adferam significationem: non sequitur, alterutram esse falsam: diuersæ quidem sint, necesse est, sed non falsæ: altera illarum falsa, quando vtraque illi conueniat nomini. Sic igitur sentiendum de hac quæstione. Inter versionem 70. & veritatem Hebraicam, etsi aliqua sit diuersitas in significationibus aliquot vel nominum, vel verborum: non eam tamen significationum diuersitatem adferre diuersitatem doctrinæ pietatis, sed pulchrè conuenire in hac doctrina 70. versionem, cum Hebraica veritate. Quare Apostoli ad comprobandam veritatem doctrinæ, non sunt vsi falso, sed illo vero, quod erat in Bibliis 70. aliquo modo diuerso ab illo vero, quod erat in Hebraicis voluminibus. Et hoc fecerunt necessitate coacti. Exemplo rem declaro. Versio Noui Testamenti vulgaris, in multis diuersa est à contextu Græco. Quibus in rebus? In fignificationibus verborum, & nominum &c phrasium. Sed numquid in doctrina pietatis? hoc est in doctrina quae ad fidem & ad mores pertinet? Minime. Idem dico de Hebraica &c 70. Apostoli igitur cum viderent versionem 70. vsitatam esse apud Gentes, & eam, quod ad doctrinam pietatis attinet, nihil diuersum continere ab Hebraica veritate, sed esse eandem prorsus: sibi autem propositum ef-set non nouas mouere quaestiones de con-textibus scripturarum, sed veritatem Euan-gelij, & doctrinam pietatis praedicare & confirmare, non testimoniis incognitis, sed notis: id certe quod de Christo praedicabant, illud confirmabant testimoniis ex 70. versione desumptis, etsi aliqua ex parte diuersa esset a verbis Hebraicae veritatis, quod hoc nihil referret, quia nihil impedimenti adfe-rebat praedicationi veritatis doctrinae: con-tra vero multum impeditus & retardatus fuisset cursus Euangelij, si diuersam attulif-sent interpretationem, ab interpretatione apud illos vsitata, nempe 70. Simile. Quem-admodum si nunc praedicandum esset Papi-stis, qui soliti sunt semper legere vulgatam editionem: si aliam adferas editionem & in-terpretationem, impedires potius cursum Euangelij, quam promoueres. Nouae enim excitarentur quaestiones de versionibus, & interim summa doctrinae negligeretur.
units.tr: I answer: the minor premise is denied. For not everything that differs from the true is strictly false, but only that which differs in such a way that it conflicts with the true. Example: Christ is God; Christ is not God. The same holds for other propositions that oppose one another contrarily, negatively, or contradictorily. But in an homonym, although it has many different meanings, they are not contrary. So even if you bring forward one meaning and I bring forward another, it does not follow that either one is false: they must indeed be different, but not false; one of them is false only when both apply to that same name. So this question should be judged in this way. Between the version of the Seventy and the Hebrew truth, although there is some difference in the meanings of certain words or names, that difference of meanings does not bring a difference of the doctrine of piety; rather, the Seventy's version agrees finely with the Hebrew truth in this doctrine. Therefore the Apostles, to confirm the truth of the doctrine, did not use what was false, but that truth which was in the Seventy's Bible, which was in some way different from that truth which was in the Hebrew volumes. And they did this, compelled by necessity. I make the matter clear by an example. The common version of the New Testament differs from the Greek text in many places. In what respects? In the meanings of words and names, and in phrases, etc. But does it differ in the doctrine of piety, that is, in the doctrine that pertains to faith and to morals? Not at all. I say the same of the Hebrew and the Seventy. So the Apostles, when they saw that the version of the Seventy was in common use among the Gentiles, and that, as far as the doctrine of piety is concerned, it contained nothing different from the Hebrew truth but was entirely the same, and since it was their purpose not to raise new questions about the contexts of the Scriptures, but to preach and confirm the Gospel truth and the doctrine of piety, using testimonies not unknown but familiar: what they preached about Christ, they certainly confirmed by testimonies taken from the Seventy's version, even though in some respect it differed from the words of the Hebrew truth. This made no difference, because it did not hinder the preaching of the truth of the doctrine at all. On the contrary, the course of the Gospel would have been much hindered and delayed if they had brought forward an interpretation different from the interpretation in use among them, namely the Seventy's. A comparison: just as if the Papists, who have always been accustomed to read the Vulgate edition, were now to be preached to; if you brought forward another edition and interpretation, you would hinder the course of the Gospel rather than advance it. For new questions would be raised about versions, and in the meantime the sum of the doctrine would be neglected.

units.la: Secunda Bibliorum versio fuit facta ab Aquila ex Hebraeo itidem in Graecum, sub Adriano Imperatore. Hic Aquila Græcus fuit natione: ac primùm factus Christianus, deinde eiectus ex Ecclesia Christi, propter vanam astrologiam, quam deserere nolebat. Hanc ob causam indignatus, abnegat Christum, & fit proselytus, ac tandem circumciditur, & Iudæus fit. Tum dat operam Hebraicæ linguæ, quam cùm fuisset assecutus, conuertit Bibliain Græcam linguam, multaq; in versione 70. corrumpit, præsertim vaticinia de Christo.
units.tr: The second version of the Bibles was made by Aquila, likewise from the Hebrew into Greek, under the Emperor Hadrian. This Aquila was a Greek by nation; he was first made a Christian, then cast out of the Church of Christ on account of a vain astrology, which he was unwilling to give up. Indignant for this reason, he renounced Christ, became a proselyte, and at last was circumcised and became a Jew. Then he applied himself to the Hebrew language, and when he had mastered it, he translated the Bible into the Greek language, and in his version he corrupted many things in the Seventy, especially the prophecies about Christ.

units.la: Tertia versio fuit Symmachi, sub Seuero Imperatore, anno post Aquilæ versionem circiter 65. Fuit hic Symmachus natione Samaritanus: cùm videret se non admodum suæ Genti gratum esse: contra propriam Gentem indignatus, & ambitionis morbo affectus, contulit se ad Iudæos, & iterum circumcisus, Iudæus fit. Ac tum suam edidit Bibliorum versionem in Græcam linguam, idque contra Samaritanos.
units.tr: The third version was that of Symmachus, under the Emperor Severus, about sixty-five years after Aquila's version. This Symmachus was a Samaritan by nation. When he saw that he was not very welcome to his own people, indignant against his own nation, and afflicted with the disease of ambition, he betook himself to the Jews, and, circumcised again, became a Jew. Then he published his version of the Bible into the Greek language, and he did so against the Samaritans.

units.la: Quarta fuit Theodotionis, sub Commo-do secundo. Hic Theodotion prius fuerat Marcionis discipulus. Sed huic postmodum sectæ infensus, ad illius euersionem, suam fecit editionem Bibliorum: atque huius editio fuit magis consentanea cum 70. Interpre-tatione, quàm vlla alia.
units.tr: The fourth was that of Theodotion, under Commodus the Second. This Theodotion had previously been a disciple of Marcion. But afterwards, hostile to that sect, he made his own edition of the Bibles for its overthrow; and this edition was more in agreement with the Seventy's translation than any other.

units.la: Quinta editio. At verò post persecutionem Seueri, temporibus Antonini, Seueri filij, qui Antoninus cognomento appellabatur Caracalla & frater Getæ, inuenta fuit quinta editio,in Hiericho,in dolio quodam occultata, sed citra autoris nomen:edita procul-dubio ab aliquo illorum piorum,qui Hie-rosolymis vixerant,& pietati operam dederant sub persecutione Seueri.Contigit hoc anno 7.regni Caracallæ.
units.tr: The fifth edition. Indeed, after the persecution of Severus, in the time of Antoninus, the son of Severus, who was called by the surname Caracalla and was the brother of Geta, a fifth edition was discovered at Jericho, hidden in a certain jar, but without the author's name. It was undoubtedly published by one of those pious men who had lived at Jerusalem and had devoted themselves to piety under the persecution of Severus. This happened in the seventh year of Caracalla's reign.

units.la: Sexta. Tempore verò Alexandri Mam-mææ[?] filij,inventa fuit alia, nempe sexta editio,idque in Nicopoli,ad Orientem sita.Erat & ipsa sexta editio in dolio occultata,& sine autoris nomine.
units.tr: The sixth. In the time of Alexander, son of Mammaea, another was found, namely a sixth edition, at Nicopolis, a city situated to the east. This sixth edition too was hidden in a jar, and without the author's name.

units.la: Hæc ex Epiphanij libro de mensuris & ponderibus,& ex Synopsi Athanasij. Athanasius verò,seu autor illius Synopseos,addit septimam editionem, quam dicit fuisse beati Luciani Martyris,& tempore Constanti-ni Magni inventam fuisse Nicomediæ in quodam armario, in pariete facto, & calce circumlito, atque hanc fuisse correctam & emendatam. Atque hæc de versionibus antiquis, ex Hebraica in Græcam linguam fa-ctis, factis[?] sunto.
units.tr: These things are taken from Epiphanius' book on weights and measures, and from the Synopsis of Athanasius. But Athanasius, or the author of that Synopsis, adds a seventh edition, which he says was that of the blessed Lucian the Martyr, and was found in the time of Constantine the Great at Nicomedia, in a cupboard built into a wall and smeared over with lime; and that this was corrected and emended. These things are said of the ancient versions made from the Hebrew into the Greek language.

units.la: De Latinis verò non est cur multa dicam, quando pauca etiam de iis scripta relique-runt Patres.
units.tr: As for the Latin versions, there is no reason for me to say much, since the Fathers have left behind only a few writings about them.

units.la: Hieronymus vertit ex Hebræo in Latinum: hanc in ipsius habemus operibus.
units.tr: Jerome translated from the Hebrew into Latin; we have this version in his works.

units.la: De vulgata quæstio diu fuit inter doctos nostri temporis disputata, cuiusnam fuerit, Hieronymi ne, an alicuius alius. Ac certè satis constat hanc diversam esse ab illa, quam Hieronymus interpretatur in suis operi-bus, bus, ut merito Munsterus cuicerit contra Steuchum, huius vulgatæ autorem minime fuisse Hieronymum. Quis verò huius fuerit autor, quando nemo hactenus potuit certò definire: neque ego hanc mihi sumam definiendi provinciam.
units.tr: The question about the Vulgate has long been disputed among the learned of our time, whether it was Jerome's or someone else's. And it is quite certain that this is different from that which Jerome translates in his works, so that Münster rightly contended against Steuchus that the author of this Vulgate was by no means Jerome. But who the author of it was, since no one so far has been able to define with certainty, I will not take upon myself the task of defining it.

units.la: Cæterum, Dei beneficio singulari, nostro hoc seculo, tot factæ sunt & editæ sacrorum Bibliorum, tam ex Hebraeo, quam ex Græco, non in Latinam tantùm, sed in omnes prope cuiusvis Nationis linguas, conversiones, hæq; fidelissimæ & pulcherrimæ, ut non sit cur veteribus invideamus. Quid verò hæc omnia demonstrant? Deum voluisse & velle, ut sua sacra Biblia legantur ab omnibus: & hoc modo una ex parte ad cognitionem veritatis, eoq; & ad salutem æternam Electi ex omnibus Nationibus perducantur: & ex altera Antichristus magis ac magis revelètur & interficiatur. Proinde mirum non est, quod is modis omnibus curat, ut Biblia, quæ possint ab omnibus intelligi, supprimantur. Nam qui malè agit, odit lucem, & eam extinctam cupit.
units.tr: Moreover, by the singular blessing of God, in our century so many translations of the sacred Bibles have been made and published, both from the Hebrew and from the Greek, not only into Latin but into almost all the languages of every nation, and these are most faithful and most beautiful, so that there is no reason for us to envy the ancients. But what do all these things demonstrate? That God has willed, and wills, that his sacred Bibles be read by all; and in this way, on the one hand, the elect from all nations are led to knowledge of the truth, and thereby to eternal salvation; and on the other hand, Antichrist is more and more revealed and destroyed. Therefore it is no wonder that he, by every means, takes care that the Bibles, which can be understood by all, be suppressed. For he who does evil hates the light, and wishes it extinguished.

units.la: Venio igitur nunc ad quæstionem, An bonum sit, ut Biblia in linguam cuiusq; Gentis propriam vertantur, nec ne.
units.tr: I now come to the question: whether it is good that the Bible be translated into the proper language of each nation, or not.

units.la: Papa negat, & merito, quia non est ei bonum: Nos verò affirmamus: Proinde hæc esto propositio.
units.tr: The Pope denies it, and rightly so, because it is not good for him. We, however, affirm it. Therefore let this be the proposition.

units.la: Ut sacra Biblia in linguam cuiusq; Gentis propriam ac popularem convertantur, non solum utile ac bonum, sed etiam necessarium est.
units.tr: That the holy Bible should be converted into the proper and common language of each nation is not only useful and good, but also necessary.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmation.

units.la: 1. Officium cuiusque Christiani hominis est, operam dare sacris Literis non solum publicè audiendis, sed etiam privatim domi legendis & meditandis, ut ante à nobis ostensum est. Atqui hanc operam dare non possunt sacris Literis Idiotæ, & linguarum Græcæ & Latinæ imperiti, nisi illæ in linguam cuique vernaculam transferantur. Est igitur non solùm utile, sed etiam necessarium, si quisq; velit suum facere officium, S. Biblia in linguam popularem transferre.
units.tr: 1. It is the duty of every Christian man to devote effort to the sacred Scriptures, not only by hearing them publicly but also by reading and meditating on them privately at home, as we have shown before. But Laymen, and those unskilled in Greek and Latin, cannot devote this effort to the sacred Scriptures unless they are translated into each person's own vernacular tongue. It is therefore not only useful but necessary, if anyone wishes to fulfil his duty, that the holy Bible be translated into the common tongue.

units.la: 2. Probo secundò Vertenda esse Biblia in linguam cuiusque Gentis propriam, ut legi ab omnibus possint.
units.tr: 2. Second, I prove that the Bible must be turned into the proper language of each nation, so that it can be read by all.

units.la: Christianam profitemur omnes religionem: Christiani igitur libri nobis omnibus sunt relegendi, hoc est, legendi & relegendi, & perpetuò perlegendi. Inde enim est nomen religionis, ut Cicero definit. Proinde officium religiosi hominis est ea quæ ad Dei cultum pertinent, legere & relegere. Quomodo verò hoc fiet, nisi Biblia in linguam cuiq; notam convertantur? Ut igitur omnes religiosi, in linguam popularem convertantur Biblia necesse est.
units.tr: We all profess the Christian religion. Therefore the Christian books must be re-read by all of us, that is, read, read again, and read through continually. For the name "religion" comes from this, as Cicero defines it. Therefore the duty of a religious person is to read and re-read those things that pertain to the worship of God. But how will this be done unless the Bible is turned into a language known to each person? So for all the religious to be served, the Bible must necessarily be turned into the common language.

units.la: 3. Omnes populi atque nationes vel ver- habent Biblia in suam quaeque linguam, vel vt conuertantur exoptant & petunt. A-gnoscunt igitur omnes, aequum & honestum & utile esse, vt in linguam popularem ver-tantur.
units.tr: 3. All peoples and nations either have the Bible in their own language or desire and ask that it be translated. All therefore acknowledge that it is fair, honourable and useful that it be turned into the common language.

units.la: 4. Tulit Deus legem eo sermone & lin- gua, quam omnes apud Hebraeos, tam pueri & foeminae, quàm docti intelligebant, lin-gua scilicet populari, idq; propter omnium illius populi hominum vtilitatem & salutem. Exemplo igitur Dei in linguam totius populi communem, vertenda sunt, quòd non possit illi esse nisi vtile. Si quae fiunt exemplis gra-uissimorum virorum, ea merito fieri credi-tur: quanto magis quae fiunt exemplo Dei Optimi Maximi? Annon etiam cùm idem voluit Deus coelestem doctrinam Gentibus communicari, curauit in linguam Graecam omnibus tunc populis cognitam, sacra con-uerti Biblia?
units.tr: 4. God gave the law in that speech and language which all among the Hebrews understood, both boys and women as well as the learned, namely the common language, and this for the usefulness and salvation of all the people of that nation. Therefore, by God's example, the Scriptures must be turned into the language common to the whole people, since this can be nothing but useful to them. If things are done by the example of very serious men, they are rightly believed to be done well; how much more so those things done by the example of God, the best and greatest? Did not God also, when he wished the heavenly doctrine to be communicated to the Gentiles, take care that the holy Bible be turned into Greek, which was then known to all peoples?

units.la: 5. Si scripturus fuisset Christus, non alia lingua scripsisset, quàm qua etiam locutus est. Est autem locutus lingua vernacula & visitata, Syriaca ex Hebraeo mixta. Ergo, &c. Idem etiam fecerunt Apostoli.
units.tr: 5. If Christ had intended to write, he would not have written in any other language than that in which he also spoke. But he spoke in the vernacular and customary language, the Syriac mixed with Hebrew. Therefore, etc. The Apostles also did the same.

units.la: 6. Finis datae scripturae est, vt per eam audi- tam & lectam & intellectam seruemur. At quomodo legetur & intelligetur, nisi in ea sit lingua, quae cuique perspecta sit Genti? Ergo vt in sua quisque eam habeat lingua, i-psa postulat salus.
units.tr: 6. The purpose of Scripture having been given is that through it we may be saved, having heard, read and understood it. But how will it be read and understood, unless it is in a language that is well known to each nation? Therefore salvation itself requires that each person have it in his own language.

units.la: 7. Cur donum variis loquendi & scriben-di linguis donatum fuit Apostolis? Ut ab omnibus intelligeretur doctrina salutis. Ergo eadem de causa in varias linguas vertenda sunt Biblia.
units.tr: 7. Why was the gift of speaking and writing in various languages given to the Apostles? So that the doctrine of salvation might be understood by all. Therefore, for the same reason, the Bible must be turned into various languages.

units.la: 8. Omnes Ecclesiæ Græcæ, Latinæ, Illy-ricæ id suo exemplo confirmant esse facien-dum. Nam quæque illarum, sua uti voluit de principio lingua in Bibliis legendis. Ergo, &c. Si his exemplis non vident Aduer-sarij omnino vertenda esse Biblia in linguam cuique Genti vernaculam, cæci sunt: si non considerant, inertes sunt: si non intelligunt, obtusi.
units.tr: 8. All the Churches, Greek, Latin and Illyrian, confirm by their example that this must be done. For each of them, from the beginning, wished to use its own language in reading the Bible. Therefore, etc. If the adversaries do not see from these examples that the Bible must altogether be turned into the vernacular of each nation, they are blind; if they do not consider, they are slothful; if they do not understand, they are dull.

units.la: 9. Exemplum Beroënsium imitandum est, ut scilicet quæ audimus in Concionibus, ea ad sacros libros examinemus. Ideo enim illud exemplum est scriptum, ut imitemur tanquā utilissimum. At quomodo quis facere hoc poterit, nisi Biblia in ea habeat lingua, quam possit intelligere? Ergo propter Idiotas in popularem linguam vertenda.
units.tr: 9. The example of the Bereans must be imitated, namely that we examine by the holy books what we hear in sermons. For that example was written so that we might imitate it as most useful. But how can anyone do this unless he has the Bible in a language he can understand? Therefore, for the sake of the unlearned, it must be turned into the common language.

units.la: 10. Tutius est legere scripturam, quàm audire concionatores. Nam ij falli possunt & fallere: illa nequaquam. At quomodo legent populi, nisi in patrium vertatur sermo-nem?
units.tr: 10. It is safer to read Scripture than to hear preachers, for they can be deceived and can deceive, whereas Scripture never can. But how will the people read, unless it is turned into their native speech?

units.la: 11. Cibus corporis nemini denegatur: cur cibus animæ suus denegetur? Denegatur autem Idiotis, præsertim ne domi ve-scantur, si non in vernaculam transferantur linguam.
units.tr: 11. Bodily food is denied to no one: why should the food of the soul be denied to them? Yet it is denied to the unlearned, especially if they cannot eat at home because it has not been turned into the vernacular language.

units.la: 1². Multis in locis nulli sunt qui possint audiri pastores: alibi sunt rari, & rariores conciones. Quid igitur tum agendum plebi Christianæ? Legendum in Bibliis. At quomodo legent, nisi in sua quisq; habeat scripturam lingua? Ergo vertenda.
units.tr: 12. In many places there are no ministers who can be heard, and elsewhere sermons are rare and even rarer. What then must the Christian people do? Read in the Bible. But how will they read, unless each person has the Scripture in his own language? Therefore it must be translated.

units.la: 13. Tales euadimus, quales solent esse libri quos legimus, & sermones eorum, quibuscum loquimur 1.Corinth.15.[?] Ergo vt omnes homines fiant boni & sancti, vt est scriptura sacra, vertenda est in eam linguam, quæ possit ab omnibus legi.
units.tr: 13. We become such as the books we read are, and the discourses of those with whom we speak (1 Corinthians 15 [?]). Therefore, so that all men may become good and holy, as holy Scripture intends, it must be turned into the language that can be read by all.

units.la: 14. Scriptura sacra sunt arma militiæ nostræ, quibus oportet nos esse armatos contra omnes hostes. Ergo vt possit quisque his armari, id quod fit legendo, meditando, & in memoriam illas recondendo, vertendæ sunt in natiuum cuiusq; populi sermonem.
units.tr: 14. The holy Scriptures are the weapons of our warfare, with which we ought to be armed against all enemies. Therefore, so that each person may be armed with them, which is done by reading, meditating and storing them in memory, they must be turned into the native speech of each people.

units.la: 15. Scriptura est lucerna ardens, ideo data, vt omnibus luceat, & exponatur videnda, Matth 5. Nemo ponit lucernam sub modio, sed in candelabro, vt luceat omnibus, qui in domo sunt. Ergo vt ab omnibus videri possit, & omnibus lucere, vertenda est in vulgarem linguam.
units.tr: 15. Scripture is a burning lamp, given so that it may shine for all and be set out to be seen (Matthew 5): "No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that it gives light to all who are in the house." Therefore, so that it can be seen by all and shine for all, it must be turned into the common tongue.

units.la: 16. Ab autoritate Pauli 1.Cor.14. Scribit in Ecclesia non esse vtendum linguis sine interpretatione: scilicet lingua ea, quæ nota est, instituenda.
units.tr: 16. From the authority of Paul (1 Corinthians 14): he writes that in the Church tongues are not to be used without interpretation; clearly, a language that is known must be established.

units.la: Argumenta aduersariorum & so-lutiones.
units.tr: Arguments of the adversaries and their solutions.

units.la: 1. Deut.31. Moses tabulas legis diuinæ in arcam inclusit, ut ibi servarentur & non ab omni-bus viderentur aut contrectarentur. Dedit autem custodiendas Aaroni & Leuitis. Voluit igi-tur scripturam a solis tantum Sacerdotibus legi, non a plebe. Quare non est vertenda, ne a plebe legatur.
units.tr: 1. Deut. 31. Moses enclosed the tables of the divine law in the ark, so that they might be kept there and not be seen or handled by everyone. He gave them, however, to Aaron and the Levites to guard. He therefore willed that Scripture be read only by the priests alone, not by the common people. Hence it should not be translated, lest it be read by the common people.

units.la: Resp. Fallacia est non causæ ut causæ. Non enim ea fuit causa inclusæ legis in ar-cam, ut à plebe ne legatur. Hoc liquet à con-trario. Nam Deut. 6. iussit eam scribi etiam in limine, & ostiis domus, imò in corde. Sed quæ fuit causa? Multæ. Prima, ut illæ ipsæ ta-bulæ à Deo acceptæ servarentur ad memo-riam sempiternam in testimonium contra Israe-lem: sic ait textus. Sed exemplum illarum scribi voluit etiam in limine & ostiis domus.
units.tr: Reply. This is a fallacy of mistaking what is not the cause for the cause. For the reason the law was enclosed in the ark was not that it should not be read by the common people. This is clear from the contrary: for Deut. 6. he commanded it to be written also on the lintel and the doorposts of the house, indeed in the heart. But what was the cause? Many. The first: that those very tables received from God should be kept for an everlasting memorial, as a witness against Israel; so the text says. But he wished the copy of them to be written also on the lintel and doorposts of the house.

units.la: Secunda, ut ea ceremonia significaret, sic legem in animo & corde esse cuique servan-dam & custodiendam, sicut in arca. Ac proin-de dedit servandam Aaroni & Leuitis, ut in-dicaret summum sacerdotem Christum vere hanc servaturum: deinde officium cum pri-mis sacerdotum esse, ut ipsi servent legem, & aliis ut servetur, sint autores, hortatores.
units.tr: Second, that this ceremony should signify that the law is to be kept and guarded in the mind and heart of each person, just as it was in the ark. And accordingly he gave it to be kept by Aaron and the Levites, to indicate that Christ, the high priest, would truly keep it; then, that the chief duty of the priests is that they themselves keep the law and be its authors and exhorters, so that it may be kept by others.

units.la: Tertia, ut ostenderet ea Ceremonia, o-mnes qui sub lege essent, & futuri erant, in-clusos esse in eam Christi fidem, quæ tandem erat revelanda. Arca enim typus fuit Chri-sti: ac proinde legem fuisse pædagogum, qui duceret ad Christum.
units.tr: Third, that this ceremony should show that all who were under the law, and were to be, were enclosed in that faith of Christ which was at length to be revealed. For the ark was a type of Christ; and accordingly the law was a tutor, leading to Christ.

units.la: 2. Moses Deut. 31. iubet Iosua & sacerdo-tibus, ut septimo quoq; anno in die solenni remis-sionis[?], fionis, coram toto populo legeretur lex Domini, ut discerent voluntatem Dei, & facerent. Si lex fuit in cuiusque manu descripta, hoc praeceptum fuit vanum. At non fuit. Ergo, &c. Apparet vo-luisse legem contineri in quadam maiestate.
units.tr: 2. Moses, Deut. 31, commands Joshua and the priests that every seventh year, on the solemn day of remission, the law of the Lord be read before the whole people, that they might learn the will of God and do it. If the law had been written out in each person's hand, this precept would have been vain. But it was not vain. Therefore, etc. It appears that he willed the law to be contained in a certain majesty.

units.la: Resp. Hoc Enthymema non valet: singulis diebus Dominicis praedicari iubet verbum Dei: Ergo nemo habet illud domi descriptum. Causa enim huius praecepti non fuit, ut simpliciter discerent, quasi tum demum legenda esset lex: pugnaret hoc cum Deut 6. Sed fuit, ut Deus publice totum populum simul, in solennitate tanta convinceret, & inexcusabilem redderet. Ad hoc faciebat solennitas diei, ceremoniae apparatus. Iis magis excitabatur populus ad Deum.
units.tr: Reply. This enthymeme does not hold: he commands the word of God to be preached on every Lord's day; therefore no one has it written out at home. For the reason for this precept was not that they should learn it simply, as if the law were to be read only then; this would conflict with Deut. 6. Rather, it was that God might convict the whole people publicly and together, in so great a solemnity, and render them inexcusable. The solemnity of the day and the ceremonial display served this end. By these means the people were more stirred up toward God.

units.la: En simile. Et Magistratus solet quotannis curare, ut leges Civitatis legantur soleniter. Ergo hoc praecepto significat, non licere cuiquam eas legere priuatim ?
units.tr: Here is a comparison. Does not the magistrate customarily arrange that the laws of the state be read solemnly each year? Does this, then, signify by this precept that it is not lawful for anyone to read them privately?

units.la: §. 2. Reg.22. Tempore Iosiae repertus fuit liber legis Dei, qui ante multos annos latuerat: Et cum fuisset repertus, magna fuit latitia toti populo. Apparet hinc, non fuisse tunc multa legis exemplaria. Ergo hoc exemplo neq;[?] nunc curandum, ut multi sint libri sancti, praesertim apud vulgum. Quare non sunt vertenda Biblia.
units.tr: §. 2 Kings 22. In the time of Josiah the book of the law of God was found, which had lain hidden for many years; and when it had been found, there was great joy among the whole people. It appears from this that there were then not many copies of the law. Therefore, from this example, there is no need now to take care that there be many holy books, especially among the common people. Hence the Bible should not be translated.

units.la: Resp. Nos loquimur de illo, quod populo Dei faciendum est iuxta Dei voluntatem, quae constat Deut. 6. Tu vero adfers exemplum de eo, quod neglectum fuit ab impiis hominibus, illorum impietate vel sa-tem[?] ignauia. Fallacia est Enthymematis ex ignoratione Elenchi. Nam ex particulari exemplo, eoque malo, non potest inferri generalis, eaque bona & pia conclusio. Resolue Enthymema in syllogismum, & fallaciam videbis. Est enim assumenda universalis hæc propositio. Omnia singularia exempla sunt imitanda. Atqui Israelita tempore Iosia non habebant nisi unum librum legis, eumque occultatum. Ergo nobis quoque idem faciendum est. Quis non videat maiorem propositionem esse salsissimam & absurdam? Sed bene sic argumentandum: Omnia Israelitica exempla bona, quæ scilicet consentanea sunt legi Dei, sunt imitanda. Nam etiam sic Apostolus: Imitatores mei estote, sicut & ego Christi. Atqui Iudæi tempore Christi passim habebant Biblia. Ergo,&c.
units.tr: Reply. We are speaking of what is to be done by the people of God according to the will of God, which is set out in Deut. 6. You, however, bring forward an example of what was neglected by impious men, through their impiety or at least their sloth. It is a fallacy of the enthymeme, an ignoratio elenchi. For from a particular example, and that a bad one, no general and good and pious conclusion can be drawn. Resolve the enthymeme into a syllogism and you will see the fallacy. For this universal proposition must be assumed: All singular examples are to be imitated. But the Israelites in the time of Josiah had only one book of the law, and that hidden. Therefore we too must do the same. Who would not see that the major premise is most false and absurd? But the argument should be framed well thus: All good Israelite examples, that is, those which agree with the law of God, are to be imitated. For the Apostle also says: Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ. But the Jews in the time of Christ had the Bible everywhere. Therefore, etc.

units.la: 4. Biblia in linguam vernaculam versa, neque ad docendum, neq; ad discendum prosunt. Ergo non sunt vertenda. Antecedens probant. Qui docent, ut sint in sacris Literis exercitati, & linguam teneant saltem latinam oportet: iis [?] ergo inutilis est versio. Qui discunt, ex Doctoribus quos intelligant, discunt. Non est igitur illis necessaria aut utilis versio.
units.tr: 4. Bibles translated into the vernacular tongue are useful neither for teaching nor for learning. Therefore they should not be translated. They prove the antecedent. Those who teach, in order to be practised in the holy Scriptures, must at least hold the Latin tongue; for them, therefore, a version is useless. Those who learn, learn from teachers whom they understand. Therefore a version is neither necessary nor useful to them.

units.la: Resp. Falsum assumtum, primo de Doctoribus. Non enim tantum est literatorum & in linguis exercitatorum, docere: sed etiam illiteratorum, ut patrisfamilias, matrisfamilias, liberos suos, Ephes.6. 2. De discen-tibus. Non est unum tantum horum ossi-cium: cium:nempe audire Doctores scripturas explicantes, sed multa: Primum, ut domi per se legant, quod explicandum est in Ecclesia. 2. Ut attentè audiant praelectiones & conciones. 3. Ut relegant accuratè per se domi, & conferant audita cum scriptis, exemplo Beroënsium. 4. Ut repetant quae audierunt, & memoriae mandent. Ad haec autem omnia, quis non videat utilem esse versionem, imò necessariam iis, qui peregrinas linguas non tenent? Quid enim si doctor sit haereticus? Retorquendum igitur est argumentum in aduersarios.
units.tr: Reply. The assumed premise is false, first concerning the teachers. For teaching is not only the task of the learned and those practised in languages, but also of the unlearned, such as a father of a family or a mother of a family teaching their children (Eph. 6. 2). Concerning the learners: this duty is not one alone, namely to hear teachers explaining the Scriptures; there are many: first, that they read at home for themselves what is to be explained in the Church; second, that they listen attentively to lectures and sermons; third, that they carefully re-read at home by themselves and compare what they have heard with the writings, after the example of the Bereans; fourth, that they repeat what they have heard and commit it to memory. For all these things, who would not see that a translation is useful, indeed necessary, to those who do not have foreign tongues? For what if the teacher is a heretic? The argument must therefore be turned back against the adversaries.

units.la: 5. Si vertantur in linguam vulgarem, fiunt contemnibiles, & exposita sunt manibus, etiam sceleratorum & immundorum hominum. Sunt autem retinenda in sui veneratione. Ergo,&c.
units.tr: 5. If they are translated into the vulgar tongue, they become contemptible and are exposed to the hands even of wicked and unclean men. Yet they are to be retained in reverence of them. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Resp. Fallacia est non causae ut causae. Causa cur datae sacrae scripturae, non ea est, ut eas tantùm eminus veneremur, sed ut eas omnes legamus, & per has ad veritatis cognitionem perveniamus, & ita per eas mundemur à peccatis, alamur in homine interno, servemur. Non possunt autem legi ab omnibus, nisi vertantur. Ergo,&c. Quod isti dicunt, perinde est, atque si diceremus, Non sunt admittendi ad pulchras balneas immundi, quia immundi sunt: Imò contrà, quia immundi sunt, ideo ij cumprimis admittendi, ut mundentur. Mundamur autem per verbum Dei, tam lectum quàm auditum. Ergo, &c. Christus mandat Iohan. 5. di-cendo, cendo, Scrutamini scripturas. Ergo ab earum lectione nemo arcendus. Deinde, quid discriminis est inter audire & legere scripturas? Licet omnibus audire, & semper, & ubique. Cur non etiam legere?
units.tr: Reply. This is a fallacy of mistaking what is not the cause for the cause. The cause for which Holy Scripture was given is not that we should venerate it only from afar, but that we should all read it, and through it come to the knowledge of the truth, and so be cleansed from sins, be nourished in the inner man, and be kept safe. But they cannot be read by all unless they are translated. Therefore, etc. What these men say is just as if we were to say: the unclean are not to be admitted to beautiful baths, because they are unclean. Rather, on the contrary, because they are unclean, they are especially to be admitted, so that they may be cleansed. Now we are cleansed through the Word of God, both read and heard. Therefore, etc. Christ commands it in John 5, saying: Search the Scriptures. Therefore no one is to be kept back from reading them. Further, what difference is there between hearing and reading the Scriptures? It is permitted to everyone to hear them, always and everywhere. Why not also to read them?

units.la: At vilescunt. Resp. Imo contrà quo melius agnoscuntur scripturæ & intelliguntur, eo in maiori habentur veneratione & honore. Ignota contemnimus: quorum autem vim agnoscimus, veneramur.
units.tr: But they become cheap. Reply. On the contrary: the better the Scriptures are known and understood, the greater the reverence and honour in which they are held. We despise what is unknown; but what we recognise the power of, we venerate.

units.la: 6. Multi sunt loci in scripturis, qui multos etiam literatos fefellerunt, ita ut eorum prãua intelligentia facti sint haeretici: quanto magis poterunt decipere imperitam multitudinem? Verbi gratia, Vt quia ait Matth. 1. Maria peperit filium suum primogenitum: Heluidius intulit, Illam igitur alios post Christum natum filios peperisse. Alij, quia Iohan. 1. Iesus appellatur filius Iosephi: inde negarunt esse Deum, sed purum hominem. Arius, quia Christus dixit se esse minorem Patre, intulit, Christum non esse ὁμοούσιον Patri: Quanto magis haec inferet etiam imperita plebs, si permittantur ei Biblia vulgaria? Imo indicabit in scripturis esse pugnantia & contradictoria, quia multi sunt loci, qui nisi a doctis concilientur, videntur pugnare. Ergo ut haec haereses & haec absurda vitentur, non sunt vertenda Biblia in linguam vernaculam, ut a plebe possint legi: ac proinde bene faciunt Pontifices, dum haec Biblia vulgaria prohibent. Hoc enim faciunt propter salutem plebis.
units.tr: 6. There are many passages in the Scriptures which have deceived even many learned men, so that through their wrong understanding they became heretics. How much more will they be able to deceive the unskilled multitude? For example: because Matthew 1 says, Mary bore her firstborn son, Helvidius inferred that she therefore bore other sons after Christ's birth. Others, because John 1 calls Jesus the son of Joseph, from this denied that he is God but a mere man. Arius, because Christ said he was less than the Father, inferred that Christ is not homoousios with the Father. How much more will the unskilled common people infer these things too, if the vernacular Bibles are permitted to them? Indeed they will point out that there are contradictions and inconsistencies in the Scriptures, because there are many passages which, unless reconciled by the learned, seem to conflict. Therefore, that these heresies and absurdities be avoided, the Bibles are not to be translated into the vernacular tongue so that they may be read by the common people; and accordingly the Pontiffs do well in prohibiting these vernacular Bibles. For they do this for the salvation of the people.

units.la: Resp. Fallacia est accidentis. Concedo enim multos esse locos, quibus multi ad sua abusi sunt perniciem, & quibus alij abuti possint: sed non hinc sequitur: Ergo prohibenda Biblia vulgaria Idiotis, ne abutantur ad perniciem propter ignorantiam. Quare non sequitur? 1. Quia potest huic errorum & hæresium morbo, bona fieri medicina. Quæ hæc est? Ut singulis Bibliorum capitibus tales addantur vel in margine, vel in fine cuiusque capitis annotationes, quibus illi difficiles & ambigui loci explicentur & illustrentur, ita ut nullam dent occasionem ad errorem. 2. Non sequitur, Multi abusi sunt & abutuntur scripturis in linguam popularem versis ad hæreses, & ad suam perniciem: Ergo non sunt permittenda. Nam hæc illario sequitur ex propositione generali falsa & absurda, quæ hæc est: Quicquid per abusum hominum hominibus nocere potest, illud hominibus concedendum non esse. Quis non videat Maiorem esse absurdam? Nam cibus & potus per abusum hominum multis hominibus nocet & adfert exitium: num propterea cibus & potus vitandus est hominibus? Sol & Luna per abusum hominum, hominibus multis sunt exitiosi. Ergo Sol & Luna tollendi e Coelo? Tollatur abusus, quia malus: non res bonæ quibus abutuntur homines. 3. Imò & ad Minorem, Quod dicis de Bibliis in linguam popularem versis, idem de Bibliis Hebraicis, & Latinis & Græcis dici potest. Multi viri docti iis abusi sunt ad hæreses: Ergo etiam Biblia Hebraica & Latina & Græca prohibenda. Apparet ergo totam hanc argumentationem esse falsam, quia falsum & absurdum assumit. Pro-inde[?] etiam non sequitur, Pontifices bene facere, quòd prohibeant Biblia: imò sequi-tur impiè facere & perniciosè & tyrannicè. Annon impiè facit, qui vetat id fidelibus, quod Deus illis iubet? Iubet Deus, ut omnes verbum Dei non solùm audiant, sed etiam legant, & scripturas scrutentur, ut antè ostensum est: ac proinde, quo possint, verti iubet in linguam omnibus notam: Impiè ergo Papa facit, quòd prohibet. Annon tyrannicè agit, qui quempiam à suorum bonorum possessione & usu arcet? Scripturæ sunt bona fidelium. Annon tyranni & hostis est crudelissimi, fame confectum & esurientem impedire, imò pœna capitis prohibere, ne quem potest domi habere cibum, come-dat? Hoc facit, qui prohibet, ne Biblia in linguam, quam possit plebs intelligere, ver-tantur.
units.tr: Reply. This is the fallacy of accident. I grant that there are many passages which many have abused to their own ruin, and which others could abuse; but it does not follow from this: therefore the vernacular Bibles should be forbidden to the unlearned, lest they abuse them to their ruin through ignorance. Why does it not follow? (1) Because a good remedy can be applied to this disease of errors and heresies. What is this remedy? It is that annotations be added to each chapter of the Bible, either in the margin or at the end of each chapter, by which those difficult and ambiguous passages are explained and illustrated, so that they give no occasion for error. (2) It does not follow that: many have abused, and still abuse, Scriptures translated into the common tongue, to their heresies and their own ruin; therefore they are not to be permitted. For this inference follows from a general proposition that is false and absurd, namely: Whatever can harm men through the abuse of men is not to be granted to men. Who does not see that the major premise is absurd? For food and drink, through the abuse of men, harm many men and bring them destruction: is food and drink therefore to be avoided by men? The sun and the moon, through the abuse of men, are deadly to many men. Therefore should the sun and the moon be removed from heaven? Let the abuse be removed, since it is evil; not the good things which men abuse. (3) Indeed, also as to the minor premise: what you say of Bibles translated into the common tongue can equally be said of the Hebrew, Latin and Greek Bibles. Many learned men have abused them to heresies: therefore the Hebrew, Latin and Greek Bibles are also to be forbidden. It is clear, then, that this whole argument is false, because it assumes what is false and absurd. Accordingly, it does not follow either that the Papists do well in forbidding the Bibles; indeed it follows that they act impiously, destructively and tyrannically. Does he not act impiously who forbids the faithful what God commands them? God commands that all should not only hear the Word of God but also read it and search the Scriptures, as was shown earlier; and therefore he commands that it be translated, as far as possible, into a language known to all. The Pope therefore acts impiously in forbidding it. Does he not act tyrannically who keeps someone from the possession and use of his own goods? The Scriptures are the goods of the faithful. Is he not the tyrant and most cruel enemy who, when a man is worn out with hunger and starving, hinders him from eating, indeed who by penalty of death forbids him to eat the food he can have at home? He does this who forbids the Bibles to be translated into a language the common people can understand.

units.la: 7. In scriptura nihil est immutandum, iuxta illud Deut. 4. Non addes, neq; minues. Atqui non possunt verti Biblia in linguam popularem, quin immutentur. Mutantur enim verba, locutiones, &c. Ergo, &c.
units.tr: 7. Nothing in Scripture is to be changed, according to that word of Deut. 4: "You shall not add, nor diminish." But the Bibles cannot be translated into the common tongue without being changed. For words, expressions, etc., are changed. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Resp. Fallacia est ex ignoratione veri sensus horum verborum Dei. Illud dictum Domini intelligitur primùm de rebus in S. scriptura traditis, de historiis, de præceptis, de promissiopromissionibus,de sacramentis. Nihiliis re-bus traditis & explicatis in sacris Literis ad-dendum est. Sed quia in Bibliis sanctis He-braicis nihil poterat mutari vel in verbis, vel etiam in literis, quin mutarentur etiam ali-quo modo res ipsæ, vsque adeo erant omnia exacte & sapientissimè scripta : idcirco se-cundario illud dictum intelligitur etiam de verbis in ipsa Hebraica lingua sancta, mu-tandis,alterandis,addendis. Caeterum,non prohibet illo dicto Dominus, ne in aliam vertantur linguam,modo fideliter,ita vt licet mutentur verba, (alioqui non posset fieri versio)res tamen ipsæ maneant:alioqui pec-cassent etiam Apostoli, cùm scripturas ci-tarunt in aliena lingua.
units.tr: Reply. This is the fallacy arising from ignorance of the true sense of these words of God. That saying of the Lord is understood first of the things handed down in Holy Scripture: of the histories, of the precepts, of the promises, of the sacraments. Nothing is to be added to the things handed down and explained in the sacred Letters. But since in the holy Hebrew Bible nothing could be changed, either in words or even in letters, without the things themselves being changed in some way, so exactly and wisely were all things written, therefore, secondarily, that saying is also understood of changing, altering or adding words in the holy Hebrew language itself. Otherwise, the Lord in that saying does not forbid that Scripture be translated into another language, provided it is done faithfully, so that the things themselves remain even though the words are changed (otherwise no translation could be made); otherwise the Apostles too would have sinned, since they quoted Scriptures in a foreign language.

units.la: 8. Hieronymus in epistola ad Paulinum, quae est de lectione Bibliorum, conqueritur, quòd scripturam sacram passim sibi omnes vendicent, garrula anus, delirus senex, &c.
units.tr: 8. Jerome, in his letter to Paulinus, which is on the reading of the Bible, complains that everyone everywhere claims Holy Scripture for himself: a chattering old woman, a raving old man, etc.

units.la: Resp. Hieronymus non improbat, quòd omnes legant scripturas sacras. Nam ad huius studium omnes hortatur : ac proinde haud vituperat, quòd in linguam vertatur illam, quam omnes intelligant : sed duo improbat: 1. Quòd quisq; audeat sacram Scripturam alios docere, antequam ipse eam discat. Alterum, quòd quis audeat illam tractare, & in illa putet se posse proficere, sine aliquo se peritiore, quiviam præmonstret:id quod ipse disertis verbis ibi confirmat, & tandem ait: Hæc à meperstricta sunt breuiter,vt intelligeres te in sacris Literis sine præmio & monstrante semitam, non posse ingredi. Subintel-lige, si posset haberi talis præuius ductor: alioqui probat contrarium in Nahum, cap. vltimo. Et ipse Hieronymus Scripturam vertit non solum in Latinam, sed etiam in pa-triam, seu Illyricam linguam.
units.tr: Reply. Jerome does not disapprove of everyone reading the holy Scriptures. For he exhorts all to the study of them; and therefore he by no means finds fault that they should be translated into the language that everyone understands. But he disapproves of two things: (1) that anyone should dare to teach others the Holy Scripture before he has learned it himself; the other, that anyone should dare to handle it, and think he can make progress in it, without some more skilled guide who points out the way: which he himself confirms in plain words there, and finally says: These things have been briefly touched on by me, so that you may understand that you cannot enter into the sacred Letters without a reward and a guide showing the path. Understand: if such a leading guide could be had; otherwise he proves the contrary in Nahum, last chapter. And Jerome himself translated Scripture not only into Latin but also into the native, or Illyrian, language.

units.la: QUÆSTIO XI. De perspicuitate sacrarum Literarum, ad intelligendum.
units.tr: QUESTION XI. On the perspicuity of the sacred Scriptures, for the purpose of understanding.

units.la: Ex iis quæ dicta sunt de lectione scriptu-rarum, deq; illarum versionibus in hunc fi-nem Dei prouidentiâ editis, vt scripturæ in-telligi ab omni hominum genere possint: consequitur optimo iure Quæstio vndeci-ma, quæ est de perspicuitate sacrarum Lite-rarum, deque earum ad intelligendum faci-litate. Nam diximus in illud Apostoli πᾶσα γραφὴ θεόπνευστος· ὠφέλιμος[?], &c. quibusnam sit utilis, audientibus, legentibus, intelligen-tibus, credentibus. Ad hoc igitur ut sit utilis, non solum audiatur & legatur, sed etiam in-telligatur, necesse est. Quomodo vero intel-ligi possit, si non ea sit suapte natura ad intel-ligendum perspicua? Est igitur hic agendum de perspicuitate sacrarum Literarum. Quæ-stio hæc explicanda nobis est, quòd aduersa-rij contendunt, scripturam esse obscurissi-mam & difficilimam intellectu, & hac ratio-ne multis dissuadent illius lectionem & stu-dium. dium. Quorsum? ut omnes à somniis & hæ-resibus Romani Pontificis pendeant.
units.tr: From what has been said about the reading of the Scriptures, and about their translations, which God by his providence has published so that the Scriptures may be understood by every kind of person, it follows with the best right that the eleventh question arises, which concerns the perspicuity of the sacred Scriptures and their ease of understanding. For we have said, on the Apostle's words, "All Scripture is God-breathed and profitable" [θεόπνευστος· ὠφέλιμος], etc., for whom it is useful: for hearers, readers, those who understand, and those who believe. In order that it be useful, then, it is necessary not only that it be heard and read, but also that it be understood. But how can it be understood, if it is not by its very nature clear for understanding? Therefore we must treat here the perspicuity of the sacred Scriptures. This question must be explained by us, because our opponents contend that Scripture is most obscure and most difficult to understand, and for this reason they dissuade many from its reading and study. To what end? So that all may depend on the dreams and heresies of the Roman Pontiff.

units.la: Quæstio igitur proponitur : An[?] scriptura sit obscura, ut non possit ab omnibus fidelibus intelli-gi : an vero ita sit suapte natura perspicua, ut à singulis fidelibus vera illius intelli-gentia percipi queat. Papistæ (ut dixi) contendunt, eam vbiq; fere ita esse per se obscuram, etiam in iis, quæ ad salutem pertinent, ut non possit nisi à magnis & exercitatis Theologis intelligi.
units.tr: The question, therefore, is put forward: whether Scripture is obscure, so that it cannot be understood by all the faithful, or whether it is so clear by its very nature that the true understanding of it can be grasped by each of the faithful. The Papists (as I have said) contend that it is almost everywhere so obscure in itself, even in those matters which pertain to salvation, that it cannot be understood except by great and trained theologians.

units.la: Nos duabus respondemus propositio-nibus.
units.tr: We answer with two propositions.

units.la: PRIMA.
units.tr: FIRST.

units.la: Scriptura sancta nulla sui parte per se ob-scura est, ita ut non possit intelligi, si ea, quæ in eius lectione seruanda sunt, seruentur.
units.tr: Holy Scripture is in no part obscure in itself, so that it cannot be understood, if those things which are to be observed in its reading are observed.

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Dico, per se, quia si alicubi obscura nobis esse videatur & sit, causa obscuritatis non hæret in scriptura, sed in nobis, quòd aut mentes habeamus excæcatas vel obtusas, aut quòd non seruemus ea, quæ seruanda sunt in lectione scripturarum.
units.tr: I say "in itself," because if at any point it seems to us to be obscure, and is so, the cause of the obscurity does not lie in Scripture but in us: either because we have blinded or dull minds, or because we do not observe those things which must be observed in the reading of the Scriptures.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmation.

units.la: 1. Quòd per se & suapte natura lumen est splendidissimum, illud certè nulla sui parte obscurum esse vel dici potest. Pugnant enim simul esse lumen splendidissimum & clarissimum, & esse obscurum. Sol certè non poest ulla sui parte esse aut dici obscurus per se & in se: sed si nobis aliquando ita videa-tur, ut cum obductus est nubibus, illud est aliunde & ex accidenti: Vel si alicui aut caeco aut lusciioso Sol non videtur clarus, vitium est non in Sole, sed in caeco aut lusciioso. Est igitur certa propositio: Quod per se, & suapte natura lumen est splendidum, illud non posse dici aut esse obscurum ulla sui parte. Atqui talis est scriptura sancta, uti mox e scripturis ipsis osten-dam. Scriptura igitur nulla sui parte obscura esse aut dici potest. Minor probatur.
units.tr: 1. What is by itself and by its very nature the most splendid light certainly cannot be, or be called, obscure in any part. For it is contradictory for a light to be most splendid and most clear and yet obscure. The sun certainly cannot be, or be called, obscure in any part of itself and in its own nature; but if at times it seems so to us, as when it is covered with clouds, that is from elsewhere and by accident; or if the sun does not appear bright to some blind or squinting person, the fault is not in the sun but in the blind or squinting person. It is therefore a certain proposition: that which is by itself and by its nature a splendid light cannot be said or be obscure in any part. But holy Scripture is such, as I will show shortly from the Scriptures themselves. Therefore Scripture cannot be, or be called, obscure in any part. The minor premise is proved.

units.la: Psal.19. Praeceptum Domini lucidum, illuminans oculos.
units.tr: Ps. 19. The commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes.

units.la: Psal 119. Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum, & lumen semitis meis. Neque haec elogia dicuntur de aliqua scripturae parte, sed de toto Dei verbo. Quomodo igitur obscurum esse aut dici potest? Ibidem: Ostium verborum tuorum illuminat, & intellectum dat permultis. Comparat verbum ostio aperto, quod permultis etiam lumen adferat.
units.tr: Ps. 119. Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my paths. Nor are these praises said of some part of Scripture, but of the whole word of God. How then can it be or be called obscure? Likewise: The opening of your words gives light, and gives understanding to many. He compares the word to an open door, which brings light even to many.

units.la: Sic 2.Pet.1. Totam scripturam vocat lu-cernam lucentem in caliginoso loco: sed habemus firmum Propheticum sermonem, cui bene facitis quod attendatis velut lucernae splendenti in obscuro loco. Ac speciatim nominat Pro-pheticum sermonem, qui tamen prae caeteris scripturae partibus videtur esse obscurus. Hunc tamen ait esse lucernam lucentem in caliginoso loco. Quid hoc est ? Ut osten-dat, non solum suapte natura esse lucidum verbum Dei, sed ita lucidum, ut ubi lucet, et-iamsi locus sit sua natura caliginosus, tene-bras tamen pellat. Quomodo igitur scriptura potest ulla sui parte appellari obscura? Ita Christus Matth.5. [?]Apostolos vocauit lucem Mundi. Quam ob causam? Propter Euan-gelium, quod illis erat concreditum, & in ipsis quasi super candelabra positum, ut toti orbi lucerent. Ideo dixit, Nemo accendit lu-cernam, & ponit eam sub modium, sed super can-delabrum, ut luceat omnibus qui in domo sunt. Sic Christus ipse cumprimis appellatus fuit lux Mundi, etiam propter doctrinam. Ioh.1. Erat lux vera. Item, Ego sum lux Mundi. Item, Lux venit in Mundum, & dilexerunt homines magis tenebras.
units.tr: So also 2 Pet. 1. He calls the whole of Scripture a lamp shining in a dark place; but we have the firm prophetic word, to which you do well to attend as to a lamp shining in a dark place. And he names specifically the prophetic word, which nevertheless seems to be more obscure than the other parts of Scripture. Yet he says this is a lamp shining in a dark place. What does this mean? To show that the word of God is not only bright by its nature, but so bright that wherever it shines, even if the place is dark by its nature, it nevertheless drives out the darkness. How then can Scripture be called obscure in any part? Likewise Christ, Matt. 5, called the apostles the light of the world. Why? On account of the Gospel which was entrusted to them, and placed in them as upon a lampstand, so that they might shine to the whole world. Therefore he said, No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that it gives light to all who are in the house. Thus Christ himself was especially called the light of the world, also on account of his teaching. John 1: There was the true light. Likewise, I am the light of the world. Likewise, The light has come into the world, and men loved darkness more.

units.la: 2. Corinth. 4. Apostolus vocat Euange-lium, lumen gloriæ Christi, Ne irradiet (inquit) eos lumen gloriæ Christi. Imò comparat illud primæ illi luci, quæ totum Orbem de principio illuminauit, pulsis tenebris omnibus: nempe, quòd sicut ante illam lucem omnia erant tenebris obducta, ut scriptura ait, Gen.1. Et tenebræ erant super faciem abyssi, sed creata illa luce, disiectis tenebris, omnia facta fuerunt conspicua: Ita ante reuelatum Euangelium, quod lumen gloriæ appellatur ab Apostolo, omnia in homine sunt tenebricosa, aduentante verò luce Euangelij, omnia quæ antea alioqui late bant, patefiunt, illustrantur, videntur. Ideo ait 2. Corinth. 4. Deus qui dixit, ut e tenebris lux splendesceret, ille est, est, qui splenduit in cordibus nostris, ad praeben-dum lumen cognitionis in facie Iesu Christi.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 4. The Apostle calls the Gospel the light of the glory of Christ: lest the light of the glory of Christ should shine on them (he says). Indeed he compares it to that first light which illuminated the whole world from the beginning, when all darkness was driven away: namely, just as before that light all things were covered in darkness, as Scripture says, Gen. 1: And darkness was upon the face of the deep, but when that light was created and the darkness scattered, all things were made visible; so before the revealed Gospel, which the Apostle calls the light of glory, everything in man is dark, but when the light of the Gospel comes, all the things which before were otherwise hidden are laid open, illuminated, and seen. Therefore he says in 2 Cor. 4: God, who said, Let light shine out of darkness, is he who has shone in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of God in the face of Jesus Christ.

units.la: Exiis igitur perspicuum est, cùm totum Dei verbum, seu tota scriptura, lumen sit clarissimum, non solùm lucernæ, sed etiam Soli, sed primæ etiam illi magnæ luci comparatū, non posse sine magna iniuria dici aliqua sui parte esse per se obscura, atq; ita obscura, ut intelligi nequeat.
units.tr: From these things, therefore, it is plain that, since the whole word of God, or the whole of Scripture, is the most clear light, not only of a lamp but also of the sun, and indeed is compared even to that first great light, it cannot, without great injustice, be said to be obscure in itself in any part, and so obscure that it cannot be understood.

units.la: 2. Ief[?] 8 Vult omnia dubia & obscura, ad legem & ad testimonium scripturarum examinari, ut agnoscantur, cùm ait, Ad legem & ad testimonium. Quomodo igitur scripturæ possunt dici vlla sui parte esse obscuræ?
units.tr: 2. Isa. 8 wills that all doubtful and obscure matters be examined by the law and the testimony of the Scriptures, that they may be recognized, when he says, To the law and to the testimony. How then can the Scriptures be said to be obscure in any part?

units.la: 3. Si aliqua sui parte scriptura esset per se obscura, ut non posset intelligi, consequetur Deum aliqua esse locutum, quæ tamen nollet intelligi. Atqui hoc est absurdum: frustra enim locutus esset, quod absurdissimum est & impium de Deo cogitare. Nihil igitur locutus est Deus, quod suapte natura, & per se obscurum ita sit, ut non queat intelligi.
units.tr: 3. If Scripture were obscure in any part by its nature, so that it could not be understood, it would follow that God had spoken some things which he nevertheless would not want to be understood. But this is absurd: for he would have spoken in vain, and it is most absurd and impious to think this of God. Therefore God has said nothing which by its nature and in itself is so obscure that it cannot be understood.

units.la: 4. Luc. 24. Aperuit Christus illis sensum, ut intelligerent scripturas, scilicet omnes. Scripturæ igitur nulla pars obscura est per se, quin possit intelligi ab iis, qui mentis oculos habent per spiritum Christi apertos. 2. Timoth. 3. Omnis scriptura utilis est ad doctri-nam, &c. De tota scriptura loquitur. Qui autem posset esse utilis si ita sit obscura, ut non queat intelligi?
units.tr: 4. Luke 24: Christ opened their minds to understand the Scriptures, namely all of them. Therefore no part of Scripture is obscure in itself, but it can be understood by those who have the eyes of their mind opened by the Spirit of Christ. 2 Tim. 3: All Scripture is profitable for teaching, etc. He speaks of the whole of Scripture. But how could it be profitable if it were so obscure that it could not be understood?

units.la: Confirmari potest idem ex Patribus. Augustinus Tom. 3. de doctrina Christiana, lib. 2. cap. 6. Magnificè & salubriter Spiritus S. scripturas ita modificauit, vt locis apertioribus fami occurreret:obscurioribus verò (id est, minus cla-ris) fastidium detergeret. Nihil enim fere de il-lius obscuritatibus eruitur, quod non planissimè alibi dictum reperiatur.
units.tr: The same can be confirmed from the Fathers. Augustine, vol. 3, On Christian Doctrine, book 2, ch. 6: The Holy Spirit has wonderfully and wholesomely arranged the Scriptures so that they meet hunger with the more open passages; but the more obscure (that is, less clear) passages remove disgust. For almost nothing is drawn out of its obscurities that is not found stated most plainly elsewhere.

units.la: PROPOSITIO II.
units.tr: PROPOSITION II.

units.la: Scriptura sacra in iis, quæ ad salutem cognitu necessaria sunt, & ad veram pertinent pietatem, ita perspicua est, vt ab omnibus spiritu Dei præditis, qui eam attentè assiduéq; legant, & voces ac phrases percipiant, intelligi facilè possit.
units.tr: Holy Scripture, in those matters which are necessary to know for salvation and which pertain to true piety, is so plain that it can easily be understood by all who are endowed with the Spirit of God, who read it attentively and constantly, and who grasp its words and phrases.

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Primò, dico in iis, quæ ad salutem cognitu necessaria sunt. Hoc adiicio propter multa alia in scripturis mysteria, quæ vt intelligantur, non satis est percepisse voces & phrases, sed alia etiam requiruntur, vt postea in regulis pro intelligentia scripturarum explicabimus. Sed in iis quæ ad salutem pertinent, est ita perspicua, vt non opus sit multis regulis.
units.tr: First, I say "in those matters which are necessary to know for salvation." I add this because of the many other mysteries in the Scriptures, which cannot be understood by merely grasping the words and phrases; other things are also required for their understanding, as we will explain later in the rules for the interpretation of Scripture. But in those matters which pertain to salvation, it is so plain that there is no need for many rules.

units.la: Secundò, Ideo dico, ab iis, qui spiritu Dei præditi sunt, quia scio, etiam perspicua, non posse tamen percipi ab homine animali, destituto spiritu Dei, 1.Cor.2.
units.tr: Second, I say "by those who are endowed with the Spirit of God," because I know that even plain things cannot be perceived by the natural man, who lacks the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2).

units.la: 3. Addo, Qui attentè assiduéq; legant, & voces ac phrases intelligant. Nam qui non legit, aut non attente assiduéque, sed perfun-ctorie legit, non potest intelligere. Qui et-iam legit, sed vocum significata & phrases non percipiat, qui potest intelligere?
units.tr: 3. I add, "who read attentively and constantly, and grasp the words and phrases." For one who does not read, or does not read attentively and constantly, but skims through it superficially, cannot understand. And one who reads but does not grasp the meanings of the words and phrases, how can he understand?

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmation.

units.la: 1. Si scriptura nulla sui parte est obscura, ut ante ostensum a nobis est: multo minus in iis, quae ad salutem necessaria sunt, & ad veram pertinent pietatem: Ut quę pertinent ad fidem, spem, charitatem, vitae innocen-tiam, bonaq; conscientiam.
units.tr: 1. If Scripture is in no part obscure, as we have shown above, then much less is it so in those matters which are necessary for salvation and which pertain to true piety: such as what pertains to faith, hope, love, innocence of life, and a good conscience.

units.la: 2. 2. Tim.3. Ab infantia sacras Literas nosti, quae te possunt facere sapientem ad salutem. Quomodo hoc efficere possunt, in pueris praesertim, si non sint perspicuae?
units.tr: 2. 2 Tim. 3: From infancy you have known the sacred letters, which can make you wise unto salvation. How can they accomplish this, especially in children, if they are not plain?

units.la: 3. Matth.28. Marc.16 Praedicate Evangelium omni Creatura, qui crediderit & baptiza-tus fuerit, servabitur. Quomodo potest esse obscura illa doctrina, quae omnibus promi-scuè praedicanda est, ut ei auditae, mox queant homines fidem adhibere?
units.tr: 3. Matt. 28; Mark 16: Preach the Gospel to every creature; he who believes and is baptized will be saved. How can that teaching be obscure which is to be preached indiscriminately to all, so that people may at once be able to give faith to it when they hear it?

units.la: 4. Summam doctrinae ad salutem necessa-riae, quam Catechesin appellant, Apostolus vocat lac parvulis exhibitū. 1.Cor.3. Lac vo-bis potum dedi tanquam parvulis, non escam. Et Heb.5. reprehendit Hebraeos, quòd summâ doctrinae ad salutem necessariae non teneant, & adhuc illa opus habeant, tanquam lacte. Quid autem durum est in lacte? quid diffi-cile? Voluit igitur Apostolus significare, doctrinam salutis non esse difficilem, non esse duram ad percipiendum & imbibendum.
units.tr: 4. The Apostle calls the sum of the doctrine necessary for salvation, which they name the Catechism, milk given to infants (1 Cor. 3): I gave you milk to drink as to infants, not solid food. And in Heb. 5 he rebukes the Hebrews because they did not hold the sum of the doctrine necessary for salvation, and still needed it as milk. But what is hard in milk? What is difficult? The Apostle therefore meant to signify that the doctrine of salvation is not difficult, not hard to perceive and to take in.

units.la: 5. 1.Corinth.2. Animalis homo non percipit ea, quae sunt spiritus Dei : Nobis autem dedit spiritum suum, ut sciamus quae nobis a Deo donata sunt. Item, Spiritualis omnia diiudicat. Ergo qui donatus est spiritu Dei, omnia quae ad salutem necessaria sunt, facile intelligit.
units.tr: 5. 1 Cor. 2: The natural man does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God; but to us God has given his Spirit, that we may know the things that have been freely given us by God. Likewise: The spiritual man judges all things. Therefore, he who has been endowed with the Spirit of God easily understands all things necessary for salvation.

units.la: 6. 1.Iohan.2. Vos unctionem habetis a sancto, & nostis omnia. Quae omnia? Omnia quae cognitu necessaria sunt. Item, Non scripsi vobis quasi ignorantibus veritatem, sed quasi scientibus eam. Et ad quos scribebat? Numquid tantum ad magnos Theologos & Doctores? Minime, sed ad omnes fideles. Ergo qui unctionem habet a sancto, hoc est, qui praeditus est spiritu Dei, is facile veritatem, eorum scilicet, quae ad salutem necessaria sunt, agnoscere potest.
units.tr: 6. 1 John 2: You have an anointing from the Holy One, and you know all things. Which all things? All things that are necessary to know. Likewise: I have not written to you as to those who do not know the truth, but as to those who know it. And to whom was he writing? Surely not only to the great theologians and teachers? By no means, but to all the faithful. Therefore, he who has the anointing from the Holy One, that is, who is endowed with the Spirit of God, can easily recognize the truth, namely of those things which are necessary for salvation.

units.la: 7. Iohan.3. Christus, cùm differuislet de renascentia, de fide in se, deque vita aeterna, idque similibus a natura defumtis: Et ea non potuisset Nicodemus percipere, quia sine spiritu Dei erat: postea subiecit dicendo: Si dixi vobis terrena, & non creditis, quomodo si dixero vobis coelestia, credetis? Terrena appellavit illa, quae dixerat de regeneratione, de fide, de vita aeterna. Cur terrena? Quia facilia & plana.
units.tr: 7. John 3: Christ, when he had spoken of new birth, of faith in himself, and of eternal life, using comparisons drawn from nature, and Nicodemus could not grasp these because he was without the Spirit of God, afterwards added, saying: If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things? He called those things earthly which he had said about regeneration, faith, and eternal life. Why earthly? Because they are easy and plain.

units.la: Ex Patribus Testimonia.
units.tr: Testimonies from the Fathers.

units.la: Chrysost. Tom.4. in 2 Thess.3. homilia 3. col.1413. Omnia clara sunt & plana ex scripturis diuinis, quacunq; necessaria sunt, manifesta sunt. Haec ille. Sed opus est, inquit Chrysostomus, lectione, auditioneq; verbi perpetua.
units.tr: Chrysostom, vol. 4, on 2 Thess., homily 3, col. 1413: All things that are necessary are clear and plain in the divine Scriptures, and are manifest. Thus he. But, says Chrysostom, there is need of constant reading and hearing of the Word.

units.la: Augusti. Tom. 3. de doctrina Christiana, libr. 2. cap.6. Magnificè & salubriter Spiritus sanctus ita sacras Scripturas modificauit, ut locis apertioribus fami occurreret (& hoc, quoad ea, quae sunt ad salutem necessaria:) obscurioribus vero, fastidium detergeret. Nihil enim fere de illius obscuritatibus eruitur, quod non planissime alibi dictum reperiatur.
units.tr: Augustine, vol. 3, On Christian Doctrine, book 2, chap. 6: The Holy Spirit has tempered the sacred Scriptures magnificently and salutarily, so that he meets hunger in the plainer passages (and this, as to those things which are necessary for salvation), but in the more obscure ones he removes disgust. For almost nothing is drawn out of their obscurities which is not found plainly said elsewhere.

units.la: Hieronym. in Ies. cap.19. Moris est scripturarum, obscuris manifesta subnectere: & quod prius sub aenigmatibus dixerat, aperta voce proferre.
units.tr: Jerome, on Isaiah, chap. 19: It is the custom of the Scriptures to append the plain to the obscure, and to state in open words what it had earlier said under riddles.

units.la: Argumenta aduersariorum.
units.tr: Arguments of the opponents.

units.la: I. 2. Corinth. 3. Cùm declarassět, cur Moyses velamen in suam poneret faciem, & quid illud significaret, mox subdit, usque in hodiernum diem idem velamen in lectione veteris Testamenti manet: nec tollitur velum, quod per Christum aboletur. Ergo saltem vetus Testamentum obscurum est, & quasi impossibile ad intelligendum.
units.tr: I. 2 Corinthians 3. When he had explained why Moses put a veil on his face and what that veil signified, he immediately adds: "to this very day the same veil remains at the reading of the Old Testament, and the veil is not taken away, since it is abolished through Christ." Therefore the Old Testament, at least, is obscure and almost impossible to understand.

units.la: Resp. Fallacia est diuisionis. Diuidis haec verba à subsequentibus, quae praecedentia explicant, cum sint coniungenda.
