Subdit Apostolus sese explicans: sed ad hunc usque diem, cum legitur Moses, velamen cordibus illorum impositum est. Cum autem conuersum fuerit (cor Israelis) ad Dominum, tolletur velamen.
units.tr: Reply: This is the fallacy of division. You separate these words from the following ones, which explain the preceding ones, and the two must be joined. The Apostle continues, explaining himself: "but to this day, when Moses is read, a veil lies upon their hearts. But when (the heart of Israel) shall have been turned to the Lord, the veil will be taken away."

units.la: Quis non videat hic, Apostolum causam, cur Israëlitæ non intelligant Mosen, transferre à lege, id est, à scriptura, in ipsos Israëlitas? Et hanc esse, quòd cum non habeant cor conuersum ad Dominum, sed auersum, illud habeant velatum excæcatumque, vt non possint intelligere? Sicut qui faciem habet auersam à sole, solem videre nequit. Aperte enim ait, cùm fuerit conuersum ad Dominum, tunc velamen detractum iri, vt possint scripturam veteris Testamenti percipere.
units.tr: Who does not see here that the Apostle transfers the cause of the Israelites' failure to understand Moses, from the law, that is, from Scripture, to the Israelites themselves? And that this cause is that, since they do not have a heart turned to the Lord but turned away, they have it veiled and blinded, so that they cannot understand? Just as one who has his face turned away from the sun cannot see the sun. For he plainly says that when it has been turned to the Lord, then the veil will be removed, so that they may perceive the Scripture of the Old Testament.

units.la: Idem confirmat subdens de Christianis, qui ad Dominum conuersi, spiritum eius acceperunt: Nos autem omnes retecta[?] facie gloriam Domini speculantes (scilicet in scripturis, & tanquam in speculo repræsentantes) ad eandem imaginem transformamur à gloria in gloriam, tanquam à Domini spiritu.
units.tr: He confirms the same, adding of Christians who, converted to the Lord, have received his Spirit: "But we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord (namely in the Scriptures, and as if represented in a mirror), are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord."

units.la: Capite autem 4. idem apertius confirmat, dicendo: Quod si Euangelium, nostrum obtectum est: iis qui pereunt obtectum est, in-quibus Deus huius seculi excæcauit mentes (ne-pe) infidelibus, ad hoc ne illos irradiet lux Euangelij gloriæ Christi. Hic etiam Apostolus culpam obscuritatis Euangelij, non in ipsum Euangelium, sed in auditores transfert: quòd scilicet sint reprobi, sine spiritu Dei, destina-ti ad perditio-em.
units.tr: In chapter 4 he confirms the same more plainly, saying: "But if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who perish, in whom the god of this age has blinded the minds (namely of unbelievers), so that the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ should not shine upon them." Here too the Apostle transfers the blame for the obscurity of the gospel not to the gospel itself but to the hearers: namely, that they are reprobate, without the Spirit of God, destined to destruction.

units.la: Huc spectat & illud Christi Matth. 11. Gratias tibi ago Pater, quòd abscondisti hæc à sapientibus, & revelasti parvulis. Hic etiam videmus, cur sapientes huius Mundi non intelligant scripturas, & mysterium Euangelij[?] non percipiant, causam hærere in ipsis sapientibus, hoc est: quia sunt nimis sapien-tes secundùm carnem. Pugnant autem inter se sapientia Dei,& sapientia humana, seu prudentia carnis Roman. 8. Prudentia carnis inimicitia est adversus Deum. Hinc fit,vt quò quis sapientior est secundùm carnem, eò minùs percipere possit sapientiam Dei, quæ in scripturis est patefacta. Vitium igitur & causa obscuritatis, non est in scripturis, sed in hominibus. Confirmatur hæc responsio alio testimonio Apostoli. 1. Corinth. 2. Animalis homo, non percipit ea, quæ sunt Dei, nec potest percipere, quia spiritualiter diiudi-cantur. Quis etiam hic non videat, causam cur Animalis homo non percipiat ea, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei, & scripturas non intelligat, in ipso hærere homine Animali? nempe quia animalis tantùm est homo, humana tantùm prudentia, & nullo Dei spiritu præditus. Scripturæ enim cùm sint à spiritu Dei, non possunt intelligi sine spiritu Dei. Quò quis autem animalior est, & prudentior secundùm carnem, eò minùs habet Spiritus Dei. Quomodo igitur possit eas intelligere? Ideo Apostolus consulit, si quis velit verè scripturas intelligere, & sapiens fieri vera & cœlesti sapientia, ponat sapientiam huius seculi. 1. Cor.3. Nemo se seducat: si quis videtur inter vos[?] sapiens esse in hoc seculo, stultus fiat, vt sit sapiens. Sapientia enim huius Mundi, stultitia est apud Deum. Ioh. 3.[?] causa etiam alia adferrur, cur multi non possint percipere Euangelium : qua a scilicet illud non amarunt. Lux venit in Mundum, & dilexerunt homines magis tenebras, quam lucem. Unde hoc? Quia cum primùm legunt verbum Dei, vident sua a gai[?] pecca-ta. Ideo ait, Erant enim opera eorum mala. Item, Qui male agit, odit lucem, & non venit ad lucem.
units.tr: To this also refers that saying of Christ in Matthew 11: "I thank you, Father, that you have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to little ones." Here too we see why the wise of this world do not understand the Scriptures and do not perceive the mystery of the gospel: the cause lies in the wise themselves, that is, because they are too wise according to the flesh. Now the wisdom of God and human wisdom, or the prudence of the flesh, are at war with each other (Romans 8): "The prudence of the flesh is enmity against God." Hence it follows that the wiser someone is according to the flesh, the less he can perceive the wisdom of God, which has been revealed in the Scriptures. The fault and the cause of the obscurity, therefore, lie not in the Scriptures but in men. This answer is confirmed by another testimony of the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 2: "The natural man does not perceive the things that are of God, nor can he perceive them, because they are spiritually judged." Who does not see here too that the cause why the natural man does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God and does not understand the Scriptures lies in the natural man himself? Namely, because man is merely natural, possessed only of human prudence, and endowed with no Spirit of God. For since the Scriptures are from the Spirit of God, they cannot be understood without the Spirit of God. But the more natural and prudent someone is according to the flesh, the less he has the Spirit of God. How then could he understand them? Therefore the Apostle advises, if anyone wishes truly to understand the Scriptures and to become wise with the true and heavenly wisdom, let him lay aside the wisdom of this age. 1 Corinthians 3: "Let no one deceive himself: if anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become foolish, that he may be wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God." John 3. Another cause is also alleged why many cannot perceive the gospel, namely that they have not loved it. "The light came into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light." Whence is this? Because when they first read the word of God, they see their own sins. Therefore he says: "For their works were evil." Likewise: "He who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light."

units.la: 2. Thess 2. Quia non fuscepcrunt dilectionem veritatis, ut salui fierent, propterea mittet illis Deus efficacitatem deceptionis, &c. Hic etiam videmus cautam, cur homines huius seculi non intelligant scripturas, esse in ipsis, non in scripturis, quia scilicet scripturas non amant, nec illarum lectione delectantur, sed alij oderunt, alij fastidiunt.
units.tr: 2 Thessalonians 2: "Because they did not receive the love of the truth, that they might be saved, therefore God will send them the working of deception, etc." Here too we see the cause why men of this age do not understand the Scriptures lies in themselves, not in the Scriptures, namely because they do not love the Scriptures and do not delight in reading them; some hate them, others loathe them.

units.la: Matth. 22. Erratis nescientes scripturas. Unde verò hæc ignoratio? Quia eas non legebant. Ideo subinde illos de hac re reprehendebat: Non legistis? Matth. 22. De resurrectione mortuorum non legistis, quod vobis dictum est a Deo dicente, Ego sum Deus Abraham, & Deus Isaac, & Deus Iacob? Vel, si legebant, perfunctorie legebant, non scrutabantur. Ideo Iohan. 5. Scrutamini scripturas. Hic etiam apparet, quòd Iudæi non intelligerent scripturas, causam fuisse in ipsis, quòd eas non legerent, aut non scrutarentur, non autem hæ-sisse in scripturis. Summa : E scripturis ap-paret, si quis illas non intelligat, culpam hærere in hominibus, non in scripturis ipsis, quæ sunt lux splendidissima.
units.tr: Matthew 22: "You are mistaken, not knowing the Scriptures." But whence this ignorance? Because they did not read them. Therefore he repeatedly rebuked them on this point: "Have you not read?" Matthew 22: "Concerning the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was said to you by God, saying: I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob?" Or, if they did read, they read perfunctorily and did not search. Therefore John 5: "Search the Scriptures." Here too it appears that when the Jews did not understand the Scriptures, the cause was in themselves, because they did not read them or did not search them, and not that the difficulty lay in the Scriptures. In sum: from the Scriptures it appears that if anyone does not understand them, the fault lies in men, not in the Scriptures themselves, which are the most brilliant light.

units.la: II. Deut. 17. Si qua difficilis causa oriatur, iubet adiri non scripturas ipsas, sed sacerdotes, qui secundum legem Dei iudicent. Si scriptura esset perspicua, supernacaneum [?] foret iubere, ut eas ad sacerdotes.
units.tr: II. Deuteronomy 17: "If a difficult case arises, it orders that they go not to the Scriptures themselves but to the priests, who shall judge according to the law of God. If Scripture were plain, it would be superfluous to order that they be referred to the priests."

units.la: Resp. Fallacia est non causa ut causa. Non ideo iussit ire ad sacerdotes, quia scriptura sit obscura, ita ut non possit omnis difficilis causa iuxta illam cognosci: sed partim, ut qui eam negligunt, ideoque ignorant, do-ceantur a sacerdotibus, partim ut, etiamsi norint, servetur tamen forma iudicij in Ec-clesia, & homines reddantur inexcusabiles. Imò hic locus euincit, scripturam esse per-spicuam, cùm ad hanc omnes difficiles iubet quæstiones examinari, & ex hac de omnibus pronunciari. Illud enim, secundùm quod res ambiguæ iudicandæ sunt, perspicuum & clarum sit, necesse est. Quomodo enim rem ambiguam & obscurā declarare queas. Atqui causæ difficiles iuxta præceptum Mo-sis iudicandæ sunt a sacerdotibus secundùm legem, hoc est, secundum verbum Dei. Quo-modo igitur ex verbo Dei iudicari possunt quæstiones omnes, nisi verbum Domini sit clarissimum? Nihil igitur ex hoc Deut. loco adversus perspicuitatem scripturarum con-cluditur, sed contrà potiùs facit pro perspi-cuitate.
units.tr: Reply: This is the fallacy of non-cause as cause. He did not order them to go to the priests because Scripture is obscure, so that every difficult case could not be known from it; rather, partly so that those who neglect it, and therefore are ignorant, might be taught by the priests, and partly so that, even if they know it, the form of judgment in the Church be preserved and men be rendered inexcusable. Indeed, this very passage proves that Scripture is plain, since it orders that all difficult questions be examined by it, and that judgment be pronounced on all things from it. For that by which ambiguous matters are to be judged must necessarily be plain and clear. For how could you make clear an ambiguous and obscure matter? But difficult cases, according to the precept of Moses, are to be judged by the priests according to the law, that is, according to the word of God. How then could all questions be judged from the word of God, unless the word of the Lord were most clear? Nothing, therefore, is concluded from this passage of Deuteronomy against the perspicuity of the Scriptures; rather, it argues for their perspicuity.

units.la: III. Rom. ii. Incomprehensibilia sunt iudicia eius: Et quis nouit sensum Domini? Hac Erasmus, vt concluderet, scripturas multis in locis obscuras esse.
units.tr: III. Romans 11: "How incomprehensible are his judgments, and who has known the mind of the Lord?" With this Erasmus argued that Scripture is obscure in many places.

units.la: Respondet Lutherus, Non ait Apostolus, incomprehensibilia esse iudicia scripturae, sed, eius, id est, Domini: Neq; ait, Quis nouit sensum scripturae, sed Domini? Damus autem libenter, iudicia Dei non revelata, esse nobis incomprehensibilia. Sed non de iis, verum de revelatis est quaestio: & haec contendimus esse perspicua, & comprehendi posse: quia in hunc etiam finem illa revelauit Deus in scripturis. Item, Damus sensum Domini, id est, voluntatem non revelatam, nemini esse perspectam & notam: verum de hac non disputatur, sed de revelata in S. Literis: Et hanc dicimus posse agnosci, & esse perspicuam. Quare hic est παραλογισμὸς ὁμωνυμίας [?]. Est enim sensus Domini duplex, reue-latus & non revelatus. Ita iudicia Domini duplicia, revelata, non revelata. Nos de revelatis in scripturis loquimur: Loci autem illi scripturae adducti, de non revelatis sunt.
units.tr: Luther replies: The Apostle does not say that the judgments of Scripture are incomprehensible, but "his," that is, of the Lord; nor does he say, "Who has known the sense of Scripture," but "of the Lord." We freely grant that the judgments of God which are not revealed are incomprehensible to us. But the question is not about those, but about those that are revealed; and these we maintain are plain and can be comprehended, because God revealed them in the Scriptures for this very purpose. Likewise, we grant that the mind of the Lord, that is, his unrevealed will, is known and perceived by no one; but this is not disputed, rather the revealed will in the Holy Letters; and this we say can be recognised and is plain. Hence here is an equivocation (paralogismus homonymiae). For the sense of the Lord is twofold: revealed and unrevealed. So the judgments of the Lord are twofold: revealed and unrevealed. We speak of the revealed things in Scripture; but the passages of Scripture adduced there concern the unrevealed.

units.la: IV. 2.Pet.3. De Epistolis Pauli verba faciens Petrus, ait, esse in illis quaedam difficilia intellectu. Non sunt igitur scripturae perspicuae.
units.tr: IV. 2 Pet. 3. Peter, speaking of the Epistles of Paul, says that there are in them certain things hard to understand. Therefore the Scriptures are not perspicuous.

units.la: Resp. Fallacia est figurae dictionis, ex ignoratione linguae Graecae, & sensus Apostolici. Primum illud (in quibus) non potest referri ad Epistolas, quasi dicat Petrus, inter Epistolas Pauli esse aliquas obscuras difficilesque intellectu: sed referrtur [?] ad quaedam fidei mysteria, quæ in Epistolis Pauli tradun-tur. Nam Græcè sic est: Quapropter, Dilecti, hæc exspectantes studete, ut immaculati ab eo reperiamini cum pace: Dominiq; nostri patientiam, salutem arbitremini: sicut & charus frater noster Paulus pro sibi data sapientia scripsit vobis: ὡς καὶ ἐν πάσαις ταῖς ἐπιστολαῖς λαλῶν ἐν αὐταῖς περὶ τούτων (de iis, scilicet de futuro aduentu, & de iis, quæ tunc ventura sunt) ἐν οἷς ἐστί δυσνόητά τινα. Illud ἐν οἷς, neutri generis est, ἐπιστολαῖς autem fœminini. Ideo dixisset ἐν αἷς, si de Epistolis locutus esset: sed ait, ἐν οἷς, scilicet τούτοις, de quibus ipse scripsit, & ait scripsisse etiam Paulum. Quare locus hic minimè concludit, Epistolas Pauli, aut alias scripturas esse obscuras, difficilesque intelle-ctu. Neque enim hic Petrus disputat de obscuritate, aut perspicuitate epistolarum Pauli, sed loquitur de mysteriis futuri aduentus Domini, de exustione cœlorum & elementorum, de nouo cœlo & noua terra: & cumprimis de potentia Domini, qua suum differt aduentum: Et in iis mysteriis, de quibus ait etiam Paulum in suis Epistolis scripsisse, dicit esse quædam, quæ non ita facilè à quovis intelligi & comprehendi possint: ac proinde quæ torqueantur ab indoctis & parum firmis ad suum exitium: sicut etiam reliquas scripturas detorquent. Quare non de epistolis & scripturis, sed de rebus ipsis loquitur.
units.tr: Reply. This is a fallacy of the figure of speech (figura dictionis), arising from ignorance of the Greek language and of the Apostle's meaning. First, the phrase "in which" (in quibus) cannot be referred to the Epistles, as if Peter meant that among the Epistles of Paul there are some obscure and hard to understand. It refers rather to certain mysteries of the faith which are taught in Paul's Epistles. For the Greek reads thus: "Wherefore, beloved, looking for these things, be diligent that you may be found by him without spot and blameless, in peace; and account the patience of our Lord as salvation, as also our dear brother Paul, according to the wisdom given to him, wrote to you; as also in all his epistles, speaking in them of these things [ὡς καὶ ἐν πάσαις ταῖς ἐπιστολαῖς λαλῶν ἐν αὐταῖς περὶ τούτων]" (that is, of the future coming, and of the things that are then to come), "in which are some things hard to understand [ἐν οἷς ἐστί δυσνόητά τινα]." The word ἐν οἷς is of the neuter gender, whereas ἐπιστολαῖς is feminine. So he would have said ἐν αἷς if he had been speaking of the Epistles; but he says ἐν οἷς, that is, τούτοις, "of these things," about which he himself wrote, and he says that Paul also wrote about them. Therefore this passage by no means proves that the Epistles of Paul, or other Scriptures, are obscure and hard to understand. For Peter is not disputing about the obscurity or perspicuity of Paul's epistles, but speaks of the mysteries of the Lord's future coming, of the burning of the heavens and the elements, of the new heaven and the new earth, and above all of the power of the Lord by which he defers his coming. And among those mysteries, of which he says Paul also wrote in his Epistles, he says there are some things which cannot easily be understood and grasped by just anyone, and which therefore are twisted by the untaught and the unstable to their own destruction, just as they twist the other Scriptures too. Therefore he speaks not of the epistles and Scriptures, but of the things themselves.

units.la: At (inquies) perinde est, quæ continen-turtur in sacris Literis esse δυσνόητα, & scripturas ipsas, τὰ ἱερὰ γράμματα esse δυσνόητα. Unde & Petrus simul coniungit, cum ait, tam illa mysteria, quàm reliquas scripturas torqueri ab indoctis. Quare optimè sequitur ex hoc Petri loco, si quæ in scripturis continentur mysteria, sunt δυσνόητα, etiam scripturas ipsas esse difficiles intellectu.
units.tr: But (you will say) it is all the same whether the things contained in the holy Letters are "hard to understand" (δυσνόητα), and the Scriptures themselves, "the holy writings" (τὰ ἱερὰ γράμματα), are hard to understand. Hence also Peter joins them together when he says that both those mysteries and the other Scriptures are twisted by the untaught. Therefore it follows very well from this passage of Peter that if the mysteries contained in the Scriptures are "hard to understand" (δυσνόητα), the Scriptures themselves are also difficult to understand.

units.la: Resp. Demus: sed quid tum? Primò, non consequetur, omnes scripturas esse difficiles intellectu, sed tantùm illas, ubi continentur hæc quædam δυσνόητα: Qua voce indicat, reliqua esse ἄνόητα, illa scilicet, quæ cuique ad salutem cognitu sunt necessaria. Quòd si hæc etiam sint alicui difficilia & obscura: ideo sunt, quia volunt ipsi ea ignorare, ut supra ait Petrus, verf.5. Nam illud, volentes nesciunt, quod cœli, &c.
units.tr: Reply. Granted; but so what? First, it does not follow that all the Scriptures are difficult to understand, but only those in which these certain "hard to understand" things are contained. By this word he indicates that the rest are "easy to understand" (ἄνόητα, that is, plain), namely those things which are necessary for everyone to know for salvation. But if even these are difficult and obscure to anyone, they are so because they wish to be ignorant of them, as Peter said above, v. 5: "For they willingly are ignorant that the heavens, etc."

units.la: Secundò, non ait, illa etiam quædam, esse ita obscura, ut non possint intelligi, sed tantùm ait, esse δυσνόητα. Fatemur autem opus esse studio, diligentia, scrutatione in intelligendis scripturis. Nullæ igitur scripturæ, ita obscuræ sunt, quin possint intelligi.
units.tr: Second, he does not say that those certain things are so obscure that they cannot be understood, but only that they are "hard to understand" (δυσνόητα). We admit, however, that study, diligence and searching are needed in understanding the Scriptures. Therefore no Scriptures are so obscure that they cannot be understood.

units.la: Tertiò, Non ait, quibusvis esse δυσνόητα. Sed duobus hominum generibus, indoctis, hoc est, imperitis scripturarum, ac minimè ἀπαιδεύτοις, & instabilibus, hoc est, qui non sunt firmi in fide, neque perseverant in lectione ac studio scripturarum: hoc est, illis, qui sunt sine spiritu Dei. Ita enim subdit Apostolus: ἀοὶ ἀμαθεῖς καὶ ἀστήρικτοι στρεβλοῦσιν, ὡς καὶ τὰς[?] [?]ἐν τὰς λοιπὰς γραφὰς πρὸς τὴν ἰδίαν αὐτῶν ἀπώ-λειαν. Quasi dicat, quia sunt indocti, imperiti scripturarum, sine spiritu Dei, & instabiles in religione: Ideo haec, non intelligentes, torquent ad suam perniciem. Vt exempli causa, potentia qua Christus suum differt aduentum, abutuntur ad suam perniciem, vt negent esse venturum, sicut supra dixit, Ven-turos irrisores, qui in suis cupiditatibus incedant, & dicant, vbi est pollicitatio aduentus eius. Ex quo enim, &c. Non sequitur igitur, scripturas omnibus esse obscuras & difficiles, sed hominibus tantùm, qui cùm sint sine spiritu Dei, sunt etiam scripturarum imperiti, & instabiles. Quare? Quia animalis homo non percipit ea quae Dei sunt: Et caro & sanguis non renelat hoc, sed Pater coelestis suo spiritu. A contrario igitur docet Petrus iis verbis, illis qui sunt praediti spiritu Dei, & [?]θεοδίδακτοι, quique perpetuò & constanter in scripturarum lectione versantur & meditantur, nihil in eis esse [?]ἀνεπίλυτον. Ratio: 1. Corinth. 2. Spiritus enim omnia scrutatur, etiam profunditates Dei. Et quas profunditates? Non omnes, vt quae non sunt reuelatae in scripturis, sed tantùm reuelatas. Nam de illis Apostolus Rom. 11. [?]ὦ βάθος· πλούτου καὶ σοφίας, ὡς ἀνεξεραύνητα, &c. Sum-ma: Primùm, Etsi scriptura per se sit perspicua: non tamen dicimus omnibus esse perspicuam, & facilem intellectu, vt sunt illi peruersi homines, de quibus loquitur Petrus. Sed quibus? iis, qui spiritum Dei habent se docentem: qui Deum invocant pro vera scripturarum intelligentia: qui diligenter & assiduè S. literas perscrutatur. Quare locus Petri, qui de perversis loquitur ho-minibus, nil concludit contra nos. Dein-de, etsi dicimus totam scripturam esse per se claram: non ideo tamen dicimus, ubique ex æquo, esse intellectu facilem: Alicubi enim etiam filiis Dei, esse intellectu difficiliorem, quàm alibi. Sed dicimus, in tam fre-quentibus locis esse intellectu facilem, ut qui veram Dei doctrinam in eis quærat, ple-nissimè eam sit inventurus.
units.tr: Third, he does not say that they are hard to understand for anyone at all, but for two kinds of people: the untaught, that is, those inexperienced in the Scriptures, and by no means "uneducated" (ἀπαιδεύτοις), and the unstable, that is, those who are not firm in the faith and do not persevere in reading and study of the Scriptures; that is, those who are without the Spirit of God. For the Apostle adds this: "The untaught and unstable twist, as also the rest of the Scriptures, to their own destruction" [ἀοὶ ἀμαθεῖς καὶ ἀστήρικτοι στρεβλοῦσιν, ὡς καὶ τὰς λοιπὰς γραφὰς πρὸς τὴν ἰδίαν αὐτῶν ἀπώλειαν]. As if he were saying: because they are untaught, inexperienced in the Scriptures, without the Spirit of God, and unstable in religion, therefore they, not understanding these things, twist them to their own ruin. For example, they abuse the power by which Christ defers his coming, to their own ruin, so that they deny that he will come, just as he said above: "There will come scoffers, walking in their own lusts, and saying: where is the promise of his coming? For since the fathers fell asleep, etc." Therefore it does not follow that the Scriptures are obscure and difficult for everyone, but only for people who, since they are without the Spirit of God, are also inexperienced in the Scriptures and unstable. Why? "Because the natural man does not perceive the things that are of God; and flesh and blood do not reveal this, but the heavenly Father by his Spirit" (1 Cor. 2). By the contrary, therefore, Peter teaches in those words that for those who are endowed with the Spirit of God, and are taught by God [θεοδίδακτοι], and who constantly and steadily occupy themselves in reading and meditating on the Scriptures, nothing in them is [ἀνεπίλυτον] insoluble. The reason: 1 Cor. 2: "For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God." And what depths? Not all of them, namely not those that are not revealed in the Scriptures, but only those that are revealed. For of those the Apostle speaks in Rom. 11: "O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God! How unsearchable [ὡς ἀνεξεραύνητα] are his judgments," etc. In summary: First, although Scripture is perspicuous in itself, we do not say that it is perspicuous and easy to understand for all people, such as those perverse men of whom Peter speaks. But for whom? For those who have the Spirit of God teaching them, who call upon God for the true understanding of the Scriptures, who diligently and constantly search the holy Letters. Therefore Peter's passage, which speaks of perverse men, proves nothing against us. Next, although we say that the whole of Scripture is clear in itself, we do not therefore say that it is equally easy to understand everywhere: for in some places it is more difficult even for the sons of God to understand than in others. But we say that in so many places it is easy to understand that whoever seeks the true doctrine of God in them will find it most fully.

units.la: V. ¶A quotidianis explicationibus. Si scriptu-ra sancta non essent obscura, sed perspicua, super-nacanei essent interpretes in Ecclesia. ¶At non sunt. Sunt igitur obscura.
units.tr: V. From the daily explanations. If the holy Scripture were not obscure but perspicuous, interpreters in the Church would be superfluous. But they are not superfluous. Therefore the Scripture is obscure.

units.la: Resp. Fallacia est non causæ ut causæ: Non enim una tantùm est causa, cur Dominus velit scripturas in Ecclesia explicari, nimirum ut simpliciter intelligantur: sed aliæ etiam sunt causæ: nempe 1. ut melius per Spiritum sanctum cordibus infigantur. Adest enim Spiritus sanctus in ministerio publico. 2. Ut publicum extet ministerium, ad quod etiam infideles accedant, & discant: & Dominus publicè arguat, doceat, consoletur. 3. Ut charitas ac dilectio per donorum communicationè magis ac magis in populo Dei exerceatur, augeatur, dum alij docent, alij discunt. 4. Non omnes sciunt scripturas legere: aliis non ita vacat: alij non tam bene intelligunt, quia imperiti, quàm pastores. Ergo non frustra ministerium, etiamsi scripturæ per se sint perspicuæ.
units.tr: Reply. This is a fallacy of a non-cause as a cause. For there is not only one cause why the Lord wills the Scriptures to be explained in the Church, namely that they may be simply understood; there are also other causes: namely, (1) that they may be more effectively fixed in hearts by the Holy Spirit, for the Holy Spirit is present in the public ministry; (2) that a public ministry may stand, to which even unbelievers may come and learn, and that the Lord may publicly reprove, teach and comfort; (3) that charity and love may be exercised and increased more and more among the people of God, while some teach and others learn; (4) not everyone knows how to read the Scriptures; some do not have the leisure; and some do not understand as well, being untaught, as the ministers do. Therefore the ministry is not in vain, even if the Scriptures are perspicuous in themselves.

units.la: VI. A variis scripturarum interpretationibus, quas adferunt Doctores.
units.tr: VI. Concerning the various interpretations of Scripture that the teachers put forward.

units.la: Doctores Ecclesiæ dissentiunt inter se in interpretationibus scripturarum. Ergo obscuræ sunt.
units.tr: The teachers of the Church disagree among themselves in their interpretations of Scripture. Therefore Scripture is obscure.

units.la: Resp. primò ad Antecedens. In necessariis ad salutem non dissentiunt veri Doctores. Est igitur fallacia à secundum quid, ad simpliciter. Secundò ad consequens. Etiamsi dissentiant nonnulli, non consequitur, scripturam esse per se obscuram. Vitium enim est in Doctoribus ipsis, non in scriptura. Quòd autem Deus permittat, ut in multis scripturarum interpretationibus inter se dissentiant Patres, hoc facit propter ipsorum & nostram utilitatem. Ipsorum, ut primò agnoscant suam in rebus diuinis imperitiam, atq; ita humilientur. Secundò, ut se exerceant in scripturis inuestigandis, & ita euitent otium, & tentationes Sathanæ.
units.tr: I reply, first, to the antecedent: the true teachers do not disagree about things necessary to salvation. So this is a fallacy moving from a qualified sense to an unqualified one. Second, I reply to the consequent: even if some disagree, it does not follow that Scripture is obscure in itself. The fault lies in the teachers themselves, not in Scripture. As for God's permitting the Fathers to disagree with one another about many interpretations of Scripture, He does so for their benefit and ours. For their benefit, first, so that they may recognise their own ignorance in divine matters and so be humbled. Second, so that they may exercise themselves in searching the Scriptures and thus avoid idleness and the temptations of Satan.

units.la: Tertiò, ut excitentur ad inuocationem.
units.tr: Third, so that they may be stirred up to prayer.

units.la: Ad nostram, ut nos inde quoque Patrum exemplo discamus, quàm simus nostra natura ineptiad ea quæ Dei sunt. Ita accendamur ad studium scripturæ, & ad Deum inuocandum pro vera scripturæ intelligentia.
units.tr: For our benefit, so that we too may learn from the example of the Fathers how unfit our nature is for the things that belong to God. Thus we may be kindled to the study of Scripture and to call upon God for the true understanding of Scripture.

units.la: VII. A multis scripturarum locis, qui ne à doctissimis quidem intelliguntur. Multa sunt in scripturis, quæ ne à doctissimis quidem intelli-guntur
units.tr: VII. Concerning many passages of Scripture that are not understood even by the most learned. There are many things in Scripture that are not understood even by the most learned.

units.la: guntur, vt quædam apud Prophetas oracula, & visiones: qualis est illa visio apud Ezechielem in cap.1 quam etiamsi præstantissimi & ingenio, & spiritu, & eruditione viri interpretentur: fatentur tamen esse obscurissimam, nec se intelligere, nisi forte ex parte, idq; tenuiter. Et alia non dissi-miles, tam in hoc, quam in aliis Prophetis. Et in Apocalypsi quot sunt obscurissima?
units.tr: Such as certain oracles and visions among the Prophets, like that vision in Ezekiel chapter 1, which even the most outstanding men, endowed with genius, spirit and learning, confess to be most obscure when they interpret it, and say that they understand it only in part, and that imperfectly. And others not dissimilar, both in this book and in the other Prophets. And in the Apocalypse, how many passages are most obscure?

units.la: Resp. Fatemur nonnulla in Prophetis præsertim, nobis esse obscurissima atque ita obscura, ut quid sibi voluerint Prophetæ illis in locis & visionibus, quisve sit illarum verus sensus, divinari quidem ab aliquo possit, sed certò à se sciri, profiteri nemo vix queat. Atque hoc præsertim verum est in iis visionibus, quæ sunt de rebus futuris, quorum complementa nondum videmus aut gustamus. Exempla occurrent legentibus Prophetas, maximè verò Ezechielem, Danielem, Zachariam, & Apocalypsin Iohannis. Sed unde hæc obscuritas? Non certè à scripturis ipsis 1. Stat enim firmum illud Petri de Prophetico sermone, quicunque ille sit, eum esse lucernam lucentem in caliginoso loco. 2. Et certè Deus non illas obtulit visiones Prophetis, ut nollet intelligi non solum ab ipsis Prophetis, quibus visiones asse[?]-rebat, sed etiam à populo, cui eas recitari volebat: imò & à nobis, in quorum gratiam scriptæ sunt. Non est igitur obscuritas hæc, proprie loquendo, in & ab ipsis scripturis Propheticis. Sed ubi & unde? In nobis, & à nobis, quòd ita obtusa fumus acie oculo-rum spiritus, ut res procul dissitas, quae illis visionibus Prophetis ostendebantur, intueri nequeamus: ac proinde ipsae etiam visiones obscurissimae nobis sunt. Ratio. Nam sicut reliquum Dei verbum non potest percipi ab illis qui sunt sine spiritu Dei.i.Corinth.2.Sic visiones Propheticae, & oracula de rebus futuris non possunt percipi sine spiritu Prophetico. Interim tamen scripturae illae Propheticae per se perspicuae sunt.Nam fac,ut illae visiones & oracula nobis proponantur, non amplius ut Prophetica,de rebus futuris: sed ut historica, ut pote de rebus, quae complementum habuerunt, aut iam habere incipiunt illae scripturae non amplius nobis ita videbuntur obscurae, sed claræ & perspicuae. Exemplis rem declaro.
units.tr: I reply: we grant that some passages, especially in the Prophets, are most obscure to us, so obscure that one may guess what the Prophets meant in those passages and visions, and what their true sense is, but hardly anyone could profess that he knows it for certain. This is especially true of those visions which concern future things, whose fulfilment we do not yet see or taste. Examples will occur to readers of the Prophets, above all of Ezekiel, Daniel, Zechariah and the Apocalypse of John. But whence this obscurity? Certainly not from the Scriptures themselves. (1) For that saying of Peter about prophetic speech, whatever it may be, stands firm: that it is a lamp shining in a dark place. (2) And surely God did not give those visions to the Prophets so that they should not wish to be understood, not only by the Prophets themselves, to whom He revealed the visions, but also by the people to whom He wished them to be read out, and indeed by us, for whose sake they were written. This obscurity, then, properly speaking, is not in the prophetic Scriptures themselves nor from them. Where, then, and whence is it? It is in us and from us, in that the eyes of our spirit are so dulled that we cannot see the things far off that were shown to the Prophets in those visions; and therefore the visions themselves are most obscure to us. The reason is this: just as the rest of the Word of God cannot be perceived by those who are without the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2.), so prophetic visions and oracles about future things cannot be perceived without the prophetic Spirit. Meanwhile, those prophetic Scriptures are clear in themselves. For suppose these visions and oracles are set before us no longer as prophetic, about future things, but as historical, as concerning things that have already come to pass or are beginning to come to pass; those Scriptures will no longer seem obscure to us, but clear and plain. I will make the matter plain by examples.

units.la: Quæ Daniel cap.2. somnium Regis expli-cans,& 7.cap.visionem suam de 4 bestiis declarans, prædixit de quatuor Monarchiis: Et quæ itidem Zacharias, cap.6. sub visione 4. Quadriigarum egredientium de medio montium,de iisdem 4.Monarchiis vaticinatus est: dubium non est,quin populo illi fue-rint obscurissima. Quare? Quia nondum po-terant res ipsas longo post tempore futuras, perspicere sine spiritu Prophetico. At nobis, qui hæc omnia videmus completa: ac proinde,qui hæc legimus, non tanquam de rebus futuris oracula, sed tanquā de præteritis rebus gestis historias:nihil est clarius illis visionibus.
units.tr: What Daniel in chapter 2, explaining the king's dream, and in chapter 7, declaring his vision of the four beasts, foretold about the four monarchies; and likewise what Zechariah in chapter 6, under the vision of the four chariots coming out from between the mountains, prophesied about those same four monarchies: there is no doubt that these were most obscure to that people. Why? Because they could not yet, without the prophetic Spirit, perceive the things themselves, which were to come far in the future. But to us, who see all these things fulfilled, and who therefore read them not as oracles about future things but as histories of past events, nothing is clearer than those visions.

units.la: Item, Quæ tam Daniel cap. ii. sub figura Antiochi, & Zacharias cap. ii. sub pastore stulto, de Antichristo prædixerunt: & quæ deinde luculentius de eodem prædixit Apostolus 2. Thessal. 2. & Johan. in Apocalypsi, cum alibi, tum cap. 13. Ea certè antequam revelatus esset Antichristus, obscurissima fuerunt viris etiam sanctissimis, & in scripturis exercitatissimis. Quamobrem ? Quia Prophetica erant, de rebus futuris: quas res, qui sine spiritu Dei erant, videre non poterant. At nobis nihil his locis clarius: quia ea loca legimus non tanquam vaticinia de rebus futuris: sed tanquam historica de præteritis & præsentibus. Idem videmus contigisse Apostolis. Multa de se, de sua morte, resurrectione, regno prædicebat Christus, quæ illi non intellexerunt, nisi posteaquàm impleta vidissent. Exemplum unum. Joh. 2. petentibus Judæis signum à Christo: soluite (inquit) Templum hoc, & in tribus diebus excitabo illud. Luc. 18. Et abscónditum erat ab oculis eorum: sed post resurrectionem recordati sunt. Hoc dictum obscurum fuit non solùm illis Judæis incredulis, sed etiam Apostolis Spiritu Dei præditis. Quare? Quia de re futura, quam non videbant, neque persuadere sibi poterant. At posteaquam resurrexisset à mortuis, atq; ita dictum illud suissel adimpletum: tunc Apostolis nihil fuit clarius, quàm Christum tunc locutum fuisse de templo corporis sui: quòd scilicet occisum [?]um illud à Iudæis, ipse esset excitaturus à mortuis, quemadmodum Euangelista ibidem subdit, & docet.
units.tr: Likewise, what Daniel in chapter 11, under the figure of Antiochus, and Zechariah in chapter 11, under the foolish shepherd, prophesied about Antichrist; and what the Apostle later set out more clearly about the same in 2 Thessalonians 2, and John in the Apocalypse, both elsewhere and in chapter 13. These were certainly most obscure, even to the most holy men and those most practised in the Scriptures, before Antichrist was revealed. Why? Because they were prophecies about future things, which those without the Spirit of God could not see. But to us nothing in these passages is clearer, because we read these passages not as prophecies of future things but as history of past and present events. We see the same thing happened to the Apostles. Christ foretold many things about himself, about his death, resurrection and kingdom, which they did not understand until they had seen them fulfilled. One example: in John 2, when the Jews asked Christ for a sign, he said: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." And in Luke 18: "It was hidden from their eyes, but after the resurrection they remembered." This saying was obscure not only to those unbelieving Jews, but also to the Apostles, who were endowed with the Spirit of God. Why? Because it concerned a future thing, which they did not see and could not convince themselves of. But after he had risen from the dead, and so the saying had been fulfilled, nothing was clearer to the Apostles than that Christ had then been speaking of the temple of his body: that is, that he himself would raise up that body, killed by the Jews, from the dead, as the Evangelist adds and teaches in the same place.

units.la: Hinc perspicuum fit, multa apud Pro-phetas dicta & visiones contineri, quæ licet ante illarum complementum hominibus spiritu Prophetico destitutis, obscurif-simæ essent: tamen per se erant perspicuæ: id quod inde apparet, quia post illarum com-plementum, nobis factæ sunt clarissimæ. Obscuritas igitur non erat in ipsis Prophe-tarum dictis, oraculis, visionibus, sed in hominibus, qui cum essent spiritu Prophe-ti-co vacui, hoc est, acie oculorum spiritus obtusa: res tam procul dissitas videre non poterant. Idem igitur sentiendum est de multis aliis, quæ tam in veteribus Prophe-tis, quàm in Apocalypsi continentur: ea esse non in se, sed nobis obscura: quia de rebus sunt futuris, quas quia expertes spiritus Prophetici non possumus cernere, idcirco harum etiam scripturarum verum ac genuinum sensum videre non possumus. Sed cum omnia suum sortita[?] fuerint cōplementum: tum omnes etiam scripturæ perspicuæ nobis fuerint, quæ semper in se nihil habent obscuritatis. Sunt enim semper lucerna lu-cis: obscuritas semper in nobis, & à nobis est. Semper enim Spiritus sanctus in scri-pturis ipsis, causas cur non intelligamus scripturas, nobis adscribit, non scripturis. Accusare igitur scripturas obscuritatis, & talis obscuritatis, propter quam intelligi ne-quant: summae est impietatis: quia nihil aliud est, quàm culpam huius obscuritatis à nobis in Deum transferre, quam tamen dif-fertè Spiritus S. in nobis hærere docet: vt aliqua ex parte ostendimus in responsione ad primum argumentum: & nunc fusius et-iam ostendemus.
units.tr: From this it is plain that many sayings, visions and oracles are contained in the Prophets, which, although before their fulfilment they were most obscure to men destitute of the prophetic Spirit, were nevertheless clear in themselves. This is shown by the fact that after their fulfilment they became most clear to us. The obscurity, therefore, was not in the sayings, oracles and visions of the Prophets themselves, but in men who, being empty of the prophetic Spirit, that is, having the eyes of their spirit dulled, could not see things so far off. Therefore the same must be thought of many other things contained both in the older Prophets and in the Apocalypse: that they are obscure not in themselves but to us; because they concern future things, which, since we lack the prophetic Spirit, we cannot discern, and therefore we cannot see the true and genuine sense of those Scriptures either. But when all these things have received their fulfilment, then all these Scriptures will also be clear to us, for they in themselves never have any obscurity. For they are always a lamp of light; the obscurity is always in us and from us. For the Holy Spirit always ascribes to us, not to the Scriptures, the causes why we do not understand the Scriptures, in the Scriptures themselves. To accuse the Scriptures of obscurity, and of such obscurity that they cannot be understood, is the height of impiety: for this is nothing other than transferring the blame for this obscurity from ourselves to God, whereas the Holy Spirit clearly teaches that it lies in us. We have shown this in part in our reply to the first argument, and now we will show it more fully.

units.la: Quod ad quæstionem de perspicuitate scripturarum attinet: hactenus demonstra-tum à nobis est, primum quidem, scripturam nulla sui parte ita per se obscuram esse, vt à fidelibus spiritu Dei præditis intelligi nequeat: multò verò minùs in iis quæ ad sa-lutem necessaria sunt. Confirmata, demon-strataque doctrina: responsum est ad argumenta aduersariorum numero septem: quo-rum primum ductum fuit ex loco 2. ad Co-rinth. 3. de velamine quod adhuc est in le-ctione veteris Testamenti. Alterum ex Deu-ter. 17. de causis difficilibus ad sacerdotes re-ferendis. Tertium à loco Pauli in Epistola ad Roman. 11. Quàm incomprehensibilia sunt iudicia eius? Item, Quis nouit sensum Domini? Quartum, ex loco Petri 2. Pet. 3. in quibus sint quædam intellectu difficilia. Quintum ductum à Ministerio verbi in Ecclesia. Sextum à multitudine diversitateque interpretationum scripturæ sanctæ, quæ tum à veteribus, tum à nostris doctoribus allatæ sunt, & adferuntur. Septimum, à locis quibusdam scripturæ, qui hucusq; à nemine fuerunt probè intellecti, & perfectè explicati.
units.tr: As regards the question of the perspicuity of the Scriptures, we have so far demonstrated, first, that no part of Scripture is in itself so obscure that it cannot be understood by the faithful who are endowed with the Spirit of God; much less is this so in those matters which are necessary to salvation. The doctrine having been confirmed and demonstrated, we have replied to the seven arguments of our opponents. The first of these was drawn from 2 Corinthians 3 concerning the veil which still lies upon the reading of the Old Testament. The second from Deuteronomy 17 concerning difficult causes to be referred to the priests. The third from Paul's passage in Romans 11: "How unsearchable are his judgments!" and likewise "Who has known the mind of the Lord?" The fourth from Peter's passage, 2 Peter 3, in which there are certain things hard to understand. The fifth drawn from the ministry of the Word in the Church. The sixth from the multitude and diversity of interpretations of Holy Scripture, which both the ancients and our own teachers have advanced and still advance. The seventh from certain passages of Scripture which up to now have been understood properly and explained perfectly by no one.

units.la: Responsiones ad singula argumenta repetere, neque necesse est, neque operæ pretium.
units.tr: It is neither necessary nor worthwhile to repeat the replies to each single argument.

units.la: Tantùm censeo vtile fore, si responsionem ad septimum breviter repetam. Res igitur ita se habet.
units.tr: I think it will only be useful if I briefly repeat the reply to the seventh. The matter stands as follows.

units.la: Fatemur nonnullas visiones & oracula de rebus futuris in scripturis, apud Prophetas contineri, quæ à nemine hactenus videntur fuisse probè intellecta, & perfectè explicata. Nam etiamsi multi in ea scripserint quod senserunt: fatentur tamen se non profiteri perfectam illorum locorum intelligentiam. Esse igitur obscura.
units.tr: We grant that some visions and oracles concerning future events are contained in the Scriptures, among the Prophets, which so far seem to have been understood properly and explained perfectly by no one. For although many have written on them what they thought, they nevertheless confess that they do not profess a perfect understanding of those passages. Therefore they are obscure.

units.la: Sed contendimus nos, causam huius obscuritatis, non hærere in ipsis scripturis Propheticis, propter illud 2.Pet.1. Et habemus firmiorem Propheticum sermonem, &c. De toto sermone Prophetico hoc dixit.
units.tr: But we contend that the cause of this obscurity does not lie in the prophetic Scriptures themselves, on account of that passage of 2 Peter 1: "And we have a more sure prophetic word," etc. He said this concerning the whole prophetic discourse.

units.la: Non igitur in ipsis scripturis hærere culpam obscuritatis.
units.tr: Therefore the fault of obscurity does not lie in the Scriptures themselves.

units.la: Vbi igitur? In nobis ipsis, vt semper Spiritus S. in scripturis docet: Et hanc esse, quòd licet spiritum Dei habeamus: tamen obtusa mentis acie sumus. Hinc fieri, vt res procul à nobis dissitas nequeamus videre, eoque nec scripturas, quæ de iis sunt, perfectè intelligere, eoq; obscuras videri.
units.tr: Where then does it lie? In ourselves, as the Holy Spirit always teaches in the Scriptures; and this is so because, although we have the Spirit of God, we nevertheless have a dull edge of mind. Hence it happens that we cannot see things remote from us, and therefore cannot understand perfectly the Scriptures that concern them, and so they appear obscure.

units.la: Hoc ita esse, hinc liquere, quia si visiones illæ nobis proponantur non amplius vt Prophetica de rebus futuris, sed vt historicæ de præteritis[?] aut præsentibus: eas non amplius nobis visum iri obscuras, sed perspicuas. Non igitur obscuritatem in scripturis fuisse, sed quod res procul distantes non possemus intueri, acie obtusa cum simus.
units.tr: That this is so is clear from this: if those visions were presented to us no longer as prophecies of future events but as historical accounts of past or present ones, we would no longer find them obscure but plain. The obscurity therefore was not in the Scriptures, but in the fact that we, having a dull sight, could not see things far distant.

units.la: Exemplis rem declaraui, primum de visionibus & vaticiniis Monarchiarum, quæ Dan.2.&7. Zach.6.leguntur. Illa antequam complerentur, visa fuisse obscura antiquis, nobis clara. Secundum, quæ de Antichristo Dan.11. sub typo Antiochi, Zach.11 sub Pastore stulto, leguntur. Tertium quæ Ioh.2.[?] Luc.18.de templo corporisChristi.Idem igitur sentiendum de aliis, quæ nondum sunt impleta, in Apocalypsi. Quare causam obscuritatis semper in nobis hærere: proinde summæ impietatis esse, scripturas accusare obscuritatis: quia hoc est culpam obscuritatis huius in Deum transferre, quam tamen Spiritus S. semper in nobis esse docet. Atque hæc de quæstione vndecima satis. Nunc sequitur
units.tr: I have illustrated the matter with examples: first, the visions and prophecies of the monarchies, which are read in Daniel 2 and 7 and Zechariah 6. Before those were fulfilled they were obscure to the ancients, but clear to us. Second, what is read of Antichrist in Daniel 11 under the type of Antiochus, and in Zechariah 11 under the foolish shepherd. Third, what is read in John 2 and Luke 18 concerning the temple of Christ's body. The same must be thought of the other things in the Apocalypse which are not yet fulfilled. Wherefore the cause of obscurity always lies in us; therefore it is the height of impiety to accuse the Scriptures of obscurity, since this is to transfer to God the fault of this obscurity, which the Holy Spirit always teaches to be in us. And so much on the eleventh question. Now follows

units.la: QVÆSTIO DVODECIMA quæ est de regulis intelligendi S.Literas, & illis proficiendi.
units.tr: QUESTION TWELVE, which concerns the rules for understanding the Sacred Letters and for making progress in them.

units.la: Sed vt melius hæ cognoscantur, expli-candæ prius sunt causæ, cur scripturæ videantur obscuræ, quas causas omnes dixi in nobis hærere, vt ex iis postea è contrario educantur regulæ perspicuitatis. Quæstio igitur est, quænam sint illæ causæ, propter quas scri-pturæ nobis videantur obscuræ: ac proinde, quæ-nam vera regula, quibus scripturas perspicuè in-telligere, inq; illis proficere possimus.
units.tr: But so that these may be better known, the causes must first be explained why the Scriptures seem obscure. I have said that all these causes lie in us, so that from them, in turn, the rules of perspicuity may afterwards be drawn out. The question therefore is: what are those causes on account of which the Scriptures seem obscure to us; and consequently, what is the true rule by which we may understand the Scriptures clearly and make progress in them.

units.la: Resp. Papistæ putant,& scribunt, primam regulam intelligendi scripturas, eamque præcipuam, esse vt recurratur pro sacra-rum Literarum intelligentia, ad Ecclesiam Catholicam. Ibi enim tantùm verum scri-pturæ intellectum retineri, iam inde ab i-nitio per Apostolos relictum [?]. Et ad hanc sententiam confirmandam adferunt testi-monium Apostoli, ex 1.Timoth.3. Ecclesia est columna & fundamentum veritatis. Verus igitur scripturarum intellectus, apud Eccle-siam Catholicam quærendus est, quòd ibi semper maneat.
units.tr: Reply. The Papists think and write that the first and chief rule for understanding the Scriptures is that one should have recourse to the Catholic Church for the understanding of the sacred Letters. For there alone, they say, the true sense of Scripture has been retained, having been handed down from the beginning by the Apostles. And to confirm this opinion they bring the testimony of the Apostle from 1 Timothy 3: "The Church is the pillar and ground of the truth." The true sense of Scripture is therefore to be sought in the Catholic Church, because it always remains there.

units.la: Deinde quædam alia argumenta ex Pa-tribus.
units.tr: Then certain other arguments from the Fathers.

units.la: Nos quoad hanc quæstionem attinet, pri-mò dicemus, quid nobis videatur: Deinde, ad extremum, Papisticam sententiam, vt ipsi eam intelligunt, refutabimus.
units.tr: As far as this question is concerned, we shall first state what seems right to us; then, at the end, we shall refute the Papistical opinion as they themselves understand it.

units.la: Principio tenenda est hæc partitio. Regulæ ad intelligendum scripturas, vtiles & verò etiam necessariæ, triplicis sunt generis.
units.tr: First of all this division must be held. The rules for understanding the Scriptures, which are useful and indeed truly necessary, are of three kinds.

units.la: Quædam præcedunt ipsam scripturarum lectionem, seu adferendæ sunt ad studium sacrarum Literarum: Quædam seruandæ in ipsa lectione. Quædam verò subsequantur, necesse est.
units.tr: Some precede the very reading of the Scriptures, or are to be brought to the study of the sacred Letters; some are to be observed in the reading itself; and some, of necessity, follow afterwards.

units.la: Hæ regulæ (vt antè dixi) colligendæ sunt ex causis, cur scripturae multis obscurae sint, ac parum in eis proficiant. Ergo primum hae causae sunt videndae, & ex singulis, singulae regulae conficientur.
units.tr: These rules (as I said before) are to be gathered from the causes why the Scriptures are obscure to many and why they make little progress in them. First, therefore, these causes must be examined, and from each single cause a single rule will be drawn.

units.la: CAPUT PRIMUM. De regulis primi generis, deque causis ob-scuritatis scripturarum, in primo genere.
units.tr: CHAPTER ONE. On the rules of the first kind, and on the causes of the obscurity of Scripture, in the first kind.

units.la: Praecipua quidem causa, cur scripturae multis sint obscurissimae, ita ut non queant ab ipsis intelligi, est, quod sunt reprobi, suntque e numero eorum, quibus non est datum, ut agnoscant mysteria Dei, sed ex illorum, qui pereunt. Docet hanc Christus & Apostoli. Matth.13. Vobis (Electis) datum est, nosse mysteria regni Dei: illis autem (Pharisaeis & aliis reprobis) non est datum: propterea per parabolas loquor eis, quia videntes non vident. Et confirmat dictum verbis Ies.[?] 6. cap. Auribus audietis, & non intelligetis. Iohan. 8. Qui ex Deo est, verba Dei audit: propterea vos non auditis, quia ex Deo non estis. 1.Cor.1. Verbum crucis (id est, Euangelium) pereuntibus quidem stultitia est: iis autem qui salui fiunt, id est, nobis Dei virtus est. 2. Cor. 2. ait, Euangelium esse odorem mortis ad mortem iis qui pereunt. Item, cap. 4. ait, Euangelium suum non esse velatum, seu opertum, nisi iis, qui pereunt. Non est igitur obscuritas in Euangelio, sed in hominibus reprobis.
units.tr: The chief cause, indeed, why Scripture is most obscure to many, so that they cannot understand it, is that they are reprobate, and belong to the number of those to whom it has not been given to acknowledge the mysteries of God, but who belong to those who perish. Christ and the Apostles teach this. Matt. 13. "To you (the Elect) it is given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God; but to them (the Pharisees and other reprobates) it is not given; therefore I speak to them in parables, because seeing they do not see." And he confirms the saying with the words of Isaiah 6: "By hearing you will hear, and will not understand." John 8: "He who is of God hears the words of God; therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God." 1 Cor. 1: "The word of the cross (that is, the Gospel) is indeed foolishness to those who perish, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God." 2 Cor. 2 says that the Gospel is "a fragrance of death to death to those who perish." Likewise, chapter 4 says that his Gospel is not veiled or hidden except to those who perish. Therefore the obscurity is not in the Gospel, but in reprobate men.

units.la: Ex hac praecipua obscuritatis causa, nullam possumus tradere regulam pro intellectu scripturarum: quia nullius est hominis efficere, ut sit Electus. Sed maximâ hinc colligimus & fidei confirmationem, & utilitatem. Fidei confirmationem: quia si Electis tantùm datum est, ut verè, perspicuè, genuinè & solidè intelligant sacras Literas: Ergo cùm sentimus, nos hac vera cognitione donatos esse, confirmamur, & debemus confirmari in fide de nostri electione. Utilitatem verò, quia hinc excitamur ad strenuè pergendum in scripturis perscrutandis: quippe qui sumus ex illorum numero, quibus datum est nosse mysteria Regni Dei.
units.tr: From this principal cause of obscurity we cannot give any rule for understanding Scripture, because it is no man's doing to make someone one of the Elect. But from this we draw the greatest confirmation and benefit for faith. Confirmation of faith: because if it has been given only to the Elect to understand the sacred Letters truly, clearly, genuinely and soundly, then, when we perceive that we have been endowed with this true knowledge, we are confirmed, and ought to be confirmed, in faith concerning our election. The benefit is that we are roused thereby to press on vigorously in searching the Scriptures, since we are of the number of those to whom it has been given to know the mysteries of the Kingdom of God.

units.la: Cæterum, quia hæc causa extra hominem est, & immutabilis: Nos autem quærimus causas, quæ in homine sunt, & quæ possunt tolli & emendari: ideo alias quæremus causas obscuritatis, ut à contrario inde colligantur regulæ, ad scripturas perspicuè rectéq; intelligendas.
units.tr: Moreover, since this cause is outside man and unchangeable, while we are seeking causes that lie in man and that can be removed and corrected, we will therefore seek other causes of obscurity, so that from their opposites rules may be drawn for understanding Scripture clearly and rightly.

units.la: Prima igitur causa, est cæcitas naturalis, qua nostrapte natura, ad ea quæ Dei sunt in-telligenda, ineptissimi sumus. 1.Cor.2.{e}Ani-malis homo non percipit ea quæ Dei sunt. Stultitia enim sunt illi: nec potest percipere: quia spiritualiter diiudicantur. Etsi enim Sol splendidissimè luceat: si tamen cæcus sis, intueri illius lucem minimè possis.
units.tr: The first cause, then, is natural blindness, by which we are, by our very nature, most unfit to understand the things of God. 1 Cor. 2: "The natural man does not receive the things of God; for they are foolishness to him, nor can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned." For although the sun shines most brightly, if you are blind you can by no means look upon its light.

units.la: Hinc igitur haurimus à contrario regu-lam ad scripturas intelligendum necessa-riam. Quænam hæc est? Preces, quibus peta-mus à Deo Spiritum suum sanctum, quo mentes nostras illuminet ad veram scriptu-rarum intelligentiam. Nam Spiritu sancto Dei cum primis opus est ad verbum Dei intelligendum. Hoc docet Christus, cùm Iohan.20. dat Spiritum Apostolis, vt intelligerent scripturas. Confirmat Apostolus 1. Corinth.2. Nos autem Spiritum Christi accepimus, vt sciamus quæ à Deo nobis donata sunt. Confirmat ratio. 2.Pet.1. Omnis scriptura non est propria interpretationis. Non enim libidine hominis allata est olim prophetia sed acti à Spiritu sancto locuti sunt sancti Dei homines. Ergo eodem spiritu opus est ad eas intelligendas. Qui sine spiritu humano est, non potest quæ homo loquitur, percipere, vt bos,&c. Sic qui sine spiritu Dei. Spiritus autem Dei inspiratur precibus, Luc.11. Quis ex vobis pater, à quo si filius petierit panem, vnum lapidem dabit illi? Si igitur vos, cùm sitis mali, nostris bona dona dare filiis vestris: quanto magis pater cœlestis dabit spiritum bonum petentibus ab ipso? Sic Iac.1. Si quis indiget sapientia, postulet à Deo. Est autem hoc perpetuo agendum, cùm accedimus ad studium sacrarum Literarum, aut ad lectionem, & ad conciones, & dicendum cum Dauide Psal.18. Da mihi intellestum, vt discam mandata tua. Item, Reuela oculos meos, vt videam mirabilia de lege tua.
units.tr: From this, then, we draw by contrast the rule necessary for understanding Scripture. What is this? Prayers, by which we ask God for his Holy Spirit, by whom he may illuminate our minds to a true understanding of the Scriptures. For above all we need the Holy Spirit of God to understand the Word of God. Christ teaches this when, in John 20, he gives the Spirit to the Apostles so that they might understand the Scriptures. The Apostle confirms it in 1 Corinthians 2: "But we have received the Spirit of Christ, that we may know the things that have been given to us by God." Reason confirms it. 2 Peter 1: "No prophecy of Scripture is of private interpretation; for prophecy never came by the will of man, but holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit." Therefore the same Spirit is needed to understand them. He who does not have the human spirit cannot perceive what a man says, like an ox, etc. So too for one without the Spirit of God. The Spirit of God is breathed into us by prayers, Luke 11: "Which of you fathers, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the good Spirit to those who ask him?" So too James 1: "If anyone lacks wisdom, let him ask of God." This, moreover, must be done continually, whenever we approach the study of the sacred Letters, or reading, or sermons, and we should say with David, Psalm 118: "Give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments." Likewise: "Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law."

units.la: Secunda causa est, nostræ carnis prudentia ac sapientia, quam dum adferimus ad lectionem & studium scripturarum, minùs fimus idonei ad veram illarum intelligen-tiam assequendam, & eo magis a nobis abs-conditur cognitio sapientiæ Dei, quo plus adhibemus nostræ sapientiæ & prudentiæ. Hanc tradit Christus Matth. 11. Abscondi-sti hæc a sapientibus, & reuelasti parvulis. Et Apostolus confirmat addita etiam ratione 1.Corinth.3. Sapientia huius Mundi, stultitia est apud Deum. Et Rom.8. Prudentia carnis, inimicitia est adversus Deum. Hæc impedimento ipsis maximè Philosophis & sapientibus huius seculi, & quicunque inanem Philosophiam sectati sunt, vt multi Patres, & Sophistæ omnes. Dum enim ea quæ Deus tradidit in scripturis spiritu suo diuino, voluerunt ipsi sua humana sapientia metiri & intelligere: in maximos lapsi sunt errores: vt non immeritò dixerit Tertullianus: Philosophos patres esse hæreticorum.
units.tr: The second cause is the prudence and wisdom of our flesh, which, when we bring it to the reading and study of Scripture, makes us less fit to attain a true understanding of it; and the more we apply our own wisdom and prudence, the more the knowledge of God's wisdom is hidden from us. Christ hands this down in Matthew 11: "You have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to little children." And the Apostle confirms it, adding also a reason, in 1 Corinthians 3: "The wisdom of this world is foolishness before God." And Romans 8: "The prudence of the flesh is enmity against God." This is an impediment above all to the philosophers and the wise of this age, and to all who have pursued vain philosophy, such as many of the Fathers and all the Sophists. For while they wished to measure and understand with their own human wisdom the things that God has delivered in Scripture by his divine Spirit, they fell into very great errors; so Tertullian rightly said: "The philosophers are the fathers of heretics."

units.la: {2}Ergo ad veram scripturarum intelligen-tiam consequendam, secunda hæc esto regula: vt scilicet, cum ad illas accedimus, omnitas. nostræ humanæ prudentiæ & ratiocinationibus renunciemus, & ceu infantes simpliciter subiiciamus nos Deo in scripturis nos docenti, captiuantes omnem cogitationem nostram in obsequium Christi.
units.tr: Therefore, to attain a true understanding of Scripture, let this be the second rule: namely, that when we approach it, we renounce all of our human prudence and reasonings, and, like infants, simply submit ourselves to God who teaches us in Scripture, taking every thought captive to the obedience of Christ.

units.la: Hanc docet Apostolus 1.Corinth.3. Si quis vult inter vos sapiens esse, stultus fiat, vt sit sapiens. Psalm.1. Beatus vir, qui non ambulauit in consilio impiorum, &c. sed in lege Domini tota eius voluntas, mens, oblectatio, [illegible, ~6 letters]. QuanQuantum prosit hæc consecratio mentis in obsequium CHRISTI, valedicto omni nostræ humanæ sapientiæ: docet Apostolus suo exemplo, Actor.9. Domine quid me vis facere? Item simili pueri, qui se totum tradit erudiendum Magistro excellenti.
units.tr: The Apostle teaches this in 1 Corinthians 3: "If anyone among you wishes to be wise, let him become foolish, that he may be wise." Psalm 1: "Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, etc., but whose will, mind and delight are in the law of the Lord." How much this consecration of the mind to the obedience of Christ profits, once all human wisdom has been bid farewell, the Apostle teaches by his own example, Acts 9: "Lord, what do you want me to do?" Likewise by the similar case of a child, who gives himself wholly to be taught by an excellent teacher.

units.la: Tertia causa obscuritatis, est præiudicium, quod ad illarum lectionem adfertur. Multi enim præter naturalem cæcitatem, præter propriam carnis sapientiam, adfe-runt etiam præiudicium, ex hominum impiorum, ut Papistarum & aliorum hæreticorum, aut etiam hominum piorum, sed multis in rebus hallucinatorum, doctrinis & consiliis conceptum, ad interpretationem scripturarum. Hoc decepti atque corrupti, scripturarum intelligentiam non aflequuntur, sed corrupti corrumpunt. Hoc vitium indicat Christus Matth.15.[?] cùm docet, Pharisæos sua traditione, de adferendis muneribus ad templum, corrupisse, & ita transgredi docuisse præceptum Dei de honorandis parentibus.
units.tr: The third cause of obscurity is the prejudice that is brought to their reading. For many, besides natural blindness and their own fleshly wisdom, also bring to the interpretation of Scripture a prejudice, conceived from the doctrines and counsels of ungodly men, such as the Papists and other heretics, or even from pious men who, however, have erred in many things. Deceived and corrupted by this, they do not attain an understanding of Scripture, but being corrupted they corrupt. Christ indicates this vice in Matthew 15, when he teaches that the Pharisees, by their tradition about bringing gifts to the temple, had corrupted and so taught the transgression of God's command to honor parents.

units.la: Atque hæc est non postrema causa, cur Hæretici, Papistæ & sectarij homines non intelligant scripturas, etiamsi diligenter legant. Quamobrem? Quia sua adferunt præiudicia & dogmata impia, ut secundum hæc scripturas interpretentur, non autem ad illas hæc examinent. Ita inter nostros, qui ita sunt suis addicti præceptoribus, ut hoc semel statuerint, illos non potuisse errare, & quicquid scripserint, optimè fuisse dictum : ij hoc praeiudicio occupati, verita-tem scripturarum assequi non possunt.
units.tr: And this is not the least cause why heretics, Papists and sectarians do not understand Scripture, even if they read it diligently. Why? Because they bring their own prejudices and impious dogmas, so that they interpret Scripture according to these, rather than examining these by Scripture. So too among our own people, who are so devoted to their teachers that they have once for all decided that those men could not have erred, and that whatever they wrote was altogether well said: these, occupied with this prejudice, cannot attain the truth of Scripture.

units.la: Tertia igitur regula,ad veram scripturarum intelligentiam, hac est : Ut scilicet ad illarum studium, sine ullo praeiudicio, vel e nostro capite, vel ex aliorum doctrinis concepto, accedamus : sed animo candido, puro, discendique cupido. Hanc docuit Apostolus Col. 2. Videte ne quis vos decipiat per inanem philosophiam secundum traditionem. Psalm.i. Beatus, qui non abiit in consilium impiorum, & in via peccatorum non stetit, & in Cathedra derisorum non sedit, &c. hoc est, qui neglectis omnibus impiorum hominum consiliis & doctrinis, ad solum Dei verbum adiicit animum, & in eo solo meditatur die ac nocte. Matth.16. Cavete a fermento Pharisaeorum. Ierem.23. Quid tritico cum paleis ?
units.tr: Therefore the third rule for a true understanding of Scripture is this: namely, that we approach its study without any prejudice, whether conceived from our own head or from the doctrines of others, but with a sincere, pure mind, eager to learn. The Apostle taught this in Colossians 2: "Take heed lest anyone deceive you through vain philosophy according to the tradition of men." Psalm 1: "Blessed is he who has not gone to the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of scoffers, etc.," that is, he who, having set aside all the counsels and doctrines of ungodly men, applies his mind to the Word of God alone, and meditates on it alone day and night. Matthew 16: "Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees." Jeremiah 23: "What has the chaff to do with the wheat?"

units.la: Quarta causa, est impietas & impœnitentia, hoc est, perseverantia in peccatis, sine ulla vera conversione ad Dominum. Hac fit, ut in iis impœnitentibus hominibus, locum habere nequeat vera sapientia, & spiritus Christi, qui illuminet ad intelligendum scripturas.
units.tr: The fourth cause is impiety and impenitence, that is, perseverance in sins without any true conversion to the Lord. From this it happens that in impenitent people true wisdom and the Spirit of Christ, who enlightens them to understand the Scriptures, cannot take hold.

units.la: Hanc docet Hos.14. Plana sunt via Domini, iusti ambulabunt per eas, impij aute corruent. 2. Timoth.3. primum ait, futuros homines pra-vos[?], impœnitentes : deinde, seductores, qui proficiant in peius, errantes, &c. quasi dicat, quae est causa, cur non proficiant in melius, in scripturis, & in pietate, sed in peius, errantes, & in errorem inducentes? Quia sunt praui homines, nempe pleni peccatis, & impoenitentes: Sic 2.Corinth.3. Ideo dixit, Velamen manere super cor Iudaeorum, quia cor habent auersum à Domino. Sic Sap. 1. In malevolam animam, non introibit sapientia, nec in corpore peccatis obnoxio habitabit. Ioh. 3. Omnis qui male agit, odit lucem.
units.tr: Hosea 14 teaches this: "The ways of the Lord are plain; the just will walk in them, but the wicked will fall." 2 Timothy 3 first says that there will be wicked men, impenitent; then seducers, who make progress for the worse, erring and so on. As if to say: what is the cause why they do not make progress for the better, in the Scriptures and in piety, but for the worse, erring and leading others into error? It is because they are wicked men, namely full of sins and impenitent. So 2 Corinthians 3: "For this reason he said that the veil remains over the heart of the Jews, because they have their heart turned away from the Lord." So Wisdom 1: "Wisdom will not enter into a malevolent soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sin." John 3: "Everyone who does evil hates the light."

units.la: Ergo cùm accedemus ad scripturas legendas & audiendas: accedamus cum vera animi à peccatis resipiscentia, cordeque ad Deum conuerso, detestati priorem vitam sceleribus plenam, & animo proficiendi in pietate.
units.tr: Therefore, when we come to read and hear the Scriptures, let us come with a true repentance of soul from sins, and with the heart converted to God, detesting our former life, full of crimes, and with a desire to make progress in piety.

units.la: Hanc tradit Apostolus 2.Corinth.3. Cùm autem conuersum fuerit (cor Israëlis) ad Dominum auferetur velamen. Sic Christus Marc. 1. primum ait, Poenitentiam agite: Deinde, Et credite Euangelio: quasi dicat, Non potestis credere Euangelio, illudque intelligere, nisi poenitentiam agatis. Hof. 14. Plana sunt viae Domini, & iusti ambulabunt in eis: impij autem corruent in eis. Psalm. 1. Beatus, qui in via peccatorum non stetit, sed in lege Domini meditatur die ac nocte: Quasi dicat, Necesse prius est, ut recedas à peccatis, si velis in scripturis proficere.
units.tr: The Apostle hands this down in 2 Corinthians 3: "But when (the heart of Israel) shall be turned to the Lord, the veil will be taken away." So Christ in Mark 1 first says, "Repent," then, "And believe the Gospel," as if to say: you cannot believe the Gospel and understand it unless you repent. Hosea 14: "The ways of the Lord are plain, and the just will walk in them; but the wicked will fall in them." Psalm 1: "Blessed is the one who has not stood in the way of sinners, but meditates on the law of the Lord day and night." As if to say: it is necessary first that you turn away from sins, if you wish to make progress in the Scriptures.

units.la: Quinta causa est, quòd multi accedunt ad studium sacrarum Literarum sine reuerentia, sineque amore veritatis & sacrarum Literarum, ex frigida potius consuetudine, quàm ex amore veritatis ac voluntatis diuinæ cognoscendæ. Hinc fit, ut non possint eam allequi[?].
units.tr: The fifth cause is that many approach the study of the sacred Letters without reverence, and without love of the truth and of the sacred Letters, out of a cold custom rather than out of love for knowing the truth and the divine will. Hence it happens that they cannot attain it.

units.la: Hanc docet 2. Thessal.2. Et quia non fusce-perunt dilectionem veritatis, ut salui fierent: ideo misit illis Deus efficacitatem deceptionis, ut credant mendacio: Quasi dicat, Tantum abest, ut qui non diligit veritatem, possit in ea proficere, ut potius contra accepturus sit spiritum seductionis, ut credat mendaciis, & in illis proficiat.
units.tr: 2 Thessalonians 2 teaches this: "And because they did not receive the love of the truth, that they might be saved, therefore God sends them a strong delusion, that they should believe a lie." As if to say: far from being able to make progress in the truth, one who does not love the truth is rather about to receive a spirit of seduction, so that he believes lies and makes progress in them.

units.la: Et hæc sequitur ex superiore, hoc est, ex impœnitentia Iohan.3. Omnis qui male agit, odit lucem, & non venit ad lucem, ne arguantur opera eius.
units.tr: This also follows from the previous point, that is, from impenitence. John 3: "Everyone who does evil hates the light, and does not come to the light, lest his works be reproved."

units.la: Regula igitur hæc esto. Vt amemus scriptu-ras, & ad earum studium accedamus cum a-more desiderioq; veritatis agnoscendæ, & retinendæ.
units.tr: Let this, therefore, be the rule: that we love the Scriptures, and approach their study with love and desire to recognize and retain the truth.

units.la: Hanc docet Salomon Proverb. 4. Dilige sapientiam, & conseruabit te. Psal.1. Beatus, cuius voluntas in lege Domini.
units.tr: Solomon teaches this in Proverbs 4: "Love wisdom, and it will keep you." Psalm 1: "Blessed is the one whose delight is in the law of the Lord."

units.la: Sexta causa est, quòd multi accedunt ad lectionem sacratum[?] Literarum, cum desiderio quidem illas intelligendi: verùm non animo seruandi & proficiendi in pietate, seu non in hunc finem, ut faciant voluntatem Dei, sed tantùm ut sciant, & ex illa aut gloriam aut quæstum sibi parent: aliqui etiam, ut oppugnent veritatem, ut hæretici. Hi etiam non possunt proficere in cognitione scripturarum.
units.tr: The sixth cause is that many approach the reading of the sacred Letters with a desire indeed to understand them, but not with the intention of keeping and making progress in piety, or not to this end, that they may do the will of God, but only that they may know, and from it gain for themselves either glory or profit; some also, in order to attack the truth, like heretics. These too cannot make progress in the knowledge of the Scriptures.

units.la: Hanc docet Christus Iohan.7. Si quis vo[?]uerit facere voluntatem Patris mei, cognoscat de doctrina mea: Quasi dicat a contrario, cui non est animus facere voluntatem Patris, quae est credere in Christum, & mandata eius seruare: is non poterit cognoscere meam doctrinam.
units.tr: Christ teaches this in John 7: "If anyone wishes to do the will of my Father, he shall know concerning my teaching." As if to say by the contrary: he who has no mind to do the Father's will, which is to believe in Christ and keep his commandments, will not be able to know my teaching.

units.la: Ergo regula sexta hæc esto: ut ad scripturarum lectionem ac studium hoc animo accedamus, non tantum ut intelligamus, sed etiam ut cognitam Dei voluntatem faciamus. Hac docet Christus Ioh. 7. Si quis voluerit facere voluntatem Patris mei, &c. Finis enim scripturæ non est, ut tantum sciamus, sed ut faciamus, ut scilicet credamus in Christum, deinde ut sancte viuamus. Tit. 2. Tu vero loquere quæ decent sanam doctrinam, Apparuit enim gratia salutifera Dei, &c. erudiens nos, ut abnegata impietate & mundanis cupiditatibus, sobrie, iuste, ac pie viuamus, &c. Sobrie, quoad nos: iuste, quoad proximum: pie, quoad Deum.
units.tr: Therefore let this be the sixth rule: that we approach the reading and study of the Scriptures with this mind, not only that we may understand, but also that we may do the known will of God. Christ teaches this in John 7: "If anyone wishes to do the will of my Father, etc." For the end of Scripture is not only that we may know, but that we may do, namely that we believe in Christ and then live holily. Titus 2: "But you, speak the things that befit sound doctrine. For the saving grace of God has appeared, etc., teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly desires, we should live soberly, justly, and piously, etc." Soberly, with regard to ourselves; justly, with regard to our neighbour; piously, with regard to God.

units.la: Hæ omnes regulæ respiciunt qualitatem legentis, seu illius, qui ad studium sacrarum Literarum accedit: qualem scilicet requirant scripturæ auditore ac studiosum. Summa est: ut accedamus ad studium scripturarum, primum hac fide, quod sumus Electi Dei, ac proinde quod velit scripturas patefacere. Secundo, accedamus mente per Spiritum sanctum illuminata, id quod obtinetur precibus. Tertio, accedamus valedicto nostræ sapientiæ humanæ, mente in obsequiū Christi captiuata. Quarto, accedamus animo, nullo praeiudicio ex doctrinis humanis contaminato. Quinto, accedamus toto corde ad Christum conuerso, cum vera poenitentia, & vera pietate, bonaq; conscientia. Sexto, accedamus animo, amore scripturarum, desiderioque veritatis cognoscendae, affecto & accenso. Postremo, non in hunc finem, vt tantum sciamus voluntatem Dei, sed vt illam faciamus.
units.tr: All these rules concern the quality of the reader, or of the one who comes to the study of the sacred Letters: namely, the kind of hearer and student the Scriptures require.
