The sum is this: that we approach the study of the Scriptures, first, with this faith, that we are the elect of God, and therefore that he is willing to open the Scriptures to us. Second, that we come with a mind enlightened by the Holy Spirit, which is obtained by prayers. Third, that we come having bid farewell to our human wisdom, with our mind taken captive to the obedience of Christ. Fourth, that we come with a mind contaminated by no prejudice from human doctrines. Fifth, that we come with the whole heart converted to Christ, with true repentance, true piety, and a good conscience. Sixth, that we come with a mind kindled and inflamed with love of the Scriptures and desire to know the truth. Lastly, that we come not to this end, that we may only know the will of God, but that we may do it.

units.la: CAPVT SECVNDVM.
units.tr: CHAPTER TWO.

units.la: NVNC dicendum est de regulis, quae in ipsa lectione seruandae sunt: ostensis prius aliis causis, cur scripturae videantur obscurae, & in eis non proficiatur.
units.tr: NOW we must speak of the rules which are to be observed in the reading itself, having first set out the other causes why the Scriptures seem obscure and why no progress is made in them.

units.la: Causa prima in hoc secundo genere est negle-ctus & intermissio lectionis sacrarum Scri-pturarum, hoc est, quòd aut nunquam, aut raro legimus scripturas: & si legere incipimus, non continuamus. Inde fit, vt cum postea vel audimus, vel legimus scripturas, obscurae & ceu res inauditae nobis videantur. Hanc indicat Christus, cùm subinde Iudaeis exprobrat, quòd non legerent scripturas.
units.tr: The first cause in this second class is neglect and interruption of the reading of the Holy Scriptures, that is, that we either never or rarely read the Scriptures, and if we begin to read, we do not continue. From this it happens that when afterwards we either hear or read the Scriptures, they seem obscure to us and as if they were unheard-of things. Christ points to this when he often reproaches the Jews that they did not read the Scriptures.

units.la: Idem contingit in aliis linguis & scientiis. Si non quotidie & diligenter legas & audias autores linguae Latinae, quomodo poteris eam allequi? Obscura tibi semper videbitur, & nil in ea proficies. Ita si non frequenter le-gas aut audias Aristotelem, si postea aliquando contingat, vt audias vel legas, semper tibi obscurus visus fuerit: Ita nunquam in eius doctrina proficies. Contrà verò, si quotidie in eo legas, tandem nihil in eius libris fuerit tam obscurum, quod tu non facile percipias. Idem nobis contingit in S.Literis.
units.tr: The same happens in other languages and sciences. If you do not read and hear the authors of the Latin language daily and diligently, how will you be able to speak it? It will always seem obscure to you, and you will make no progress in it. So too, if you do not read or hear Aristotle frequently, and afterwards it happens at some time that you hear or read him, he will always have seemed obscure to you; thus you will never make progress in his teaching. On the contrary, if you read him every day, in the end there will be nothing in his books so obscure that you do not readily grasp it. The same happens to us in the Sacred Writings.

units.la: Prima igitur regula in hoc altero genere est: ut assiduè, diligenter & sine intermissione legamus scripturas, easq; diurna & nocturna versemus manu. Nam licet non statim omnia intelligamus, vel phrases, vel res ipsas: non ideo tamen desperandum, illarumve lectio est intermittenda, sed continuanda. Hac enim ratione tandem fiet, Deo opem ferente, ut nobis assuefactis scripturarum phrasibus, historiis, doctrinis, nihil in eis futurum sit obscurum.
units.tr: The first rule, therefore, in this second class is: that we read the Scriptures constantly, diligently and without interruption, and that we turn them over by day and by night. For although we do not at once understand everything, whether the phrases or the things themselves, we must not on that account despair, nor should we give up reading them, but continue. For in this way it will at last come about, God lending his aid, that once we have become accustomed to the phrases, histories and doctrines of Scripture, nothing in them will remain obscure.

units.la: Hanc regulam tradit Spiritus sanctus ubique, cùm subinde mandat, ut audiamus scri-pturas: Audite (inquiens) verbum Domini. Hac de causa Deuter.6 iubet, ut legem Domi-nihabeant scriptam etiam in liminibus & ostiis domus, gestent ante oculos, in brachiis, &c. ut sci-licet quotidie & omni momento in ea lege-rent.
units.tr: The Holy Spirit everywhere lays down this rule, when he repeatedly commands us to hear the Scriptures: Hear, he says, the word of the Lord. For this reason Deuteronomy 6 orders that they should have the law of the Lord written also on the doorposts and gates of the house, and carry it before their eyes, on their arms, etc. that is, that they might read it every day and at every moment.

units.la: Josuæ 1. Non recedat volumen legis ab ore tuo, sed meditaris in eo die ac nocte. Psalm.1.Beatus, qui in lege Domini meditatur die ac nocte. Prouerb.2. Si sapientiam innocaveris[?], & inclu-naveris cor tuum prudentia: si quaesieris eam, quasi pecuniam, & sicut thesauros effoderis illam: tunc intelliges timorem Domini, & scien-tiam Dei invenies. Sapient.6. Si indagaueris scientiam ut aurum, facile assequeris eam. Ioh. 5. Scrutamini scripturas, &c. 1. Timoth. 4. Dum venio, attende lectioni & doctrinae. Apostolus suo exemplo idem confirmat 2. Timoth. 4. τὸν φιλόνλω οὐ ἀπέλιπον ἐν Τρωάδι παρὰ Κάρπῳ ἐρχόμενος φέρε, ἡ τὰ βιβλία, μάλιστα τὰς μεμβράνας. Romae erat captiuus, & solicitus erat de scriptis & Bibliis.
units.tr: Joshua 1: Let not the book of the law depart out of your mouth, but meditate on it day and night. Psalm 1: Blessed is he who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night. Proverbs 2: If you call out for wisdom, and incline your heart to understanding; if you seek her as silver, and search for her as for hidden treasures: then you will understand the fear of the Lord, and find the knowledge of God. Wisdom 6: If you search for wisdom as for gold, you will easily attain it. John 5: Search the Scriptures, etc. 1 Timothy 4: Until I come, give attention to reading and teaching. The Apostle confirms the same by his own example, 2 Timothy 4: The cloak which I left at Troas with Carpus, when you come, bring, and the books, especially the parchments. He was a prisoner at Rome, and was anxious about the writings and the Bibles.

units.la: Debet igitur quisque, etiam aliis rebus occupatus, aliquot horas singulis diebus suffurari, quibus duo saltem capita, sine in-termissione in scripturis legat, idque attente & praemissis precibus: Vnum in Nouo Te-stamento, mane si possit: & alterum in veteri, antequam eat cubitum. Ac licet (vt an-te dixi) non omnia mox intelligat: non id-eo tamen hanc intermittat lectionem. Nam quod hodie non potuisti percipere, cras af-sequeris: quia scriptura seipsam aperit & ex-plicat illis, quorum manibus quotidie versa-tur: Et Deus reuelat suo tempore, quae ante simpliciter credidimus. Exemplum in Ma-ria virgine, & Apostolis: item in Eunucho Actor. 8.
units.tr: Therefore everyone, even when occupied with other things, ought to snatch some hours each day, in which he may read at least two chapters of the Scriptures without interruption, and this attentively and after prayers first offered: one in the New Testament, in the morning if he can; and another in the Old, before he goes to bed. And although (as I said before) he does not at once understand everything, he must not on that account give up this reading. For what you could not grasp today, you will attain tomorrow; because Scripture opens and explains itself to those whose hands turn it over daily; and God reveals in his own time what we formerly believed simply. An example is in the Virgin Mary and the Apostles, and likewise in the eunuch, Acts 8.

units.la: Secunda causa, quód multi, etsi legant Bi-blia, tamen quia verborum significata & phrases, rationesque dicendi scripturarum ignorant: idcirco ipsas etiam scripturas non intelligunt, & obscurissimae illis videntur. Ut sunt permulti, qui nouunt quidem lege-re,& legunt vel Latinè, vel Graecè, aut etiam Hebraicè: interim quae legunt, non intelli-gunt: gunt: idque propterea quòd verborum significata, figuras locutionum, phrasiumque proprietates ignorent.
units.tr: The second cause is that many, although they read the Bible, nevertheless, because they are ignorant of the meanings of words and the phrases and modes of speaking of the Scriptures, therefore do not understand the Scriptures themselves, and they seem most obscure to them. There are very many who indeed know how to read, and read either in Latin, or in Greek, or even in Hebrew, yet they do not understand what they read, and this precisely because they are ignorant of the meanings of words, the figures of speech and the proper usages of expressions.

units.la: Hanc ignorantiam reprehendit Christus saepe in Apostolis, vt Matth.16. quòd non intellexerint quid sit fermentum Pharisaorum: vt Luc. 22. quòd ignorent, quid velit, cum ait, Emat gladium: gladium scilicet Spiritus, fortitudinem animi, quia periculum imminebat: vt Iohan. 11. quid nomine dormitionis Lazari: vt Iohan. 4. quid nomine cibi: vt Iohan. vltimo, quòd nescierint distinguere inter affirmatiuam & interrogatiuam locutionem: sì eum volo manere donec veniam, quid ad te? Arguitur ergo in omnibus ignoratio Grammaticæ.
units.tr: Christ often rebukes this ignorance in the Apostles: as in Matthew 16, that they did not understand what the leaven of the Pharisees was; as in Luke 22, that they did not know what he meant when he said, "Let him buy a sword" — namely, the sword of the Spirit, fortitude of mind, since danger was at hand; as in John 11, what was meant by the sleep of Lazarus; as in John 4, what was meant by the food; as in the last chapter of John, that they did not distinguish between an affirmative and an interrogative expression: "If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you?" In all these, therefore, the ignorance of grammar is rebuked.

units.la: Regula igitur necessaria est, vt qui accedunt ad studium sacrarum Scripturarum, afferant cognitionem eius linguæ, in qua lecturi sunt Biblia, & dicendi modos obseruent atque discant. Nam cùm verba sint vasa rerum, & earum quæ in animo sunt passionum notæ: qui possis mysteria pietatis in Bibliis contenta, intelligentia consequi, nisi verborum teneas & locutionum significationes? Hac de causa Dominus non tantùm iubet vt audiamus & legamus: sed etiam vt intelligamus: cum ait per Prophetas, Audite & intelligite. Vt verò ipse intelligeretur, Hebraico populo locutus est Hebraicè per Prophetas: Græcis, Græcè per Apostolos.
units.tr: A necessary rule, therefore, is that those who come to the study of the Holy Scriptures should bring a knowledge of the language in which they are going to read the Bible, and should observe and learn its modes of speaking. For since words are the vessels of things, and the signs of the passions that are in the mind, how could you attain understanding of the mysteries of godliness contained in the Bible, unless you hold the meanings of words and expressions? For this reason the Lord not only commands that we hear and read, but also that we understand, when he says through the Prophets, Hear and understand. And that he might himself be understood, he spoke in Hebrew to the Hebrew people through the Prophets, and in Greek to the Greeks through the Apostles.

units.la: Hanc regulam confirmat Apostolus 1.
units.tr: The Apostle confirms this rule

units.la: Cor. 14. cùm prohibet vti linguis ignotis in Ecclesia, nisi addatur[?] explicatio per notiorem linguam. Hanc ob causam plurimum profue-rit ad veram scripturarum cognitionem, si quis det operam illis duabus linguis, quibus locutus est Spiritus sanctus: Hebraicæ, propter vetus: Græcæ, propter nouum Testamentum. Melius enim significata verborum, & proprietates locutionum in quavis lingua percipiuntur ab illis, qui eam tenent linguam. Et exempla nostri temporis, vt de veteribus taceamus, id aperte demonstrant. Cur nostro tempore tam bene intellecta & explicata Biblia, quàm vnquam post tempora Apostolorum?
units.tr: in 1 Corinthians 14, when he forbids the use of unknown tongues in the Church, unless an explanation is added in a more familiar language. For this reason it will be of great profit to the true knowledge of the Scriptures if anyone devotes effort to those two languages in which the Holy Spirit spoke: Hebrew, on account of the Old Testament; Greek, on account of the New Testament. For the meanings of words and the proper usages of expressions in any language are better perceived by those who hold that language. And the examples of our own time, to say nothing of the ancients, clearly demonstrate this. Why in our time are the Bibles so well understood and explained, as never since the times of the Apostles?

units.la: Præter alias causas hæc est non postrema, quia Dominus multos donauit perfecta v-triusq; linguæ cognitione. Proinde consul-tissimum[?] est, vt adolescentes in cognitione harum linguarum instituantur diligenter.
units.tr: Among other causes this is not the least, because the Lord has granted to many a perfect knowledge of both languages. Therefore it is most advisable that young people be carefully trained in the knowledge of these languages.

units.la: Si qui tamen sunt, vt quamplurimi sunt, qui neutram teneant linguam: optimas ac-cipiant versiones, siue Latinas, vt qui tenent Latinam: siue vulgares, vt qui suam tantum vernaculam intelligunt linguam. Atque, vt de Latinis dicam versionibus: quod ad nouum Testamentum attinet, omnibus aliis præfero versionem egregij & excellentis viri, fratrisque obseruandi, Theodori Bezæ. Quod ad vetus, Tigurinam, quæ vna cum versione vulgata, & annotationibus Vatabli, impressa olim etiam fuit ab honorandæ memoriæ Roberto Stephano. His, qui linguas non tenent, consulo, vt hæc emant & legant. Nulla enim meliora purioraq;,& ea re vtilia[?] raiis reperiuntur,quod sciam,hoc tempore.
units.tr: If there are some, as there are very many, who hold neither language, let them take the best translations, either Latin ones, for those who hold Latin, or vernacular ones, for those who understand only their own mother tongue. And, to speak of the Latin translations: as far as the New Testament is concerned, I prefer to all others the version of that distinguished and excellent man and brother worthy of honour, Theodore Beza. As for the Old, the Tigurine version, which was once printed together with the Vulgate version and the annotations of Vatablus, by the late Robert Estienne, of honoured memory. I advise those who do not know the languages to buy and read these. For, so far as I know, no better or purer ones, and therefore none more useful, are to be found at this time.

units.la: Atque hæc esto generalis regula, aduersus obscuritate, quæ in verbis sita est. Non enim omnes hic prosequor: de illis alij fusiùs : Et Augustinus etiam scripsit in lib. de doctrina Christiana 2.3[?]. In secundo docet, quàm vtilis sit cognitio linguarum Hebraicæ & Græcæ. In tertio tradit regulas discernendi figuratas, à propriis: ac docet, nihil figuratè alicubi dictum fuisse in scripturis, quod alibi in eisdem scripturis non possit per proprias explicari locutiones.
units.tr: And let this be the general rule against the obscurity which lies in words. I do not pursue all of these here; others have treated them at greater length. Augustine too wrote in his book On Christian Doctrine, book 2 and 3[?]. In the second he teaches how useful the knowledge of the Hebrew and Greek languages is. In the third he gives rules for distinguishing figurative from proper expressions, and teaches that nothing is said figuratively anywhere in the Scriptures which cannot elsewhere in the same Scriptures be explained by proper expressions.

units.la: Quod verò attinet ad obscuritatem, quæ in rebus ipsis sita esse videtur: aliæ sunt huius causæ, & ideo aliæ etiam aduersus hanc regulæ tradendæ sunt.
units.tr: As for the obscurity which seems to lie in the things themselves, the causes of this are different, and therefore different remedies must also be given against this kind of obscurity.

units.la: Tertia igitur causa, cur scripturæ videantur obscuræ, nec queat sincerè intelligi: est, quoniam non tenetur scopus totius scripturæ sacræ, in quem scilicet tam Prophetæ, quàm Apostoli, tam vetus, quàm Nouum collimat Testamentum. Hic scopus est Christus. Ioh.5. Scrutamini scripturas: quia illæ (omnes) testificantur de me (tanquam de scopo omnium illarum.) Act.10. Huic testimonium perhibent omnes Prophetæ. Rom.17. Finis legis est Christus. Matth.17. Transfiguratus fuit in medio Mosis & Eliæ, vt ille, in quem & Lex & Prophetæ semper respexerunt.
units.tr: Third, then, the reason why the Scriptures seem obscure and cannot be understood sincerely is this: the scope of all Holy Scripture is not held in view. This is the aim at which the Prophets and the Apostles alike, the Old Testament and the New, both aim. This scope is Christ. John 5: "Search the Scriptures, for they (all of them) bear witness to me" (as to the scope of all of them). Acts 10: "To him all the Prophets bear witness." Romans 17 (sic): "The end of the Law is Christ." Matthew 17: "He was transfigured in the midst of Moses and Elijah, as that one to whom both the Law and the Prophets always looked."

units.la: Cùm igitur Christus sit omnium scripturarum scopus, quomodo quis intelligere scripturas possit, qui Christum non agnoscat pro scopo utriusque Testamenti? Hanc ob causam Iudæi non intelligunt scripturas, vt ait Apostolus. 2 Cor.3. Sed velamen est super cor eorum, quia ignorant Christum, a quo auersa sunt illorum corda.
units.tr: Since Christ, therefore, is the scope of all the Scriptures, how can anyone understand the Scriptures who does not acknowledge Christ as the scope of both Testaments? For this reason the Jews do not understand the Scriptures, as the Apostle says: 2 Corinthians 3: "But a veil lies over their heart, because they do not know Christ, from whom their hearts are turned away."

units.la: Hac de causa Ariani, Seruetiani, &c. non possunt scripturas intelligere: quia ignorant Christum quis sit, verus scilicet Deus. Hac de causa Papistæ: quia eis absconditus est Christus, vt perfectus Seruator.
units.tr: For this reason the Arians, the Servetians, and so on, cannot understand the Scriptures, because they do not know who Christ is, namely true God. For this reason the Papists cannot: because Christ, as the perfect Saviour, is hidden from them.

units.la: Regula igitur est, vt sciamus Christum illum esse, in quem omnes resoluendæ sunt scripturæ. Lex pædagogus est ad Christum, Galat 3. Ideo enim ipsa conuincit nos peccati, & reos esse mortis ostendit, vt ducat ad Christum. Euangelium nil prædicat, nisi Christi. 1.Cor.2. Nihil iudicaui me scire, inter vos, nisi Iesum Christum, & hunc crucifixum.
units.tr: The rule, therefore, is that we must know that Christ is the one into whom all the Scriptures are to be resolved. "The Law is our schoolmaster to Christ," Galatians 3. For it convicts us of sin and shows us to be guilty of death, so that it may lead us to Christ. The Gospel proclaims nothing but Christ. 1 Corinthians 2: "I determined to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified."

units.la: Quarta causa: quod nescient distinguere inter se duas præcipuas partes totius scripturæ, hoc est, Legem & Euangelium, earumque officia: sed confundunt inter se, & miscent, cum sint discernendæ hæ partes.
units.tr: The fourth reason: they do not know how to distinguish between the two principal parts of the whole of Scripture, that is, the Law and the Gospel, and their offices; but they confuse and mix them together, when these parts ought to be distinguished.

units.la: In hac re plurimum peccabant Iudæi, tempore etiam Apostolorum: cùm legem proponebant tanquam Euangelij doctrinā. Hac eadem de causa, Papistæ non intelligũt scripturas: quia vbi Christus, officio fungens Mosis & legis, docet, opera ad salutem esse necessaria: ibi putant, Christum Euangelicam tradere doctrinam, de via nostrae salutis: Ut cùm ait Matth.19. Si vis ad vitam in-gredi serua mandata.
units.tr: The Jews, even in the time of the Apostles, sinned greatly in this matter, when they put forward the Law as the doctrine of the Gospel. For this same reason the Papists do not understand the Scriptures: where Christ, acting in the office of Moses and of the Law, teaches that works are necessary for salvation, there they think Christ is delivering the evangelical doctrine concerning the way of our salvation, as when he says in Matthew 19: "If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments."

units.la: Item cùm Apostolus Rom. 2. Non audi-teres legis, sed factores iustificantur apud Deum. Valde peccant Papistæ in legendis & explicandis scripturis, hanc ob causam, quòd nesciunt distinguere inter legem & Euangelium.
units.tr: Likewise, when the Apostle says in Romans 2: "It is not the hearers of the Law, but the doers, who are justified before God." The Papists greatly err in reading and explaining the Scriptures, for this reason: that they do not know how to distinguish between Law and Gospel.

units.la: Hanc causam indicat Apostolus ad Gal.1. cùm ait, Pseudoapostolos peruertisse Euangelium. Quomodo? doctrina legis, tanquam doctrina esset Euangelij.
units.tr: The Apostle indicates this cause in Galatians 1, when he says that the false apostles perverted the Gospel. How? By teaching the doctrine of the Law as if it were the doctrine of the Gospel.

units.la: Regula igitur quarta est seruanda, ut scilicet diligenter & probè retineamus & obseruemus in legendis scripturis, vbinam lex & vbi Euangelium loquatur: Ideo etiam 2. Timoth.2. air, Episcopum oportere esse ὀρθοτομοῦντα [?] τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας, id est, bene & rectè secantem & diuidentem.
units.tr: The fourth rule, therefore, is to be observed: namely, that we diligently and properly keep in mind and observe, in reading the Scriptures, where the Law speaks and where the Gospel speaks. Thus also 2 Timothy 2 says that the bishop must be "ὀρθοτομοῦντα [?] τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας," that is, cutting straight and rightly dividing the word of truth.

units.la: Quinta causa, ex quarta fluit, & est, quòd non teneant summam & finem doctrinæ legis, & doctrinæ Euangelij. Cùm hanc plerique omnes ignorent & in hanc tamen tota resoluatur scriptura: quî possunt sacram Scripturam intelligere? quî fieri aliter potest, quin videatur iis hominibus obscurissima, confusa, intricata? Hinc fit, ut vagentur per inanes stultas, & inutiles quæstiones.
units.tr: The fifth reason follows from the fourth, and it is that they do not hold the sum and the end of the doctrine of the Law and the doctrine of the Gospel. Since most people are ignorant of this, and yet the whole of Scripture is resolved into it, how can they understand Holy Scripture? How can it happen otherwise than that the Scripture seems to them most obscure, confused, and entangled? Hence it comes about that they wander into empty, foolish, and useless questions.

units.la: Hanc docet Apostolus, cùm loquitur de Pseudoapostolis, quòd neglecta sana doctrina, attendant fabulis, & inutilibus quæstio-nibus. 1.Tim.1.4.6 2.Tim.2. Tit.3.
units.tr: The Apostle teaches this when he speaks of the false apostles: that, neglecting sound doctrine, they attend to fables and useless questions. 1 Timothy 1:4, 6; 2 Timothy 2; Titus 3.

units.la: Tenenda est igitur summa doctrinæ le-gis & Euangelij, pro optima regula, ad intel-ligendam sacram Scripturam, pernecessaria.
units.tr: The sum of the doctrine of the Law and of the Gospel must therefore be held, as the best rule, most necessary for understanding Holy Scripture.

units.la: Summa autem legis in Decalogo conti-netur. Eius officium est, detegere peccata nostra, & nos reos esse mortis demonstrare.
units.tr: Now the sum of the Law is contained in the Decalogue. Its office is to uncover our sins and to demonstrate that we are guilty of death.

units.la: Rom.3. Per legem enim cognitio peccati. Finis, ut desperatos de nobis, adducat ad Christum seruatorem. Galat. 3. Lex pædagogus ad Christum.
units.tr: Romans 3: "For through the Law comes the knowledge of sin." Its purpose is that, having despaired of ourselves, we might be led to Christ the Saviour. Galatians 3: "The Law is our schoolmaster to Christ."

units.la: Summa Euangelij primum in symbolo habetur breuiter comprehensa, deinde in precatione Domini. Euangelij officium est docere 1.quid Deus Pater: quid Filius: quid Spiritus pro nobis effecerint. Et hæc est ceu fundamentum totius ædificij Christiani. 2. Docere, quam sibi Ecclesiam collegerit Christus: quæ, qualis, & vbi hæc sit:eam esse sanctam, ac proinde studendum sanctitati. 3. Quæ priuilegia quæ beneficia huic præstiterit, remissionem peccatorum, carnis resurrectionem, vitam æternam.
units.tr: The sum of the Gospel is first briefly comprehended in the Creed, and then in the Lord's Prayer. The office of the Gospel is to teach: (1) what God the Father, what the Son, and what the Spirit have accomplished for us; and this is as it were the foundation of the whole Christian edifice. (2) To teach what Church Christ has gathered for himself, what kind it is, and where it is; that it is holy, and therefore that we must strive after holiness. (3) What privileges and benefits he has bestowed upon it: forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, eternal life.

units.la: Finis, ut nos retineat in fide in Christum: in charitate erga proximum, inq; studio bonæ conscientiæ & puri cordis retinendi.
units.tr: The end is that it may keep us in faith in Christ, in love toward our neighbour, and in the zeal of keeping a good conscience and a pure heart.

units.la: Eodem spectat precatio Dominica. Hæc igitur doctrina est retinenda, & hac vtendum est in legendis scripturis, vt huc omnia dirigantur, si quis cupit illas intelligere, & in eis proficere.
units.tr: The Lord's Prayer also looks to this. This doctrine, therefore, is to be held, and we must use it in reading the Scriptures, so that everything is directed toward it, if anyone wishes to understand them and to make progress in them.

units.la: 1.Cor.1. Finis παραγγελίας[?], quam tradebat Timotheo, est charitas in corde puro, conscientia bona, fide non ficta.
units.tr: 1 Corinthians 1: "The end of the charge which he delivered to Timothy is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and faith unfeigned."

units.la: Tit.3. constituit hanc summam. 1. in fide, quòd sumus per Christum redempti, & salui gratis, sine operibus nostris. 2. in studio bonorum operum, vt Deus in nobis glorificetur: sicut alibi etiam ait.
units.tr: Titus 3 sets out this sum: (1) in faith, that we have been redeemed and saved through Christ, freely, without our works; (2) in the zeal for good works, so that God may be glorified in us, as he also says elsewhere.

units.la: Sexta causa, quia in scripturis interpretandis non vtuntur regulis praescriptis, à Spiritu S. in ipsis scripturis. Hæ duæ sunt.
units.tr: The sixth reason: because in interpreting the Scriptures they do not use the rules prescribed by the Holy Spirit in the Scriptures themselves. There are two of these.

units.la: Prima, Fidei ἀναλογία. Hanc tradit Apostolus Roman. 12. Siue[?] quis habet Prophetiam (hoc est, donum interpretandi scripturas) iuxta analogiam fidei, scilicet interpretetur. Sensus est, vt qui scripturas interpretatur, ita interpretetur, vt illa interpretatio conueniat cum fide, hoc est, cum summa doctrinæ fidei, quam quisque Christianus tenere omninò debet. Quæ hæc est? Ea, quam clarè & perspicuè, sine ambagibus, sine tropis, sine inuolucris habemus in symbolo explicatam. Item in Decalogo, quod ad præcepta tam de cultu Dei, quàm de ratione vitæ nostræ cum proximo gerendæ, attinet. Item in precatione Dominica, quantum attinet ad inuocationem. Hæc est enim summa doctrinæ, fideique Christianæ, quam Apostoli prædicabant, & iuxta quam singulos catechizabant, vt alias demonstraui.
units.tr: The first is the analogy of faith. The Apostle hands this down in Romans 12: "Whether anyone has prophecy (that is, the gift of interpreting the Scriptures), let him prophesy according to the analogy of faith." The sense is that whoever interprets the Scriptures should interpret them so that the interpretation agrees with faith, that is, with the sum of the doctrine of faith which every Christian must absolutely hold. What is this? That which we have explained clearly and plainly, without circumlocutions, without tropes, without veils, in the Creed. Likewise in the Decalogue, as far as concerns the precepts both about the worship of God and about the manner of conducting our life with our neighbour. Likewise in the Lord's Prayer, as far as concerns invocation. For this is the sum of the doctrine and faith of Christians, which the Apostles preached, and according to which they catechized individuals, as I have shown elsewhere.

units.la: Contra hanc peccant, qui scripturas interpretantur citra & contra hanc regulam, ita ut eorum interpretationes non sint cum hac doctrina consentaneæ. Exempla:ut
units.tr: Those who interpret the Scriptures apart from and against this rule sin, so that their interpretations are not consistent with this doctrine. Examples:

units.la: Qui verba Cœnæ, Hoc est corpus meum, ita interpretantur, ut dicant, corpus Christi ubique esse, eoque etiam in pane. Non est hæc interpretatio secundum analogiam fidei: pugnat enim cum primis fidei articulis: Christus est factus homo, & Ascendit in Cœlum: Et inde venturus est ad iudicandum vivos & mortuos.
units.tr: Those who interpret the words of the Supper, "This is my body," in such a way as to say that the body of Christ is everywhere, and therefore also in the bread. This is not an interpretation according to the analogy of faith: it fights against the first articles of faith: "Christ was made man, and ascended into heaven, and from there he will come to judge the living and the dead."

units.la: Qui verba Christi de peccatrice: Ideo di-co tibi, remittentur ei peccata multa, quoniam dilexit multum, ita interpretantur, ut doceant, propter meritum charitatis nostræ, peccata remitti: pugnat hoc cum analogia fidei: (Credo remissionem peccatorum. Si remissio est: igitur gratuita est, non propter merita nostra. Ille enim dicitur tibi remittere debitum, qui nulla à te accepta solutione, liberat te debito. Qui verò propter solutionem acceptam, aut propter opus à te præstitum solutionis loco, nomen expungit: non potest tibi debitum remisse[?]. Doctrina igitur, quam Papistæ è scripturis colligere conantur de meritis, propter quæ peccata remittuntur, pugnat ex diametro cum analogia fidei, de remissione peccatorum. Item pugnat cum alio articulo fidei, cum dicimus de Christo, passus & mortuus est pro nobis. Nam quòd postea sequitur, Credo remissionem peccatorum, vitam æter-nam, nam,&c. illatio est ex praecedentibus: quasi dicat, Credo in Iesum Christum, qui passus & mortuus est pro nobis. Credo igitur propter Christi passionem & mortem, remissionem peccatorum dari, & vitam aeternam. Quod si propter Christi passionem & mortem: non ergo propter nostram charitatem, aut merita. Quare omnino pugnat cum analogia fidei.
units.tr: Those who interpret the words of Christ concerning the sinful woman, "I say to you, her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much," in such a way as to teach that sins are forgiven on account of the merit of our love, fight against the analogy of faith: "I believe the forgiveness of sins." If it is forgiveness, then it is gratuitous, not on account of our merits. For he is said to forgive you a debt who frees you from the debt without any payment received from you. But he who strikes out the name on account of a payment received, or on account of a work performed by you in place of payment, cannot forgive you the debt. Therefore the doctrine which the Papists try to gather from the Scriptures about merits, on account of which sins are forgiven, fights diametrically against the analogy of faith concerning the forgiveness of sins. It also fights against another article of faith, when we say of Christ, "he suffered and died for us." For what follows, "I believe the forgiveness of sins, eternal life," and so on, is an inference from what precedes, as if one were to say: I believe in Jesus Christ, who suffered and died for us. I believe therefore that forgiveness of sins and eternal life are given on account of Christ's passion and death. But if it is on account of Christ's passion and death, then not on account of our love or merits. Wherefore it wholly fights against the analogy of faith.

units.la: Apparet igitur, causam cur Papistae scripturas in doctrina de iustificatione, remissione peccatorum, consecutione vitae aeternae, non intelligant sed corrumpant, esse, quoniam ad illarum explicationem non adhibent primam hanc regulam Apostoli, ut scilicet, eas interpretentur iuxta analogiam fidei.
units.tr: It is therefore clear that the reason why the Papists do not understand but corrupt the Scriptures in the doctrine of justification, the remission of sins, and the attainment of eternal life is that they do not apply to their explanation this first rule of the Apostle, namely that they interpret them according to the analogy of faith.

units.la: Hanc eandem ob causam Samosateniani & Servetiani, aliique non intelligunt scripturas, sed corrumpunt, quae sunt de Deitate Christi, dum illas ita interpretantur, ut negent, Christum fuisse verum Deum, antequam conceptus esset de Spiritu sancto in utero Virginis: & docent, eum iam esse Deum, non essentialiter & naturaliter, sed per privilegium & per participationem Deitatis Patris. Pugnat cum analogia fidei: Credo in Iesum Christum, filium eius (Dei Patris) unigenitum. Postea: Qui conceptus est de Spiritu sancto, &c. Primò, Si credimus in Christum: Ergo Deus est: quia fiducia in solum Deum collocari debet. Secundò, Si fatemur primò fuisse Filium Dei, deinde conceptum ex Maria virgine. Fuit igitur ante Mariam. Tertio, Si filius vnigenitus: Non est igitur per priuilegium, & per gratiam, sed per naturam. Nam per gratiam, alij etiam sunt multi filij Dei.
units.tr: For the same reason the Samosatenes and the Servetians, and others, do not understand but corrupt the Scriptures concerning the Deity of Christ, while they interpret them in such a way as to deny that Christ was true God before he was conceived of the Holy Spirit in the womb of the Virgin; and they teach that he is now God, not essentially and naturally, but by privilege and by participation in the Deity of the Father. This contradicts the analogy of faith: I believe in Jesus Christ, his (God the Father's) only begotten Son. Afterwards: who was conceived of the Holy Spirit, etc. (1) First, if we believe in Christ, then he is God, since trust must be placed in God alone. (2) Second, if we confess that he was first the Son of God and then was conceived of the Virgin Mary, then he existed before Mary. (3) Third, if he is the only begotten Son, then he is so not by privilege and grace but by nature; for by grace there are many other sons of God.

units.la: Satis igitur luculenter apparet, hanc vnam esse ex præcipuis causis, cur permulti scripturas non intelligant, sed peruertant: nimirum, quòd illas non examinent, nec interpretentur iuxta analogiam fidei. Quare quicunq; vult scripturas probè intelligere, & in eis proficere: hæc Apostolica regula semper in legendis & interpretandis scripturis vtatur necesse est. Proinde hortor omnes, vt benè teneant doctrinam, quæ in putis[?] Catechismis traditur ex verbo, & vehementer laudo Catechesin Ecclesiæ Heidelbergensis & totius Palatinatus.
units.tr: It therefore appears quite clearly that this is one of the chief causes why very many do not understand the Scriptures but pervert them: namely, that they do not examine them or interpret them according to the analogy of faith. Therefore, whoever wishes to understand the Scriptures properly and to make progress in them must necessarily always use this apostolic rule in reading and interpreting the Scriptures. Accordingly I urge all to hold fast to the doctrine that is taught from the Word in the catechisms, and I warmly commend the Catechism of the Church of Heidelberg and of the whole Palatinate.

units.la: Altera interpretandi scripturas regula est, diligens & accurata scripturarum, quæ de eadem suntre, inter se collatio: hoc est, vt scripturas obscuriores, per scripturas clariores interpretemur & explicemus. Est enim scriptura, id est, Spiritus S. in scripturis, sui ipsius interpres: quo quis melior inueniri potest?
units.tr: The second rule of interpreting the Scriptures is the diligent and careful comparison of the Scriptures that concern the same matter with one another; that is, that we interpret and explain the more obscure Scriptures through the clearer Scriptures. For Scripture is, that is, the Holy Spirit in the Scriptures, its own interpreter: who could be found a better one?

units.la: Hanc docuit Christus, primùm, cùm dixit Iohan. 5[?]. Scrutamini scripturas, quia illa de me testificantur: quasi dicat, Examinate diligenter omnes scripturas, præsertim quæ loquuntur de Messia, & conferte cum eis, quæ ego de me prædico, quæve doceo: Et agnoscetis, me illum esse, de quo scripturæ loquuntur. Deinde, hanc eandem regulam docuit Chri-stus, suo exemplo, Matth. 4. Cùm enim Sa-than illum horreretur, ut se deiiceret e pin-naculo templi, & ad hoc abusus esset scriptu-ra, dicendo: Scriptum est enim, quoniam Angelis suis, &c. Hunc locum Psalmi interpretatus est alio loco scripturæ, dicendo, scriptum est etiam Deuter. 6. Non tentabis Dominum Deum tuum. Hoc dicto voluit concludere, non sic esse intelligendum dictum Psalmi, uti Sa-than explicabat, quasi liceret Christiano se-se in discrimen vitæ coniicere, sine causa, quia scriptum sit, Angelis suis mandabit de te, &c. Nam aperte Deus vetat, ne quis illum tentet: tentat autem, qui sine causa, se-se in manifestum vitæ discrimen coniicit. Nihil autem in scripturis inter se pugnans docetur. Non potest igitur illud Psalmi dictum intelligi in eum sensum, in quem citatur à Sathana. Quomodo igitur? Tunc Deum custodire homines per suos Angelos, cùm homines non tentant Deum: sed in sua vocatione ordinaria ratione modoque conue-nienti versantur & ambulant. Item, Matth. 19. Legem Dei per Moysen de libello repu-dij, docet per aliam scripturam, ex Genesi, non esse sic intelligendam, quasi Deus probaret Diuortium, quavis de causa factum, ut Pharisæi interpretabantur, quòd hoc pu-gnet cum prima coniugij institutione: sed ob duritiam cordis Judæorum, fuisse latam illam legem, ut quando contra Dei præce-ptum illas dimittere vellent, nec possent propter duritiam cordis à suo proposito amoueri: saltem dimitterent cum libello re-pudij, quo libello darent testimonium pro-bitatis, honestatis, & fidei, uxoribus, quas di-mittebant, & ita illarum honori consule-rent. En quomodo scripturas per scripturas interpretetur.
units.tr: Christ taught this, first, when he said in John 5. Search the Scriptures, for they testify of me: as if he said, examine diligently all the Scriptures, especially those that speak of the Messiah, and compare them with what I declare and teach about myself; and you will recognize that I am the one of whom the Scriptures speak. Then Christ taught this same rule by his own example, Matt. 4. For when Satan urged him to cast himself down from the pinnacle of the temple, and abused Scripture for this purpose, saying: For it is written, that he shall give his angels charge concerning you, etc., he interpreted this passage of the Psalm by another passage of Scripture, saying: It is also written, Deut. 6, You shall not tempt the Lord your God. By this saying he meant to conclude that the words of the Psalm are not to be understood in the sense in which Satan explained them, as if a Christian were allowed to thrust himself into danger of life without cause, because it is written, He shall give his angels charge over you, etc. For God plainly forbids anyone to tempt him; and he tempts God who without cause thrusts himself into manifest danger of life. Now nothing mutually contradictory is taught in the Scriptures. Therefore that saying of the Psalm cannot be understood in the sense in which Satan cites it. In what way, then? God keeps men by his angels when men do not tempt God, but live and walk in their ordinary calling, in a suitable manner and way. Likewise, Matt. 19. Christ teaches, through another passage from Genesis, that the law of God given through Moses concerning the bill of divorce is not to be understood as if God approved divorce made for any cause whatever, as the Pharisees interpreted it, since this would contradict the first institution of marriage; but that, because of the hardness of the Jews' hearts, that law was enacted so that when they wished to dismiss their wives contrary to God's command, and could not be turned from their purpose because of the hardness of their hearts, they would at least dismiss them with a bill of divorce, by which they would give a testimony of the uprightness, honesty and fidelity of the wives whom they dismissed, and thus would provide for their honor. See how one interprets Scripture through Scripture.

units.la: Matth. 22. illa Prophetarum vaticinia de Christo, quòd nasciturus esset filius Davidis, interpretatur per aliud Propheticum oraculum ex Psal. 110. nempe per verba Davidis, cùm Messiam suum vocat Dominum, dicendo: Dixit Dominus (id est, Deus Pater) Domino meo (id est, Messiæ) sede à dextris meis. Docet enim hoc dicto, quatenus Christus sit filius Davidis, nempe secundùm carnem, ut loquitur Apostolus: secundùm autem aliam naturam, nempe divinam, maiorem esse Davide.
units.tr: Matt. 22. interprets the prophecies of the Prophets about Christ, that the Son of David was to be born, through another prophetic oracle from Ps. 110, namely through David's words when he calls his Messiah Lord, saying: The Lord (that is, God the Father) said to my Lord (that is, the Messiah): Sit at my right hand. For by this saying he teaches that, in so far as Christ is the son of David, namely according to the flesh, as the Apostle says, yet according to the other nature, namely the divine, he is greater than David.

units.la: Act. 17. Laudat Spiritus S. quòd Berhoënses doctrinam Apostolicam iuxta scripturas Prophetarum interpretabantur & examinabant.
units.tr: Acts 17. The Holy Spirit commends the Bereans because they interpreted and examined the apostolic teaching according to the Scriptures of the Prophets.

units.la: Hanc eandem regulam docet Apostolus, primùm præcepto, cùm ait 1. Timoth. 4. Attende lectioni. Præcipit enim hic pro vera scripturarum intelligentia assequenda, ut attendat lectioni scripturarum, hoc est, ut pia sedulitate scripturas cuoluat, inter se cõ-ferat. ferat. Item, exemplo suo:ubique enim scri-pturas scripturis explicat. Exemplum.
units.tr: The Apostle teaches this same rule, first by precept, when he says in 1 Tim. 4, Attend to reading. For he here commands, in order to attain true understanding of the Scriptures, that one attend to the reading of the Scriptures, that is, that one turn over the Scriptures with devout diligence and compare them with one another. Likewise, by his own example: for everywhere he explains Scriptures by Scriptures. Example.

units.la: Heb.2.illud Psalm.8.de Christo, Minui-sti eum paulo minus ab Angelis, hoc est, aliquanto inferiorem fecisti, quomodo sit intelligendum, exponit, nempe quoad humanitatem, in qua passus est: non autem simpliciter. Quomodo hoc explicat & interpretatur? Per alias scripturas. Ostendit enim in primo capite, eum esse Deum, & creatorem etiam Angelorum: & ideo secundum hanc naturam, maiorem esse Angelis. Scriptum est enim: Et adorent eum omnes Angeli eius. Item, Et ad Angelos quidem (id est, de Angelis) dicit, Qui facit Angelos suos spiritus, &c. Item, Tu autem Domine (alloquitur Christum) terram fundasti, & opera manuum tuarum sunt Coeli, eoque & Angeli. Secundo autem capite ostendit ex vaticiniis scripturarum, esse hominem: & secundum hanc naturam minorem factum esse Angelis, per passionem.
units.tr: Heb. 2, the saying of Psalm 8 about Christ, You made him a little lower than the angels, that is, you made him somewhat inferior, he explains how this is to be understood, namely with respect to the humanity in which he suffered, and not absolutely. How does he explain and interpret this? Through other Scriptures. For he shows in the first chapter that he is God and also the creator of the angels, and therefore, according to this nature, greater than the angels. For it is written: And let all his angels worship him. Likewise, And of the angels indeed (that is, concerning the angels) he says, Who makes his angels spirits, etc. Likewise, But you, Lord (he addresses Christ), have founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands, and so also the angels. In the second chapter, however, he shows from the prophecies of the Scriptures that he is man, and that according to this nature he was made less than the angels through his suffering.

units.la: Eandem regulam confirmat Diuus Petrus 2. Pet.cap.1. Vult scripturam Propheticam, esse interpretationem eorum, quae ipsi docebant Apostoli, dicendo: Habemus autem firmiorem sermonem Propheticum, cui recte fa-citis, quod attendatis, &c. Nimis prolixus fo-rem, si vellem omnes scripturas percurrere noui Testamenti, & ostendere, quas Christus & Apostoli soliti semper fuerint scripturas per scripturas interpretari, & conciliare obscuriores per clariores, collatione locorum, qui de eadem sunt re vel persona. Satis est demonstrasse, hanc regulam veram, & a Spiritu sancto.
units.tr: The divine Peter confirms the same rule, 2 Pet. 1. He wishes the prophetic Scripture to be the interpretation of what the Apostles themselves taught, saying: We have also a more sure prophetic word, to which you do well to take heed, etc. I would be too long-winded if I wished to run through all the Scriptures of the New Testament and show how Christ and the Apostles were always accustomed to interpret Scripture through Scripture, and to reconcile the more obscure with the clearer by comparing places that concern the same matter or person. It is enough to have shown that this rule is true and from the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Eandem regulam confirmant Patres: ut praeter alios Augustinus de doctrina Christiana, tam in 2. quam in tertio libro: multis in locis docens, debere nos per clariora, explicare obscuriora: & figurate dicta, per proprie dicta. Est igitur certissima & optima regula, eoque necessaria ad intelligentiam scripturarum.
units.tr: The Fathers confirm the same rule, among others Augustine in On Christian Doctrine, both in the second and in the third book, teaching in many places that we must explain the obscure by the clearer, and figurative sayings by plain sayings. It is therefore a most certain and best rule, and therefore necessary for understanding the Scriptures.

units.la: Hoc vero confirmatur exemplis eorum, qui hanc regulam negligunt. Omnes enim hallucinantur in intelligentia scripturarum, quia hac non utuntur regula, & non conferunt scripturas cum scripturis. Liquet ex-emplis.
units.tr: This indeed is confirmed by the examples of those who neglect this rule. For all go astray in understanding the Scriptures who do not use this rule and do not compare Scriptures with Scriptures. The examples make this clear.

units.la: 1. Ariani & similes ex dicto Christi, Pater maior me est, & aliis similibus, colligunt, Christum non esse verum Deum, Patri ὁμο-ούσιον[?], coæternum, & coæqualem. Quare? quia non contulerunt haec loca cum aliis, quae sunt magis perspicua de æterna Deitate Christi: qualis est Roman. 9. loquens de Christo, ait eum esse ex Patribus Israelitarum secundum carnem, deinde mox subdit alteram naturam divinam, dicendo, Qui est DEVS benedictus in saecula.
units.tr: First, the Arians and the like gather from Christ's saying, The Father is greater than I, and other similar sayings, that Christ is not true God, consubstantial (homoousion) with the Father, coeternal and coequal. Why? Because they did not compare these passages with others that are more plain concerning the eternal Deity of Christ: such as Rom. 9, where, speaking of Christ, he says that he is from the fathers of Israel according to the flesh, and then immediately adds the other, divine nature, saying, Who is God blessed for ever.

units.la: 2. Blandrata & alij nebulones Seruetiani rident Trinitatem, id est, doctrinam hanc, quod tres, Pater, Filius, & Spiritus S. unus sunt Deus, quod scriptum sit 1. Cor. 8. Nobis autem unus est Deus, qui est Pater, & unus Dominus Iesu. Sed si conferrent hunc locum cum aliis de eadem re loquentibus, non ita hallucinarentur, vt est ille 1.Ioh.5. Tres sunt qui testificantur in cœlo, Pater, Sermo, & Spiritus sanctus, & hi tres vnum sunt.
units.tr: 2. Blandrata and other scoundrels of the Servetian school mock the Trinity, that is, this doctrine that Father, Son and Holy Spirit are three and yet one God, on the ground that it is written in 1 Cor. 8: "But to us there is one God, who is the Father, and one Lord Jesus." But if they compared this passage with others speaking of the same matter, they would not go so astray as they do in 1 John 5: "There are three who bear witness in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, and these three are one."

units.la: 3. Græci locum de Spiritu sancto, qui est Iohan.15. Spiritus qui a Patre procedit, &c. male sunt interpretati, dum inde concluserunt Spiritum non procedere a Filio. Vnde hic error? Quia non contulerunt alios de eodem spiritu locos: Iohan.16. Si autem abiero, mittam eum ad vos. Item Rom.8. Spiritum quem appellauit Dei, eundem mox vocat Spiritum Christi. Gal.4. Misit Deus Spiritum Filij sui in corda vestra. Quem Spiritū Patris Christus dixerat se missurum: Hic Paulus ait, Deū (Patrem) misisse Spiritum Filij sui.
units.tr: 3. The Greeks have badly interpreted the passage about the Holy Spirit in John 15, "the Spirit who proceeds from the Father, etc.", when they concluded from it that the Spirit does not proceed from the Son. Whence this error? Because they did not compare the other passages about the same Spirit: John 16, "But if I go away, I will send him to you"; likewise Rom. 8, "the Spirit whom he calls the Spirit of God, he soon calls the Spirit of Christ"; Gal. 4, "God has sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts." The Spirit whom Christ had said he would send from the Father: here Paul says that God (the Father) sent the Spirit of his Son.

units.la: 4. Papistæ loca de bonis operibus perfi-mè[?] interpretantur, dum ex illis concludunt, Nos seruari per opera. Vnde hic error? Quia non conferunt scripturas cum scripturis il-lis, quæ omninò negant, nos saluos esse factos ex operibus. Tit 3. Non ex operibus iusti-tiæ, quæ fecerimus nos, sed secundum suam misericordiam saluos nos fecit. Neque hic valet ex-ceptio. Fecit per solam misericordiam nos saluos ex parte, id est, quoad se, & inchoatiuè: sed requirit à parte nostra, vt per opera salu-tem perficiamus. Nam quomodo saluos nos fecit, sed tantum ex parte? Seruare non est virtutem merendi salutem tribuere, sed à morte & peccato gratis liberare.
units.tr: 4. The Papists interpret the passages about good works perversely, when they conclude from them that we are saved by works. Whence this error? Because they do not compare those Scriptures with those which utterly deny that we have been made safe by works. Titus 3: "Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us." Nor does the objection hold here, that he saved us by mercy alone only in part, that is, as far as he himself is concerned and inchoatively; while from our side he requires that we complete our salvation through works. For how has he saved us, if only in part? To save is not to grant the power of meriting salvation, but to free freely from death and sin.

units.la: §. Libertini perperàm interpretantur di-cta Apostoli, Nos seruari fide sine operibus, dum talem intelligunt fidem, quæ non sit efficax per opera : Vt cùm dicit Apostolus Rom. 3. Colligimus igitur hominem iustifica-ri per fidem sine operibus. Vnde hic error? Quia non conferunt loca similia, vt illud Galat. 5. Fides, quæ per dilectionem operatur. Si hunc locum cum illo ad Romanos contulissent: intellexissent cùm excludit Apostolus opera, eum non excludere ea à fide, sed à vi iustificandi. Illud enim sine operibus in dicto, Col-ligimus igitur, iustificari hominem per fidem, non refertur ad fidem, sed ad verbum iustifi-cari.
units.tr: §. The Libertines wrongly interpret the Apostle's words, "We are saved by faith without works," when they understand such a faith as is not effective through works. As when the Apostle says in Rom. 3: "We conclude therefore that a man is justified by faith without works." Whence this error? Because they do not compare similar passages, such as Gal. 5: "faith which works through love." If they had compared that passage with the one to the Romans, they would have understood that when the Apostle excludes works, he does not exclude them from faith but from the power of justifying. For the phrase "without works" in the saying "We conclude therefore that a man is justified by faith" does not refer to faith, but to the verb "is justified."

units.la: 6. Idem dico de illis, qui verba Cœnæ ita interpretantur ad literam, vt statuant, alij quidem, mutari substantiam panis, in substantiam corporis Christi: alij verò, ipsum Christi corpus verè esse in ipso pane, aut coniunctum cum pane. Vnde hic error? Inde, quòd præterquam non interpretantur hæc verba iuxta analogiam fidei, non etiam ea conferunt cum aliis scripturis, quæ tum de aliis sacramentis, tum de hoc Cœnæ mysterio loquuntur. Nam si hoc facerent, viderent, & nullam ibi fieri mutationem substantiæ in substantiam: & corpus Christi, vel sanguinem, quoad suam substantiam, minimè esse in pane vel vino: sed esse in cœlo, & ibi perpetuò manere, vt in Actis testatur Petrus.
units.tr: 6. I say the same of those who interpret the words of the Supper so literally that some hold the substance of the bread is changed into the substance of Christ's body, and others hold that the very body of Christ is truly in the bread itself, or joined with the bread. Whence this error? Because, besides not interpreting these words according to the analogy of faith, they do not compare them with other Scriptures which speak both of the other sacraments and of this mystery of the Lord's Supper. For if they did this, they would see that no change of substance into substance takes place there, and that the body of Christ, or his blood, as to their substance, is by no means in the bread or wine, but is in heaven and remains there perpetually, as Peter testifies in Acts.

units.la: Nam 1.in Sacramentis veteris Testamen-ti, quae eadem fuerunt cum nostris, quod rem ipsam attinet, licet signa essent diuer-sa, nullam videmus factam fuisse substan-tiae mutationem: nullam etiam rerum, quarum erant signa, realem crassamve cum si-gnis coniunctionem: & tamen easdem cum nostris habent locutiones. Circumcisio foe-dus dicebatur & erat, nulla tamen substantiae mutatio: nulla foederis in ea inclusio, sed si-gnum tantum foederis Agnus pascha dice-batur & erat: ibi tamen nulla mutatio sub-stantiae: neque realiter pascha, id est, transi-tus Domini, erat in Angelo. Idem de Manna cibo, quem omnes ederunt, & de aqua, quae e petra fluxit, & de qua omnes biberunt, di-co. Ergo neque in nostris sacramentis vllam debuissent isti imaginari aut μετουσίαν[?] aut συμ-βασίαν[?]. 2. Debuissent conferre verba huius sacramenti, cum verbis alterius sacramenti, nempe baptismi. Lauacrum dicitur & est re-generationis. Tit.3.cum tamen sit duntaxat sa-cramentum regenerationis, & sigillum Spi-ritus sancti, per quem fit regeneratio.3. De-buissent etiam conferre cum verbis de eo-dem sacramento, in aliis locis: vt cum illis, quibus hoc sacramentum explicauit Chri-stus apud Iohan. 6. vbi corpus & carnem suam vocat panem, ibi tamen nulla vel cor-poris CHRISTI in panem, vel panis in cor-pus Christi mutatio, aut vnius in alio inclu-sio, vel realis coniunctio indicatur. Item cum illis Apostoli 1 Corinth.10. Panis quem frangimus,nonne communio corporis Christi est? Ibi certe Apostolus nullam statuit aut docet vel transsubstantiationem, vel crassam aut substantialem corporis Christi cum pane coniunctionem. Sed ubique tam in sacramentis veteris Testamenti, quàm in sacramentis Novi, symbola diversa sunt à rebus quarum sunt symbola, & nullam cum rebus ipsis realem substantialemque habent coniunctionem, sed tantum spiritualem. Perceptio etiam symbolorum fit corpore: perceptio rerum, quarum sunt symbola, fit animo & spiritu per fidem. Cur non igitur idem sentiendum de sacramento Coenæ? Ergo vi-demus hanc veram, tutam, optimamque esse interpretandi rationem, cum scripturas per scripturas diligenti collatione inter-pretamur. Quare haec sexta regula omnino re-tinenda est, si velimus scripturas probe intelligere, & nunquam hallucinari: nimirum ut eas interpretemur & iuxta analogiam fidei, & per ipsas scripturas, diligenti similium locorum inter se collatione. Fusius & multis exemplis hanc sextam regulam explicare libuit: propterea quòd fit pernecessaria, & interim tamen à magnis etiam viris negligi-tur.
units.tr: For, first, in the sacraments of the Old Testament, which were the same as ours as far as the thing itself is concerned, although the signs were different, we see that no change of substance was made, nor any real or gross conjunction of the things of which they were signs with the signs; and yet they have the same manner of speaking as ours. "Circumcision was called and was a covenant," yet there was no change of substance, no inclusion of the covenant in it, but only the sign of the covenant. "The Passover lamb" was called and was the Passover, yet there was no change of substance there; nor was the Passover, that is, the passing over of the Lord, really in the angel. I say the same of the "manna" food which all ate, and of the "water" which flowed from the rock and which all drank. Therefore they ought not to have imagined in our sacraments either a "metousia" or a "symbasis." Second, they ought to have compared the words of this sacrament with the words of another sacrament, namely baptism: "It is called and is a laver of regeneration" (Titus 3), although it is only the sacrament of regeneration and the seal of the Holy Spirit, through whom regeneration takes place. Third, they ought also to have compared them with words about the same sacrament in other places: such as those by which Christ explained this sacrament in John 6, where he calls his body and flesh bread; yet there no change of the body of Christ into bread, or of bread into the body of Christ, nor an inclusion of one in the other, nor a real conjunction, is indicated there. Likewise the Apostles in 1 Cor. 10: "The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?" There the Apostle certainly establishes or teaches neither a transubstantiation nor a gross or substantial conjunction of the body of Christ with the bread. But everywhere, in the sacraments of the Old Testament as much as in those of the New, the signs are different from the things of which they are signs, and they have no real or substantial conjunction with the things themselves, but only a spiritual one. The perception of the signs also takes place with the body; the perception of the things of which they are signs takes place with the mind and spirit through faith. Why then should we not think the same of the sacrament of the Supper? Therefore we see that this is the true, safe and best method of interpreting, when we interpret Scriptures through Scriptures by diligent comparison. "Therefore this sixth rule must be wholly retained, if we wish to understand the Scriptures rightly and never to go astray: namely, that we interpret them both according to the analogy of faith and through the Scriptures themselves, by diligent comparison of similar passages with one another." It has pleased me to explain this sixth rule more fully and with many examples, because it is most necessary, and yet meanwhile it is neglected even by great men.

units.la: Septima causa, cur in scripturarum intel-ligentia multi hallucinentur, est: quòd in interpretandis scripturis, non se continent intra terminos scripturarum, sed excedunt, extra illos vagantes. Et cùm dico terminos scripturæ, intelligo terminos tam verbo-rum, quàm rerum & sententiarum. Nam aliis etiam vti verbis, quàm scriptura vtatur, causa est multorum errorum. Peccant in hac re maximè omnium Papistæ. Vnde enim tot errores & idololatriæ, & cumprimisin Missa ? Inde quòd intra terminos scripturarum non se continuerunt: sed multras[?] & res & voces acceperunt ab Ethnicis. Exempla sunt infinita & omnibus obuia: ideo non multis immorabor. Ita peccant illi,qui dum volunt carnalem corporis Christi præsen-tiam stabilire, vagantur extra terminos & locutiones scripturarum: & aiunt, corpus Christi esse vbique: alij, corpus Christi factum esse partem Trinitatis. Vnde hæc mon-stra atque portenta? Quòd non se continent intra terminos scripturæ. Vbi vnquam scrip-tura sic locuta est? Redite, redite fratres ad caulas, & intra eas continete vestras cogita-tiones & linguas. Regula igitur retinenda, vt in scripturis intelligendis & interpretandis, contineamus nos intra ipsarum terminos, tam reales quàm etiam verbales. Hanc tradit Deut.4.& 5. Non declinetis neq; ad dextram neq; ad sinistram. 1. Timoth. 6. iubet vitari βέβηλας[?] κενοφωνίας.
units.tr: The seventh cause why many go astray in understanding the Scriptures is this: that in interpreting the Scriptures they do not keep themselves within the limits of the Scriptures, but go beyond them, wandering outside them. And when I say the limits of Scripture, I mean the limits of words, of things and of meanings alike. For to use words other than those Scripture uses is also a cause of many errors. The Papists sin in this matter most of all. Whence come so many errors and idolatries, and above all in the Mass? From this, that they did not keep themselves within the limits of the Scriptures, but took both things and words from the heathen. The examples are endless and obvious to all, so I will not dwell on many. Thus they sin who, while they want to establish a carnal presence of Christ's body, wander outside the limits and manner of speaking of the Scriptures: some say that the body of Christ is everywhere; others that the body of Christ has become a part of the Trinity. Whence these monsters and portents? Because they do not keep themselves within the limits of Scripture. Where has Scripture ever spoken in this way? Return, return, brothers, to the folds, and keep your thoughts and tongues within them. The rule to be retained, therefore, in understanding and interpreting the Scriptures, is that we keep ourselves within their limits, both real and verbal. Deuteronomy 4 and 5 hands this down: "Do not turn aside either to the right hand or to the left." 1 Timothy 6 commands us to avoid profane and empty babblings [βέβηλας κενοφωνίας].

units.la: Octava causa, cur veram intelligentiam scripturarum non assequamur, est in multis superbus doctorum virorum & interpre-tum contemtus: hoc est, quòd omnes con-temnant temnant interpretes:in aliis, quòd nimium addicti sint suis interpretibus, eosq; sine iudicio legant.
units.tr: The eighth cause why we do not attain the true understanding of the Scriptures is the proud contempt of learned men and interpreters: that is, on the one hand, that some despise all interpreters, and on the other, that others are too attached to their own interpreters and read them without judgment.

units.la: In primo genere sunt Anabaptistæ & alij, qui omnes contemnunt interpretes, & improbant tot scribi commentarios: Ita fit, vt dum contemnunt dona Dei, quæ per varios suos seruos communicat Ecclesiæ, maneant prorsus imperiti scripturarum, vel præposterè eas intelligant. In altero genere sunt primùm Papistæ, qui ita suis Patribus sunt addicti, & Monachi suis quisque Doctoribus, Thomæ, Ægydio, Scoto, vt ab eorum expositionibus, vel latum vnguem discedere non licear. Deinde sunt plerique etiam inter nostros, quibus religio est, ab interpretationibus suorum præceptorum vel minimum deflectere. Ita fit, vt & ipsi sponte se priuent vera scripturæ intelligentia: Et dum suos præceptores in omnibus, & per omnia volunt tueri, turbas excitant in Ecclesia. Res est perspicua vel me tacente.
units.tr: To the first kind belong the Anabaptists and others, who despise all interpreters and disapprove of so many written commentaries. So it happens that, while they despise the gifts of God, which he communicates to his Church through his various servants, they remain wholly ignorant of the Scriptures, or understand them backwards. To the second kind belong first the Papists, who are so bound to their Fathers, and the monks to their own teachers, Thomas, Giles, Scotus, that they do not dare to depart a hair's breadth from their explanations. Then there are also many among our own people who consider it a matter of conscience to deviate even the slightest bit from the interpretations of their teachers. So it happens that they too voluntarily deprive themselves of the true understanding of Scripture; and while they want to defend their teachers in everything and at all points, they stir up disturbances in the Church. The matter is plain, even without my saying so.

units.la: Regula igitur tenenda est, quæ duplex ha-bet membrum: primum est, Vt in inter-pretandis scripturis ipsos etiam interpretes consulamus, sed cum primis optimos & sinceriores. Nam hos excitat in Ecclesia Deus propter nostram vtilitatem. A-ctor. 8. Eunuchus ait, se non posse intelligere Esaiam sine interprete. Roman. 10. ait Apo-stolus: Quomodo credent, nisi audiant? Quomodo audient sine praedicante. Item cap. 11. Laudat interpretes in Ecclesia : sed docet quomodo debeant interpretari, scilicet iuxta analogiam fidei. 1. Corinth. 14. iubet, ut si cui revelatum aliquid fuerit, alius taceat & audiat. Et quid fuerunt Prophetae, nisi interpretes Mosis? Ephes. 4. c[?] Alios Apostolos, doctores, &c. Et quotidie etiam, sedens ad dextram Patris, dat Doctores Ecclesiae. Qui igitur contemnit pios Doctores & interpretes, Christum contemnit: Et qui Christum, Patrem etiam. Et eo ingratiores nunc fuerimus nos in Christum, quam veteres: quo nunc excellentiores dedit nobis interpretes, quam unquam ante hac post Apostolos, Ergo amplectamur interpretes.
units.tr: The rule, therefore, must be kept, and it has two parts. The first is that, in interpreting the Scriptures, we consult the interpreters themselves, but above all the best and purest of them. For God raises these up in the Church for our benefit. In Acts 8 the eunuch says that he cannot understand Isaiah without an interpreter. In Romans 10 the Apostle says: "How shall they believe, unless they hear? And how shall they hear without a preacher?" Likewise in chapter 11 he praises interpreters in the Church, but teaches how they ought to interpret, namely according to the analogy of faith. In 1 Corinthians 14 he orders that if something has been revealed to someone, the other should keep silent and listen. And what were the prophets but interpreters of Moses? In Ephesians 4 he says: "Some apostles, some teachers, etc." And even today, sitting at the right hand of the Father, he gives teachers to the Church. Therefore whoever despises pious teachers and interpreters despises Christ, and whoever despises Christ despises the Father also. And we are now the more ungrateful toward Christ than the ancients, since he has given us more excellent interpreters now than ever before since the Apostles. Therefore let us embrace the interpreters.

units.la: Alterum membrum huius Regulae est: ut cum iudicio eos legamus & audiamus persuasi eos esse homines, & potuisse ac posse errare: ac proinde eatenus illorum interpretationes amplectamur, quatenus videmus esse allatas iuxta analogiam fidei, & ex aliis erutas esse scripturis. Nam sic egerunt omnes veri interpretes. Moses legem a Deo acceptam populo interpretatur: sed ibi nil vides diuersum ab eo, quod acceperat in monte. Prophetae interpretantur legem Moses: sed nihil ibi diuersum a lege Moses. Nehemiae 8. Esdras suggestum conscendit, explicat legem, sedet in Cathedra coram tota Ecclesia. Sed quid ibi audis, nisi verbum Dei? Christus Luc. 4. interpretatur Esaiam alia sæpiùs loca: sed semper iuxta scripturas & per scripturas. Item Luc. ultimo, incipiens à Mose, Prophetis & Psalmis, interpretabatur illis scripturas. Sunt igitur audiendi interpretes, sed cum iudicio, & eatenus admittendæ illorum interpretationes, quatenus sunt & iuxta analogiam fidei, & per alias scripturas confirmatæ.
units.tr: The second part of this rule is that we read and listen to them with judgment, being persuaded that they are men, and that they could err and still can err; and accordingly we embrace their interpretations only so far as we see that they are brought forth according to the analogy of faith and drawn from other Scriptures. For this is how all true interpreters have acted. Moses interprets for the people the law received from God, but there you see nothing different from what he had received on the mountain. The prophets interpret the law of Moses, but there is nothing in them different from the law of Moses. In Nehemiah 8, Ezra mounts a platform, explains the law, and sits in the chair before the whole Church. But what do you hear there, except the word of God? Christ in Luke 4 interprets Isaiah, and other passages often, but always according to the Scriptures and through the Scriptures. Likewise in the last chapter of Luke, beginning from Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms, he interpreted the Scriptures to them. Therefore interpreters are to be heard, but with judgment, and their interpretations admitted only so far as they agree with the analogy of faith and are confirmed through other Scriptures.

units.la: Hanc regulam tradit Apostolus. 1. Thess. 5[?]. Prophetiam nolite spernere. Ecce primum membrum nostræ regulæ. Omnia probate, quod bonum est, tenete. Ecce alterum.
units.tr: The Apostle hands down this rule in 1 Thessalonians 5: "Do not despise prophesying." Here is the first part of our rule. "Test all things; hold fast what is good." Here is the second.

units.la: Notandum tamen etiam, quomodo vten-dum sit interpretibus. Sunt qui sentiant, primùm consulendum esse optimum aliquem interpretem in illud caput, quod suscepisti legendum: Deinde examinandum contextum: quò facilius possis tunc adiutus opera interpretis, percipere sensum scripturæ.
units.tr: It must be noted, however, also how interpreters are to be used. There are those who think that one should first consult some excellent interpreter on the chapter you have undertaken to read; then examine the context, so that, helped by the work of the interpreter, you may more easily perceive the sense of the Scripture.

units.la: Sed ego contrà sentio, primùm, dandam nobis esse operam, ut invocato Christo, qui suum nobis largiatur spiritum, contextum ipsum per nosipsi examinemus, an forte sine interprete intelligere valeamus: consultis lexicis & libris de tropis scripturarum, si quid occurrat obscurum in verbis: consultis verò historiis, & aliarum artium libris, si quid talium rerum scitu necessarium occurrat: ac tum demum ad legendum etiam optimum aliquem interpretem, vel interpretes, si unus non sufficiat, accedamus. Est hæc ratio multis nominibus vtilior meo iudicio, licet laboriosior.
units.tr: But I, on the contrary, think that, first, we ought to take pains, with Christ invoked, who grants us his Spirit, to examine the context itself by ourselves, to see whether perhaps we can understand it without an interpreter: consulting lexicons and books on the tropes of Scripture if anything obscure occurs in the words; and consulting histories and books of the other arts if anything of such matters that needs to be known occurs. And only then should we come to read also some excellent interpreter, or interpreters if one is not enough. This method, in my judgment, is more useful in many respects, although more laborious.

units.la: Atq; hæ sunt regulæ generales. Nam magis speciales persequi non tantum nimi'j[?] ef-set laboris, sed etiam inutile: quia obrueren-tur studiosorum animi magna præceptionum & regularum multitudine. Nunc propius accedo.
units.tr: These are the general rules. For to pursue the more special ones would be not only too much labor but also useless, since the minds of students would be overwhelmed by a great multitude of precepts and rules. Now I come closer to the point.

units.la: Nona causa, cur multi veram scripturæ intelligentiam non consequantur, est: quod in legendis scripturis, quia omni carent Dia-lectica, vel naturali, vel artificiali, cum accipiunt librum aliquem, aut epistolam, aut caput scripturæ legendum & interpretandum, non obseruant scopum autoris in eo libro vel capite, neque argumentum seu summam, neque media, quibus sua explicat vel probat: sed ita confusè legunt, perinde atque si etiam Spiritus sanctus ibi per Prophetas aut Apostolos confusè & sine vllo scopo, sine arte ac methodo locutus sit. Inde fit, vt sententias quidem aliquas inde colligant & percipiant: sed quid sibi velit Spiritus S. in eo libro vel capite, prorsus nesciant. Ita parum proficiunt in vera scripturarum cognitione: imo ignorato scopo & propósito Spiritus S. multa in diuersum torquent sensum. Est hæc ignoratio causa multorum & maximorum errorum. Exemplum.
units.tr: The ninth cause why many do not attain the true understanding of Scripture is this: when they take up some book, or epistle, or chapter of Scripture to read and interpret, they lack all dialectic, whether natural or artificial, and so do not observe the scope of the author in that book or chapter, nor its argument or summary, nor the means by which he explains or proves his points. Instead they read so confusedly, just as if the Holy Spirit had also spoken there through the prophets or apostles confusedly and without any purpose, without art or method. Hence it happens that they indeed gather and perceive some sentences from it, but what the Holy Spirit means in that book or chapter they utterly do not know. Thus they make little progress in the true knowledge of the Scriptures; indeed, ignoring the aim and purpose of the Holy Spirit, they twist many things into a wrong sense. This ignorance is the cause of many and very great errors. An example:

units.la: Luc.7. Papistæ, quia ignorant scopum, in quem illam proposuit parabolam Christus de duobus debitoribus: ideo fit, vt cum postea concludit : Ideo remittentur ei peccata multa, quia dilexit multum, inde colligunt, hominem iustificari propter opera charitatis.
units.tr: In Luke 7 the Papists, because they ignore the purpose for which Christ put forth the parable of the two debtors, therefore, when he concludes afterwards: "Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much," they infer from this that man is justified on account of works of charity.

units.la: Regula igitur hac esto aduersus hanc mul-ta ignorantia, multorumque errorum causam: ut cum aliquam, verbi gratia, epistolam aut caput, sumimus nobis legendum: primo il-lud percurramus, & curemus, ut intelligamus vocum significata & locutionum vim ac proprietates, & si quae alia sint, quorum cognitio petenda sit ex Grammaticis, vel Dialecticis, vel historiis, vel Mathematicis, vel aliis artibus: illa ex iis libris cognoscantur. 2. loco obseruemus, quis sit scopus au-toris in ea epistola vel capite: id quod fieri nequit, nisi prius toto perlecto libro vel capite. Scopus autem est ille finis, in quem omnia, quae scribit autor, immediate referuntur, & in quem ipse collimat. 3. Argu-mentum colligatur. Est autem argumentum, summa eorum, quae in eo libro vel Epistola, vel capite tractantur. 4. Rationes sive media, quibus argumentum illud probatur & tractatur. Exemplum in Epistola ad Romanos, 1. Videnda vocum significata: & in primis, quid significet Apostolo lex, Eu-angelium, spiritus, caro, lex peccati, lex spiri-tus vitae. 2. Scopus Apostoli fuit hic, tollere discordias & simultates ex Ecclesia Romana inter fratres ex Gentibus & inter fratres ex Iudaismo excitatas: ortas autem ex superbia utriusque partis. Nam Iudæi insolescebant contra Gentiles quòd ipsi essent ex populo Dei, ex quibus Christus, quibus datæ scripturæ, &c. ut Roman. 9. ostendit Apostolus: cùm reliqui essent ex idololatris & alieni à fœdere. Gentiles etiam præ se contemnebant Iudæos, quòd propter ingratitudinem & alia scelera, maximè propter occisum Messiam, maxima ex parte essent illi reiecti: ipsi verò in illorum locum vocati, ut Paulus ostendit Rom. 11. de ramis excisis & infitis. Scopus igitur Apostoli fuit, utrumque populum humiliare: & utraque parte humiliata, tollere discordias: & iis sublatis, ad concordiam & amicitiam eos revocare, ut vivant in fide Christi, & pace fraterna: Unde concludens Epistolam ait, Salutate vos invi-cem in osculo sancto. Hic fuit scopus.
units.tr: The rule, therefore, against this great ignorance and cause of many errors, let it be this: when we take up some epistle or chapter, for example, to read, first, let us run through it and take care to understand the meanings of the words and the force and proper usages of expressions, and whatever else there is whose knowledge is to be sought from grammarians, or dialecticians, or historians, or mathematicians, or other arts: let these be learned from those books. Second, let us observe what the author's scope is in that epistle or chapter, which cannot be done unless the whole book or chapter has first been read through. The scope, however, is that end to which everything the author writes is immediately referred, and at which he himself aims. Third, the argument is to be gathered. The argument is the summary of what is treated in that book, epistle, or chapter. Fourth, the reasons or means by which that argument is proved and treated. Example in the Epistle to the Romans: (1) the meanings of the words are to be seen, and especially what the Apostle means by law, gospel, spirit, flesh, the law of sin, the law of the Spirit of life. (2) The Apostle's scope was this: to remove the discords and quarrels stirred up in the Roman Church between brothers from the Gentiles and brothers from Judaism, arising from the pride of each party. For the Jews were growing arrogant against the Gentiles because they were of the people of God, from whom Christ came, to whom the Scriptures were given, etc., as the Apostle shows in Romans 9, while the rest were idolaters and strangers to the covenant. The Gentiles, too, held the Jews in contempt, because for their ingratitude and other crimes, especially for killing the Messiah, they had for the most part been rejected, and they themselves had been called into their place, as Paul shows in Romans 11 about the broken off and grafted branches. The scope of the Apostle therefore was to humble both peoples; and with both parties humbled, to remove the discords, and with these removed, to call them back to concord and friendship, so that they might live in the faith of Christ and in brotherly peace. Hence, concluding the Epistle, he says: "Greet one another with a holy kiss." This was the scope.

units.la: 3.
