Argumentum verò totius Epistolæ, est summa eorum quibus utitur ad obtinendum suum scopum, hoc est, ad retundendam utriusque populi superbiam, & utrumque humiliandum, adducendumque eò, ut in fide Christi, & fraterna charitate viverent. Quæ est hæc summa? Ea duobus constat capitibus, cognitione hominis, & cognitione Dei ac Christi. Primùm enim probat, omnes esse ex æquo peccatores, & reos mortis æternæ, ita ut nemo servari posset ex suis operibus: Non esse igitur, cur alter adversus alterum efferatur. Deinde argumento ducto à cognitione Christi, & eius gratiæ ac iustitiæ, probat, Christum, licet secundùm carnem sit tantùm ex semine Dauid, & promissus tantùm Israëlitis: tamen quatenus saluator est, pertinere illum, & effecta promissionum, tansad [?] Gentes, quàm ad Iudæos: ita vt quicunque credat in Christum, siue Iudæus, siue Gentilis: per hanc fidem, eamq; solam seruetur. Imò etiam, quòd aliquis credat in Christum: hoc neque Iudæum, neque Gentilem habere à se, sed ex gratuita Dei electione. Omnium igitur excludi gloriationem. Quare non esse, cur alter aduersus alterum insolenter efferatur: cùm omnes ex æquo gratis per Christum, fide in eum diuinitùs accepta, seruentur. Argumentum igitur, hoc est, summa eorum, quæ ibi tractat Apostolus, est: Omnes esse ex æquo peccatores, & reos iræ Dei, mortisque æternæ: Quòd si qui seruentur, tam- ex uno, quàm ex altero populo: seruari omnes ex sola Dei gratia, per fidem in Christum, & non ex operibus: idque propterea, quòd Deus illos ante Mundi constitutionem ad hanc salutis gratuitam participationem in Christo gratis elegerit, reiectis aliis omnibus.
units.tr: 3. The argument of the whole Epistle, however, is the sum of the things by which he gains his aim, that is, to break down the pride of each people, to humble both, and to bring them to live in the faith of Christ and in brotherly love. What is this sum? It consists of two heads: the knowledge of man, and the knowledge of God and of Christ. For first he proves that all are equally sinners and liable to eternal death, so that no one could be saved by his own works. Therefore there is no reason why one should be puffed up against the other. Then, from the argument drawn from the knowledge of Christ, and of his grace and righteousness, he proves that Christ, although according to the flesh he is only from the seed of David and was promised only to the Israelites, nevertheless, insofar as he is Saviour, pertains to the Gentiles as much as to the Jews, and the effects of the promises likewise; so that whoever believes in Christ, whether Jew or Gentile, is saved through this faith and by this alone. Moreover, that anyone believes in Christ is something that neither Jew nor Gentile has from himself, but from God's free election. Therefore all boasting is excluded. Hence there is no reason why one should be arrogantly puffed up against the other, since all are equally saved freely through Christ, by faith in him divinely received. The argument, that is, the sum of what the Apostle treats there, is this: All are equally sinners, and liable to the wrath of God and to eternal death. But if some are saved, whether from the one people or from the other, all are saved by the grace of God alone, through faith in Christ, and not by works; and this is because God, before the foundation of the world, freely elected them to this gratuitous participation in salvation in Christ, all others having been rejected.

units.la: 4. Media porrò, quibus vtrumque hoc totius argumenti membrum explicat, probat, tractat, sparsa sunt in tota epistola. Quod primum membrum argumenti attinet, omnes ex æquo esse peccatores: principiò conuincit Gentes peccati ex iudiciis Dei super illas, maximè spiritualibus, vt sunt varia & fœda vitia. Item, ex lege naturali, quæ illarum conscientias accusat. Per legem vero Mosis, ipsos Iudæos. Quod vero ad alterum caput argumenti attinet, nempe omnes qui iustificantur, iustificari sola Dei gratia per fidem: partim rationibus a natura ductis, partim variis testimoniis veteris Testamenti probat. Hæc sunt media, quibus suum tractat argumentum. Nisi quis hæc obseruet[?] de principio, leget quidem et vagabitur, et multa bona colliget ex epistola: sed perfectum et integrum fructum nō percipiet, ignorato scopo et argumento Apostoli. Exemplum. Unde enim factum, ut Papistæ non intelligant Epistolam ad Romanos, eoque statuant, homines iustificari per opera moralia: Et Paulum, cum negat hominem iustificari ex operibus legis, ita interpretentur, quasi a iustificatione nostri, opera tantum legis ceremonialia excludantur, non autem moralia? Quia scopum et argumentum Apostoli non perceperunt in ea epistola, fuisse ut ostenderet, neminem hominum habere, cur glorietur coram Deo, et alter aduersus alterum insolescat[?], maxime in negotio salutis æternæ: idque propterea, quod omnes ex æquo sint peccatores, et omnes ex æquo egeant gloria Dei. Quomodo hoc potuisset concludere, si aliqui per opera moralia possent iustificari et seruari? An non illi, qui plus habuissent moralium bonorum operum, potuissent excipere: At nos habemus cur gloriemur aduersus eos, qui iis carent operibus Videmus igitur, quàm necessaria fit hæc regula, ad veram scripturæ cuiusvis intelligentiam.
units.tr: 4. The means, moreover, by which he explains, proves and treats each part of this whole argument are scattered through the whole epistle. As for the first part of the argument, that all are equally sinners: he first convicts the Gentiles of sin from the judgments of God upon them, chiefly spiritual ones, such as their various and foul vices. Likewise from the natural law, which accuses their consciences. Through the law of Moses, he convicts the Jews themselves. As for the second part of the argument, namely that all who are justified are justified by the grace of God alone through faith, he proves it partly by arguments drawn from nature and partly by various testimonies of the Old Testament. These are the means by which he treats his argument. Unless someone observes these things from the beginning, he will indeed read and wander, and gather many good things from the epistle, but he will not receive its perfect and whole fruit, since the aim and argument of the Apostle remain unknown. An example: whence does it come that the Papists do not understand the Epistle to the Romans, and so hold that men are justified by moral works; and when Paul denies that a man is justified by works of the law, they interpret it as if only the ceremonial works of the law were excluded from our justification, but not the moral? Because they did not grasp the aim and argument of the Apostle in that epistle, which was to show that no man has ground to glory before God, and that one should not be arrogantly puffed up against another, especially in the matter of eternal salvation; and this because all are equally sinners and all equally lack the glory of God. How could he have concluded this if some could be justified and saved by moral works? Would not those who had more of the moral good works be able to except themselves? But we have reason to glory against those who lack those works. We see, therefore, how necessary this rule is for the true understanding of any Scripture.

units.la: Exemplum particularis alicuius loci.
units.tr: An example of some particular passage.

units.la: Luc. 7. ex illis verbis CHRISTI, Remittuntur ei peccata multa, quia dilexit mul-tum, Papistæ collegerunt, propter opera charitatis remitti peccata. Vnde hæc impia doctrina, & falsa verborum Christi interpretatio? Non solum inde, quòd neque iuxta analogiam fidei, neque secundum alias scripturas interpretati sunt verba Christi: sed etiam inde, quòd non tenuerunt scopum Christi in ea parabola. Non is fuit, vt doceret, quibus mediis peccata remittantur: sed vt concluderet, illam fœminam non esse amplius peccatricem, vt putabat Pharisæus: ac proinde, neque se male fecisse, quòd sineret se à tali fœmina tangi, cùm non amplius sit peccatrix, sed iustior Pharisæo. Quare illa verba: Et ideo dico tibi, Remittuntur ei peccata multa, &c. non sunt simplex sententia, qua doceat, propter charitatem remitti peccata: sed conclusio, ex superioribus illata, quæ à posteriori, id est, ab effectu charitatis demonstrat, mulieri illi remissa esse peccata omnia, eoque iustam esse, & iustiorem Pharisæo. Sed quia Papistæ non spectarunt scopum: ideo & locum illum sua interpretatione corruperunt, & impium inde dogma collegecollegerunt. Liquet igitur, quàm necessaria sit hæc regula de obseruando semper scopo & argumento.
units.tr: In Luke 7, from those words of Christ, Her many sins are forgiven, for she loved much, the Papists gathered that sins are forgiven on account of works of charity. Whence this impious doctrine and false interpretation of the words of Christ? Not only because they have interpreted the words of Christ neither according to the analogy of faith nor according to other Scriptures, but also because they did not keep the aim of Christ in that parable. His purpose was not to teach by what means sins are forgiven, but to conclude that that woman was no longer a sinner, as the Pharisee thought, and therefore that he had not done wrong in allowing himself to be touched by such a woman, since she was no longer a sinner but more righteous than the Pharisee. Therefore those words: And so I say to you, her many sins are forgiven, etc. are not a simple statement by which he teaches that sins are forgiven on account of love, but a conclusion drawn from what precedes, which demonstrates from the effect, that is, from the effect of love, that all her sins had been forgiven to that woman, and that she was therefore righteous, and more righteous than the Pharisee. But because the Papists did not regard the aim, they corrupted that place by their interpretation and gathered from it an impious dogma. It is clear, therefore, how necessary this rule is, of always observing the aim and argument.

units.la: Hanc docet Christus Iohan. 5. Scrutamini scripturas, quia illæ testimonium perhibent de me.
units.tr: Christ teaches this in John 5: Search the Scriptures, for they bear witness of me.

units.la: Decima causa, cur permulti genuinum sa-lutaremq; sensum sacrarum Literarum non assequantur, est: quòd alij nimium inhærent τῷ ῥητῷ etiam cùm figuratæ sunt locutiones: & nullum in sacris Literis admittunt sensum, nisi quem verba sonant, quem literalem vocant, cùm tamen necessaria sit allegoria: Alij verò contrà, plus quàm par sit, allegoriis & tropologiis addicti sint, etiam vbi solus sufficit literalis: Ita fit, vt neque illi, neque isti in scripturarum cognitione proficiant, & mentem Spiritus sancti non percipiant. In primo genere multa peccabant Iudæi, etiam tempore Prophetarum & Apostolorum, & nunc etiam grauissimè peccant. Exemplum. Vt in præceptis de mactandis pecudibus, & offerendis Deo, denique in tota lege ceremoniali, nihil aliud intelligebant, nec volebant intelligere, nisi quod sonabat littera, externam illarum pecudum mactationem, & externas ceremoniarum laruas præcipi, cùm tamen Deus sub illis ceremoniis aliud intelligi voluerit, nempe, Christum cum primis (vt satis abundè & perspicuè docet Apostolus, cùm alibi, tum in Epistola ad Hebræos) & nostri mortificationem. Item vaticinia de RegnoChristi spirituali, sed sub typo regni alicuius temporalis & amplissimi: ad literam tantum volebant intelligi. Inde factum, ut negarint, & adhuc negent, Messiam venisse, & nostrum Iesum esse Messiam: propterea quod non vident, vaticinia illa, ad literam & iuxta illam suam crassam[?] interpretationem accepta, adimpleta esse. In hoc etiam primo genere peccant saepe Papistae, & alij cum illis, ut notum est, & maximè in verbis Coenae, cùm illa ad literam ita interpretantur, ut ea interpretatio cum analogia fidei, & aliis pugnet scripturis. Sic etiam Ori-genes, cùm illa verba Matth. 19. de castratis: ita ad literam interpretatus est, ut se castrandum curarit, Eufeb.lib.6 c.8.
units.tr: The tenth cause why very many do not attain the genuine and saving sense of the sacred Letters is this: that some cling too much to the τῷ ῥητῷ [the literal word] even when the expressions are figurative, and admit in the sacred Letters no sense except what the words sound, which they call literal, although allegory is necessary; others, on the contrary, are addicted to allegories and tropologies more than is fitting, even where the literal sense alone suffices. Thus it happens that neither these nor those make progress in the knowledge of the Scriptures, and do not perceive the mind of the Holy Spirit. In the first kind the Jews erred much, even in the time of the Prophets and Apostles, and now also they err most gravely. An example: in the precepts about slaughtering cattle and offering them to God, and finally in the whole ceremonial law, they understood and wished to understand nothing except what the letter sounded, namely that the external slaughter of those animals and the external masks of ceremonies were commanded, although God wished something else to be understood under those ceremonies, namely, first of all Christ (as the Apostle teaches abundantly and clearly, both elsewhere and in the Epistle to the Hebrews), and the mortification of ourselves. Likewise the prophecies about the spiritual Kingdom of Christ, given under the type of some temporal and very large kingdom, they wished to be understood only according to the letter. Hence it came about that they denied, and still deny, that the Messiah has come, and that our Jesus is the Messiah, because they do not see that those prophecies, taken literally and according to their own crude interpretation, have been fulfilled. In this first kind the Papists also often err, and others with them, as is well known, and especially in the words of the Supper, when they interpret them so literally that the interpretation fights with the analogy of faith and with other Scriptures. So also Origen, when he interpreted literally those words of Matthew 19 about eunuchs, so that he took care to have himself castrated (Eusebius, book 6, ch. 8).

units.la: In fecundo genere peccarunt multi patres, atque inprimis Origenes: terminos enim excessit in scripturis interpretandis ἀλ-ληγοεικῶς[?] ubi opus erat tantum literali sensu: ut satis notum est.
units.tr: In the second kind many of the Fathers erred, and above all Origen; for he went beyond the limits in interpreting the Scriptures allegorically, where only the literal sense was needed, as is well enough known.

units.la: Sic Papistae sacras Literas depravant saepenumerò suis interpretationibus & impiis allegoriis: ut illas, quae sunt de connubio Sacerdotum. 1.Timoth.3. Oportet Episcopum esse unius uxoris virum, aiunt, id est, unius Episcopatus Episcopum. Sic Haeretici alij, etiam tempore Apostolorum: ut qui dicta de resurrectione mortuorum, interpretabantur de spirituali animorum à peccatis resurrectione. Videmus peccatum fuisse, & adhuc peccari in utramque partem.
units.tr: Thus the Papists often corrupt the sacred Letters by their interpretations and impious allegories, as with those passages about the marriage of priests: 1 Timothy 3, A bishop must be the husband of one wife, they say, that is, a bishop of one bishopric. So also other heretics, even in the time of the Apostles, who interpreted the words about the resurrection of the dead as a spiritual resurrection of souls from sins. We see that this was a fault, and is still committed in both directions.

units.la: Regula igitur decima tenenda est & seruanda in lectione scripturarum. Quænam? Scia-mus scripturam, præter literalem, vt vocant, sensum, qui cumprimis semper spectandus & quærendus est, nonnunquam etiam opus habere allegorico, quem alij vocant spiri-tualem. Nam alij duo, quos multi probant, anagogicus & tropologicus seu moralis, ad allegoricum reducuntur. Hos enim tantum duos sensus reperio in scripturis, & traduntur à Spiritu sancto.
units.tr: The tenth rule, then, must be held to and observed in reading the Scriptures. Which one? We should know that Scripture, besides the literal sense, as they call it, which always has to be looked for and considered first, sometimes also needs the allegorical sense, which others call spiritual. For the other two senses, which many approve, the anagogical and the tropological or moral, are reduced to the allegorical. I find only these two senses in the Scriptures, and they are handed down by the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Literalis sensus est ille, quem ipsa vocabu-la sua consueta significatione, iuxta mentem Spiritus sancti, significant. Addo iuxta men-tem Spiritus sancti, quia si fit contra mentem Spiritus S. non potest esse verus scripturæ illius sensus: verbi gratia, cùm pugnat cum analogia fidei & aliis scripturis. Ut cùm Deus in scripturis dicitur dormire, habere caput, oculos, &c. Item, Si oculus tuus te scandalizauerit, erue illum. Sensus quem immediatè signifi-cant hæc verba, non potest dici literalis. Quare? quia non est iuxta mentem Spiritus sancti: cùm pugnet cum analogia fidei, & scripturis apertis. Alibi enim habemus, Deū non esse corpus, sed spiritum: neque dormi-re. Est igitur literalis sensus duplex: alius pro-prius & simplex: alius figuratus: verbi gratia, vt horum verbotum, Qui credit in me, habet vitam æternam, sensus est proprius & litera-lis, quem immediatè verba sonant. Horum autem Iohan.6. Qui manducat meam carnem, habet vitam æternam: sensus non literalis, sed figuratus est: Qui credit in me, habet vitam æternam. CHRISTVS enim ibidem explicat, quid sit manducare carnem suam, credere in se, illumque se vt cibum animæ reti[?]ere. Ergo etsi fit figuratus, literalis tamen esse non definit, quia de eadem est re. Nam oportet, vt sensus literalis semper sit verus & pius: non est autem semper pius & verus ille, qui immediatè è verbis colligitur, cùm sunt figuratè dicta. Ergo non potest ille esse verus literalis sensus, sed ille, qui ex figurata locutione colligitur iuxta mentem Spiritus sancti de eadem semper re. Hic sensus li-teralis semper in primis, & ante omnia quæ-rendus est, & solus valet ad dogmata pro-banda.
units.tr: The literal sense is the one which the words themselves signify in their usual meaning, according to the mind of the Holy Spirit. I add "according to the mind of the Holy Spirit," because if it runs contrary to the mind of the Holy Spirit it cannot be the true sense of that passage; for example, when it clashes with the analogy of faith and with other plain passages of Scripture. So when God is said in Scripture to sleep, to have a head, eyes, and so on; likewise, "If your eye offend you, pluck it out." The sense which these words signify immediately cannot be called literal. Why? Because it is not according to the mind of the Holy Spirit, since it conflicts with the analogy of faith and with plain Scripture. For elsewhere we have that God is not a body but a spirit, and does not sleep. The literal sense is therefore twofold: one proper and simple, the other figurative. For example, in the words "He who believes in me has eternal life," the sense is proper and literal, which the words immediately sound. But in John 6, "He who eats my flesh has eternal life," the sense is not literal but figurative: he who believes in me has eternal life. For Christ himself there explains what it is to eat his flesh: to believe in him and to receive him as food for the soul. So even though it is figurative, it does not cease to be literal, because it concerns the same matter. For the literal sense must always be true and godly; but that sense which is gathered immediately from the words is not always godly and true when the words are spoken figuratively. Therefore that cannot be the true literal sense, but the one which is drawn from the figurative expression according to the mind of the Holy Spirit about the same matter. This literal sense is always to be sought first and before all else, and it alone is valid for proving doctrines.

units.la: Allegoricus est, qui ex vero & pio literali sensu, postea per quandam similitudinem & consensionem colligitur, sive ad dogmata pertinens, sive ad mores. Est enim proprie allegoria, cùm præter id quod verè dicitur & fit, aliud etiam significatur, vel ad dogmata, vel ad mores pertinens.
units.tr: The allegorical sense is that which is drawn afterwards, by a certain likeness and correspondence, from the true and godly literal sense, whether it pertains to doctrines or to morals. For properly speaking there is allegory when, besides what is truly said and done, something else is also signified, pertaining either to doctrine or to morals.

units.la: Galat. 4. In Genesi est historia, Abraham duos filios habuisse ex duabus uxoribus. Literalis sensus verus & pius, iuxta mentem Spiritus S. est ille, quem immediatè significant verba historiæ. Ex hoc sensu tamen Apostolus per similitudinem alium colligit sensum, quem allegoriam vocat, de duobus Testamentis, idque per similitudinem inter illas duas uxores, & duo Testamenta, ut ipse expli-cat. Ideo allegoricus semper ex literali vero & pio, colligendus est, per similitudinem: Habet enim allegoria fundamentum in lite-terali vero sensu.
units.tr: Galatians 4. In Genesis there is the history that Abraham had two sons by two wives. The true and godly literal sense, according to the mind of the Holy Spirit, is the one which the words of the history immediately signify. From this sense, however, the Apostle by likeness draws another sense, which he calls allegory, concerning the two Testaments; and he does this by likeness between those two wives and the two Testaments, as he himself explains. Therefore the allegorical sense must always be drawn from the true and godly literal sense, by likeness; for allegory has its foundation in the true literal sense.

units.la: Est & hic duplex: unus qui colligitur ex literali sensu verarum historiarum, rerumque verè gestarum: alius, qui colligitur ex vero sensu literali verborum, sive proprio, sive figurato.
units.tr: This too is twofold: one which is drawn from the literal sense of true histories and things truly done; the other, which is drawn from the true literal sense of words, whether proper or figurative.

units.la: Exemplum primi, ut allegoria quæ est in Gal.4. Item, ut ille, qui ex historia Ionæ colligitur à Christo, de se: futurum se in corde terræ tribus diebus. Primùm historia est ve-ra, & res verè gesta: Deinde ex illo literali sensu, per similitudinem quandam colligi-tur sensus allegoricus. Exemplum secundi: ut ex verbis & præcepto de circumcidendo puero, literalis sensus colligitur, verè præ-putium carnis fuisse circumcidendum He-bræis. Hic sensus est verè literalis: quia so-nant hunc verba, & est iuxta mentem Spiri-tus S. Sed ex hoc alius colligitur allegoricus, isque etiam iuxta mentem Spiritus S. nempe circumcidendum esse cordis præputiū. Præ-cepti de mactandis hostiis sensus literalis est, oues fuisse mactandas. Sed hinc allegoricus & spiritualis, debere mortificare nos ipsos, & offerre Deo hostiam sanctam, &c. Hic sen-sus ad dogmata probanda per sese nil valet, sed potius ad probata iam confirmanda & exornanda, sicut & Apostolus facit ad Gal. 4.
units.tr: An example of the first is the allegory in Galatians 4. Likewise, that which Christ draws from the history of Jonah concerning himself: that he would be in the heart of the earth for three days. First, the history is true and the thing really happened; then from that literal sense an allegorical sense is drawn by a certain likeness. An example of the second: from the words and the command about circumcising the child, the literal sense is drawn, that the foreskin of the flesh was truly to be circumcised among the Hebrews. This sense is truly literal, because the words sound it and it is according to the mind of the Holy Spirit. But from this another allegorical sense is drawn, and that too according to the mind of the Holy Spirit: namely, that the foreskin of the heart is to be circumcised. The literal sense of the command about slaying sacrifices is that sheep were to be slain. But from this comes the allegorical and spiritual sense: that we ought to mortify ourselves and offer to God a holy sacrifice, and so on. This sense is of no use in itself for proving doctrines, but rather for confirming and adorning things already proved, just as the Apostle does at Galatians 4.

units.la: Tenenda igitur hæc regula ad veram intelligentiam scripturarum necessaria: Non semper inhærendum nudæ literæ, sed & verum literalem sensum esse eruendum, qui aliquando proprius est, aliquando figuratus: sæpe etiam allegoricum esse quærendum.
units.tr: This rule, therefore, is to be held as necessary for the true understanding of Scripture: one must not always cling to the bare letter, but the true literal sense must also be drawn out, which is sometimes proper and sometimes figurative; and often the allegorical sense is also to be sought.

units.la: Venio nunc ad regulas tertij generis, quibus utendum est post lectionem & intelligentiam scripturarum. Hæ sunt tres.
units.tr: I come now to the rules of the third kind, which are to be used after reading and understanding the Scriptures. There are three of these.

units.la: Prima, est gratiarum actio. Prima enim causa, cur Deus multos donata cognitione scripturarum privet, est ipsorum ingratitudo: quòd scilicet pro hoc beneficio non agunt debitas gratias, neque animo, neque verbis. Debemus igitur gratias agere mox Deo, tum universè pro aliis beneficiis innumeris, tum propriè pro hac vera scripturarum intelligentia, qua nos donavit: & has quidem gratias agere ex animo, si verè agnoverimus, quantum hoc sit beneficium, cognitio scilicet vera & salutaris verbi Dei, hoc est, voluntatis divinæ, & mysteriorum Cœlestium. Tale actantum est beneficium, ut nullum hoc maius invenire possit in toto terrarum Orbe. Maximum & incomparabile beneficium fuit, dedisse Filium in mortem pro salute nostra: sed quid nobis hoc profuisset, nisi per veram scripturarum intelligentiam hoc nobis revelasset & revelaret? Ergo si pro minimis quibusque beneficiis agendæ sunt gratiæ Deo: quantò magis pro hoc immenso, quod est cognitio scripturarum? Ac deinde simul est precandus Deus, vt quam largitus est cognitionem scripturæ, eam etiam infigat cordibus nostris per Spiritum suum sanctum, vt nunquam excidat.
units.tr: The first is thanksgiving. For the first cause why God deprives many of the knowledge of Scripture which he has given them is their ingratitude: namely, that they do not give due thanks for this benefit, either in heart or in words. We ought therefore to give thanks to God at once, both generally for his countless other benefits, and specifically for this true understanding of the Scriptures by which he has blessed us. And we give these thanks from the heart if we have truly recognised how great a benefit this is: namely, the true and saving knowledge of the Word of God, that is, of the divine will and of the heavenly mysteries. So great is this benefit that one cannot find a greater in the whole orb of the earth. It was a great and incomparable benefit that God gave his Son to death for our salvation; but what would this have profited us, unless through a true understanding of the Scriptures he had revealed it to us and still reveals it? Therefore, if thanks are to be given to God even for the smallest benefits, how much more for this immense one, which is the knowledge of the Scriptures? And then at the same time God is to be entreated that he would also fix in our hearts, through his Holy Spirit, the knowledge of Scripture which he has bestowed, so that it may never fall away.

units.la: Hanc regulam docet Apostolus, cùm gratias agit Deo pro Corinthiis, quòd eos Deus diuites effecerit in omni sermone, & in omni scientia. Idem in Epistola ad Philippenses, Colossenses, &c. Et precatur, vt crescant in omni cognitione Dei.
units.tr: The Apostle teaches this rule when he gives thanks to God for the Corinthians, that God has made them rich in every word and in all knowledge. The same in the Epistle to the Philippians, the Colossians, and so on. And he prays that they may grow in all knowledge of God.

units.la: Secunda causa, cur multi post acceptam cognitionem veritatis, veramque scripturarum cognitionem, in ea non perseuerent nec proficiant, est: quia non retinent verbum in animo, neque in eo meditantur, illudq; non ruminant. His quoque Deus tandem illam etiam, quam videbantur habere scientiam rerum, eripit vti ingratis, qui thesaurum hunc nihili faciunt, neque conseruandum curant.
units.tr: The second cause why many, after receiving the knowledge of the truth and a true knowledge of the Scriptures, do not persevere in it nor make progress, is that they do not retain the word in their mind, nor meditate upon it, nor ruminate on it. From these too God at length takes away even that knowledge of things which they seemed to have, as from the ungrateful, who make this treasure of no account and do not take care to keep it.

units.la: Regula igitur esto, vt verbum iam intelle-ctum Dei beneficio, ruminemus & medite-amur: & meditando ac ruminando, memoriæ & animo infigamus nostro. Hanc docet Dauid Psalm. 1. Beatus, qui meditatur in lege Domini die ac nocte.
units.tr: The rule, therefore, is that we should ruminate and meditate upon the word of God already understood by God's benefit, and by meditating and ruminating fix it in our memory and mind. David teaches this in Psalm 1: "Blessed is he who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night."

units.la: Tertia ac postrema causa, cur multi à cognita veritate, iusto Dei iudicio, deficiant, est aliud genus ingratitudinis, quòd scilicet vita & moribus non curent cognitam veritatem exprimere, sed veritatem detinent in iniusti-cia, vitaq; scelerata contaminant.
units.tr: The third and last cause why many fall away from the truth once known, by the just judgment of God, is another kind of ingratitude: namely, that they do not take care to express in life and morals the truth they have known, but hold the truth in unrighteousness and defile it with a wicked life.

units.la: Hanc ob causam Deus ea etiam cognitio-ne spoliat tanquam indignos, penes quos tantus maneat thesaurus.
units.tr: For this reason God also strips them of that knowledge, as unworthy persons with whom so great a treasure should not remain.

units.la: Hanc causam tradunt sacræ Literæ: Amos & reliqui Prophetæ ideo Israelitas spoliatum iri cognitione scripturarum, quia scelerate viverent, & cognitione verbi abuterentur ad suas iniquitates, longe ante prædixerunt. Proinde Amos dixit, Deum immissu-rum famem non panis, sed verbi sui. Roman. 1. Idem de gentibus testatur Apostolus, ea etiam Dei cognitione, quam ex creatarum rerum contemplatione, Dei beneficio, consecuti fuerant, spoliasse, & in reprobum sensum tradidisse, factosq; fuisse insipientes ac stultos: quia scilicet veritatem in iniusticia detinerent, & quia cum Deum cognouissent, non sicut Deum glorificaret. 1.Tim.1. idem testatur de quibusdam, præsertim de Hymenæo & Alexandro, Ideo naufragium fecisse circa fidem, id est, doctrinam fidei, quia bonam reiecissent conscientiam. Quid? quòd & Aristoteles fatetur in Ethicis, scientiam Ethicam tolli corruptione morum? quantò magis cognitionem scripturarum, veramq; Theologiam?
units.tr: Sacred letters hand down this cause: Amos and the other prophets foretold long before that the Israelites would be stripped of the knowledge of Scripture because they lived wickedly and abused the knowledge of the word for their iniquities. Accordingly Amos said that God would send a famine, not of bread, but of his word. Romans 1: the Apostle likewise testifies of the Gentiles that they had been stripped even of that knowledge of God which, by God's benefit, they had gained from contemplating created things, and had been given over to a reprobate mind, and had become foolish and senseless: because, namely, they held the truth in unrighteousness, and because, though they had known God, they did not glorify him as God. 1 Timothy 1: the same testifies of certain persons, especially Hymenaeus and Alexander, that they suffered shipwreck concerning the faith, that is, the doctrine of the faith, because they had rejected a good conscience. What of this, that Aristotle also admits in the Ethics that ethical knowledge is destroyed by the corruption of morals? How much more the knowledge of the Scriptures and true theology?

units.la: Sap.1. certè legitur, sapientiam non habita-turam in corpore subdito peccatis.
units.tr: Surely it is written in Sap. 1: "wisdom will not dwell in a body subject to sins."

units.la: Tertia igitur regula pro retinenda vera scripturarum cognitione, & augenda in nobis,est exercitium pietatis;hoc est,ut quæcunque legimus & intelligimus, ad nostrum accommodemus usum[?]: sive legis præcepta & exempla: sive Euangelij promissiones & consolationes : has ad corroborandam f-dem: illa ad instituendam vitam, bonamque retinendam conscientiam: alioquin inutilis, imo detrimetofa[?] fuerit nobis cognitio scri-pturarum. Nam finis,cur ea nos donet Deus, est, ut eam ad nostrum trahamus usum[?], ut li-quet Rom.4. Non est tantum scriptum propter Abrahamum, &c. 1.Cor.10. Hæc autem scripta sunt ad correctionem nostram. 2. Tim.3. Omnis scriptura diuinitus inspirata utilis est, &c. ut perfectus sit homo Dei, ad omne opus bonum perfecte instructus.
units.tr: The third rule, then, for retaining true knowledge of the Scriptures and increasing it in ourselves, is the exercise of piety. That is, whatever we read and understand we should apply to our own use: whether the precepts and examples of the law, or the promises and consolations of the Gospel. The latter serve to strengthen faith, the former to form the life and keep a good conscience. Otherwise knowledge of the Scriptures would be useless to us, indeed harmful. For the purpose for which God gives them to us is that we should turn them to our own use, as is clear from Rom. 4: "It was not written for Abraham alone, etc." 1 Cor. 10: "These things were written for our correction." 2 Tim. 3: "All Scripture is divinely inspired and profitable, etc., that the man of God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work."

units.la: Est igitur scripturis & fides fulcienda, corroboranda, stabilienda in Christum : & vita renouanda, bonaque conscientia retinenda.
units.tr: Therefore faith must be supported, strengthened and established in Christ by the Scriptures, and life must be renewed and a good conscience kept.

units.la: Hoc enim exercitio pietatis , ipsa etiam scripturarum cognitio & doctrina in nobis conseruatur.
units.tr: For by this exercise of piety, the very knowledge and teaching of the Scriptures is also preserved in us.

units.la: Hanc docet Apostolus 1.Tim.1. Retine fidem & bonam conscientiam, qua repulsa nonnulli fidei naufragium fecerunt.
units.tr: The Apostle teaches this in 1 Tim. 1: "Hold fast faith and a good conscience, which some, having rejected them, have suffered shipwreck of the faith."

units.la: 2. Tim.1. Bonum depositum custodi per Spiritum S. qui habitat in nobis, ambulando scilicet & viuendo non secundum carnem, sed secundum spiritum. Docet vitæ sanctitate quæ secundum spiritum, custodiri depositum scientiæ Dei.
units.tr: 2 Tim. 1: "Guard the good deposit through the Holy Spirit who dwells in us," that is, by walking and living not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit. He teaches that the deposit of the knowledge of God is guarded by a life of holiness, which is according to the Spirit.

units.la: 1.Pet.1. Hæc (de fide,veritate,pietate, charitate, ritate, & aliis Christianis virtutibus loquens) si vobis adsint (inquit) & exercerent: non constituent vos sine fructu in Domini nostri Iesu Christi cognitione. Ioh.14.v.21. Qui tenet praecepta mea, & seruat ea, is est, qui diligit me: Qui autem diligit me, diligetur a Patre meo, & ego diligam-eum: & manifestabo (scilicet clarius & plenius) ei me ipsum. Ergo profectus in cognitione Christi & scripturarum, est merces quae datur exercitio pietatis & dilectioni Christi. Ergo quàm haec tertia regula post lectionem scripturarum sit semper necessaria, vi-demus.
units.tr: 1 Pet. 1: "If these things (speaking of faith, truth, piety, charity, and other Christian virtues) are in you and abound," he says, "they will not leave you barren in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ." John 14:21: "He who holds my commandments and keeps them, he is the one who loves me; and he who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him, and will manifest (that is, more clearly and fully) myself to him." Therefore, progress in the knowledge of Christ and of the Scriptures is the reward given to the exercise of piety and love of Christ. Thus we see how this third rule is always necessary after the reading of the Scriptures.

units.la: Haec habui, quae dicerem de regulis accedendi ad lectionem scripturarum: legendi scripturas: & conferuandi in nobis cognitionem scripturarum, inque illis pro-ficiendi.
units.tr: These are the things I had to say about the rules for approaching the reading of the Scriptures, for reading them, and for preserving in ourselves the knowledge of the Scriptures and advancing in it.

units.la: Reliquum est, vt antequam finem huic quaestioni de regulis intelligendi & inter-pretandi scripturas, imponam: refutem Papistarum sententiam hac de re, multis in li-bris scriptam.
units.tr: It remains, before I put an end to this question of the rules for understanding and interpreting the Scriptures, to refute the opinion of the Papists on this matter, which they have written about in many books.

units.la: Aiunt causam, cur nos non recte scriptu-ras intelligamus (hoc enim praesupponunt) & interpretemur, esse, quod pro illarum in-telligentia, ad Ecclesiam Catholicam non recurramus: ac proinde primam ac praeci-puam, recte intelligendi scripturam, hanc esse regulam, vt scilicet ad Ecclesiam Catho-licam recurramus: Ibi enim tantum verum scripturae sensum retineri: vt qui ibi etiam tantùm iam inde à tempore Apostolorum, per Apostolos fuerit relictus.
units.tr: They say that the reason we do not rightly understand and interpret the Scriptures (for they presuppose this) is that we do not have recourse to the Catholic Church for their understanding. Hence the first and chief rule for rightly understanding Scripture is this: that we should have recourse to the Catholic Church, for only there is the true sense of Scripture preserved, which has been handed down there alone from the time of the Apostles, through the Apostles.

units.la: Pro confirmanda hac sententia, adferunt illud Apostoli ex 1. Tim.3. Ecclesia est fundamentum & columna veritatis.
units.tr: To confirm this opinion they bring forward the saying of the Apostle from 1 Tim. 3: "The Church is the pillar and ground of the truth."

units.la: In Ecclesia igitur Catholica quærendus est verus sensus scripturarum: quòd apud illam solam semper maneat.
units.tr: Therefore the true sense of the Scriptures is to be sought in the Catholic Church, because it always remains with her alone.

units.la: Secundò quædam ex Tertulliano & Irenæo, recurrendum ad Ecclesias Apostolicas pro interpretatione scripturarum, & cognitione veritatis.
units.tr: Secondly, they bring forward passages from Tertullian and Irenaeus, that one must have recourse to the Apostolic churches for the interpretation of Scripture and the knowledge of the truth.

units.la: Tertiò, quædam ex historia Tripartita l. 9. cap.19.
units.tr: Thirdly, they bring forward something from the Tripartite History, book 9, chapter 19.

units.la: Resp. Refutatio huius sententiæ pendet ex cognitione huius nominis ECCLESIÆ CATHOLICÆ. Primò significat cœtum fidelium à condito orbe, & vbique locorum, ad colendum Deum collectorum.
units.tr: Reply. The refutation of this opinion depends on understanding the meaning of the name "CATHOLIC CHURCH." First, it signifies the assembly of the faithful gathered from the beginning of the world and from all places to worship God.

units.la: Si in hac significatione Ecclesiam accipiunt: dico, sententiam Papisticam de recurrendo ad Ecclesiam Catholicam, pro af-sequenda vera scripturarum intelligentia, pugnare cum verbo Dei, esse iniquam, & impossibilem.
units.tr: If they take the Church in this sense, I say that the Papistical opinion, that one should have recourse to the Catholic Church in order to attain the true understanding of Scripture, is contrary to the Word of God, unjust, and impossible.

units.la: Cum verbo Dei pugnat. Nam verbum Dei docet, verum scripturarum intellectum, quærendum esse apud Deum, primùm in Cœlo precibus: Deinde apud eundem Deum in scripturis ipsis loquentem, sedula scripturarum lectione & collatione, quemadmodum paulò antè ostendimus: non autem apud Ecclesiam Catholicam ubiq; diffusam.
units.tr: It is contrary to the Word of God. For the Word of God teaches that the true sense of Scripture is to be sought from God: first in heaven by prayer; then from the same God speaking in the Scriptures themselves, by diligent reading and comparison of the Scriptures, as we showed a little earlier; but not from the Catholic Church spread everywhere.

units.la: De primo , quòd precibus sit quærendus a-pud Deum, liquet. Docet enim Apostolus 1.Cor.2 Non nisi per Spiritum sanctum pos-se apprehendi & intelligi S. Scripturam. Hunc verò spiritum vult Dominus à se peti precibus,& obtineri,ut est Luc.11.Ideo Apo-stolus diligenter precatur Ecclesiis spiritum sapientiæ & revelationis, ad sciendum quæ sit spes vocationis Christi, quæ latitudo & profunditas: ad probandum quæ sunt præstantia,&c. Videan-tur loci Ephes.1.& 3. Phil.1. Col.1. Sic Da-uid Psalm.119.
units.tr: As to the first point, that it is to be sought from God by prayer, this is clear. For the Apostle teaches that Scripture cannot be apprehended and understood except through the Holy Spirit. This Spirit the Lord wills to be asked for and obtained by prayer, as in Luke 11. Therefore the Apostle earnestly prays that the churches may receive "the spirit of wisdom and revelation, to know what is the hope of Christ's calling, what its breadth and depth are, to prove what things are excellent, etc." Let the passages in Eph. 1 and 3, Phil. 1, Col. 1 be consulted. So David in Psalm 119.

units.la: De secundo : quòd scilicet diligenti scri-pturarum lectione & collatione ac scruta-tione quærenda sit vera scripturæ intelli-gentia,etiam liquet:Iohan.5. scrutamini scri-pturas,&c. 1.Timoth.4. Attende lectioni. Actor.17. 2.Pet.1. Docet ibi certè Apostolus, per ipsum Dei scriptum verbum, tanquam per lucernam accensam & lucentem, reliqua omnia, ut obscura & tenebricosa, illuminan-da & declaranda esse : ac proinde omnes, qui pia diligentia sacras Scripturas legunt, & peruestigant : eos posse non solùm illas intelligere ad salutem : sed etiam omnem aliam doctrinam ex illis sibi discernere & confirmare. Sic Christus & Apostoli suam doctrinam per testimonia Prophetarum confirmabant, tanquam per notiora & clariora. Pugnat igitur cum verbo Dei, quæ-rendum esse intellectum scripturæ alibi, quàm apud Deum precibus, & in scripturis ipsis.
units.tr: As to the second: that the true understanding of Scripture is to be sought by diligent reading, comparison and searching of the Scriptures, this is also clear. John 5: "Search the Scriptures, etc." 1 Tim. 4: "Attend to reading." Acts 17. 2 Pet. 1. There the Apostle certainly teaches that all other things, as obscure and dark, are to be illuminated and made clear through the written Word of God itself, as through a lamp lit and shining. And therefore all who read and diligently search the sacred Scriptures with pious care are able not only to understand them unto salvation, but also to discern and confirm for themselves all other doctrine from them. Thus Christ and the Apostles confirmed their doctrine by the testimonies of the Prophets, as by things better known and clearer. It is therefore contrary to the Word of God to seek the understanding of Scripture elsewhere than from God by prayer and in the Scriptures themselves.

units.la: 2. Pugnat cum ratione, & est iniquum, Deus enim, vt Pater noster, scripturam suam nobis proposuit vt filiis: in quem finem? vt nos sapientes reddat ad salutem, & ad omnia bona opera. 2. Tim. 3. Ergo proposuit eam claram & perspicuam, vt si velimus voluntatem Patris cognoscere, eam possimus e scripturis percipere. Nam hoc postulat nostra salus. Proinde ante ostendi, scripturam esse perspicuam, praesertim in iis, quae ad salutem nostram pertinent. Quis inter nos pater est, qui si filiis suis loqui sciat & possit perspicuè, & sua mandata tradere clara: velit eis loqui obscurè, ita vt si velint ea intelligere praecepta, cogantur huc atque illuc ad varios homines, qui ea explicent, recurrere? Nemo certè, praesertim si in illis scriptis & praeceptis tota liberorum salus consistat: sed ita sua tradet praecepta liberis suis, vt quisque illorum, si velit diligenter audire & legere, ea etiam possit intelligere. Annon igitur iniquum, aliter sentire de nostro Cœlesti Patre, nostri amantissimo sapientissimoque? eum ita obscurè loqui nobis voluisse, vt si velimus illius mandata & voluntatem intelligere, cogamur ad omnes homines ubique & in omni tempore recurrere? Nam quid est Ecclesia Catholica, nisi Cœtus fidelium, ubiq; & in omni tempore, in fide CHRISTI collectus? Pugnat igitur etiam cum ratione, verum scripturæ intellectum quærendum esse apud Ecclesiam Catholicam.
units.tr: 2. It is contrary to reason and unjust. For God, as our Father, has set forth his Scripture to us as to his children. To what end? That he might make us wise unto salvation and unto all good works (2 Tim. 3). Therefore he has set it forth clear and perspicuous, so that if we wish to know the will of the Father, we may be able to perceive it from the Scriptures. For our salvation requires this. Hence I showed before that Scripture is perspicuous, especially in those things which pertain to our salvation. Who among us is a father who, knowing how and being able to speak to his sons plainly and to deliver his commands clearly, would wish to speak to them obscurely, so that if they want to understand those precepts they are forced to run here and there to various men to explain them? Surely no one, especially if the whole salvation of the children consists in those writings and precepts; rather he would deliver his precepts to his children so that each of them, if he is willing to listen and read diligently, could also understand them. Is it not therefore unjust to think otherwise of our heavenly Father, who loves us most and is most wise, that he wished to speak to us so obscurely that if we want to understand his commands and will, we must have recourse to all men everywhere and at all times? For what is the Catholic Church but the assembly of the faithful, gathered everywhere and at all times, in the faith of Christ? It is therefore also contrary to reason that the true understanding of Scripture is to be sought in the Catholic Church.

units.la: 2. Est etiam res impossibilis. Nam Ecclesia Catholica, ut dixi, congregatio est fidelium omnium, quotquot unquam fuerunt à condito Orbe. Fieri autem non potest, ut omnes isti simul congregati inveniantur, & ab iis veram scripturæ intelligentiam petamus. Est ergo ἀδιάλωτον[?], ut in Ecclesia Catholica quæramus verum scripturæ sensum.
units.tr: 2. It is also an impossible thing. For the Catholic Church, as I said, is the congregation of all the faithful, of all who have ever been from the beginning of the world. But it cannot happen that all of them are found gathered together at once, and that we ask from them the true understanding of Scripture. It is therefore impossible that we should seek the true sense of Scripture in the Catholic Church.

units.la: At, inquient, non ita intelligimus, recurrendum esse ad omnes fideles: sed ut scripturas interpretemini & intelligatis iuxta sensum Catholicæ Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: But, they will say, we do not mean that one must have recourse to all the faithful, but that you should interpret and understand the Scriptures according to the sense of the Catholic Church.

units.la: Resp. At ubi expressus est sensus scripturæ iuxta mentem Catholicæ Ecclesiæ. Si aliquis extaret talis liber: aliquid suaderent certi, & possibile. Sed nullus extat. Ergo rem impossibilem proponunt. At, inquiunt, habemus Patres, Ecclesiæ Catholicæ Doctores: ab il-lis petatur.
units.tr: Response: But when the sense of Scripture according to the mind of the Catholic Church has been clearly set out, if some such book existed, they would be suggesting something certain and possible. But none exists. Therefore they propose an impossible thing. "But," they say, "we have the Fathers, the teachers of the Catholic Church: let the answer be sought from them."

units.la: Resp. Si nomine Catholicæ Ecclesiæ Patres intelligitis, & iubetis nos stare illorum interpretationibus: rem etiam proponitis, primo pugnantem cum verbo Dei, deinde iniquam, & impossibilem simul. Cum verbo Dei pugnantem: quia Apostolus 1. Thes. 5. iubet quidem, ne prophetias & interpretes contemnamus: sed iubet etiam, ut cum iudicio legamus: omnia probemus, si ea tantum, quæ bona, sunt, teneamus. Prohibet igitur, vt pendeamus ab interpretationibus Patrum, sine iudicio & delectu[?].
units.tr: Response: If by the name of the Catholic Church you mean the Fathers, and you bid us abide by their interpretations, you propose a thing which, first, contradicts the Word of God; second, is unjust; and at the same time impossible. It contradicts the Word of God, because the Apostle in 1 Thess. 5 indeed bids us not to despise prophesyings and interpreters, but also bids us read with judgment: "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good." He therefore forbids us to depend on the interpretations of the Fathers without judgment and discrimination.

units.la: Deinde Patres inter se non consentiunt in explicationibus scripturarum: imo saepe nec singuli secum. Quomodo igitur possumus esse certi, eos tradere sensum illum scripturarum, quem Catholica Ecclesia probat?
units.tr: Then, the Fathers do not agree among themselves in their explanations of Scripture; indeed often not even each one with himself. How, then, can we be certain that they hand down that sense of Scripture which the Catholic Church approves?

units.la: Praeterea apparet multas ab illis scripturarum interpretationes allatas, quae minime sint consentaneae cum ipsis scripturis, & cum analogia fidei: qualis est illa interpretatio Syricij Papae, in illum Pauli locum ad Rom.8. Qui in carne sunt, Deo placere non possunt: hoc est, (vt ipse Syricius interpretatur) qui sunt in matrimonio: Et habetur in Tom.1. Concil. inter decreta Syricij, cap.7. An non haec interpretatio pugnat cum verbis Apostoli, Heb.13. Coniugium honorabile est inter omnes, & cubile impollutum: & aliena a mente Apostoli eo in loco ad Rom. Qualis & illa Hieronymi contra Iouinianum, in illum Pauli locum 1.Cor.7. Bonum est homini, mulierem non tangere: hoc est (inquit ille) malum est & peccatum, mulierem tangere. Innumerae apud Patres reperiuntur scripturarum interpretationes, aliae absurdae, aliae impiae. Annon igitur iniquum est, iubere, vt Patrum interpretationes, simpliciter recipiamus.
units.tr: Besides, it appears that many interpretations of Scripture have been put forward by them which are by no means consistent with Scripture itself and with the analogy of faith. Such is that interpretation of Pope Siricius on that passage of Paul in Romans 8: "Those who are in the flesh cannot please God," that is (as Siricius himself explains it) those who are in marriage. And it is found in Tom. 1 of the Councils, among the decrees of Siricius, chapter 7. Does not this interpretation conflict with the words of the Apostle in Hebrews 13: "Marriage is honourable among all, and the bed undefiled"; and is it not foreign to the mind of the Apostle in that place in Romans? Such also is that interpretation of Jerome against Jovinian, on that passage of Paul in 1 Cor. 7: "It is good for a man not to touch a woman"; that is (he says) it is evil and a sin to touch a woman. Countless interpretations of Scripture are found among the Fathers, some absurd, some impious. Is it not therefore unjust to bid us simply accept the interpretations of the Fathers?

units.la: Tertio, Si etiam nomine Ecclesiae intelligatis particulares Ecclesias, quae in diuersis sunt locis, quae inter Catholicas numerantur, tut[?], & ad eas iubeatis nos ite pro vera scri-pturæ intelligentia.
units.tr: Thirdly, if by the name of the Church you mean the particular churches which exist in various places and are counted among the Catholic ones, and bid us go to them for the true understanding of Scripture...

units.la: Resp. Hoc etiam fieri nequit, & est iniquum. Nam etsi aliàs fuerint puræ: nunc certè omnes sunt corruptæ variis abusibus, erroribus, præsumtionibus, vt etiam olim scripsit Augustinus T.2.ad Ianuarium.
units.tr: Response: This also cannot be done, and it is unjust. For although they may once have been pure, now indeed all of them are corrupted by various abuses, errors and presumptions, as Augustine also wrote long ago in his second volume, to Januarius.

units.la: Quarto, At licet aliæ, vt Græcanicæ, sint corruptæ: non tamen Ecclesia Romana: Et de hac loquimur: ad hanc recurrendum. Est enim illa Ecclesia, de qua Matth.16. Et super hanc Petram (Petrum) ædificabo Ecclesiam meam, & porta inferi non prævalebunt ei. Et Papæ, successores sunt Petri, de cuius fide dixit Christus Luc.22. Rogaui pro te, Petre, vt non deficiat fides tua.
units.tr: Fourthly, but although other churches, such as the Greek, are corrupt, the Roman Church is not: and it is of this that we speak; to this we must have recourse. For it is that Church of which Matthew 16 says: "And upon this rock (Peter) I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it." And the Popes are the successors of Peter, of whose faith Christ said in Luke 22: "I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail."

units.la: Resp. Vetus est cantilena Romanensium, & toties refutata, vt pudeat me respondere ad has nugas. Summa tamen hæc est.
units.tr: Response: This is an old refrain of the Romanists, and so often refuted that I am ashamed to answer these trifles. Nevertheless, the sum of it is this.

units.la: Primo, falsum est, Romanam Ecclesiam manifestè integram & puram in doctrina: imò nulla corruptior, vt jam totus novit orbis. Quod ad mores attinet: nulla scelerarior[?].
units.tr: First, it is false that the Roman Church is manifestly whole and pure in doctrine; indeed none is more corrupt, as the whole world already knows. As for morals, none is more wicked.

units.la: Secundo, iniuria fit Christo, & Spiritui S. Quod Christus de tota Ecclesia Electorum dixit, Porta inferi non prævalebunt ei, &c. illud de Ecclesia speciatim Romana dictum interpretari, tali præsertim, qualis est hæc præsens: Et super petram, interpretari super personam Petri.
units.tr: Second, injury is done to Christ and to the Holy Spirit. What Christ said of the whole Church of the Elect, "The gates of hell shall not prevail against it," etc., to interpret it as said specifically of the Roman Church, especially in such a form as this present one: "upon this rock," to interpret it as "upon the person of Peter."

units.la: Tertio, probari nequit, Papas esse succes-sores Petri, etiam in loco & Episcopatu: im-pium pium vero & impudentissimum, dicere esse successores in doctrina: quasi Petrus hanc, quam ipsi docent, etiam ipse docuerit. Sacrilegum autem, si Papæ sibi spiritum Petri vsurpent. Nam ab operibus eorum cognoscetis eos, &c. Et Decr. dist. 40. per totum: maxime Can. 2. Non est facile. Item c. 2. q. 7. c. 28. Non omnes. Non sanctorum filij sunt, qui tenent loca sancta, sed qui exercent opera eorum. Non sunt igitur successores sanctorum, omnes qui eorum tenent loca, sed qui spiritum & fidem eorum retinent.
units.tr: Third, it cannot be proved that the Popes are successors of Peter, even in place and bishopric; to say that they are successors in doctrine is impious, and indeed shameless in the extreme, as if Peter had taught what they teach. It would be sacrilegious, moreover, if the Popes usurped the spirit of Peter: "For by their works you will know them," etc. And Decretum, dist. 40, throughout, especially canon 2, "Non est facile"; likewise c. 2, q. 7, c. 28, "Non omnes": "They are not the children of the saints who hold holy places, but those who practise their works." Therefore not all who hold the places of the saints are their successors, but those who retain their spirit and faith.

units.la: Quarto, Donum interpretandi non est alligatum Romæ & ad Episcopos Romanos: sed Deus dat cui vult, etiam non Episcopis. Num. 11. Quis tribuat, ut omnis populus prophe-tet? Et det eis Dominus spiritum suum? Amos 7. Non sum Propheta, neque filius Propheta sum: & tamen prophetabat. 2. Pet 1. Prophetia non est privata interpretationis: sed opus est spiritu illo, quo etiam Prophetæ locuti sunt. Hanc autem dat, cui vult Deus, 1. Cor. 12.
units.tr: Fourth, the gift of interpreting is not tied to Rome and to the Roman bishops; God gives it to whom he wills, even to those who are not bishops. Numbers 11: "Would that all the people might prophesy! Would that the Lord would put his Spirit upon them!" Amos 7: "I am no prophet, nor the son of a prophet," and yet he prophesied. 2 Peter 1: "No prophecy is of private interpretation"; but there is need of that Spirit by whom even the prophets spoke. Now he gives this to whom God wills, 1 Cor. 12.

units.la: Cùm igitur in toto terrarum orbe nullos habeamus vel homines, vel libros, qui possint nos facere certiores de vero intellectu scripturarum, nisi ipsas sacras Literas: manifestum est eos errare, qui docent, eum esse quærendum in sola Ecclesia Catholica. Multò gravius, qui docent, intelligendas esse scripturas secundum doctrinam, quam nunc tenet & prædicat Ecclesia Romana: quemadmodum audio ex viris fide dignissimis nunc fieri in Italia. Paucis ab hinc annis fuit omnibus interdictum lectione Bibliorum: sed si qui vellet legere, praesentaret se coram Episcopo & inquisitore: & hic juraret, se Biblia non aliter intellecturum aut explicaturum, nisi secundum doctrinam, quam nunc tenet & praedicat Ecclesia Romana: hoc est, quae loca ipsa interpretatur de purgatorio, de Missae sacrificio, de confessione, de coelibatu, &c. eadem quoque ipse, qui velit lege-re Biblia, juret se intellecturum & interpretaturum. O Diabolicam tyrannidem.
units.tr: Since, then, throughout the whole world we have no men or books which can make us more certain of the true meaning of Scripture, except the sacred Scriptures themselves, it is plain that those err who teach that it is to be sought in the Catholic Church alone. Far more gravely err those who teach that Scripture must be understood according to the doctrine which the Roman Church now holds and preaches, as I hear from most trustworthy men is now happening in Italy. A few years ago the reading of the Bible was forbidden to all; but if anyone wished to read, he presented himself before the bishop and the inquisitor, and this man swore that he would not understand or expound the Bible otherwise than according to the doctrine which the Roman Church now holds and preaches: that is, which interprets those passages about purgatory, about the sacrifice of the Mass, about confession, about celibacy, etc. In the same way the man who wishes to read the Bible must swear that he will understand and interpret it thus. O diabolical tyranny!

units.la: Confutatur etiam haec sententia & regula Papistica ex Augustino. D. Augustinus Tomo 3. scripsit 4. libros de doctrina Christia-na: ac tribus prioribus tradidit regulas quas-cunque potuit, & quascunque iudicavit fore ad veram scripturae intelligentiam conse-quendam utiles. Illis enim tribus libris voluit docere, quomodo Concionator, seu doctor Ecclesiae posset verum sacrae Scripturae sensum consequi. In quarto autem, quomodo posset aliis illum utiliter proponere. Inter omnes autem illas regulas, nunquam haec posuit, quam nunc tradunt Papistae. Non vi-dit igitur Augustinus esse utilem, multo minus necessariam. Summa autem omnium illorum librorum haec est, quam nosse non in-utile fuerit.
units.tr: This Papist opinion and rule is also refuted from Augustine. St. Augustine in his third volume wrote four books on Christian doctrine; and in the first three he set down whatever rules he could, and whatever he judged useful for attaining the true understanding of Scripture. For in those three books he wished to teach how a preacher or teacher of the Church could attain the true sense of Holy Scripture. In the fourth, however, how he could usefully set that forth to others. Among all those rules, however, he never laid down the one that the Papists now hand down. Augustine therefore did not see it to be useful, much less necessary. The sum of all those books, which it will not be useless to know, is this.

units.la: Primo libro summatim docet: tenendum esse cum primis scopum scripturarum omnium: hunc esse, charitatem in Deum & proximum per Christum: 2. nec solum te-nendum esse mente & intelligentia, sed etiam usu & exercitatione. In iis enim duobus præceptis, exercendum nobis esse: Et 3. sic rebus præsentibus esse vtendum, vt per eas, geminam hanc charitatem in nobis & in aliis promoueamus. Hæc est summa primi libri. Docet in summa, quales & quali animo debeamus accedere ad lectionem scripturarum, si velimus eas recte intelligere, & in eis proficere. Et hæc regula est ne-cessaria.
units.tr: In the first book he teaches in summary that the aim of all Scripture must above all be held: that this is love toward God and neighbour through Christ; second, that one must hold to it not only in mind and understanding but also in practice and exercise. For in those two precepts we must exercise ourselves. And third, that present things must be so used that through them we may promote this twofold love in ourselves and in others. This is the summary of the first book. He teaches, in brief, with what kind of character and mind we ought to approach the reading of Scripture, if we wish to understand it rightly and make progress in it. And this rule is necessary.

units.la: In secundo libro docet, multum utilitatis ad veram scripturarum cognitionem adfer-re, mediocrem saltem linguarum, quibus de principio scriptæ fuerunt, cognitionem. 2. diligentem interpretationum diuersarum collationem. 3. mediocrem artium libera-lium, bonarumque disciplinarum cognitionem. Sed inprimis, vt animus vera pietate, mansuetudine & spontanea obedientia veritati inhæreat: Et in charitate Dei & proximi, firmas agat radices, firmumq; ponat fundamen-tum.
units.tr: In the second book he teaches that a good deal of benefit toward a true knowledge of Scripture is brought by at least a moderate knowledge of the languages in which it was first written; second, a diligent comparison of various interpretations; third, a moderate knowledge of the liberal arts and good disciplines. But above all, that the mind should cling to the truth with true piety, meekness and willing obedience, and should put down firm roots and lay a firm foundation in love of God and neighbour.

units.la: In tertio, magnam docet diligentiam & cautionem in scripturis legendis adhiben-dam esse: 1. vt singula verba & locutiones recte discernantur: vt quænam propriæ, quæ metaphoricæ & figuratæ sint. 2. Vt discer-nantur signa sacramentorum, à rebus ipsis: ne signa pro rebus accipiamus, & contra. Et præterea alia, etiam habet hæc verba, contra Papistas. cap.9. Ut autem literam sequi, & signa pro rebus, quae iis significantur, accipere, servulus infirmitatis est : ita inutiliter signa interpretari, male vagantis erroris est : Et ibi mentionem fecerat Baptismi & Cœnæ. Deinde tradit alias regulas, tum ex Ticonio, tum ex suo iudicio, quae omnes eo spectant, ut sensus scripturae omnibus in locis, proprie deprehendi & percipi possit. Nunquam autem haec regula citatur ab Augustino, quam Papistae tanquam praecipuam, & summe necessariam urgent: ut scilicet quaeratur primum, quid universalis Ecclesia de unoquoq; scripturae loco senserit. Vidit enim hoc fore impossibile. Sed hoc in summa & perpetuo docet, ut obscuriora per clariora explicando, scripturas per scripturas interpretemur: atque ita genuinus scripturae sensus inveniatur. Magnificè enim & salubriter (lib. 2. cap.6.) Spiritus S. ita Scripturas sacras modificaunt, ut locis apertioribus fami occurreret: obscurioribus autem fastidia detergeret. Nihil enim fere de illius obscuritate erui tur quod non planissime dictum alibi reperiatur.
units.tr: In the third book he teaches that great diligence and caution must be applied in reading the Scriptures: (1) that individual words and expressions be correctly distinguished, so that we know which are proper, which metaphorical and figurative. (2) That the signs of the sacraments be distinguished from the things themselves, so that we do not take signs for things, and the reverse. And besides, he has these other words, also against the Papists, chap. 9: But to follow the letter, and to take signs for the things signified by them, is the mark of a slavish weakness; and to interpret signs uselessly is the mark of a wildly wandering error. And there he had made mention of Baptism and the Supper. Then he hands down other rules, both from Ticonius and from his own judgment, all of which aim at this: that the sense of Scripture may be properly grasped and perceived in all places. This rule, however, which the Papists urge as chief and most necessary, namely that one should first inquire what the universal Church has thought about each passage of Scripture, is never cited by Augustine. For he saw that this would be impossible. But in summary and throughout he teaches that we should interpret Scripture by Scripture, explaining the obscure by the clearer, and so the genuine sense of Scripture is found. For magnificently and beneficially (book 2, chap. 6) the Holy Spirit so tempers the sacred Scriptures that the plainer places meet hunger, while the obscurer ones remove weariness. For almost nothing is drawn out of its obscurity that is not found said most plainly elsewhere.

units.la: Nunc respondeo ad illorum fundamenta.
units.tr: Now I answer to their foundations.

units.la: 1. Tim.3. Ecclesia est columna & stabilimentum veritatis : Ergo ad illam recurrendum pro cognitione veritatis.
units.tr: 1 Tim. 3. The Church is the pillar and ground of the truth. Therefore one must have recourse to it for the knowledge of the truth.

units.la: Resp. ad Antecedens. Ideo dicitur columna & stabilimentum veritatis, quatenus fundamento verbi superstructa est, & in eo, quod certissimè continetur in scripturis, firma consistit. Quòd si aliqua in re erret, & declinet à veritate: eatenus non est columna veritatis, & ea re audienda non est. At quam dabis mihi Ecclesiam, de qua certus sim, quòd non erret vlla in re?
units.tr: Answer to the antecedent. It is called the pillar and ground of the truth insofar as it is built upon the foundation of the Word and stands firm in what is most certainly contained in the Scriptures. But if it errs in any matter and departs from the truth, then to that extent it is not a pillar of the truth, and it is not to be heard in that matter. But what Church will you give me of which I may be certain that it errs in no matter whatever?

units.la: 1. Ad consequentia: Cùm ais, Ergo ad Ecclesiam recurrendum est pro cognitione veritatis: interrogo ad quam? Ad Catholicam? Est impossibile. Ad hanc vel illam? Non sequitur illatio, & est ὁμωνυμία in nomine Ecclesiæ: pro vniuersali Electorum, & pro particulari. Illud enim dictum Apostoli, intelligitur de Ecclesia in genere, id est, de Electis, qui sunt vera Ecclesia, & in veritate persistunt. Illatio autem fit de particularibus Ecclesiis, vbi etiam hypocritæ, imperiti scripturarum, qui non sunt Ecclesia. Item, Ecclesia, quæ est columna & stabilimentum veritatis, aliter non intelligit nec interpretatur scripturas, quàm per Spiritum sanctum, & diligentem scripturarum perscrutationem & collationem.
units.tr: 1. As to the consequence: when you say, "Therefore one must have recourse to the Church for the knowledge of the truth," I ask: to which one? To the Catholic Church? That is impossible. To this or that one? The inference does not follow, and there is an equivocation in the name "Church": it is used of the universal body of the elect and of a particular church. That saying of the Apostle is understood of the Church in general, that is, of the elect, who are the true Church and persist in the truth. The inference, however, is drawn about particular churches, where there are also hypocrites and the unlearned in the Scriptures, who are not the Church. Likewise, the Church, which is the pillar and ground of the truth, does not understand or interpret the Scriptures otherwise than through the Holy Spirit and diligent searching and comparing of the Scriptures.

units.la: Ad dicta Tertulliani, & Irenæi, recurren-dum ad Ecclesias Apostolicas: antè responsum à nobis fuit, in Quæstione 8. quæ fuit de perfectione scripturarum, in responsione ad argumenta tertiæ classis, nempe ab authoritatibus Patrum ducta. Summa est:
units.tr: As to the sayings of Tertullian and Irenaeus, that one must have recourse to the apostolic churches: we have answered this before, in Question 8, which concerned the perfection of the Scriptures, in the answer to the arguments of the third class, namely those drawn from the authority of the Fathers. The summary is:

units.la: 1. Non esse has Ecclesias, quales illæ, de quibus illi Patres.
units.tr: 1. These churches are not such as those of which those Fathers spoke.

units.la: 2. Non de omni veritate, & de omni scripturæ sensu, eos fuisse locutos: sed de præci-puis fidei articulis.
units.tr: 2. They did not speak of every truth and of every sense of Scripture, but of the principal articles of the faith.

units.la: 3. Tunc demum prouocasse ad Eccle-siam : cùm Hæretici reiiciebant scripturas.
units.tr: 3. They appealed to the Church only when the heretics rejected the Scriptures.

units.la: 4. Ideo ad illas prouocasse, quia apud il-las manebat veritas. Dent igitur tales Eccle-sias: efficiant, vt apud illas maneat veritas: Tunc recurremus ad illas.
units.tr: 4. They appealed to it because the truth remained among them. Let them therefore produce such churches, let them bring it about that the truth remains among them: then we will have recourse to them.

units.la: Tripartita historia lib.9.cap.19. liquet: Com-munem (inquiunt) fuisse veterum conciliorum consuetudinem, vt si quando olim inter Catholicos & hæreticos concertatio oriretur de vero scripturarum intellectu, diligenter inuestigaretur, quid Patres, qui precesserant ad tempora usque Apostolorum, de illis scripturis sensissent. Ergo idem debet etiam nunc fieri: & petenda vera scripturarum intelligentia à Patribus.
units.tr: It is clear from the Tripartite History, book 9, chap. 19: "It was (they say) the common custom of the ancient councils that, if ever a dispute arose between Catholics and heretics about the true sense of the Scriptures, it was carefully investigated what the Fathers, who had gone before back to the times of the Apostles, had thought of those Scriptures. Therefore the same ought to be done now too, and the true understanding of the Scriptures should be sought from the Fathers."

units.la: Resp. 1. Falsum est assumtum. In eo loco, quem citant ex historia Tripartita, tantùm legimus, Agelium quendam, Episcopum Nouatianum hoc dedisse consilij, idque per Sisinnium suum lectorem, vt hoc quærere-tur ab Arianis : An doctores Ecclesiæ, qui ante illam fuissent sectam, recipere, eorumq; auctoritate acquiescere vellet, nec ne. Sed nihil profuit. Imò contra se res habet. Patres enim in conciliis semper soliti fuerunt sua defendere, & hæreticorum refutare dogmata, per S. literas, vt liquet. Et sic Constantinus ille Magnus in Concilio Nicæno hortatus est Patres, vt est apud Eusebium. Item Tripart. hist. lib. 2. cap. 5.
units.tr: Answer. First, the assumption is false. In the passage they cite from the Tripartite History we read only that a certain Agelius, bishop of the Novatians, gave this advice, and that through his reader Sisinnius, it was to be asked of the Arians whether they wished to receive the teachers of the Church who had lived before that sect, and to rest upon their authority, or not. But it did no good. Indeed, the matter stands against them. For the Fathers in councils were always accustomed to defend their own positions and to refute the doctrines of heretics by the sacred letters, as is clear. And so the great Constantine himself, in the Council of Nicaea, exhorted the Fathers, as is recorded in Eusebius. Likewise Tripartite History, book 2, chap. 5.

units.la: Hoc quidem fatemur, in Conciliis posterioribus Patres semper solitos fuisse, pro confirmanda sua sententia, post sacras Literas, etiam Patrum antiquorum, & veterum conciliorum auctoritatem, veterumq; Eccle-siarum consuetudines citasse: sed nunquam sine scripturis praemissis. Ac quod attinet ad interpretationes scripturarum, illud etiam damus: antiquos Patres in expositionibus eorum locorum, qui de praecipuis erant capitibus religionis Christianae, ut de Trinitate, de Deitate Christi, &c. inter se convenisse: sed in reliquis locis, non ita. Quare ex antiquitate nihil contra nos afferri potest.
units.tr: We indeed grant this: in the later councils the Fathers were always accustomed, to confirm their own opinion, to cite, after the sacred Scriptures, also the authority of the ancient Fathers and of the ancient councils, and the customs of the ancient Churches; but never without the Scriptures going before. And as far as the interpretations of Scripture are concerned, we also grant this: the ancient Fathers agreed among themselves in the expositions of those passages which concerned the principal heads of the Christian religion, such as the Trinity, the deity of Christ, etc.; but in the remaining passages, not so. Therefore nothing can be brought against us from antiquity.

units.la: Haec habui quae dicerem primum de regulis, quibus debemus muniti ad scriptura-rum lectionem accedere: Deinde de iis, quae in ipsa scripturarum lectione servandae sunt, ut probe intelligantur, ac postremo de iis, quas post intellectum aliquem scripturae lo-cum per Dei gratiam, servare utile & necesse est, ad retinendam veram scripturarum intelligentiam. Atq; haec de duodecima quaestione satis iunto[?].
units.tr: These are the things I had to say: first about the rules by which we ought to be armed when approaching the reading of the Scriptures; then about those things which are to be observed in the very reading of the Scriptures, that they may be properly understood; and lastly about those things which, after some passage of Scripture has been understood by the grace of God, it is useful and necessary to keep, in order to retain the true understanding of the Scriptures. And so let this suffice on the twelfth question [?].

units.la: Finem autem hic imponere tractationi de scripturis constitui: quia certis & necessariis de causis ingrediendum nobis est ad tractandum locum communem de Deo.
units.tr: I have decided, however, to end the treatment of Scripture here, because for certain and necessary reasons we must proceed to treat the common topic concerning God.

units.la: Si quis vero miretur, cur quaestiones 18. collegerim ex loco Apostoli 2. Timoth. 3 de scripturis tractandas: Et ego iam 12. tantum explicaexplicauisse videar: is sciat, in iis duodecim reliquas quoque fuisse explicatas.
units.tr: But if anyone wonders why I have gathered eighteen questions from the passage of the Apostle, 2 Timothy 3, to be treated concerning the Scriptures, and I seem to have explained only twelve so far: let him know that the remaining ones too were explained among those twelve.

units.la: Nam quastio prima, fuit de partitionibus Bibliorum, deque libris Canonicis & Apocryphis.
units.tr: The first question was about the divisions of the Bibles, and about the canonical and apocryphal books.

units.la: Secunda, de mediis, quibus agnosci possit, quae scriptura sit Canonica θεόπνευστα[?], quae minus.
units.tr: The second, about the means by which it may be recognized which Scripture is canonical, θεόπνευστα [?], and which less so.

units.la: Tertia, de autoritate scripturae, cum hac fi-mul etiam alia quastio tractata est de auto-ritate Ecclesiae in scripturam. Ita ex duabus unam fecimus.
units.tr: The third, about the authority of Scripture; with this was also treated another question, about the authority of the Church over Scripture. Thus we made one out of two.

units.la: Quarta, de iis, quibus scriptura fuit inspirata, id est, de scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis. Sed cum hac quaestio de linguis, quibus fuit inspirata & scripta. Item, de antiquitate scripturae. Ita etiam hic ex tribus fecimus unam.
units.tr: The fourth, about those to whom Scripture was inspired, that is, about the ecclesiastical writers. But with this question was joined one about the languages in which it was inspired and written. Likewise, about the antiquity of Scripture. Thus here too we made one out of three.

units.la: Quinta, de Origine & progressu verbi in Ecclesia.
units.tr: The fifth, about the origin and progress of the Word in the Church.

units.la: Sexta, de causis, cur primum voce tantum, deinde etiam scripto propagari Deus voluerit suum verbum.
units.tr: The sixth, about the causes why God willed that his Word be propagated first by voice only, and then also in writing.

units.la: Septima, de fine, propter quem datae S.Literae: Cum hac etiam quastio de utilitate scripturae.
units.tr: The seventh, about the end for which the Holy Letters were given; with this question was also joined one about the usefulness of Scripture.

units.la: Octava, de perfectione scripturarum: Sed cum hac quaestio: An ullum dogma extra scripturas admittendum in religione.
units.tr: The eighth, about the perfection of the Scriptures; but with this question: whether any doctrine is to be admitted in religion outside the Scriptures.

units.la: Nona, de legendis cuique etiam domi suae scripturis: cum hac quaestio de officio do-cendi scripturas, an sit omnium.
units.tr: The ninth, about whether the Scriptures are to be read by each person even in his own home; with this question about the duty of teaching the Scriptures, whether it belongs to all.

units.la: Decima,de versionibus Bibliorum: & an verti debeant in linguam popularem.
units.tr: The tenth, about the versions of the Bibles, and whether they ought to be translated into the vernacular tongue.

units.la: Undecima,de perspicuitate sacrae Scriptu-rae:Cum hac,quaestio de officio interpretandi scripturas:an sit superuacaneum in Ecclesia,nec ne, in responsione ad quintum argumentum.
units.tr: The eleventh, about the clarity of Holy Scripture; with this question about the duty of interpreting the Scriptures, whether it is superfluous in the Church or not, in the answer to the fifth argument.

units.la: Duodecima,de regulis intelligendi scriptu-ras.
units.tr: Twelfth, on the rules for understanding the Scriptures.

units.la: Nunc nihil aliud superest,quàm ut adhortationem Apostoli,unde totam hanc de scripturis tractationem collegimus, in nostrum convertamus usum,& ea excitemus nos ipsi, ad perfistendum in iis, quae didicimus ab Apostolis: & perseueremus in sancta lectio-ne,studioque Scripturarum sanctarum. Permane (inquit) tu in iis quae didicisti, & quae tibi concredita sunt, &c. Quam gratiam nobis omnibus,pro suo beneplacito, praestet DEUS OPT. MAX. per filium suum unigenitum Dominum nostrum.
