units.tr: Nothing remains now except that we turn the exhortation of the Apostle, from which we have drawn this whole discussion of Scripture, to our own use, and stir ourselves up to persevere in those things we have learned from the Apostles, and to continue in the holy reading of, and zeal for, the holy Scriptures. "Continue" (he says) "in those things which you have learned, and which have been entrusted to you, etc." May God, the best and greatest, grant this grace to us all, according to his good pleasure, through his only-begotten Son our Lord.

units.la: AMEN
units.tr: AMEN

units.la: D. HIER. ZANCHII PRÆFATIUNCULA ANTE DISPUTATIONEM DE LIBRIS Canonicis & Apocryphis, habita 10. Decemb. an 69.
units.tr: D. HIER. ZANCHII PRÆFATIUNCULA ANTE DISPUTATIONEM DE LIBRIS Canonicis & Apocryphis, habita 10. Decemb. an 69.

units.la: Antiquissima est non solum huius no-strae Amplissimae universitatis, sed etiam omnium aliarum Scholarum bene in-stitutarum consuetudo: Ut quæ priùs placi-de, & sine ullius contradictione in Scholis tradita a Doctoribus & explicata fuerunt: ea deinde in publicis disputationibus, omnibus non tam diiudicanda, quam argumentis etiam discutienda, certis temporibus pro-ponantur: idque duplici potissimum de cau-sa: quarum una est, ut veritas contrariis va-riisque argumentis discussa, magis ac magis elucescat & confirmetur.
units.tr: This custom is very ancient, not only in this our most distinguished university but in all other well-ordered schools: namely, that what has first been taught and explained by the teachers in the schools, calmly and without anyone's contradiction, should then be put forward at set times in public disputations, to be examined not only by everyone's judgment but also discussed by arguments. This is done chiefly for two reasons. The first is that truth, examined by opposing and various arguments, may shine forth and be confirmed more and more.

units.la: Altera, ut studiosorum adolescentum ingenia disputando acuantur, & in dignoscendis refutandisque Sophisticis Elenchis ac para-logismis exerceantur. Habet igitur hæc consuetudo magnam utilitatem, ac proinde lau-dem etiam non paruam.
units.tr: The second is that the wits of young students may be sharpened by disputing, and exercised in recognising and refuting sophistical fallacies and paralogisms. This custom therefore has great usefulness and, consequently, no small praise.

units.la: Cùm verò hoc utilissimum sit in omnibus disciplinis: tum verò maximè in Theologia, quæ & plures semper habet adversarios, & doctrinam utiliorem magisq; necessariam. Nam sicut nihil est salutarius doctrinâ de re-ligione, si pura & certa habeatur: ita nihil perniciosius, si impura & incerta sit. Hæc cùm ita se habeant: non sunt igitur huiuscemodi disputationes negligendæ,ne-que negligi sine maguo studiosorum damno possunt.
units.tr: Although this is most useful in all disciplines, it is especially so in theology, which always has more opponents and a teaching that is more useful and more necessary. For just as nothing is more salutary than the doctrine of religion if it is held pure and certain, so nothing is more pernicious if it is impure and uncertain. Since these things stand thus, such disputations are not to be neglected, nor can they be neglected without great loss to the students.

units.la: Quare cùm Ego quoque ad hoc sim vo-catus,vt pro mea virili studeam huic Scholæ prodesse,nolui vos carissimos Adolescentes, & reliquos nobiles auditores his disputatio-num fructibus defraudare, neque etiam su-mus in posterum, Deo faciente, defrauda-turi.
units.tr: Wherefore, since I too have been called to this task, that I should strive with all my manly strength to benefit this school, I have not wished to defraud you, most dear young men, and the other noble hearers, of the fruits of these disputations; nor, God willing, shall we defraud you of them in the future.

units.la: Proposuimus igitur primo loco Theses de scripturis Canonicis & Apocryphis dis-putandas. Sicut enim scriptura est fundamentum totius Theologiæ: sic disputatio de scripturis prima est, quæ diligenter discuti mereatur, vt confirmati in certitudine scrip-turarum,studiosius eas legamus,& in eis toto animo versemur, die ac nocte.
units.tr: We have therefore proposed, in the first place, theses to be disputed concerning the Canonical and Apocryphal Scriptures. For just as Scripture is the foundation of all theology, so the disputation concerning the Scriptures is the first that deserves to be carefully discussed, so that, confirmed in the certainty of the Scriptures, we may read them more eagerly and dwell upon them with our whole mind, day and night.

units.la: Cæterum quia ordo & modestia ornamentū sunt omnium nostrarum actionum: idcirco vos adolescentes, vestra proferetis argumenta ordine, & modestè, vt soletis.
units.tr: Moreover, since order and modesty are the ornament of all our actions, therefore you young men will put forward your arguments in order and modestly, as you are accustomed to do.

units.la: Recitabuntur aut primùm Theses pro consuetudine Scholæ, & breuiter partim explicabuntur, partim confirmabun-tur. Audite igi-tur.
units.tr: The theses will be read first, according to the custom of the school, and will be briefly explained in part and confirmed in part. Listen, therefore.

units.la: THESES. DE LIBRIS CANONICIS ET APOCRYPHIS.
units.tr: THESES. CONCERNING THE CANONICAL AND APOCRYPHAL BOOKS.

units.la: De quibus praeside D. Hieronymo Zanchio, respondit VVolffgangus VVeigkius Spirensis, quarto idus Decemb. Anno 1569.
units.tr: On which, under the presidency of Master Hieronymus Zanchius, Wolfgang Weigkius of Speyer defended the theses on the fourth day before the Ides of December, in the year 1569.

units.la: PROPOSITIO I.
units.tr: PROPOSITION I.

units.la: VOlumen illud, quod in more positum est ut Graeca voce apud omnes βίβλια appellatur, in partes secatur duas: quarum una continet libros, qui Canonici appellantur: altera illos, qui apocryphi.
units.tr: The volume which, as is customary, is called by the Greek word βίβλια by all men, is divided into two parts: one of which contains the books called canonical, the other those called apocryphal.

units.la: Canonici vocantur, quos constat in Ecclesia esse θεοπνεύστως[?]: ac proinde qui pro certo Canone omnis doctrinae de Religione recepti sunt. Apo-cryphi autem, quos non ita constat: ac proinde tanquam indigni, non quidem, quos domi quisq; sua legat, sed qui in numero Authenticorum ha-beantur, reiecti sunt.
units.tr: Canonical are called those which are agreed to be in the Church θεοπνεύστως[?]: and accordingly those which have been received as the fixed canon of all doctrine concerning religion. Apocryphal, however, are those about which there is no such agreement: and accordingly they have been rejected as unworthy, not indeed those which anyone may read at home, but those which are held in the number of the authentic books.

units.la: Ex veteri quidem Testamento, quos Ecclesia tam ante quam post Christum citra ullam dubitationem pro θεοπνεύστοις[?] agnovit, iis sunt. Libri quinque Moisis. Iehosua. Iudicum. Rhuta. Samuelis duo. Regum duo. Παραλειπομένων[?] duo. Esdrae duo priores. Esthera capita nonem, & priores decimi capitis versus tres. Iob. Psalmi. Proverbia. Ecclesiastes. Canticum Cantico-rum. rum. Iesaias, Ieremias, cum Threnis. Ezechiel, Danielis duodecim priora capita, excepto trium puerorum cantico. Et duodecim minores Prophetæ.
units.tr: Of the Old Testament, those are the books which the Church has acknowledged, both before and after Christ, without any doubt as θεοπνεύστοις[?]: the five books of Moses; Joshua; Judges; Ruth; two books of Samuel; two of Kings; two of Chronicles [Paralipomena]; the first two books of Ezra; Esther, nine chapters and the first three verses of the tenth chapter; Job; the Psalms; Proverbs; Ecclesiastes; the Song of Songs; Isaiah; Jeremiah, with the Lamentations; Ezekiel; the first twelve chapters of Daniel, except the Song of the Three Children; and the twelve minor Prophets.

units.la: Quos igitur non ita agnouit pro θεοπνεύστοις[?], sunt reliqui, nimirum Iudith a. Tobias. Esdræ tertius & quartus. Sapientia Salomonis. Sapientia Iesu filij Sirach, qui Ecclesiasticus Latinis dicitur. Baruch. Epistola Ieremiæ. Danielis caput 13. & 14. Item canticum trium puerorum, quod est capiti tertio Danielis adiectum. Esthera, a tribus versibus decimi capitis, reliquum. Libri quinq; Machabæorum.
units.tr: Those, then, which the Church has not so acknowledged as θεοπνεύστοις[?] are the remainder, namely: Judith; Tobit; the third and fourth books of Ezra; the Wisdom of Solomon; the Wisdom of Jesus the son of Sirach, which is called Ecclesiasticus by the Latins; Baruch; the Epistle of Jeremiah; chapters 13 and 14 of Daniel; likewise the Song of the Three Children, which is added to the third chapter of Daniel; the remainder of Esther from the three verses of the tenth chapter; and the five books of the Maccabees.

units.la: Ex nouo autem Testamento, de quibus nunquam fuit dubitatum, ij sunt, Euangelia secundum Matthæum, Marcum, Lucam, Ioannem. Acta Apostolorum. Epistola Pauli. Petri prima. Et prima Iohannis. De quibus autem aliquando, sunt reliqui.
units.tr: Of the New Testament, about which there has never been any doubt, these are: the Gospels according to Matthew, Mark, Luke and John; the Acts of the Apostles; the Epistles of Paul; the first Epistle of Peter; and the first Epistle of John. Those about which there has at some time been doubt are the remainder.

units.la: Etsi vero certioris quodam modo sint auctoritatis illi, de quibus nunquam, quam isti, de quibus aliquando fuit dubitatum: Horum tamen nullum esse censemus, qui merito debeat inter Apocryphos connumerari.
units.tr: Although indeed those about which there has never been doubt have a somewhat more certain authority than those about which there has at some time been doubt, we judge that none of these latter deserves to be numbered among the Apocrypha.

units.la: Porrò quatuor sunt precipua, per quæ agnoscimus, quinam sint θεόπνευστοι[?] 1. Traditio Ecclesiastica 2. Auctoritas scriptorum, 3. Dignitas scripturarum, 4. Et Lumen Spiritus sancti, dignitatem scriptura patefacientis, & eam cer-tum esse Dei verbum persuadentis.
units.tr: Moreover, there are four principal means by which we recognise which are θεόπνευστοι[?]: (1) Ecclesiastical tradition; (2) the authority of the writers; (3) the dignity of the Scriptures; (4) and the light of the Holy Spirit, which reveals the dignity of Scripture and persuades us that it is the certain Word of God.

units.la: Scriptura enim sacra, sicut afflatu Spiritus S. fuerunt revelata & conscripta: ita[?] citra eius lu-men nobis persuaderi, & pro certo Dei verbo à nobis vere agnosci non possunt.
units.tr: For Holy Scripture, just as it was revealed and written down by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, so too without His light cannot be made persuasive to us, nor can it truly be recognised by us as the certain Word of God.

units.la: Proinde ad hoc, ut simus vere persuasi hosce libros certum esse Dei verbum: dicimus, neq; Ecclesiasticam Traditionem, neq; Scriptorum auctoritatem, neq; etiam scriptura ipsius dignita-tem, per se sufficere: sed necessarium esse lumen Spiritus Sancti.
units.tr: Therefore, in order that we may be truly persuaded that these books are the certain Word of God, we say that neither ecclesiastical tradition, nor the authority of the writers, nor even the dignity of Scripture itself, suffices by itself; but the light of the Holy Spirit is necessary.

units.la: Confirmamur vero in cognitione priorum per testimonia posteriorum.
units.tr: Moreover, we are confirmed in the knowledge of the former by the testimonies of the latter.

units.la: Habent autem Canonici libri auctoritatem ad statuenda & probanda fidei dogmata. Apo-cryphi vero, etsi utiliter legi possunt, & ad dogma-ta iam probata, confirmanda adhiberi: illam tamen non habent auctoritatem, quam Ca-nonici.
units.tr: The canonical books, however, have authority to establish and prove the dogmas of faith. The apocryphal books, although they may usefully be read and employed to confirm dogmas already proved, do not, however, have that authority which the canonical books have.

units.la: Fides enim ex auditu est: auditus autem per verbum Dei. Solos vero libros Canonicos constat esse verbum Dei.
units.tr: For faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the Word of God. It is agreed, however, that only the canonical books are the Word of God.

units.la: Merito itaq; ij etiam soli CANON omnis doctrinæ[?] de Religione constituti sunt.
units.tr: Rightly, therefore, these alone have been established as the CANON of all doctrine concerning religion.

units.la: TIT. 1.v.9. duplex Episcopi, (seu Ecclesiastici Doctoris traditur officium. Unum, ut sanam tradat & explicet doctrinam: hæc autem alia non est, quam quæ in S. tradita est Literis, & ab Apostolis in Ecclesia electa. Alterum, τὴς ἀντιλέγοντας ἐλέγχειν[?], hoc est, ut contradicentes firmis argumentis euincant & eorum sophismata refutent.
units.tr: Titus 1.9: The office of a bishop (or ecclesiastical teacher) is said to be twofold. The first is to teach and expound sound doctrine; and this doctrine is nothing other than what has been handed down in Holy Scripture and chosen in the Church by the Apostles. The second is τὴς ἀντιλέγοντας ἐλέγχειν [to refute those who speak against it], that is, to overcome the contradictors with firm arguments and to refute their sophisms.

units.la: Merito certè hæc duo tradit Apostolus, duo esse Ecclesiastici Doctoris officia. Duo enim etiam sunt Auditorum genera. Alij pij & electi, qui sana & simplici doctrina contenti, nihil præterea quærunt, & si quid quærunt, non animo contradicendi, sed discendi quærunt.
units.tr: Surely the Apostle rightly hands down these two as the two offices of an ecclesiastical teacher. For there are also two kinds of hearers. Some are pious and chosen, who, content with sound and simple doctrine, seek nothing further; and if they do seek anything, they seek it not with a mind to contradict, but to learn.

units.la: Alij impij & reprobi, qui nunquam contenti, semper contradicunt veritati, & nouas quotidie in Ecclesia excitant rixas.
units.tr: Others are impious and reprobate, who are never content, always contradict the truth, and every day stir up new quarrels in the Church.

units.la: Respectu prioris generis Auditorum ait, oportere Episcopum esse tenacem illius sermonis, qui ad doctrinam facit, ut possit etiam exhortari per doctrinam sanam.
units.tr: With respect to the first kind of hearers, he says that the bishop must hold fast to the word that accords with doctrine, so that he may also be able to exhort by sound doctrine.

units.la: Respectu alterius generis hominum, ait oportere etiam τὴς ἀντιλέγοντας ἐλέγχειν[?].
units.tr: With respect to the other kind of people, he says that it is also necessary τὴς ἀντιλέγοντας ἐλέγχειν [to refute those who speak against it].

units.la: Ergo cùm vos detis operam Theologiæ, ut fiatis aut Ecclesiarum pastores, aut Scholarum Professores, utrumque vobis necessa-rium est. In hunc finem curatur etiam, ut & lectiones habeatis fere quotidie, & disputationes certis temporibus. Illas, ut quotidie proficiatis in cognitione verae & sanae doctrinae: Has, ut in ratione disputandi, & suo tempore Haereticos convincendi, exerceamini.
units.tr: Therefore, since you devote yourselves to theology, in order to become either ministers of the Churches or professors in the schools, both of these are necessary for you. To this end it is also arranged that you have lectures almost every day, and disputations at set times: the former so that you may make daily progress in the knowledge of true and sound doctrine; the latter so that you may be exercised in the method of disputing and in refuting heretics at the proper time.

units.la: Ergo vestri etiam est officij, ut sicut in lectionibus diligentes estis: sic etiam in disputationibus haud sitis negligentes. Si non pu-blicè, tam frequentes, ut forte desideratis, ha-beantur: domi saltem inter vos privatas & modestas disceptationes instituere debetis.
units.tr: Therefore it is also part of your duty that, just as you are diligent in the lectures, so you should not be negligent in the disputations. If they are not held publicly as often as you perhaps desire, you ought at least to conduct private and modest debates among yourselves at home.

units.la: Cæterum tria observanda sunt in disputationibus: unum, ut scopus non fit nobis φιλονικία[?], sed veritatis perfectio: Alterum, ut modestia in dicendo seruetur: Tertium, ut ad formam syllogisticam omnia componantur argumenta.
units.tr: Moreover, three things are to be observed in disputations: first, that our aim not be contentiousness φιλονικία [love of victory], but the perfection of truth; second, that modesty be preserved in speaking; third, that all arguments be framed in syllogistic form.

units.la: DE SCRIPTVRAE SAN-ctæ authoritate, perfectione, perspicuitate, lectione.
units.tr: On the Authority, Perfection, Perspicuity and Reading of Holy Scripture.

units.la: Disputatæ in Academia Heidelb. V. Idus De-cemb. Anno 1570.
units.tr: Disputed in the Academy of Heidelberg, on the 5th of the Ides of December, in the year 1570.

units.la: Respondente Danide Pareo Silesio.
units.tr: Respondent: Daniel Pareus of Silesia.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: DOCTRINA illa Papistica, scripturam san-ctam suam ab Ecclesia habere authoritatem, & huius maiorem esse quam illius, impia & sacrilega est.
units.tr: That Papist doctrine, that Holy Scripture has its authority from the Church, and that the Church is greater than it, is impious and sacrilegious.

units.la: Probatio à Respondente scripta, & ante disputationem pro vetusto Academiæ more recitata:
units.tr: Proof, written out by the Respondent and read aloud before the disputation, according to the old custom of the Academy:

units.la: Autoritas est dignitas quædam seu vis, propter quam persona vel res aliqua digna est & habetur honore vel fide. Et sic Scripturæ sanctæ autoritas est dignitas vel vis illa, propter quam ipsa Scriptura sancta est & habetur pro fide digna, seu pro verbo Dei, ac proinde est ἀξιόπιστος [?]. De hac dignitate quæritur inter Papistas & orthodoxos, habeatne eam scriptura in se, an ab Ecclesia. Papistæ posterius affirmant: & Ecclesiæ dignitatem, quàm ipsius Scripturæ maiorem esse contendunt. Utrumque ut impium & sacrilegum damnatur hac Thesi. Ac prius quidem propter manifesta Scripturæ testimonia & euidentes rationes. Christus Iohan.17. de Euangelica loquens doctrina,etiam ante-quam à mundo reciperetur : Verbum, inquit,tuum est Veritas. Et cap. 5. Ego ab homine testimonium non accipio. Ergo verbum Dei non ideo est verum quia ab Ecclesia recipitur,vel ab hominibus testimonium habet. Et Paulus Eph.2.dicit, Ecclesiam super fundamentū Prophetarum & Apostolorum ædificatam esse. At fundamentum non nititur ædificio, sed ædificium fundamento. Non igitur Scriptura Prophetica & Apostolica Ecclesiæ, sed contrà Ecclesia scripturæ authoritate nititur. Accedit his alia ratio, quòd scriptura non est ab Ecclesia profecta, sed à Deo inspirata, qui ipsa est veritas. Non igitur ab Ecclesia, sed à Deo autore ac fonte omnis veritatis, ipsa quoq; Scriptura indu-bitatam veritatem habet. Et quis non videt totam religionem nostram Turcarum & a-liorum impiorum sannis & ludibrio expo-ni, si certantes cum illis ideo tantùm nobis credi postulemus, religionem nostram esse veram ac fide dignam quia Ecclesia(quæ hominibus constat) asseuerat. Eadem certè specie ipsi negabunt, qua à nobis asseuerabitur. Posterius similiter manifestam falsitatem & blasphemiam habet. Quid enim minus est veritati consentaneum, quàm diuinam au-toritatem[?] humana inferiorem esse? quid magis impium, quàm Deo in Scriptura loquenti fidem derogare, nisi Ecclesiæ, hoc est, miserorum hominum suffragium accedat ? Atque hoc idem sequenti Thesi dicitur.
units.tr: Authority is a certain dignity or power, on account of which a person or thing is worthy of, and held in, honour or belief. So the authority of Holy Scripture is that dignity or power by which Holy Scripture itself is held worthy of belief, or as the Word of God, and is therefore trustworthy [ἀξιόπιστος]. The question about this dignity is raised between the Papists and the orthodox: whether Scripture has it in itself, or has it from the Church. The Papists affirm the latter, and contend that the dignity of the Church is greater than that of Scripture itself. Both positions are condemned by this thesis as impious and sacrilegious. The first is condemned on account of the plain testimonies of Scripture and the evident reasons. Christ, in John 17, speaking of the evangelical doctrine even before it was received by the world, says: "Your word is truth." And in chapter 5: "I do not receive testimony from man." Therefore the word of God is not true because it is received by the Church, or because it has testimony from men. And Paul, in Eph. 2, says that the Church is built upon the foundation of the Prophets and Apostles. But the foundation does not rest upon the building; the building rests upon the foundation. Therefore the prophetic and apostolic Scripture does not rest upon the Church; rather the Church rests upon the authority of Scripture. To these is added another reason: Scripture did not proceed from the Church but was inspired by God, who is truth itself. Therefore Scripture has its indubitable truth not from the Church but from God, the author and fountain of all truth. And who does not see that our whole religion would be exposed to the mockery and ridicule of the Turks and other impious people, if, when contending with them, we demanded that they believe only this: that our religion is true and worthy of belief because the Church (which consists of men) affirms it? Certainly they would deny it with the same right with which we affirmed it. The latter likewise carries manifest falsehood and blasphemy. For what is less consistent with truth than that divine authority should be inferior to human authority? What is more impious than to detract from faith in God speaking in Scripture, unless the suffrage of the Church, that is, of miserable men, is added? And the same is said in the following thesis.

units.la: Est enim perinde, ac si dicas, Deum ab hominibus habere authoritatem, & hominum maiorem esse quam sit Dei.
units.tr: For it is just as if you said that God has authority from men, and that men are greater than God is.

units.la: Probatio.
units.tr: Proof.

units.la: Nam Dei authoritas etiam verbi Diuini est Dignitas, quam qui ab Ecclesiæ testimonio suspendit, reuera Deum hominibus subiicit: contra dicta: Iohan. s.[?] Ego testimonium maius habeo, vt 1.Iohan.s.[?] vers.9. Si testimonium hominum accipimus, testimonium Dei maius est. Nam hoc est testimonium Dei quod testificatus est de Filio suo, nempe in Scriptura sacra.
units.tr: For the authority of God is also the dignity of the divine Word; whoever makes it depend on the testimony of the Church in fact subjects God to men. Against this: John 5, "I have a greater testimony," and 1 John 5:9, "If we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater. For this is the testimony of God, which he has testified concerning his Son," namely in holy Scripture.

units.la: Contrà igitur nos contendimus, quicquid authoritatis habet Ecclesia, totum hoc illi esse a Deo, eiusq; verbo.
units.tr: Therefore, on the contrary, we contend that whatever authority the Church has, all of it is from God and from his Word.

units.la: Probatio.
units.tr: Proof.

units.la: Docet hoc Apostolus Eph. 2. cùm Ecclesiam extructam esse dicit super fundamentum Prophetarum & Apostolorum. Nititur ergo non scripta Ecclesia: sed alieno fundamento, quod est Scriptura sancta sustentatur. Hinc est, quòd Prophetæ, quoties sibi credi volunt, exclamant: Audite cœli quid Dominus loquatur: Factum est verbum Dominiad Prophetam Iesaiam: quia nimirum Dei autoritas per se est ἀξιόπιστος: Hominibus vero tanquam Dei legatis, fides non habetur, nisi Dei verbum loquantur, & loqui intelligantur.
units.tr: The Apostle teaches this in Eph. 2, when he says that the Church has been built upon the foundation of the Prophets and Apostles. It therefore rests not on itself but on a foundation not its own, which is sustained by Holy Scripture. Hence it is that the Prophets, whenever they want to be believed, cry out: "Hear, O heavens, what the Lord speaks" (Isa. 1:2); "The word of the Lord came to the prophet Isaiah." Because, doubtless, the authority of God is trustworthy in itself; but men, as envoys of God, are not believed unless they speak God's Word and are understood to speak it.

units.la: Proinde licet Ecclesia authoritatem habeat, Scripturas S. ab aliorum scriptis discernendi, deq; illis testificandi: & vero illas etiam interpretandi: nullam tamen habet, eis vel addendi vel detrahendi, deq; illis, vt loquuntur, dispensandi potestatem, multo vero minus hanc habet Papa Romanus.
units.tr: Accordingly, although the Church has the authority to distinguish the holy Scriptures from the writings of others, and to bear witness concerning them, and indeed to interpret them, it has no power either to add to them or to take away from them, or to dispense them, as they say, and much less does the Roman Pope have this.

units.la: Probatio.
units.tr: Proof.

units.la: Autoritatem discernendi Scripturas sa-cras ab aliorum scriptis: & testificandi de il-lis, non pro suo quidem arbitratu, sed iuxta mentem Spiritus in illis loquentis, Ecclesiae non derogamus, quia ipse Spiritus sanctus ei hanc tribuit 1.Corinth.10. Iudicate vos quod aio. 1.Corinth.12. Vnicuique datur declaratio Spiritus ad vtilitatem: alij quidem dona sa-nationum, alij vero discretiones spirituum. 1.Iohan.4. Probate spiritus an ex Deo sint. 1.Thess.5[?].21, Omnia probate, quod bonum est, tenete.
units.tr: We do not detract from the Church's authority to distinguish the holy Scriptures from the writings of others, and to bear witness concerning them, not indeed according to its own judgment but according to the mind of the Spirit speaking in them; for the Holy Spirit himself grants this to it: 1 Cor. 10, "Judge for yourselves what I say." 1 Cor. 12, "To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good: to one indeed the gifts of healing, to another the discernment of spirits." 1 John 4, "Test the spirits, whether they are from God." 1 Thess. 5:21, "Test everything; hold fast what is good."

units.la: De iure etiam interpretandi scripturas iuxta analogiam fidei ad omnes, in Ecclesia facultate ἑρμηνευτικῇ praeditos pertinente, lo-quuntur hæc dicta 1.Corinth.12. Alij datur Prophetia, alij interpretatio linguarum. Rom.12. Habentes autem diuisa dona, pro gratia quæ nobis data est per Prophetiam, prophetemus pro analogia fidei. Matth. 28. Euntes docete omnes gentes. At vero potestatem Scripturis addendi vel detrahendi aliquid, neque Ecclesia neque quisquam Angelorum habet: ac multo minus Papa Romanus: quod toties testatur Spiritus sanctus, ut mirum sit, unquam homines eo temeritatis venire potuisse, quo Pontificios progressos videmus. Deuter. 6. grauissime à Deo cohercetur ea hominum temeritas: Non addetis ad verbum quod ego præcipio vobis, neque detrahetis quicquam ex eo, ut custodiatis præcepta Iehouæ Dei vestri. Deut. 5. Ne declinetis ad dextram vel ad sinistram. Galat. 1. Si vel Angelus de Cœlo Euangelizauerit vobis præter id, quod accepistis, anathema est. Apoc. 22. Si quis addiderit ad hæc, imponet ei Deus plagas scriptas in libro isto: & si quis abstulerit aliquid ex verbis libri Prophetæ huius, auferet Deus partem eius ex libro vitæ, & ex urbe sancta, & ex iis, quæ scripta sunt in libro isto.
units.tr: The words also speak of the right to interpret the Scriptures according to the analogy of faith, which belongs to all in the Church who are endowed with the hermeneutical faculty: 1 Cor. 12, "To another is given prophecy, to another the interpretation of tongues." Rom. 12, "Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us, let us prophesy according to the analogy of faith." Matt. 28, "Go and teach all nations." But neither the Church nor any of the angels has the power to add anything to Scripture or to take anything away from it, and much less does the Roman Pope have it. The Holy Spirit so often bears witness to this that it is astonishing that men could ever have come to such a degree of recklessness as we see the Papists have advanced to. Deut. 6 most gravely restrains this human rashness: "You shall not add to the word that I command you, nor take anything from it, that you may keep the commandments of Jehovah your God." Deut. 5, "Do not turn aside to the right hand or to the left." Gal. 1, "If an angel from heaven preach to you anything beside what you have received, let him be accursed." Rev. 22, "If anyone adds to these things, God will add to him the plagues written in this book; and if anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God will take away his part from the book of life, and from the holy city, and from the things written in this book."

units.la: Est autem doctrina salutis tam abunde in sacris Literis tradita, ut quicquid ad salutem cognitu necessarium est, illud totum in eis contineatur.
units.tr: The doctrine of salvation, however, is so abundantly delivered in the holy Writings that whatever is necessary to know for salvation is wholly contained in them.

units.la: Cum enim Deus caueat, ne quicquam addatur suæ doctrinæ: docet eam ita esse perfectam, ut nihil ei addi possit aut debeat.
units.tr: For since God takes care that nothing be added to his doctrine, he teaches that it is so perfect that nothing can or ought to be added to it.

units.la: 7. Quare in doctrina per Spiritum sanctum in sacris Literis tradita, ita Christi Ecclesia acquie-scendum est, ut extra illam nihil tanquam ad sa-lutem necessarium admittere debeat.
units.tr: 7. Therefore, in the doctrine delivered in the sacred Writings by the Holy Spirit, the Church of Christ must so rest content that it ought to admit nothing outside it as necessary to salvation.

units.la: Probatio.
units.tr: Proof.

units.la: Necessaria ad salutem vocamus, quæcun-que ad verum Dei cultum externum & internum pertinent, ut sunt fides in Christum, Timor Dei, studium bonæ conscientiæ, legitimus Sacramentorum usus, &c. Hæc omnia in verbo Dei scripto tam plenè perse-ctèque sunt tradita, ut neque possit neq; fas sit quicquam ab hominibus addi. Esset enim Deo nimis contumeliosum, dicere, eum non integram cultus sui, & salutis nostræ rationem in verbo suo patefecisse: & manifestè id vel omnipotentiæ eius, vel summæ bonitati derogaret. Aut enim non potuit, aut non voluit nobis perfectam scriptură tradere, quorum utrumque de Deo cogitare nefarium est. Et si quid deest, vel Legi vel Euangelio deerit: sed Legi nihil deesse, manifestum est: quia requirit dilectionem Dei ex toto corde & qua maior & perfectior esse nulla potest. In cæteris quoque obedientiam longè per-fectiorem sancit, quàm quæ ab vlla creatu-rarum præstari possit. Nec Euangelio addi aliquid potest: quoniam qui fecundum illud credit in Filium, habet vitam æternam. Pertinent huc etiam dicta Iohan.15.[?] Omnia, quæ audiui à patre meo, nota feci vobis. Act.20. Non subterfugi quominus annunciarem vobis omne consilium Dei. Item illa, quæ omnes additiones & detractiones à verbo Dei prohibent, qualia sunt, quæ ex Deuteronomio & Apocalypsi ad Thesin 1 V. recitaui.
units.tr: We call necessary for salvation whatever pertains to the true external and internal worship of God, such as faith in Christ, the fear of God, zeal for a good conscience, the lawful use of the sacraments, etc. All of these have been handed down in the written Word of God so fully and perfectly that nothing can or may rightly be added by men. For it would be too great an insult to God to say that he has not revealed in his Word the complete account of his worship and of our salvation; and this would clearly detract either from his omnipotence or from his supreme goodness. For either he could not, or he would not, deliver to us a perfect Scripture; and to think either of these about God is impious. And if anything were lacking, it would be lacking either in the Law or in the Gospel. But that nothing is lacking in the Law is evident, because it requires love of God with the whole heart, and no love can be greater or more perfect. Likewise, in the other matters it enjoins an obedience far more perfect than any creature could render. Nor can anything be added to the Gospel, since whoever believes in the Son according to that word has eternal life. To this also belong the sayings of John 15: "All that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you." Acts 20: "I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God." Likewise those passages which forbid all additions to and subtractions from the Word of God, such as those I have recited from Deuteronomy and from Revelation, in Thesis 1 V.

units.la: Cum verò tanta sit Scripturæ sanctæ perfectio, vt sola ad salutem & cultum Dei sufficiat: manifestum est, concidere ac facesserc debere traditiones humanas alienas à verbo Dei, vel cum eodem pugnantes, quales hodie à Pontificiis multæ pro verbo Dei obtruduntur: ac citra conscientiæ violationem non credi, omitti vel mutari posse, quicquid vel non expressè in scriptura est traditum, vel ex verbis eius rectè intellectis bona consequentia deduci nequit. Sic enim postulat discrimen, quod est inter Propheticos atque Apostolicos libros, & aliorum scripta, vt illi soli, tanquam verbum Dei immediatè inspiratum & revelatum, & tanquam regula fidei, atque canones omnis doctrinæ in Ecclesia recipiantur: Hæc verò eatenus tantùm fidem mereantur, quatenus cum norma illorum congruunt.
units.tr: Since, then, the perfection of Holy Scripture is so great that it alone suffices for salvation and the worship of God, it is clear that human traditions foreign to the Word of God, or fighting against it, must be cast down and removed, such as the many which are today foisted upon us by the Papists as the Word of God; and that, without violating conscience, nothing can be believed, omitted or changed which either is not expressly handed down in Scripture or cannot be rightly deduced from its words by good consequence. For the distinction that exists between the Prophetic and Apostolic books and the writings of others requires this: that the former alone be received, as the immediately inspired and revealed Word of God, and as the rule of faith and the canons of all doctrine in the Church; while the latter merit belief only so far as they agree with the norm of those.

units.la: {§} Neque solum abunde, verum etiam perspicuè tota salutis doctrina in sacris Literis prodita est.
units.tr: {§} The whole doctrine of salvation is set forth in the Holy Scriptures not only abundantly but also clearly.

units.la: {¶}[?] Est enim scriptura Lux, eaq; splendidissima, quemadmodum & de lege præter alios testatur Dauid, & de Euangelio Apostolus.
units.tr: {¶}[?] For Scripture is a light, and that a most brilliant one, as David testifies of the law, among others, and the Apostle of the Gospel.

units.la: Probatio.
units.tr: Proof.

units.la: Hæ Theses de perspicuitate scripturæ propter Pontificios confirmandæ sunt: qui scripturam in fundamento salutis accusant obscuritatis, ut suas etiam præstigias & Sera-phicas glossas cum scriptura necessario re-cipienda esle obtineant. Quanta uero cum contumelia Spiritus sancti id faciant, qui ubique in uerbo suo nobiscum quasi balbu-tit, & ad ruditatem nostram se demittit: nulli qui Scripturam sanctam unquam recte legit, obscurum esle potest. Dauid Psal.119. Legem Dei uocat lucernam pedum nostrorum, & lumen semitarum nostrarum, lucem quæ in-telligentiam paruulis conferat. Salomon Prouerb.1. testatur, se scribere ad dandam simplicibus solertiam, pueris scientiam & prudentiam: sapientiam foris clamare, & in plateis edere uocem suam: Paulus 1.Cor.1.& 2.dicit, se à Christo missum esle ad prædican-dum Euangelium, non cum sermonis peri-tia, neque cum eminentia facundiæ aut per-suasoriis humanæ sapientiæ verbis, ne ina-nis reddatur crux Christi: Et alibi 2.Cor.4. Euangelium uocat lumen gloriæ Christi. Petrus Propheticum sermonem, qui tamen non parum obscuritatis habere uidetur, lu-cernam uocat lucentem in caliginoso loco. Denique, si obscura est Scriptura sancta, uel in Lege vel in Euangelio ea obscuritas erit. Non in lege. Quid enim clarius, quam quòd Deum diligere iubemur ex toto corde & proximum sicut nos ipsos? Nec in Euangelio: Nihil enim obscuritatis habet hæc totius Euangelij summa: Sic Deus dilexit mundum, vt fiiuum suum daret, vt omnis qui credit, non pereat, sed habet vitam æternam. Item: Qui credit in filium, habet vitam æternam: qui non credit filio, non videbit vitam, & ira Dei manet super eum.
units.tr: These theses on the clarity of Scripture must be maintained against the Papists, who accuse Scripture, as the foundation of salvation, of obscurity, so that they may obtain that their own deceits and Seraphic glosses be necessarily received along with Scripture. But how great an insult they offer to the Holy Spirit in doing this, who everywhere speaks with us in his Word as if lisping, and lowers himself to our rudeness! No one who ever reads Holy Scripture rightly can find it obscure. David, Psalm 119, calls the law of God a lamp to our feet and a light to our paths, a light that gives understanding to little ones. Solomon, Proverbs 1, testifies that he writes to give shrewdness to the simple, knowledge and discretion to the young; that wisdom cries out abroad and raises her voice in the streets. Paul, 1 Cor. 1 and 2, says that he was sent by Christ to preach the Gospel, not with skill of speech, nor with eminence of eloquence or with persuasive words of human wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be made void. And elsewhere, 2 Cor. 4, he calls the Gospel the light of the glory of Christ. Peter calls the prophetic word, which nevertheless seems to have no small obscurity, a lamp shining in a dark place. Finally, if Holy Scripture is obscure, whether in the Law or in the Gospel that obscurity will be found. Not in the Law: for what is clearer than that we are commanded to love God with the whole heart and our neighbour as ourselves? Nor in the Gospel: for this summary of the whole Gospel has no obscurity: "God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes should not perish but have eternal life." Likewise: "He who believes in the Son has eternal life; he who does not believe the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him."

units.la: Quare impie etiam & tyrannicè ab illis fit, qui ne Scriptura sancta aut in populares linguas conuertatur, aut conuersa imprimatur, vendatur legatur, legibus cauent.
units.tr: Therefore it is wicked and tyrannical on the part of those who by law forbid that Holy Scripture be translated into the vernacular tongues, or, once translated, be printed, sold or read.

units.la: Probatio.
units.tr: Proof.

units.la: Papistarum tyrannidem scriptura ipsa damnat, quoties diligentem lectionem & meditationem omnibus & singulis præcipit Deut.6.& 11. Docete ea filios vestros, inquit Deus, vt serió loquantur de eis, cum desides domi tuæ: & cum es in itinere: cum cubitum vadis & cum surgis: scribes ea quoque super postes domus tuæ & in portis tuis. Præceptum hoc est morale ad omnes pertinens. Pfal. 1. Dauid beatum eum prædicat, qui legem Dei meditatur die ac nocte. Pf.119. felicem eum, qui meditatur eloquia Domini. Deut. 17. inter partes officij regij nu-merameratur assidua legis diuinae lectio & meditatio, Iohan. 5. Christus omnibus & singulis praecipit, ut scrutentur scripturas. Act or. 8. Eunuchus Aethiops lectione scripturarum, & institutione Philippi ad fidem Christianam conuertitur. Act. 17. Berhoenses Christiani ex concione domum reuersi doctrinam Pauli ad scripturas examinant. Act. 2. Apostoli dono linguarum ornantur, ut omnibus nationibus & linguis vernaculo idiomate doctrinam salutis explicare possint. 1. Cor. 14. Paulus vetat peregrinas linguas sonare in Ecclesia sine interpretatione. Ergo in vernaculas conuerti scripturam necesse est.
units.tr: Scripture itself condemns the tyranny of the Papists, whenever it commands everyone, each and every one, to read and meditate diligently on it: Deut. 6 and 11. "Teach these things to your sons," says God, "so that they may speak of them seriously, when you sit idle at home, when you are on a journey, when you go to bed and when you rise; write them also upon the posts of your house and on your gates." This precept is moral and pertains to all. Ps. 1: David calls blessed the man who meditates on the law of God day and night. Ps. 119: happy is he who meditates on the words of the Lord. Deut. 17: constant reading and meditation on the divine law are numbered among the duties of the royal office. John 5: Christ commands all and each to search the Scriptures. Acts 8: the Ethiopian eunuch is converted to the Christian faith by reading the Scriptures and by the instruction of Philip. Acts 17: the Christians of Berea, returning home from the sermon, examine the teaching of Paul by the Scriptures. Acts 2: the apostles were endowed with the gift of tongues, so that they could explain the doctrine of salvation to all nations and languages in their own vernacular tongue. 1 Cor. 14: Paul forbids foreign tongues to be sounded in the Church without interpretation. Therefore it is necessary for Scripture to be translated into the vernacular.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Neq; enim Scriptura sancta certis tantum hominum generibus, sed toti Ecclesiae, eoq; singu-lis fidelibus tradita & commendata sunt, idque non tam, ut illis salutis doctrina asservetur, quam ut ex eius tum legendis tum audiendis indies magis ac magis, quæ sit Dei voluntas, à singulis co-gnoscatur.
units.tr: For Holy Scripture was delivered and commended not only to certain kinds of men, but to the whole Church, and therefore to each and every believer; and this not so much so that the doctrine of salvation might be preserved for them, as so that each one may learn, by reading and by hearing it day by day more and more, what the will of God is.

units.la: Probatio.
units.tr: Proof.

units.la: Finem lectionis, auditionis, ac meditatio-nis Scripturarum esse salutem nostram, testa-tur Christus Iohan. 5. Scrutamini Scriptu-ras: nam videmini vobis in illis vitam æter-nam habere. At salutis æternæ neque acqui-sitio præcipitur, neque fruitio promittitur certis duntaxat hominibus, aut hominum generibus, puta Pontificibus, Cardinalibus, Episcopis, Monachis, &c. sed tori Ecclesiae, & singulis fidelibus Matth. 7. Contendite ingredi per angustam portam Mar. 16. Quicunque crediderit & baptizatus fuerit salvus erit. Omnibus ergo Ecclesiae domesticis scripturae sunt traditae & commendatae, idque geminae utilitatis causa: quarum una est, ut in illa tanquam in turri fortissima & inexpugnabili doctrina salutis integra defendatur, & pura conseruetur: si quidem nunquam defuturi sunt hostes, qui eam deiicere, vel saltem labefactare conentur. Ideo Apostolus 1. Tim. 3. Ecclesiam στῦλον [?] ἱδραίωμα τῆς ἀληθείας, hoc est, columnam & stabilimentum veritatis appellat. Altera est ut earum lectione & meditatione agnitio veri Dei, & studium salutis nostrae magis magisq; in nobis crescat & excitetur Pial.1. Beatus qui meditatur legem Dei dies ac noctes. 2. Tim. 3. Permane in iis quae didicisti, sciens, quòd à pueris sacras Literas noueris, quae te possunt perfectum reddere ad salutem, per fidem, quae est in Christo Iesu.
units.tr: That the purpose of reading, hearing and meditating on the Scriptures is our salvation, Christ testifies in John 5: "Search the Scriptures, for you think that in them you have eternal life." But neither the attainment of eternal salvation is commanded, nor its enjoyment promised, to certain persons only, or kinds of men, such as Pontiffs, Cardinals, Bishops, Monks, etc., but to the whole Church and to each believer: Matt. 7: "Strive to enter by the narrow gate." Mark 16: "Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved." Therefore the Scriptures have been delivered and commended to all the members of the Church, and this for a twofold benefit. The first is that in them, as in a most strong and impregnable tower, the doctrine of salvation may be defended whole and preserved pure, since enemies will never be lacking who try to overthrow it or at least weaken it. Hence the Apostle in 1 Tim. 3 calls the Church "the pillar and ground of the truth" [στῦλον καὶ ἑδραίωμα τῆς ἀληθείας], that is, the column and foundation of the truth. The second is that by reading and meditating on them the knowledge of the true God and the zeal for our salvation may grow and be stirred up more and more in us. Ps. 1: "Blessed is he who meditates on the law of God day and night." 2 Tim. 3: "Continue in the things you have learned, knowing that from childhood you have known the holy letters, which can make you wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus."

units.la: DE LIBRIS APOCRYPHIS veteris Testamenti, Patrum iudicia.
units.tr: ON THE APOCRYPHAL BOOKS of the Old Testament: the judgments of the Fathers.

units.la: Israelitica Ecclesia semper constans fuit in sententia, hos non esse Θεοπνεύστους[?].
units.tr: The Israelite Church always remained constant in the view that these are not divinely inspired [θεόπνευστοι].

units.la: In nouo etiam Testamento nullus ex iis li-ber, aut ex libris locus citatus à Christo fuit, aut ab Apostolis. Imò nec ulla mentio reperitur facta fuisse.
units.tr: In the New Testament too, none of these books, nor any passage from them, was cited by Christ or by the Apostles. Indeed, no mention of them is found to have been made.

units.la: Est autem huius Ecclesiæ tam constans, vniuersale & perpetuum de iis rebus iudi-cium, iudicio eorum, qui post Christum & Apostolos in Ecclesia Christiana secuti sunt, præponendum his de causis.
units.tr: Now the judgment of this Church, so constant, universal and perpetual on these matters, is to be preferred to the judgment of those who followed after Christ and the Apostles in the Christian Church, for the following reasons.

units.la: Primò, quia illa Ecclesia vicinior fuit scri-ptoribus, quàm posterior. Ideo melius etiam potuit cognoscere, & certius iudicium facere, an tales scripserint necne: & quales ij fuerint, qui scripserunt.
units.tr: First, because that Church was nearer to the writers than the later ones were. Therefore it was also better able to know, and to make a more certain judgment, whether such men wrote or not, and what kind of men those were who wrote.

units.la: Secundò, quia nulla inter ipsos legitur fuisse iudiciorum discrepantia: secus fuit inter Patres, post Christum.
units.tr: Second, because no disagreement of judgments is read to have existed among them; it was otherwise among the Fathers after Christ.

units.la: Tertiò, quia peritiores suæ linguæ, & phraseon Spiritus S. inque Scripturis exercitiores, quàm nostri Patres fuerint. Melius ergo potuerunt iudicare.
units.tr: Third, because they were more skilled in their own language and in the phrases of the Holy Spirit, and more practised in the Scriptures, than our Fathers were. They therefore could judge better.

units.la: Quartò, quia diligentiores fuerunt in seruandis Traditionibus Maiorum, quàm nostri. Gal. 1. Certior igitur Traditio Israelitice Ecclesiæ, quàm nostræ.
units.tr: Fourth, because they were more diligent in preserving the traditions of their ancestors than ours are. Gal. 1: The tradition of the Israelite Church is therefore more certain than ours.

units.la: Quintò, quia neque Apostoli ullam dederunt significationem, illos sibi probari.
units.tr: Fifth, because the Apostles gave no sign that these books were approved by them.

units.la: Sextò, Quia etiam post Christum nemo ex Iudæis ad Christum etiam conuersis, potuit agnoscere tales libros pro θεοπνεύστοις[?]. Vi de testimonio Iosephi de Antiquitate, lib.1. aduersus Appionem Alexandrinum, pag. 919. Ait, viginti duos esse, primùm quinque libros, Mosis. Secundò prophetarum tredecim. Tertiò tyrannos.
units.tr: Sixth, because even after Christ no one among the Jews, even those converted to Christ, could recognise such books as divinely inspired [θεοπνεύστοι]. See the testimony of Josephus in On the Antiquity, book 1, against Apion the Alexandrian, page 919. He says there are twenty-two: first, the five books of Moses; second, thirteen of the prophets; third, the hymns.

units.la: Qui post Artaxerxen scripti, non habitos fuisse fide dignos à Iudæis. Pro prioribus omnes paratos, si opus sit, mori. Eadem recitantur ab Eufeb.hist.lib.3.cap.10.
units.tr: Those written after Artaxerxes were not held by the Jews to be worthy of trust. For the former ones, all are ready, if need be, to die. The same things are recited by Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 3, chapter 10.

units.la: Denique siue spectes traditionem Maiorum, illorum est certior, de iis libris, quàm nostra: siue autoritatem scriptorum, melius potuerunt illi, vtpote Iudæi & viciniores, iudicare siue dignitatem scripturarum: illis fuit magis perspecta, quàm nostris, ob dictas causas: deinde, quia non minùs spiritus habuerunt in iudicandis libris, quàm nostri.
units.tr: Finally, whether you look at the tradition of the ancestors, theirs is more certain than ours about these books; or whether you look at the authority of the writers, they were better able to judge, as Jews and nearer in time; or the dignity of the Scriptures: that was more clearly perceived by them than by us, for the reasons mentioned; and furthermore, because they had no less of the Spirit in judging the books than we have.

units.la: Vetustiores inter nostros Patres, & peritiores linguæ sanctæ, exercitatiores etiam in scripturis, iudicium Israeliticæ Ecclesiæ secuti sunt, idque iudicio ex ipsis libris concepto. Qui verò dissentiunt, iuniores & imperitiores fuerunt.
units.tr: The older ones among our Fathers, and those more skilled in the holy language and also more practised in the Scriptures, followed the judgment of the Israelite Church, and that judgment formed from the books themselves. Those who dissent were younger and less skilled.

units.la: Meliton Sardensis Episcopus sub Antonino Imperatore, circa annum Domini 160. idem scriptum reliquit, nisi quòd sapientiam Salomonis inter Canonicos enumerat. Nec habet Eftheram. Eusebius hist.lib.4.c.26.
units.tr: Melito, Bishop of Sardis, under the Emperor Antoninus, around the year of the Lord 160, left the same writing, except that he counts the Wisdom of Solomon among the canonical books. Nor does he have Esther. Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 4, chapter 26.

units.la: Origenes idem in Psal.primum, teste etiam Eufeb.histor.lib.6.cap 25.non habet Sapientiam Salomonis, sed Epistolam Hieronymi. Addit,præter istos sunt libri Machab.
units.tr: Origen, on the first Psalm, likewise, as Eusebius also testifies, Ecclesiastical History, book 6, chapter 25, does not have the Wisdom of Solomon, but the Epistle of Jeremiah. He adds that besides these there are the books of the Maccabees.

units.la: Epiphanius in panar.Tom.1.lib.1.hæref.8. pag.9 Sed habet Epistolam Hieronymi, Baruch. Addit sapientiam Salomonis, & Jesu filij Sirach, ambiguæ esse apud illos lectionis & alios etiam Apocryphos. Idem libro de Mens.& ponderibus pag.606.lat. Aperte sapientiam Salom.quem πανάρετον[?] vocat, re-iicit inter Apocryphos.
units.tr: Epiphanius, in Panarion, vol. 1, book 1, heresy 8, page 9. But he has the Epistle of Jeremiah and Baruch. He adds the Wisdom of Solomon and that of Jesus son of Sirach, and says that the reading of these is ambiguous among them, and of others also that are Apocryphal. The same in his book On Measures and Weights, page 606 of the Latin. Clearly, he rejects the Wisdom of Solomon, whom he calls "all-virtuous" [πανάρετον], among the Apocryphal books.

units.la: Hilarius in Prolog.in Psal pag.479. Addit Epistolam Hieronymi, & nihil ex Daniele & Hesthera excipit. A quibusdam addi To-biam & Iuditham.
units.tr: Hilary, in the Prologue to the Psalms, page 479. He adds the Epistle of Jeremiah, and excepts nothing from Daniel and Esther. Tobit and Judith are added by some.

units.la: Cyprianus (Ruffinus est) in symb. Apo-stol.pag.377. eos duntaxat, quos & nos nisi quòd nihil excipit ex Ieremia: sed neque no-minat Epistolam.Neque ex Daniele.Sed ne-que nominat.Neq; ex Hesthera.
units.tr: Cyprian (it is Rufinus) in On the Apostles' Creed, page 377: only those whom we also accept, except that he excepts nothing from Jeremiah; but he does not name the Epistle. Nor from Daniel. But he does not name them. Nor from Esther.

units.la: Hieronymus in Prolog. in libr. Regum, quem vocat Galeatum & præponi solet Bibliis: Non alios, quàm quos nos posuimus: & ait: Hic prologus scripturarum, quasi Galea-tum principium, omnibus libris, quos de Hebræo vertimus in Latinum, convenire potest, ut scia-mus quicquid extra hos est, inter Apocryphos esse ponendum.
units.tr: Jerome in the Prologue to the books of Kings, which he calls Galeatus and which is usually placed before the Bibles: "Not others than those which we have set down," and he says: "This prologue of the Scriptures, as a helmeted beginning, can apply to all the books which we have translated into Latin from the Hebrew, so that we may know that whatever is outside these must be placed among the Apocryphal."

units.la: Ecclesia Romana. Nam semper probauit hunc prologum Hieronymi, & Bibliis semper præfigendum curauit.
units.tr: The Roman Church. For it has always approved this prologue of Jerome, and has always taken care to have it prefixed to the Bibles.

units.la: Concilium Laodicenum, can. 59. initio PontifiPontificatus Damasi celebratum. Concilii Tom.1.pag.380. Eosdem, nisi quòd Esdræ libros nullos numerat: sed apparet ex verbis immediatè præcedentibus, vbi ait, Paralipomenon libri duo : Esdræ: voluisse dicere, itidem duo. Proinde in contextu est. Item ex Daniele aut Esthera nihil excipit.
units.tr: The Council of Laodicea, canon 59, celebrated at the beginning of the pontificate of Damasus. Council, vol. 1, page 380. It counts the same books, except that it lists no books of Ezra; but it appears from the words immediately preceding, where it says "two books of Paralipomenon; Ezra," that it meant to say likewise two. Therefore it is in the context. "Likewise it excepts nothing from Daniel or Esther."

units.la: Biblia Græca antiquissima, omnes hos, quos inter Apocryphos posuimus, ipsa quoque habent, seorsum à Canonicis positos & separatim.
units.tr: The most ancient Greek Bibles also have all these which we have placed among the Apocryphal, set apart from the canonical and separately placed.

units.la: Et, si damus septuaginta Interpretes, omnia Biblia sacra, & non tantùm Mosen, in Græcam transtulisse: apertissimo est argumento, hos tantùm quos adhuc Hebraicè habemus, esse sacros. Nam in vetustissimis etiam manuscriptis Exemplaribus, non alij habentur, quàm isti.
units.tr: And if we grant that the Seventy interpreters translated all the sacred books, and not only Moses, into Greek, this is the clearest argument that only those which we still have in Hebrew are sacred. For in the most ancient manuscript copies also, no others are found than these.

units.la: POSTERIORVM IVDI-cium de Machabaorum [?] libris.
units.tr: The later judgement concerning the books of the Maccabees.

units.la: GElasius Papa in Catalogo Bibliorum, excludit à Canone secundum librum Machabæorum. Vide Concil. Tom.1. p,991.
units.tr: Pope Gelasius, in his catalogue of the Bible, excludes the second book of the Maccabees from the canon. See the Councils, vol. 1, p. 991.

units.la: Augustinus Tom.7. contra secundam Epistolam Gaudentij, lib.2. cap.22. Col.553.B, vbi improbat factum Raziæ, qui se præcipitem dedit ex fenestra, 2.Machab.14. ait, primùm, hanc scripturam, quæ appellatur Machabæorum, non haberi apud Iudæos, sicut Legem, Prophetas, & Psalmos, quibus Dominus minus testimonium perhibet, tanquam testibus suis, Luc.14. sed receptam esse ab Ecclesia non inutiliter, si sobrie legatur vel audiatur.
units.tr: Augustine, vol. 7, against the second letter of Gaudentius, book 2, chapter 22, col. 553 B, where he disapproves of the deed of Razias, who threw himself down from a window (2 Macc. 14). He says, first, that this writing, which is called that of the Maccabees, is not held among the Jews as the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms are, to which the Lord gives more testimony, as to his own witnesses (Luke 24); but that it has been received by the Church, not uselessly, if it is read or heard soberly.

units.la: Certè, si verè esset scriptura illa Machabeorum diuina, non dixisset Augustinus, Si sobrie legatur. Idem Tom.5. de Ciuitate Dei, lib.18. cap.38. fatetur libros Machabeorum, non esse de canone Hebræorum, neque paris autoritatis, cum Lege, & Prophetis: & id-cò sobrie esse legendos.
units.tr: Certainly, if that writing of the Maccabees were truly divine, Augustine would not have said "if it is read soberly." The same author, vol. 5, On the City of God, book 18, chapter 38, confesses that the books of the Maccabees are not part of the canon of the Hebrews, nor of equal authority with the Law and the Prophets, and that for this reason they are to be read soberly.

units.la: ARGUMENTA PRO LI-bris Apocryphis, primum in genere: deinde speciatim.
units.tr: ARGUMENTS FOR THE APOCRYPHAL BOOKS, first in general, then in particular.

units.la: TOmo Concil.i.[?]inter Canones Apostolorum est canon 84. ubi connumerantur sacri libri, inter eos sunt etiam libri Machabeorum tres.
units.tr: In the Council volume, among the Canons of the Apostles, is canon 84, where the sacred books are enumerated; among them are also the three books of the Maccabees.

units.la: Resp. primùm, si recipis hos Canones pro Apostolicis. Ergo neque Tobias, neque Judith, neque sapientia Salomonis, neque Baruch, inter Canonicos connumerari possunt. Nam ij ibi non connumerantur.
units.tr: I reply, first: if you accept these canons as Apostolic, then neither Tobit, nor Judith, nor the Wisdom of Solomon, nor Baruch can be counted among the canonical books, for those are not enumerated there.

units.la: Secundò, sed canones Apostolorum non esse liquet multis argumentis, quæ in præsentia adferre in medium non est necesse. Certè si Apostolorum essent canones, Hiero-nymus diligentissimus Ecclesiasticorum scriptorum obseruator, horum fecisset mentionem. Item Eusebius & alij Patres. Præterea, Si Apostolorum essent, non ausi fuissent Patres & Concilium Laodicenum, libros Machabeorum, è numero sacrorum Bibliorum excludere. Neq; etiam duas Clementis epistolas, è numero canonum noui Testamenti. Nam ibi duæ Clementis Epistolæ, & præceptiones quædam, inter libros Canonicos noui Testamenti connumerantur.
units.tr: Secondly, that the canons of the Apostles are not genuine is clear from many arguments, which it is not necessary to bring forward at present. Certainly, if they were canons of the Apostles, Jerome, the most diligent observer of ecclesiastical writers, would have made mention of them. Likewise Eusebius and the other Fathers. Moreover, if they were the Apostles', the Fathers and the Council of Laodicea would not have dared to exclude the books of the Maccabees from the number of the sacred Bible. Nor would they have dared to exclude the two letters of Clement from the number of the canons of the New Testament. For there the two letters of Clement and certain injunctions are enumerated among the canonical books of the New Testament.

units.la: Gelasius Papa, omnes habet pro Canonicis, excepto Machabeorum. Ita Athanasius in synopsi.
units.tr: Pope Gelasius holds all of them to be canonical, except the Maccabees. So Athanasius also in his synopsis.

units.la: Auguft Tom.3. de doctrina Christiana, lib.2. cap.8. omnes quos vos reiicitis inter Apocryphos, ipse inter canonicos ponit.
units.tr: Augustine, vol. 3, On Christian Doctrine, book 2, chapter 8: all those which you reject among the Apocrypha, he himself places among the canonical books.

units.la: Idem Concilium Carthaginense tertium, can.47. & est in Concil. Tom.1. pag.431. omnes itidem admittit inter Canonicas scripturas.
units.tr: The same, the Third Council of Carthage, canon 47, which is in the Councils, vol. 1, p. 431, likewise admits all of them among the canonical Scriptures.

units.la: Innocentius Papa itidem omnes inter decreta ipsius. In epistola ad Exuperium Tholosanum Episcopum, cap.7.
units.tr: Pope Innocent likewise (lists) all of them among his own decrees, in his letter to Exuperius, Bishop of Toulouse, chapter 7.

units.la: Resp. Ex iudicis horum posteriorum, non potest concludi aduersus iudicia priorum, iis de causis.
units.tr: I reply: from the judgements of these later writers, nothing can be concluded against the judgements of the earlier ones, for these reasons.

units.la: 1. Quia priores secuti sunt iudicium Ecclesiæ Israeliticæ, qua nemo melius potuit de iis libris iudicare.
units.tr: 1. Because the earlier writers followed the judgement of the Israelite Church, and no one could judge better about those books than it.

units.la: 2. Quia Ecclesiæ illæ priores, fuerunt etiam puriores, & melius potuerunt de libris sacris iudicare, tanquam præditæ maiori spiritu, & exercitatiores in scripturis.
units.tr: 2. Because those earlier churches were also purer, and were better able to judge the sacred books, as endowed with greater spirit and more practised in the Scriptures.

units.la: 3. Quia viciniores Apostolis:idcirco certius potuerunt nosse, qui autores & scriptores librorum, qui non, &c.
units.tr: 3. Because they were nearer to the Apostles, and so could more certainly know which authors and writers wrote the books, and which did not, etc.

units.la: Huc regula Tertulliani, Id esse verum, quodcunque prius: id esse adulterum, quodcunq; posterius.
units.tr: Here is Tertullian's rule: that is true which is earlier; that is adulterated which is later.

units.la: Et loquitur de traditionibus Ecclesiasticis.
units.tr: And he speaks of ecclesiastical traditions.

units.la: 4. Quia illi priores, longè melius inter se conueniunt de hac quæstione, quàm posteriores.
units.tr: 4. Because those earlier writers agree among themselves on this question far better than the later ones do.

units.la: 5. Augustinus ipse tradit regulam de libris Canonicis dignoscendis, Tom.3. de doctrina Christiana, lib.2.cap.8.
units.tr: 5. Augustine himself gives a rule for distinguishing the canonical books, vol. 3, On Christian Doctrine, book 2, chapter 8.

units.la: In Canonicis autem scripturis (scilicet diiudicandis) Ecclesiarum Catholicarum (id est, verè piarum) quamplurium autoritatem sequatur: inter quas sanè illæ sunt, quæ Apostolicas sedes habere, & Epistolas accipere meruerunt.
units.tr: In judging the canonical Scriptures, he says, one should follow the authority of the many Catholic Churches (that is, those truly pious), among which are certainly those which have deserved to have Apostolic sees and to receive Epistles.

units.la: 1. Tenebit igitur hunc modum in scripturis Canonicis, ut eas quæ ab omnibus accipiuntur Ecclesiis Catholicis, præponat eis, quas quædam non accipiunt.
units.tr: 1. He will therefore keep this method in the canonical Scriptures: that he should place before the others those which are received by all the Catholic Churches, rather than those which some do not receive.

units.la: 2. In eis verò, quæ non accipiuntur ab omnibus, præponat eas, quas plures gravioresq; (Ecclesiæ) accipiunt, eis, quas pauciores, minorisq; auctoritatis Ecclesiæ tenent.
units.tr: 2. But among those which are not received by all, he should place before the others those which more and weightier (churches) receive, rather than those which fewer churches of lesser authority hold.

units.la: 3. Si autem alias invenerit à pluribus, alias à gravioribus haberi (quanquam hoc inveniri non possit) æqualis tamen authoritatis eas habendas puto.
units.tr: 3. But if he finds that some are held by more and others by weightier (churches) (though this cannot be found), I think they should be held to be of equal authority.

units.la: Regula hæc Augustini intelligenda est in diiudicandis scripturis, ex sola Ecclesiastica traditione & iudicio: ut primò, quæ omnibus probantur, primum etiam locum teneant.
units.tr: This rule of Augustine is to be understood in judging the Scriptures from ecclesiastical tradition and judgement alone: so that, first, those which are approved by all should also hold the first place.

units.la: Secundò, quæ à pluribus & grauioribus approbantur, secundum locum.
units.tr: Second, those which are approved by more and weightier churches, the second place.

units.la: Tertiò, si verò quædam à grauioribus, aliæ à pluribus, hæ paris sint authoritatis. Duo prima membra ut iustissima admitto. Sed tertium non probo. Quasi verò numerus suffragiorum, debeat grauitati æquari. Scimus non esse numeranda, sed ponderanda suffragia. Si hoc in politicis: quantò magis in diuinis & Ecclesiasticis?
units.tr: Third, if some are held by weightier churches and others by more, these are of equal authority. I accept the first two members as most just, but I do not approve the third. As if the number of votes should be equal to weight! We know that votes are not to be counted but weighed. If this holds in political matters, how much more in divine and ecclesiastical ones?

units.la: Iuxta verò duo priora membra, omninò consequitur veram esse nostram sententiam, quæ conformis est Ecclesiis prioribus.
units.tr: Moreover, according to the first two members, it wholly follows that our opinion is true, which agrees with the earlier Churches.

units.la: 1. Quos nos ut Canonicos defendimus, ij fuerunt omnibus Ecclesiis in Israel probati, & improbati quos non probamus.
units.tr: 1. Those whom we defend as canonical were approved by all the Churches in Israel; those whom we do not approve were disapproved.

units.la: 2. Iidem fuerunt omnibus Ecclesiis, usque ad Concilium Nicenum probati. Nullam enim de iis contentionem legimus, usq; ad illa tempora.
units.tr: 2. The same were approved by all the Churches up to the Council of Nicaea. For we read of no dispute about them up to those times.

units.la: 3. Ab authoritate. Multò grauiores fuerunt, & maioris authoritatis illi priores, quàm posteriores.
units.tr: 3. From authority: those earlier writers were far weightier and of greater authority than the later ones.

units.la: 4. Accedit, quòd etiam inter posteriores, nostræ Ecclesiæ maioris sunt authoritatis, iudicij, eruditionis, quàm quæ mille ab hinc & amplius annis.
units.tr: Add to this that even among the later writers, our Churches are of greater authority, judgement and learning than those which (were) a thousand years and more ago.

units.la: Nostræ autem Ecclesiæ, ita sentiunt, uti nos proposuimus in thesibus. Nulla est enim inter eas differentia de libris veteris Testamenti.
units.tr: Our Churches, moreover, think as we have set out in our theses. For there is no difference among them concerning the books of the Old Testament.

units.la: Sed hoc argumento contraria omnium iudicia refelluntur.
units.tr: But by this argument the contrary judgements of all are refuted.

units.la: Illi tantum sunt Canonici, quos in Ecclesia Dei constitit & constat, esse θεόπνευστοι [?]. Quos enim Canonicos nos, Paulus vocat θεοπνεύστους [?]: & Petrus ait, sanctos Dei homines, Spiritu S. inspiratos, locutos esse, eoq; & scripsisse.
units.tr: Only those are canonical which it has been and is agreed in the Church of God are θεόπνευστοι [theopneustoi, God-breathed]. For those whom we hold to be canonical, Paul calls θεοπνεύστους [theopneustous, God-breathed]; and Peter says that holy men of God, inspired by the Holy Spirit, spoke, and therefore also wrote.

units.la: Atqui sicut nunquam ante Christum, sic neq; tempore Christi & Apostolorum, agniti fuerunt pro θεοπνεύστοις [?] isti de quibus controvertitur: neque etiam postea, neq; nunc, apud fratres, ex Iudaismo ad Christum conversos, utut [?] sanctissimos & doctissimos, & multos, constitit, aut constat.
units.tr: Yet just as these disputed books were never recognised as θεοπνεύστοι [theopneustoi] before Christ, so neither in the time of Christ and the Apostles, nor afterwards, nor now, has it been or is it agreed among the brethren converted from Judaism to Christ, however holy and learned they are, and however many.

units.la: Liquet hæc Assumtio.
units.tr: This assumption is clear.

units.la: 1. Ex Iosepho, contra Appionem Alexandrinum.
units.tr: 1. From Josephus, against Apion the Alexandrian.

units.la: 2. Ex scriptis Apostolicis, in quibus nulla unquam fit mentio.
units.tr: 2. From the Apostolic writings, in which there is never any mention of them.

units.la: 3. Experientia. Nullus enim unquam Hebræus frater admittit sponte, & ex iudicio, pro Canonicis hos, quos nos Apocryphos esse contendimus. Neq; unquam sperandum est fore, ut admittant, etiam cum Ecclesia fuerit refertissima Iudæis, ut ad finem Mundi. Constantissimi enim in hac sunt sententia, quam tuemur. Quomodo igi-tur sunt, aut futuri sunt in Ecclesia Cano-nici. Confirmatio. Et, si Canonici autoritatem habent apud omnes fideles, ij autem non habuerunt vnquam, aut habent apud Iudæos fratres: oportet igitur aut hos fratres non esse pios & fideles: aut hos libros non esse Canonicos.
units.tr: 3. From experience. For no Hebrew brother ever admits of his own accord, by judgement, as canonical those which we contend are Apocryphal. Nor is it ever to be hoped that they will admit them, even when the Church is most crowded with Jews, until the end of the world. For they are most steadfast in this opinion, which we uphold. How then are, or will they be, canonical in the Church? Confirmation: if the canonical books have authority among all the faithful, but these have never had authority, or do not have it, among the Jewish brethren, then either these brethren are not pious and faithful, or these books are not canonical.

units.la: SPECIATIM DE LIBRIS veteris Testamenti Argumenta.
units.tr: CONCERNING THE ARGUMENTS OF INDIVIDUAL BOOKS OF THE Old Testament.

units.la: Sed quid? quòd etiam antiquorum illorum priorum Patrum testimoniis euincitur, certos quosdam libros, non esse Apocryphos, quos tamen vos inter Apocryphos reponitis?
units.tr: But what of the fact that the testimonies of those earliest Fathers also prove that certain books are not Apocryphal, although you class them among the Apocrypha?

units.la: TOBIAS.
units.tr: TOBIT.

units.la: Hieronymus ad Cromalium & Eliodorum (& est præfatio in Tobiam, præfixa Bibliis) scribit se transtulisse in illorum gratiam Tobiam, eumq; vehementer laudat.
units.tr: Jerome, writing to Chromatius and Heliodorus (this is the preface to Tobit, placed before the Bibles), says that he translated Tobit for their sake, and he praises it greatly.

units.la: Resp. Non probat vt Canonicum, sed tanquam vtilem.
units.tr: Reply: He does not commend it as canonical, but as useful.

units.la: Instant. 1. At ait, Iudæos illum secuisse de Catalogo sacrarum Scripturarum. Ergo antea annumerabatur.
units.tr: Objection 1: But he says that the Jews removed it from the catalogue of the Sacred Scriptures. Therefore it was previously counted among them.

units.la: Resp. Quasi verò, quæcunq; discernuntur, non etiam secari ex aliis dicantur, tametsi nunquam fuerint coniuncta, publica autoritate.
units.tr: Reply: As if whatever is distinguished were not also said to be cut off from others by public authority, even though they were never joined together.

units.la: Instant. 2. At ait, inter Hagiographa mancipatum librum hunc per Hebræos. Hagiographa autem sunt Canonica. Resp. Hagiographa scriptum est pro Apocrypha, aut ipse Hieronymus ita usurpa-vit. Liquet:quoniam primò ait, Hebræos illum secuisse ex Catalogo sacrarum Scriptu-rarum.
units.tr: Objection 2: But he says that this book was assigned by the Hebrews among the Hagiographa, and the Hagiographa are canonical. Reply: The word Hagiographa is used for the Apocrypha, or Jerome himself used it in that sense. This is clear, since he first says that the Hebrews removed it from the catalogue of the Sacred Scriptures.

units.la: Instant. 3. At Hebræos, qui secuerunt hunc librum è Catalogo, vocat Pharisæos: & ait, se malle Episcoporum iussionibus deservire, quàm Pharisæorum iudicio non dis-plicere.
units.tr: Objection 3: But he calls the Hebrews who removed this book from the catalogue Pharisees, and he says that he would rather obey the orders of the bishops than not displease the judgment of the Pharisees.

units.la: Resp. Non illos qui distinxerunt libros, vocat Pharisæos, sed illos, qui improbant quòd Hieronymus hunc librum non Canonicum, verteret in Latinum, & Ecclesiis legendum obtruderet.
units.tr: Reply: He does not call those who distinguished the books Pharisees, but those who disapprove that Jerome translated this book, which is not canonical, into Latin and forced it upon the churches to be read.

units.la: Instant. 4. At multi Patres ex hoc libro citant.
units.tr: Objection 4: But many Fathers cite from this book.

units.la: Resp. Quasi verò non etiam ex Philosophis citemus, & ex Poëtis.
units.tr: Reply: As if we did not also cite from the philosophers and the poets.

units.la: IVDITHA.
units.tr: Judith.

units.la: Hieronymus in præfatione in hunc librum, ait à Niceno Concilio in numerum sacrarum Scripturarum fuisse connumeratum, ac proinde se illum vertisse.
units.tr: Jerome, in his preface to this book, says that it was counted among the sacred Scriptures by the Council of Nicaea, and that for this reason he translated it.

units.la: Resp. Fieri potest, & credo Hieronymo. Sed nomine S. Scripturarum, non intellexit Canonicos libros, qui citra dubitationem habentur pro verbo Dei: alioqui cur Hieronymus non hunc etiam inter Canonicos connumerauit, sed nominatim inter Apo-cryphos copulauit. Intellexit igitur, librum esse à Concilio Niceno agnitum pro libro vero & vtili, & qui à fidelibus non debeat inter profanos haberi.
units.tr: Answer: This may well be so, and I believe Jerome. But by the name of the sacred Scriptures he did not mean the canonical books, which without doubt are held to be the word of God; otherwise why did Jerome not reckon this book among the canonical ones, but expressly joined it with the Apocrypha? He therefore understood that the book was acknowledged by the Council of Nicaea as a true and useful book, which should not be regarded by the faithful as profane.

units.la: Regula. Multa in summa sunt, quæ fuerunt admissa ab Ecclesia, tanquam veræ historiæ, sed non tanquam dictatæ à Spiritu sancto.
units.tr: Rule: There are many things in the sum of the book which the Church admitted as true history, but not as dictated by the Holy Spirit.

units.la: BARVCH.
units.tr: BARUCH.

units.la: Ambrosius de fide ad Grat. lib 1. pag. 49 ad-scribit Ieremiæ, & ex hoc citat illud cap. 3 [?]. Posthac in terris visus est, &c. & esse à Spiritu sancto docet. Item Epiphan. lib. 1. hæres. 8. inter Canonicos habet.
units.tr: Ambrose, in his work On Faith to Gratian, book 1, page 49, ascribes it to Jeremiah, and on this basis cites that passage from chapter 3: Afterwards he was seen on earth, etc. He also teaches that it is from the Holy Spirit. Likewise Epiphanius, in book 1 of Heresies, number 8, counts it among the canonical books.

units.la: Resp. Primùm, fallitur Ambrosius, cùm attribuit Ieremiæ. Secundò, Illius & huius iudicium, non præualet iudicio Ecclesiæ If-raeliticæ, & Hieronymi, tot tantorumq; alio-rum Patrum.
units.tr: Reply: First, Ambrose is mistaken when he attributes it to Jeremiah. Second, his judgment and that of Epiphanius do not outweigh the judgment of the Hebrew Church, of Jerome, and of so many great Fathers besides.

units.la: EPISTOLA IEREMIÆ.
units.tr: THE EPISTLE OF JEREMIAH.

units.la: Inter Canonicos ponit Origenes in Psalmum primum, & citatur etiam ab Eusebio Cæsar. lib. 6. c. 25.
units.tr: Origen places it among the canonical books in his commentary on Psalm 1, and Eusebius of Caesarea also cites it, in book 6, chapter 25.

units.la: Epiphanius idem facit in Panar. lib 1. hæ-res.8.
units.tr: Epiphanius does the same in the Panarion, book 1, heresy 8.

units.la: Hilarius in Psalmos idem facit, pag. 429.
units.tr: Hilary does the same in his commentary on the Psalms, p. 429.

units.la: SAPIENTIA SALOMONIS.
units.tr: THE WISDOM OF SOLOMON.

units.la: Melito connumerat inter Canonicos.
units.tr: Melito counts it among the canonical books.

units.la: Eusebius lib. 4. c. 26.
units.tr: Eusebius, book 4, ch. 26.

units.la: Augustinus Tom. 7. de prædestinatione Sanctorum, cap.14. dat huic libro magnum testimonium & laudem.
units.tr: Augustine, Vol. 7, On the Predestination of the Saints, ch. 14, gives this book great testimony and praise.

units.la: Basilius etiam contra Eunomium.
units.tr: Basil also, against Eunomius.

units.la: Et Ambrosius de fide ad Grat. citant pro Deitate Christi.
units.tr: And Ambrose, in his book On Faith to Gratian, cites it in support of the deity of Christ.

units.la: Refp. At hanc non habet Origenes, & reiicit Epiphanius, licet [illegible, ~9 letters] appellet inter Apocryphos.
units.tr: Reply: But Origen does not have it, and Epiphanius rejects it, although [illegible, about nine letters] he calls it one of the Apocrypha.

units.la: Item Hieronymus ait, credi esse Philonis.
units.tr: Likewise Jerome says that it is believed to be by Philo.

units.la: Sed existo libro citantur sententiae ab Apostolis, ait Catharinus.
units.tr: But from this book, Catharinus says, sayings are cited by the Apostles.

units.la: Refp. Non constat. Secundo, Etiam ex poetis profanis citauit Apostolus.
units.tr: Reply: This is not established. Secondly, the Apostle also quoted from profane poets.

units.la: DANIEL DE SVSANNA ET BELO.
units.tr: DANIEL: SUSANNA AND BEL.

units.la: Hieronymus Tom.2. contra Ruffinum in Apol. lib.2. pag.227. non improbat, sed tan-tum ait, se retulisse quid Hebraei dicant.
units.tr: Jerome, in Vol. 2 against Rufinus, in the Apology, book 2, p. 227, does not disapprove of it, but only says that he has reported what the Hebrews say.

units.la: Refp. Innuit quidem sibi non improbari iudicium Hebræorum, sed tamen non pro-bat vt Canonicum.
units.tr: Reply: He indeed indicates that the judgment of the Hebrews is not disapproved by him, but nevertheless he does not prove it as canonical.

units.la: DE LIBRIS NOVITE-stamenti Patrum iudicia.
units.tr: ON THE BOOKS OF THE NEW TESTAMENT: THE JUDGMENTS OF THE FATHERS.

units.la: LAodicenum Concilium Can.59[?]. Con-cil. T.1. Omnes nullo excepto pro Canonicis habuit.
units.tr: The Council of Laodicea, Canon 59 [?], in Councils, Vol. 1: it held all of them, none excepted, as canonical.

units.la: Cyprianus (Ruffinus) in Symb. Aposto-lorum pag.377. omnes inter Canonicos col-locat: & totam Ecclesiam sic sentire docet.
units.tr: Cyprian (Rufinus), on the Apostles' Creed, p. 377, places all of them among the canonical books, and teaches that the whole Church thinks so.

units.la: Hieronymus in Epist. ad Paulinum, quae Bibliis semper solita fuit praefigi, omnes admittit pro sacris. Tantum dicit Epistolam ad Heb.à plerisq; extra numerum poni:sed ipse eam admittit. T.ʒ. [?] in epistola ad Dardanum, p.86. Item in epistolam ad Gal.cap.1.pag.159. Athanaf. in synopsi, versa à doctissimo Musculo. vide sup p.35.
units.tr: Jerome, in his Letter to Paulinus, which was always customarily prefixed to the Bibles, admits all of them as sacred.
